## Mr Duisenberg's opening statement at the press conference held on 22 December 1998

Introductory statement by the President of the European Central Bank, Dr W F Duisenberg, press conference held in Frankfurt on 22/12/98

Ladies and gentlemen, the Vice-President and I are here today to report on the outcome o meeting of the Governing Council of the European Central Bank at which we took the opportun finalise a number of issues of a rather technical or legal nature ahead of the forthcoming Weekend.

Let  me  first  turn  to  the  Governing  Council's  discussion  on recent  economic,  monetary  and financial developments and the decisions that the Governing Council has taken today in t field of monetary policy .

On 1 January 1999 the ESCB will assume responsibility for defining and implementing the monetary  policy  of  the  euro  area.  The  Governing  Council  of  the  ECB  deemed  it  appropria announce  in  advance  the  interest  rates  that  will  apply  to  the  monetary  policy  instrume ESCB as from the start of Stage Three. This should eliminate any remaining uncertainties a monetary  policy  stance  of  the  ESCB  and  contribute  to  a  smooth  changeover  to  Stage  Thr Economic and Monetary Union.

As you have already been informed, the following decisions were taken:

- First, the Governing Council decided to conduct the first main refinancing operatio ESCB as a fixed rate tender and to set the level of the interest rate for this operat line with the key central bank rates prevailing at the end of Stage Two. This operati initiated  on  4  January  1999,  the  allotment  decision  will  be  taken  on  5  January, settlement will take place on 7 January. The first longer-term refinancing operatio announced  on  12  January.  The  Governing  Council  has  already  decided  that  it  wil conducted through the single variable rate auction procedure.
- Second, with respect to the interest rates on the ESCB's standing facilities, which ar to form a corridor for movements in short-term money market rates, the Governing Co decided that the interest rate for the marginal lending facility will be set at a leve the interest rate for the deposit facility at a level of 2%. These are the rates o standing facilities at the start of Stage Three, i.e. 1 January 1999.
- Third, however, as a transitory measure, between 4 January and 21 January, the inter for the marginal lending facility will be set at a level of 3.25% and the interest deposit  facility  at  a  level  of  2.75%.  This  exceptional  narrow  corridor,  of  50  bas between the marginal lending facility and the deposit facility aims at smoothing the of  market  participants  to  the  integrated  euro  area  money  market  during  the  initial Monetary Union. The maintenance of such a narrow corridor is not desirable beyond the term,  since  it  would  hamper  the  development  of  an  efficient  euro  area  money  ma Therefore, the Governing Council intends to terminate this measure following its mee 21 January 1999. In summary, let me provide the following explanations for these decisions. I will start with issues related to the narrow corridor; thereafter, I will comment on the interest rates.

With respect to the interest rates on the ESCB's standing facilities , which are designed to form a corridor for movements in short-term money market rates, the Governing Council had to co two aspects. First, it needed to signal clearly its monetary policy intentions. These were setting the rate for the marginal lending facility at 4.50% and the rate for the deposit

for  the  start  of  Stage  Three.  Hence,  the  corridor  for  movements  in  short-term  interes asymmetric  towards  the  upper  boundary.  Determining  these  rates  was  also  necessary  in  or provide successors to the official national central bank rates previously used as refere certain legislation and contracts in some Member States. Second, however, the Governing C also had to consider the possibility that market participants may need some time to get new environment for monetary policy. In principle, cross-country deviations of short-term rates will not exist in Stage Three, as intra euro area arbitrage should be expected to However, the many novelties related to the changeover make it difficult to foresee whether area money market will indeed work in a fully integrated way from the very first day of St For this reason, the Governing Council has decided to use a relatively narrow corridor rates on the standing facilities of the ESCB in the first three weeks of Stage Three as device to reduce the maximum range of fluctuations in the overnight interest rate. Concerning the decision to set the level of the interest rate for the first main refinancing operation of the ESCB at 3%, it may be recalled that on 3 December 1998, in a coordinated decision, all central banks participating in the single monetary policy lowered their key interest rates the exception of the Banca d'Italia, which reduced the discount rate to 3.5%). As explain ECB at that time, this joint reduction had to be seen as a de facto decision on the leve rates  with  which  the  ESCB  will  start  Stage  Three  and  which  it  intended  to  maintain foreseeable future. It was based on the common assessment that these interest rate reduct line with maintaining price stability in the euro area over the medium term. In this connec be pointed out that a rate of 3% is very low by historical standards. This should be see indication that the ESCB does not want to give any signal for a further easing in the future. At today's meeting, taking account of the latest monetary, financial and economic Governing Council confirmed these views. At this juncture, there are no signs to suggest t rates  of  increase  in  the  HICP  of  around  1%  would  either  decelerate  significantly  or,  c accelerate to levels which are inconsistent with the definition of price stability provided in October 1998.

## Let me provide you with a more detailed record of our assessment .

The information coming from the data on monetary aggregates signals a relatively smooth path for M3 growth in 1998, compatible with continued price stability. In particular, the latest moving average annual growth rate of M3 stood at around 4.5%. This was exactly in line w reference value set by the Governing Council at its last meeting.

With  respect  to  the  other  pillar  of  the  ESCB's  monetary  policy  strategy,  the broadly  based assessment  of  the  outlook  for  price  developments  and  risks  to  price  stability ,  various  indicators confirm  the  assessment  of  developments  in  monetary  data. ## 1 Preparations for the changeover to the single currency

## Mr Jalan looks towards a more vibrant banking system

Inaugural address by the Governor of the Reserve Bank of India, Mr Bimal Jalan, to th Bank Economists [apostrophe?]Conference (BECON'98) held at Bangalore on 16/12/1998.

## Introduction

I am happy to join this special gathering of bankers and deliver the inaugural addr conference of bank economists . This year's meeting of bank economists is particularly impor as it is being held against the background of one of the worst meltdowns of the financ experienced by a number of economies.

The  recent  financial  market  developments  show  that  we  have  come  to  live  in  a  wor considerable uncertainty, where prudence and foresight get rewarded while errors, in judgements and bad decisions impose severe costs on the individual financial interme well as on the financial system as a whole. In today's liberalised financial environme investors and financial intermediaries are widely dispersed, not necessarily confined t boundaries.  This  has  made  capital  extremely  fluid  and  highly  sensitive  to  polic performance of the financial systems of the recipient countries. Pursuing policies an that  ensure  improved  efficiency  and  continued  stability  of  the  financial  system  has critical importance in the present context of a more open world economy.

In  India,  over  the  past  few  years,  we  have  made  substantial  progress  towards  improv performance of our financial system and putting in place a new financial regime which r on  detailed  controls  and  directions  and  more  on  initiative,  autonomy  in  decision-mak accountability. Policy initiatives since 1992 in this regard have been directed at buil and ensuring the safety and stability of the financial system. Compared with the expe many developing countries embarking on financial sector reform, we have trodden caut and in an orderly fashion, which has helped us in minimising the adjustment costs inv the process. This, however, should not lead to any complacency, particularly in the con present  fluidity  of  international  capital  markets  and  the  increased  vulnerability  of economies  to  sharp  fluctuations  in  macroeconomic  situations.  These  disturbances  tend exaggerated if the financial system is fragile and lacks depth in absorbing internal shocks.

It is important to note that the number and frequency of bank failures in the world hav rapidly in recent years. These failures have occurred both in countries which followed more open policies as well as the ones exercising control in different degrees. Recent in East Asia and elsewhere have brought to fore the criticality of a financial system's ensuring sustainability of openness in invigorating economic growth. In one important also  marks  a  departure  from  the  excessive  emphasis  laid  on  the  proposition  that liberalisation per  se will  lead  to  higher  growth.  While  developing  financial  institution markets  is  important  for  growth,  it  may  not,  however,  prove  sufficient  to  provide outcomes if the safeguard systems are not very sound and the financial system is unstabl

It is in the above context that the theme of this year's bank economists' conference, strengthen the Indian financial system, assumes critical importance. Indeed this is a most developing countries at present. Many of them have initiated a fresh round of s reforms in their financial systems. A number of international agencies, including the

I would like to acknowledge with thanks the help of Shri M.S. Mohanty and Shri Partha Ray of the Reserve India in the preparation of this lecture.

International Settlements (BIS), are also currently engaged in identifying factors th vulnerability of financial systems and devising new safety standards that would help stability. In India, the second Report of the Narasimham Committee has recently addr number of vital issues pertaining to the health and stability of the financial system a that is necessary to strengthen it. Some of these recommendations have been implemented recent monetary and credit policy announcements.

As professional bankers and economists, you are no doubt seized of the challenges that developments in international financial markets have posed for the Indian financial sys has been our experience of financial reforms so far? Where do we stand in terms of stability considerations? What are the tasks ahead if the Indian financial system is to competitive strength substantially and strengthen itself to withstand the pressures of What role should the bank economists be playing in this environment? Let me try and ad few of these issues in my remarks this morning.

## A Review of Directions

The significance of the financial system for an economy arises from at least three major s First,  it  performs  various  transformation  functions  relating  to  intermediation  of  f economy. Secondly, it provides the mirror image of the underlying real economy and th macroeconomic balances. Thirdly, it is one industry whose basis of operation is underp public trust. The strength of this bond between the banking system and people in genera on how the financial viability of the banking system is perceived. The organisation an of  financial  markets  should  be  such  that  they  reflect  the  underlying  fundamentals economy. The financial system as a whole must remain sound and stable in order to enjoy level of public confidence.

Until recently, the improvement in various transformation functions of the financial s the focal point of reform initiatives in many developing countries. The basic issue w create a competitive environment for the financial system and to put in place a poli which would lead to improved allocative efficiency of the financial sector and enhanc saving and investment activities of the economy for attaining faster rates of economic financial  markets  developed  and  matured,  the  two-way  interaction  between  the  financi nonfinancial policies grew in importance. In the recent years, the increased market e the financial system and its vulnerability to macroeconomic shocks have highlighted the greater internal controls and the need for strengthening prudential norms and regulati environment  of  rising  importance  of  cross  border  capital  flows,  perceptions  and  expe play major roles in shaping events and this consideration can be particularly heighte financial system is perceived to be weak and unsound. It is not surprising that finan initiatives  globally  have  now  moved  to  the  strategic  considerations  of  ensuring  c stability of the financial system.

In India, since the formal announcement of the first initiative of financial sector r Union  budget  of  1991-92  to  the  Second  Report  of  the  Narasimham  Committee  in  1998 considerable ground has been covered in putting in place a financial system which can requirements of a more competitive and open economy. By and large, financial reforms i have proceeded in four major directions.

First, setting the policy conditions right and removing the operational constraints of system.  What  the  reform  process  has  tried  to  achieve  is  to  lower  the  share  of  pr resources in the total resources of the banking system through gradual liberalisation

reserve ratio and the statutory liquidity ratio. While the medium term target of 25% an for the CRR and SLR, respectively, have been, by and large, achieved, these ratio level higher  than  what  would  perhaps  look  ideal  in  the  international  context.  Our  relati reliance  on  the  cash  reserve  ratio  has  been  necessitated  by  the  needs  of  monetar operations. As financial markets develop, allowing for a greater role for the interes economy, the dependence on this instrument of monetary policy would need to come down future.

The second directional change has been in the area of creating a more competitive envi in  the  financial  sector  through  reform  measures  such  as  relaxation  of  entry  and  ex reduction in public ownership in the banking industry and letting banks access the capi in order to meet their funding requirements. The objective is to bring out the best re of pricing and quality of banking services over a period of time.

The third important direction of reform has been the strengthening of market institu allowing  greater  freedom  to  financial  intermediaries.  These  reforms  have  taken  the gradual  liberalisation  of  interest  rates,  development  of  money,  capital  and  debt  ma giving operational flexibility to banks in the management of their assets and liabiliti course,  to  prudential  guidelines.  In  simple  terms,  these  changes  imply  a  greater exposure  of  individual  financial  institutions  to  the  domestic  and  international environment.

In this connection, a distinction needs to be made between two types of market develo which  have  implications  for  the  financial  system.  One  is  developments  in  resp macroeconomic fundamentals of the economy which impact on the interest rate, exchange and other asset prices. This is a normal phenomenon in any economy and has implications balance  sheets  of  the  financial  intermediaries.  Institutions  which  do  not  have  an approach  in  anticipating  events,  undertaking  pre-emptive  actions  and  designing  a response to unanticipated developments can find themselves in a difficult situation, p in times of a large degree of fluctuations in macroeconomic variables. The dangers p market and credit risks arising out of macroeconomic shocks need to be given special at a liberalised financial system. Our reform initiatives in this area are still in the The second type of market developments which have implications for the financial sector to asset price bubbles, which may be related to a high concentration of bank lending two sectors which have a boom and bust cycle of their own. This form of market exposure unhealthy and lead to irreparable shocks. Although the impact of such cycles on our system is quite limited, international experience suggests that, unless prudential mea place, banks can be potentially vulnerable to asset price pressures that can generat risks for the financial system.

The fourth important element of reform concerns the 'safety' aspects of the financia This is the core of the challenges facing the financial system at present. When the ref was started in 1992, there was a massive problem of cleaning the balance sheets of ban had deteriorated over the years. Successive reform initiatives in this area have bee prescribing certain prudential standards for the financial system and addressing certai weaknesses  which  could  minimise  their  recurrence  in  future.  Measures  such  as  in recognition  norms,  asset  classification,  meeting  minimum  capital  adequacy  standards recapitalisation and devising a supervisory framework are steps in the direction of en safety of the financial system.

## Where Do We Stand?

The  key  indicators  of  banking  sector  performance  during  the  past  few  years  mark noticeable  changes.  For  example,  the  net  profit  of  the  scheduled  commercial  banks percentage of their total assets has been turned around from a negative figure of -1 average during 1992-93 and 1993-94 to a positive of 0.5% during 1994-95 to 1997-98. I case of most public sector banks, business per employee and profit per employee have improvement in the recent period. Certain other indicators also look good. By 1997, a public sector banks had achieved the minimum capital adequacy norm of 8%. The gross an non-performing assets of the banking system as a percentage of advances declined to 1 8.2%, respectively, by March 1998. In terms of percentage to total assets, gross and performing assets declined to 7.0% and 3.3%, respectively, by March 1998.

I think the present statistics are not unfavourable for the banking system as a who second report of the Narasimham Committee has observed, 'this improvement has arreste deterioration in these parameters that had marked the functioning of the system earlier in  view  the  current  macro  economic  and  international  financial  situation,  the  Commit noted that:

'There is still, however, a considerable distance to traverse. The process of streng banking system has to be viewed as a continuing one. There is no finite end to impro levels of efficiency and profitability. In fact, the situation is one where the syste constantly  with  changes  in  the  broader  environment  in  which  it  functions  and  fac challenges that these developments impose on it' (p. 18).

The  banking  sector  indicators  in  India  need  to  be  seen  against  the  backdrop  of  i vulnerability  of  the  financial  systems  of  developing  countries  and  the  need  for  imp efficiency and stability. The Narasimham Committee has presented a detailed analysis of problems and challenges facing the Indian banking system and made wide-rangi recommendations for improving and strengthening its functions. Let me shortlist a few k which must concern us at this stage.

The Indian banking system is still perceived as a relatively high cost banking. This is the relatively high operating cost of the banking system. A comparative analysis indi while the average operating cost of banks as a percentage of assets was about 2.3% during 1990-91 to 1995-96, it was 1.1% in China, 1.6% in Malaysia, 1.9% in Thailand, 1. Japan  and  2.1%  in  G10  Europe.  One  of  the  major  problems  posed  by  a  relatively intermediation  cost  in  our  case  is  that  it  gives  rise  to  uneconomical  banking.  It necessity of maintaining a relatively high interest income spread and a high real le This adversely affects financial intermediation and growth in the economy.

Operating  costs  depend  on  labour  productivity,  technology,  innovation  and  organis effectiveness of a bank to harness various static and dynamic economies from the pro process. On the economy-wide scale, these factors differentiate the weak from the stron system  and  provide  internal  strength  and  stability  to  the  system.  Without  gaining advantage  in  this  respect,  it  is  difficult  to  think  of  a  significant  improvement  in system in future.

A key issue relates to the banking sector's non-performing assets (NPAs). The amount o and net NPAs have been on the rise, although the rate of their growth has been below th rate  of  expansion  of  advances.  Apart  from  absolute  size,  the  distribution  of  non-p

assets  is  skewed  across  banks.  Still  a  large  number  of  public  sector  banks  have performing assets ranging between 10 to 20% of net advances. The Narasimham Committee underlined the need to reduce the average level of net NPAs for all banks to 3% by 200 zero  for  banks  with  international  presence.  I  think  this  is  an  important  requireme banking system and is crucial to maintaining the viability of the system in future. A t strategy  identified  by  the  Committee  viz.,  to  reduce  the  backlog  NPAs  and  improv management efficiency and stricter enforcement of prudential norms, has to be acted upon with this challenge.

Another critical aspect is the soundness of the banking system and how this is reflec practices and principles followed by banks. Prudential norms and supervision are neces they are no substitute for the internal control system and sound business practices. Th distinguish  between  a  normal  business  risk  and  an  abnormal  one,  managing  such  risk defining a prudent limit for risks are essential functions for the bankers. For a long banking did not have a tradition of dealing with various forms of market risks. The cr of managing such risks has now come into the open, especially against the experience recent East Asian crisis, where markets fell precipitously because banks and corporate accurately measure the risk spread that should have been reflected in their lending act did they manage such risks or provide for them in their balance sheets. In India, t Bank has recently issued comprehensive guidelines to banks for putting in place an asse management system. Formal guidelines will be issued shortly in the light of suggestions from banks. But, ultimately risk management is a culture that has to develop from wi internal management systems of the banks. Its critical importance will come into sha once  current  restrictions  on  banks'  portfolios  are  further  liberalised  and  are  subj pressure of macro economic fluctuations.

While developing a system of internal control and risk management is of critical impor the banking system, there is no escaping the fact that a permanent improvement in the Indian  banking  is  not  possible  without  addressing  the  long-term  structural  weaknesse system. Our banking system operates with a large continent-wide network of branches, scale economies in the banking industry are limited, owing  to the fragmented organi structure. Today, size is becoming increasingly important for strategic business planni sphere of the economy. The banking sector is no exception. When competition is the key is the market structure and regulation that need careful attention. Furthermore, given tier financial system of our economy, and the complementarity and synergetic relation these different tiers, it is difficult to isolate the efficiency of the banking system long-term financial institutions, cooperatives, rural banks and non-bank financial com more  meaningful  reorientation  of  objectives  and  functions  of  various  tiers  of institutions  would  be  necessary  in  dealing  with  the  long-term  issue  of  enhanc competitiveness  of  the  system  as  a  whole.  It  is  also  important  to  ensure  that  the structure  of  Indian  banks  is  such  that  managerial  decision-making  is  not  affected economic  considerations,  and  banks  are  able  to  raise  sufficient  capital  in  line increasing volume of business.

Another crucial issue, especially in the present context, relates to banks' special rol delivery system. There is no inherent conflict between the canons of sound banking and proactive role in credit disbursements to promote growth. These two objective complementary to each other. High growth leads to high credit off-take and credit av conditions influence growth prospects of an economy. Ultimately, it is the credit busi is central to the profitability of the banking system. To the extent that excessive

among bankers restricts credit growth in the economy, it has adverse effects on the pr of the banking system as well as on economic growth.

Credit disbursement to the rural sector and small-scale industries require special att banks. The Gupta Committee recommendations involving greater flexibility and discretion lending  banks  in  the  agricultural  sector  in  matters  of  collateral,  margin,  securi certificate, composite cash credit limits etc., have to be implemented by the banks exp Similarly,  special  treatment  has  to  be  accorded  to  small-sector  units  in  improv accessibility to institutional finance with a view to enabling them to emerge as profi the banking system. Given its critical importance in the manufacturing and export act the  economy,  it  is  unlikely  that  the  banking  system's  profitability  and  efficiency without  exploiting  the  opportunity  provided  by  the  small-scale  industrial  sector.  T Committee has recently made a comprehensive set of recommendations for improving the cr delivery system for small-scale industries, which are being implemented in phases.

## The International Context

An important effect of the Asian economic crisis, and of the recent developments in J been  that  there  is  now  a  much  greater  international  focus  on  the  soundness  of  the banking system in all countries - developed and developing. Unlike previous financial c persistent crisis in the real economy in East Asia and also Japan is generally belie been accentuated by the weakness in the financial sector rather than the other way r health of the banking sector and the prudential and regulatory framework are thus no matter  of  domestic  concern  only.  A  country's  ability  to  access  capital  markets  as investments abroad is likely to depend on whether the domestic financial system is per broadly conform to international prudential and supervisory norms. In fact, the world themselves are being put to a severe test by the changing nature and ramifications o crises in several parts of the world. What were earlier considered to be the ideal prud for preventing individual bank failures have been proved to be severely inadequate to systemic instability or prevent the contagion effects.

In various international fora, an intensive effort is now underway to evaluate the exi and practices being followed by banking systems in different countries and to assess these norms have helped or prevented instability in the banking system. India has b participating  in  these  discussions  and  is  helping  in  the  formulation  of  norms  and which  take  into  account  the  views  of  the  developing  countries,  where  market  structu growth  objectives  are  different  than  in  industrial  countries.  Issues  currently  und include: the corporate governance system in banks, risk management, banking regulati supervision,  transparency  and  accountability  and  public  policies  relating  to  moral banking sector. The Basle Core Principles for Effective Banking Supervision have underlined the need  to  adhere  to  25  basic  principles  for  adopting  an  effective  supervision  syste aftermath  of  the  East  Asian  crisis.  More  detailed  work  is  now  in  progress  after  t publication  of  three  reports  by  the  Willard  Group,  constituted  by  the  Bank  for  Int Settlements, on enhancing transparency and accountability, strengthening financial sys managing international financial crises.

The Willard Group reports have argued for improving the credibility and accountabilit banking system through more transparent accounting practices and better disclosure norm have  drawn  attention  to  the  need  to  develop  a  stable  and  efficient  financial  syste strengthening the corporate governance system and risk and liquidity management among and putting in place a proper safety net arrangement for the banking system. They h

argued for a more organised approach in preventing international financial crises an orderly system of creditor and debtor coordination and effective solvency laws.

The recent international consensus on preserving the soundness of the banking system ha around  certain  core  themes.  These  are:  effective  risk  management  systems,  adequate provision, sound practices of supervision and regulation, transparency of operation, public policy intervention and maintenance of macroeconomic stability in the economy.

An important issue which we, along with other countries, would need to address is how t that individual banks govern themselves according to the best practices in corporate go This, as mentioned before, involves according utmost importance to prudent business pr such  as  developing  an  effective  internal  control  system,  monitoring  and  managing  the range of financial and commercial risks, and instituting a proper system of asset an management in order to avoid term mismatches in portfolios. A proper cushion needs to by way of capital reserves against market exposure and capital size should set a limit exposure of an individual financial institution. Apart from capital adequacy standard international norms of banking regulation and supervision require a more proactive rol regulator in enforcing an effective mechanism for evaluating, monitoring and managing the financial system. This in turn would need stricter accounting, valuation and repor on the part of banks.

The Basle core principles have also identified a number of challenging areas for regu supervisors,  which  must  be  satisfied  to  ensure  orderly  conduct  of  financial  syste promote its soundness and stability. Transparency in banking operation is also somethi has  to  receive  top  priority  given  the  current  nature  of  capital  markets.  Transpa accountability  demand  realistic  valuation  of  assets,  public  disclosure  norms  and  p reporting by banks to help depositors and investors form an informed opinion about the the financial system, thereby enabling them to react in an orderly fashion to asset pr Moreover, public intervention policies in the form of explicit or implicit guarantees be such that they do not lead to 'moral hazard' in the form of undue risk-taking by b laxity in observing market disciplines.

India  must  remain  in  the  forefront  of  the  movement  for  ensuring  soundness  of  the  b system by adopting best practices and best international standards of performance and p Actions  have  already  been  initiated  in  this  direction.  The  challenge  now  is  to  acce process  so  that  the  banking  and  the  financial  system  in  our  country  can  contribut sustained growth of the real economy with price stability.

## Role of Bank Economists

Before I conclude, let me say a word about the role of Bank economists in facilitating process. This annual conference is a testimony to the economic talent that our bankin has  developed  over  the  years.  Almost  all  our  banks  have  economic  research  departmen economic cells which are staffed by highly qualified economists with long experience in and the financial sector. The issue that I would like to pose before this conference making the best and most effective use of economists working in the banking sector to the functioning of banks, and for that matter, the operational efficiency of the finan a whole? In commercial organisations like banks, economics departments have the advant not being excessively burdened with day-to-day problems of running the banks or ensur safety and profitability of individual transactions. They are in a position to take longer-term view of the comparative or competitive advantage of their individual banks

as identify areas of portfolio weaknesses and the costs/benefits of various kinds of s products offered by them. They also have the opportunity to study from their vantage p from a practical angle the working of the financial system and various improvements ne strengthen the financial intermediation function.

However,  for  bank  economists  to  be  able  to  perform  these  functions,  it  seems  tha reorientation of the role that is assigned to them is necessary. There is also a ne 'attitudinal' change on the part of economists themselves. Those who work in the comm banking sector have to be prepared to accept operational responsibility, to work in th to familiarise themselves fully with the commercial aspects of their bank's work. Their to  be  operationally  relevant,  and  it  must  contribute  to  the  financial  soundness operations. This is possible if bank economists also have branch-level experience and e of working in non-economic departments with line responsibility.

At present, the role of economists in our banking sector seems to be too narrowly defi are viewed as keepers of data, particularly macroeconomic data, and undertake periodic or analysis of macroeconomic trends in the economy. They are seldom involved in undert any operational work or in developing strategic policy choices or even in treasury exchange  functions.  All  over  the  world,  with  deregulation  and  globalisation  of  the sector, the role of economists in the banking sector has been changing and becoming m more  focussed  on  the  analysis  and  valuation  of  the  risk  associated  with  various  alt particularly in emerging economies that are subject to greater volatility in the financ India, however, the role of economists has been somewhat slow in changing.

It may perhaps be useful for this conference to initiate a process of discussion on issues  and  to  reassess  the  role  that  members  of  this  distinguished  body  can  play  i forward the process of reform in our country. The challenges ahead are gigantic, but th exciting. Given the determination, I have no doubt that India can have one of the mos financial systems in the world.

## Mr McDonough discusses the role of central banks in the global financial markets

Remarks  by  the  President  of  the  Federal  Reserve  Bank  of  New  York,  Mr  William McDonough, before the Economic Club of New York, New York City, on 14/12/98.

Good evening, ladies and gentlemen. I am delighted to be here tonight and to share the with my good friend Dick Grasso. Dick and I have worked together for many years now, have come to value greatly both his warm friendship and his thoughtful counsel.

Dick has spoken eloquently about how equity markets have developed globally over the several years and some of the concerns he has going forward. For my part, I will foc global debt markets and the interests of central banks in the stability of these markets

The role of central banks in the fixed-income and related capital markets may not be im obvious because, one can argue, debt markets are a zero-sum game. One side of a trad what the other loses. If only it were as easy as that! In fact, trading in the globa serves an important purpose and it does not follow that central banks have no inter stability of these markets. Quite the contrary. Opening statement by the Governor of the Reserve Bank of Australia, Mr I.J. Macfarlane, House of Representatives Standing Committee on Economics, Finance and Publi Administration in Sydney on 15/12/98.

## Thank you, Mr Chairman,

It is a pleasure to be here in front of your Committee again. As you mentioned, the nee adjustments to the composition of the Committee after the October Federal election me we are meeting about five weeks later than our normal timetable. Given the uncertainty timing of the hearing, and the importance we attach to regular communication with the about the economy and the Bank's activities, we decided to keep to the regular time releasing our Semi-Annual Statement on Monetary Policy , which came out in early November.

So there is a substantial gap between the Statement and this hearing. On the whole, we feel that our Statement still represents a reasonable summary of our views on events that had taken over the preceding six months. The world has not changed dramatically since the Statement was issued. We have, however, made an adjustment to the stance of monetary policy, follow December Board meeting. This was as a result of our continual process of evaluating i information, and our assessment of the outlook for the year ahead, and the various risk to  our  forecasts.  Our  judgement  was  that,  even  though  most  of  the  data  coming  in suggesting  growth  was  running  ahead  of  earlier  expectations,  the  likelihood  was  that would decline in 1999. At the same time, the likelihood of overshooting the inflation judged to have declined. Hence, we viewed a small further easing of policy as a prudent

The good economic outcomes over the past year will, I suspect, be a recurring featur discussion today. It might be helpful, therefore, if I start by reviewing the forecas seven months ago and make some observations about how recent developments compare wit them.

What I said last time could be summarised as:

- GDP would grow by about 3 per cent during 1998;
- the unemployment rate would remain relatively stable;
- we had passed the trough of inflation and it would rise gradually, reaching about by the end of the year; and
- the current account deficit would average about 5½ per cent of GDP for 1998.

I  also  said  that  I  thought  this  combination  of  events  would  be  a  reasonably  good  r Australia in view of the difficult external situation we were facing, particularly amon export  markets.  In  the  event,  the  external  situation  did  not  get  any  better,  but economic performance has exceeded our expectations, and, to the best of my knowledge expectations of virtually all forecasters.

It now looks as though GDP growth during 1998 will be about 4 per cent, rather than t cent that seemed likely in May. A good deal of the additional growth is attributable outcomes than we had expected in the June and September quarters. The remainder is a re upward revision to earlier data across most of the recent quarters. Consistent with t than expected growth, the rate of unemployment has continued to edge down, rather than flat. Over the past three months it has averaged 7.9 per cent, compared with 8.1 per first quarter of 1998 and 8.7 per cent in the first quarter of 1997.

On inflation, it seems clear that the trough has passed, and our best guess for the ri over the four quarters to December 1998 is, in round figures, still about 2 per cent. true to say that inflation shows signs of not increasing by as much as historical r might have led us to expect, given the fall in the exchange rate. I would summarise the situation as being one where the forecast errors were within th ranges that occur with forecasts of this type. The thing we can take some comfort from, is that no-one can accuse us of being Pollyannas because in each case the outcome was better than the forecast. Growth has been stronger, the widening in the current acco smaller and, at the margin, the rise in inflation slightly smaller than we had expected.

I now propose to make a few general comments about how we are expecting future event unfold.  Over  the  course  of  the  year  before  the  Asian  crisis  commenced,  that  is  1996 economy grew by 4½ per cent. In the first year affected by the Asian crisis - 1997/98 4¼ per cent. Despite starting 1998/99 at a similar pace, we have to accept that we w able to continue at this rate. Growth through 1998/99 is more likely to be somewhere 2½ and 3 per cent. Some slowing seems to be inevitable, given the weaker outlook for the world economy. Si last met in May, most forecasters have revised down expectations. The IMF, to take j example, has revised down its forecast for world growth in 1998 from 3 per cent to 2 and for 1999 from 3¾ per cent to 2½ per cent. If these estimates are a reasonable guide external  environment  will  remain  difficult  and  income  from  external  sources  constrai course, domestic demand has been, and remains, much stronger than external demand, a Australia's expenditure has run ahead of national income over the past year. But that be expected to continue to grow at the same pace indefinitely, and so both domestic dem GDP growth must be expected to come down over coming quarters. With slower growth in offing, we expect that the unemployment rate will flatten out. Of course, we said that now we are suggesting it will occur at a slightly lower rate of unemployment than we expected.

We expect the four-quarters-ended increase in the CPI to be about 2½ per cent by the e financial year - that is, in the short term, we expect inflation performance to be co our  target.  Of  course,  any  forecast  of  inflation  beyond  that  period  is  only  as  g assumption about the future path of the exchange rate.

Given  the  current  tendency  towards  lower  commodity  prices,  we  are  assuming  some  fur widening in the current account deficit to about 5½ per cent of GDP in 1998/99. With a figure of this size, it would not be surprising to see a quarter or two of it running cent of GDP. I made the same comment in March this year, and again in May at our pre hearing. I expected that it would have come to pass by now, but it has not. It would n me, however, if it does happen some time in the next year.

This set of outcomes, or something like it, would represent a good performance for an in  its  eighth  year  of  expansion  facing  a  difficult,  but  not  disastrous,  external  en expect that it would be well received by the domestic and international investment co though one can never take this for granted. And, of course, if the assumptions we ar about the world economy turn out to be too optimistic, all bets would be off.

I now come to the second part of my testimony, in which I attempt to answer the questio we have done better than most other countries in Asia or the Pacific Rim. In doing

conscious that the story is not yet over, so this is really an interim report. I thi factors have been involved and I will list them in no particular order. As we go throu will become apparent that they are all intertwined.

First, I think the Asian crisis hit at a time when the Australian economy was in good s for cyclical reasons. By mid-1997, the economy was growing strongly and inflation was than our target. Had we not received a contractionary impulse from the Asian crisis, we been facing the need to tighten policy because of a potential overheating. No-one will but it is a possibility. I am conscious that attributing our performance over the past our good starting point is rather superficial because it does not explain why the start so good. But I will come back to that later.

Second, I think we have benefited from the flexibility of our exporters, who have swit the contracting Asian markets into the expanding North American and European ones, and number of other markets we do not usually think of as being important to us. The natur exports - with so much of them being commodities - has helped, but the efforts of our companies and authorities should not be ignored. Third,  Australia  has  benefited  from  a  greatly  improved  perception  of  the  soundness economic policies. The fact that the budget has moved back into surplus - where it sho the mature phase of an economic expansion - has been important. So has nearly a decade inflation. Also important on this occasion has been the recognition that Australia sco such factors as its regulation of banks, other financial institutions and stock exchan its  underlying  body  of  commercial  law  and  accounting  practice  is  at  or  close  to  wo practice.

Not only have the international capital markets taken a better view of Australia, but w to have more confidence in ourselves. In the past three months, they have tended to rise m again  as  figures  about  the  economy  have  confirmed  that  it  has  performed  better  tha expected.

The fourth explanation for why growth has held up is a catch-all one - the economy just be more flexible and adaptable than before. The only clear evidence of this is that pr whether labour productivity or total factor productivity - has increased faster in the earlier decades. For example, total factor productivity has increased at an average an 1.7 per cent during the expansion of the 1990s, compared with 0.7 per cent in the 1980 per cent in the 1970s. To me, this suggests that the painful adjustments that have been the past decade or so are paying off. By this, I mean the changes that have been made t competition  in  previously  sheltered  industries.  This,  of  course,  includes  great orientation, but also greater competition in utilities and transport, which has redu other  industries.  It  also  includes  the  downsizing  of  the  public  sector,  which  ha resources. Finally, our labour relations practices and wage setting machinery now have of flexibility that has surprised the sceptics.

I now come to a fifth factor, which most commentators view as being important - name fact that in response to a contractionary external shock, the Australian dollar was all down. This is the way the textbooks say the situation should be handled, and is in sha to the severe domestic squeeze that can result in the cases of countries with fixed or exchange rates.

The domestic economy has benefited from the lower exchange rate because exporters' inc have been held up and the incentive to export maintained (while at the same time assis industries that are competing against imports). The domestic economy has also benefited we have not had to put up interest rates in order to maintain our external parity (a exchange rate) or to prop up a floating rate that threatened to fall so far that it w undesirable  inflationary  consequences.  Raising  interest  rates  in  response  to  an contractionary shock is not something that you normally would want to do, although in circumstances it may become necessary.

I can assure you all that we were never rela followed the Australian dollar on virtually a daily basis for 15 years, I know that yo take it for granted. On each occasion, stabi re-established and, unlike the experience of the mid-1980s, we did not raise interest this does not mean that that option was not on the table. Why out this way?

The  answer,  I  think,  is  that  we  are  beginning  to  receive  the  big  dividend  that  low provides.

title: Mr Tietmeyer looks at the euro as a stabiliser in the international economic system  (Central Bank Articles and Speeches, 4 Dec 98)
description: Speech by the President of the Deutsche Bundesbank, Prof Hans Tietmeyer, given at the conference of the Luxembourg Institute for European and International Studies and the Pierre Werner Foundation in Luxembourg on 4/12/98.
text:
## Mr Tietmeyer looks at the euro as a stabiliser in the international economic system

Speech  by  the  President  of  the  Deutsche  Bundesbank,  Prof  Hans  Tietmeyer,  given  at conference of the Luxembourg Institute for European and International Studies and the Werner Foundation in Luxembourg on 4/12/98.

I

There are just 28 days left until the start of monetary union, which is perhaps the mos monetary event since the end of the Bretton-Woods system.

Some people may be thinking: 'Just another 28 days, and then we've done it!' before he sigh of relief as they relax in their armchairs.

That is a very human reaction, especially when one considers the great efforts and obs the advances but all the reverses on the way to greater monetary cooperation in Europe a

Thirty years ago the subject of monetary union was already a topic on the agenda of the Community, which in those days consisted of just six member countries. It was at that the road to monetary union was first jointly mapped out by you, Pierre Werner, and the Group named after you - in which I myself had the honour of working.

Luxembourg and its political representatives were always advocates of progress towards going but clearly stability-oriented integration.

Important insights which were gained at that time are still highly relevant today. For e currencies  of  the  participating  states  can  be  welded  together  to  form  a  permanent monetary union only

- if there is an adequate degree of ongoing economic convergence between the countrie
- if there are common preferred structures in monetary policy and the same priorities and
- if there is broad agreement on the basic political stance.

The  way  forward  proposed  at  that  time  was  different  to  some  extent  than  the  path charted  in  Maastricht.  It  was  envisaged  that  political  integration  would  develop  p economic integration.

However, the consultations following the submission of the Werner Plan showed clearly t politicians  at  that  time  were  not  prepared  to  abandon  national  sovereignty  on  t considerable scale demanded. So the first attempt to launch monetary union fell at this

On January 1, 1999 monetary union will therefore be launched at the second attempt. A of conditions have changed in the meantime:

- Eleven countries will be taking part, as opposed to just six at the time of the fir
- These  11  countries  are  only  part  of  the  overall  European  Union.  Hence  there  w differences in the level of monetary integration within the EU.
- And the political framework for integrating the single currency is a rather loose s

The euro will have to cope with this as best it can.

For the goal is not merely to ensure that the euro is stable at the beginning. The goal that the euro remains stable over the long term. And in the long term it is highly prob euro will need a stronger political underpinning.

II

It is gratifying that the financial markets already seem to have largely accepted the eu

At any rate, the euro has passed its first test.

The markets apparently have confidence in the preannounced exchange rates. So far ther been no marked tensions between the exchange rates of the future participating currencie

And  the  euro  has  already  begun  to  show  the  first  benefits.  In  the  context  of  prob developments in the financial markets which in some cases reached crisis-like proport euro has acquired the reputation of a safe haven - even before the actual launching of union - which has led to correspondingly low capital market rates in the future euroland

None of these things should be taken for granted. They are the result of

- the rigorous stability orientation of the Maastricht Treaty,
- the large degree of convergence that has already been achieved in the monetary s policies of the central banks,
- the careful preparatory work, and
- the determined efforts that have been made to date to achieve greater convergence policy, too.

The safe haven function which the euro area has performed so far clearly demonstrates introduction of the new currency is undoubtedly a 'global event'. And a lot of hopes placed on the future international role of the euro.

Clearly, the enlarged financial market in euroland will result in a wider range of pro broader choice of investment opportunities.

To what extent these greater opportunities will actually be used - especially by ent depends on other conditions as well.

These include the legal framework laid down by the EU and by the national parliaments countries concerned, the different traditions in respect of financial market structu questions of taxation.

It  remains  to  be  seen  just  how  quickly  traditional  financial  market  structures  mo together.

And another thing which remains to be seen is the use to which enterprises will put th capital market. For example, will there be a tendency towards greater concentration as to exploit 'economies of scale' in euroland?

And what about the other question which central bankers are often asked in connection international role of the euro:

How fast and to what extent will the euro become a major international investment and currency? Can the euro take over the D-Mark's role as the second most important investm reserve currency?

Naturally,  the  euro  will  play  a  significant  international  role  as  an  investment  a currency.  If  this  does  not  turn  out  to  be  the  case,  it  will  be  an  enormous  -  an conceivable - surprise as well as a bitter disappointment.

The fact that the euro area is already regarded as a safe haven confirms this assump simply a fact of life that major international currencies are used by investors from ti a safe haven.

However, this can also be a problem in certain situations, especially for the exchange r

But it is the future stability of the euro that will determine its actual role in the conce currencies. And two key criteria for this will be

- sensible monetary policy decisions by the ECB Governing Council, and
- stability-oriented behaviour in those aspects of economic policy which remain a responsibility, especially fiscal and wage policies.

Given such a policy mix, the euro can assume a major international role - in line wit and economic importance of euroland - and also make its contribution to global stabilit

## III

And that brings me to the subject of this conference: 'The euro as a stabiliser in the economic system.'

This title expresses great expectations of the future single currency.

- In what sense - if at all - does the international economic system need a stabilise
- And if it needs one, how can a currency help to meet such a need?

Let me begin with the second question: as a general principle, currencies cannot solve problems relating to the global real economy.

And as far as the first question is concerned, it must be said that, while the worl setting is difficult at the moment, there is certainly no cause to talk of a fundamenta

In recent weeks the financial markets have at least calmed down a little. The world crisis which many people predicted looks unlikely to occur at the moment.

It is true that a number of countries are currently suffering crises entailing consi growth losses:

- In the South-East Asian countries this is a direct consequence of the financial cr the moment there are some encouraging signs of an improvement in certain countries.
- Japan  continues  to  suffer,  in  particular,  from  the  structural  problems  whi accumulated  in  its  financial  sector.  Happily,  it  has  now  taken  steps  to  put  it sector in order. These now need to be implemented resolutely.

- In Russia the transformation of the centrally planned economy into a market econom virtually come to a halt.
- And  in  Latin  America  contagion  effects  manifested  themselves  in  the  wake  of uncertainty  in  the  financial  markets.  Fortunately,  the  financial  markets  are renewed confidence and are tending more to reward the marked structural advances in a number of countries.

Nevertheless, these regional crises have clearly left their mark on the global econom process.

On the one hand, that does not mean that an overall world economic crisis is looming. T state of the US and European economies clearly contradicts such gloomy views.

On the other hand, it is becoming more apparent that the international setting has cr extraordinary  risks  and  uncertainties  which  are  beginning  to  retard  the  pace  of expansion in the industrial countries.

There  are  some  indications  that  the  euro  area,  too,  cannot  fully  escape  the  global pressure.

Fortunately, this comes at a time when the internal monetary conditions in Europe ar favourable. The goal of price stability has largely been achieved. Moreover, there seem obvious threat to maintaining price stability in the foreseeable future.

That has given European monetary policy the opportunity for a further round of cuts i bank interest rates.

As you know, for some weeks now the euro area as a whole has already experienced a per considerable decline in the average interest rate. This is the result of the so-call convergence of central bank interest rates.

At the beginning of this week the Council of the European Central Bank made a comprehe assessment of the monetary and economic situation in the euro area. This very thorough on the ECB Governing Council, as well as yesterday's discussion on the Bundesbank's C Bank Council, came to the same conclusion: an additional coordinated rate cut is app which clears the horizon for a level of 3% for the start and the first stage of the eur

Therefore, this cut also has to include those currencies whose interest rate already bottom of the current range. The Bundesbank's decision to cut the repo rate by 30 basis our contribution to that coordinated action.

The decision is compatible with both the monetary situation and the overall economic co The early announcement of the interest rate level for the launch of the euro may hel expectations  in  the  financial  markets.  But  of  course,  the  rate  cut  cannot  solve structural  problems  in  most  of  the  euro  countries.  This  is  particularly  true  of  th problems on the labour markets.

Naturally, it is not only Europe that is suffering structural problems and, therefore, challenges.

To a large extent, it was structural problems occurring in the monetary and banking sec played a major calamitous role in the outbreak and course of the regional crises.

- Many of the countries affected had excessively rigid exchange rate pegs.
- Many of the countries affected placed their own monetary policy too much at the ser these problematical exchange rate pegs.
- Many of the countries affected have structural deficiencies in the area of financ supervision, in particular.

These structural problems in the monetary sector have to be solved first and foremost suitable policy measures in these countries themselves.

## How else could these internal structural problems be solved than

- through a confidence-building economic policy,
- through a stability-oriented central bank policy, and
- through a greater measure of realism in the exchange rate pegs,
- through an overhaul of the financial sector and an improvement of banking supervisi

Naturally,  international  cooperation  can  also  help,  but  not  so  much  through  c arrangements like the euro as through strengthening the overall functioning and viabil financial markets. This entails above all

- improving international cooperation in the field of supervision,
- improving the transparency of the financial markets.
- involving private sector creditors in the task of overcoming crises, and

All this will sharpen the markets' risk awareness and strengthen their functioning and

But considerable structural problems exist in the industrial countries, too.

In  the  USA  the  already  low  private  saving  ratio  has  fallen  further  in  recent  year showing a negative ratio of late. Despite the country's balanced budget, the imbalances trade have not therefore been reduced.

And in most of the euro countries unemployment remains too high. The euro will not be solve this problem on it own. Instead the euro requires flexibility and competitiveness economy.

It is the politicians who must tackle these internal structural problems. In the long the  best  contribution  that  can  be  made  towards  achieving  sound  financial  markets prospering world economy.

V

Boldly  undertaking  the  necessary  reforms  in  the  euro  area  will  at  the  same  time  pre ground for sustained favourable growth and employment prospects.

Given more flexible structures in the markets, a lastingly stable euro will be able to the undoubtedly  large  potential  for  economic  benefits,  and  then  it  will  also  be  abl political integration.

To sum up: the euro is not the final aim of European integration. Even in 28 days' ti remain a future-oriented project.

For it is not just a question of introducing the euro. The euro also requires ongoin stability.  And  the  euro  requires  a  sufficient  degree  of  political  consensus  on  th economic dynamism and flexibility. Only in this way can potentially dangerous political be avoided in the long run.

We are investing great hopes and expectations in this future-oriented project associat euro. All those involved are responsible for doing what is necessary to ensure that t and expectations are fulfilled.

title: Mr Crockett considers what regulatory consequences should be drawn from the most recent crises in financial markets  (Central Bank Articles and Speeches, 20 Nov 98)
description: Remarks by the General Manager of the Bank for International Settlements, Mr Andrew Crockett, to the European Banking Congress in Frankfurt/Main on 20/11/98.
text:
## Mr  Crockett  considers  what  regulatory  consequences  should  be  drawn  from  the  most recent crises in financial markets

Remarks  by  the  General  Manager  of  the  Bank  for  International  Settlements,  Mr  And Crockett, to the European Banking Congress in Frankfurt/Main on 20/11/98.

You have asked me to talk about the regulatory implications of recent crises. Before I important that we understand the relative roles of regulators and bank management in excesses  and  managing  risks  appropriately.  As  you  all  know,  the  regulatory  and  supe focus has shifted in recent years from quantitative controls and explicit rules to mon soundness through the quality of internal controls and the banks' risk management cultu this, greater emphasis has been placed on responsibility of bank management and stakeh through market discipline, to ensure prudent operations. I think we all agree that ban and market participants are better equipped and 'incentivised' for this task than super there is no going back to a world of quantitative controls.

At the same time, it is understandable that the ability of banks to repeatedly walk ope massive overexposure should lead to questions being asked about the wisdom of this ch regulatory and supervisory focus. I will not address this question here. But if the wider financial community is to resist pressures for re-regulation, it is necessary t pay much greater heed to the responsibilities for prudent operations that are now more theirs and theirs alone.

What  regulatory  consequences  should  be  drawn  from  the  most  recent  crisis  in  the financial markets?

Coming  to  the  question  you  asked,  I  think  it  is  useful  to  distinguish  between  the emerging  markets  and  the  recent  heightened  volatility  in  financial  markets  in  a economies. Even though there are undoubted linkages between them, the regulatory implic to be drawn are rather different.

Concerning what has happened in emerging markets, there are at least three basic less recent  experience.  The first is  that  structural  weaknesses  in  the  financial  system  can  be costly. The second is that there are important feedbacks between macroeconomic instabilit problems in the financial sector. And the third is that financial instability can spread contagio from  country  to  country.  The  Asian  crisis  began  when  the  overvalued  Thai  baht  had devalued. The currency crisis then interacted with financial system weaknesses to produ economic recession. And the difficulties in Thailand were rapidly propagated across th and beyond.

From this experience, the most important regulatory consequence to be drawn is the n rapid strengthening of financial systems. Among the most important shortcomings of fi systems  in  Asia  were:  severe  currency  and  maturity  mismatches;  excessive  concentrat lending; insider and politically directed lending; inadequate accounting and loan cla procedures; weak capitalisation; and unsatisfactory supervision.

Correcting these fundamental problems will be neither quick nor easy. A strong financia requires  the  development  of  deep-rooted  'credit  culture',  in  which  lending  instrum properly related to the risks they are used to finance. Lenders need to become bett assess borrowers on an arm's-length basis, understanding their businesses and their var matching  cash  flow  to  debt  servicing  obligations  and  appreciating  the  appropriate

collateral.  And  supervisors  need  a  strengthened  capacity  to  identify  and  correct  s vulnerability.

Fortunately, there now exists a standard by which banking systems and supervisory arran can be judged. This is the 'Core Principles for Effective Banking Supervision' issued l the Basle Committee on Banking Supervision. Virtually all countries have now accepted principles and pledged to adopt them. This is not the place to go into the Core Pr detail. But let me just note four aspects of them that are of key importance. First , they cover all phases  in  the  life  of  a  bank,  from  initial  licensing,  through  ongoing  supervision, closure procedures. Second , they apply to both domestic and internationally active banks. Third , the rules are applicable to banks operating in emerging markets as well as to those of countries. And fourth , they have been developed by an internationally representative grou supervisors. The Core Principles therefore have the comprehensiveness and the legitimac as the basis for a thorough-going strengthening of banking systems worldwide.

The difficult part, of course, will be implementation. A major effort will be require banks, national supervisory authorities and international organisations and expert gr BIS  and  the  Basle  Committee  will  play  their  part  both  in  implementation  and  in  pr training and technical assistance to help countries bring their systems up to scratc primary responsibility for overseeing implementation of the Principles falls to the IMF Committee will be drawing up a compliance methodology for use by the IMF in its survei activities. And as regards training, we have recently announced the establishment of Financial Stability Institute, which will be headed by Mr John Heimann, who is well k the banking community and Mr Erik Musch, former Secretary General of the Basle Committe hope this Institute will make an important contribution to disseminating best superviso and supporting the effort to strengthen banking systems.

I now turn to the lessons to be learned in the industrial countries from the rather episode  of  market  turbulence  that  began  in  mid-August.  The  Russian  debt  moratoriu 17 August sparked a widespread flight to quality, which was followed by a generalised d of liquidity in many markets. This prompted fears that lenders would 'disengage', lea credit crunch.

Fortunately, markets have more recently gained a certain measure of stability. But w certainly try to understand what went wrong and how we can avoid such episodes in the One problem was that lenders had unrealistic expectations about the extent to which th to emerging markets would be protected. It is therefore important that cross-border l assessed on a stand-alone basis, and that supervisors make sure that the pricing and ma of such exposures are not undertaken on a false basis. In other words, a tightening-u risk procedures is called for.

Another  source  of  difficulty  was  that  the  models  used  to  assess  market  risk  were  b simplistically on established statistical correlations. They did not take adequately other types of risk, such as liquidity, volatility and event risk. Widely used value-a caused financial intermediaries to liquidate assets when volatility in asset prices in selling, in turn, caused volatility to increase further and resulted in additional se that most market participants used the same basic model led to common reactions, amp herd-like behaviour. Consideration therefore has to be given to ensuring that common be by market participants does not exacerbate market instability.

It  has  to  be  recognised  that  all  model-based  approaches  to  controlling  market  risk assumptions, explicit or implicit, about market liquidity. The drying-up of liquidity i market turbulence, as market participants seek to disengage from exposure, invalidate premise on which risk management is built. It is therefore all the more important that approaches to risk containment are supplemented by stress-testing.

## How do you think national governments have fared in implementing BIS rules?

The scorecard in this connection is not very good. If one looks back at the history of or  15  years,  financial  crises  have  succeeded  themselves  with  depressing  regularity emerging markets, there are [15] cases in which the direct resolution costs of bank crises have exceeded 10% of GDP. And among the industrial countries, systemic strain been  just  as  evident.  The  Savings  and  Loan  debacle  in  the  United  States;  the  Scand banking crisis; financial fragility in Japan; and individual cases of failure or sev such as Barings and Crédit Lyonnais: all these episodes show there is much to be don advanced countries also.

## Let me make a few simple points:

First , capital ratios do not mean much without prudent and consistent accounting practic after time, banks have failed even though they had shortly before declared strong capi And whole banking systems have been declared sound at a certain moment, only to have s weaknesses revealed shortly afterwards. The reason, of course, is accounting practices bad  loans  to  be  called  good.  It  is  of  the  utmost  importance  that  asset  impairment recognised.

Second ,  the  Basle  rules  are  not  just  a  matter  of  capital  requirements.  Banking  is management  of  risk.  Banks  need  systems  and  controls  at  all  levels  that  foster  the measurement  and  monitoring  of  risk,  and  permit  risk  to  be  accurately  priced  and  ri controlled. This goes well beyond the maintenance of certain balance-sheet ratios whic know, are at best an imperfect measure of the riskiness of a portfolio.

Third , good supervision is no substitute for a developed 'credit culture'. The best sup the world cannot enforce a culture when the basic soil is not receptive. As I noted onus here lies squarely with banks' management and their boards of directors.

Fourth , to keep a banking system healthy, it is necessary to have clear procedures fo with institutions that get into difficulties. Too often, troubled banks are allowed operation  as  losses  mount  and  their  capital  erodes.  Forbearance  is  used  to  put  of decisions in the hope that things will somehow get better on their own. Industrial cou been just as guilty as developing ones in this regard. Early intervention procedures th to be spelled out so that institutions in difficulties are dealt with before they infec system.

Let me conclude: the international financial system has had a close shave. With luck, a management from now on, there is a good chance that things will now get better. But t important lessons to be learned if the system is to be made more resilient on a durable
