In the 'Branch Plan' draw 1978  the  Bank  explicitly  announced  the  objective  of  fostering  competition  in  the industry: the opening of branches was envisaged primarily in the areas where the conce of loans and deposits was highest, and not infrequently monopolistic.

Thus the Bank of Italy placed competition at the centre of its policy aimed at incr efficiency and solidity of the banking and financial system well before it was grant antitrust powers in 1990.

The precondition for the change in the Bank's approach was the abandonment of the id widely held after the crisis of the thirties, not only in Italy and not only among cen that competition, or 'excess' competition, caused banking instability and was antino respect to stability. On the contrary, and especially in the conditions of internatio typical of the Italian economy in normal circumstances, an inefficient banking system i be prone to systemic instability, even though oligopoly allows it to be profitable. stimulus to achieve profitability and hence a congruous capital base through efficie clearly be detected in the increase in competition in the domestic banking and financia Increased competition therefore became the key intermediate objective, the fulcrum of of Italy's monetary, exchange rate and supervisory policies. Without competition, in th there cannot be efficiency; without efficiency, in the long run there cannot be stab banking  and  financial  industry.  A  further  consideration,  rooted  in  the  economic  the which antitrust legislation is based, was that laisser faire and competition were not the same thing,  that  the  former  could  override  the  latter  (especially  in  an  industry  with  e scale), and that deregulation was likely to be more effective if set within the fram economic  and  institutional policy aimed  at  protecting  and  strengthening  competition  and ultimately imposing it on producers who might well not like it. The attribution to t Italy of responsibility for implementing antitrust law in the banking field was thus no anomaly to be removed later. It was the natural, institutional, recognition of a state had  already  existed  for  tens  of  years.  Above  all  it  sanctioned  a  principle  tha consolidated and applied more widely: not only are prudential supervision and the prot competition not in conflict, but they are rigorously complementary.

The declarations of intent, the strategic decisions, the single acts with which the B interpreted and applied these general criteria in practice have been many and spread o years. They cannot all be listed here, but I shall briefly indicate the most important summary points:

- the first, absolutely fundamental, step was taken at the beginning of the eighti reaffirmation of the notion of banks, both publicly and privately-owned, as enter the wake of the transposition of the EEC's First Banking Directive of 1985, the i finally  settled  in  a  judgement  handed  down  by  the  Court  of  Cassation  in  1989 transformation of publicly-owned banks into companies limited by shares followe provided for in Law 218 of 1990;
- between 1985 and 1990, while the amendments to the law that would lead to the Banking  Law  of  1993  were  being  enacted,  administrative  measures  were  adopt attenuating or eliminating the restrictions in fields such as branching, fund-r lending beyond the short term, and the creation of new banks. The growth of ind banks was increasingly related, by way of solvency and gearing ratios, to the am capital they were able to bring into play;
- starting in the early eighties, the quantity, the quality and the diffusion of th disclosed by banks to customers and the market were enhanced;
- by the end of 1988 the shift from direct administrative instruments to indirec instruments in implementing monetary policy had been completed;
- in response to the need to place growing volumes of public debt with domestic inv steps were taken to create efficient money and bond markets. The share of bank d in households' financial assets fell from 53 per cent in 1979 to 34 per cent in stands at 25 per cent today;
- the removal of exchange controls was started in 1988 and completed in 1990, wit result  that,  for  the  first  time  in  its  history,  Italy  had  a  fully  convertible complete freedom of both short and long-term capital movements.

All the indicators show that the degree of competition in the Italian banking system significantly in the eighties. Between 1979 and 1989 the average number of banks pre each  province  rose  from  20  to  27.  The  concentration  of  the  loan  market  fell  by  15 nationwide and by 20 per cent in the Centre and South. The differential between the bank lending rate and the pre-tax yield on Treasury bills narrowed from 5 percentage 1980 to less than 1 point in 1989 and this happened in a period which saw the riskines credit increase slightly. The spread between lending and deposit rates also narrowed, initially from more than 9 percentage points in 1980 to less than 7 points in 1989. these developments resulted in the margins on credit business coming under pressure.

In 1990 the law establishing the Competition Authority (Law 287/1990) made the Bank of responsible for the antitrust function in the banking sector. The choice was made in v specific technical nature of banking and the complementary nature of prudential supervi the protection of competition. In the United States, with its century-long tradition legislation, the situation is similar since the Federal Reserve or the Office of the C the  Currency,  according  to  the  banks  involved,  are  responsible  for  evaluating  t competitive  effects  of  mergers.  The  Department  of  Justice  cooperates  with  the  reg authorities and in extreme cases may bring a legal action against an operation. In Eu

worth mentioning the case of the Netherlands, where, in establishing a Competition Aut the beginning of this year, the law provisionally assigned the protection of competi banking  and  insurance  industries  to  the  respective  supervisory  authorities.  Other authorities are also beginning to recognize the specificity of the banking sector and, a have issued special instructions for the evaluation of bank mergers.

The growth in competition has continued in the decade that is drawing to a close. Foll decision taken by the Bank of Italy in 1990 to liberalize banks' branch networks by ab the  system  of  'branch  plans',  the  number  of  branches  increased  as  never  before,  ri 10,000, or more than 60 per cent, to 25,600 in June of this year. At the end of 1989 1,173 banks in Italy, of which 83 were medium-term credit institutions or sections. By June the number had fallen by more than 20 per cent to 937, of which 120 belonged to groups. In recent years the process of consolidation has involved large commercial ban in response to the prospect of an integrated European market with a single currency. Th number of banks present in each province has risen further to 30.

During the nineties the differential between the average bank lending rate and the pr on Treasury bills has tended to remain close to its level at the end of the eighties owing to the rather weak performance of the economy, this decade has seen a sharp inc the  average  riskiness  of  loans  and  a  deterioration  in  the  quality  of  banks'  assets. stability of the differential between bank lending rates and the yield on government s further evidence of the increasing competition within the banking industry.

The differences between the lending rates applied in the various parts of the country narrowed in the last four years after peaking in the second half of 1994. The differen the rates on short-term lira loans in the North and the South is currently around 2 points for non-financial companies and about 1.5 points for producer households. The entirely attributable to the greater average riskiness of lending in the South and the takes to recover credits there. The ratio of bad debts to total loans disbursed to cus South  is  22  per  cent,  as  against  7  per  cent  for  borrowers  in  the  Centre  and  North. carried  out  at  the  Bank  of  Italy  show  that,  after  adjusting  for  the  risks  that  mat geographical  differential  disappeared  in  the  early  nineties.  The  spread  between  len deposit rates has narrowed further and now stands at 4.5 percentage points.

The growth in competition has contributed to a substantial redistribution of banks' sh loan market. The major changes that occurred after the ceiling on bank loans was remov followed by further large shifts in the two years 1989-90 and from 1995 onwards. In the years the market shares that changed hands each year were equal to around 4 per cent of loan portfolio on average, excluding the amounts directly affected by mergers. The in competition has led to banks adopting more aggressive supply policies and growth st more closely attuned to demand.

## Mergers and acquisitions in the Italian banking system

Between 1990 and 1997 the Bank of Italy, pursuant to the provisions of antitrust law ap the banking sector, examined some 300 proposed mergers and acquisitions. The banks in grew steadily larger. In the last four years the banks involved accounted for 7 per banking  system's  total  assets  on  average  each  year.  The  consolidation  process  has particularly  pronounced  impact  on  the  southern  banking  system,  partly  as  a  result acquisition of the control of local banks in difficulty by banks situated in the Centre

In ten cases the Bank of Italy decided to examine proposed mergers in order to verify wh operation was likely to create or strengthen a dominant position and prejudice compet four  of  these  cases  the  go  ahead  was  made  conditional  on  measures  aimed  at  prot competition in the market in question.

Another ten examinations concerned agreements suspected of being detrimental to compet The investigation of industry-wide standard terms and of payment instruments were esp important in this respect. In its recently published findings on the rules governing t PagoBANCOMAT card, the Bank of Italy identified several circumstances that were potent anti-competitive and made its approval of the agreement conditional on a number of chan will help to make the market more competitive.

The Bank of Italy also investigated five alleged abuses of dominant positions. In fou cases the banks were accused of using their exclusive right to provide tax-collection gain undue competitive advantages in neighbouring credit markets. In the fifth case took  action  to  prevent  the  bank  from  exploiting  its  dominant  position  to  expand  it network abnormally with the aim of obstructing the entry or growth of competitors in th in question.

In  addition  to  its  normal  examination  activity,  in  1996  the  Bank  of  Italy  invest possibility that banks were coordinating their pricing policies, but found no eviden practices. In 1997, in agreement with the Competition Authority, it conducted a gene finding inquiry into the corporate services sector.

In the nineties the consolidation of the Italian banking system has proceeded primarily of mergers and amalgamations, of which there had been 265 by the end of 1997. Acquisiti the control of banks that subsequently continued to operate as separate entities also important  role,  with  a  total  of  91  such  takeovers.  Even  where  these  operations  have significantly reduced operating costs, they have allowed capital to be used more effic brought tax benefits, increases in fee income and improvements in the quality of the bank's loan portfolio.

Mergers between banks which are not present in the same markets, or with only limited increase competition. By contrast, the 'market power' effect tends to prevail over the effect where the merging banks both have a large presence in the same market. These f confirm the continued importance of the physical closeness of customers to their banks need for the attention that the competition authorities pay to local markets.

Mergers  inevitably  impact  the  payment  system  and  the  stability  of  the  banking  sec diminishing the number of participants in the payment system, they tend to reduce the v transactions  to  be  settled.  The  setting  of  operational  and  technological  standards exploiting network economies may well be easier. On the other hand, larger banks are cause more serious problems in the event of insolvency: the overall effect of merger stability of the payments system will depend on how they affect the riskiness of the banks.

## Competition, consolidation and costs

Competition, consolidation and reorganizations have helped to curb operating costs in r the total assets of the banking system. In the three years from 1995 to 1997 this rat 2.4 per cent, compared with 3 per cent in the second half of the eighties.

Nonetheless, partly as a result of the rigidity of the Italian labour market, the co between Italian banks and their counterparts abroad, which is attributable primarily to incidence of staff costs, has not narrowed in the nineties. In 1997 bank staff costs am per cent of gross income in Italy, compared with an average of 38 per cent in France, and Spain.

The agreements between employers and the trade unions to reduce the cost of labour, pr by the Bank of Italy and promoted by the Government, have not yet been given effect in wage agreement linking earnings more closely to a bank's performance. Significant cost as  well  as  increased  revenues,  can  be  achieved  by  modernizing  structures,  reorg production processes and developing innovative distribution networks. Other banking s have invested a substantial volume of resources, deriving in part from savings in sta technological innovation, thereby acquiring competitive advantages on several fronts.

The  increase  in  competition  in  banking  markets,  further  intensified  by  foreign  inter accustomed  to  operating  on  a  larger  scale  and  with  smaller  interest  rate  spreads,  h reduced the profitability of Italian banks' traditional activities. The fall in net i which began several years ago and will be accentuated by the introduction of the euro been  offset  by  a  lasting  increase  in  revenues  from  innovative  activities:  corporat services and finance, the administration and management of households' savings, and bus the international securities markets.

In the first half of the eighties Italian banks' return on equity was in excess of 14 p with that of the other leading European banking systems. Since then it has fallen, reac of around 1 per cent last year. Apart from the level of costs, the large loan losses i last few years have made a major contribution to the decline in profitability. The ris of the Italian banking system is 13 per cent, well above the requirement of 8 per cent in the Basle Capital Accord. Only a very few banks are below this limit and the total around 500 billion lire.

The decline in profitability has nonetheless reduced the flow of internally-generated with which to finance growth and merger operations. The larger banks have suffered esp in this respect: at the end of last year they held less than one third of the free banking system, as against 80 per cent of its total assets. The lack of free capital, tangible  and  financial  fixed  assets  and  available  for  acquisitions,  will  curtail  t modernizing the system and pursuing efficiency.

The intermediate objective pursued over the last twenty years has been largely achieved more  competition,  there  have  been  numerous  mergers  and  a  start  has  been  made reorganization projects  that  promise  to  improve  efficiency.  Competition  has  produced effects on the prices of banking products and services, holding them down and making more uniform. But other benefits have been, still are, slow in coming: lower costs, in competitiveness, profits and fresh capital generated by efficiency and the quality of se

The  picture  is  thus  chiaroscuro.  Disappointment  should  only  be  felt  by  those  who recognize that competition fosters efficiency but cannot guarantee it where producers ability to respond - à la Leibenstein - to the competitive stimulus. It is necessary to how much inertia has to be overcome in a complex process that is more cultural than jur institutional, in short the 'passage' from oligopoly to competition of an industry that information asymmetries, bilateral customer relationships and the reputation of produc journey  was  bound  to  be  laborious  and  slow,  especially  in  Italy's  case.  The  Italia

system arrived at the world economic crisis of the seventies after two postwar decades its  oligopolistic  nature  had  become  deeply  rooted,  while  the  economy  had  enjoye extraordinary  boom.  The  model  formulated  by  Donato  Menichella  and  Raffaele  Mattioli 'worked' in a certain sense; it had met, albeit with the inefficiencies that were th corollary, the demand for credit and money of the Italian economy in that buoyant pha subsequent resistance to change cannot be entirely attributed to the reluctance of any face the forces of competition or to the natural tendency to continue to do things in th

To  give  way  to  counterfactual  criticism  based  on  hindsight  -  such  as,  the  injec competitive  enzymes  should  have  been  much  larger  and  more  intense  -  would  be  not  on sterile but also debatable in theory and risky in practice. It is analytically doubt would have been possible, given the context. It is sufficient to mention just one aspec earlier: the uniform treatment of banks and enterprises and of banks in the public a sectors became a part of Italian law - as a result of the judgement of 1989 - ten years supervisory authority had clearly stated the principle. The risk at the practical level point banking competition will be seen as a missed opportunity, and that this will lead of renouncing it in the future.

The position of the Bank of Italy is to proceed, if possible with greater determination taken twenty years ago - not only because the single market, the euro and their rules option, and not only because the law in force in Italy today mandates this course, but that the progress that has already been made is in the right direction, even though com its own, it is worth repeating, does not guarantee an optimal financial system.

The Bank of Italy will devote more resources, a revised internal administrative structu on banking competition, and additional analyses serving to underpin new intervention task  of  fostering  competition  in  the  markets  in  which  banks  operate  and  the  merge autonomously plan.

Two changes that are already under way will also produce their effects. Mutually rei they should, together with competition in the markets for banking products, stimulate achieve the cost reductions and quality improvements that are necessary. The first cha privatization  of  the  banks  that  are  still  under  public  control,  the  second  concer procedures aimed at preventing moral hazard and the neglect of costs.

The transfer of the ownership of banks to the private sector is the precondition for c contested in the market. In the last few years the process of privatizing public banks pace, in parallel with the growth in mergers. Including the operations that are curr organized, the share of the banking system's assets in the hands of banks of which the authorities  or  foundations  own  the  majority  of  the  capital  will  shortly  fall  to  20 against 70 per cent ten years ago. BNL is about to be privatized. The Monte dei Paschi foundation, the only one that still owns all the capital of a major bank, has recentl place some of its capital in the market and to seek a stock exchange listing.

The prospect of contestability opened up by bank privatizations has been strengthene changes to the legal framework introduced by the Consolidated Law on Financial Markets, came into force in July of this year. The new rules serve to increase the disclosure of enhance the efficiency of the financial markets and the contestability of control - in listed companies partly through the revision of the provisions governing takeovers. The commercial banks listed on the stock exchange; they account, directly and indirectly and unlisted subsidiaries, for 50 per cent of the banking system's total assets. In a

are 10 cooperative banks listed on the stock exchange, accounting for 10 per cent of t and another 7 banks are listed on the ristretto market.

Although the Community authorities recognize the specific features of the banking sect application of Article 92 of the Treaty to banks tends to be rigorous. The authorizat aid to some large European banks has been made conditional on their disposing of assets the  business  and  equity  interests.  The  fact  that  bankers  will  be  able  to  count  les support means they will have to adopt even more stringent criteria of autonomous, so prudent management.

The  number  of  banks  in  distress  that  have  been  consolidated  (by  means  of  mer amalgamations  and  takeovers)  or  placed  under  special  administration  or  in  liquidat increased in the nineties, in both absolute and relative terms. The ratio of the num banks to the total number rose from 1.5 per cent in 1990 to an average of 4.3 per cen and 1997; the ratio of their assets to the total assets of the banking system rose from to nearly 6 per cent. The increase in the number of such interventions with respect t banks has been partly due to the increased emphasis on the preventive nature of sup action. Since the action is taken when the troubled bank still has a net value, it is p for  market-based  solutions  and  hence  to  reduce  the  burden  borne  by  the  deposit  pro system or the public finances. The proportion of troubled banks subjected to restruct were liquidated rose from 6 to 16 per cent between 1990 and 1997. In terms of their a ratio rose from just a few percentage points at the beginning of the decade to 11 per ce

The potential for the development of the financial sector, in both quantitative and terms, that the Italian economy requires and that it can achieve is considerable, prob than in most other European countries. The Bank of Italy remains committed to ensure, instruments  the  law  provides,  that  this  further  development  takes  place  in  a  co environment and in conditions of greater efficiency.

description: Speech by the Governor of the Bank of England, Mr. E.A.J. George, given at the Institute of Directors Annual Dinner in London on 19/11/98.
text:
## Mr. George gives an assessment of where the UK economy has come from and where it is headed

Speech by the Governor of the Bank of England, Mr. E.A.J. George, given at the Insti Directors Annual Dinner in London on 19/11/98.

My  Lord  and  President,  Deputy  Lord  Mayor,  Your  Excellency,  My  Lords,  Ladies  an Gentlemen.

Let me put some of the recent newspaper headlines alongside the facts, in order to put perspective.

First, on the world economy, the headlines read:

- Meltdown warning in the wake of economic slowdown.
- Last ditch bid to avert global crisis.
- G7 nations try to halt slide to depression.

And these are just the supposedly serious newspapers!

The facts are that world output growth is expected by the IMF to be 2% this year and 21 - compared with 4% in 1997. And the OECD expects growth in the OECD area of 21/4% th year, 13/4% in 1999, recovering to 21/4% in the year 2000 - compared with 3% in 1997. certainly is a very marked slowdown, but it is hardly meltdown or recession.

And on our own economy - the headlines read:

- Recession looms.
- The economy is hurtling headlong towards recession.

And even:

- It's official - the economy is shrinking.

The facts are that for the past 6½ years the British economy as a whole has grown at a annual rate of over 3% - which is well above its long term trend rate of some 2% - or, optimistic, some 2½%. And we were still growing, at an annual rate of some 2% in each last two quarters, on the latest published data.

At  the  time  these  headlines  were  written  a  month  or  so  ago  not  one  of  the  28  inde professional forecasting organisations surveyed by Consensus Forecasts was expecting ou fall in 1999; and their average expectation was for 1% growth next year. That is broad with our own latest best guess in the MPC. Your own most recent IOD forecast in Sept suggested  slightly  stronger  growth  next  year.  It  is  true  that  Consensus  Forecasts revised down their mean expectation - to just over ¾% growth; but even now only one of contributors expects output to fall.

On unemployment in the UK the headlines read:

* Jobs gloom deepens as layoffs soar.* More jobs go as recession looms.* Jobless up a pain hits Britain.

And the facts? At the time these headlines were written, the unemployment rate, both n and in virtually every region of the UK, apart from the South East and East Anglia, lowest it has been since at least the early 1980s.

## I could go on.

Headlines: UK heads for credit crisis. Closed for credit. Credit card sales dive. Fact building society lending up by 0.7% in the latest month (September) and by 8.8% over t year. Credit card lending was up by over 26% on a year ago.

Headlines: House prices hit as recession clouds gather. Facts: house prices rose by 6.7 past year on the Halifax index and by 7.5% according to the Nationwide.

Now I say all this, President, not to draw attention to the proclivity of headline writ economic/financial commentators, to sensationalise. My serious point is that, especiall of  unusual  uncertainty  as  at  present,  we  all  need  to  focus  more  carefully  than  ev evolving  facts,  and  on  the  more  probable  outcomes  and  not  allow  ourselves  to  be preoccupied with extreme, even if possible, outcomes.

Against that background, let me offer you my own assessment of where the UK economy come from and where it is headed.

Since the recession of the early 1990s the economy as a whole has, as I say, grown at a annual rate of just over 3% - well above trend. During this period we were steadily re the spare capacity created by the recession, and this was reflected in a gradual impr the labour market - in a net increase in employment of 1.7 mn people since the end of in a persistent fall in unemployment to - as I say - the lowest rate for nearly 20 year underlying consumer price inflation has averaged 2.7% over the past 5 years, the low since the early 1960s - and it has been exactly on target - at 2½% - in each of the past

About 2 years ago it began to become evident that demand and output growth, in the econ a whole, was picking up speed. And as we moved into and through 1997, it became increa obvious that unless we acted to tighten monetary policy, in order to moderate the rate we risked overheating, particularly in the labour market, where reports of shortages skilled but even of unskilled workers, were becoming widespread.

The situation was seriously complicated by an increasing imbalance between the domest the internationally exposed sectors of the economy. Domestic demand for goods, and part for services, was unsustainably strong, and large parts of the economy were doing very the back of that - though they didn't make too much of a song and dance about it. B sectors,  those  most  exposed  to  international  competition  -  most  of  agriculture,  larg manufacturing and some service sectors - were already then having a much more difficul Understandably,  they  were  more  vociferous.  They  had  been  hit,  initially,  by  the  exa strength of sterling against the major European currencies in the run up to decisions euro. And they were hit, subsequently, by the successive waves of turmoil spreading thr world economy which saw exchange rates fall and demand dry up in Asia and elsewhere.

So, faced with this dilemma, what were we to do? It is true that the external factors they were in a more fundamental sense, in terms of the imbalance in the economy - did restraining  influence  on  overall  aggregate  demand  and  on  inflation,  and  that  meant somewhat more time than we would otherwise have had to moderate the growth of domes demand. But even allowing for that we in fact had no choice but to tighten policy.

It wasn't that we didn't know that the internationally-exposed sectors were under the we'd have had to be blind as well as deaf not to have known. Our problem was that if held back more than we did, in order to shelter the exposed sectors, we would have put economy - including the sectors we were trying to protect - at risk of accelerating in that would have meant eventually having to tighten policy more abruptly, which would more certainly have plunged the economy into serious recession, a bit further down the r

The harsh reality is that monetary policy can only target the economy as a whole realistically  seek  to  shelter  particular  businesses  or  particular  sectors  or  parti however much we might all wish it were otherwise. And, in relation to the economy as a the effective choice in the situation we faced was not whether or not to tighten, but tighten sooner, and by less, or later, by more.

So we raised interest rates through the second half of last year - and again in June we could through our tactics, to minimise any further unwanted upward pressure on sterli

## But things have now clearly moved on.

The outlook for the world economy deteriorated further through the summer under the imp a series of new shocks. Japan, the world's second largest economy, slipped further into Russia - which had only weeks earlier embarked on an IMF program - saw the collapse o rouble  and  default  on  its  debt.  And  acute  nervousness  spread  through  many  of  the financial markets. Although there has been some improvement in sentiment over the past or two, and although the US and European economies continue to expand, the likelihood r that world economic growth will be significantly slower than had been expected earlie summer. Slower growth of world activity is bound to prolong the restraining external growth and inflation in the UK, even though the exchange rate has now started to weaken

At the same time there are also now clearer signs of overall slowdown in our own econom evidence for this is less obvious in the backwards-looking economic and monetary data t in the forward-looking surveys, but even so the data suggest that we are beginning easing  of  pressure,  including  an  easing  of  pressure  in  the  labour  market.  And  the themselves now point to a slowdown in service sector growth, including retail distri well as a sharper decline in manufacturing output.

This prospect is consistent with the reports which we receive directly from the Bank's regional agents and their 7000-odd industrial and commercial contacts around the countr

Of course we pay very careful attention to this forward-looking evidence of development economy alongside the data, and, like others, we have revised down our forecasts fo growth and inflation. And we have eased monetary policy quite sharply in the past two in the light of that evidence.

Our current best guess - published in last week's Inflation Report is that, after the cuts,  the  growth  of  overall  output  next  year  will  be  around  1%,  picking  up  thro Millennium  to  around  trend  in  the  second  half  of  the  year  2000.  Meanwhile,  we  e underlying inflation to remain close to the target rate of 21/2% - though perhaps a l that rate during the course of next year. Now no-one likes to see the economy slowing d some  slowdown  was  necessary  at  this  point  in  the  economic  cycle  in  order  to  avo inflationary upsurge. And if in fact it proves to be as mild as most of the forecasts own - suggest, it will be a huge improvement on anything we have seen at this stage in for decades.

It is true of course that the economy may turn out to be weaker than in our central That projection is the MPC's very carefully considered view as to the most probable o but there is considerable uncertainty around it; and the risks are somewhat more on than on the upside. We don't have a crystal ball. And we don't pretend to know at all just how things will in fact turn out - that's why we publish our forecasts in the f with a wide range of uncertainty around the central case. The people to watch out for i are those who do claim to know precisely. What we have to do, in actually operating m policy is to monitor all the relevant evidence as it emerges for signs that the econom to  be  either  stronger  or  weaker  than  we  expect,  and  modify  our  view  of  the  prosp inflation -  and  our  monetary  policy  -  in  the  light  of  that.  And  in  that  context assurance, which I gave recently to the TUC in Blackpool, that we will act symmetrica will be - have been - just as rigorous in reducing interest rates with the overall evid to the balance of risks to inflation on the downside, as we have been - and will ag raising rates with the evidence pointing to a significant or sustained overshoot of target.

Now  there  are  those  -  perhaps  even  one  or  two  of  you  here  this  evening  -  who  rega assurance  as  cold  comfort.  It  misses  the  point  -  they  say  -  because  the  present  ap monetary policy focuses too narrowly on inflation. What we want - they say - is a m policy which puts more emphasis on growth and employment. You hear this complaint not in this country but increasingly these days in Continental Europe. I must say, Presid leaves me totally bemused.

What it suggests is that growth and price stability are seen as alternatives - you ca more of one if you're prepared to accept a bit less of the other. I must confess that debate had advanced beyond that point and that we really had learned from bitter experi there is no trade-off of this sort. In anything other than the short term you can't hav the other.

We've  tried  all  too  often  in  the  past  to  increase  the  growth  rate  of  the  economy pumping up demand - without sufficient regard to the underlying, supply-side, capacit economy  to  meet  that  demand.  The  result,  repeatedly  was  inflationary  boom  followe inevitable bust, and this repeated experience itself engendered a pervasive and damagi termism,  in  both  industrial  and  financial  business  behaviour.  That  simply  made  the worse next time around. What we - and the Bundesbank, and the ECB in future - have to do  is  to  keep  overall  demand  growing  broadly  in  balance  with  the  underlying  suppl capacity  of  the  economy,  aiming  to  dampen  rather  than  aggravate  the  economic  cycle consistent price stability - certainly not falling prices but not accelerating price in is the measure of our success in achieving that broader objective over time. The deb about the ends, it is about the means. Price stability has never to my mind been simpl itself - it would be a pretty dry and unsatisfying objective if that were all that we w whole point about price stability - even when, as now, it involves a temporary slowdow growth of activity - is that it is a necessary condition for the sustainable growth o employment and rising living standards, which are of course the truly good things of which we surely all want to see. That is, I think, what we have seen over recent years.

## Mr. Yam focuses on how Hong Kong is coping with financial turmoil

Text of the 'Inside Asia Lecture 1998' by the Chief Executive of the Hong Kong Mone Authority, Mr. Joseph Yam, JP, organised by The Australian, Sydney on 23/11/98.

## Introduction

It  is  a  great  pleasure  to  be  in  your  beautiful  city  once  again,  and  an  honour  t opportunity to speak to such a distinguished audience. Sydney and Hong Kong - both v international cities with spectacular ports - have much in common. We enjoy growing c and economic links and, although some 4,500 miles distant, we are both part of the same Less  happily,  our  economies  have  both  taken  a  hammering  from  the  financial  crisis  t recently rocked the region. My focus in this talk will be on how the regional crisis Hong Kong, and, equally important, on the ways in which it has not affected Hong Kong.

## The Asian Financial Crisis

The complex causes that so suddenly turned the Asian miracle into an Asian mess will n be debated for many years to come. The devastating effects of the massive exodus of capi the region have been clear enough. In the worst hit economies currencies have devalue much as 70%. Stock markets have declined to the levels of ten years ago. Asset pric sharply deflated, economies have contracted, and unemployment has risen. The region is through  its  worst  financial  crisis  since  the  Second  World  War.  Optimists  already stabilization of the situation and light at the end of the tunnel, and they may well deepening  recession  in  Japan,  emerging  problems  in  Latin  America,  and  questions  abou stability  of  the  U.S.  and  European  markets  still  raise  serious  concerns  that  what regional crisis may swell into a crisis of global proportions.

Hong Kong is located at the very heart of the East Asian region, and our economy is in and increasingly, linked with the other economies in the region. It is therefore hardl that we should have experienced some considerable stress as a result of the Asian crisi last  year  we  have  seen  a  roughly  50%  decline  in  the  value  of  property  and  stocks, unemployment,  and  a  forecast  contraction  of  4%  in  our  GDP  for  1998.  Although  the  s market and property prices have seen something of a rebound during the last month, the what has become an extensive economic adjustment continues, and is likely to continue f time.

It is necessary to stress, however, that this is an adjustment, not a collapse, and t one of the least dramatic, and least traumatic, of all the upheavals in the region. terms, the Hang Seng Index has, since the crisis erupted last July, seen the smallest any stock market in the region. Our banking system has remained stable and solvent. rates have risen, but not as far as they have elsewhere: they are currently marginally US dollar interest rates at the short end and at a premium of about 100 basis points f money.  Inflation  is  declining,  not  rising.  And,  where  other  currencies  have  seen  s devaluations,  the  Hong  Kong  dollar  has  remained  stable.  In  fact,  it  remains  the  on convertible currency in Asia that has not experienced devaluation: the linked exchan $7.8 Hong Kong dollars to the U.S. dollar - is as solid as ever. The tenacity and credi link is, in my view, one of the main reasons why Hong Kong has weathered the crisis bet most of its neighbours. We are as committed as we have ever been to preserving the link have demonstrated, throughout the turmoil of the last year, that we have the machinery form of an effective currency board - to enable us to keep the link.

We are also committed to maintaining our position as the world's freest economy. Hong has built its reputation on free market principles. We are proud of this reputation, an these principles because we know how much our prosperity depends on them. Whatever u other economies might have for them, exchange controls are out of the question for Hong the Basic Law, which sets out our basic principles of government, expressly prohibits t even if it did not, we know that, at least for Hong Kong, any attempt to introduce th turn inwards on ourselves, would spell the end of our prosperity.

But free market principles cannot mean markets that are left defenceless against mani One troubling aspect of the Asian crisis, and a sign of larger problems in the worl system, has been the extreme volatility in markets created by the rapid flows of highly funds  around  the  world.  As  markets  in  the  region  became  more  vulnerable,  these increasingly took on a predatory character and became more and more subtle in their p and  sophistication.  This  August,  as  you  know,  the  Hong  Kong  financial  markets  becam target of a well planned attack by international hedge funds. We took unconventional a fend off that attack and to fortify our financial system against future attacks. Not these  actions  have  been  the  cause  of  extensive  controversy,  and  of  a  great misunderstanding.  Let  me  attempt  to  present  the  issue  from  Hong  Kong's  perspectiv outlining what happened in August and explaining why we took action.

Oddly enough, Hong Kong became a target because of the transparency of its financial we were singled out for our efficiency and predictability rather than for any fundamen Under our rule-based currency board system, any change in the Hong Kong dollar monetary must be strictly matched, at the linked exchange rate, by a corresponding change in th of foreign reserves held by the currency board. This is an autopilot mechanism, in wh the HKMA have minimal discretion: the currency board simply acts passively in respon capital flows. Under the autopilot mechanism, an expansion of the monetary base causes rates  to  fall;  a  contraction  causes  them  to  rise.  The  crucial  element  in  the  mon influencing the rise and fall of interest rates is the aggregate balance that banks ma clearing  accounts  held  with  the  currency  board.  Notwithstanding  the  enormous  volum transactions that goes through our banks, the aggregate balance is minimal, because our infrastructure  is  so  efficient.  We  have  a  real-time  interbank  payment  system  and  no requirements,  so  that  banks  in  Hong  Kong  do  not  need  to  maintain  large  balances  i clearing accounts with the currency board: in August the aggregate balance was as low billion. This meant that the aggregate balance, and hence interbank interest rates, sensitive to speculative attack.

We saw a series of such attacks over the past year, when various currency speculators t short positions against the Hong Kong dollar with the aim of destabilizing the linked rate. On all these occasions the attacks drove up the interbank interest rates to ver To the extent that the speculators had to borrow in the interbank market to fund their Kong  dollar  positions,  the  interbank  interest  rates  were  high  enough  to  force  the speculators to abandon the attacks, unwind their short positions, and incur substantial finely tuned currency board  system  worked  well,  but  the  interest  rate  volatility  was during one attack, on 23 October 1997, the overnight interest rate shot up to nearly stock market took a nosedive, and the HKMA was sharply criticized for relying on this tool, the interest rate, to defend the Hong Kong dollar.

In August the speculators adopted a more sophisticated ploy. They introduced a form of play aimed at playing off the currency board system against the stock and futures mark to avoid being squeezed by high interest rates, they prefunded themselves in Hong Kong

in the debt market, swapping US dollars for Hong Kong dollars with multilateral institu have raised Hong Kong dollars through the issue of debt. At the same time, they accu large short positions in the stock index futures market. They then sought to enginee conditions in the money market by dumping huge amounts of Hong Kong dollars. This sel was intended to cause a sharp interest rate hike, which in turn would have sent the st plummeting. The collapse of the stock market would have enabled them to reap a hand profit from the futures contracts they had taken out.

A few figures will help give some idea of the scale of this attack and the vulnerabil Kong's markets at the time. We estimate that the hedge funds involved had amassed in ex HK$30 billion in currency borrowings, at an interest cost of around HK$4 million a da also held an estimated 80,000 short contracts, which translated into the following calc every fall of 1,000 points in the Hang Seng index they stood to make a profit of HK$4 they could have engineered that fall within 1,000 days they would have broken even. could have achieved it within 100 days they would have netted HK$3.6 billion. All the do was to wait for the best moment to dump their Hong Kong dollars, to drive up inter and send a shock wave through the stock market. August was an opportune time: turnover stock  market  had  shrunk  to  about  a  third  of  its  normal  level;  there  was  bad  news government  announced  that  first-quarter  GDP  growth  had  been  negative;  and  rumours  w flying around predicting the devaluation of the Renminbi and the severing of the link the Hong Kong dollar and the US dollar.

We acted swiftly to defeat the manipulators at their own game with a series of measu threw them off their guard, drove them out of the market, and raised the defences agai attacks. First, drawing on the official reserves, we went into the stock and futures ma second half of August we accumulated US$15 billion worth of shares: I am happy to say t now  worth  US$19  billion,  but  our  aim  was  not  to  make  money;  it  was  simply  to  d manipulation  by  making  sure  that  it  did  not  pay  off.  That  objective  was  achieve manipulators were forced to close out their short positions, in many cases with heavy l we  followed  through  with  a  package  of  technical  measures  to  strengthen  our  currency arrangement to make our money market less susceptible to manipulation. These measure working  well.  Further  reforms  are  being  introduced  in  the  securities  and  futures  m reduce the possibility of market dislocation.

Our actions served their purpose of deterring market manipulation. We could not passi through  the  speculative  attack  and  see  our  markets  overshoot  to  produce  profits manipulators, and our entire financial system brought to the brink of collapse. We do n that our intervention in the markets was not a controversial act. This was not a decis enjoyed taking. It involved many risks, not least among them the risk of being misund Our critics, both at home and abroad, have accused us of intervening with the aim s propping up the stock market; of being too afraid to face the pain from the necessary i volatility under a strict currency board system operating in difficult conditions; even introduce a novel form of state ownership by acquiring a substantial interest in Hon major corporations. The essence of these charges is that what we did in August marked of our long-standing and hugely successful philosophy of non-intervention in the market

I  think  it  is  now  increasingly  recognized  throughout  the  world  that  what  we  did  w necessary and effective. But let me emphasize this: our actions in August were not t non-interventionism, not an abandonment of our free market principles, but a measure ensure  that  those  principles  prevailed.  Free  markets  cannot  mean  markets  that  can  b manipulated, particularly by large players operating in small markets. We did the mini

was  necessary  to  preserve  the  integrity  of  our  linked  exchange  rate  system  and  al financial markets properly to perform the role of financial intermediation. Our respons to keep the markets free and fair for all investors. Not to have acted would, in my been  the  very  height  of  irresponsibility,  and  would  have  seriously  damaged  Hong  K credibility as an international, and freely accessible, financial centre.

We now have a substantial shares portfolio. We have put that portfolio under the manage a separate company at arms length from the HKMA to ensure that there is no conflict of between our shareholdings and our daily operations as a regulator. Our intention is these shares very gradually in a way that will have no impact on the markets. This mean holding on to them for some time. Meanwhile, the markets have stabilized, and th Seng Index has, like other markets, been enjoying something of a resurgence over the weeks.

## Hong Kong's Economic Strengths

I believe that in the future we shall be able to look back on our actions in August and as  a  resounding  reaffirmation  of  our  resolve  to  maintain  our  fifteen-year  record  of stability through the linked exchange rate. The link was introduced in October 1983 at uncertainty over Hong Kong's future and declining confidence in the Hong Kong dollar. T has survived successive political and economic shocks, both global and regional. It i weathering the current crisis, the greatest test so far: it will, I believe, come out o resilient than ever, fortified by the technical refinements to our currency board syste important, be strengthened by the clear message that we have given about our determin maintain it.

The link is the lynchpin of our monetary system and a vital factor in our prosperity. explaining why the stability of the Hong Kong dollar is so important to our economy, an is that we have been able to maintain this stability at a time when the fixed exchange many other freely convertible currencies in the region have collapsed.

We are a predominantly externally-oriented economy, and an economy that comes the close any in the world to running itself on pure free market principles. The annual value of trade is at least two and a half times that of our gross domestic product: most of it t of re-exports. We import nearly all of our daily needs, including food and water. We ex of our manufactured products, together with a large range of financial and other servic an  international  financial  centre  with  huge  capital  inflows  and  outflows,  and  no controls.

In  such  an  economic  environment,  volatile  exchange  rates  would  introduce  instabili unpredictability without bringing any corresponding advantages, except possibly to tho foreign exchange industry. Businessmen would face greater currency risks in their inte transactions and would be forced to hedge their considerable currency exposures at gr Sharp gyrations in the exchange rate, and the kind of overshooting that we have see recent currency devaluations elsewhere would seriously undermine the stability of our system, and confidence in it. Nor is devaluation necessary to help make us more comp even given the fact that many of our neighbours have seen currency devaluations of bet and 80 per cent. Currency devaluation is not the only means to achieve economic adju and the argument that Hong Kong is losing out by maintaining the link makes little s such  an  externally  oriented  economy.  Hong  Kong  is  achieving  its  adjustment  through variables. Asset prices and the cost of production, particularly in the form of land

have  come  down  very  sharply.  Wages  are  easing.  Manufacturers  and  service  providers increasingly  able  to  lower  their  costs  while  at  the  same  time  seeking  improveme productivity.

It is therefore quite misleading to claim, as many sceptics do, that without currency Hong Kong cannot be competitive. We have chosen an alternative route towards adjustment we consider ourselves fortunate that we have the capacity to make that choice. This comes from the fundamental strengths that make it possible for us to run an effective board. These fundamentals can be reduced to four basic, and some what obvious, points are so obvious, in fact, that they are too often overlooked in the narrow discussion prospects for the link, and it is worth setting them out.

First, our ample foreign currency reserves. These are the fruits of strict fiscal dis has produced surpluses year after year, and of prudent investment. Our reserves current to US$88.4 billion, the third largest in the world, after Japan and the Mainland of C are equivalent to more than seven times the currency in circulation, one of the highes the world.

Secondly, we pursue a prudent fiscal policy, with small government and no external de have a simple tax structure, a low tax rate, and a public sector expenditure that accou 18% of GDP.

Thirdly, our financial system is sound. The banking system is strong and solvent, and we cope  with  the  interest  rate  movements  necessary  under  the  currency  board  system. adequacy ratios among locally incorporated banks average around 18%, and their problem ratio is about 3.7%. Our standards of prudential supervision are among the highest in t

Fourthly, Hong Kong's economy is flexible and responsive. Because they are governed by market  principles,  the  markets  respond  quickly  to  interest  rate  changes  and  other making the economy resilient in absorbing external shocks and capable of adjusting effi validate the linked exchange rate.

These are Hong Kong's economic strengths. Not all economies have them, or would necess wish to have them, but they have enabled us to maintain a monetary system appropriate t Kong's  unique  needs  and  capable  of  withstanding  the  storms  that  any  open  and  exte oriented economy must necessarily expose itself to.

One  of  our  greatest  underlying  economic  strengths  is  our  relationship  with  the  Main China,  a  relationship  which  helped  fuel  rapid  growth  in  both  economies  over  the  l decades. Our two economies maintain extensive and highly productive economic links yet same  time  operate  entirely  separate  economic  systems  under  the  one  country,  two  sy formula. Not much more than a year ago, just before the Asian financial crisis erupted eve of the transfer of sovereignty over Hong Kong, pessimists were depicting this relat a  weakness  rather  than  a  strength:  they  were  predicting  extensive  meddling  by  the Government, and consequently a loss of autonomy and dynamism in Hong Kong. They hav been very wrong on this. The track record so far has been impressive, and all the more the succession of crises over the last year.

As far as Hong Kong's monetary system is concerned, the transfer of sovereignty has more, not less, autonomy for Hong Kong. Whereas before the handover monetary policy o required close consultations with the Secretary of State in London, the Central Gover

Beijing has left such matters entirely in the hands of the HKSAR Government. Furtherm has strongly and clearly reiterated its support for what we are doing, its confidence i to  manage  things  on  our  own  and  its  preparedness  to  help  in  the  unlikely  event  tha needed.  Our  fundamental  policies  are  enshrined  in  the  Basic  Law:  among  these  are independence; maintenance of Hong Kong as an international financial centre; and a f system  governed  and  protected  by  locally  enacted  laws.  Most  important,  the  Basic prescribes a separate currency for Hong Kong - the Hong Kong dollar - which is to contin freely exchangeable and fully backed by reserves. These points are worth stressing, bec has been much misunderstanding about Hong Kong's position.

## The challenges ahead

I believe we should also look to the future, and not just dwell on current anxieties the political fall-out from our recent measures against market manipulation. As I see i two main challenges ahead. One is the challenge before every economy in the region, in Hong Kong, to pull ourselves out of the economic difficulties that now face us. The o challenge to the global financial community as a whole.

For Hong Kong, the challenge is to see through the economic adjustment that is now in continue to promote our competitiveness, and to plan for economic recovery. There is n that this is a painful process. Nor can there be any pretence that the current downturn quickly, whatever the positive signs in the markets over the past few weeks. In the markets we need to be vigilant against future attacks and to introduce further safegu financial system. These safeguards will include improvements to cross-market surveill Hong Kong, and an in-depth exploration of possibilities for further strengthening the of the currency board system - an exercise which is now making good progress. More wide need to continue to develop Hong Kong's position as a premier international financia Practical measures recently announced by the Chief Executive of the HKSAR will help i they include schemes ranging from the upgrading of the security and efficiency of ou financial infrastructure to the expansion of research facilities in the form of a mone affiliated to the HKMA.

The emphasis in all of this is not on intervention, but on facilitation. As a governmen direct  the  form  that  economic  growth  should  take:  we  simply  strive  to  provide  t environment that we can to enable growth to take place. In the financial sphere that stable  currency,  a  credible  and  secure  banking  system,  and  markets  that  sustain,  ra undermine, economic development. There is much that we can do - and have done - local achieve these aims. But increasingly, the solutions have to be global solutions, beca events of the last year have amply demonstrated, some of the most intractable problem our financial systems straddle borders and thrive in the cracks and holes between jur Globalization - the breaking down of economic barriers - has brought many benefits, par to our own region. But it has also brought risks and instabilities that can only be ta co-operation between governments.

Over  the  last  two  months  an  international  consensus  has  emerged  about  the  dange unmonitored, highly leveraged cross-border capital flows. In August we talked about the to small or medium markets, such as Hong Kong. Since the LTCM debacle in September, focus has been on the damage that huge international hedge funds, which are subject to no regulation, are capable of inflicting even on the larger markets. We now have a si which the global financial market is outgrowing its infrastructure, or, to quote Charl of  the  London  School  of  Economics,  'Finance  is  rapidly  becoming  global;  but  laws

regulations are national.' The world financial community has now awoken to the danger seems to be unanimous on the point that action is needed. The G7 communique in late O calling for strong global action to promote greater transparency in highly leveraged fu a step in the right direction. This has been reiterated at the APEC Summit last week Lumpur. The challenge will be in translating these calls into an effective system to the kind of turmoil that has ravaged economies throughout our region does not repeat it the larger aim of this co-operation should be not just to draw up defensive measures, b positive opportunities for building a new global financial order appropriate to the n twenty-first century.
