title: Mr. Meister reports on the Year 2000 problem from the perspective of German banking supervisors  (Central Bank Articles and Speeches, 30 Oct 98)
description: Luncheon speech by Mr. Edgar Meister, a member of the Directorate of the Deutsche Bundesbank, at the Year 2000 meeting of European central banks and financial regulators organised by the Joint Year 2000 Council and the Deutsche Bundesbank in Frankfurt/Main on 30/10/98.
text:
Mr.  Meister  reports  on  the  Year  2000  problem  from  the  perspective  of German  banking  supervisors Luncheon  speech  by  Mr.  Edgar  Meister,  a  member  of  the Directorate of the Deutsche Bundesbank, at the Year 2000 meeting of European central and financial regulators organised by the Joint Year 2000 Council and the Deutsche Bund in Frankfurt/Main on 30/10/98.

I

I  am  pleased  to  contribute  to  this  conference  on  the  Year  2000  and  how millennium date change poses a very significant risk for financial institutions and mark

The  media  have  now  been  reporting  regularly,  and  sometimes  with  flas headlines, on the many problems which the Y2K problem or 'millennium bug' can pose to economy and public administration. One has visions of planes crashing, assembly lines to a standstill, pensioners being asked to register for school, babies receiving old contracts becoming null and void, or deliveries being interrupted.

We are all well aware that the Year 2000 problem impacts on the whole econo and  the  public  administration.  Therefore,  joint  action  must  be  taken  now  if  we  are potentially serious problems down the road.

Acting in my role as a central banker and as chairman of the Banking Superv Committee  of  the  European  Central  Bank,  my  primary  concern  is  on  the  role  fina institutions play in this context. That is why I want to take this opportunity to giv overview on the implications of the problem on the financial sector and a brief summar measures  taken  by  German  banking  supervisors  to  promote  and  intensify  the  necessary 2000 preparations.

II

In the banking and insurance sectors, the impact of systems being insuffi Year  2000  compliant  can  be  particularly  drastic.  Some  vivid  examples  are  the  possib interest and redemption payments on loans being calculated inaccurately, statements of and  insurance  periods  being  updated  incorrectly,  cheques  and  credit  cards  being  rej ATMs (automated teller machines), and futures contracts being cancelled.

However,  the  more  pressing  risks  are  to  be  found  in  the  danger  that  pay systems  might  collapse,  liquidity  bottlenecks  might  occur,  and  the  number  of  credit might increase, owing to Year 2000 problems on the part of banks' customers. For this banking supervisors have alerted the banking industry to the possibility of significant customers' behaviour occurring at the end of 1999 as far as their demand for cash goes. public confidence in the ability of the financial sector to solve the Year 2000 pro trigger increased withdrawals of deposits and demand for cash.

The particularly close technical and financial interdependency within the b sector, as well as with all sectors of the economy (owing to the banks' corporate c makes  it  necessary  to  take  particularly  comprehensive  action.  Not  only  must  the  bank systems be reassessed but also the Year 2000 preparations being made by their business p

There  is  a  further  factor  that  compounds  the  situation:  Germany  and  the member states of the forthcoming European Monetary Union must deal with the dual chall of preparing their computer programs for the changeover to the single European currenc

the same time take the necessary preparations for the century date change. Numerous p show up here, and what we nowadays call 'synergy effects' are the result. They will s limited, yet they do clearly exist, such as in cashless payments.

For  one  thing,  there  is  a  heightened  awareness  of  how  to  handle  such  c country  and  cross-system  conversion  processes,  for  which  there  is  hardly  any  hi precedent. For another, completely new procedures such as the cross-border TARGET sys have been developed. In these systems, it was possible to take timely account of the c to the Year 2000, which will take place in 427 days. The absolute necessity of prepar systems  anew  for  the  euro  has  allowed  the  Bundesbank  and  the  credit  instituti simultaneously  make  virtually  countless  EDP  systems  in  the  accounting  sections  and offices' Year 2000 compliant.

The  practical  experience  which  must  almost  inevitably  be  gained  during weekend of the changeover to the euro from 1998 to 1999 will also provide welcome knowl that can be used for the century date change. It will probably once again become clear involved that the interplay of different systems can be different in real life than in however realistic it may be. The Year 2000 changeover has a different type of complex the introduction of the euro, since there is an interaction between different EDP ap system  components  and  external  software  components,  as  well  as  processor-driven  sys Substituting  the  euro  for  the  DM  will  involve  the  organisation  of  workflows  and  op procedures; in computer-related terms, that means new software must be installed. Howe the changeover from December 31, 1999 to January 1, 2000, the hardware components of EDP systems, i.e. the nearly innumerable number of chips, must be transformed.

The Bundesbank and the credit institutions, which were already required to pioneering role when the euro was introduced, are again forced to play a key role in financial sector ready for the millennium date change. Responsibility for the overall c of the exchange of information and ideas on this problem among the various sectors of though, is in the hands the Federal Government. (To this end, the Federal Ministry of E has set up, among other things, a Year 2000 expert group in its ministry, in which repr of the most important sectors of industry and administration affected by the problem ar participating.)

## III

What measures are German banking supervisors taking to help the financial s achieve a successful crossover to the new millennium?

German banking supervisors do not and cannot even dare to guarantee that b will be fully compliant; rather the emphasis is on ensuring that

- banks' senior management have focused on the scale of the problems fac their institution,
- they are taking responsibility for solving them,
- the banks systematically plan the relevant projects and implement them timely manner, and
- they  have  contingency  plans  in  place  to  rectify  any  slippage  or  s failure.

Since the beginning of their Year 2000 activities in 1994-95, and particular 1997, the Bundesbank and the Federal Banking Supervisory Office have been leaning on

banking industry to press ahead with its Year 2000 preparations with great intensity. the state of the banking industry's preparations for the Year 2000 is also a major fo ongoing banking supervision.

On-site validation procedures through independent auditors during audits banks' annual accounts for as early as the year 1997 constitute one important point. An important  action  is  a  Year  2000  survey  conducted  in  June  1998.  The  Federal  Ban Supervisory  Office  and  the  Bundesbank  asked  all  the  approximately  3,600  credit  inst under supervision and 200 stockbrokers in Germany about their Year 2000 preparations analysis of the preparations is supplemented by personal discussions of banking supervi individual  credit  institutions,  particularly  those  having  branches  and  subsidiari Immediate  actions  are  taken  where  the  existence  of  the  institution  is  in  jeopardy insufficient preparations for the Year 2000.

With regard to the timetable, German banking supervisors have not set any of target dates, yet they have made it perfectly clear in discussions and surveys that testing of these systems should be completed by mid-1999. This target date will also b the final prudential assessment of the state of preparations of individual credit insti

Although legal problems, particularly liability issues, are being given i attention in connection with the Year 2000 problem, no legislative changes are curren envisaged, because the legal system is flexible enough to cope with these problems.

Ladies and gentlemen, the turning of the clock at midnight on December 31, cannot  be  postponed  -  as  you  all  know.  Time  is  a  scarce  asset  with  regard  to  the preparations. As all credit institutions are depending on each other to be sufficiently issue  is  hardly  a  factor  of  competition.  On  the  contrary,  an  exchange  of  experi information is crucial in order to enhance the efficiency of the changeover work. Ther Federal Banking Supervisory Office and the Deutsche Bundesbank have been playing a proa role in coordinating the efforts across the financial institutions: at their instigat Credit  Committee  ( ZKA )  established  a  forum  comprising  several  banking  associations exchanging  experience  on  the  Year  2000  problem  at  the  expert  level.  The  Federal  Ba Supervisory Office and the Deutsche Bundesbank are involved in the forum's work.

Supporting  the  banking  industry  in  its  efforts  to  solve  the  Y2K  problem ongoing process that will continue until the crossover takes place. Nevertheless, I mu that  the  ultimate  responsibility  lies  with  the  management  of  the  individual  in themselves.  This  is  why  handling  the  Year  2000  problem  responsibly  is  a  criterion Federal Banking Supervisory Office when assessing whether or not banking business is conducted properly.

IV

I could go on and on about the supervisory aspects of the Y2K problem. Howe a luncheon speech does not seem to be the appropriate setting to go into too much detai

Furthermore,  when  I  look  at  the  impressive  programme  of  this  conference seems to me that all the important elements of this topic will be covered by this mor afternoon's panels.

However, looking at a lunch as a social event, one aspect of the Y2K pro comes to my mind that is not covered by today's programme and that might be worth bring your attention - if nothing else, at least as a potential problem in the course of th change that deserves thought. Let me call it the social aspect of the Y2K problem.

New Year's Eve 1999/2000 will be a social event of major proportions, accor to some people even an event of biblical significance. Millions of people will drive e of many organised New Year's parties or to pay a visit to relatives or friends in order the new millennium. Are you aware of the fact that there are about 30 different dataembedded chips in a modern-day automobile?

Getting  to  the  parties  before  midnight  should  not  be  a  big  problem.  How imagine what will happen to the mood of the parties if cars stop working after the m date changes, which would mean the parties would have to continue, but the second an glasses of champagne would only be lukewarm at best because all the refrigerators ar order?

V

However, looking at some  humorous side effects of the problem does not mak any less serious for society in general. Looking at the international banking system as believe that we have already made considerable headway in limiting the possibility t disruptions will have systemic consequences for our markets. However, we must all cont work hard in the time remaining to ensure that the existing threat can be averted to possible extent.

In  that  spirit,  ladies  and  gentlemen,  I  would  like  to  conclude  my  remar commend  the  Joint  Year  2000  Council  for  organising  such  regional  conferences.  They account of the fact that in a globalised economy, a worldwide effort is necessary to s face the challenges of the Year 2000 computer problem.

title: Mr. Hartmann's welcoming remarks at the Year 2000 meeting in Frankfurt  (Central Bank Articles and Speeches, 30 Oct 98)
description: Welcoming remarks by Wendelin Hartmann, a member of the Directorate of the Deutsche Bundesbank and Chairman of the G-10 Committee on Payment and Settlement Systems, at the Year 2000 meeting of the European central banks and financial regulators organised by the Joint Year 2000 Council and the Deutsche Bundesbank in Frankfurt/Main on 30/10/98.
text:
## Mr. Hartmann's welcoming remarks at the Year 2000 meeting in Frankfurt

Welcoming  remarks  by  Wendelin  Hartmann,  a  member  of  the  Directorate  of  the  Deutsch Bundesbank and Chairman of the G-10 Committee on Payment and Settlement Systems (CPSS), at the Year 2000 meeting of the European central banks and financial regulators organis Joint Year 2000 Council and the Deutsche Bundesbank in Frankfurt/Main on 30/10/98.

Ladies and gentlemen, On the occasion of a regional conference of the Joint 2000 Council, I warmly welcome you here to Frankfurt. As chairman of the CPSS and a mem of  the  Joint  Year  2000  Council  it  is  an  honour  and  a  pleasure  for  me  to  act  as  ho distinguished  audience.  Thank  you  all  for  coming  to  Frankfurt  from  Europe,  Israel  a United  States.  I  wish  you  a  pleasant  stay  on  the  Main,  and  I  hope  our  meeting  give opportunity not only to gain new insights but also to produce some useful results that us to meet the enormous challenges that still lie before us.

## Joint Year 2000 Council

In April 1998, the Basle Committee on Banking Supervision, the Committee Payment and Settlement Systems, the International Association of Insurance Supervisors International Organization of Securities Commissions announced the formation of the Joi 2000 Council. The sponsors´ decision was motivated by their recognition of the severi challenges posed by the century-date change and of the potentially grave implication financial markets associated with a lack of readiness.

The Joint Year 2000 Council views its main task as being that of ensuring level of attention to the Year 2000 challenge within the global financial supervisors´ At a number of regional meetings - of which this Frankfurt conference is one - financi regulators and supervisors from both within and outside Europe have an opportunity t strategies and experiences, to discuss possible contingency measures and establish cont national and international private sector initiatives. The first regional event took pl for the Asia-Pacific region in mid-October. The present Frankfurt meeting gathers regul supervisors from all over Europe. Further conferences are to be held in Miami for The A in Riyadh for the Middle East, and in Pretoria for the African continent.

The  programme  of  our  conference  today  includes  three  panel  discussions. first one, on 'the challenges to the private and public sector relating to Y2K problem' Year 2000 issues in a more general manner, whereas the second on 'remediation and tes and  the  third,  on  'contingency  planning'  treat  specific  aspects  related  to  Y2K.  I summary panel we will try to find an answer to the question: 'Where do we go from h (Good question, indeed.)

A press conference will take place after the first panel at 10.30 am. Our J 2000  Council  chairman,  Mr  Roger  W.  Ferguson  Jr,  Member  of  the  Board  of  Directors, Washington, and I are going to present the Year 2000 problem and its implications for t financial markets via all media to a - hopefully - broad public.

Around 12:30 you will be invited to lunch here at the hotel. Mr Edgar Me Member of the Board of the Deutsche Bundesbank and chairman of the Banking Supervisi Committee of the European Central Bank, is going to give a luncheon address.

Scope and impact of the Year 2000 problem

Although generally well known, it has to be repeated: the cause of the Yea computer  problem  is  ridiculously  simple.  In  the  days  when  computer  memory  was  sca programmers got into the frugal habit of using only two digits to write a date, so th represented as 98. But, as 99 is a higher number than 00, millions of computers simpl place the year 2000. Instead, they may read the first year of the new millennium as th of the century, or as a date that does not exist. Even if they pass that test, they s notice that 2000, unlike most centennial years, is a leap year. Thus, at the century-d or even before - a large number of computer systems, software programs and embedded devices currently used will produce errors or will malfunction - unless the date or pro is  modified.  With  regard  to  embedded  processors,  any  operation  that  functions  usin sensitive technology may be affected, be it medical pacemakers, heating systems, elec transportation.

For financial market participants, the Year 2000 problem is especially acute financial institutions rely heavily on automation to manage information, it will be even impossible to conduct business if automated applications fail to work properly. number and complexity of the date-dependent computerprograms in use, the remediation e will often have to be colossal.

The interdependence of the world's markets and economies makes the Year 200 risk a true global problem and perhaps the biggest challenge ever faced by the world's industry. Difficulties are bound to arise in every region across the globe, and could h (if temporary) economic effects. Unless resolute steps are taken to resolve the Year 2 in all parts of the world, serious consequences are inevitable.

## The Bundesbank's preparation for Y2K

Although  you  may  get  a  different  impression  from  recent  media  reports, Germany  preparation  for  the  century-datechange  is  in  full  swing  and  not  at  all  be progress  in  other  Western  European  countries.  Let  me  describe  briefly  the  activiti financial sector, seen from a central banker's perspective.

The  Bundesbank  -  like  other  EU  central  banks  -  is  confronted  with  the problem in many respects. Internal preparatory work for the Year 2000 change started time. The Bank's management set July 1, 1999 as the deadline for making all affected and  technical  devices  year-2000-proof.  By  that  date,  all  computer-infrastructure (systems and networks) and data-processing application procedures will be available i year 2000-proof versions. An earlier date is not possible, because conversion work f Three of European monetary union is to be completed as a priority. In this context, by lot  of  preparatory  work,  mainly  in  applications  for  accounting  and  payment  system automatically be included with respect to Y2K.

With regard to the context of national payment and settlement systems, how the Bundesbank acts as a key service provider but also as a central co-ordinator fo payments.  The  Bank's  clearing  facilities  offer  all  credit  institutions  involved  in competitively neutral payment service for settling large-value and retail payments. Nat have a strong interest in the smooth functioning of our IT- infrastructure. So I am h you that the Bundesbank has created a test environment for its public and private clie already  in  use.    In  the  area  of  large-value  payments  as  in  the  other  procedures  of

access,  the  Bundesbank  is  offering  interface  tests  for  verifying  year-2000-compati interbank  settlements.  The  electronic  access  test-centers  are  also  available  for Customers  and  software  manufacturers  can  make  direct  arrangements  with  the  relevant center  for  the  tests  to  be  conducted.  In  the  field  of  retail  payments,  the  Bundesb primary  'interface',  provides  its  customers  with  the  year-2000-compatible  process payment data. It will also ensure that its data-processing procedures are robust enou individual customer systems fail to operate in a year-2000-compatible manner.

As you all know, the Bundesbank is responsible for monetary policy in Germ till the end of this year, but will also continue to form part of the banking supervi after the start of Stage Three of European monetary union. In his luncheon address, my Mr Edgar Meister, who is in charge of the Bundesbank´s Banking Supervision Department, chairman of the ECB-Committee on this subject, is going to outline the Bank's actions field in detail.

## Co-ordination with other institutions' activities

The Bundesbank is not only a part of the financial sector, but also a fis for the government. At the administrative level, the Bank isworking closely with othe institutions  to  ensure  the  year-2000-compatibility  of  public  authorities.  The  activ public financial sector are managed by the Ministry of Finance. In June 1998, a 'Ye Forum' was called into being by the German banking and insurance supervisory authoriti Bundesbank and private banking associations as a platform for regulators and official a credit institutions to exchange their views and experiences.

The government activities relating to the Y2K challenge as a whole are bei ordinated  by  the  Ministry  of  Economics.  In  this  position,  the  ministry  is  also  over preparatory activities of the industrial sector in Germany. Special attention is being readiness  of  core  infrastructure  providers  because  of  their  major  significance  for activity in general. In particular, given the financial sector's heavy depen telecommunications,  water,  energy  and  transportation,  any  failure  to  meet  the  Yea challenge  in  any  of  these  sectors  could  lead  to  serious  disruptions  at  the  nat international levels. In addition to that, it would probably adversely affect all cont of the entire economy. As you know, our latest Joint Year 2000 Council Bulletin also fo this matter, and I hope that we will have an opportunity to attract public attention i at the forthcoming press conference.

## Preparations at the European level

At the European level, the Bundesbank, being a member of the ESCB, is tak part in the activities of the ECB to ensure the Year-2000-compliance of ESCB-wide syste applications.  The  necessity  for  the  ECB  and  the  ESCB  to  give  EMU  top  priority  pos additional challenge to their activities in connection with Y2K. However, all the new and  accounting  systems  which  will  be  implemented  next  year  will  be  Y2K-proof,  so  t should be possible to cope with the remaining challenges during 1999.

In operational terms, the newly developed large-value-payment system TARGET is  going  to  function  by  joining  together  the  15  EU  central  banks´  existing  real-t settlement (RTGS) systems, using what is known as the Interlinking System. S.W.I.F.T. is being used as the carrier for the 'Interlinking System' , S.W.I.F.T. is therefore going to

greater  technical  responsibility.  That  will  mainly  include  ensuring  steady  and  tr operation  -  in  particular,  we  are  relying  on  S.W.I.F.T.  having  a  firm  grip  on  the challenge. This will be ensured by a joint task force of several central banks under t of the National Bank of Belgium. As S.W.I.F.T. is the main service-provider world-wide financial industry, a smooth transition to the next millennium is of paramount importa all.

Since  our  schedule  today  only  allows  me  the  time  to  make  a  few  welcomi remarks,  I  don't  want  to  make  a  short  story  long.  I  hope  that  we  will  all  work  su together at this conference, and thereby contribute to minimising the Year 2000 risk.

title: Mr. Kelley gives an economic assessment of the countdown to Y2K  (Central Bank Articles and Speeches, 29 Oct 98)
description: Remarks by Mr. Edward W. Kelley, Jr., a member of the Board of Governors of the US Federal Reserve System, at the Annual Economic Symposium at Houston Baptist University on 29/10/98.
text:
Mr. Kelley gives an economic assessment of the countdown to Y2K Remarks by Mr. Edward W. Kelley, Jr., a member of the Board of Governors of the US Federal Re System, at the Annual Economic Symposium at Houston Baptist University on 29/10/98.

I am pleased to be back with you today to participate in this annual ec symposium hosted by the Houston Baptist University and the Federal Reserve Bank of Da These  are  challenging  times  for  economic  policymakers,  and  there  are  many  issues  cu facing our nation's central bank. One of them is the Year 2000 computer problem, and th subject  for  today.  Much  has  been  written  on  this  topic,  and  I  am  sure  that  everyon familiar  with  the  basic  issue  -  specifically,  that  information  generated  by  compute inaccurate, or that computers and other electronic systems may malfunction because they correctly process Year 2000 dates. I will dwell no further on the nature of the problem rather attempt to focus on the likely economic impact of this problem. The economic st very  large,  and  the  spectrum  of  possible  outcomes  very  broad,  ranging  from  minim extremely serious. For the truth of the matter is that this episode is unique: We reall previous experience with a challenge of this sort to give us reliable guideposts.

Although the lack of a precedent may be unnerving, that certainly does not from the obligation to attempt to analyze how the millennium bug is affecting and will economy.  This  economic  puzzle  has  many  complex  pieces  -  some  of  them  quite  inscruta before the event - and my task this morning is to assemble for you the tidbits of infor we do have into a coherent picture of where the Y2K problem appears likely to take us. turn first to the reasons why the Year 2000 problem is so difficult to manage. Then I s the actions that are being taken by government and businesses to deal with the millen and the effects these measures are having on economic activity at the present time. Fin turn - not without some trepidation, I might add - to the spectrum of plausible outcom Year 2000, as I see it. As you shall shortly hear, I believe the Y2K pessimists hav recognized the attention that is being given to this problem and the significant progr already been made. Given what we know today, I am cautiously optimistic that the mill bug will not cause major economic disruptions when it bites.

## The Difficulty of Managing the Y2K Problem

Why  has  it  been  so  difficult  for  people  to  come  to  terms  with  the  Year problem? At the most basic level of any organization - be it public or private, large o Y2K problem was all too easy to ignore. It is a hidden threat, cloaked in the arcane l computer  programs  and  in  embedded  microchips.  As  such,  it  was  difficult  at  first  fo management in the corporate world and the public sector to recognize the serious natu problem. This was compounded by the fact that the costs and benefits of the situatio individual operation are not easily quantified nor are they attractive. But after an in denial, the majority of US business leaders now have recognized the problem and are action to correct it. Nonetheless, given the pervasiveness of the problems involved, I even the most thoroughly prepared organizations are worried that something important m missed. Indeed, many organizations are developing elaborate workarounds and other conti plans as insurance against Y2K disruptions. Thus, uncertainty about the ultimate effect Y2K remediation programs already is affecting corporate investment and production pla obviously will be with us until at least January 2000.

The second feature of the millennium bug that makes it so difficult to ana the interrelated character of many computer systems. An individual company may be sat

that it has done all it can to fix its own systems, but it still may feel very vulnerab taken by its suppliers and customers. In an environment where just-in-time inventory and electronic data interchanges (EDI) have linked economic activities very closely tog firm's failure has the potential to ripple through significant segments of the chain o services, and distribution. Thus, greater coordination of Y2K remediation activities w benefits for everyone.

But  it  is  clearly  impossible  to  coordinate  the  Y2K  activities  of  mill individual  establishments.  To  help  fill  this  void,  numerous  organizations  have  eme clearinghouses of information, and I have high hopes for efforts such as 'National Y2K Week',  which  was  just  sponsored  by  the  Small  Business  Administration  (for  the  Presi Council  on  the  Year  2000),  together  with  a  number  of  private  groups.  Other  institut functioning  as  vehicles  for  system  testing.  Witness  this  past  summer's  inception  of Reserve payment system testing with its depository institution customers, and similar the Securities Industry Association. Bank supervisors, including the Federal Reserve, a their banks accountable for the effectiveness of their Y2K efforts, and I can assure yo will be consequences for banks that do not fulfill their obligations. But many organi on their own to test their critical systems with their key suppliers and customers.

Because this situation is both complex and fragmented, it is a very difficu quantify the aggregate costs of Y2K remediation. Similarly and perhaps more important also  have  no  national  scorecard  on  how  effective  our  economy  is  being  in  our  remed efforts.  Under  these  circumstances,  it  is  not  hard  to  understand  why  the  millenniu viewed as such an unpredictable phenomenon, and why it has attracted so much gloom and commentary.

## What is Being Done?

So, what is being done? The short answer is a lot is being done. Let me with you our understanding of the status of efforts by the private sector, government e the  world  community  to  deal  with  the  Year  2000  problem.  As  far  as  the  private  se concerned,  efforts  to  deal  with  the  millennium  bug  have  been  intensifying.  In  my  te before  Congress  in  April,  I  suggested  that  the  private  sector  might  spend  approxima billion over the next two years to tackle the Y2K problem. This figure was based on a r the available corporate filings with the SEC as well as our own guestimates for firms are private, did not discuss Y2K expenditures in their 10-K reports, or stated that programs were not having a 'material' influence on their bottom line. We have updat research using the latest quarterly reports, and we were pleased to find a larger pe firms discussing the costs of their Year 2000 strategies, and I am confident these fund used effectively. While our estimate of the '$50 billion bug' seems still to be reason expect to see this figure move upward over time.

I also perceive that the tools available to companies to address Y2K issu increased substantially. Over the past six months, most major computer hardware and s companies have released documentation of the Y2K readiness of their products on thei sites. Similarly, most of the major computer publications now have elaborate 'how to' g their  web  pages  that  will  aid  consumers  and  small  businesses  in  their  efforts  to  m systems Year 2000 compliant. Commercial software producers also have been busy, and software  products  are  becoming  available  to  aid  programmers  in  repairing  code.  I  ho believe people are availing themselves of these new resources. To paraphrase an old ad have brought the Y2K horse to water, and he appears to be drinking!'

As far as financial institutions are concerned, I am encouraged by the progr has been made over the past year, and there is every reason to be confident that our system  will  be  ready.  Based  on  a  review  of  all  depository  institutions  completed  b banking  regulatory  agencies,  the  vast  majority  are  making  satisfactory  progress  in  t 2000 planning and readiness efforts. About four percent were rated 'needs improvement fewer than one percent were rated 'unsatisfactory'. In these cases, the agencies hav intensive supervisory follow up, including restrictions on expansionary activities by deficient organizations. While we can be confident institutions are addressing the pro important to recognize that regulators cannot be responsible for ensuring or guarant Year 2000 readiness and viability of the banking organizations that we supervise. Ra boards  of  directors  and  senior  management  of  banks  and  other  financial  institutions responsible  for  ensuring  the  institutions  they  manage  are  able  to  provide  high  qu continuous service in January 2000.

The Federal Reserve System has itself made significant progress on Y2K iss meeting all of the goals that we have set for ourselves. In addition to completing an i of the Y2K readiness of all banks subject to our supervisory authority, we have renov own  mission-critical  applications,  nearly  completed  work  on  all  others,  and  are completion of our internal testing. As mentioned, we have opened our mission-critical s customers  for  testing  with  us  and  have  progressed  significantly  in  our  contingency efforts. This has required much hard work on the part of many people, but it is pay visible ways.

As in the private sector, activity to fix computer systems maintained by the government is intensifying. Progress has been made in many areas, but the President's on  the  Year  2000  agrees  that  much  work  still  needs  to  be  done.  Reviews  of  federa programs have highlighted needed areas of improvement, and the Congress has budgeted a $5½ billion for Y2K fixes. Legislation also has been enacted that would facilitate the Y2K information among businesses and clarify the legal liability of reporting Y2K re information. All of these are positive developments.

With the notable exception of the recent dress rehearsal in Lubbock, I must that  far  less  is  known  about  the  effectiveness  of  the  Y2K  preparations  by  state governments. Attention often is focused on high-profile systems such as the nation's control  computers  or  the  electric  power  grid,  but  there  are  many  smaller,  yet  quit electronic  systems  maintained  by  states  and  municipalities  that  also  are  very  vulne example, innumerable vitally important computer-controlled utility systems are operated government units. And, as any Washington commuter will tell you, one or two malfuncti traffic signals can cause serious congestion, confusion, and delay, and the complete b of traffic management systems likely would cause near total gridlock. To try to get a Y2K remediation activity at the state level, we surveyed the web pages of all fifty st District of Columbia and Puerto Rico. As best we can tell, the states that reported Y2K are budgeting $1 to $2 billion for this purpose. However, five states had no referen preparedness and 23 states did not cite the cost estimates for their programs. Thus, b and other anecdotal evidence I have seen, I suspect that much work still needs to be d area as well.

On the international level, there is both good news and bad. The governmen various  industrialized  nations  have  stepped  up  their  own  internal  Y2K  awarenes

remediation  programs  over  the  past  six  months,  and  international  cooperation  is  int through efforts such as the Joint Year 2000 Council, chaired by my colleague Federal Governor Roger Ferguson. Most large multinational corporations report they are well a their preparations worldwide. However, the conversion to the euro and world financial obviously are deflecting all too much attention away from Year 2000 issues, and I wo time will simply run out for some countries - particularly in the developing world. A risks exit for some level of disruption to international trade and capital flows.

## How are Year 2000 Preparations Affecting the Economy?

Corporate efforts to deal with the Y2K problem are affecting economic activ a  variety  of  ways.  On  the  positive  side,  an  important  element  in  some  Y2K  programs accelerated replacement of aging computer systems with modern, state-of-the-art hardwa software. Such capital expenditures should raise the level of productivity in those and, in general, the need to address the Y2K problem has increased the awareness on th senior  executives  of  the  complexity  and  importance  of  managing  corporate  inform technology resources. The increased replacement demand also has contributed to the spec recent growth in this country's computer hardware and software industries. But, ultima are largely shifting the timing of these investment expenditures: Today's added growth 'borrowed' from spending at some time in the future. And, while accelerating some sy investments, many institutions will 'freeze' their systems in the middle of 1999 forgoing  the  installation  of  major  new  hardware  and  software  systems  as  we  approac millennium. This certainly will also influence spending on technology - shifting some o 1999 and into 2000.

While a shift in the timing of investment spending may help to solve the 2000 problem for some firms, it certainly will not be sufficient. Most organizations d the option of simply scrapping their existing computer systems and replacing them wit new  'turn-key'  hardware  and  software.  To  one  degree  or  another,  we  all  rely  on  el proprietary  software  systems  that  have  been  developed  over  many  years,  and  these  pro must  be  debugged  by  a  skilled  programmer.  This  obviously  is  a  very  labor-intensiv time-consuming process, and organizations have had to boost their IT staffs to carry work. The good news is that many got an early start on this problem and are now well a their repair and testing programs. The bad news is that there is no corresponding incr firm's  marketable  output,  and  this  lowers  the  overall  level  of  productivity  in  the boosts its costs, and reduces its profitability.

One area in which uncertainty about Y2K readiness is likely to have notic effects on economic activity in 1999 is in the management of inventories. As the mil approaches, I expect businesses will want to hold larger inventories of goods as insura Y2K-related  supply  disruptions.  Such  a  shift  from  'just-in-time'  inventory  managemen 'just-in-case'  posture  is  likely  to  prompt  an  increase  in  orders  and  production  dur These stocks subsequently would be run off in the first half of 2000. We at the Fed, fo will do precisely that in our management of the production of new currency.

While  Year  2000  preparation  efforts  may  give  a  temporary  boost  to  econom activity in some sectors, the net effect on the aggregate economy probably is negative. the  obviously  very  valuable  ability  to  maintain  its  operations  across  the  millenn quantifiable benefits accrue to the firm - and overall productivity gains are reduced hours devoted to reprogramming and testing. Conservative estimates suggest that the net

Y2K remediation efforts might shave a tenth or two a year off the growth of our nation' labor productivity, and a more substantial effect is possible if some of the larger Y2K costs turn out to be accurate. The effects on real gross domestic product are li somewhat smaller than this but could still total a tenth of a percentage point or so a next two years.

## What is the Spectrum of Plausible Outcomes for Economic Activity in 2000?

As we have discussed, a great deal of work either is planned or is under deal  with  the  Year  2000  problem.  But  what  if  something  slips  through  the  cracks, experience the failure of 'mission critical' systems? How will a computer failure in o the economy affect the ability of others to continue to operate smoothly? How severe the consequences of Y2K problems emanating from abroad? The number of possible scenario this type is endless, and today no one can say with confidence how severe any Y2K disr could be or how a failure in one sector would influence activity in others. That said, turn to a discussion of the spectrum of plausible outcomes for economic activity in 2000.

What will happen as the millennium rolls over? A few economists already suggesting that Y2K-related disruptions will induce a deep recession in 2000. That prob stretch,  but  I  do  not  think  we  will  escape  unaffected.  I  anticipate  that  there  wil production problems and disruptions to commerce, and perhaps some public services, th reduce the rate of GDP growth early in 2000. Certainly a mild inventory cycle seems ve to  develop.  But,  just  like  the  shocks  to  our  nation's  physical  infrastructure periodically,  I  would  expect  the  Y2K  shock  to  our  information  and  electronic infrastructure is most likely to be short-lived and fully reversed.

We  have  many  examples  of  how  economic  activity  has  been  affected  by disruptions to the physical infrastructure of this country. Although the Y2K problem unique, some of these disruptions to our physical infrastructure may be useful in orga thinking about the consequences of short-lived interruptions in our information infrast early 1996, a major winter storm paralyzed large portions of the country. Commerce grou halt for up to a week in some areas but activity bounced back rapidly once the roads we again. Although individual firms and households were adversely affected by these disrup the aggregate, the economy quickly recovered most of the output lost due to the storm instance,  the  shock  to  our  physical  infrastructure  was  transitory  in  nature,  and,  c recovery  process  was  under  way  before  any  adverse  'feedback'  effects  were  produced. year's strike by workers at the United Parcel Service is a second example. UPS is a maj in the package delivery industry in this country, and the strike disrupted the shippin many businesses. Some sales were lost, but in most instances alternative shipping serv found  for  high-priority  packages.  Some  businesses  were  hurt  by  the  strike,  but  its economic activity was small in the aggregate.

Obviously an important element in any forecast for the Year 2000 is the deg which the failure of the computer system at one institution causes ripple effects on th others. If the disruptions that occur are not isolated events, as I have assumed, but key sectors of the economy by interacting with each other, then an outright decline in in the first quarter of 2000 could be a plausible outcome.

The  more  dire  of  the  Y2K  scenarios  would  involve,  among  other  things, perpetuation  and  intensification  of  these  feedback  effects.  In  such  an  event,  p disruptions could turn out to be a national or international phenomenon and could spr one industry to another. Under these circumstances, the decline in economic activity wo to be longer lasting, and a recession - typically defined as a decline in real gross dom in  two  consecutive  quarters  -  could  ensue.  But  let  me  quickly  stress  that  I  do  not recession scenario has a very high probability. It is possible, but a lot of things hav for it to occur, and much is being done to prevent its occurrence.

## What can Monetary Policy Do About the Millenium Bug?

What can monetary policy do to offset any Y2K disruptions? The truthful ans is 'not much'. Just as we were not able to plow the streets in 1996 or deliver package the central bank will be unable to reprogram the nation's computers for the year 2000. problem is primarily an issue affecting the aggregate 'supply' side of the economy, wh Federal Reserve's monetary policy works mainly on aggregate 'demand'. We all understand creating more money and lowering the level of short-term interest rates gives a boost t sensitive  sectors  (such  as  homebuilding),  but  these  tools  are  unlikely  to  be  very  e generating  more  Y2K  remediation  efforts  or  accelerating  the  recovery  process  if  s experiences some type of Year 2000 disruption. We will, of course, be ready if people hold more cash on New Year's Eve 1999, and we will be prepared to lend whatever sums ma needed to financial institutions through the discount window under appropriate circumst to provide needed reserves to the banking system. And, if a serious Y2K disruption sho significant feedback effects on aggregate demand - as I outlined in the recession scen obviously would be a role for the Federal Reserve to play in countering the downturn. is nothing monetary policy can do to offset the direct effects of a Y2K disruption.

## Conclusion

In summary, as I stated at the outset of my remarks, I am cautiously optimis the  United  States  will  weather  the  Year  2000  storm  without  major  disruptions  to  ec activity. Some of the more frightening scenarios are not without a certain plausibil challenge  were  being  ignored.  But  it  is  not  being  ignored  -  as  this  symposium  toda illustrates. An enormous amount of work is being done in anticipation of the rollov millennium.  As  the  world's  largest  economy,  the  heaviest  burden  of  preparation  falls United  States.  But  it  is  truly  a  worldwide  issue,  and  to  the  extent  some  are  not prepared  and  experience  breakdowns  of  unforeseeable  dimension,  we  shall  all  be  af accordingly. We at the Federal Reserve intend to do our utmost, and we hope and trus will do likewise.

title: Mr. Stals discusses the importance of credit extension for macroeconomic financial stability  (Central Bank Articles and Speeches, 29 Oct 98)
description: Address by the Governor of the South African Reserve Bank, Dr. Chris Stals, at a Breakfast Meeting of the Institute of Credit Management in Johannesburg on 29/10/98.
text:
Mr.  Stals  discusses  the  importance  of  credit  extension  for  macroeconomic financial stability Address by the Governor of the South African Reserve Bank, Dr. Ch Stals, at a Breakfast Meeting of the Institute of Credit Management in Johannesburg on 2

## 1. A 'credit' economy

Modern economies are often described as 'credit-based' economies. This is a reflection  of  the  functioning  of  modern,  sophisticated  economies  in  which  money  pla important part as a means of exchange, as an instrument of payments and as a store of va

The  availability  and  the  use  of  credit  facilitates  the  exchange  of  go services,  the  production  processes  and  the  growing  importance  in  all  modern  econom financial services. One can hardly visualize a modern economy that works without credit.

The normal characteristic of credit is that one participant in the economy, individual, a corporate body or a governmental institution, denies himself the immedia purchasing power already in his possession, and makes this purchasing power on a tem basis available to another participant in the economy who has an immediate need for th the purchasing power. This kind of transfer of purchasing power from savers (the len users (borrowers) will never create macroeconomic distortions in the economy. On the c as already mentioned, it supports maximum economic growth and development in the countr

This basic form of credit extension encouraged the development over many ye of financial savings institutions, financial intermediaries, institutional investors, etc. that serve as useful conduits for transferring purchasing power from savers to u for  consumption  or  for  real  or  financial  investment  purposes.  The  financial  authori countries have a responsibility to oversee these financial institutions, mainly with th protecting the general public, be they lenders or borrowers, against exploitation that an  unreasonably  low  remuneration  for  savers,  exorbitantly  high  costs  for  borrowers financial losses for both.

Together  with  the  development  of  these  specialised  financial  intermedi financial markets emerged where the transfer of savings from lenders to borrowers can t in a more competitive environment with greater transparency and more general partici These  markets,  such  as  the  stock  exchanges,  bond  markets,  markets  for  derivative short-term  money  markets  play  a  very  important  part  in  the  optimum  allocation  of resources in modern economies. Financial authorities also have a vested interest in o these financial markets to ensure orderly conditions, the effective and efficient tran from borrowers to lenders and the maintenance of orderly and stable conditions in the ma

A further development in this process of the transfer of purchasing power savers  to  users  of  funds,  took  place  with  the  development  of  cross-border  or  inte transfers of purchasing power. Savers in the more mature economies of the world whe demand for purchasing power is relatively low, found it increasingly attractive to mak the  less-developed  economies  where  they  could  earn  much  higher  interest  rates. cross-border movement of funds introduced a new dimension in the credit extension proc the form of exchange rates for foreign currency transfers. The financial authorities o countries now obtained more than just an overseeing function in the credit extension Rightly or wrongly, governments were in the past seen to be responsible for the fixi

exchange rate, and for ensuring that convertibility of national currencies into othe will at all times be possible.

There is one further form of credit extension that has become of vital imp for  macroeconomic  financial  management,  and  that  is  the  extension  of  bank  credi simultaneously also creates money. Banks are not normal financial intermediaries tha funds from savers and then make loans out of these funds to borrowers. Banks can create to make loans, and in the process can increase the total purchasing power in the econom

In summary, therefore, the  presence  of  credit  facilities,  financed  out  o savings, is an essential and necessary element of all modern economies. The financial a should have no more than an overseeing function in the management, organisation and i administration of the whole process of credit extension. As far as both financial int and  financial  markets  are  concerned,  the  authorities  should  restrict  their  interven creation of a protective and transparent legal and accounting framework within which in and markets can function effectively.

However,  the  financial  authorities  have  more  than  just  an  overseeing  fun when  it  comes  to  international  credit  extension  activities,  and  to  the  creation  of banking institutions.

## 2. Bank credit extension

Excessive bank credit extension lay behind many of the global financial pro of recent times. In a number of the East Asian countries, controls on banking institu rather  lax  and  enabled  them  to  increase  their  total  credit  to  governments  and  priv borrowers by substantial amounts over a protracted period of time. In the process, int were  kept  artificially  low  and  banks  on  an  increasing  scale  relied  on  foreign  borr supplement their liquidity base for the continuing expansion of total credit.

In the end, when foreign investors became reluctant to continue to provi liquidity base for the credit extension by the banks, the financial systems crumbled. I the final collapse was forced by:

- A  withdrawal  of  foreign  deposits  from  banks  and  of  foreign  portfo investments from the capital markets of the affected countries.
- Foreign credit previously extended to the East Asian countries was ther withdrawn.
- A reduction in the amount of liquidity available within banking institut they lost foreign deposits and had to fund the withdrawal of other inves from the capital markets.
- Forced  reductions  in  the  amount  of  credit  banking  institutions  could available to their clients, many of whom were overborrowed and could meet the demand for the repayment of loans.
- An unavoidable depreciation of exchange rates and sharp rises in interes which forced losses on borrowers of foreign and domestic fund Overborrowed  institutions  were  forced  into  liquidation,  and  in  the  pr transferred their losses to their lenders.

The consequences of this credit crunch are now well-known. In many of the Asian  countries,  negative  real  economic  growth  rates  are  now  experienced  as  p consolidations and reforms of banking and financial structures are taking place.

The East Asian financial crisis, which quickly spread to other emerging ma to the smaller more stable developed economies of the world and recently also to major centres such as New York provided a stark reminder of how important sound credit manage is  for  the  protection  of  macroeconomic  financial  stability  in  individual  countries, world at large.

No  country  can  procure  permanent  and  sustainable  economic  growth  at  a  hi level if this growth is dependent on the creation of an increasing amount of credit, banking  institutions.  Not  only  lenders  (banking  institutions)  and  borrowers  (priva institutions and individuals) can be destroyed in the process, but also total financia even total economies can break down under the burden of too much credit.

Central banks have the unenviable task of judging at all times what amou additional  bank  credit  will  in  prevailing  circumstances  be  reconcilable  with  the  ob maintaining  overall  financial  stability.  Economies  normally  provide  early  warning  si excessive credit extension, such as rising inflation or unaffordable increases in imp withdrawal of foreign funds from the country. It is important not to ignore such signal

## 3. Other lessons from the global financial crisis

The  recent  turmoil  in  world  financial  markets  provided  important  lessons only for central bankers, but also for credit managers in private sector financial ins following  three  lessons  must  have  come  to  the  notice  of  many  a  private  sector  f institution:

- (i)  Risk  management  models  based  on  past  experience  or  on  rigid  comput programmes  do  not  necessarily  provide  adequate  protection  against  poten losses  in  the  new  environment  of  financial  globalisation.  Experience discretion cannot be replaced by models and machines.
- (ii) The value of collateral against credit extension can disappear overni the Russian example).
- (iii)  Excessive  leveraging  must  be  avoided  at  all  times,  and  particularl present  environment  of  volatile  global  changes  (vide  the  example  of Long-Term Capital Management Fund).

Governments,  central  banks,  market  managers,  private  sector  institutions private individuals all have learned once again from this experience that the excess credit sooner or later leads to disaster. At this juncture, the world economy is paying in the form of depressed growth for being reminded of these basic truths.

## 4. Credit extension and the South African economy

Although the South African economy was also severely affected by the curr world financial crisis, a sound banking system, well-managed financial institutions and financial  markets  protected  the  country  against  the  almost  total  collapse  of  the  ec happened in a few other countries.

The Reserve Bank has some concern, nevertheless, for the increasing use of credit to maintain expenditure levels. The recent financial crisis forced exorbitantly rates on the South African economy and borrowers of funds could not avoid sharp rises cost of servicing existing debts. The world financial crisis therefore hopefully also grim warning to all South African borrowers and lenders that excessive debt positions avoided.  Neither  the  Reserve  Bank  nor  the  Government  can  guarantee  low  interest  ra overall  financial  protection  in  the  new  environment  of  a  worldwide  integration  of markets.

It will also be foolish for South Africa now to try to revive the domestic by creating an excessive amount of additional credit extended by banking institutions i global financial environment. Such a policy could easily lead South Africa also on th overall economic disaster, as more than one country in the rest of the world experience past year.

## 5. Conclusion

I believe that members of this Institute of Credit Management are aware potent  danger  of  excessive  debt  positions,  be  it  for  countries,  governments  or  priv borrowers. The discipline of controlling this dangerous element of modern, sophisticate economies,  is  not  a  responsibility  only  of  the  central  bank.  It  is  not  only  a macroeconomic  policy,  but  also  one  for  institutions  operating  at  the  micro-level.  W make a contribution towards protecting our country from falling in the debt trap of borrowing by applying sound principles in the management of our debt positions.

title: Mr. Ferguson speaks on the future of the financial services sector  (Central Bank Articles and Speeches, 27 Oct 98)
description: Remarks by Mr. Roger W. Ferguson, Jr., a member of the Board of Governors of the US Federal Reserve System, at the College of Management of the University of Massachusetts in Boston, Massachusetts on 27/10/98.
text:
Mr. Ferguson speaks on the future of the financial services sector Remarks by Mr. Roger W. Ferguson, Jr., a member of the Board of Governors of the US Federal Re System,  at  the  College  of  Management  of  the  University  of  Massachusetts  in  Bos Massachusetts on 27/10/98.

## Some Observations on the Future of the Financial Services Sector and Related Public Policy Issues

Let  me  first  thank  you  for  your  invitation  to  speak  today  at  this  very conference.  The  future  of  the  financial  services  sector  holds  great  interest  fo participants  as  well  as  bank  regulators,  given  the  remarkable  changes  affecting  the Developments in this sector will affect all of us.

We  are  all  acutely  aware  of  the  trend  toward  the  blurring  of  lines  th separated the various parts of the financial sector, particularly commercial banking, banking, and insurance. Most recently, we are faced with the prospect of the formation financial conglomerates, composed of amalgams of firms that have previously operated the roughly defined boundaries of their respective industries. In addition, we have w substantial  degree  of  consolidation  through  mergers  in  the  commercial  banking  and industries.

I  will  begin  my  remarks  today  by  discussing  historical  experience conglomeration in the US, and the underlying conditions necessary for conglomeration successful business strategy. I will then offer some thoughts regarding what the financ sector may look like in the future. Finally, I will address some of the issues that Reserve as a supervisor and regulator will need to consider.

There are several conclusions that I would like to highlight. The first i movement to financial conglomerate may prove to be transitory. Second, basic financial management skills will likely remain the most important determinant of a company's vi and success. Third, even in a world of financial conglomerates there will be room for and  more  nimble,  participants.  Finally,  the  supervisory  and  regulatory  structure  wil evolve to meet these new challenges, but regulatory authorities should remain vigilan out our duties, particularly in enforcing the antitrust laws.

## II. Will Financial Service Conglomerates be Successful?

## The Historical Context of Conglomeration

The concept of the financial conglomerate is receiving a great deal of att this  time  because  of  the  diminishing  distinctions  across  financial  industries.  How success of such conglomerates is certainly not guaranteed, based on historical experien illustration, one need only look back to the conglomerate merger movement in the in sector during the 1960s. Large conglomerate firms such as LTV, Gulf and Western, Textro Litton Industries became conglomerates through numerous mergers, heralded with great f from  the  business  press.  By  the  1970s,  such  proclamations  sounded  hollow,  as conglomerate firms' equities were pummeled as their corporate structure proved unsucc This period was followed by a decade of spin-offs as the conglomerates sought to str their operations and return to their original areas of expertise - and this reversal o greeted with considerable enthusiasm by the business press.

Much closer to home, we should also recall that the retail financial sect through a phase of conglomeration about 15 years ago, in the movement toward the 'fin supermarket'.  The  acquisitions  of  Coldwell  Banker  and  Dean  Witter  by  Sears,  Shearso American Express, Schwab by Bank of America, and Bache by Prudential come to mind. Desp the enthusiasm for the financial supermarket in the early 1980s, by the end of the d concept  had  stagnated,  and  the  press  instead  reported  the  benefits  of  specializatio provision of niche services.

I  believe  this  past  experience  with  business  conglomerates  in  the  US  s temper  our  views  of  the  inevitability  of  today's  financial  conglomerates.  There  ar challenges to managing much larger, more diversified firms, as well as benefits. This strategy is surely not for all financial services firms.

## Business Conditions Necessary for Financial Conglomerates to Succeed

The difficulties associated with operating a financial conglomerate are su by the business conditions that are necessary for such a conglomerate to succeed. We ha of course, of the potential economies of scale and scope in managing information that m large firms to reduce the unit costs of doing business. We are also aware of the potent marketing, where economies of scope on the supply side allow firms to sell multiple pr their customers, and on the demand side allow consumers to conveniently purchase bund services.  Since  a  number  of  conglomerates  of  the  past  have  been  unable  to  improve separate delivery of services - including financial services - it is unclear whether te other changes have altered the nature of financial products or managerial capabilities to result in significantly improved exploitation of scope economies.

The potential benefits of reducing risk through sectoral and geogr diversification are another motivation for conglomeration. I have little doubt that in the  potential  for  diversification  gains  exists.  However,  we  have  heard  very  little expertise needed to merge the risk management practices of previously separate financi While merging risk management practices may be straightforward for firms consolidating an industry, such a readjustment is likely far more complex for firms originating i industries.

Furthermore,  the  challenges  of  managing  a  merger  of  diverse  firms  and operation of the resulting conglomerate are substantial. The operation of a conglomerate requires the ability to integrate the financial activities, research and investments, pricing decisions, compensation practices, cost containment activities, a of  an  extremely  large  and  diverse  organization.  Before  any  steps  toward  conglomerat taken, each potential participant in such a merger must judge whether this extraordin skills is to be found in any managerial team.

However,  having  raised  the  cautionary  flags  about  the  prospects  for  fin conglomerates, I should add that various considerations suggest that the financial con format  in  the  future  may  be  successful  for  at  least  some  firms.  From  the  mana perspective,  technological  developments  should  help  provide  more  detailed  informati monitoring the various activities of the firm and allow the application of more sophis management models. Past experience with conglomeration may also provide new insights managing  product  integration  more  effectively.  On  the  demand  side,  retail  customer

become  more  receptive  to  one-stop  shopping  as  the  range  of  services  increases  and opportunities for accessing these services become available.

## III. How Might the Financial Services Sector Evolve?

The  extraordinary  changes  occurring  in  the  financial  sector  make  projec about how the sector will evolve quite speculative. Nevertheless, it is useful to consi future might look as both industry participants and regulators plan to meet that futu like  to  offer  some  prognostications  based  both  on  systematic  projections  using  h experience and on analogies and informal observations of current trends.

## Systematic Projections on Consolidation

The commercial banking industry, which is the largest single component of financial sector, has experienced massive consolidation since 1980. For example, the n banking organizations in the US fell from around 12,300 in 1980 to just under 7,200 by of  1997.  Not  surprisingly,  the  percentage  of  banking  assets  held  by  the  top  10 organizations rose from about 20 percent in 1980 to nearly 35 percent in 1997, while held  by  the  top  25  increased  from  about  33  to  53  percent.  Despite  the  large  amo consolidation and increase in banking concentration at the national level, banking con within local market areas (MSAs and non-MSA counties) has, on average, hardly changed the  past  decade.  For  example,  the  average  Herfindahl-Hirschman  Index  (HHI)  in  MS decreased from 1990 to 1949 between 1985 and 1997, while in non-MSA counties it decre from  4357  to  4114  (thrifts  excluded).  The  stability  of  average  local  market  concent noteworthy  because  research  suggests  that  competition  for  retail  customers  takes substantially at the local market level, and concentration is a determinant of competit

Based on these trends and the fact that tremendous new opportunities for mergers have been created by the removal of restrictions on interstate banking under t Neal  Interstate  Banking  and  Branching  Efficiency  Act  of  1994,  I  would  expect consolidation to occur in banking. Based on historical experience, some Fed economist projected  that  in  a  decade  or  so  about  3,000-to-4,000  banking  organizations  will Importantly, most of these firms would be smaller organizations.

In  addition  to  commercial  banking,  other  financial  service  sectors  hav experienced movements toward consolidation. Insurance companies and securities firms ha experienced merger waves in recent years, though not to the extent of commercial bankin more moderate pace of consolidation in nonbank financial industries is likely due to th of  preexisting  restrictions  on  geographic  expansion.  Like  banking,  insurance  underwr characterized by a broad size distribution of firms, from several large national insur smaller local or technically specialized firms. Investment banking is more heavily con due  to  the  greater  geographic  expanse  of  the  markets  for  their  services,  and  du considerable benefits of portfolio diversification. Extending current patterns into th can only expect a continuation of the trend towards consolidation.

## Informal Projections on Conglomeration

As  I  noted  earlier,  in  addition  to  a  continuing  consolidation  in  banki elsewhere  in  the  financial  sector,  there  is  also  a  tendency  toward  increased  congl Given the prospects for legislation expanding the product lines available to banks, I w surprised at a wave of cross-industry mergers within the financial sector, particularl largest firms, that results in the formation of financial conglomerates.

In order to consider the form of the financial sector in the future, I b very  important  to  distinguish  between  retail  financial  services  (i.e.,  those  for  hou small businesses) and wholesale or large-scale corporate financial services. The custo of these two sectors differ dramatically, as do many of the products used.

Despite  their  differences,  both  the  retail  and  wholesale  sectors  have  mo expand their product offerings. In retail financial services, the desire by banks to product offerings is both a response to new products developed by other industries (for the  emergence  of  annuities  in  the  insurance  industry),  as  well  as  a  response  to  c substitution  of  other  products  (such  as  mutual  funds)  for  traditional  bank  products traditional savings accounts).

At wholesale firms, we have witnessed the push into securities underwritin the establishment of offices throughout the world in an effort to respond to the financ large corporate customers. Because of the very large scale required to serve a wholesa consisting of a relatively small number of sizable customers, relatively few very large likely  remain  active  in  the  wholesale  portion  of  the  financial  sector.  Of  course, wholesale institutions may operate in the retail portion as well, although the latter not necessitate the extraordinary size of these firms. In addition, there are clearly that achieve enviable results by serving just one need, say M&A advice, for large busine

The existence of both retail and wholesale institutions will have a direct on  the  future  of  financial  services.  In  contrast  to  wholesale  institutions,  ret institutions are able to operate profitably on a small scale. Given the continuing stro of many retail customers to deal with local offices, especially for many services of institutions, small retail financial institutions will likely be able to serve the need and small businesses in local markets.

Such  niche  players  would  play  an  important  role  in  a  retail  financial composed of perhaps several thousand relatively small retail financial institutions, smaller number of large financial firms that offer wholesale products, or both whole retail products. The large firms that offer retail services would likely operate offic the country. This scenario would not be unlike that which we observe quite frequentl nonfinancial retail sector. Restaurants, department stores, convenience stores and sup are examples of locally based markets with a strong presence of large national or regi operating alongside a large number of small local sellers.

## IV. What Do Conglomeration and Consolidation Mean for the Federal Reserve?

Now I would like to consider some of the issues that are raised by the evolu the financial services sector for the Federal Reserve. Clearly the Federal Reserve m along with the industry it supervises and regulates.

## Reducing Moral Hazard through Increased Market Discipline

A  key  concern,  which  is  a  challenge  internationally  as  well  as  in  dom supervision, is the well-known 'moral-hazard' problem. Moral hazard occurs when a firm on  greater  risk  than  is  prudent,  because  it  does  not  bear  the  full  cost  of  adopti position.  Instead,  the  cost  of  this  risk  is  borne  by  the  financial  safety  net,  whi banking system consists of access to federal deposit insurance, the Fed's discount win Federal Reserve payments system guarantees. While this safety net in my judgment will remain firmly in place, incentive-compatible policies should be developed and applied more of the cost of risk-bearing onto the firms themselves. Such policies would seek t and improve the role of 'market discipline' in constraining bank risk taking.

One widely discussed idea for increasing market discipline is to require a issue a minimum amount of subordinated debt to non-related parties. The basic idea is t set of uninsured bank liability holders who will have risk preferences similar to tho supervisors, and who would thus discipline bank risk taking to a similar degree. In changes  in  the  price  of  a  bank's  subordinated  debt  might  prove  to  be  a  useful  sign market's  evaluation  of  a  bank's  financial  condition.  Such  signals  could  perhaps  be supervisors as an aid in identifying problem banks. While a policy of 'mandatory subo debt' is not without its problems and implementation difficulties, it is certainly wort discussion.

A  second  way  that  market  discipline  could  be  encouraged  is  through  finan reporting and transparency guidelines, which provide the market with the information n to make informed transactions. This improved information is essential for market disc function. Greater transparency by itself will not alleviate the moral hazard problem insured deposits, since fully informed investors may be willing to make deposits in a an overly risky portfolio, as long as their deposits are insured. However, transparency the need for some types of direct regulation in uninsured financial activities. If th financial institutions are apparent to the market, the institutions will adjust their optimally to maintain the ability to attract capital. Improved disclosure by domestic international institutions would increase the information that allows investors to as they bear.

## Communicating with Other Regulators

If the financial services sector moves further in the direction of conglo the Federal Reserve will experience an ever greater need for communication with regul different financial industries. Regulators of the banking industry will need to coor agencies  governing  the  securities  and  insurance  industries.  Communication  with  ins regulators will present a particular challenge, since in the US insurance is regulated at  the  state  level.  Furthermore,  international  communication  among  central  banks  an financial regulators is already essential. This need can only become greater as market financial  services  continue  to  extend  across  national  borders.  Indeed,  the  need intervention could be reduced through preventive measures that include ongoing communic and coordinated improvements in supervisory methods. Ensuring Competition

Also important is the role of encouraging competition through implementati the Federal Reserve's bank merger policy. This role is particularly important at a banking and the financial sector in general are experiencing an unprecedented merger mo that is radically restructuring these industries. Before discussing newer analyses that called upon to perform, let me emphasize that I think that we must continue to be e vigilant  to  protect  local  market  competition.  Applicants  should  remember  that  we  m impacts on local market structure considering both HHI and concentration ratios. Tran satisfying one of those measures may not satisfy the other measure. Small increases i share as measured by HHI may mask the high market share of the dominant competitor. In cases, I would expect that mitigating factors, even for small increases in market sha extremely strong to gain approval.

The  task  of  enforcing  bank  merger  policy  will  become  potentially  mo challenging if financial conglomeration occurs, since the analysis of competition rel correct definition of the relevant geographic and product markets. Thus, increasing n financial  conglomerates  that  sell  traditional  retail  banking  services  along  with  in securities will make the analysis of competitive effects of mergers more difficult. In will  remain  important  to  distinguish  between  markets  for  large-scale  wholesale  produ markets for household- and small-business-oriented retail banking products. We will als consider the effects that networks, such as ATM and point-of-sale networks, and other electronic banking have on competition for financial services. Finally, as financial r become  increasingly  complex,  we  must  work  to  reduce  market  inertia  that  could  l competition  by  restricting  customers'  ability  to  choose  freely  among  providers  of services. Domestic competition is particularly important not only because it increases of our fellow citizens, but also because other reforms, such as those based on market probably  work  best  in  a  competitive  market.  Also,  domestic  competition  is  one  of  t powerful forces that gives rise to international competitiveness.

## Reducing Systemic Risk through Improved Supervision

Finally,  the  Federal  Reserve  must  continually  improve  the  bank  supervi process in order to help manage risk that could be introduced into the financial sys changes occurring in the financial sector. The effects of consolidation and conglome systemic risk cannot be ignored. If risk is not managed properly within the consolidate repercussions could extend beyond a single institution and well into the financial sec the moral hazard problem could be largely solved, so that financial firms bear the costs of the risks they adopt, these firms may fail to internalize the costs borne financial system when their portfolio decisions result in bad financial outcomes. The r damage can be held in check only by sound supervisory practices.

I do not have time to do more than quickly mention some of the important ef that the Federal Reserve is pursuing in order to improve bank supervision. Much of ou along with that of other bank supervisors, is focused on improving our ability to mo supervise  the  risk  management  practices  of  banks  and  banking  organizations.  Closely work is aimed at devising capital standards that more accurately reflect the realitie banking world. Through it all, I would emphasize that old-fashioned supervision, the which is the on-site examination, remains central to our supervisory strategy. Improve discipline,  increased  communication  with  other  supervisors,  and  enhanced  stability greater diversification are necessary. But improved supervision is also critical, and there is simply no substitute for a well-trained and highly motivated examiner 'on the g

## V. Conclusion

In  closing,  I  would  like  to  reemphasize  the  importance  of  the  basic  ski remain  centrally  important  in  the  financial  services  sector.  Regardless  of  the  exte nature  of  conglomeration,  technological  development,  and  new  financial  instruments, fundamental business practices will remain essential: credit underwriting and risk ma skills, cost control, and appropriate pricing practices. While technological improveme aid in nearly all these areas, only sound management practices will allow industry part take  advantage  of  any  advances  in  technology.  At  the  same  time,  fundamental  princip supervision  and  regulation  must  be  applied,  including  sound  credit  standards  and examinations,  to  ensure  the  safety  and  soundness  of  the  financial  sector.  Finally, should implement antitrust policy in a manner that will ensure competitive prices and s the financial sector evolves and consolidates. Despite the importance of vigorous super regulation, I and my colleagues on the Board are quite sensitive to the fact that it i to  judge  the  wisdom  of  management  decisions  and  business  strategies  beyond  ensuring public policy standards regarding supervision and regulation are met. I look forward to and participating in this sector's evolution into the next century. I thank you once opportunity to discuss these issues with you today.
