title: Ms. Rivlin discusses the state of the world economy and its implications for the United States  (Central Bank Articles and Speeches, 22 Oct 98)
description: Remarks by Vice-Chair of the US Federal Reserve System, Ms. Alice M. Rivlin, at the State University of New York-Brockport and Buffalo State College in Buffalo, New York on 22/10/98.
text:
Ms. Rivlin discusses the state of the world economy and its implications the United States Remarks by Vice-Chair of the US Federal Reserve System, Ms. Alice M. Rivlin, at the State University of New York-Brockport and Buffalo State in Buffalo, New York on 22/10/98.

I am delighted to be here today and to have this opportunity to talk with y particularly  pleased  to  be  here  with  my  friend  Congressman  John  LaFalce,  who  brings energy and good sense to the Congress, especially to the hard work of the Banking Com which is where I see him most frequently.

I want to talk with you this morning about the turmoil in the world econom what it might mean for us here in the United States. Why should people in upstate Ne care  about  the  economy  of  Thailand  or  Russia  or  Brazil?  What  can  we  do  to  keep  our economy strong?

We are all used to the cliche that the world is getting smaller, that the age has brought us closer and put us in instant touch with remote parts of the globe. that cross-border trade and investment have increased enormously in recent years, brin greater prosperity and greater interdependence.

Still, when bad news from Asian economies began flashing across our screen the summer of 1997, it didn't seem to have much to do with us. Currencies with odd nam the baht and the ringgit were said to be plunging, stocks prices on the Hang Seng or were falling, by the end of the year Korean banks were negotiating with their creditors at home the economy was doing better than it had in a generation. The news from Asia like a small dark cloud appearing on the horizon in the middle of a sunny day at an festivity. It might mean rain, but with any luck it would go away.

We have been enjoying a truly extraordinary performance of the US econom Since the beginning of the 1990s, we have had a long period of growth that didn't se sputtering out. In fact, growth accelerated in 1997 and early 1998, which is not the u for a 'mature' business cycle. We have seen few signs of strain or imbalance. Althoug areas,  including  Upstate  New  York,  have  lagged,  we  have  experienced  mostly  good  gro across the country and across sectors of the economy.

Unemployment has been very low - lower than most economists thought it cou remain for long without igniting inflation. Wages have been increasing, but not so fa rise caused rapid escalation of costs. The slowdown in the rise of health benefit cos total  compensation  increases  to  moderate  levels.  Productivity  increases  have  been  o compensation growth, keeping profits growing, at least until quite recently. Most rema all, inflation has been falling and not showing any clear evidence of accelerating again

Even  the  Asian  crisis  at  first  seemed  an  ill-wind  whose  timing  was  ac blowing us some good. Some Americans felt the negative impact early, especially manufac whose exports to Asia declined and farmers who saw their prices drop on world markets a demand  fell  off.  At  the  national  level,  however,  our  economy  was  clearly  growing unsustainable rate, and some slowdown was actually welcome. We were in danger of runnin of workers. Sooner or later cost pressures would lead to inflation. The primary econ seemed to be overheating, not slow growth.

Indeed, the Federal Reserve was concerned enough to tap the brakes by raisi short  term  interest  rate  in  March  1997  before  the  Asian  crisis  hit  that  summer.  W probably have felt called on to raise rates again later in 1997, but by then it seeme slower growth in Asia would cut US net exports, and restrain our economy enough to inflation and any pressures. Good productivity performance, falling commodity prices, c with low inflation expectations and the high value of the dollar, all made it less risk reduced the necessity of the Federal Reserve taking preemptive action against inflation rates again.

The  stock  market's  remarkable  rise  both  reflected  and  perpetuated  the  ge good feeling about the US economy. Even the Asian crisis raised the price of US sto investors took their money out of Asian markets and bought US securities instead. To US  equity  values  were  outrunning  reasonable  expectations  of  profits,  especially  if, forecasters expected, the economy slowed down. But increased wealth of consumers stimu consumption and the low cost of equity stimulated investments, so chances of future pro enhanced. Some worried that high equity values were a bubble that would inevitably bu this concern was mitigated by: (1) lack of strong evidence that stock prices were part speculative phenomenon that included real estate and other assets, as in some previo periods; (2) the apparent new maturity of small investors, who talked and acted as th were in the equity market for the long haul. All in all, it was a sunny day at the fair.

All of this good news generated an occasionally silly debate about whether was in 'new era' in which all the old rules had been suddenly repealed, or whether th 'new paradigm,' which usually seemed to mean 'no paradigm' or 'the sky's the limit'.

The more sensible version of the discussion went something like this. The lots of reasons why the economy might be both more productive and less inflation prone used to be:

- more global competition
- deregulation  of  airlines,  trucking,  telecommunications;  decline  of  barriers financial services
- the  computer  and  telecommunication  revolution  (finally)  making  cost  savi possible, not just in manufacturing, but in services
- more  flexibility  and  incentives  built  into  wages,  less  unionization,  out-so specialized services, use of temporary and part-time employees
- high levels of investment, including human investment - on-the-job and other training.

In economists' terms, there was hope that productivity might have moved on higher  growth  trend.  Faster  productivity  growth  would  mean  a  higher  standard  of  liv Americans in the future. It would mean that growth could be faster without setting off (perhaps  closer  to  3  percent  a  year  than  2  percent)  and  that  unemployment  could  be without inflationary consequences. That would be very good news.

It was too soon to be sure that the apparent productivity trend increase wo up or that less inflation was becoming the norm. It was certainly true that some eleme unusual combination of favorable inflation factors were likely to reverse. Health cos might  accelerate  again;  the  dollar  might  weaken  and  cause  import  prices  to  rise;

commodity prices might go up again. Still, the US economy seemed to be performing remar well.

Then ill-wind from Asia turned to a gale, sweeping through currency and markets all around the world and affecting our own financial markets as well. The stoc dropped  5  percent  in  one  day  in  August,  then  bounced  wildly  around.  A  general  'fl quality'  drove  long-term  interest  rates  down  on  Treasuries,  but  rates  on  riskier instruments went up. The market mood changed to pessimism and risk aversion.

Meanwhile, across the Atlantic, the initial storm warnings from Asia, wer first dismissed by many Europeans as far away and not their problem - distant thunder o shore. European economies are less heavily involved with Asia than we are and, besid ill-wind was blowing them some good in the form of lower oil and other commodity price major  countries  on  the  continent  were  working  hard  on  the  details  of  monetary  uni organizing  a  multi-national  central  bank;  they  were  struggling  earnestly  to  get  de inflation down. The basically simple idea of having a common currency and a common ce bank proved very difficult to achieve technically and politically, but they had done rates  were  finally  picking  up  and  even  high  French  and  German  unemployment  rates  w beginning to recede. Europeans were optimistic that the common currency, and the inc competition  and  deepening  capital  markets  it  was  likely  to  engender,  would  energiz economies even more and lead to higher growth. This unpleasant weather on the horizon s at first a minor distraction. But the lightening bolt in Russia was more difficult to right there on their borders.

In Japan, the Asian crisis had a much greater impact and came at a much w time. Japan is closely involved with other Asian countries and suffered both financia and  loss  of  markets  for  Japanese  goods.  They  were  already  struggling  with  slow  gro banking system in need of overhaul and a political party structure in need of rejuven Asian crisis precipitated deep recession in Japan. The world economic turmoil could n come at a moment when the Japanese were less able to deal with it.

In  the  last  few  months,  we  have  learned  so  much  about  the  downside  of increasingly  interdependent  world  that  it  is  important  to  remind  ourselves  that  the enormous. Increasing volumes of trade and cross-border investment have raised the stan living in many emerging countries at an astonishing rate. Trade and foreign investme moved the countries of southeast Asia in less than a generation from traditional agr modern  industrial  societies  with  far  less  poverty,  much  more  skilled  work  forces  an standards of living. At the same time, we and other industrial countries have benef growing markets for our exports, higher profits on our capital and lower prices for variety of goods we import.

When  things  are  going  well  in  an  interlinked  world,  one  country's  prosp reinforces another's. The rapid growth of emerging market countries, especially in As last  couple  of  decades,  led  to  greatly  increased  trade  among  them  as  well  as  with countries. The self-reinforcing growth seemed so positive that investors began to view in emerging markets as not much more risky than investing in their own more familiar in country markets. Capital flowed freely to finance projects in emerging market countr lenders demanding only slightly higher interest rates than they would have required t home.

But  the  downside  of  interdependence  is  that  when  something  goes  wrong, impact also spreads quickly from one country to another, through trade channels, prices markets.  Asian  countries  in  trouble  quickly  cut  their  imports  from  each  other  and industrial world. The reduced Asian demand for food, oil and raw materials was felt by in the US and Canada, Australia and New Zealand; by producers of oil in Mexico and Venez Nigeria and Russia and the Middle East; by copper producers in Chile and exporters of i raw materials in Africa and elsewhere. Companies in Rochester and Buffalo found thei falling.

As the contagion spread, investments in many emerging market countries began look less promising. Investors became generally more cautious and began looking for saf to put their money - like buying US government bonds - even at low rates of return. As US companies affected, they became less eager to finance them as well.

We've learned a lot in the last few months about the power of contagious l confidence in an interlinked world. The meltdown in Russia was the clearest case. Russ an important economic and trading power in itself. Losses to major money center banks, in Europe, though magnified by unexpected interrelations with hedge funds and other ope were not in themselves destabilizing. But what apparently mattered was the surprise, bo suddenness and unpleasantness of the Russian default and of the fact that the Western were so powerless. No one thought the US and its allies would take the political risk Russia fall apart. In the end, there was nothing they could do to stop it.

The Russian collapse led investors to pull back just about everywhere. Some had  borrowed  to  invest  in  Russia  had  to  sell  assets  in  other  markets  to  cover  loss simply said to themselves, 'If it can happen in Russia, it can happen anywhere; I had my money to a safe place.' The result was plummeting markets in Latin America, South A Asia and elsewhere, more difficulties for the countries struggling to recover.

It is now clear that the Asian crisis that started in Thailand in the summe - and seemed like a remote event of no great significance to most Americans - has set o reaction reaching around the world. Much of Asia is in deep recession, the Russian econ collapsed  with  negative  repercussions  for  many  of  its  neighbors,  growth  is  slowing America. Risk aversion of investors has made it difficult for any country, company or perceived as at all risky to get capital or to borrow, even at high rates. Countrie Mexico and Argentina, considered quite strong a few months ago, are under mounting pre Brazil  has  had  to  raise  interest  rates,  use  much  of  its  foreign  exchange  reserves currency  from  depreciating;  the  high  interest  rates,  in  turn,  have  greatly  exacerbat budget deficit, and the deteriorating outlook has led to fears that investors will pul out and bankers refuse to roll over debts. Economic collapse in Brazil, which is Latin largest economy, could precipitate serious trouble in other Latin American countries reverberate back around the globe to deepen the trouble of Asia, including Hong Kong, and  Japan.  Another  round  of  deepening  deterioration  would  surely  put  intense  down pressure on the US economy by cutting our exports, depressing equity markets and weak investor and consumer confidence. As Chairman Alan Greenspan has said, we cannot expec be an 'oasis of prosperity' in a deteriorating world economy. Even if we could stay pr alone, we should not want to take the risk that deteriorating economies in the rest o would augment unrest, terrorism and international conflict that could engulf the United

What's to be done? In the near term there are clearly two priorities:

- GLYPH<222> Stop the contagion so that emerging market countries can begin to get back on thei
- GLYPH<222> Keep the world's largest economy from slowing down too much - for our own sake a the world's.

There  is  no  easy,  simple  answer  to  stopping  contagion,  if  indeed  there answer. What would be the elements of a plan?

First, countries most in danger of being the next to fall have to be willi up to their vulnerability quickly. (There is no point in moaning, 'It's not our fault, anything wrong; we just got caught in the world backwash.' That's partly true, but not They  have  to  be  willing  to  call  in  their  creditors  to  negotiate  rollovers,  ask  t conditional loans, offer significant and credible internal reforms in return. Nowhere i

Second, private creditors have to see their long-run interest in hanging in concessional terms, rather than joining a stampede for the exits.

Third, the international financial institutions and the industrial countri find more funding to tide these countries over the crises if they give evidence of wi accept strict conditions. Congress' passage of the IMF quota increase and the New Arran to Borrow remove a major uncertainty about the effectiveness of collective action and s a lot to restore confidence that the chain reaction of economic deterioration can be st

Keeping our own economy growing would be important even if the rest of t world were not depending on us so much. Slower growth and rising US unemployment woul mean fewer opportunities for Americans to earn income and move to higher skilled and paid  jobs,  less  chance  for  families  to  move  out  of  poverty  and  from  welfare  to  wor growth  or  recession  in  US  would  also  have  serious  consequences  for  the  rest  of  the reducing our ability to buy and invest abroad and exacerbating economic downturn everywh

At present, the chance of recession in the US does not seem high. Recent g has  been  strong  and  balanced  with  few  indications  of  strains  and  speculative  exces typically go with boom/bust cycles. Most forecasters expect the US economy to slow; the that it will not slow too much.

The  Federal  Reserve,  recognizing  that  the  balance  of  risks  has  shifted overheating to cooling off, has cut short term interest rates twice. Other industrial follow our lead (Canada already has); although the major continental European countr easing is less appropriate for them as they consummate their monetary union.

It is clearly important for the Japanese to get their economy moving again being part of the problem and be part of the solution - as Americans and Europeans ha pointing out, none too politely, for months.

The Japanese were not shy, when they were riding high in the '70s and '80 offer advice to the Western industrialized countries about modernizing our manufactur management practices, working harder, getting budget deficits down. So there may be a p element to the US and European shrillness about how important it is for the Japanes aggressive fiscal stimulus to get their economy going again and to restore confidence and immediate restructuring of their banking system. Neither is going well. A series o

announcements, mostly focussed on increasing government spending for public works has yet succeeded in stemming the economic slide. A next step might be a significant tax with  Japanese  consumers  and  investors  both  feeling  anxious  about  the  future,  ther guarantee that even a large tax cut would result in much near term spending.

Japanese banking system restructuring is going slowly, although it does se be moving toward resolution. We are fine ones to talk, since we let our much smaller sa loan crisis fester for a long time before facing up to it. With hindsight, the Japanes restructured their banks much more easily three or four years ago. The worst time to r failing  banks  is  when  macroeconomic  conditions  are  reducing  the  value  of  their  asse further. Drastic action now may make the recession worse in the short run, but it may a only hope for restoring confidence and financial health in the future. Let's suppose turns around: the contagion is stopped, Asian and other emerging market countries begin again; Japan pulls out of recession and begins to contribute with its recovery to rec neighbors; North America and Europe sustain healthy economies. Then the big question i to  avoid  such  a  costly  episode  happening  again.  The  real  costs  are  not  monetary; disrupted human lives and hopes. Millions of people in emerging market countries are s without  jobs,  food,  basic  necessities,  children  are  not  going  to  school,  young  peop learning skills, and are facing uncertain futures.

title: Mr. Wellink gives a central banker's view of price stability and monetary policy  (Central Bank Articles and Speeches, 23 Oct 98)
description: Speech by the President of the Netherlands Bank, Dr. A.H.E.M. Wellink, on the Alumni Day of the Tinbergen Instituut in Rotterdam on 23/10/98.
text:
## Mr. Wellink gives a central banker's view of price stability and monetary poli

Speech by the President of the Netherlands Bank, Dr. A.H.E.M. Wellink, on the Alumni Day o Tinbergen Instituut in Rotterdam on 23/10/98.

## Introduction

It was only recently that some predicted that central bankers would soon be themselves  in  never-never  land.  They  alleged  that  the  considerable  technological  advanc since the Second World War would make for structurally higher growth and low inflation. The economy had supposedly landed in an age of no inflation. But here the question arises whe really  is  a  new  era,  and  if  it  is,  how  it  was  brought  about.  Before  we  go  into  these however, we need to look at the definition of price stability, as well as at the concept such.

## Price stability in central bank terms

It goes without saying that European monetary policy is concerned above all price  stability  within  the  euro  area.  That  is  after  all  the  mandate  given  by  the  EC  T European Central Bank. The euro's exchange rate against, let us say the US dollar or the yen, is not targeted. The euro zone is a comparatively closed economy where, contrary to have been used to in our open European economies, the exchange rate plays a relatively mi in  price  determination.  The  emphasis  laid  on  the  internal  value  of  the  euro  is  th contribution which the European System of Central Banks (ESCB) can make to the stability international monetary system.

In their quest for internal price stability, the monetary authorities base th notably on movements in the consumer price index (CPI). They do so for several reasons. T with, there are various technical advantages to the CPI, such as its high publication frequ availability and transparency. The latter is reflected in its well-founded weighting sch covers a considerable proportion of final spending, viz. household consumption. This makes a more attractive gauge than the broadest measure of inflation available, viz. the GDP de GDP deflator is, however, no match for the CPI when it comes to monetary policy-making, be its  figures  become  available  with  a  considerable  lag  and  not  as  frequently.  Moreove movements  over  time  lose  some  of  their  comparability  because  of  shifts  in  the  package spending. But the CPI is useful for another, more basic reason as well. At the end of the banks are most interested in the ultimate net result of the gamut of price rises within t i.e. the increases in the prices paid by households for goods and services. In this conte of raw materials are, for instance, of a lesser importance. It must be kept in mind that an  earlier  stage  of  the  production  process  need  not  necessarily  bring  about  tensions economy, because they can be compensated for by other factors (such as increasing product competition).

However, this does not mean that central banks should not look at other price as well. On the contrary. Movements in import prices may be barely relevant to the euro they  are  of  importance  to  small,  open  economies.  Because  import  prices  in  a  small  an economy are determined largely by exchange rate developments, the latter may have a consid influence  on  the  general  price  level.  That  even  goes  for  the  euro  zone,  for  example, exchange rate of the US dollar - in which the prices of numerous commodities are expres subject to heavy fluctuations. Likewise, movements in the prices of non-final goods and

such  as  commodities  and  energy,  can  be  relevant  for  central  bankers  because  they  may indication of inflationary tensions.

It is becoming harder for central bankers to do their work because doubts have about the traditional gauges of inflation. What is going on? The measurement of inflation the attention of the academic world, as well as that of the central banks. Take, for i Boskin Report published in the United States, and a comparable report published under the of the Deutsche Bundesbank. These studies indicate that the CPI has been systematically ov in the United States by about 1 percentage point, and in Germany by three-quarters of a p point.  It  is  worthwhile  taking  a  closer  look  at  this  matter,  because,  from  the  point monetary policy, the importance of any distortions of the CPI increases in a world where has  dropped  to  low  levels.  After  all,  the  lower  the  rate  of  inflation,  the  greater significance of any statistical distortion. With inflation in the euro zone coming out at last twelve months, measurement errors of the magnitude which I mentioned earlier sugge Europe is currently wavering between inflation and deflation.

The  errors  made  in  measuring  inflation  are  due,  first  of  all,  to  the  (fo progressing increase in product quality. This is known in academic circles as the quality not easy to distinguish between the price rises and quality improvements of sophisticated such  as  computers  and  telecommunications  equipment.  For  marketing  reasons,  technolog innovations  may  be  very  highly  priced,  for  one  thing  because  the  development  costs  need recovered. Later generations of IT tools, by then mass-produced, are invariably much chea their predecessors. Falling prices and an impressive expansion of investment and profitab go hand in hand, which is a fairly unusual phenomenon macroeconomically. The variety of pr and their ever-shorter life cycle add to the risk that distortions in price indices increas

The second cause of statistical distortions in inflation is the growing impo services; this is known as the services bias. In 1997, more than 65% of the nominal val within the Dutch economy was accounted for by the services sector. In 1950, it had still than 50%. The shares of the agricultural sector and manufacturing industry have shrunk acc Within the services sector, the greatest expansions are accounted for by business service and  telecommunications.  The  problem  is  that  it  is  not  easy  to  determine  the  output  vo services, which can usually only be calculated in a roundabout way. Because the growth of underestimated, price movements in the services sector are systematically overestimated be these  measurement  problems.  This  (unduly)  low  estimation  of  output  growth  is  corroborat studies made by the Netherlands Bureau for Economic Policy Analysis. According to them, th productivity  of  business  services  in  the  Netherlands  between  1991  and  1995  came  out  at 1.5%. Compared to the increase in productivity in manufacturing industry in the same pe 1.75%, this figure is implausibly low. The problems inherent in measuring the CPI are comp further by the fact that services have come to make up an increasingly large share of t product.

The  third  factor  causing  measurement  problems  with  regard  to  inflation  may termed  the  substitution  bias.  In  practice,  the  composition  of  the  package  of  goods  and purchased by consumers changes fairly rapidly. That is especially true in this day and age and improved products being marketed all the time. The package composition underlying the adjusted  for  such  changes  only  once  every  five  years.  The  basket  of  goods  and  services calculate the CPI has recently been harmonised within the European Union. This harmonise will be used by the ESCB as a measure of inflation in their monetary policy-making. This me the differences between the national definitions used by statistical agencies have decline

the process of harmonisation has not yet been completed. The harmonised CPI in fact cov narrow an area in terms of goods and services. Several components which are relevant to th price level are not included. Take, for example, rent increases.

## Consequences for monetary policy

In view of the problems attending the measurement of inflation, people are r question whether central bankers still have sufficient insight into inflationary develop subsequently, whether central bankers are still capable of conducting adequate monetary Such concerns are valid notably in times of low inflation, when the statistical distortion speaking about carry extra weight.

In a market economy, any difficulties encountered in the calculation of the i the general price level need not necessarily give rise to problems right away. An entrepr has decided to purchase new computer hardware will not be swayed by possible statistical di in the CPI. Neither will you or I, when we visit the supermarket on Saturdays to stock up o The essential thing is that entrepreneurs, consumers and other economic agents have prope into the value of individual goods.

But there is a catch. An inflation gauge which is closely monitored by a centr may  influence  the  behaviour  of  economic  agents.  Contracts  and  labour  agreements  often explicitly to an officially published inflation figure. Via this route, distortions in me can thus affect functioning of the economy. In other words, it is of the utmost importanc for the monetary authorities, that price rises be gauged as accurately as possible.

In spite of the uncertainties inherent in measuring inflation, the monetary au in formulating their policies, make use of a gauge that seeks to encompass the general p How otherwise can one ascertain whether price stability has been achieved. Moreover, mo policy should in principle take effect at the macroeconomic level. However, in order to possible measurement errors, price stability - as indicated by the inflation measure used more broadly by the central bank. The Governing Council of the European Central Bank has re defined price stability as a rise in the (harmonised) consumer price level of less than 2% hand, this definition, which is in line with that used in most countries of the euro area measurement errors occur while, on the other, it stresses that it is one of the tasks of System of Central Banks to prevent deflation. Some caution is in order when it comes to u word  'deflation'.  In  purely  technical  terms,  deflation  may  be  defined  as  a  fall  in  pr conjures up much more than that, viz. the depression of the 1930s. A slight decrease of t price level need not of course be attended by an overall collapse of demand. In 1987, fo consumer prices in the Netherlands dropped by around 0.5%, a development which had a pos impact on the economy because disposable income in real terms grew more than expected.

Returning  to  our  measurement  problem,  we  cannot  conclude,  on  the  basis  of information  now  available,  that  the  distortions  in  the  official  price  indices  have substantially over time. That would have landed the monetary authorities with real problem example,  inflation  had  been  increasingly  overstated,  monetary  policy  would  have  been tightened, with negative effects for economic growth and the employment situation. Howev cannot but admit that it has become more difficult over the past few decades to measure o price developments in the services sector in particular.

## A brave new world?

Now let us take a look at actual inflation. We can see from the various inflat in Europe, and even throughout the world, that there are few factors which could make f inflation. In the European Union and the United States, inflation has been structurally re the early 1980s, thanks to budgetary consolidation in both these areas, the deregulation of product  markets,  and  a  further  liberalisation  of  international  trade  and  capital  market international  competition.  In  those  -  large  -  parts  of  the  world  which  have  been  affec financial and economic crisis, deflation is in evidence.

This brings me back to the question which I posed at the beginning of this a what indications are there that we now find ourselves in a new era of permanently higher gr lower inflation, or to cite Alan Greenspan, in a new economy. This question is prompted no the  developments  in  the  United  States  where  -  so  far  -  high  growth  has  been  attended inflation.

But one swallow does not make a summer, as the saying goes. And that is true o United  States,  too.  Those  who  feel  that  high  growth  and  low  inflation  have  come  to permanent fixture may be suffering under some delusion. After all, viewed over the long neither the duration of the upswing in the United States, nor the increase in productivity of inflation are unique. In fact, if the signs are not misleading, the American economy wou be over the hill. Since the early 1950s, the expansion phases of the American business cy on average lasted five years, two of them lasting longer than the current phase. Though ac the rise in labour productivity over the past few years (of 1-1.5%) still compares unfavo the 3% average recorded during the first two decades following the Second World War. And, inflation is concerned, it may be noted that it was low until the mid-1960s, averaging current developments in the United States, which are now beginning to tarnish somewhat, t have much more in common with the situation in the first half of the post-war period (tho are  also  quite  a  few  differences),  and  can  hence  hardly  be  called  exceptional.  It  is  a imperative to exercise caution when averring that inflation has been banned forever, be current low rate of inflation in the United States and Europe is accounted for largely commodity prices, which is temporary in nature. Obviously a role is also played by the c demand in South-East Asia in particular and its repercussions elsewhere. That is why th telling  what  the  underlying  inflation  rate  would  be  if  there  were  greater  economic  eq worldwide. For example, suppose oil prices in 1998 and 1999 continued to be at their 19 ($19.2 per barrel UK Brent). That is 30% more than the current price. Inflation in the Union would then come out at 1.8% this year, instead of the current estimate of 1.5%. inflation would then rise to 2.4% (according to the Netherlands Bank's EUROMON model).

## Conclusion

Let me conclude. Central bankers will never be at a loss for something to d look at the current financial and economic crisis. And although the inflation genie will from the bottle for the time being, central banks will need to keep an eye on price moveme time. Monetary policy is not asymmetrical, as some might feel, in the sense that a central takes action when prices soar. Falling prices, too, may be detrimental to the economy, an some reaction from the central bank.

It is under these very conditions - low inflation worldwide and even deflation areas - that measurement problems with regard to price movements, though not insurmountable

prove a nuisance. Although the central banks still have at their disposal sufficient mo economic beacons by which to steer their course, there is work to do for the statistical ESCB and the academic world. If problems with measuring inflation mean that inflationary t may be hard to assess reliably, we must do all we can to ensure that the quality of the p published is at least maintained and, where possible, improved.

title: Mr. Stals reviews the position of South Africa against the background of the global financial crisis  (Central Bank Articles and Speeches, 22 Oct 98)
description: Address by the Governor of the South African Reserve Bank, Dr. C. Stals, at the Fifth Annual General Meeting of the South Africa - Canada Chamber of Business in Johannesburg on 22/10/98.
text:
Mr. Stals reviews the position of South Africa against the background of th global financial crisis Address by the Governor of the South African Reserve Bank, Dr. C. Stal the  Fifth  Annual  General  Meeting  of  the  South  Africa  -  Canada  Chamber  of  Business Johannesburg on 22/10/98.

## 1. Background

As  could  have  been  expected,  this  year's  Annual  Meetings  of  the  Internati Monetary Fund and the World Bank held in Washington D.C. during the first week of October, dominated by a discussion of the global financial crisis.

What started off more than a year ago as an East Asian crisis gradually exten other emerging market countries and eventually also affected a number of smaller well-de economies. The most recent extension was an infliction on the financial systems of some industrial  countries,  such  as  the  United  States  of  America.  What  started  off  as  a  mor problem  of  the  countries  surrounding  the  depressed  economy  of  Japan,  indeed  became  a  g problem that is now demanding the serious attention of the entire international community. be a depressing thought, but it is nevertheless one of the more encouraging outcomes of t annual  meetings  of  the  IMF  and  the  World  Bank.  Now  that  so  many  countries,  and  also  m industrial countries, are more directly involved in the financial crisis, there is a grea finding a solution.

## 2. The causes of the problem

Many reasons have been advanced for the world financial debacle. Apart from adverse effects of a protracted recession in the Japanese economy, East Asian countries wer for lax macroeconomic financial policies, for insufficient disclosure of information on for movements and debt positions, for bad governance at government and private sector levels crony capitalism.

Private international investors were blamed for irresponsible speculative att the  foreign  exchange  rates  of  countries,  destabilizing  activity  in  the  financial  mar reluctance to share in the burden of eventual collapse and adjustment.

The International Monetary Fund has been criticized and is still under attac many quarters for not diagnosing the problem at an earlier stage, and for the way the Fund handled the crisis situation in individual countries. The medicine prescribed by the Fund 'conditionalities') is blamed for killing the patient, rather than curing the illness.

Recent  developments  added  a  further  dimension  and  exposed  a  possibly  mor important basic cause for the global financial dilemma, and that is the excessive leverag that  certain  financial  institutions  were  allowed  to  create  in  funding  international  c including  speculative  investments  in  emerging  markets.  The  near-collapse  of  the  hedg Long-Term Capital Management (LTCM) in the United States of America in September exposed a astonishing  balance  sheet  position  for  an  important  operator  in  the  world  financial  ma balance  sheet  for  a  non-bank  financial  intermediary  that  used  more  than  $50  of  borrowe (mostly bank funds) for every one dollar of own capital!

Finally, the nature and functioning of the present international financial s floating exchange rates, unrestricted capital movements and liberalised financial markets

being questioned. This system, which gradually developed through an evolutionary process o past two decades after the final demise of the system of fixed par values in the 1970s, has in elements that encourage periodic occurrences of international financial instability. Pa smaller economies of the world find it increasingly difficult to maintain orderly domesti conditions in an environment of financial globalisation, financial market integration and control liberalisation.

The truth is perhaps that no solitary cause can be singled out as the only r the development of the present international financial crisis. The erosion in the quality took place over a long period of time and the possible causes identified above most pro contributed  to  the  weakening  and  eventual  foundering  of  the  system.  The  restoration  of stability in the international financial markets is therefore a cumbersome and complex pr will take some time to achieve. The seriousness of the problem, however, demands a worl concerted  effort  that  can  best  be  accomplished  by  working  through  the  available  e infrastructure of the IMF and the World Bank.

## 3. Implications of more recent developments in the crisis

Three important events over the past few months contributed to a deepening o crisis, but at the same time also to a better understanding of the situation.

Firstly, the decision of Malaysia to reintroduce rather restrictive and compr exchange controls on international capital movements focused attention on the real danger movement towards national protectionist and economic isolation policies. It is true that traditionally a country with a high domestic savings rate and is therefore less dependant investment  for  the  financing  of  its  own  internal  economic  development.  It  is  also  tru presence of serious internal political division in Malaysia to some extent discredited Mr recent economic policy measures. International investors, however, could not ignore the s the danger of a wider and more general recourse to direct governmental controls over inte capital  movements,  particularly  over  the  more  volatile  short-term  capital  flows  that disrupted the economies of so many of the emerging and developing countries of the world.

Secondly,  the  default  by  Russia  in  respect  of  the  redemption  of  its  sho domestic and foreign sovereign debt caught many investors by surprise. A huge overnight de the discounted value of Russian government bonds that was previously regarded as secure co for large banking loans extended to Russian borrowers forced massive losses on investors, a large provisions for bad debts from international banking institutions. The Russian deb than anything else exposed the vulnerability of the world's banking system in the current s global financial turmoil. It also partly exposed the role of hedge funds and short-term sp this evolving global drama. More than one short-term non-banking financial intermediary and few banks were caught with their pants down in the Russian debacle, and were forced to abso losses.  The  clear  warning  was  for  greater  caution  in  the  games  they  play  in  this environment of the global financial markets.

Thirdly, the near collapse of Long-Term Capital Management and the decision of American Federal Reserve Bank System to get involved in the subsequent rescue operation o non-bank financial institution, exposed a new dimension of the emerging world financial remains a highly debatable issue of why the Federal Reserve was prepared to attach its nam not its funds, to the rescue of LTCM. The only reason can be that the Fed was gravely c about possible adverse implications for the American banking system of a liquidation of LT

it turned out to be, LTCM managed about $5 billion of selected clients funds, but had inves financial markets more than $250 billion of borrowed funds, mostly raised on a short-te from American banking institutions.

Both  the  American  authorities  and  representatives  of  the  hedge  fund  movem recently went out of their way to explain that LTCM was not representative of the industr most other hedge funds maintained much more reasonable leverage positions on their balance The  vulnerability  of  the  world's  financial  system,  and  of  many  reputable  multinational institutions, was nevertheless rudely exposed by the LTCM affair. The real explanation that this stage be demanded from the American financial supervisory authorities is therefore no Fed  got  involved  in  the  rescue  operation  of  LTCM,  but  rather  why  such  excessive  gearin permitted by a financial institution that in the end turned out to hold a major systemic American banking system, and indeed for the emerging global financial system as a whole.

The  moment  that  the  Fed  decided  to  support  the  rescue  operation  for  LTCM, whole ball game changed as far as the future role of hedge funds is concerned. The fact become necessary for the monetary authorities of the most important financial structure in to lend their support to the rescue of an institution such as LTCM, surely recognises the of this type of institution for monetary policy in general, and for the protection of ove stability in particular. But then it also demands financial disciplines and the adherence requirements  of  financial  prudency,  capital  adequacy  and  risk-aversion  policies  fro institutions.

The  epicentre  of  risk  exposure  in  the  present  global  financial  crisis  has partly shifted from the East Asian or emerging and smaller developed economies of the w some  of  the  world's  major  financial  centres.  Important  international  banking  institut become so involved in the problem of excessive leverage and speculative investments in th financial  markets  that  they  now  also  have  to  implement  major  and  painful  internal  rest programmes. A few examples of such forced financial reform programmes already surfaced in r weeks and more will most probably follow. Maybe we are now much closer to finding a soluti the international financial crisis of the past year, which can surely no longer be bla macroeconomic mismanagement in the smaller economies of the world. LTCM exposed one of th major sources of global financial instability.

## 4. In search of a solution

The causes of the current world financial crisis are complex and widespread solution therefore is not a simple one. In particular no quick solution is available.

It must firstly, be taken into account that the adverse developments in the markets will continue to have secondary effects that will, for some time to come, exert influence  on  global  real  economic  activity.  Forecasts  for  world  economic  growth  in  199 systematically been scaled down from a rather ambitious 4 per cent made towards the end year to only about 2 per cent at this stage. In a number of East Asian economies, growth w be negative this year.

Secondly,  the  restructuring  of  the  banking  systems  in  a  number  of  the  af countries  will  take  some  time  before  normality  will  be  restored.  As  is  known,  the Government has just recently provided an amount of more than Yen 60 trillion to recapita

Japanese banking system. In the meantime only modest amounts of new bank loans will be ava for the financing of consumption and investment.

Thirdly, the deleveraging process to reduce the absurd excessive gearing ra some mega-sized financial institutions can only be accomplished by a reduction in world l Taking account of the magnitude of the problem of over-leveraging as evidenced by the b sheet information recently released for LTCM, this can become a major constraint on the ava of new funds in the global financial market over the next year.

Against  this  background,  the  world  can  only  extricate  itself  from  this  c problem by a coordinated effort applied from three different levels:

Firstly, many macroeconomic deficiencies were exposed in a number of countr that  in  the  end  suffered  most  from  the  global  financial  crisis.  It  is  dangerous  to  ge shortcomings  as  they  would  obviously  differ  from  country  to  country  and  would  therefor require  specialised  treatment  suitable  to  the  underlying  situation  in  each  one  of  t economies.  A  number  of  countries  such  as  Thailand,  Korea  and  the  Philippines  have  al addressed  their  problems  with  appropriate  adjustment  programmes,  and  are  beginning  to benefits from often painful corrective measures. These adjustments provide for more disclo transparency, enhanced financial regulation and supervision, recapitalising of banking in more restrictive monetary and fiscal policies, exchange rate adjustments and improved gov in macroeconomic management in general.

Secondly  ,  all  the  criticism  against  the  multinational  institutions,  and  pa against the IMF, is not without foundation. These institutions did not keep up with the a process of financial globalisation in recent years, and with the rapid integration of wo markets. Economic policy models that may have been appropriate in the old system where c banks  and  governments  could  still  exert  strong  influences  on  the  direction  of  major aggregates such as interest and exchange rates and could effectively control changes in supply and in bank credit extension cannot be applied without adjustment in the new worl market forces now dominate the scene. Some changes in the global financial system have b necessary and urgent. These institutions are now concentrating on increasing their resou IMF quotas, on improving their surveillance functions and on revising the 'architecture' existing infrastructural frameworks.

Thirdly , after the LTCM affair, there is an urgent need for multinational ban other  financial  institutions  to  revise  their  own  internal  risk  control  models.  The  act Malaysia recently to reintroduce exchange controls on international capital movements and facto default by Russia in its inability to redeem its public debt eroded almost overnight what was regarded as secure collateral in terms of normal banking practices. The develop more suitable risk management models cannot be left entirely to the official financial sup the world - private sector financial institutions should on their own initiative improve financial disciplines and controls.

## 5. South Africa's position in the international financial crisis

The South African economy was also badly affected over the past six months by deteriorating international financial situation. As non-resident investors reduced their South African bonds, we had to ride with the storms. Although the authorities 'leaned ag wind', South Africa ended up with:

- a decline in the value of the rand. Changes in the exchange rate of the ra some turbulent fluctuations resulted in a currency that is now about 18 p weaker than at the beginning of this year;
- higher interest rates. The level of interest rates also moved up and down b stands at about 7 full percentage points above the level of six months ago;
- some decline in overall liquidity in the banking sector which, however, again in recent weeks;
- a  depressed  real  domestic  economy.  Growth  in  real  gross  domestic  produ slowed down already last year and was further restrained by the recent ad developments in the financial markets.

During this testing period, some structural weaknesses in the South African ec were once again exposed, but also some inherent strengths for which we should be grateful include a sound and well-managed domestic banking sector and financial markets that provid liquidity,  the  mechanisms  and  the  resilience  to  adapt  to  the  rapidly  changing  int environment.

South Africa's approach to this worldwide financial market problem is to remai of the system and to lend our support for a global initiative to solve the problem.

Action at the level of national governments, the multinational financial ins and private sector financial market operators is necessary to restore stability in the gl system:

- Governments must recognise, analyze and define deficiencies in th macroeconomic  policies  and  identify  weaknesses  in  their  financial  struct and  must  take  the  necessary  steps  on  a  case  by  case  basis  to  strengthe system at the national level. Problems are different from country to count no  standard  macroeconomic  module  can  be  prescribed  on  a  global  basis  f universal application.
- The multinational institutions should concentrate on the obvious shortcomin the present infrastructure for international payments, international capi and the determination of exchange rates. The process of financial globali worldwide financial market integration and liberalisation of financial inst moved faster than the global authorities themselves did with their contr surveillance  systems.  The  approach  now  should  not  be  for  the  markets  to stopped in their progress, but rather for the authorities to catch up.
- Private  sector  financial  market  operators,  including  multinational  ba institutions,  hedge  funds  and  institutional  fund  managers,  must  in  thei interest reconsider and review their modus operandi in the markets. In part risk  management  models  must  provide  for  the  volatile  global financ environment in which they now operate.

Many encouraging signs emerged from the discussion in Washington D.C. to indic that progress is now being made at all three levels, and that greater stability is gradual the world financial system. South Africa, like many other countries in a similar situation, these signs of hope with great interest.
