title: Mr. Reddy reports on the recent performance of the Indian economy  (Central Bank Articles and Speeches, 1 Oct 98)
description: Speech by Dr. Y.V. Reddy, a Deputy Governor of the Reserve Bank of India, entitled, 'Managing Capital Account' in Hyderabad on 01/10/98.
text:
Mr. Reddy reports on the recent performance of the Indian economy Speech by Dr.  Y.V.  Reddy,  a  Deputy  Governor  of  the  Reserve  Bank  of  India,  entitled, 'Managing  Capital Account' in Hyderabad on 01/10/98.

On behalf of the Reserve Bank of India, I would like to convey my warm greetin all the delegates from various South Asian countries. I have special pleasure in welcoming guest, Governor A. S. Jayawardhene.

The forex markets in many parts of the world are going through a turmoil d currency crises, which are intensively affecting more and more countries. Many of these c characterized  by  volatile  capital  flows  -  though  the  underlying  causes  for  such  crises Currently,  there  is  a  raging  debate  on  the  issues  relating  to  managing  capital  flows, reopening many issues such as the merits of capital controls, and the adequacy of the in financial  architecture.  There  are  references  to  India  also  in  this  debate  and  intere expressed  on  how  we  are  managing  our  capital  flows.  I  will,  therefore,  share  with perceptions on the following issues.

## First, why is it that India has remained relatively unaffected by the Asian crisis?

Second, what role did policy relating to capital flows play in imparting stab put it differently, what was the policy and operational framework in managing capital flo was the current account handled to ensure effective management of the capital account? Wha the strategies for crisis avoidance? What were the means adopted to meet extraordinary situ

Third, in view of emerging global developments, can India continue to be wha been described as an island of tranquility amidst a sea of turbulence in the emerging econ put it differently, what are the immediate prospects for India in the external sector?

## India and Asian Crisis

The  performance  of  the  Indian  economy,  by  all  accounts,  has  been  by  and  l impressive both in terms of growth and stability. During the period 1992-97, the annual av GDP growth rate was 6.8 per cent. Our annual average growth rate during this period was than the developing countries' average at 6.4 per cent. Our inflation during the period 1 8.7  per  cent,  which  compares  favourably  with  the  developing  countries'  average.  Our account deficit as a percentage of GDP was only 1.3 per cent during this period. Foreign reserves went up from US$ 9.2 billion in 1991-92 to US$ 26.4 at end-March 1997.

The  data  that  I  have  just  presented  will  show  that  our  fundamentals  are making us less vulnerable to contagion, and this is clear from our performance in 1997 when the crisis struck East Asia. During 1997-98, real GDP growth has been estimated at cent, a decline from the previous year's growth of 7.5 per cent, mainly attributable to decline  in  agricultural  output.  The  rate  of  inflation  as  measured  by  the  wholesale  p declined in 1997-98 to 5.3 per cent on a point-to-point basis. In 1997-98, the current acc continued to be low at 1.7 per cent of GDP and there was accretion to foreign exchange re the tune of US$ 3 billion.

The  reason  as  to  why  we  escaped  the  contagion  can  be  analysed  in  terms  of policies that we have been pursuing in areas where serious concern has been expressed in th of the Asian crisis. Investment as a percentage of GDP has been reasonably steady in the r

at around 27 per cent on average, and about 95 per cent of this was financed by domestic s managing  our  external  account,  we  ensure  a  sustainable  current  account  deficit,  strict reliance on short-term external debt, limit access to external debt, and emphasise produc such debt. We do encourage Foreign Direct Investment and portfolio investments through f institutional investors as the main sources of non-debt-creating capital inflows. Also, t rate is market determined. The RBI closely monitors it, and when warranted makes purchas sales of foreign currency to ensure orderly conditions in forex markets. We undertook, ea reform period, financial sector reforms - especially banking reform, which included stre the  regulatory  framework,  imposing  prudential  norms  and  reducing  non-performing  assets discourage  banks'  investments  in  real  estate  and  stock  markets.  Corporates'  exposure especially external debt, is within reasonable limits. As compared with other central ban widely  recognised  transparency  in  operations  of  the  Reserve  Bank  of  India.  There  is,  t reason to believe that it is not just chance but sound macroeconomic management which sa from the South-East Asian contagion. It is nonetheless necessary for us to learn from the of the Asian crisis.

## Policy Frame

The broad approach to reform in the external sector after the Gulf crisis was in the Report of the High Level Committee on Balance of Payments chaired by Dr. C. Rangar currently  the  Governor  of  Andhra  Pradesh.  It  recommended,  inter  alia:  liberalisation  o account transactions, leading to current account convertibility; compositional shift in c away  from  debt  to  non-debt-creating  flows;  strict  regulation  of  external  commercial  bor especially  short-term  debt;  discouraging  volatile  elements  of  flows  from  non-resident gradual liberalisation of outflows; and disintermediation of the Government in the flow o assistance. The Committee also recommended the introduction of a market-determined exch rate regime while emphasing the need to contain the current account deficit within limits. framework  for  the  external  sector  based  on  the  Rangarajan  Committee  Report  was  implemen along with policy changes in the trade, industrial and financial sectors.

Under trade policy, there has been a virtual elimination of licensing, a pr shift of restricted items of imports to Open General Licence (OGL) and a lowering of tarif Industrial policy has been characterised by delicensing, removal of monopoly clauses defin industrial houses and removal of most reservations for public sector enterprises. The ref area of the financial sector were guided by the recommendations of the Narasimham Commi Alongside the deregulation of the banking industry, including entry for new private sector general thrust of monetary policy has been towards reduction in pre-emptions, greater re open  market  operations,  deregulation  of  interest  rates  and  widening  and  deepening  of  f markets. Simultaneously, measures have been undertaken to strengthen the institutional fr in  banking,  non-banking  financial  companies,  financial  institutions  and  stock  markets prudential  norms,  capital  adequacy  stipulations,  improvements  in  payments  and  sett mechanisms  and  strengthening  of  the  supervisory  framework.  Institutional  measures  have included  recapitalisation  of  banks,  improvements  in  debt  recovery  and,  most  importa setting-up of the Board for Financial Supervision and strengthening Bank's supervisory mech A second Narasimham Committee has given a road map for further reform of the banking sector

We have taken various measures to ensure that the banking system does not get maturity mismatch bind. With a view to encouraging banks to mobilise longer-term deposi increased  the  interest  rate  ceiling  on  FCNR-B  deposits  above  one  year  while  simultan reducing the ceiling on such deposits below one year. Banks have been asked to monitor un

foreign  currency  exposures  of  their  clients.  Draft  guidelines  for  asset-liability  manag been prepared and after discussion with banks will be put in place. We are monitoring the position in the economy very closely.

Fiscal  adjustment  has  been  undertaken  and  a  very  significant  measure  is  th system of automatic monetisation of the fiscal deficit was replaced by a system of ways a advances.

In brief, reform in the external sector was meshed with reform in other relate and, within the external sector reform, capital flows were managed, keeping in view the efficiency and stability. There was a fairly smooth movement from an administered exchan system to a market-determined exchange rate, and the Reserve Bank always ensures that vo and speculative elements are curbed through both direct and indirect measures.

## Operational Framework

Based on the policy frame and the projected financing requirement for each management  of  the  capital  account  is  operationalised  through  procedures  for  foreign investment, portfolio investment, external commercial borrowings, NRI deposits and outflows

The broad approach to targeting of foreign direct investment has been through route, i.e. automatic and non-automatic. Where the approval is automatic, activities and ownership are listed, while in regard to the rest, a case-by-case approval by a high-power adopted.

Portfolio investments are restricted to select players, viz. FIIs. They could, some restrictions, operate in equity and debt markets. FIIs are permitted to invest in equi a ceiling of 10 per cent for individual FIIs in a single company and 30 per cent collectiv ceiling in a single company. Indian corporates are permitted, again through a process of a individual cases satisfying general guidelines, to access funds through global depository r euroconvertibles.

The  approach  to  external  commercial  borrowings  has  been  one  of  prudence,  wi self-imposed ceilings on commitments and a careful monitoring of the cost of raising fund as  their  end  use.  External  commercial  borrowings  are  subject  to  a  'dual  route',  viz component  of  automatic  and  a  major  part  through  case  by  case  approval,  based  on  the  si sector.  Short-term  debt,  including  trade-related  payments  beyond  180  days,  is  subject case-by-case approval of purpose, amount and terms. An overall annual ceiling is kept for flows - both for short-term and medium to long-term.

In respect of NRI deposits, control over inflows is exercised through specific interest rates or interest rate ceilings for different maturities in respect of deposits i while, more generally, variable reserve requirements are stipulated to encourage or discou flows.

As regards external assistance, both bilateral and multilateral flows are adm by the Government of India.

In  respect  of  capital  outflows,  the  approach  has  been  to  facilitate  direct investment through joint ventures and wholly owned subsidiaries and provision of financial

to promote exports, especially project exports from India. There are dual routes, namely and  case-by-case  and  there  is  an  aggregate  annual  ceiling  for  such  approvals.  Export exchange earners have also been given permission, on a selective basis, to maintain foreig accounts and use them for permitted purposes which facilitate their overseas business prom growth.

## Current Account Management

When  India  adopted  current  account  convertibility  in  1994,  it  was  recognise emphasised by the Rangarajan Committee, that there could be capital outflows in the guise o account transactions. Hence, certain safeguards were built into the regulations relating account transactioins.

First, the requirement of repatriation and surrender of export proceeds was co Exporters were, however, allowed to retain a portion of their earnings in foreign currenc in  India  which  could  be  used  for  approved  purposes,  thereby  avoiding  costs  of  conversi reconversion.

Second, all authorised dealers were allowed to sell foreign exchange for unde current account transactions which could be readily identified and supported by some docu evidence.

Third, indicative value limits were given for different kinds of transactions amounts  sold  were  reasonable  in  relation  to  the  purpose.  For  higher  amounts,  the  banks approach  the  RBI.  This  operational  framework  for  the  current  account  enabled  eff management of the capital account.

Fourth,  the  RBI  has  been  taking  an  active  interest  in  the  development  of  m government securities and forex markets. A proactive interest in the development of these has also enabled effective management of the current and capital accounts.

Fifth, while ensuring orderly and cautious deregulation, every effort has been improve the information base on major transactions in the forex markets with respect to and  magnitude.  Constant  improvements  are  made  to  ensure  the  appropriateness,  timelines quality  of  the  information  base.  The  insistence  on  adequate  and  timely  details  from  a dealers  in  forex  markets  also  helped  in  fine  tuning  the  management  of  the  current  and accounts.

It must be noted that we insist as a general rule that foreign currency transac place for financing defined underlying transactions. No doubt, genuine hedging of exposur specified conditions is allowed. Transactions merely involving currency exchange or with speculative motives are viewed with serious disfavour. This consistent approach has lent to the management of both current and capital transactions.

As explained by Governor Jalan, the objective of the current policy in regard foreign exchange market is to maintain orderly conditions in the financial markets. The aimed at preventing any destabilizing speculation in the market while at the same time f foreign exchange transactions at market rates for all permissible purposes.

## Crisis avoidance

It would not be appropriate to conclude that managing capital flows on the lines, however efficient, will ensure that there would be total tranquility in the capital even with a managed capital account, we had to contend with occasional surges in capita between 1993 and 1997. In general, the short-term response has taken a number of forms, viz of reserve requirements, reviewing the pace of removal of restrictions on capital inflows, of end-use specifications, liberalization of capital outflows, partial sterilization throu operations,  and  deepening  the  foreign  exchange  market  by  routing  an  increased  volum transactions through the market.

The prolonged stability in the exchange rate of the rupee from March 1993 under stress in the second half of 1995-96. In response to the upheavals, the RBI interve market to signal that the fundamentals were in place and to ensure that market correcti exchange rate was orderly and calibrated. Exchange market intervention was supported by mo policy action to withdraw liquidity. The pressures intensified towards the end of January the first week of February 1996. The Reserve Bank undertook a number of measures to enco the faster realization of export proceeds and to prevent an acceleration of import paym interest  rate  surcharge  on  import  finance  was  raised,  the  scheme  of  post-shipment  expo denominated in foreign currency was scrapped and the RBI continued to intervene actively spot, forward and swap markets.

The  year  1997-98  and  the  first  quarter  of  1998-99  posed  severe  challenge exchange rate management in the face of the threat of external contagion and other unce Distinct phases of exchange rate movements and response by the RBI can be identified. Durin to  September  1997,  excess  supply  conditions  prevailed  in  the  market  and  the  Reserve undertook large net purchases of foreign currency. From September 1997 to mid-January 1998, exchange  market  pressure  was  staved  off  through  sales  of  foreign  currency,  coupled administrative measures such as restricting certain forward contracts and monetary policy Mid-January  to  April  1998  marked  the  return  of  stability  and  enabled  the  rolling-back monetary measures introduced in January 1998.

When the foreign exchange market was characterised by considerable uncertaintie May  to  June  1998,  several  measures  were  announced  by  the  RBI  in  June  1998  to  reverse demand/supply mismatches in the market. The market responded positively to these measures, August 1998 there were fluctuations in the exchange rate in view of international developme RBI again undertook strong administrative and monetary measures, which included an increa the repo rate and the cash reserve requirement of banks.

A vigilant and proactive policy by the RBI was, therefore, essential to avoid a highly unsettled atmosphere in international currency markets.

## Managing Extraordinary Events

An extraordinary situation arose consequent upon the imposition of sanctions the issue of Resurgent India Bonds (RIBs) is an interesting example of management of the account in such a situation. The RIBs were designed to compensate for the extraordinary e 1998-99,  which  may  result  in  some  shortfall  in  the  normally  expected  level  of  capital though the current account deficit would continue to be well within 2 per cent of GDP. Du sudden developments in 1998-99, a temporary disruption in capital flows, especially debt f

anticipated. Instead of dipping into currency reserves, which might affect sentiment adv cutting the current account deficit through drastic import cuts, which would affect rea activity, the alternative was to enhance debt flows at the least possible cost. There w offset the adverse negative market sentiment created in the international capital markets downgrading  of  India's  sovereign  rating  to  non-investment  grade.  This  could  be  don demonstrably raising debt resources at a cost lower than that any organised financial in was prepared to provide in the context of the rating downgrade. Raising resources through borrowing was considered to be time-consuming and in any case inadvisable as a maiden of under adverse circumstances. At the same time, it was necessary to ensure that amounts so were restricted quantitatively to meet essential needs as a replacement for normal debt keeping an option for premature closure. Furthermore, we had to ensure that the borrowing appropriate  medium-term  maturity,  say  five  years.  RIBs,  which  are  essentially  in  the  n foreign currency deposits on a par with FCNR-B, were devised in the light of these consider was  also  necessary  for  the  RBI  to  ensure  that  these  funds  did  not  disrupt  the  money, government securities market.

There have been three main points of criticism regarding RIBs, i.e. cost of RIBs, substitution of FCNR-B deposits and exchange rate guarantee.

A total amount of $ 4.23 billion has been mobilised at a moderate cost in the difficult  international  environment  and  the  recent  downgrading  of  our  credit  rating.  S called it the deal of the year. To quote an international investor, '… the cost at which been raised imply a perceived sovereign rating three to four notches higher than current comparison sake China's 2003 Yankee Bond Issue, rated A3 by Moody's trades at a spread of basis points (on August 21) over the ten year US Treasury implying a dollar yield of 7.90 and the RIB issue is not even sovereign risk.'

On the second point, as most of the banks that have actively mobilised RIBs m aware  by  now,  there  has  been  limited  substitution  from  FCNR-B  deposits  and  moreover,  t extent there has been substitution, it would result in elongation of the maturity of dep years, while at the same time bringing into the country actual foreign exchange that is pr unswapped.

In  regard  to  the  exchange  guarantee  extended,  it  is  recognised  that  under circumstances, issuance of such a guarantee is inadvisable. However, it can be legitimatel the  recent  times  have  been  far  from  normal.  In  return  for  a  specific  guarantee  on  R Government  can  claim  benefits  in  four  ways,  viz.  addition  to  forex  reserves,  sup macroeconomic environment and sentiment, indirect support for its own borrowing programme resources for infrastructure development, including for public sector entities. It can al that the Government bears exchange risk in regard to bilateral and multilateral flows for i onlending. Moreover, given the Indian track record on prudent macroeconomic management, burden of the exchange guarantee could be said to be manageable.

## Prospects

The trend growth rate of real GDP in India during the nineties so far has a 6.1 per cent per annum as against 5.4 per cent in the 1980s. Taking the entire 17-year p 1980-81  to  1997-98,  India's  trend  growth  has  averaged  5.8  per  cent  per  annum,  whi significantly higher than the trend, annual average rate of 4.7 per cent for the developi and  2.4  per  cent  for  the  advanced  countries.  The  performance  during  1997-98  also  re

considerable  resilience  and  inner  strength  to  meet  the  macroeconomic  challenges  posed  b domestic and external developments. The performance of various sectors clearly suggests growth of real GDP during the current year (1998-99) would be about 6.5 per cent - an im figure, especially in the current international environment.

As regards prices, we have an impressive record of maintaining a modest single annual inflation rate during the 1980s and most of 1990s. However, during the current annual inflation rate has been a little over 8 per cent on a point-to-point basis as at 1998. The principal sources of current inflation lie in the primary articles group, within contributions were from fruits and vegetables, oilseeds and cereals. The price situation se to reflect a shortage of supplies of certain primary articles and is perhaps attributabl factors.

There were some concerns earlier in the current year that interest rates coul significantly  due  to  the  large  borrowing  programme  of  the  Government.  However,  most  of market borrowing requirement of the Government for this year has already been met with very marginal increase in yields on government paper. Moreover, the genuine credit requir the productive sectors would be comfortably met by the significant accretion in bank deposi

During the 1980s the average current account deficit was of the order of 2.0 of GDP. Even when we faced the Gulf crisis we had a current account deficit of a mere 3.2 Since then, it has remained well below 2 per cent. In 1997-98, despite large uncertainties, account deficit remained modest at about 1.7 per cent of GDP. In 1998-99, the relatively lo oil prices in international markets and trends in invisible receipts should help maintain account deficit at a sustainable level of about 2 per cent of GDP. This order of curre deficit is clearly sustainable and we expect it to be financed by capital flows. In additio the comfort of a reasonable level of foreign currency reserves, which we would not hesitat curb speculative activities and ensure orderly conditions in the market.

During 1997-98, we added $ 3 billion to our foreign currency assets despite pa of  over  $  2  billion  effected  directly  from  reserves  under  the  FCNR-A  deposits  schem repayments  to  the  IMF.  During  1998-99  also,  despite  all  the  turbulence,  we  have  increa foreign currency assets marginally from $ 25,975 million as at end-March 1998 to $ 26,135 as on September 18, 1998.

We fully recognise that the uncertain international financial and economic si poses considerable policy challenges. Of late, there have been some unfavourable developm the Russian economy and in a few Latin American countries. The developments in the indu countries, in particular Japan, are also being closely watched as they impact not only account, but also capital flows. On the whole, the international scene has been unfavo developing countries. However, in so far as markets in India are concerned, the response fairly reasonable and has been less volatile than other countries in the region.

From the presentation I have made on prospects, it should be evident that Indi position to meet the challenges of possible adverse international developments. The recent the  Resurgent  India  Bonds  is  a  clear  testimony  to  the  confidence  which  investors  have country.  We  fully  recognise  that  there  is  no  room  for  complacency,  but  we  do  believe economic fundamentals, prudent management as well as the operational framework of capital will ensure the reasonable stability in the external sector that has been the hallmark of I process.

In conclusion, the relative tranquility of the Indian economy in the face of crisis  was  neither  an  accident  nor  a  stroke  of  luck.  The  management  of  the  capital  ac displayed  pragmatism  and  a  contextual  response  to  a  changing  environment.  The  prospect 1998-99  indicate  continued  stability  in  our  external  sector,  consistent  with  our  recor performance. In fact, I expect that the second half of the current fiscal year will be b first half, in terms of sentiment and economic performance.
author: Y V Reddy

title: Mr. Macfarlane comments on the future international financial architecture  (Central Bank Articles and Speeches, 14 Oct 98)
description: Talk by the Governor of the Reserve Bank of Australia, Mr. I.J. Macfarlane, to the East Asia Economic Summit in Singapore on 14/10/98.
text:
Mr. Macfarlane comments on the future international financial architecture Talk by the Governor of the Reserve Bank of Australia, Mr. I.J. Macfarlane, to the E

Economic Summit in Singapore on 14/10/98.

…

In my ten minutes here I will try and cover what I see as the main chan perspective about what we formerly termed the Asian crisis, and then say a few words future international financial architecture.

- The main change is that since August this year we no longer think of an crisis but we now think of either an emerging markets crisis or a genera financial crisis.
- A second important change is that the western policy establishment ca longer  believe  that  the  root  cause  of  the  problem  is  the  inadequacy financial  infrastructure  and  governance  of  some  formerly  rapidly  gro Asian countries. Of course, not everyone used to believe this, but ther some very influential institutions that thought this way.
- Everyone is now aware that contagion is a much stronger force than form thought. Contagion is an essentially irrational force which tars large g countries with the same brush, and causes fear to overrule reason.
- Given the bigger role for contagion, more and more people are asking whe the international financial system as it has operated for most of the basically unstable. By now, I think the majority of observers have come conclusion that it is, and that some changes have to be made.

With  pretty  well  everyone  now  conceding  that  changes  have  to  be  made,  y would think it would be a relatively simple matter to move on to the next step. But it because there are still big differences of opinion about how serious the problem is.

- One school of thought held that the main thing required to restore stabi to  improve  transparency,  particularly  the  Government's  transparency  to private sector - e.g. by more frequent and accurate publication of fig international reserves. This school of thought also gave a fair bit of improving the quality of bank supervision in emerging market countries. explains the motivation behind two of the three working groups set up b G22 in April.
- But an increasing majority think something more is required, and the promising approach here goes under the general title of burden sharing the private sector (the G22's third working group). I would like to say more about this because I think it will be necessary if we are to mak progress.

If we go back and think of the Thai, Korean or Indonesian crises, we can s problem if there is no formal system of burden sharing. Once the currency doubts start term  lenders  knew  that  if  they  could  get  their  money  out  fast  enough  they  would  mi currency losses and loan losses. So when each loan had to be rolled over it was not ren capital  flowed  out.  Each  day  this  happened  the  exchange  rate  came  under  further  dow

pressure, which encouraged further capital flight. Everyone wanted to be out before the reached where the exchange rate was so low, interest rates were so high, and insolvenc so rife, that those who could not get out of the door would be big losers. This process maximum fall in the exchange rate.

Something clearly has to be done in terms of managing the crisis to redu incentives  for  everyone  to  try  to  be  the  first  one  out  of  the  door.  Some  system  of followed by an orderly workout involving rollovers, reschedulings and, in extreme cas equity swaps is clearly required. No country wants to be the first one to do this, an action could cause panic in other countries à la Russia. What is needed is a system th cooperation between the host country, private lenders and the IMF. We saw an example o effective this can be for Korean bank-to-bank debt late last year.

Ideally, this should not be on an ad hoc basis, as it was in Korea, but s thought  out  well  in  advance,  with  the  possibility  of  such  workouts  included  i documentation.  This,  of  course,  would  increase  the  cost  of  borrowing  by  emerging  m economies, but that would be no bad thing. One of the problems over the last five years it became too cheap and too much of it was done. It would be better than excessive followed by capital flight as we have seen over the past few years.

This is all becoming reasonably conventional thinking now and, as I said contained in the third Working Party Report of the G22. But it was not that long ago suggestions  along  these  lines  were  greeted  with  the  response  that  it  was  out  of  th because it involved interfering with the free movement of capital.

I would like to conclude by mentioning two other things that have changed the past year.

## First, hedge funds.

As recently as three months ago if you complained about the activities of funds you were regarded as paranoid and you received a sermon on the dangers of shooti messenger, etc.

Now, no one has got a good word to say for them, and they are likely to so brought into either:

- the disclosure net, or
- some form of supervision via their connections with banks.

Second, I see a clear improvement in future crisis management in the way the is talking with Brazil.

Unlike the Asian crises, I don't see any country in future putting itself in of the IMF without knowing pretty clearly beforehand what the IMF conditions will b doesn't like the conditions, for example, because they are too wide-ranging, it will n Fund. If it is comfortable with the conditions, it will be able to sign up from day one

This way, we should be able to avoid the long periods of semi-public hag over conditions that characterised the Asian crises and did so much to frighten the ma pushing exchange rates down excessively.

title: Mr. Yam discusses the political process of monetary management in Hong Kong  (Central Bank Articles and Speeches, 20 Oct 98)
description: Text of the Thirteenth Susan Yuen Memorial Lecture delivered by the Chief Executive of the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, Mr. Joseph Yam, JP, at the Hong Kong Management Association on 20/10/98.
text:
Mr. Yam discusses the political process of monetary management in Hong Kong Text of the Thirteenth Susan Yuen Memorial Lecture delivered by the Chief Execut the  Hong  Kong  Monetary  Authority,  Mr.  Joseph  Yam,  JP,  at  the  Hong  Kong  Management Association on 20/10/98.

…

1. I am particularly pleased to be here this evening to deliver the Thirtee Yuen Memorial Lecture. I never had the privilege of meeting the late Mrs. Susan Yuen. reading her brief history in the material published by the Hong Kong Management Associa found out that she and I both came to Hong Kong from the Mainland in 1949. And we b became the first Chief Executives of HKMAs - the Hong Kong Management Association in h case and the Hong Kong Monetary Authority in my case. But I fear that I shall never ach distinction of having a Memorial Lecture dedicated in my name. And certainly at the age I am content not to have to ponder such matters. It is a sufficient honour to have bee celebrate with you Susan Yuen's distinguished record of public service.

2. I would like to talk about the political process of monetary management with your theme of 'Managing Economic Turbulence in Asia'.

## Controversy

3. I am sure you are aware of the controversy over how we managed the finan turmoil  that  we  have  been  facing.  There  have  been  many  complaints  about  a  wide  ran issues. Our critics have told us that we should not have squeezed so hard on interes October and that we should not have increased the cost of borrowing for business and f who  have  to  service  their  home  mortgages.  We  should  have  introduced  our  measures strengthen our monetary and financial systems earlier. We should not have departed f free market policy and intervened in the stock and futures markets. That there was a 'sense of crisis' in how we handled the situation. These are the more significant criti

4.  I  can  fully  understand  the  sentiment  behind  these  criticisms.  The  peo Hong Kong have been suffering the worst conditions we have had to face for many years. the most patient and understanding community will have grievances when the value of the they hold has been halved while they have to pay significantly higher interest costs liabilities. Furthermore, income has not been growing, and, for some, it has been shrin worse still, the probability that they may lose their jobs has doubled in the past year.

5. So, whatever the cause of this difficult situation, whether or not it events outside the control of the authorities, it is considered, and rightly so, the re caring government to do what it can to relieve these grievances. Refusal or reluctance even for very sound reasons in the larger long-term public interest, is not looked u Even in cases where the authorities managed to be innovative, perhaps to an extent not expected of bureaucrats, and did the right thing, there is always the easy, popular bu question of why action was not taken earlier.

## The Political Process of Monetary Management

6.  In  Hong  Kong,  the  grievances  of  the  community  are  enthusiastically effectively aired by politicians. Whether directly or indirectly elected, the politic

mandate of the people and the people of Hong Kong are well served by them. But one o peculiarities of the system of Hong Kong is that the politicians, although having the the people, do not actually have the authority to direct government policies. A conse this  is  that  the  Administration  is  always  kept  on  its  toes,  much  more  so  than  in  m jurisdictions. There are lively debates on almost all issues of significance, not to that  are  controversial.  This  obviously  has  the  benefit  of  ensuring  that  the  Admi performs to its best ability. But the inevitable disadvantage is simply that there can of everything, to the extent of eroding rather than enhancing the efficiency and effec government. But this is the reality of Hong Kong today and we all have to live with it.

7. The management of any public issue of significance involves first gett technicalities right, then explaining them patiently and clearly to all those concern handling skillfully the politics surrounding it. More often than not, handling the po most  difficult  part.  You  can  be  100  per  cent  right  technically  and  you  can  spend explaining all the fine details, relating them to the policy objective and the public i you are not skillful enough in the handling of the politics of the issue, particular whose success the confidence of the people plays a crucial part, all your efforts might A totally different perception than that intended could well result, undermining the success of what you are trying to achieve.

8.  Let  me  focus  specifically  on  the  management  of  the  political  pr concerning monetary issues. I must say that this task is, for the HKMA, becoming incr difficult and time-consuming. Monetary issues are unfortunately very technical and elu they affect everybody. Money is dear to the heart of everyone. We work hard to earn it use it everyday, which can often be, thank goodness, the more pleasant aspect of it. naturally to us, the price and the value of money are things that we should be concer Here, already to a layperson or to the average politician, we are being esoteric. What of money? What is the value of money? And what are the differences between the two? should we be concerned about them? These are very legitimate questions. And they are not easy questions to answer or easy concepts to put across.

9. So, imagine trying to explain, and obtain support for, the following p 'to dampen interest rate volatility and lessen the interest rate pain by redefining base to include debt paper discountable at the HKMA through overnight repurchase agree and fully backed by foreign reserves without departing from the monetary rule of curren arrangements which requires the monetary base to change only with a corresponding chan foreign reserves'. This really is a mouthful. And to some, I must have been speaking Gr I can assure you that the wording of the proposal is precise and technically 100 per c In fact, this was exactly what we did when we introduced the seven technical measures September to strengthen our monetary system. And the proposal has worked well so far. B the proposal been presented in those terms, I think even the most learned academics wo taken some time to figure out what we were up to.

10. The likely result is that nobody would be willing to comment on the pr for fear of exposing ignorance on the subject. This might be considered a good result, ourselves being able to achieve what in our professional opinion should be done. An community has faith in the HKMA, confident that we know what we are doing, we may even public support. But it is also a risky result. First of all, we can of course be wron naive to think that we can be right all the time. Nobody can be. We can only be less w more importantly, public support should not be built merely upon faith in an esoteric

HKMA being professional and acting in the best interest of Hong Kong. Whatever reputati HKMA has been able to achieve, domestically and internationally, such support could ne sustained  for  long.  We  do  run  a  system  that,  at  times,  inflicts  considerable  pa community.  Many  of  the  decisions  taken  by  the  HKMA  are  unpopular.  The  pain  and  t unpopular decisions may become too severe to bear just on the foundation of faith, part the peculiar political setup of Hong Kong.

11.  An  essential  part  in  the  management  of  the  political  process  conce monetary issues, therefore, is to promote a better general understanding on those issu not easy. Not only are those issues technical, but they are also changing all the ti rapid  changes  in  the  global  financial  scene.  Financial  liberalization  and  the  globa financial markets, encouraged by the advance of telecommunications and informa technology, have drastically changed the behaviour of money. On top of all this, we complication that Hong Kong's monetary system has really only started to take shape in ten years or so, as monetary reform measures were introduced to modernize it so it co with the demands and expectations of modern finance. But these difficulties are not ex not trying. And we have tried; although I must confess, on the basis of the reaction fr the politicians to the actions we have taken recently, that the returns on our efforts better general understanding of monetary issues in Hong Kong have not been impressive.

12. So we must try harder, and we will. There are then the questions on ho the areas in which we need to concentrate our efforts. On the former I shall seek advic colleagues. On the latter, the recent episode surrounding our operations in the stock markets, culminating in the defeated Motion Debate in the Legislative Council on 30 Se 1998  to  review  the  HKMA,  provides  excellent  guidance.  If  one  filters  away  the  nois political posturing, including the rather unpleasant and unnecessary personal attacks three areas that require attention.

## Basic Monetary Concepts

13.  The  first  area  that  requires  attention  concerns  various  concepts  in monetary management that need to be more effectively put across. This is essential if d on the technical issues are to be more meaningful. I am aware that this is not inten lecture on monetary economics, so let me just bring out one or two of them here for ill

14.  Under  our  linked  exchange  rate  system,  stability  in  the  exchange  r ensured  through  the  control  on  what  is  called  the  monetary  base.  If  you  were  to representative grouping of the community, say, the Legislative Council, what the monet is, I would be surprised if more than ten per cent of the group could come up with t answer. Many would be tempted to relate this to the various definitions of the money because that is the term mostly heard in commentaries on money and finance. But they a different things. The crucial part of the monetary base and the money supply, however are in fact on the different sides of the balance sheet of the banking system. Put this group of academics and you would probably, on the contrary, get as many definitions as people in that group.

15. This confusion is understandable and, at least partly, in the context Kong, a reflection of the rather peculiar institutional framework for monetary manageme past that is now, one hopes, history, with the ten years of reforms to our monetary s may be surprised to hear this. It was not until the end of 1996 that the monetary bas

Kong was properly defined. This was when, on the occasion of the introduction of Rea Gross  Settlement  for  interbank  transactions,  all  licensed  banks  were  required  to clearing  account  with  the  HKMA  instead  of  with  a  commercial  bank.  Yet  we  have  be somehow, controlling, or we claimed to have been controlling, the monetary base ever s linked exchange rate system was established in October 1983.

16. Even assuming that the definition of the monetary base is well under there is then the important question of how it should be controlled. Herein lies one interesting subjects in monetary management and that is the choice between discretionar with people making decisions, and automatic rule-based control with no discretionary d involved.  Associated  with  this  are  considerations  concerning,  and  possibly  another between, flexibility in management and the credibility of the monetary system. Even t professionally  competent  central  banker  can  be  wrong.  A  system  that  involves  discre decisions is therefore subject to human errors of judgement that may undermine the cred the system, and some would go as far as to argue that this would eventually lead to fai system. On the other hand, an entirely rule-based system without any discretion is infl may  not  serve  the  best  interest  of  the  community,  even  though  short-term  interes sometimes  be  involved  -  witness  the  many  calls  for  lowering  interest  rates  even  w exchange rate is under pressure.

17. Another related conceptual issue that needs to be put across clearly is classical currency board system, as structured in the old colonial era, whilst still sound, has long become impracticable in coping with the complexities of modern finance. old days, transactions were conducted predominantly with the use of physical cash. And focus of attention in currency board theory was merely that the issue of cash should 100  per  cent  by  foreign  reserves  and  rather  simplistically  that  cash  arbitrage  would exchange  rate  stable.  There  was  nothing  much  about  the  monetary  base  and  the  adjus process in response to capital flows involving movements in domestic interest rates. T also  did  not  take  into  account  the  many  and  much  larger  volumes  of  transactions  no conducted with the use of electronic money and settled electronically without the use o cash.  As  a  result,  the  crucial  part  of  the  monetary  base  is  no  longer  the  amount circulation but a much smaller yet highly leveraged element in the form of the aggregat that banks have in their clearing accounts maintained with the currency board, that is t

18. The old theory also did not take into account the need for the currenc to be controlling the interbank payments system and therefore performing the role as pr liquidity  to  the  banking  system.  As  a  result  when  our  currency  board  arrangements modernized  through  monetary  reform  in  the  past  ten  years,  many  of  our  actions misunderstood even by leading monetary economists. But to be fair, even we ourselves we entirely sure about a few things, as we moved into the uncharted waters of modern c board theory and practice.

19.  Yet  another  conceptual  issue  to  be  put  across  clearly  is  the  fact inevitable cost of fixing the exchange rate through currency board arrangements is in volatility. An external shock involving any substantial flows of funds into or out of will lead to interest rate changes. The larger the flow the sharper the changes, in a much dictated by the market. And as there is little or no discretion on the part of th interest  rates,  the  HKMA  was  in  fact  not  responsible,  for  example,  for  overnight  i interest rates hitting 280% last October. We did not squeeze interest rates. It was th the Hong Kong dollar who squeezed interest rates and, on that occasion, squeezed themse

well, along with the innocent borrowers. Interest rate volatility can be dampened by di action, but that would undermine the credibility of the system. Alternatively this cou by  further  modifying  our  currency  board  arrangements  and  incurring  the  cost  in  the greater fluctuation in our foreign reserves while eschewing the exercise of discretion the objective of the seven technical measures we took in early September to make our less susceptible to manipulation.

20. I do not wish to continue to bore you with these conceptual issues. Al they are technical, they are essential if there is to be sensible and meaningful disc monetary management in Hong Kong. I shall be stepping up the efforts of the HKMA to pro a better understanding of them.

## Transparency

21. The second area that requires attention in the political process of management concerns the transparency of the HKMA. To at least the minority of those mem of  Legislative  Council  who  supported  the  defeated  Motion  to  review  the  HKMA, transparency of the HKMA was found to be lacking. Although the Motion was defeated, the that transparency was an issue, even to the minority of the Legislature, is quite surp It is perhaps not something that I can afford to ignore. However, compared with othe banks, the HKMA must be among the most transparent in the world. In monetary manageme specifically, I am quite sure that we are the most transparent in the world. I know central bank that discloses information about the monetary base, and operations affecti real-time basis. There is also an abundance of information published in the HKMA's series  of  monthly,  quarterly  and  annual  reports,  and  in  the  ad  hoc  publications  o monetary and banking issues. Figures on foreign reserves are published monthly and so shall be publishing the balance sheet of the Exchange Fund also on a monthly basis.

22. Perhaps this minority view was based on the practice, now becoming q common  in  other  central  banks,  that  the  proceedings  of  monetary  policy  committee published, so that the public is made aware of how monetary policy decisions are taken entrusted with the authority to make them. There are the examples of the Federal Open Committee (FOMC) of the Federal Reserve Bank in the United States and the Monetary Po Committee  of  the  Bank  of  England.  The  minutes  of  their  meetings  are  published  wit appropriate time lag. In Hong Kong we do not have an equivalent of the FOMC or the Mone Policy Committee. This is simply because we do not have an independent monetary polic an independent body making that policy. We do not have a system whereby the HKMA has take discretionary decisions to determine interest rates or to specify monetary target therefore not been a need for a mechanism for public scrutiny of discretionary decision there is nothing to scrutinize.

23. Our monetary system is rule-based. To the extent that there is a need t mechanism for public scrutiny, it should be aimed at ensuring that the HKMA adheres rules  and  does  not  indulge  secretly  in  discretionary  monetary  management.  We  have  a volunteered this mechanism in providing real time information on the monetary base. C and  forecasts  of  changes  to  the  monetary  base  are  announced  almost  immediately  aft relevant transactions have been conducted. There is no parallel with this practice i jurisdiction.

24. But the process of modernization of our currency board arrangements is to be a continuous one, in the light of possible rapid and significant changes in the financial architecture. The Financial Secretary as controller of the Exchange Fund, and Monetary Authority under his delegated authority, are responsible for making decisions area, in consultation with the statutory Exchange Fund Advisory Committee (EFAC). Rece with the agreement of the Financial Secretary, a subcommittee of the EFAC on currency operations chaired by me has also been set up to advise, among other things, on curren arrangements.

25. Whilst it can be argued that transparency in this area of work would enhance the credibility of the system and the HKMA, it must, however, be noted that pr in this area are likely to be market sensitive. It will not be easy to strike a balance obviously try. I shall shortly be making a proposal to the Financial Secretary initi minutes of meetings of the subcommittee, other than those concerning market sensitive i be published, with an appropriate time lag. Consideration will also be given to the sub conducting public hearings to receive opinions and suggestions on monetary management members of the public. In the light of experience of this practice, consideration can l to do the same for the minutes of meetings of the EFAC.

## Accountability

26.  The  third  area  that  requires  attention  in  the  political  process  of management  concerns  the  accountability  of  the  HKMA.  Here  again,  there  are  cer characteristics peculiar to Hong Kong. Unlike arrangements in other jurisdictions, the the institution responsible for issues generically called central banking, is not a bo by  law.  The  legal  entity  is  the  Monetary  Authority,  as  a  person,  appointed  by  the Secretary to assist him in the performance of his duties under the Exchange Fund Ordi have the honour of being the person who has been so appointed. That means I am accounta the  Financial  Secretary  for  my  actions  when  exercising  the  authority  delegated  to  m Financial Secretary under the Exchange Fund Ordinance. The Financial Secretary is advi the EFAC appointed by the Chief Executive of the HKSAR, whose authority has been delega to the Financial Secretary.

27.  It  is  through  the  Financial  Secretary  that  the  Monetary  Authori accountable to third parties, and the form this takes is determined by the Financial S the Financial Secretary wants me to appear before the Legislative Council and formally report to the Council every six months, as suggested by some, I am quite happy to do so Financial Secretary must of course make an assessment of whether the implications of practice are acceptable. He must take a view on whether this would introduce an ave political interference in the work of the HKMA, in particular in monetary management. H also take a view on whether this would undermine the effectiveness of the relationship the Administration, in particular himself, and the HKMA.

28. Insofar as getting things done at the technical level is concerned, fo in achieving the broad policy objectives of monetary and banking stability, and the de of  the  financial  infrastructure,  the  existing  relationship  between  the  Administrati HKMA has worked well. The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate has remained very stable and banking  system  robust,  and  Hong  Kong  now  has  one  of  the  most  sophisticated  finan infrastructures in the world.

29.  It  is  of  course  up  to  the  Administration  to  consider  whether,  for reasons,  the  unusual  arrangements  for  the  appointment  of  the  Monetary  Authority  an framework defining his accountability should be looked at. But it should be remember those unusual arrangements had the agreement of the Legislative Council as recently as when it approved the required amendments to the Exchange Fund Ordinance. Admittedly, details of the amendments then reflected expediency dictated by political considerati time. But the arrangements have worked well for Hong Kong.

30. The Administration may feel that there is a need for the existing arran to be replaced by a separate Ordinance establishing an institution called the HKMA, h own board and clearly defined functions. This appears sensible and is at least consi arrangements  in  other  jurisdictions.  But  it  is  my  strong  view  that,  should  this  be desirable for whatever reasons, the opportunity should be taken to achieve greater an autonomy  for  the  HKMA.  There  should  be  more,  and  not  fewer,  safeguards  against  poli interference in the work of the HKMA. The Administration has indicated that it will matter  forward  in  due  course  and  no  doubt  the  Legislature  will  be  consulted  whe Administration has formulated more concrete proposals. My advice, for what it is wort proceed cautiously and in quieter times when market conditions are less unsettled.

31. Thank you very much again for giving me the honour of delivering the S Yuen Memorial Lecture.

title: Mr. Meyer reports on increasing global financial integrity: the roles of market discipline, regulation and supervision  (Central Bank Articles and Speeches, 22 Oct 98)
description: Speech by Mr. Laurence H. Meyer, a member of the Board of Governors of the US Federal Reserve System, at the 16th Annual Monetary Conference, Cato Institute, Washington, DC on 22/10/98.
text:
Mr.  Meyer  reports  on  increasing  global  financial  integrity:  the  roles market discipline, regulation and supervision Speech by Mr. Laurence H. Meyer a member of the  Board  of  Governors  of  the  US  Federal  Reserve  System,  at  the  16th  Annual  Mone Conference, Cato Institute, Washington, DC on 22/10/98.

Recent developments, both at home and abroad, have reinforced the importanc efforts to increase the stability of global banking and financial markets. The central promoting the stability of the global banking system is sometimes viewed as bringing systems around the world up to best practice standards, as exemplified in the superv regulatory frameworks of advanced industrial economies. While this is, to be sure, a pr least  for  internationally  active  banks  around  the  world  -  let  me  offer  a  more  comp framework for thinking about enhancing the stability of the global banking system.

First,  best  practices  is  a  dynamic,  not  a  static  concept.  The  rapid  c banking  markets  and  practices,  and  more  generally  in  financial  markets  and  instr challenges  supervisors  and  regulators  around  the  world  to  adapt  in  order  to  main effectiveness of regulatory standards and supervisory practices. Best practices simpl better over time or they will soon not be good enough.

Second, best practices may not be the same for all banking organizations time to think about not only enhancing the contributions of market discipline, reformi standards  and  enhancing  supervisory  practice  at  the  largest  and  most  complex  ba organizations,  but  also  about  differentiating  how  we  regulate  and  supervise  these  i relative to small and medium-sized banks.

Third, we have to continue to work on appropriate global norms and make gre progress in achieving greater convergence to best practices - including, perhaps, dif practices  for  different  classes  of  institutions  -  around  the  world.  This  means investments in developing the standards, in technical assistance, and in monitoring com

I am going to apply this broader perspective on global banking to three pi an efficient and effective supervisory and regulatory framework for banking: market di regulation,  and  supervision.  First,  I  will  discuss  the  potential  for  enhanced  dis improved incentives to increase the effectiveness of market discipline in controlling by banks. Second, I will discuss the importance of reforming our international capital as an example of dynamic best practices. Third, I want to emphasize the important role supervision.

## I. Market Discipline: Information and Incentives

There appears to be a renaissance in appreciation of the contribution of discipline in banking. This undoubtedly reflects a growing awareness that recent develop banking  and  financial  markets  have  made  regulatory  standards  less  effective  and  supe more challenging, that it may be simply impossible to adapt regulatory standards and su practices fast enough to keep pace with market developments.

Of  course,  market  discipline  does  not  come  easy  to  banking.  We  start establishing a safety net for banks, including deposit insurance, access to a lender o and payment system guarantees. This immediately reduces the incentives of market parti to monitor the risk-taking of banks and, in turn, encourages excessive risk-taking by

then  put  in  place  a  regulatory  and  supervisory  framework  to  counter  these  moral incentives.  And,  when  we  are  done,  we  complain  about  the  absence  of  market  discipl appreciate that this sounds just a bit contradictory.

I could be more consistent and perhaps more appreciated at this institute i the dismantling of the federal safety net and the full return to reliance on market dis is clear that society has made one of those irreversible choices and will not choose deposit insurance, the discount window, a Federal Reserve payments system, or bank supe and regulation. Moreover, my reading of history suggests that, despite the strong indi the success of market discipline, the cost of the associated financial market disturba economic  activity  are  too  high  for  market  discipline  to  be  the  sole  regulator  of understand  opinions  differ  on  this,  just  as  they  must  when  supervisors  and  regulat judgments to act at specific times. But, what is worth understanding is that there is agreement that moral hazard is a significant problem, that the markets are increasingly making it more difficult for supervisors and regulators - and that supervision and regu significant costs and inefficiencies. As a result, we must begin to increase our relian discipline both as a governor and as an indicator.

When I talk about market discipline, some hear a call for a substitution market discipline for less regulation and supervision. Listen more closely. My concern task  of  regulation  and  supervision  has  become  more  challenging  and  we  therefore  ha increase the effectiveness of our overall regulatory and supervisory framework to keep p referring here to the increased size, breadth and geographic scope of banking and to it globalization and complexity. I want to achieve this increased effectiveness by enhanci discipline, modifying our regulatory standards, and adapting supervisory practice. We an efficient regulatory framework, one that achieves its objectives at the lowest cost. are opportunities to achieve the same degree of stability through increased reliance and reduced emphasis on regulation and supervision, we should, of course, do so. But ri my focus is on increasing the overall effectiveness of the framework and in relying a possible on market discipline and improved capital standards to get this job done.

It is one thing to extol the virtue of markets and another thing to find make them work more effectively in controlling risk-taking in banking, at least in the the safety net. The time has come to move beyond rhetoric to specific actions. Within t Reserve System we have a variety of working groups and committees working to this end also have the benefit of ongoing work and recent reports by the Basle Committee on B Supervision and the Group of 22. I expect that these efforts will result in concret soon.

Market discipline is about information and incentives. Market participant have  access  to  reliable  and  timely  information  on  the  financial  conditions  and  pro banking firms, and both the market participants and the firms must have incentives to r this information. With respect to information, we need to consider what additional d would contribute to enhanced market discipline. Providing incentives is important beca incentives can encourage banks to provide voluntarily the information the market demands

I have not come with a specific set of recommendations for improved disclo But  two  common  principles  apply  here  as  well  as  to  issues  related  to  regulatory  ref adaptation of supervisory practice. Banking systems in emerging economies have a long go to catch up to global norms with respect to disclosure. Banks that want to play

markets should meet international standards with respect to transparency and disclosure systems in developed economies, in turn, should not be resting on their laurels when i transparency  and  disclosure.  Here  again  'best  practices'  has  to  be  understood  as  a process. The increased complexity of banking, the speed with which risk positions can and the increased size and breadth of banking organizations all seem to point to the us improving disclosure to provide the raw material the markets need to continuously re changing risk profiles.

Improved  disclosures  about  risk  management  practices,  risk  profiles,  and management performance -coupled with disclosures about regulatory capital and components,  risk-weighted  assets  and  related  matters  -  could  provide  transparency  t facilitate  market  discipline.  Timely  disclosure  of  this  information  would  enable participants and supervisors to better assess how institutions maintain sound capital i their changing risk exposures. Some of these types of disclosures are among those set f recent  Basle  Committee  paper  on  Enhancing  Bank  Transparency.  International  disclo standards  should  include,  for  example,  guidelines  for  reporting  non-performing  loa provisioning  for  non-performing  loans,  and  for  classifying  the  quality  of  loans.  U international banking statistics to provide more detailed data on international expos enhance  the  ability  of  both  supervisors  and  market  participants  to  assess  the  vulne domestic banking systems to financial shocks from abroad. It would also be useful to better information about the complex activities of the largest, internationally active as securitizations, credit risk modeling and credit derivatives.

The second foundation of market discipline is incentives. One promising dir might be to require at least the largest and most complex banks to issue minimum amo subordinated debt as a way of enhancing market discipline. To a degree I view this as a for  specific  steps  to  enhance  market  discipline,  to  emphasize  that  we  have  to  move rhetorical  praise  for  markets  to  specific  steps  to  harness  the  role  of  markets  in risk-taking by banks. There may be other approaches that can accomplish this task, as g better than subordinated debt. But, right now, I do believe there is considerable pr subordinated debt requirement.

An appealing aspect of this approach is that subordinated debt holders, so they are not bank 'insiders,' face only downside risk, and thus their risk preferenc close to those of the FDIC. Subordinated debt holders would therefore be expected to market discipline on the bank that is quite consistent with what bank supervisors are t including  encouraging  banks  to  disclose  more  information  about  their  financial  con Observed risk premiums on subordinated debt could perhaps be used to help the FDIC set accurate risk-based deposit insurance premiums, and such debt would provide an extra of protection to taxpayers. An additional benefit of having subordinated debt traded o market,  at  least  if  the  market  for  subordinated  debt  was  sufficiently  liquid,  is movements  would  provide  a  clear  signal  of  the  market  evaluation  of  the  bank's  fi condition that would serve as an early warning signal to aid supervisors.

Such an approach would most likely be limited to the largest banks for at le reasons. First, it is the increased size of banking organizations and the financial i the  largest  and  most  sophisticated  banks  that  are  challenging  the  effectiveness  of regulatory and supervisory framework. Second, it is unclear just how deep and liquid for bank subordinated debt would be and what access small and medium-sized banks would

to this market. This suggests that an operationally feasible program of mandatory sub debt would require a considerable amount of further thought.

## II. Reforming Capital Standards

Market discipline, as I noted, is a complement to the regulation and supe required by the safety net. The foundation for bank regulation has long been capital Since 1998, these have been international standards as embodied in the Basle Accord.

Capital  standards  can  be  thought  of  as  a  way  of  reinforcing  market  disc because they shift more of the risk to shareholders relative to taxpayers. In this way, closest relative to market discipline among bank regulations. That is the good news abo standards. The bad news is they are becoming increasingly less meaningful and progre undermined as a result of regulatory capital arbitrage.

Regulatory  capital  arbitrage  refers  to  the  gaming  of  the  capital  standa exploitation of loopholes that allows banking organizations to lower the amount of cap given level of risk. Regulatory capital arbitrage has been encouraged by the limitati excessive rigidity in the current capital standards. To be sure, it serves as a kind o preventing the capital rules from distorting bank behavior in non-economic ways. But arbitrage  also  undermines  the  effectiveness  of  our  capital  rules  and  creates  some distortions.

Banks engage in regulatory capital arbitrage mainly through securitizatio credit derivatives. These vehicles offer improved opportunities for banks to manage t and liquidity. Securitizations allow banks to transfer the risk of an underlying loan p markets, retaining their role in the origination of loans, but transferring more of funding to the capital markets. Credit derivatives are another vehicle for shifting som of the underlying loan pool, while avoiding disclosure of an effective loan sale an harming a customer relationship.

There are two problems with the use of securitization and credit derivative banks  often  use  these  vehicles  to  reduce  capital  charges  by  more  than  they  reduce associated with the underlying loan pool. This is the problem of limited transferenc Banks generally retain the risk of 'first dollar' or 'second dollar' loss on the unde via  various  credit  enhancements.  Indeed,  through  devices  such  as  'remote  originatio 'indirect credit enhancements' the regulatory capital associated with retained risks c low, even zero. As a result, some refinement in the capital treatment of securitization derivatives is needed to better match the capital with the retained risk by banking orga

But  the  second  problem  is  the  more  difficult  one.  Securitizations  and derivatives are basically exercises in cherry picking. That is, they allow banks to tra quality assets out of their banking book. Banks do so for good reason, to be sure. T because our current capital standards apply the same risk weight to all non-mortgage l the  regulatory  capital  charges  for  the  highest  quality  loans  are  often  well  in  ex economic capital that banks internally allocate to such loans. In a world of increased banks have to use every opportunity to manage their risks and capital to best advantage means  either  not  originating  such  high  quality  loans  or  finding  ways  to  make  the  r capital  converge  to  their  estimate  of  the  economic  capital  of  such  loans. arbitrage is a safety valve because it allows banks to stay in the business of making quality loans.

It  is,  of  course,  important  to  force  banks  to  recogniz promptly  when  they  occur;  it  is  even  better  to  make  sure  that  the  probability  of occurring is contained to begin with. To this end US supervisors now conduct examinat bank risk measurement and management processes, not just examinations of bank assets. also reflects the new dynamics of bank risk-taking, the prospect of rapid change in risk  because  of  the  changed  nature  of  bank  practices,  changes  in  the  technology  th changes through markets, and changes in financial instruments. money the old-fashioned way: poor credit judgments and bad luck. We should not lose s this as we adopt new procedures and techniques.

## IV. Conclusion

Banks  in  emerging  economies  are  increasingly  becoming  players  in  glob banking. There  is  an  important  role  in  this  pr international  standard  setting,  technical  assistance,  and  monitoring  compliance  wi standards.

At the same time, consolidation, globalization, and the increased complexi breadth of activities are increasing the challenge of regulating and supervising banks world. Best practices must therefore keep pace with market developments. I believe that for  dynamic  best  practices  involves  enhancing  the  role  of  market  discipline,  re international capital standards, and improving supervisory practice.

text:

I would like to start by adding my voice to those who have already welcomed to this Conference and to the city of Sydney. It goes without saying that there could more propitious time for the international leaders in the field of bank supervision to When we first started planning this Conference a couple of years ago, we did not know it would attract a lot of interest or would be greeted with a yawn. We now know it is and  we  in  the  Reserve  Bank,  and  our  colleagues  at  the  Australian  Prudential  Regu Authority, with whom we are jointly hosting the Conference, are sure that you will be very interesting couple of days.

It  is  hard  to  pick  up  a  newspaper  these  days  without  seeing  the  word  'c prominently displayed in a headline somewhere. First, we had the Asian crisis, then it being an emerging markets crisis, and now we hear so much talk of a world financial cr interesting that, so far, the focus is on the word 'financial' and not on the more g 'economic'. One consequence of these two trends is that the contrast b economic  health  and  concerns  about  the  financial  sector  is  as  marked  in  the  world powerful economy - the United States - as elsewhere. There is a big challenge, therefo bank supervisors of the world, and it seems to be equally large whether they are dealin least, or the most, sophisticated of the world's banking systems.

I see two main challenges for the world's economic policymakers - one for short term and one for the medium term.

In the short run, the challenge is to get through the current crisis - to m more dominoes fall through contagion. The region at risk is clearly Latin America, eve many of these countries are now running infinitely better macroeconomic policies tha have been imagined a decade ago. One helpful recent development is the acceptance that there should be behin scenes discussions between a potential borrower and the IMF. If an IMF package does pr be necessary in the case of Brazil, for example, it will already have had its voice h will know exactly what the conditions are in advance. It thus should be able to sign One and so avoid the situation that occurred in Asia where countries put themselves in of the IMF without knowing what the conditions would be. Thus, the handling of the Br situation seems to be benefiting from one of the lessons of the Asian rescue packages.

What can bank supervisors do to assist in the resolution of the present si Given that a major part of the problem is an increase in risk aversion by lenders and 'credit crunch', it seems to me that bank supervisors will inevitably have a very big i the outcome. become even more risk averse than they currently are. This will require great sensitiv part of supervisors, and I am sure you will all rise to the challenge.

The second big challenge to all of us involved in international finance is a better system for the long run. None of us should be happy about how events have u over the past five years, and none of us could deny the claim that the internationa system is prone to periods of extreme financial turbulence that leave lasting economic c

Soon, however, more thoughtful people saw the source of the instability as the combination of two things - large movements of short-term capital taking place in that had small and not very well developed financial infrastructures.

We now know that there is a third important factor at work as well - ba developed countries (often in conjunction with hedge funds) have been taking much bigge than their supervisors or their shareholders thought.

How do we go about devising a better system or, in current parlance, designi new international financial architecture? Obviously, this will be a very large task, an offer a few observations here this morning.

First,  we  all  recognise  that  access  to  the  international  capital  market balance,  bestowed  enormous  benefits  on  participating  countries,  particularly  dev countries. The world is a much better place when it is outward looking - historical epo large  international  transfers  of  capital  were  taking  place  were  those  where  living around  the  world  were  rising  fastest  and  where  poverty  declined  most. It goes without saying that Australia is completely its  policy  of  permitting  the  free  movement  of  international  capital  and  sees  no  cas change.

On the other hand, it is simplistic to insist on the totally free movement in all countries and in all circumstances. To do so would be to ignore the lesson f crises, to further risk the stability of the system and to invite a reaction which woul worse  off.  We  need  to  devise  a  system  for  maximising  the  benefits  to  be  gained international capital while limiting the risks. Within  developed  countries,  a  number  of  institutions  have  been  designe encourage investment and risk-taking - the joint stock company, the concept of limited bankruptcy laws and, of course, central banks as lenders of last resort. These are all necessary  parts  of  a  developed  financial  system,  and  help  provide  the  right  balance encouraging  enterprise  while  at  the  same  time  preventing  individual  financial  distr turning into widespread financial panic. I want to conclude by sympathising with you as bank supervisors because of inherent difficulty of the task you face. To some extent, the biggest challenge is countries furthest behind world best practice up to standard, and the Core Principles

title: Mr. Meister reviews the response of bank supervisors to the growing competition within EMU  (Central Bank Articles and Speeches, 12 Oct 98)

text:
Mr.  Meister  reviews  the  response  of  bank  supervisors  to  the  growing competition within EMU Lecture delivered by Mr. Edgar Meister, a member of the Board the Deutsche Bundesbank, at the Bank of Greece in Athens on 12/10/98.

I

'panta rhei', 'all is flux'

Ladies  and  gentlemen,  these  words,  attributed  to  Heraclit,  readily  cross mind on the eve of EMU, both with respect to the previous course of events in the E integration  process  and  with  respect  to  the  events  still  lying  ahead.  As  so  often politicians and businessmen must adjust to legal and structural changes, which on this have been triggered by the forthcoming European Monetary Union. Germany joins EMU nex year, and Greece will follow as soon as possible (that is likely to be in the year 20 has  already  immortalised  itself  on  the  Euro  banknote).  In  the  field  of  banking  sup Greece will from the outset be a genuine 'in' country, or actually is one already: th harmonisation  of  banking  law  encompasses  all  EU-countries.
