However,  I  will  offer  a  few  guesses  on  Asia's  prospects.  I  will  also  offe observations on the nature of the adjustments and transitions now being worked through especially within the financial sectors of the affected countries.

## The Asian Growth Story

The Asian growth story, over three decades or more, has been extraordinary, sustained annual expansions of the order of 7 to 10 percent. That is more than just a stati Not only has Asian economic success supported growth in the rest of the world, it has driving force in the most profound process of poverty alleviation in human history. In well-organised economies, simply adding more inputs will lead to more outputs. Certainly, Asians became wealthier, and were able to enjoy rapidly improving material well-being. Bu was, in Krugman's view, no miracle. There was no productivity steroid.

The last year or so has generally given strength to Krugman's analysis. In cru rather simplistic terms, the Asian formula worked so long as those new inputs were dire areas where the real value added, at the micro level, was sufficient to support real gr macro level. Asia was able to generate high savings rates, and to maintain similarly hig investment. But as investment increased, to 30 or 40 percent of GDP in many cases, the q that investment began to deteriorate. In so doing, they wou socialise the losses, and spread the impact of the economic collapse over the next decade course, as conditions improve, and perceptions grow that the worst of the shock is ove investors will be increasingly willing and able to reinvest, enabling the governments to from direct ownership and retire at least some of that debt.

Whatever  view  one  takes  of  the  desirability  of  public  investment  in  fin institutions, it is difficult to see how this particular option can be avoided given the m problems that have emerged, and the profound lack of confidence on the part of private which  now  exists.  Indeed,  this  process  of  public  capital  injections  is  already  well  un Korea, Thailand and Indonesia. Japan, it seems, is still struggling with the concept.

Asia's domestic private investors, for the most part, have taken such an enorm to net worth that it is difficult to imagine them being an early or substantial source of banks. In any event, the need for new equity extends well into the non-financial business and  even  with  Asia's  renowned  savings  capacity,  the  short-term  need  for  private  savin exceeds the local capacity to supply.

That  leaves  only  foreign  investment  in  Asian  financial  systems  and  industry substantial and available avenue for prompt recapitalisation and rapid economic recovery. investment would bring more than just capital. The region needs skills, experience, risk ma systems, accounting and auditing systems, diversification of ownership risk and, perhaps b else, high reputation and confidence in creditworthiness. Foreign investors can provide all

Certainly, foreign investment in the region's financial systems is already oc However, my impression is that it is not always openly welcomed. I am well aware of all national  reservations  about  foreign  investment,  and  I  don't  approach  this  issue  with ideological  view  of  the  subject.  But  it  does  seem  that  without  a  more  liberal  and  w approach to foreign investment, the recovery will be slower because the region's equity exceed the capacity of domestic sources - public and private - to provide.

Before  private  investors,  of  either  domestic  or  foreign  origin,  are  enti recapitalising the region's banks, there will have to be substantial progress on issues o standards,  audit  standards,  transparency,  and  legal  underpinning  of  bankruptcy  proceedi commercial  law  more  generally.  Investors  will  not  invest  unless  reasonably  confident  t understand the risks they are accepting (which, as recent events prove, isn't the same as investors  will  assess  those  risks  accurately).  Reducing  those  risks  is  one  of  the  most activities that governments in the region can now engage themselves in.

## Concluding Comments

Asia has suffered a shock which, by any historical comparison, is severe. Re from that shock will take time and perhaps the most useful thing that can come from the e now is to extract the available lessons and try to ensure that recovery is sound, durab susceptible to such crises in future.

Asia  2000  Executive  Director  Philip  Gibson  in  a  recent  speech  pointed  to fundamental strengths of Asian countries, in terms of their cohesiveness, willingness to invest, commitment to improvement, especially through education, and commitment to recovery

of those qualities are evident, and all will be necessary over the next couple of years takes root.

To my mind, there are two key lessons emerging from the Asian experience, these are now being reinforced by events elsewhere around the world.

- The crucial importance of a strong, well-capitalised financial sector, wit systems for recognising and managing risk. The experience is showing us ag just how financial system stress can amplify difficulties in the rest of the
- Asset price booms may be enjoyable on the way up, but are terribly destru when the bubble finally pops.

If  those  two  lessons  are  well-learnt,  and  applied  in  future  policy  making, future will be even more robust and durable than its past.

title: Mr. Bäckström speaks on the topic 'EMU - a further step in financial integration'  (Central Bank Articles and Speeches, 29 Sep 98)
description: Address by the Governor of the Bank of Sweden, Mr. Urban Bäckström, at the Danish-Swedish Business Council in Copenhagen on 29/9/98.
text:
## Mr. Bäckström speaks on the topic 'EMU - a further step in financial integration'

Address by the Governor of the Bank of Sweden, Mr. Urban Bäckström, at the Danish-Swedish Busi Council in Copenhagen on 29/9/98.

Stage Three of EMU will soon be here. Something that many people felt was impossi just a few years ago is now taking place. The EMU project is probably the greatest change that happened in the domain of exchange rate policy. The economies of eleven countries are being together by a single currency. Both the population and the economy of the euro area will be on the United States. Today, the euro area's share of the industrial countries' output is about 3 the United States has 35 per cent.

The introduction of the euro will affect conditions for the financial system th Europe. But the advent of a single currency should not be discussed as an isolated phenomeno financial sphere. The move to Stage Three is simply accentuating a process that is already in 1980s and '90s we have seen the beginnings of a financial revolution on a global scale. This been a combined consequence of financial deregulation, a general globalisation of trade and pr major developments in technology and new demographic trends.

In my address today I shall be pointing out discernible trends in the developmen financial system and how this process is being reinforced by the coming European Monetary Uni conclusion  I  shall  consider  what  this  requires  of  economic  policy,  its  decision-makers  an authorities.

## A financial revolution

It is hardly an exaggeration to say that a revolutionary process of financial tran and development has got under way in the past decade, with consequences that we probably cann fully  foresee.  Deregulation,  globalisation,  advanced  information  technology  and  new  metho valuation and risk management have initiated a dynamic process in which financial markets, ins and instruments are interacting. There are clear similarities with the expansion of real econ past  hundred  years;  a  stream  of  new,  more  efficient  and  specialised  production  processes communication facilities are leading to a growing volume of trade. Basically, the financial t internationalisation  are  a  natural  development  of  the  market  economy,  a  logical  consequ persistently  rapid  economic  transformations  that  call  for  new  financial  solutions  for  hous firms.

## Challenges for banks

The foreseeable developments will alter or at least affect the future role of ba trends in traditional banking are already discernible.

Competition for bank deposits is  growing  in  that  people  are  increasingly  choos place assets in securities, either directly or via mutual funds. Specialised agents of various niche  banks,  have  also  entered  this  field.  Savings  instruments  that  attract  customers  are provided, at least in Sweden, by food chains and petrol companies.

In the case of loans, a growing proportion of credits is being arranged in the markets.  Then  there  is  more  uncertainty  about  the  social  security  system's  future  ability adequate pensions. The demographic trends are also entailing changes in saving behaviour; a proportion of people in the industrialised world are approaching retirement and are more pron than to borrow.

Cross-border investment is rising. People in Sweden, for example, are placing thei term savings to a growing extent in assets issued abroad. At the same time, non-residents are their holdings of Swedish financial assets.

Furthermore, technological advances are making it possible to supply traditional b services without the aid of a large branch network. This in turn makes new banking establishm costly than before and a bank with just a few branches or a business concept based on telepho Internet can gain a competitive advantage in certain segments of the market. Products are also more sophisticated and their construction and production are increasingly dependent on special how that may become available outside the banks.

The  speed  of  these  processes  varies  from  country  to  country.  The  structure  of earnings is already changing, with a growing share from a range of commissions compared wi traditional income from net interest.

There is nothing to suggest that the rate of and pressure from these changes will in the years ahead. On the contrary, international integration seems to be becoming more int establishment of EMU means that this trend will accelerate.

## EMU affects the financial system

The introduction of the single currency will affect the financial system in vari The most obvious change is the end to exchange transactions between the national currencies in area. This also means an end to forwards and swaps in these currencies. By itself, this will l on the earnings of European banks.

The coming of the euro will also affect financial activities in Europe more pro and may necessitate a number of changes. The euro area will constitute a larger and more unifor with a population of about two hundred million. This market, moreover, is likely to attract inv other European countries and other parts of the world.

Via growing competition, a larger market normally leads to lower costs and incr liquidity. With more investors and the elimination of exchange risks, it will cost less to div by placing them in more countries. In other words, savers in one country will transfer some of to other countries. This process has, in fact, already begun. Briefly, then, all at once there larger and much more liquid European capital market that in time may resemble the US market and nature.

A competitive factor that has been important for national banks-familiarity with domestic monetary policy-will disappear when the single currency is introduced. This could le centralisation of trading in treasury bonds. It is quite conceivable that in time, treasury bo are concentrated to one or two financial centres in Europe.

The  elimination  of  exchange  risk  means  that  risks  of  other  types  will  attrac attention.  I  am  thinking  in  particular  of  liquidity  and  credit  risks.  This  could  well development of trans-national European markets for different categories of bonds, for example, bonds, housing bonds and local authority bonds. A contributory factor here will probably be a for investors to spread risks by diversifying portfolios so that potential losses are limited trading in these instruments that will be affected. New knowledge will have to be acquired by t players.

Share  trading  is  already  showing  clear  effects  of  EMU.  Stock  exchange  mergers occurring here and there in Europe. Another expression of what is at least a related tendenc participation in the national stock exchange. At the same time, the two principal competitive share dealing will continue to apply, namely local customer  relationships  and  knowledge  of

accounting, taxes and laws in the company's home country. But even these factors will be mod investors learn more about conditions in other countries, harmonisation between countries cont the production of goods and services is increasingly globalised.

Even this very summary review illustrates how the changeover to a single curren Europe  will  affect  conditions  for  the  financial  system.  The  financial  markets  will  becom accompanied by increased competitive pressure. Some activities will be modified or disappear Others will be concentrated to one or a few financial centres. But there will probably also b activities.

These developments will leave their mark even in countries that do not join the eu but are adjacent to it. This, too, is a process that has already begun. Banks are being merg units. Cost-cutting has come to the fore. Modes of distribution are being overhauled along wi up of specialist knowledge. Systems for pricing different products are being changed.

## Financial transformation not straightforward

Today there is a widespread conviction that free trade in goods and services en prosperity in the long term. In the same way, most things suggest that in time, free trade in field leads to increased economic growth.

But we have also learned that the transformation and development of the financia are not without problems. In the past decade there have been bank crises in a number of countr as several heavy corrections and large fluctuations in money, equity and currency markets ar world.

There  is  nothing  inherently  new  about  financial  crises.  On  the  country,  they occurred from time to time for many centuries. Experience shows that free trade and transform the financial field require a great deal from economic policy, its decision-makers and various as  well  as  extensive  cooperation  between  countries.  This  is  all  the  more  the  case  in  tha increasingly integrated financial system, mistakes in one part of the world may quickly lead t repercussions elsewhere.

## Many financial crises in the past decade

The financial problems at present in countries in Asia and other parts of the wor many respects similar to the situation in Mexico a couple of years ago, as well as to the Swed the early 1990s. Financial problems arise in an economy essentially as follows.

Banking involves accepting deposits from the non-bank public and transforming t short-run  savings  into  loans  with  longer  maturities  to  households  and  firms.  This  transfor maturities is normally an economic benefit for society as a whole. The banks provide payment and mediate credits.

However, the commercial practice of borrowing short and lending long is associated risks. If people perceive a bank's position as uncertain and withdraw their savings, the bank obtain liquidity elsewhere; otherwise it will have to suspend payments and ultimately go bankr latter event the bank ceases to contribute to the workings of the economy. If this happens bank, the economic consequences may not be serious. If it involves the whole of the banking however, economic activity may be profoundly weakened. That is why banking operations need t safeguarded.

One safety measure is the possibility, in exceptional circumstances, of the cent intervening as the lender of last resort. This is a matter of providing liquidity-as long as fundamentally solvent-when the stability of the entire financial system is threatened. In tha

possible to avoid more serious economic consequences and, provided the problems underlying the are managed, stabilise the situation in the banking system and the economy in general.

However, a central bank's unique possibility of providing liquidity is restrict national currency. If a country has an external deficit and revenue from exports does not cov to make up the difference it has to borrow in foreign currency. The vulnerability this involves the  loans  are  short-term,  sizeable  and  have  been  channelled  via  the  banking  system  to  l investment projects. If a country in this situation encounters problems with the renewal of fo the central bank will have limited opportunities of coming to the rescue with liquidity unles to have sufficient foreign exchange reserves or borrowing facilities.

That is more or less what has happened in the countries that have recently been problems.  Sudden  shifts  in  confidence  as  to  a  country's  real  economy,  the  value  of  its  as political system are examples of factors that have triggered crises in economies that have b vulnerable.

In some countries the State has been able to obtain foreign loans and thereby co liquidity to banks with problems. Meanwhile, these countries have made their own efforts to i confidence-enhancing measures that would stabilise the situation.

Other countries have been obliged to turn to the international community, headed International Monetary Fund, for assistance with foreign liquidity. Private banks have also bee as one might expect considering that they are the banks which have exposures in these coun return, the countries have been required to take measures so that confidence can be restore words, the underlying problems must be tackled. By itself, liquidity support does not suffice.

The  required  measures  include  the  orderly  winding  up  of  insolvent  banks,  a  cl account of the problems, a reduction of current-account deficits, a consolidation of governmen so that expenditures for restoring the financial sector can be covered, and a construction policy that guards against the risk of the country been suddenly hit by massive currency outflo a situation one cannot expected the necessary adjustment to be painless or free from difficult

Attempts  by  a  country  to  isolate  itself  from  the  international  exchange  of  f services would probably lead in time to effects on growth and prosperity that are just as d protectionist measures in other fields. A country that chooses to impose controls for a time w hard to re-enter the international credit market once the crisis had subsided. Currency restr type we have seen some examples of recently therefore lead the country that introduces them int end.

When problems of this type arise in one country, the effects are liable to spread countries. Recently we have seen a global increase in various asset risk premia as a conseque turbulence in Asia and the problems in Russia. This has affected countries that geographically way away from the countries in question. A part of the adjustment of risk premia probably rep normalisation. It is not to be expected that stock markets around the world can generate capita after year that deviate from the long-term development of corporate profits. Neither is it u that the terms on which countries borrow should become more differentiated than before to re various risks involved. But adjustments of this type are seldom smooth. Exaggerations in one sometimes give way to excesses in the opposite direction. The so-called flight to quality th connection with financial turbulence in parts of the world is a sign that investors want a ra of portfolio risks. This leads to increases in risk premia.

One way of adjusting portfolio risk is to sell shares and buy treasury paper. Tha financial turbulence often has a negative effect on shares prices, accompanied by a downward m in long-term - and sometimes even short-term - interest rates. Moreover, in a particular coun its economic fundamentals look good, such a situation can give rise to downward pressure on

exchange rate and share prices at the same time as interest rates rise. That suggests that cer are reducing all types of holding in the country in question, which is a signal to the countr makers that more must be done to enhance general economic policy's credibility.

## High standard of discipline throughout economic policy

While it is obviously important to discuss how a financial crisis, if it occurs, managed, it is at least as important to minimise the risks of a crisis ever materialising. T particular when the financial system is undergoing rapid developments. The transformation in E the coming years must therefore be followed closely.

One key factor is economic policy in general. An economy characterised by low, s inflation, sound government finances and good economic policy  credibility  also  provides  a  g stable economic environment. This in turn promotes a sound development of the financial domain.

By itself, however, this is not enough. Another highly important matter is the app government supervision of the financial sector. Even central banks that are not directly enga supervision must monitor tendencies in the financial field in order to fulfil their primary tas price stability and financial system stability. There are several reasons for this.

Monetary  policy  is  implemented  through  the  financial  system's  agents.  The  ban ability to transmit monetary policy effectively may be jeopardised if they have problems. The c of the banks in the payment system - as the channel for payments of every type - makes it impo the banks are financially healthy and operate efficiently and reliably. Otherwise the traffic i liable to be disturbed. If the problems become so great as to constitute systemic risk, it is the central bank to consider support for liquidity. Moreover, in that central banks provide systems for large-value payments, they also have a direct, operative function in the payment s inter-bank payments are channelled through the settlement system, which is thus the hub of t payment system.

In Sweden the Riksbank now regularly publishes a Financial Market Report, in which present our appraisal of the financial system's development and stability. The Report is thu monitoring one of our primary functions - the promotion of a safe and efficient payment syste are some parallels here with the Inflation Report, which we publish regularly as part of the other primary function - safeguarding a stable value of money.

The  rapid  pace  of  financial  developments,  particularly  in  the  international  p system, also calls for extensive international cooperation. The issue of financial system sta up for detailed discussion in various fora in connection with the coming annual meetings of Bank and the International Monetary Fund. The central banks also cooperate on matters of thi the framework of the Bank for International Settlements in Basle, Switzerland, where represent central banks throughout the world meet regularly once a month.

## Conclusion

To sum up, the financial system is undergoing a rapid transformation and develop The middle of the 19th century is commonly associated with the industrial revolution. Perha historians will see the late 20th century as the era of the financial revolution. Europe's mo single currency will accelerate the trend.

The transformation and development of the financial system will ultimately contrib future prosperity. But experience has taught us that it is a development which needs to be mon closely and presupposes a high degree of discipline in economic policy. It requires a great decision-makers in the political system and the supervisory authorities, as well as from thos work in central banks.

Developments  in  the  financial  field  are  creating  large  opportunities.  But  it important to bear in mind that major, far-reaching changes normally entail risks. In view of every agent in the financial system needs to act wisely and discerningly. Only in this way c benefits be drawn from the opportunities that financial developments are providing.

description: Address by the Deputy Governor of the Bank of Sweden, Mr. Lars Heikensten, at the Autumn Conference arranged by the Centre for Business and Policy Studies on 14/10/98.
text:
Mr. Heikensten discusses monetary policy Address by the Deputy Governor of the Bank of Sweden, Mr. Lars Heikensten, at the Autumn Conference arranged by the Centre for Bus and Policy Studies on 14/10/98.

First a word of thanks for the opportunity to attend this meeting. The autumn conf are a fine tradition to which it is a pleasure to contribute.

On previous occasions I have used the opportunity to look back over the past ye discuss what the Riksbank has been doing, including how monetary policy is conducted. Then tried to look ahead and pick out some issues of importance for monetary policy in the longer ru

My approach this year will be broadly the same. First a review of what has hap since last autumn, with comments on how the Riksbank's assessment of inflation has evolved o year. Then, as previously, a look at the question of how we communicate policy and how it h perceived in financial markets.

On  this  occasion  we  are  in  the  throes  of  an  international  financial  crisis,  w uncertainty as to what its real economic effects may be. Contagious effects of the crisis ha become  larger  and  larger.  Looking  back,  one  can  clearly  see  how  the  economic  forecasts  o observers have swung during the year, from a phase of concern about a future increase in in pressure to a phase of strong anxiety that the global economy will be hit by a recession.

Against this background I shall be discussing the current monetary policy appraisa Swedish economy, together with some factors of importance for the final assessment. First, ho shall briefly outline monetary policy's line of thought.

## Forecasts and probabilities

Monetary policy's overriding objective is to safeguard the value of money. The a rate of inflation, measured as the change in the consumer price index, is to be kept at 2 pe takes time for the Riksbank's monetary measures to work in full, our actions have to be based on an assessment of inflation's future path. The policy horizon - the period in which most of of monetary policy materialises - is around twelve to twenty-four months.

The Riksbank's assessment of future inflation is presented continuously in our I Reports. Since the first Report was presented in October 1993, the content has been develope Riksbank has, for example, become increasingly explicit in its assessments. In the first tw Report contained a more general account of how the inflation indicators and inflationary pres economy were developing. From November 1995 onwards the Riksbank has been attaching numbers t its inflation assessments.

In the June 1996 Report the inflation assessment was underpinned for the first ti an  overall  picture  of  the  cyclical  position.  A  further  step  was  taken  in  September  1997, inflation assessment was supplemented with a path for inflation in the forecast period. In the our main path for inflation was flanked by uncertainty intervals. The probabilities of inflati various alternative paths are weighed into the overall picture on which monetary policy dec based.

How, then, are the uncertainty intervals calculated? In practice, our forecasters assessments  of  a  range  of  variables,  taking  into  account  both  their  current  uncertainty  an compares with their normal uncertainty. This information is then incorporated in a fairly sim model that is used to estimate future inflation. The probability distributions we obtain in th course, highly subjective but they do give a consistent picture of how the Riksbank evaluate risks.

While we are on the subject of the inflation assessments, it is particularly im bear in mind that they are predicated on the repo rate being unchanged throughout the forecast forecast  path  for  inflation  that  deviates  from  the  target  -  or  the  large  deviations  that intervals  represent  as  conceivable  paths  -  constitutes  a  diagnosis  that  may  indicate  treat called for, repo rate adjustments are used to bring inflation into line with the target. In r the uncertainty about future inflation is not as great as the uncertainty intervals might su consequence is that our inflation forecasts become out of date as soon as the Riksbank alte rate.

## Assessments in the past year

Much  has  happened  in  the  past  year  as  regards  economic  developments  and  th conditions for monetary policy. The Riksbank, along with other official observers and market fo has revised its assessments in the light of the increasingly widespread effects of the internat

- Last autumn most observers counted on a strong economic trend, both in Sweden an in the rest of the world. The crisis that had erupted in Southeast Asia was ex lead  at  most  to  a  welcome  easing  of  international  price  pressure.  In  the  S economy,  some  indicators  last  autumn  pointed  to  rising  inflationary  pressur particular, a gradual increase in capacity utilisation was judged to lead i inflation above the Riksbank's target. Inflation expectations, moreover, were to move up, having previously stabilised after a falling trend for a number o In the December Report it was judged that inflation would exceed the target in The Riksbank raised the repo rate 0.25 percentage points.
- At  the  same  time,  the  Riksbank  underscored  that,  due  to  uncertainties  i assessment, the outcome might differ from the main scenario. On the one hand exacerbation of the crisis in Asia could result in weaker inflationary pressur other, there were risks that high wage increases and weak productivity growth fuel the rate of inflation. These two alternative scenarios were judged to be probable.
- During the spring the picture of inflation changed by degrees. In the March Repo inflation prospects had altered somewhat in connection with the mounting cris Asia  and  low  import  prices.  Subdued  inflation  expectations  and  restrained demands  pointed  in  the  same  direction.  In  view  of  a  weak  development international  activity,  it  was  foreseen  that  full  capacity  utilisation  in  t economy would not be reached until the end of the forecast period, when infl was  assumed  to  be  marginally  above  the  target.  This  called  for  a  readine undertake some cautious tightening of the monetary stance later in the year.
- At  the  same  time,  the  spectrum  of  risks  had  shifted,  with  less  risk  of  i exceeding its expected path but a continued risk of development being weaker in the main scenario. In view of the uncertainty, the Riksbank chose to await developments.
- At the beginning of the summer we observed that inflation was following a lower path than we had assumed in the main scenario in March. Weaker import prices w contributing to this but so were other factors. Transitory effects - lower int and changes in indirect taxes and subsidies - were particularly prominent. Mor on account of lower wage increases and stronger productivity growth than expe earlier, it seemed that inflation in the longer run would be somewhat lower t Riksbank had predicted. With the outlook for productivity, it was likely tha surplus capacity would continue to exist during the whole period.

All in all, inflation prospects one to two years ahead were accordingly more s than  before  and  predicted  inflation  was  below  the  target  throughout  the  fo period. In addition, there was judged to be a large risk of inflation being path in the main scenario. Under these circumstances the repo rate was lowered percentage points.

Notwithstanding  these  revisions,  the  economic  outlook  for  the  near  future  ha changed much in the past year, with expectations of good growth during 1998, to an increasing account of rising domestic demand. These predictions have been fulfilled. During the year, how uncertainty about growth prospects further ahead has risen, above all in the late summer and au

## Transitory effects and lower import prices

Another matter to note is that although the cyclical picture has proved fairly acc path of inflation during 1998 has been markedly lower, mainly on account of large changes in t effects and import prices.

At the beginning of the year it was foreseen that the transitory  effects would  largely cancel out, with no impact at all on the course of inflation during 1998. With the spring dec tobacco taxes and property tax, however, it was assumed that the transitory effects would act curb on inflation. In the June Report it was foreseen that the transitory effects would have impact on inflation during 1998 of as much as 1.2 percentage points; in the September Report t was adjusted upwards to 1.3 percentage points. For 1999 and 2000 the transitory effects on infl assumed to be marginal.

Import prices have also been more subdued than expected. In the December assessment last year the Riksbank assumed that during the forecast period the annual contribution to inf import prices would amount to about half a percentage point. Some downward revision was mad March, followed by a further adjustment in June, when it was envisaged that the impact of impo on the CPI would not be sizeable. The lower outcome and the adjusted forecasts mainly reflec fall  for  raw  materials,  though  the  international  price  trend  for  manufactured  products  has weaker than expected, presumably in part as a consequence of the Asian crisis.

Rents are another CPI item that has been more subdued than foreseen in the spring. the beginning of the year, the rate of rent increases has dropped to levels that are historica partly attributable to lower mortgage interest costs and lower expectations for wages and infl also reflects the cut in property tax and decreased heating costs.

Wages seem to have developed more or less as the Riksbank foresaw. Today we count an annual wage rise of 3.5-4 per cent in the period 1998-2000; that is only a little below o last December before the wage negotiations had been completed. Opinions differ as to the effe the Riksbank's actions may have had on the latest wage round. In the light of contacts with lab representatives, my view is that monetary policy's influence on the wage settlements was posi this was by no means the only factor. Contributions to the low outcome seem to have been made wage round having been conducted both centrally, with efforts to hold wage formation togethe throughout  the  labour  market  then  at  least  in  large  segments,  and  decentralised  to  indivi Whether this model can be repeated is another matter.

Transitory  effects,  import  prices  and  rents  account  for  2  percentage  points substantial  downward  revision  of  inflation  in  1998  by  a  total  of  2.2  percentage  points  be Inflation Reports in December 1997 and this September. The same factors are responsible for ab of the downward adjustments for 1999 and 2000 between the forecasts in March and June.

Monetary policy increasingly understood, but problems last spring

For some years now the Riksbank has been working hard to communicate the line thought behind its decisions both to the general public and to market players. This is intended the general understanding of how monetary policy functions and what it can do and also preven as possible, market disturbances on account of uncertainty. The more clearly the market unders way  of  thinking,  the  smoother  should  short  interest  rates  adjust  to  new  information  about prospects.

A comparison of market expectations (as expressed in implied forward  interest with the actual repo rate can serve as a indicator of the market's error in foreseeing the r predictive error has, on the whole, decreased. With a reservation for other effects on this i various interest rate premia that may fluctuate over time, this suggests a growing understan policy.

With a longer time horizon, the predictive error naturally tends to be larger. Wi year  horizon  the  error  presumably  has  less  to  do  with  imperfect  communication  or  a  l understanding of how our policy functions; it is no doubt more a matter of shifts in the whol economic activity and inflation. Things are somewhat different in a three-month perspective; errors then presumably also arise from misinterpretations of the Riksbank's signals.

During  the  past  year  the  repo  rate  has  been  raised  once  and  lowered  once.  Thi required a great deal of the Riksbank  in  the  way  of  communicating  policy  to  the  outside  w explaining the reasons for its measures.

A  study  of  the  market's  prices,  predictions  and  statements  shows  that  the  rep increase in December 1997 was broadly expected. It was, in fact, just at last year's Conferenc an important piece of signalling took place. As regards the repo rate cut in June, on the ot pattern of market expectations changed relatively late. description: Presentation by the President of the Deutsche Bundesbank, Prof. Hans Tietmeyer, at The Wall Street Journal's Seventh Annual Conference on the Americas in New York on 2/10/98.
text:
Mr. Tietmeyer discusses prospects for Latin America in a volatile world Presentation by the President of the Deutsche Bundesbank, Prof. Hans Tietmeyer, at The Wall Journal's  Seventh Annual Conference on the Americas in New York on 2/10/98.

First of all, I would like to thank you most sincerely for your kind invitation to conference. The fact that a European central banker is speaking at a conference on the Americ evidence of advanced globalisation. We are living in one world, even if some of the conditio Geologists claim that our two continents are moving away from each other, even though it is less  than  one  inch  a  year.  Fortunately,  that  is  true  only  in  a  geographical  sense.  Econom continents are moving closer together. For that reason, it is undoubtedly true to say that th oasis of prosperity in today's world - even if Europe looks like an island of stability at p course, our future, too, depends on the further outlook for the world economy.

The global economy is marked at present by a number of crises and critical situ The history, forms and implications of these crises have many dimensions. Understandably, t many questions to which final answers cannot yet be given.

That starts with a precise analysis of the processes involved. Why do the market later in some cases and earlier in others? How do the internal weaknesses of countries intera operation of the financial markets upon the outbreak of, and during, a crisis?

There are a particularly large number of questions on the economic implications. quickly  and  how  sustainably  can  the  affected  countries  overcome  the  crisis  of  confidenc successfully can other emerging markets escape the risks of contagion? How much does the turb retard growth in the traditional industrial countries? What are the long-term effects on the and financial structures?

Finally, we have to ask about the lessons to be learned. How can the emerging ma bring their internal structures better into line with their degree of integration into the g What role can international cooperation play in preventing and overcoming crises?

These  and  other  difficult  questions  are  dominating  the  current  international However, some fairly sweeping comments can be heard in the debate. People who say that the fi markets are to blame, that globalisation must be stopped or even reversed. Such views are, of simplistic and inconsistent with the realities involved. But there are indeed legitimate que asked of the global financial system. At all events, the international community would do we careful consideration to how it can improve the way in which the financial markets work.

Now, in a tempest it is especially important to maintain a clear sense of direc every serious analysis, the following two insights should provide the guiding lights: Globa markets  bring  significant  benefits  overall.  Free  capital  movements  are  an  important  and  wo achievement.

The free movement of capital has been crucial in promoting the global integrat output and trade. It has been instrumental in bringing about a marked increase in internati investment and has led to a rapid spread of know-how. Free capital movements have made the more  prosperous  overall.  Capital  is  being  used  more  efficiently  because  the  pool  for  gath allocating  resources  has  become  larger.  And  investment  decisions  are  geared  more  closely economic  yield  of  projects.  Finally,  the  free  movement  of  capital  has  helped  policymakers countries to maintain internal economic discipline. The fact that there is a comparatively hi price stability in many parts of the world is undoubtedly also due to open borders and more c from abroad. No one should forget those benefits, let alone want to sacrifice them.

On the other hand, it is nevertheless correct to say that the global markets are players and partners. They pose internal challenges which may sometimes be hard. And the inter financial markets are prone to exaggerate at times, on occasion with great severity. Nowada market players are very short-termist in their actions, which can considerably heighten risk herd behaviour in both euphoria and in moments of doubt. Above all, financial crises give rise contagion. Countries may be infected even though they have very few economic links with the o location of the crisis.

Naturally, it is understandable that market players regard a crisis in one cou reason  to  re-examine  opportunities  and  risks  across  the  board.  Problems  are  caused,  howeve markets  do  not  make  enough  distinctions  and  fail  to  take  adequate  account  of  conditions  wh specific to the individual country. I hope very much that the international financial markets take due consideration of the evident structural progress made by many countries over the past especially in Latin America. Apart from that, exaggerations in one direction or the other are dangerous for the players in the financial markets themselves - as has been revealed yet agai here during the past few days.

II

What can be done against financial turbulence? First and foremost, financial cri not  an  ineluctable  fate.  Internal  weaknesses  or  shortcomings  nearly  always  play  a  considera Conversely, it is also true to say that there is no universal patent remedy.

But  this  much  is  certain:  long-term  domestic  stability  and,  above  all,  the  e credibility of internal policies are the best protective measures. Whatever we currently discu seriousness  and  commitment  at  the  international  level,  even  the  best  possible  architecture finance needs sound foundations. Those indispensable foundations are provided by convincing lo domestic policies on the part of the countries themselves.  That  means:  sound  public  financ prices, sound banking and financial sectors, and competition and flexibility in the domestic labour markets. It cannot be said often enough: internal policies must be in order. That is point for any architecture. They are, so to speak, both the foundations and the supporting pill

Greater  and,  above  all,  improved  transparency  is  just  as  essential  for  monitor quality of those foundations and pillars as is regular surveillance by the IMF as part of t consultations. More than hitherto, the financial sector and its supervision should also be t examination, not just classical macropolicy.

Of course, one must not expect that greater transparency and strengthened survei by the IMF will mean a perfect world in future. Countries' internal structures are rarely idea something which a global financial system has to come to terms with. Therefore, external arra among  currencies  and  between  a  country  and  the  global  financial  markets  are  naturally importance. However, these must be viable in the real world.

For example, stable exchange rates are undoubtedly desirable. They provide enter and financial investors with planning certainty. In certain cases, exchange rate pegging may b that purpose. Moreover, an exchange rate peg may, for a time, help to import stability fro Ultimately, however, that borrowed credibility has to be paid back by internal performance. A country must also know that in today's dynamic world there may easily arise an unavoidable adjust the exchange rate - not just the nominal exchange rate but also the real one. And that why every country has to examine critically whether it has sufficient internal flexibility to h exchange rate peg by means of strenuous internal adjustment. Hence, it is questionable whether a currency board is wise for a country in transition which still has a considerable road to development from a centralised command economy to a market economy. A currency board only make sense if it is credible over a lengthy period of time. And it is credible only if the domestic

is sound enough to stand a temporary monetary contraction if the necessity arises. That scarce be the case in Russia at the moment.

External arrangements have to be particularly realistic. That is becoming incre apparent  nowadays  in  the  question  of  the  liberalisation  of  the  financial  markets  in  the economies. Without doubt, liberalising capital movements is the right direction to take. But if financial sector has major problems in handling extensive capital flows in a sound manner, th has to be asked about the pace and sequencing with which a country opens itself up.

The subject of controls on capital movements is very much to the fore in the de present, especially for some of the Asian countries in crisis. At the end of the day, every c assess for itself which path it will follow. It is understandable if a country is concerned a too dependent on hot money - at least, as long as the domestic financial sector is not fully de

No one should indulge in any illusions, however. Administrative controls are not thing in today's world. The markets will be permanently on the lookout for ways of circumventi controls.  And,  mostly,  the  markets  are  more  inventive  than  the  controllers.  Controls  o movements also exact a price in most cases. In order to be effective, controls must be comp broadly designed. That implies that effective controls also adversely affect desirable capita to some extent. And controls on capital movements may have the effect of retarding the strengt internal structures. Admittedly, in some cases and for specific areas, it may make sense to b developing suitable domestic structures. But that time also has to be used. Otherwise, buying backfire. For instance, controls might encourage corruption and cronyism.

For that reason, even controls of capital inflows represent a certain degree of though  there  are  arguments  for  regarding  them,  under  particular  conditions,  as  a  contri preventing crises and to limiting the potential for a setback. But controls of capital outflo of crisis management are of a different nature. They may directly attack investors' confidenc of a crisis escalating might become unpredictable.

## III

Whatever  shape  the  future  architecture  might  take,  there  are  two  indispen preconditions  for  a  sound  world  financial  system:  countries  having  a  sound  domestic  polic appropriate  external  arrangements  with  the  other  currencies  and  with  the  global  markets. foundations hold, then it naturally make a lot of sense to go one step further and to ask how cooperation can make the world economy more efficient.

A thorough debate on this issue can be very beneficial if a 'New Architecture' 'New  Bretton  Woods'  does  not  imply  throwing  the  baby  out  with  the  bath  water  but  does  m reforming the existing architecture. Since the general principles of the current system are correct. But they have to be applied coherently. And they have to be generally adopted.

A lot can and should be done. With a growing number of countries participating i international division of labour and in the global allocation of capital, the world needs m rules. A lot of work on defining such appropriate rules has already been done during the past would just like to remind you of the Basle Capital Accord or of the Core Principles for Effecti Supervision.  The  crucial  challenges  are  to  ensure  that  such  rules  are  actually  implemente countries and to ensure that the national authorities are in a position to have the required ch effect by the market players.

In particular, in order to improve the efficiency of financial markets, clear ru promote transparency in terms of the positions of both the countries and the players. Recent indicates that the issue of greater transparency is actually a matter for both.

So,  without  any  doubt,  there  is  a  strong  case  for  close  international  coop However, there is one condition for its success. In the longer term, cooperation can only be p it strengthens and does not weaken its own foundations.

There is the one part of those foundations which it must not attack: countries' soundness.  It  would  therefore  be  short-sighted  to  urge  a  country  or  currency  area  to  relax policy more than is reasonable internally. Sooner or later, that extracts a penalty. This is t learned from the current problems in Japan, which have their origin, not least, in a relaxe policy  in  the  late  eighties.  At  that  time,  Japan  understood  its  low  interest  rates  as  a  c international cooperation. And pressure to do so came at that time from the United States. The the bubble economy. The Japanese financial sector is still suffering from its excessive effec burden not just for Japan but for the world as a whole.

Moreover,  there  is  the  other  part  of  the  foundations  which  international  coop should not  undermine  either:  the  appropriate  arrangements  among  countries  themselves  and  wi financial  markets.  International  action  should  improve,  and  not  harm,  the  operation  of  the markets. But that is precisely what happens if there are public bail-outs of investors in t crisis. They encourage moral hazard, thus weakening the efficiency of the markets. Therefore, financed bail-outs ultimately attack the economic basis of legitimacy for free capital markets.

My criticism of some of the IMF's past activities is not new. In the case of Mexi to some extent, in the crises of a few Asian countries, financial resources have been thrown too quickly and too extensively and private investors have not been adequately involved or o late on. We  need  the  IMF,  above  all international  monetary  promoter  of  open  borders  and  free  markets  and  as  an  advocate  of  sou transparent policies on the part of its members. text:
Mr. Tietmeyer's statement as Governor of the Fund for Germany Statement by  the  President  of  the  Deutsche  Bundesbank,  Prof.  Hans  Tietmeyer,  at  the  Joint Discussion in Washington, D.C. on 6/10/98.

The situation in the world economy, without doubt, has turned out to be difficult than we expected a year ago in Hong Kong. In some regions, growth has slowed and global financial markets have become more volatile. It must be recognized, however, existing international economic and monetary system has brought advantages to all of u past  .  Particularly  those  countries  that  are  at  present  undergoing  temporary  setb benefited from the inflow of foreign investment. This has been reflected by impressive a last year - sustained economic growth in the emerging markets.

It is true that globalization is bringing several new challenges but, ov advantages  for  people  throughout  the  world  are  clearly  prevailing.  The  response  to problems should, therefore, not be to question international integration, which would the progress in development that has been achieved so far. Rather, the international and monetary system should be developed further in such a way that it will be ready challenges of the 21 st century.

## II

There  is  certainly  no  panacea  for  overcoming  the  present  problems.  We  kn today that the problems in the countries currently undergoing crises are different in so from those of the eighties. Therefore, the prescriptions must in some respects be dif being no longer solely an issue of macroeconomic stabilization following periods of l and  monetary  policies,  but  also  one  of  good  governance,  a  reliable  legal  framework financial markets, efficient banking supervision and the phenomenon of an excessive structured private debt. Market economies in particular, require a reliable legal fra well-functioning institutions. It has become evident that restoring confidence also req and political reforms.

Especially at this juncture, we need a strong IMF, both in crisis preventio crisis management. Regrettably some responses to the crises in recent years and mont have contributed to the distortion of the incentive structures for financial market lulled investors into a false sense of security. Excessively large financial assistanc can  undermine  the  proper  working  of  the  markets.  Consequently,  market  players  may  e underestimate  the  risks,  trusting  in  government  guarantees  or  a  bail-out  by  the  int community. This moral-hazard problem has to be taken seriously. In future, therefore, t sector must be integrated better and earlier into crisis management and bear full respo its actions.

IMF  programs  up  to  now,  regrettably,  have  not  always  produced  convinci results. Not in all cases did the Fund's conditionality address the underlying causes In particular, its financial support was not sufficiently effective whenever the count did  not  clearly  subscribe  to  radical  corrective  measures.  Ultimately,  it  is  the themselves, which are responsible for the success of their programs. Shortcomings in t efforts cannot be offset by providing international liquidity.

The  free  movement  of  capital  is  a  key  element  in  the  efficient  allocat resources and therefore a precondition for increasing prosperity worldwide. For this continues  to  be  appropriate  to  give  the  IMF  a  mandate  for  the  liberalization  o movements.

Experience  in  many  industrial  countries  and  emerging  markets  clearly  sho however,  that  liberalization  must  be  accompanied  by  the  establishment  of  stable  f markets and efficient prudential structures. The World Bank and the IMF can and must major role in that respect. Capital controls, however, are normally not an effective i monetary policy.

## IV

I am concerned that the present difficulties might trigger pressur protectionism, not only in crisis regions but also in other countries. To give in to t would be highly detrimental to the prospects for a worldwide recovery. Therefore, it is keep markets open, even if competition intensifies.

Similarly, it is also crucial to avoid a renewed round of competitive depr In the long run, nobody would benefit, but everyone would suffer. The exchange rate po to be credible and in line with the development of the fundamentals.

## V

On  January  1,  1999,  for  eleven  countries  of  the  European  Union,  the  s European currency will become a reality. This will create a currency area with a popu almost 300 million. The euro, the future European currency, will start on an - all in economic basis, notwithstanding that unemployment is still too high. The commitment of countries to a stability-oriented fiscal policy and continuing structural reform is a k term success of the European Monetary Union and also for continued improvement of pros for growth and employment. Also, the incoming euro must inherit the stability of the For this purpose, it is important that the European Central Bank is committed to th objective of price stability and enjoys genuine independence, secured under internation stable and strong euro is a major contribution by Europe to the stability of the glob system and to ongoing economic prosperity.

## VI

The  involvement  of  the  World  Bank  in  overcoming  the  financial  crises Southeast Asia and in Russia is of great importance. The World Bank has unique exper addressing the underlying structural problems. At the same time, its main task, to fig should not be neglected.

We should not forget that many countries, including the poorest ones, have implementing structural measures with great effort and commitment for a number of year is the largest concessionary aid fund in the world. Countries trust its advice and financial support which lays the foundation for sustained growth and fighting poverty.

It will be very difficult to fully integrate these countries into the worl without  efficient  institutions  in  the  financial  sector,  without  a  coherent  developme

government strategy and without a reliable legal framework. This has been demonstrated by recent crises.

IDA's  development  policy  mandate  and  its  success  in  implementing  refor programs  encourage  us  to  successfully  conclude  the  current  negotiations  for  th replenishment by the end of the year. Also against the backdrop of the current negotia note with great concern that armed conflicts jeopardize the first fruits of structural arduous reconstruction measures.

In the wake of the financial crises, structural shortcomings have also sur the World Bank's income development. The negative trend in the World Bank's profitab must be tackled quickly so that it can regain its former scope for action. The recently a measures for improving the profitability of the Bank are a major step in the right direc

## VII

For the IMF to play its key role in the international monetary system, the in quotas agreed in Hong Kong must be speedily implemented. This must have absolute pri Germany has already notified the IMF of its consent to the quota increase. We hope tha will follow without further delay so that the IMF will again have sufficient quota re soon as possible. The IMF's key role in overcoming the crises should encourage all mem fulfill their obligations speedily. The New Arrangements to Borrow (NAB) should also into force as soon as possible. This 'reserve tank', however, can only be a supplement the quotas, and by no means a substitute. Germany is prepared to notify its consent to Similarly, we are prepared to ratify the special one-time allocation of SDR.

## VIII

The activities of the IMF and the World Bank complement each other. They not  competing  organizations.  Close  cooperation  between  the  IMF  and  the  World  Bank particularly important when responding to crisis situations in order to avoid conflict We therefore welcome the ongoing efforts to improve cooperation between the two institu

I would like to take this opportunity to thank management and staff of th and the World Bank for their sometimes extremely difficult work during the past month may rest assured that Germany will continue to attach great importance to the work of and  the  World  Bank.  Finally,  I  am  pleased  to  join  my  fellow  governors  in  welcomin Republic of Palau as a new member.

title: Mr. Thiessen discusses global uncertainties and the Canadian economy  (Central Bank Articles and Speeches, 23 Sep 98)
description: Remarks by the Governor of the Bank of Canada, Mr. Gordon Thiessen, to the St. John's Board of Trade in St. John's, Newfoundland on 23/9/98.
text:
Mr.  Thiessen  discusses  global  uncertainties  and  the  Canadian  economy Remarks by the Governor of the Bank of Canada, Mr. Gordon Thiessen, to the St. John's of Trade in St. John's, Newfoundland on 23/9/98.

I  am  delighted  to  have  been  invited  to  speak  to  the  Board  of  Trade  on occasion when the Bank of Canada's Board of Directors is meeting here in St. John's.

This past year, we have had to deal with the implications for our economy a currency of increased global uncertainty and pressures arising from the problems that in  Southeast  Asia.  I  am  sure  that  the  effects  of  these  developments,  especially  o commodities, such as oil and nickel, are already very familiar to Newfoundlanders.

To understand what is going on, we need to look at the nature of the forc are currently affecting our economy. We also need to correctly identify cause and effe comes  to  the  decline  in  the  external  value  of  our  currency  over  the  past  12  mont commentary on this subject has not always been helpful.

I  would  like  to  start  my  presentation  with  a  quick  review  of  intern developments, focusing on the extent to which the problems in Southeast Asia have persi spread. Next, I will discuss the implications of these developments for the Canadian and give you the Bank's latest assessment of the outlook. I can tell you now that I bel key trends in our economy remain positive. Lastly, I will talk about the decline in t value of the Canadian dollar and about the response of monetary policy to that decline.

## The world around us

For over a year now, volatility and uncertainty have been the main traits international environment in which Canada operates.

The financial crisis started in Southeast Asia in the summer of 1997, then to  South  Korea,  and  in  turn  exacerbated  the  domestic  economic  difficulties  that  Ja already facing. Recently, Russia has been added to the list of afflicted countries, an countries in Latin America are under pressure.

As  with  the  crisis  in  Asia,  the  financial  problems  in  Russia  have  rever around the world through foreign exchange, stock, and bond markets, touching off conc still further contagion.

It is certainly easier now, with the benefit of hindsight, to see the exte many investors from industrial countries were attracted to higher-yield investments in market  countries,  without  fully  appreciating  the  risks  involved.  When  investors substantial losses in certain markets, they sought to reduce their exposure to emergi more generally. But this rapid withdrawal of funds brought to the surface areas of we some of these economies, making investors still more nervous. The recent events in Russ prime example of this process.

The  apparently  contagious  nature  of  these  developments  has  led  to  s pessimistic predictions of recession in the world economy. How concerned should we be this?

While the international environment has turned out to be more difficult tha people had thought earlier, let me reassure you that it is certainly not all negative.

To be sure, the situation in Japan is worrisome - not only because of that economic importance but also because of its strong trade and financial links with othe Asian economies. But, and this is an important but, Japan has the capacity and the wherewithal to turn its situation around. With resolute action to speed up the impleme measures to deal with its ailing banking sector and to kickstart its domestic economy, concerns would dissipate.

More importantly, economic activity in the United States has been very robu is expected to remain healthy. In Canada, too, and in Europe the situation is positi certainly not insignificant, for North America and Europe together account for more tha world output. And recent declines in medium- and long-term interest rates to record l are helping to sustain domestic spending in all industrial countries.

With  this  as  background,  I  would  now  like  to  turn  to  the  impact  of international  developments,  and  of  the  associated  uncertainties  and  pressures  in markets, on Canada.

## How is our economy faring?

The international developments of the past year have affected our economy than previously anticipated. And there is no doubt that those Canadian industries and r depend on the production of primary commodities are facing considerable difficulties.

To appreciate this particular link between recent international developmen the Canadian economy, let me point out that Asia, including Japan, absorbs between 30 per cent of the world output of certain key primary materials. So it is not surprisin commodity prices have been hit hard by the Asian crisis. The recent events in Russia, w major commodity producer, have added to the uncertainty about the outlook for the world and prices of primary commodities.

Because  of  all  this,  the  US  dollar  prices  of  commodities  that  are  impor Canada have fallen by about 15 per cent over the past 12 months. While commodities ar important  to  us  than  they  used  to  be,  they  still  make  up  about  30  to  35  per  cen merchandise exports.

Although Canadians have to deal with these difficulties coming from abroad, important  to  remember  that,  overall,  our  economy  is  still  in  good  shape.  This  is, foremost, because some basic aspects of our economic situation have improved markedly last few years. We now have a low rate of inflation, a fiscal surplus, and a declining high)  public  debt-to-GDP  ratio.  As  well,  Canadian  businesses  have  undertaken  m restructuring  and  investment  initiatives  to  increase  their  productivity.  Because fundamental strengths, we are now better positioned to weather sudden shocks.

As for the near-term outlook, there are also a number of positive elements picture. Economic activity in the United States, our main customer, remains high. And Canada, the latest indicators suggest continued expansion in consumer spending and b investment, supported by higher employment and low medium- and long-term interest rates

This  year,  the  Canadian  economy  will  not  repeat  the  4  per  cent  gro experienced through 1997. But it may still expand by 2½ to 3 per cent (fourth quarter o quarter). Clearly, a good deal of uncertainty surrounds any estimate at this juncture international situation. For one thing, it is difficult to judge how quickly and effe will deal with its problems, and what this will mean for the rest of Asia. The extent o from the recent spreading of the crisis to Russia and the pressures in parts of Latin also  uncertain.  But,  at  the  same  time,  most  forecasters  have  consistently  underesti resilience of the US economy, and may still be doing so.

## Implications for the Canadian dollar

One of the most talked-about economic events in Canada over the past year been the decline in the external value of our currency. At its lowest point, in late the Canadian dollar had depreciated by about 13 per cent against the US dollar and by m 7 per cent against the German mark from its average value in the first half of 1997, Asian  crisis  erupted.  Since  that  low  point  in  late  August,  the  Canadian  dollar  has somewhat against the US dollar.

## What has caused these movements?

Exchange rates will typically reflect developments in Canada and abroad. Th is  important  to  keep  in  mind  that  the  recent  movements  in  the  Canadian  dollar consequence of developments that have occurred over the past year. They are not the cau difficulties we are now facing, as some of the recent commentary seems to suggest.

It is also important to note that our exchange rate is the price of the dollar  expressed  in  terms  of  the  currency  of  another  country,  usually  the  US  dollar exchange  rate  will  be  influenced  by  events  affecting  both  countries.  If  we  are  to interpret  movements  in  the  Canada/US  exchange  rate,  we  must  also  look  at  what  has happening  to  the  United  States,  not  just  to  Canada.  And  that  makes  any  interpretati complex.

Until  very  recently,  the  US  dollar  has  been  exceptionally  strong  again currencies.  In  part,  this  reflected  the  buoyancy  of  the  US  economy.  But  in  the  dif uncertain global environment of the past year, the strength of the US dollar also cam role as the major international currency. After the Asian crisis, and with renewed vi days following the events in Russia, international investors sought shelter in US do Indeed, the turmoil in financial markets in late August seemed to be the result of a reassessment of risks by investors following the announcement of the Russian debt morat

Thus, to the extent that the depreciation of our currency reflected the app of the US dollar against all currencies, the cause was the global flight of funds into U

But that is not the whole story. The downward pressure on our currency ove past year was also related to events that were seen as affecting Canada more specific explained earlier, one important event was the marked decline in the prices of the ke commodities we export.

The drop in these prices has meant lower incomes and wealth for Canadians. profit  outlook  for  many  of  our  resource  industries  has  deteriorated  and  product employment in those industries are likely to be affected. And the market value of comp those sectors has reflected these developments. Moreover, lower net export earnings f primary commodities imply, all else being equal, a larger deficit in our balance of i payments and a greater need for foreign borrowing than would otherwise be required.

All these commodity-related developments have led to downward pressure on o exchange rate. And the lower dollar spreads the wealth and income effects of falling c prices across the economy.

In  effect,  a  lower  Canadian  dollar  means  higher  domestic  prices  for  all goods that are imported and for many of the import substitutes we produce here. For level of income, these higher prices imply a decline in living standards for Canadian Retailers who feel unable to pass on these price increases to consumers will have to ab in lower profits which, in turn, will mean lower returns for their shareholders.

The bottom line is that the decline in commodity prices has made us less w than we were before. And we have to adjust to this reality.

These effects are unavoidable, even if we were able to prevent the Canadian from falling. In fact, if the currency were not allowed to move at all, the adjustmen slower and more costly, taking place through reductions in wages which usually involve fluctuations in output and employment. Under a floating exchange rate, the process is by some downward movement in the dollar which spreads the burden of adjustment. Over years,  this  has  been  an  important  justification  for  a  flexible  exchange  rate  in  Can adjusting  through  exchange  rate  movements  to  the  shocks  that  periodically  hit  our  e makes for a generally smoother and fairer process than adjusting through reductions i employment, and wages.

But I do not want to leave you with the impression that foreign exchange ma always know the appropriate value for a currency. They sometimes push too far once a established in one direction or another. Indeed, I believe that during this latest epi financial turbulence, markets exaggerated the commodity connection of the Canadian doll example,  our  exports  of  highly  manufactured  goods,  apart  from  the  important  motor  v sector, have grown by nearly 20 per cent over the past 12 months, and now represent a per cent of our merchandise trade. This development seems to have been largely overlooke

## Monetary policy response

So, what can and should the Bank of Canada do about the exchange rate in t of international financial turbulence and major external shocks?

First of all, let me remind you that the objective of Canadian monetary pol hold the rate of inflation within a range of 1 to 3 per cent. This target, jointly agre government and the Bank of Canada, reflects the conclusion that low inflation will con a stronger, more stable economic performance over time.

If we are to fulfill our commitment to keep inflation low and stable, mo policy  must  remain  focused  on  that  objective.  The  exchange  rate  and  interest  rates

channels through which monetary policy operates and they must be allowed to adjust t achieve the inflation targets.

But what if the momentum of currency movements pushes the Canadian dollar beyond  any  level  that  is  justified  on  economic  grounds?  Judgments  as  to  what  is,  o justified are very difficult to make, but there are times when the good economic news g the face of a persistent currency decline.

On those occasions, Canadian authorities need to remind investors of the p trends in our economy. And to reinforce the message, the Bank may intervene, on behalf Minister of Finance, to support the currency by buying Canadian dollars in the foreign market. But we do know that this kind of intervention will be effective only if a good investors share our belief that the currency movement has been overdone.

The Bank can also respond to currency declines with Bank Rate changes. Th are  two  sets  of  circumstances  in  which  this  would  be  appropriate.  The  first  is magnitude  of  the  currency  decline  threatens  to  push  the  economy  off  a  sustainabl inflationary  growth  path.  Remember  that  a  declining  currency  is  a  source  of  stimulu economy, because it encourages exporters and producers of import substitutes to expan activities. That is why the Bank always puts the exchange rate and interest rates toget to measure the amount of monetary stimulus in the economy. If a declining currency l monetary conditions that are persistently too easy and inconsistent with the inflation Bank will offset that with higher short-term interest rates.

The second situation that would prompt a Bank Rate increase is when there potential loss of confidence in the Canadian dollar. If confidence is undermined, both and foreign investors will move out of investments denominated in Canadian dollars unl are compensated with substantial premiums in interest rates. Higher premiums, which t into higher medium- and long-term interest rates, are very costly for the economy. It w of  such  concerns  that  the  Bank  responded  strongly  to  the  decline  in  our  currency  du Mexican crisis in early 1995.

The recent Bank Rate increase at the end of August was also designed to cou potential loss of market confidence. In this case, investor nervousness was exacerbat financial crisis in Russia and was reflected in a sharp decline in our currency and ris and long-term interest rates. Since the Bank Rate increase, the Canadian dollar has rec medium- and longer-term interest rates have come down.

## Concluding comments

I have placed a great deal of emphasis on recent international developments remarks today because the implications of these developments for the Canadian economy a exchange rate are important and complex.

Let me summarize my main points.

For the past year, our economy has had to cope with the fallout from the crisis, which has turned out to be more widespread and prolonged than most of us had pr Although we are having to deal with these difficulties and with the ongoing global un and pressures, it is important to remember that there is still a significant positi

Canada's external environment coming mainly from a resilient US economy. And there is considerable underlying buoyancy in our domestic economy. What's more, the improvement our basic economic foundations puts us in a better position than before to withstand t adversity.

In addition to pressure from the worldwide strength of the US dollar, some downward movement in the Canadian dollar over the past year was a reflection of the im lower commodity prices on our economic well-being. However, by early August, it appeare investors  were  exaggerating  the  importance  of  these  effects  and  losing  sight  of  th positive  fundamentals  in  our  economy.  The  Bank  intervened,  buying  Canadian  dollars encourage market participants to pause and reassess their views of the Canadian economy that pause was overwhelmed by a new wave of nervousness precipitated by the events in in mid-August, the Bank raised the Bank Rate to forestall a loss of confidence in th and thus reverse a costly increase that was taking place in medium and long-term inter Since then, these interest rates have come down.

Let  me  conclude  by  pointing  out  that,  despite  all  the  recent  attention Canadian  dollar  because  of  exceptional  external  developments,  the  fundamental  foc monetary policy remains on keeping the trend of inflation in Canada inside a target ran 3 per cent. Low inflation is the best contribution the Bank of Canada can make towards overall  economic  performance  over  time.  It  also  provides  the  best  underpinning  for Canadian dollar in the long run.
