title: Mr. Bäckstöm remarks on the Swedish economy  (Central Bank Articles and Speeches, 7 Oct 98)
description: Address by the Governor of the Bank of Sweden, Mr. Urban Bäckström, at Svenska Handelsbanken's seminar in New York on 7/10/98.
text:
Mr. Bäckstöm remarks on the Swedish economy Address by the Governor of the Bank of Sweden, Mr. Urban Bäckström, at Svenska Handelsbanken's seminar in New Yor on 7/10/98.

First of all I should like to thank Svenska Handelsbanken for the invita meet with you today here in New York. I arrived late yesterday from the 1998 Annual Meet the International Monetary Fund in Washington D.C. The discussions in Washington over weekend focused on the current problems in the world economy. At the centre was of cour crises in emerging markets that began in Thailand last year, which spread to other eco East Asia and Russia and which most recently have been pressuring economies in Latin Am Lately,  we  have  also  seen  some  contagion  effects  spreading  to  the  industrial  co Stockmarkets have been falling and there have also been some problems in connection wi Long-Term Capital hedge fund.

However, today I will talk about the Swedish economy. I shall be using a broad brush to paint you a picture of how our economy has developed in recent years an conclude by saying a few words about the present situation in my country.

## Positive trend in recent years

The Swedish economy is now entering its sixth consecutive year of favour growth. The average annual GDP growth rate since the summer of 1993 is almost 3 per This is an improvement compared to the average that has characterised our economy in t twenty-five years. It has been accompanied by external surpluses that are larger than years, making it possible to repay foreign debt. Government finances, moreover, now surplus instead of the earlier deficits, which means that government debt is already be in relation to GDP.

The latest figures show that prices in Sweden's economy are virtually stat The falling trend in market interest rates in recent years has been a major factor here reduced house mortgage interest expenditure and thereby temporarily exerted a downward effect on inflation. The underlying price trend is not, in fact, as low as the CPI figures m but that does not alter the conclusion that in the years ahead, inflation will continue

If Sweden sticks to disciplined fiscal and monetary policies, together wi ways of enhancing economic policy's credibility, we have a real opportunity of reinst tradition of price stability that existed in Sweden prior to the 1970s and 80s. Let m short historical background to our current economic policy strategy.

## Tradition of price stability

In the period from 1830 to the late 1960s, the annual rate of inflation i averaged around 2 per cent. So if one disregards the 1970s and 80s, low inflation has norm for almost a century and a half. There are indeed grounds for saying that price st long Swedish tradition.

The tradition of price stability did not obstruct the economy's developmen is shown by the fact that from the mid 19th century up to the late 1960s growth in Sw

among the highest in the world. It is rather the case that the favourable outcome was p low inflation and the stability this represents.

The decades immediately after World War Two were particularly notable for h growth,  low  inflation,  external  balance  and  an  optimistic  mood  that  resulted  in  the economy's successive expansion. That was a prosperous period with a good, stable eco trend, a rising standard of living and high employment.

After  the  collapse  of  the  Bretton  Woods  system  in  the  early  1970s  it  p difficult  to  establish  an  equally  robust  fixed  exchange  rate  regime.  A  firm  anchor existed for economic policy in general and wage formation in particular. Sweden experi series of devaluation cycles, with an expansionary fiscal policy, inefficient wage for growing structural problems. With the deregulation of the financial sector the problem all too evident.

During the 1970s and 80s economic growth in Sweden became weaker than in other countries. But the economy still became overheated and this, together with an exp public sector activities, meant that unemployment was restrained for the time being .

The  situation  was  of  course  unsustainable.  An  inflationary,  speculative cannot grow indefinitely; sooner or later it is bound to burst. There was also a limit resources for financing employment.

## New direction in economic policy

In the late 1980s there was a growing awareness that something would have t done. The structural problems, high inflation and relatively low growth called for an policy realignment.

This realignment involved a variety of measures. The tax system was refor and so were certain components of transfers. Sweden, moreover, applied for membership European Union. Sweden's currency was linked to the ecu and in the autumn of 1992, duri wave of currency speculation, the exchange rate was defended. Short term interest ra raised to high levels. The idea was to demonstrate the determination to re-establish lo

However,  Sweden's  economic  policy  realignment  coincided  with  a  profound economic crisis. Output fell around 5 per cent over a three-year period, open unemploym up  to  over  9  per  cent  and  total  unemployment  to  around  13  per  cent,  figures  that completely  unknown  in  modern  Sweden.  The  government  finances  deteriorated  sharply  a budget  deficit  reached  a  high  of  more  than  12  per  cent  of  GDP,  which  was  almost  w precedent  in  the  industrialised  countries.  In  the  middle  of  this  crisis,  moreover, whole of the banking system was threatening to collapse. In the light of the crisis Asian economies, all this sounds very familiar.

Researchers  will  no  doubt  be  studying  whether  this  dramatic  setback  in Swedish economy could have been managed differently. Some things could definitely have arranged  in  another  way  both  in  the  late  1980s  and  once  the  crisis  was  over  us  in nineties.

But the vital conclusion is, I believe, that the roots of the profound cris a  long  way  into  the  past.  An  economic  policy  realignment  was  essential;  a  credible oriented policy had been lacking ever since the collapse of the Bretton Woods system in 1970s. It was high time to put this right.

## Making the new regime credible

After  the  long  period  of  high  inflation,  together  with  extensive  eco problems and massive government deficits, the task of inspiring confidence in economic new direction proved difficult at first. Economic agents listened to the new approach w and hesitation.

As we know from other countries, however, creating confidence in a new reg with low inflation is a rather long process that takes time. Moreover, if the work inflation low and government finances in order is to be combined with low interest r stable growth, it is a task that never ends.

In recent years the low-inflation regime has gained increased credibility. B disciplined monetary policy for price stability, a major contribution to this has com consolidation of government finances. In just a few years a budget deficit at 12 per c has been turned into today's surplus.

In order to underscore its ambitions for public finances, the Government long-term  objective:  as  the  average  level  over  a  business  cycle,  government  finance generate a surplus at 2 per cent of GDP. A surplus will make it possible to reduce pub that  future  challenges  which  the  Swedish  economy  may  encounter  can  be  accepted  wit leading to problems for government finances.

Considering the public debt that has accumulated in the 1990s and the fac government finances in Sweden are relatively sensitive to cyclical factors, I find th reasonable.

Besides  the  increased  awareness  of  the  importance  of  stable  finances, conditions for achieving Sweden's budget target have been improved by institutional cha the budget process. Sweden now has a budget process that is inherently more disciplined thereby contribute to maintaining sound finances.

Further steps are being taken to consolidate economic policy's focus on st The independence which the Riksbank already has in practice is to have a formal legal of next year. The monetary policy objective of price stability will be enshrined in l Riksbank will be accountable for fulfilling it.

This new Riksbank legislation has already been approved once by the Riks (Sweden's parliament) and the final decision is due this autumn. The reform is backed political parties, whose combined representation in the newly elected Riksdag is over 80

According to the timetable for the new legislation, the Riksdag's final d will be made sometime in the middle of November. It will be followed by the appointment Riksbank's new Governing Board, which will consist of eleven Delegates. One of its majo

will be to appoint the Riksbank's new Executive Board. This Board will consist of six members who will direct the Riksbank and decide monetary policy as of January 1999.

## The present situation

Sweden's monetary policy is conducted in a flexible exchange rate regime and an explicit inflation target. We sometimes use the following simple rule of thumb to what governs our actions: if the overall assessment of inflation indicates that in one time the rate of inflation will deviate from the 2 per cent target, then the repo r adjusted accordingly. Our approach is symmetrical, which means that it is equally impo avoid undershooting the target, as it is to avoid overshooting it.

The Riksbank's appraisal of inflation up to the autumn of 2000 and the mon policy conclusions that can be drawn from this are presented in the Inflation Report we last  week.  In  order  to  visualise  the  consequences  for  the  future  path  of  monetary  p report is based on the working assumption of an unchanged repo rate. As the Swedish k judged to be undervalued at present, we also assume that the exchange rate follows a represents a gradual appreciation.

The technical assumption of an unchanged repo rate and the presumed path fo exchange  rate  are  then  incorporated  in  the  main  scenario  for  inflation.  As  inflati course is not a straightforward matter, we also include assessments of uncertainties. picture of inflation prospects amounts in practice to an estimate of probabilities.

The assessments in the main scenario imply favourable economic fundamentals: a growth  rate  between  2.5  and  3  per  cent  between  1998  and  2000,  low  inflation  and  a government surplus. Domestic demand in the main scenario is expected to generate a rel limited increase in inflation's underlying rate, from 1.1 per cent at present to 1.6 p end of next year and 2 per cent in the autumn of 2000.

The  12-month  change  in  CPI  inflation  is  expected  to  be  somewhat  below  t inflation target in one to two years time but the figure at the end of the period is approximately 2 per cent. All this means that at the end of the period under review, relatively well in line with the Riksbank's target.

It should be underscored, however, that the assessment of inflation prosp more  difficult  than  usual  on  account  of  the  financial  turbulence.  This  naturally  r international unrest but the political situation after the general election in Sweden h mark on price setting, above all in the currency market.

Inflation prospects and the future path of monetary policy accordingly dep two - contrary - factors: on the one hand, the international economic trend could be w we have counted on and thereby lead to lower inflation; on the other, a sustained weak rate  that  has  no  counterpart  in  a  weaker  real  economy  could  generate  increased  inf pressure.

Our  monetary  policy  conclusion  is  that  we  will  go  on  analysing  the  cour events and appraise monetary policy continuously in the light of new information. Hopef analysis  in  the  Inflation  Report  should  give  an  indication  of  our  line  of  reasoning

inflation outlook in Sweden and the future path of monetary policy that is as clear as the global economy's present state of uncertainty.

The unsettled situation in international financial markets has meant that are shifting to currencies which are historically secure. As a result, other currencie those of smaller economies, have weakened. This tendency has been evident for the Sw krona in recent weeks and very clear in the last few days. The recent path of the Swedi not consistent with the development of our economy's fundamentals. Under these circumst the Riksbank has chosen to use currency interventions to underscore that the movements krona's exchange rate have been unduly abrupt and exaggerated.

title: Mr. Heikensten discusses independence and transparency in monetary policy  (Central Bank Articles and Speeches, 25 Sep 98)
description: Speech by the Deputy Governor of the Bank of Sweden, Mr. Lars Heikensten, at the City Executive Club in Gothenburg on 25/9/98.
text:
Mr. Heikensten discusses independence and transparency in monetary policy Speech  by  the  Deputy  Governor  of  the  Bank  of  Sweden,  Mr.  Lars  Heikensten,  at  the Executive Club in Gothenburg on 25/9/98.

This morning, rather than discuss current monetary policy, I shall be cons some questions that have to do with monetary policy's long-term conditions.

Next year, a proposal that has received the preliminary approval of the R (Sweden's parliament) will make the Riksbank more independent. Here, Sweden is particip in a development that has been in progress in the industrialised countries for a couple - monetary policy decisions are being delegated to the central banks. This has been both because monetary policy is considered to focus too one-sidedly on a single objec because the increased independence is said to limit democratic influence unduly. It may be appropriate to review the arguments behind the changes and comment on what they requ the Riksbank.

A discussion of the process towards more independent central banks - and considerations that underlie this process - must take monetary policy's objective as point. I shall therefore begin by discussing why low inflation is important. Then I sh the arguments for central bank independence and outline the changes that are in train i Finally I shall put the case for the importance of monetary policy transparency.

## Why low inflation?

From  time  to  time  in  the  debate,  the  importance  of  having  low  inflati monetary policy's objective is called into question. The critics consider that the f inflation is overdone and results in an unnecessary restriction on growth and employ allow me to motivate the wisdom of focusing monetary policy just on low inflation.

The Riksbank's basic function is to provide Sweden with a stable and eff payment system. In practice, this amounts to being accountable for maintaining a fixed money and ensuring that the banks provide money in satisfactory way. If the payment sy to function properly, however, it must have a solid reputation. If people believe, for e the value of money will be appreciably eroded, or will fluctuate markedly, they will uncertain and confidence in the payment system will be weakened. That can result in decisions.

In other words, low inflation renders the economy more efficient and mak easier  for  households  and  firms  to  arrive  at  long-term  decisions.  A  look  at  the  s Sweden in the 1980s will illustrate this. High inflation, recurrent cost crises and cycles made economic development erratic, with weak investment and productivity as a More and more misplaced investments were made as a 'bubble' grew and when the proper market subsequently collapsed, Swedish society was burdened by heavy adjustment costs.

Inflation  also  leaves  its  mark  on  the  distribution  of  income  and  wealth inflation tends to widen existing differences in wealth because it varies in its impact types of earnings and saving. A person who has savings in a bank and earns a fixed wage is a loser from inflation, whereas someone who can save in real assets, for ins home-owner, stands to gain from rising inflation. Once again, Sweden in the 1970s and '

good example: prices rose sharply for houses and tenant-owned dwellings, while bank were eroded. Inflation widened the gaps.

So  far,  so  good,  most  people  would  say.  Few  desire  a  return  to  the  e inflationary and speculative economy. A knottier question is just what rate of inflation

In Sweden we have chosen to focus policy on an annual CPI inflation rate of cent.  As  monetary  policy  is  not  capable  of  directing  inflation  exactly,  when  the  t established in 1993 it was surrounded by a tolerance interval of ±1 percentage point.

This  target  is  well  in  line  with  the  rate  of  inflation  that  other  ind countries, not least in Europe, are aiming for, though there are some minor difference well in line with a statement some years ago by Mr. Alan Greenspan, head of the US F Reserve, to the effect that inflation should be so low that economic agents need not w it when making economic decisions. Perhaps that is as close to the truth as one can com

## Policy for low inflation

Low inflation has been the normal state of affairs in the Swedish economy. the past one hundred years the rate has fluctuated around two per cent. It is only in period, more exactly from the late 1960s onwards, that inflation has taken off. The s happened  in  other  countries.  Part  of  the  reason  seems  to  have  been  that  economis politicians changed their view of what monetary policy could achieve. At that time man considered that monetary policy could induce permanently higher employment; more jobs c be brought about simply by letting inflation rise. What they overlooked was the centr primary function of safeguarding the payment system's stability.

History has also clearly demonstrated that this strategy does not work; i countries, unemployment rose parallel with inflation. In Sweden the rate of inflation r digit figures, accompanied by the erratic economic development which meant that we dr down the 'growth league'. Then, when the inflation bubble burst, unemployment rose.

What the economists and politicians had not allowed for was how rising inf would leave its mark on expectations of future inflation. The original idea - that high via lower real wages, would result in higher demand and employment - did not hold in th run when firms and households realised that their elected representatives and central fuelling  inflation.  In  the  original  scenario,  the  higher  inflation  was  supposed unexpectedly and therefore would not result in wage compensation. In practice, the i inflation affected expectations of future inflation, for which employees demanded compe With the higher nominal wages, real wages rose again and labour demand fell back. A si rose where prices and wages chased each other in an upward spiral. Unemployment remain the best case at its initial level.

When  it  was  realised  that  monetary  policy  could  not  generate  permanen increased  employment,  politicians  and  people  in  general  had  to  think  again.  The  at stimulate  increased  economic  activity  and  employment  by  means  of  fiscal  and  mone measures had failed. This line therefore had to give way to a policy that focused on p stable fundamentals for economic development. One of these fundamentals is low inflati central banks were in the best position to shoulder the task of safeguarding the value

Sweden switched to the same track as other countries in the early 1990s. was directed at price stability with the explicit ambition of thereby laying a good fo future growth and employment. The next few years were onerous for Sweden's economy. T bill for the excesses of the 1980s had to be paid at a time when global activity was and Europe was hit by currency crises. Since the summer of 1993, however, events have different turn. Growth above the rate in the boom years in the late 1980s has been comb lastingly low inflation. Employment is now picking up but in order to push unemployment towards the earlier, very low levels, changes are presumably needed in the workings of t market and wage formation.

## Increased independence for the Riksbank

Today,  therefore,  most,  though  not  all,  economists  and  politicians  are  b agreed that monetary policy has a very limited potential for permanently altering th employment. But monetary policy is capable of influencing growth temporarily. So for tho decide economic policy, there is always the temptation to try to strengthen economic a the short run and push unemployment down. In order to restrict the scope for such a governments  and  parliaments  in  most  industrialised  countries  have  taken  the  initia decided to make their central banks more independent. This is often combined with a price  stability  objective.  Some  countries  have  also  established  procedures  for  asse exacting accountability.

Experience shows that the countries with a far-reaching delegation of mon policy  have  had  a  favourable  development  of  inflation.  It  is  probably  not  just  t framework  that  has  resulted  in  low  inflation.  Central  banks  have  been  most  succes countries where the aversion to inflation is strongest and most widespread.

Central bank independence is thus, you might say, a straightjacket that parl and governments have put on themselves. Paradoxically, it is just by tying their hands that the legislators have actually given monetary policy more scope to pay some heed to considerations.  This  is  so  as  a  result  of  greater  independence  and  because  everyone assured that inflation will continue to be low in the future. In actual fact, a cre target  strategy  normally  caters  to  cyclical  factors.  An  economic  slowdown  tends accompanied by a weakening of inflationary pressure, making it possible to ease the m stance. The stance is then tightened again when inflationary pressure rises. In this w policy can contribute to economic growth, without unnecessary upsets, at a rate that is with the development of productivity, employment and so on.

A government bill proposing increased formal independence for the Riksbank of 1999 was presented to the Riksdag in November 1997. Five political parties in the Ri behind the proposals and they have also given the constitutional amendments their pre approval.

The new legislation accordingly gives the Riksbank the constitutional funct conducting monetary policy. The constitutional provisions also state that the Riksbank take  instructions  from  authorities  concerning  the  construction  of  monetary  poli Riksbank's  current  obligation  to  hold  consultations  with  the  government  prior  to  i decisions of monetary and exchange rate policy is converted into an obligation to in government. The price stability objective is incorporated in the Riksbank Act, which

that the objective of monetary policy is to safeguard the value of money and promote a efficient payment system.

The greater independence also involves changes in the Riksbank's managemen Instead of being directed, as at present, by a Governing Board appointed by the Riksd will be an Executive Board with six full-time members, chaired by the Riksbank Governo the Executive Board that will manage the Riksbank and be accountable for all monetary decisions. Unlike the system in the United Kingdom, besides acting as a committee for m policy  decisions,  the  Executive  Board  will  be  responsible  for  managing  the  whole Riksbank.

Even  under  the  new  law,  however,  the  Riksbank  will  still  have  a  Govern Board.  It  will  consist  of  eleven  members,  instead  of  eight  at  present,  and  will  ha supervisory  role.  Its  principal  functions  will  be  to  monitor  and  control  the  activ Riksbank, appoint the Executive Board and, if necessary, dismiss any member of the Exe Board who no longer fulfils the conditions required for the performance of duties or i serious misconduct.

In this context I also want to say something about the timetable this autu the new legislation requires. As usual, our newly elected Riksdag will appoint a new G Board in accordance with the existing procedure. As previously, these eight Delegates w the Riksbank and decide monetary policy, up to the turn of the year. When the const amendments have been approved a second time, the Riksdag will appoint a Governing Bo under the new order; this will probably be done in late November or early December. Bef end of 1998 the new Governing Board - which for a month or so will accordingly exist side with the current arrangement - must then appoint the members of the new Executive The new Governing Board and the new Executive Board will then take over from 1 Janu 1999.

As  there  will  be  little  time  for  the  two  new  Boards  to  prepare  their  ne initial  decisions,  preliminary  work  will  have  to  be  done  this  autumn.  Matters  that Governing  Board  will  have  to  decide  at  its  first  meeting  include  the  Riksbank's procedure, while at more or less the same time the Executive Board will have to fin details of work at the Bank: which matters can be delegated further down the organisat matters should be drafted in the Bank and similar questions. At its first meeting, mo Executive  Board  will  have  to  decide  the  frequency  of  its  meetings,  which  tasks  its members are to be responsible for and how the Board is to communicate with the general

## Importance of transparency

This brings me to the degree of transparency in monetary policy. In recent the Riksbank has worked to make monetary policy more transparent, with good communicat with market players and the general public.

A basic reason behind our drive for transparency is the need for clarity. Th that clarity in monetary policy will make the policy more effective. If market agents understand how we are reasoning, there will be less risk of unnecessary fluctuations rates and the exchange rate. That in turn should help to make general economic devel more stable. In drastic terms one could say that we aim to make the markets so familiar

analytical framework and our deliberations that the available information would enable set the interest rate on their own.

Another reason for transparency has to do with the Riksbank's social fun This responsibility is augmented in that the increased independence has the force of then all the more important to develop and communicate the arguments behind the Riksb actions. This is a prerequisite for a sound discussion and evaluation of our policy and the Riksbank accountable if the policy is not conducted in a reasonable way.

More generally, moreover, the Riksbank should continue to work for increa transparency in order to promote a widespread understanding of what we are doing. In the discussion, for instance, there is some criticism of the low-inflation target. The Rik to  be  unduly  focused  on  combating  inflation  at  the  expense  of  growth  and  employment therefore need to persist with an open dialogue to explain that we, too, desire and st economic growth but that the best thing monetary policy can do to this end is just e stable framework for other components of economic policy.

The  internal  work  at  the  Riksbank  also  calls  for  external  transparency. away with a hush-hush attitude to outsiders makes a frank internal discussion easier. C goals are also a help in focusing internal work and analysis on the relevant issues.

The open presentation of a clear line of thought simplifies the education The Riksbank's line consists of an explicit inflation target and an account of the fac consider affect inflation; it also includes how monetary policy measures are construc light of the inflation assessment. Current forecasts and assessments are presented in t Inflation Reports. In between we try to comment, in speeches and other ways, on any cha our appraisal of inflation.

Unfortunately,  a  soundly  constructed  line  of  thought  does  not  always  su From  time  to  time  we  are  highly  uncertain  about  how  the  available  information  sho interpreted. That is something which we and all economic agents must learn to live w exact statement may not be possible in such situations.

One matter connected with the independence and transparency of the Riksbank whether  or  not  the  Riksbank  should  publish  minutes  of  its  discussions  and/or  sho decision-makers have voted. One reason why this issue has attracted so much attention is no doubt that the new Bank of England legislation stresses the monitoring of how i members have voted.

The Riksbank's new Executive Board will clearly have to adopt a position on matter. So permit me to raise a couple of relevant aspects. It seems to me that a disti made between requiring accountability on the one hand and clarity or distinctness of the other.

- As  regards accountability, it  is  clearly  important  how  individual  members vote. The Governing Board's long-term influence over Riksbank policy wi after all, be exerted primarily through the composition of the Executive It follows that the Governing Board - presumably the general public as needs to be in a position to assess how different members of the Exec Board have acted. The knowledge that voting is made public no doubt a

- makes every member of the Executive Board all the more keen to arrive a personal conclusion about the difficult issues that have to be resolved.
- As regards transparency , on the other hand, what matters most in my opinion is to have a clear line of thought, as I outlined earlier, and on this ways of communicating how assessments change over time. The latter can done  in  Inflation  Reports  and  speeches,  as  at  present,  as  well communiqués  after  board  meetings,  etc.  In  this  context,  information  a how  the  individual  board  members  have  voted  is  not  so  self-eviden important.

There will doubtless be reason to return to this issue. The conclusion from discussion  is  not  automatic.  A  good  combination  of  the  two  perspectives  above  is  p feasible. A further consideration is the need to create an Executive Board that functio not only when it comes to making wise monetary policy decisions but also in the Riks effective management.

## Concluding remarks

Since the early 1990s the Riksbank has clearly had the task of establishin stability in Sweden. Strong confidence in the Riksbank means that monetary policy is achieve the desired results without resorting to emphatic interest-rate signals. In an with low inflation and high credibility, monetary policy may be in a better position fluctuations in growth and employment.

Confidence  in  the  low-inflation  policy  does  seem  to  have  been  establi Inflation has been low and inflation expectations are in line with the inflation tar fiscal  policy  is  contributing  to  this  but  so,  of  course,  is  a  monetary  policy consistently on low inflation. The credibility of policy is, however, a continuous qu process will be facilitated by the Riksbank's statutory independence but the Riksbank m for example, work continuously to communicate its policy deliberations clearly and dist

The conditions for policy are affected by many factors. A labour market and formation that function better make it possible to combine low inflation with higher em Fiscal policy is another central matter; it needs to be sustainable in the long run a also help to counter any signs of incipient overheating.

If some component of economic policy fails to promote the inflation targe burden on monetary policy will be heavier. Stronger measures by the Riksbank will be ne a clear demonstration of the determination to achieve low inflation. Insufficient supp inflation target and policies that are not permanently sustainable would then be a burd for the Riksbank but for the economy in general.

title: Mr. Chon speaks on the topic 'Korea: moving on from the crisis'  (Central Bank Articles and Speeches, 8 Oct 98)
description: Address by the Governor of the Bank of Korea, Mr. Chol-Hwan Chon, at the 1999 Emerging Markets Roundtable hosted by Euromoney on 8/10/98.
text:
Mr. Chon speaks on the topic  'Korea: moving on from the crisis' Address by the Governor of the Bank of Korea, Mr. Chol-Hwan Chon, at the 1999 Emerging Marke Roundtable hosted by Euromoney on 8/10/98.

I  am  very  happy  to  be  with  you  today  to  explain  our  efforts  to  reshap economic and financial fabric of Korea. This is all the more so since I am keenly consci vital role that you as investors play in the international economy.

Just under a year ago, Korea faced a very difficult situation. But the wor specific Korean problems now appear to be over. Some sectors of the economy are grad returning to a stable track. Let me take this opportunity to express my hearty thanks t for your cooperative support. I hope that my words today will help you gain a clear what has been happening in the Korean economy.

## Development and Causes of the Crisis

The  alarm  bells  should  already  have  been  sounding  by  the  mid-nineties. trade and capital market liberalization, firms had found themselves drawn into the glob Nevertheless, they did not adjust to the new environment in which the market ruled, bu pursued the expansion strategies of an earlier development era. Also, the government establish  a  market  system  well  geared  to  the  changing  world.  The  consequent  ambitio imprudent investment brought high growth at first, but deepened the high costs-low ef structure of the Korean economy.

Deteriorating corporate sector competitiveness pushed up the ratio of the account deficit to GDP from 1 percent in 1994 to 4.7 percent in 1996. Furthermore, fr last year, a number of highly leveraged large companies that had been hit by sluggish low profitability finally collapsed under their huge debt. These failures in turn und soundness of financial institutions with large corporate exposures. A vicious downwar was set in motion.

Meanwhile,  the  contagion  of  the  Thai  baht's  devaluation  last  July  spread wildfire.  This  further  unsettled  foreign  investors  who  had  been  apprehensively  eye weakening of both companies and financial institutions in Korea. Reflecting this, S& Moody's  downgraded  Korea's  long-term  sovereign  rating  very  sharply  last  October,  w caused foreign investors to withdraw their credit lines hastily. Liquid foreign exchan drained away rapidly leaving Korea on the brink of national insolvency. The governmen had to turn to the IMF in late November.

The jury is still out on what actually caused the Korean crisis, but there major contributory factors; namely, inefficiency caused by a failure to observe market the  loss  of  market  confidence  caused  by  a  lack  of  transparency,  and  inappropriate responses to the evolving problems.

The first of these was perhaps the most fundamental. The Korean economy h been largely government-directed for many years and lacked true market discipline. In p

rapid growth, 'big' had been the name of the game so that the principle of too-big-t become an unwritten law.

Financial institutions, under the government's wing, routinely made loans corporate  sector  without  thoroughly  screening  investment  plans.  Workers  and  deposito turned  a  blind  eye  to  market  principles.  Moral  hazard  was  widespread  and  high  co efficiency problems persisted.

The second factor I mentioned was, however, the more immediate cause of financial  crisis.  The  accounting  and  disclosure  systems  of  Korea  fell  short  of  glob making it difficult to grasp a true picture of firms' condition. This lack of transpa symptoms of a crisis emerged, led to a rush for the exit since no discrimination could to  quality.  But  it  should  be  also  borne  in  mind  that  before  the  crisis,  this  obscu foreigners to invest in Korea without scrutinizing carefully the actual status of firms

Last, but not the least, was that the policy responses to the looming cr woefully inadequate; that they were mistimed; and that the markets were sent confusing by inconsistencies among them. One prime example was the retention of a narrow currency despite the mounting downward pressure on the won. This several times brought the f exchange market to a halt as the won hit its lower limit shortly after opening. Anothe was the dithering over what to do with the distressed Kia group. The failure to procee fairly and on the basis of market principles destroyed the incumbent administration's credibility.

## Response to the Crisis

Economic policies have since last December been closely coordinated with IMF. On the macroeconomic policy front, the Bank of Korea raised its market interventi from 12 percent to over 30 percent to stabilize the foreign exchange market. Korea also a free-floating exchange rate system.

Along with stringent macroeconomic policy, structural reforms are now under throughout the financial and corporate sectors.

The  focus  of  financial  sector  restructuring  is  on  the  exit  of  unsound  f institutions,  the  resolution  of  the  overhang  of  bad  loans  and  the  strengthening  of supervision and disclosure requirements.

Five  ailing  banks  have been  resolved  through  a  'Purchase  and  Assumption' formula.  Korea  First  Bank  and  Seoul  Bank  whose  capital  was  reduced  in  January  w recapitalized  by  the  government's  subscription  of  public  enterprise  stocks.  Governme shares in these two banks will be sold under open bidding to domestic and foreign i before  the  end  of  October.  Sixteen  out  of  thirty  merchant  banking  corporations,  wh contributed  to  the  crisis,  have  been  already  shut  down,  and  a  number  of  distressed financial institutions, such as securities companies and insurance companies, have been suspended.

Also, the bank and merchant banks now in business are being monitored on progress of their target BIS ratios and rehabilitation plans, which include

recapitalization  and  sharp  reductions  in  branches  and  staff.  With  this  pressure  to capital adequacy ratios and improve competitiveness, a wave of mergers is taking plac financial industry. This is supported by the government through the purchase of non-pe loans and capital injection. Three large mergers among banks have already been announce consolidation of the banking sector is likely to continue for some time.

To improve transparency, standards for the classification of non-performing the accumulation of loan loss provisions, and disclosure have all been brought into internationally accepted standards.

By revising the General Banking Act, the government allowed a foreign inve to hold more than 10% of a bank's total stocks with the permission of the Financial Su Commission.

Restructuring of the corporate sector is now underway across many dimensions

First, all new mutual guarantees among companies belonging to a chaebol, wh were a main tool in fund-raising for them, have been forbidden since April 1998. Membe will  also  be  obliged  to  retire  all  outstanding  cross-payment  guarantees  completely 2000.

Second,  commercial  banks  are  playing  a  vital  role  in  the  exit  of  faile through  agreements  between  large  firms  and  their  main  creditor  banks  on  improving  c structure. A first round which slated fifty-five non-viable firms from sixty-four conglo exit was announced last June. These firms will have their credit lifelines turned off b of fresh bank credit and the calling-in of loans. The process will continue in the futu

Third, the chaebol will have to provide combined financial statements fro fiscal year 1999. This should strip away the veil that has hidden their true position. to corporate governance, the rights of minority shareholders have also been greatly stre

Fourth,  ceilings  on  foreign  investment  in  Korean  equities  have  now  b abolished and hostile takeovers by foreigners allowed. Foreigners may now also buy and estate on a national treatment basis. This September, with the passage of the 'Foreign Promotion Act', all foreign investors in foreign investment zones are given full exemp corporation tax and income tax for the first seven years of operation, and after that exemption for a further three years.

All  of  these  efforts  are  focused  on  shifting  our  economy  from  a  governm directed to a market-oriented system. We all recognize that rebuilding the economy on principles is the one and the only way to achieve a lasting recovery from the crisis.

## Recent Economic Trends

Since  the  outbreak  of  the  crisis,  we  have  striven  for  foreign  exchange stabilization and overall structural reform. As a result, the exchange rate has gradua stability.  The  won  tumbled  to  about  2,000  won  per  dollar  at  one  stage  but  has  reco to around  the  1,300  to  1,400  won  range  thanks  to  the  big  improvement  in  supply-dem conditions in the foreign exchange market helped by the large current account surplus

with the improved exchange market conditions, market interest rates have been easing their pre-crisis levels. For example, the CP rate dropped from a peak of over 40 pe December to 11 percent level recently.

But  the  real  sector  has  been  going  through  serious  hardships  with  the  m erosion of consumer and investor confidence, a deepening credit crunch, sharply negati growth, a continuing stream of corporate insolvencies, and a steep rise in unemployment.

During the second quarter of 1998, the GDP growth rate registered -6.6 pe The number of the unemployed increased to 1.58 million in August, which was more than times the level of a year ago. And there is a concern that the present asset-price d trigger more general deflation with the loss of purchasing power.

It is true that structural adjustment is never without pain. However, a prolonged  depression  could  sap  the  country's  growth  potential.  And  with  no  adequate safety net in place, a steep run-up in unemployment could unleash social unrest.

Concerned to prevent such scenarios, the Korean government decided to incr public spending in agreement with the IMF.

However, the government initiative should not be interpreted as full-scale priming.  The  overwhelming  stress  is  still  on  structural  reform.  The  worry  is  that  t depression might stand in the way of structural reform itself. A mild stimulus would, in con be beneficial for the structural adjustment process.

This year will see sharply negative growth for the Korean economy. But prov restructuring is successful, there should be a renewal of confidence in the country on international investors. Macroeconomic fundamentals should then start to look a bit bet second half of next year, with a shift to mildly positive GDP growth, albeit at a meager

## Concluding Remarks

To sum up, Korea has made a concerted national effort to recover from the through  bold  structural  reforms.  I  think,  however,  there  was  some  trial  and  error conceived policies were adopted in the process of the structural reform. As you are wel is very difficult to complete reform at a stroke without making mistakes, because refor fairness in the sharing of the pain among all parties. I can, though, assert that K determined to bring about a sound and vital economy on the basis of the market mechanis me  then  earnestly  request  you  not  to  write  off  the  future  of  Korea  because  of shortsighted policies or temporary setbacks in pursuing structural reform.

A  recent  survey  by  the  prominent  journal  'The  Economist'  pointed  out  t Koreans were optimistic and were confident that the future would be better although t dissatisfied  with  present  life.  This  attitude  was  cited  as  a  driving  force  for  Asi development, by the translation of future hopes into reality through hardwork and thrif

Korea, which has endured many ordeals throughout its long history, will another  economic  miracle  with  this  courage  and  hope.  I  hope  that  you  will t ke  note  of  our efforts and be active in your support.

title: Mr. McDonough describes the role of the FRBNY in the events leading up to private-sector recapitalization of Long-Term Capital Management  (Central Bank Articles and Speeches, 1 Oct 98)
description: Testimony by the President of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, Mr. William J. McDonough, before the Committee on Banking and Financial Services of the US House of Representatives on 1/10/98.
text:
Mr. McDonough describes the role of the FRBNY in the events leading up to private-sector  recapitalization  of  Long-Term  Capital  Management Testimony  by  the President of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, Mr. William J. McDonough, before Committee on Banking and Financial Services of the US House of Representatives on 1/10/

Good morning Mr. Chairman and members of the Committee. I am pleased to appear before you today to describe the Federal Reserve Bank of New York's role in the leading up to the recent private-sector recapitalization of Long-Term Capital Managemen fund, Long-Term Capital Portfolio.

I  will  cover  four  points.  First,  I  will  provide  some  background  on  Long Capital's financial problems. Second, I will explain our judgment that an abrupt and close-out  of  Long-Term  Capital's  positions  would  have  posed  unacceptable  risks  t American economy. Third, I will explain the limited role we played in facilitating th sector resolution to this private-sector problem. Fourth, I will identify some of th should concern us as we begin to understand the lessons of this experience.

## Background

Long-Term Capital is an investment partnership that was started in 1994. many of the characteristics of a 'hedge fund' in that it borrows money to leverage its is only available to wealthy investors. The strategy of Long-Term Capital was to use mathematical formulas to identify temporary price discrepancies between different inter For example, the firm might notice that the yield on corporate bonds relative to Treas was higher than the range observed in recent years. If Long-Term Capital believed the relationship would reassert itself, it would buy corporate bonds and sell short Treasu the spread narrowed as expected, the firm would profit. If, however, the spread con widen,  the  firm  would  incur  losses.  This  basic  strategy  and  many  complex  variatio followed across many interest rate products in the US and many overseas markets as we firm  was  active  both  in  traditional  securities  markets,  and  perhaps  more  importa derivative product markets such as futures, swaps, and options. Anticipating that some would move in their favor and some would move against them, the firm relied on diversif across  a  large  number  of  product  and  geographic  markets.  Long-Term  Capital  proved successful at this strategy, generating returns in excess of 40 percent in 1995 and 1 somewhat less in 1997.

Perhaps their success went to their heads. Long-Term Capital took on large larger positions. They also leveraged their investments at higher levels, returning ca investors but not, apparently, reducing risks. We now also know that they took on si positions  in  equity  markets,  through  both  swap  and  options  contracts.  The  reputation Long-Term Capital partners, as traders and economists, and their initial success, appe contributed to so many counterparties' willingness to deal with them.

While hubris may have set them up for a fall, it was the extraordinary ev August in global markets that appears to have tripped them.

On August 17, the Russian government announced an effective devaluation of ruble and declared a debt moratorium, shocking investor confidence all over the worl subsequent days and weeks, equity and debt markets the world over became increasingly vo

with  US  equity  markets  falling  and  the  spreads  between  US  Treasury  securities  and yielding debt instruments widening sharply. The  partners  at  Long-Term  Capital  responded  that  they  would  prefer  to  pres information themselves and called me to arrange such a presentation.

After conferring with Chairman Greenspan and Secretary Rubin, we agreed tha visit to Long-Term Capital's offices was needed. The team also came to understand the impact which Long-Term Capital's posi were already having on markets around the world and that the size of these positions w greater than market participants imagined.

## The New York Fed's Judgements

Mr. Chairman, I would like now to turn to my second point, and focus expli on the question of our judgment that the abrupt and disorderly close-out of Long-Term C positions would pose unacceptable risks to the American economy.

There are several ways that the problems of Long-Term Capital could have b transmitted to cause more widespread financial troubles. Had Long-Term Capital been su put  into  default,  its  counterparties  would  have  immediately  'closed-out'  their  pos counterparties would have been able to close-out their positions at existing market pri if any, would have been minimal. Market moved sharply and losses would have been exaggerated. Several billion dollars of losse have been experienced by some of Long-Term Capital's more than 75 counterparties.

These direct effects on Long-Term Capital's counterparties were not our pri concern. While these losses would have been considerable, and would certainly have ad affected the firms experiencing them, this was not, in itself, a sufficient reason for involved.

Two factors influenced our involvement. In light of these risks, the responsible public policy objective was to ge those with a direct financial interest in an orderly rescue of Long-Term Capital, to problems openly and objectively, to provide a sounding board for solutions, and if nec calming influence. In my view, we achieved this objective.

## What did the New York Fed do?

Because  events  were  moving  swiftly,  and  with  my  approval  and  support,  m colleague Mr. Fisher invited representatives of the three firms, which we felt had t knowledge of the situation at Long-Term Capital and a strong interest in seeking a solu early morning meeting on September 22nd. Continuing discussions which commenced the day before, Mr. Fisher explain our interest in being aware of developments and in reducing the risk of an abrupt an close-out of Long-Term Capital. They discuss approaches to stabilizing Long-Term Capital including the concept of a 'collective ind consortium  approach.  However,  they  all  agreed  that  work  on  a  collective  option  shou preclude parallel efforts by anyone; indeed, that if any firm or group of firms wish forward and take Long-Term Capital itself or Long-Term Capital's positions onto their sheets that this would be the most desirable outcome. In the absence of any other sol firms dispatched two working groups to Long-Term Capital's offices in Connecticut to c the feasibility of 'lifting' the fixed-income and the equity positions out of Long-Term third  working  group  met  at  one  of  the  firm's  offices  downtown  to  develop  the  ide consortium approach. By mutual agreement another firm, UBS, a Swiss bank, was added to core group and to each of the three working groups. However, no one from the New York participated in any of the working groups.

At no point in this early morning meeting, nor at any stage last week, wa discussion of the use of public monies - Federal Reserve or otherwise. No Federal Re government guarantees, actual or implied, were offered, discussed or solicited.

Later that afternoon, we participated in a conference call to review the pr the working groups. Two of the working groups concluded that a 'lifting' of the fixed and equity positions was not feasible. The third group developed a consortium approach was deemed feasible. Every one agreed that the consortium approach should be 'last dit that parallel solutions should still be encouraged.

The  term conditions were debated, altered in some places, and ultimately refined so that the could present it to a wider group. At  about  8:30  p.m.,  a  meeting  of  a  wider  group  involving  13  firms  be Meanwhile, some representatives of the Core Group called Long-Term Capital to discus terms and conditions of the consortium approach. Federal Reserve officials did not part any conversations with Long-Term Capital regarding the terms and conditions. ## Issues that should concern us

It is far too early to state categorically the lessons to be learned from Capital. What I can say is that we are focused on three specific issues, all relating t how we are able to observe it through the eyes of our bank examiners. ## The Federal Reserve's Roles in the Payments System

This  is  an  exciting  time  to  have  a  conference  on  payment  system  strat because there are real opportunities for rapid change over the next few years in the wa payments, especially retail payments in the United States. You will be discussing some opportunities and possibilities over the next few days with experts on the forefront You  will  hear  presentations  that  describe  new  worlds  in  which  payments  are  made efficiently, more conveniently, with greater security and less fraud than they are nowgiant corporations and sophisticated techies, but by ordinary folks and average enterpr about their daily activities.

But  while  there  are  opportunities  and  possibilities,  there  are  also  e uncertainties,  both  about  the  direction  that  technological  change  will  take  and willingness and ability of individuals and institutions to embrace these changes. It possible that a decade from now we will have a radically different retail payments sys United States than we have now. It could be a system that depends very little on paper and air transportation of paper messages. It could instead be one in which both consu businesses, not to mention governments, make almost all of their payments by electroni from wherever they happen to be. On the other hand, it is also possible that not much w to retail payments over the next decade or at least that change will not accelerate fro pace.  Some  of  the  people  in  this  room  could  be  back  here  in  ten  years  assessing promising innovations of the late 1990's never came into general use, and why, althoug debit  and  automated  clearinghouse  (ACH)  payments  continued  to  expand  rapidly,  billio paper checks were still being written and physically transported for presentment.

In part - although only in part - the outcome depends on us, on the peopl room,  and  the  enterprises  and  institutions  we  represent.  It  depends  on  how  effecti imaginatively we all do our individual jobs and on whether we find constructive ways together.

I happen to be one of those who thinks change in retail payments could acc quite rapidly in the next few years and that paper check volume could begin to decline the relatively near term. I say could rather than will because I realize that predic made many times before and has always proved wrong. I guess like so many others I am struck by the absurdity of moving so many little pieces of paper around the country messages  could  be  sent  so  much  more  efficiently  by  electronic  means.  Every  time  I Reserve Bank and watch those high speed sorters working so hard and the trucks coming out to the airplanes, I think, 'This is a really impressive, fast and cost-effective paper, but why are we moving paper?' The 'we,' of course, is not just the Federal Rese all those banks and clearing houses and other participants in the system. And the answ we are all moving all this paper is that customers want us to move it and are willin have it done. But the answer still doesn't make a whole lot of sense.

There are several interrelated reasons why change could be expected to acc in the retail payments arena in the near future.

- First, of course, is the rapidity with which technology is evolving and c dropping  in  computing  and  telecommunications.  Many  types  of  information including payments information, can be transmitted much faster and cheaper was possible even a year or two ago, and there seems to be no end to the p in sight.
- But the avalanche of technological progress may actually be holding up a leap forward in the efficiency of retail payments. Because the network ef important and the players who have to commit to a new technology to make viable are quite numerous, change may come slowly at first. Potential playe be confused by the multiplicity of options and reluctant to commit if they likely that something faster, cheaper and more convenient may come along s It's  like  hanging  on  to  your  old  television  for  a  while  in  hopes  that generation of models will give you a lot more definition for less money.
- A second reason is that the restructuring of the whole financial services across  geographic  and  product  lines  is  providing  a  huge  opportunity  for institutions  to  rethink  how  they  transmit  information  and  make  and  re payments.  This  restructuring,  combined  with  the  onrush  of  technology  and heavy emphasis across all business sectors on competitiveness, cost reducti efficiency, could accelerate the substitution of electronic for paper based at the consumer as well as business level.
- But in the short-run, restructuring, like rapid technological change, may slow things down just because information technology people and their top b simply have too much to think about at once. Coping with mergers, the year and  the  transition  to  the  Euro  --  not  to  mention  wild  swings  in  the  f markets -- may not allow radical changes in payments technology to get m attention in the next year or two.
- A third reason to expect acceleration of change in retail payments is the e growth  of  the  Internet  and  its  increasing  use  for  shopping  and  bus transactions. The number of consumers and small businesses using the Inte routinely  for  transactions  that  require  payments  could  skyrocket  if different types of industries move in this direction at once.

- GLYPH<224> It is possible that paying taxes, trading securities and making some k purchases on the Internet could become routine activities of a large fra the population quite quickly (the way making phone calls and driving a became  routine  quite  quickly  for  earlier  generations). over into increased demand for (or reduced resistance to) electronic pay methods for non-Internet transactions as well.

- The key unknown here is how fast average people become comfortable with PCS lose their anxiety about electronic transmission and storage of data and ov the feeling that if something isn't written on paper and saved in a drawer real.
- The usual assumption is that computer literacy is age- and income-related a it will take a long time before older and less affluent (or at least les people get comfortable with electronic payments and paperless transactions we  could  be  in  for  some  surprises  as  governments  move  quickly  to  electr benefit payments, which mainly affect older and less affluent groups. The most rapidly grow demographic group currently on the Internet is retirees.

For all of these reasons, I would be willing to bet that, despite the rela pace  of  change  in  retail  payments  over  the  past  several  decades  and  despite  Ame long-standing affection for the convenience, flexibility and familiarity of the paper c likely to get to some sort of tipping point early in the next century (less than a deca after which electronic retail payments quite quickly become the norm and the volume of falls rapidly.

This does not mean that I see retail payments moving to some single elec payment instrument that would substitute for the check in all or most of its uses. Some  of  these  systems  are  in  use  already,  some  wil discussed today, others are not yet ready for prime time. Some will be developed by the system, some by non-banks in cooperation, or even in competition, with depository insti

So what will be the role of the Federal Reserve in all this? As you know, Fed committee which is explicitly focussed on this question. We issued a report last Ja are continuing to discuss how the Fed can best contribute to the efficiency and safety payments system to which all depository institutions have access. The Committee now co of Presidents McDonough and Minehan, Governors Kelley and Ferguson and myself. You wi hear from Governor Ferguson tomorrow afternoon.

We see our role as working closely with the other participants in the pa process to help modernize the retail payments system and facilitate the transition over efficient, convenient, and primarily electronic system.

We spent quite a lot of time and energy last year discussing whether we exit the business of processing check and ACH payments. We decided to stay in and us operational presence to help modernize both check and ACH and to work actively with oth evolve a vision of a more efficient future payments system and help remove obstacle realization.

## In practice, what does that mean?

First, it means increased efforts by the Federal Reserve Banks - as prov check and ACH services - to develop new products that reduce costs and to price and them effectively. In the first instance, that means focussing on ECP with truncation an in order to meet market demand and gain experience with different technologies. We h learn a great deal more about whether the wider use of these products can reduce the check collection by substituting electronic technologies for the transportation and pr paper. We are involved in several pilot studies of ECP, including one which we hope wil all  depository  institutions  in  the  whole  state  of  Montana.  Montana  has  small  banks dispersed over great distances. It seems like the right place to see whether, if vir institutions participate, it would be cheaper and more satisfactory to send images el rather than to move paper over thousands of miles.

Like others who have been studying the business case for ECP and imaging, believe the jury is still out. It is not clear that moving the whole national check pro to ECP (with or without imaging) would provide net societal benefits even if the willin resources to do it could be found. So you will see us working hard, in collaboration w in the industry, to explore, in practical ways, the potential advantages and disadvantag

You will also see us working hard, in collaboration with NACHA and others improve ACH service, make it more user friendly and increase its use.

You will see us trying, through surveys, focus groups and other tools, more about how consumers and businesses use different types of retail payments and ho think about them. As we have worked on positioning the Fed to help move the nation payments system of the future, we realized that many of our assumptions about the comp and use of retail payments, paper checks in particular, are based on information co survey in 1979 and were likely seriously out of date. We and the industry need more information on which to base strategies going forward.

We will also be reaching out to participants in the payments system in a va groupings to talk about alternative visions of the payments system of the future, what regulatory and technological barriers there might be to getting there and what we might do to reduce those barriers.

We certainly do not see the Fed managing the process of transition to a mor electronic payments system. We believe strongly that innovations must come primarily fr private sector and be tested in the marketplace to see if they meet customer needs at prices. But there are times when progress can be stymied by legal or regulatory barrier absence  of  technological  standards,  especially  standards  that  allow  communication competing systems. ## What is Electronic Banking?

I will begin by defining what I mean by electronic banking. I would propos we use a very broad definition. Thus, at one end I would include telephone banking, cre ATMs, and direct deposit, all of which are fairly mature and familiar products, but on certainly electronically based. Recent Federal Reserve research on the use of the ACH shows that while A volume continues to increase at double-digit rates, a significant untapped market rema than  half  of  households  surveyed  earlier  this  year  receive  one  or  more  payments  vi deposit and about one-third of all businesses surveyed offer this payment option (wi three-quarters of medium and large companies offering it). More than one-third of hou surveyed use ACH direct payment and only 13 percent of businesses offer this payment (although almost three-quarters of utility companies offer it). Users of both direct direct debit report very high satisfaction levels; nonusers cite more difficult probl and  lack  of  availability.  In  addition,  nonusers  of  direct  payment  expressed  concern option would diminish their control over payments, as well as reduce privacy and securit

It  is  interesting  to  note  that  when  one  looks  at  the  incidence  of  c complaints received by the Federal Reserve Board, electronic banking does not stand o troublesome  area.  For  example,  through  July  of  this  year,  only  two  percent  of  t complaints involved electronic funds transfer transactions. For the entire year of 1997 and one-half percent of all complaints were so directed.

## What Might the Future Hold?

So, what, on balance, should we expect in the future? It is useful to con question in the context of both the typical product life cycle as well as in relation key factors for the success of new payment services. Some retail payment services, such value products, are at the beginning of the product life cycle, and it is not clear wh succeed  and  eventually  have  mass  acceptance  and  which  will  fall  by  the  wayside.  P payment  is  somewhat  farther  along  the  life  cycle  curve,  but  still  has  relatively  l penetration.

The  most  interesting  group  of  technologies,  in  my  judgment,  are  those have recently moved out of their limited niche markets into mass adoption. A short l include the Internet, which is a whole new distribution system in itself; debit cards existing  credit  card  and  regional  ATM  networks;  and  on-line  investing,  which  relies Internet. The Internet really only blossomed into mass adoption in the mid to late 1990 advent of numerous simple tools for 'surfing the web.' On-line investing has just begu into  early  mass  adoption.  Some  apparent  reasons  for  its  success  include  our  long  e boom, a graying population looking towards retirement, significantly lower transaction the provision of associated investor information and services. Finally, heavily market debit cards that provide consumers with global merchant access and the convenience of card have fueled debit's sharp volume gains.

As our research indicates, one electronic banking service that has moved we mass  adoption  is  direct  deposit.  Users  value  the  convenience,  reliability,  and  secur means of payment. Credit cards have moved even further along in the product life cycle.

This  brings  me  to  two  key  factors  underlying  the  successful  adoption  of payments method. The first key factor, as we have seen with direct deposit, ATMs, debi and  on-line  investing,  is  that  reaching  a  critical  customer  mass  is  highly  depend comprehensive infrastructure. There must be a distribution system that saturates the ta and has resolved most 'soft' infrastructure issues--standards, protocols, and legal f before widespread consumer availability will occur. Debit cards and on-line investing h this  a  step  further  to  reduce  the  time  from  product  introduction  to  early  mass  ad piggybacking  upon  existing  networks.  These  infrastructure  issues  are  critical  becaus electronic banking products that customers can use is the obvious first step in havin that customers will use. Similarly, resolving some of these 'soft' infrastructure ques the balance in risk-reward calculation that providers must make in deciding whether t new product introductions.

Second,  for  customer  preferences  to  shift  to  a  new  payment  mechanis customers must perceive that, on net, the new mechanism is more advantageous to them existing alternatives. Is the new product more convenient to use? More secure? Less ex Does it facilitate better recordkeeping? Before customers try a new payment product, not be in a position to compare fully how it stacks up with respect to these attribute payment method they currently use. Unfortunately, in many cases they cannot easily comp relative  cost  of  the  new  payment  method  with  an  existing  method.  In  this  regard, somewhat puzzling that some banks that advocate the migration of retail payments from p electronics nonetheless have pricing structures that appear to run counter to that obje

## Competitive and Market Issues Raised by Payments System Developments

The  evolution  of  the  retail  payments  system  raises  several  interesting related  to  competition.  First  is  the  tension  between  cooperation  and  competition providers. Cooperation may help ensure interoperability across products of competing providers and increase providers' willingness to accept new technologies and payment innovations,  which  can  reduce  the  risk  and  cost  for  each  participant.  Competition coordination  among  providers  may  provide  the  market  with  a  broader  choice  of  pay innovations, but may delay user acceptance and the associated economies of scale and prices that may result from volume growth.

A related issue is how the evolution of retail payments and the increasing on electronics will affect the competitive balance between small and large financial i To date, small institutions have proved very adept at maintaining their competitive via effects  of  the  widespread  use  of  some  of  the  more  recent  innovations  in  electronic however,  are  unclear.  For  example,  PC  banking  may  free  smaller  institutions  from  a dependence  on  'bricks  and  mortar,' and thus greatly expand their geographic r Alternatively, it may be that large institutions will have an advantage in being able t technical overhead and manage the security concerns required to offer a wide range of services on the Internet.

Electronic  banking  may  also  have  implications  for  Federal  Reserve  polic several arenas outside of the payments system. While it is too early to say with any cer the implications of electronic banking will be, and my comments must therefore be t highly speculative, I would like to give you a feel for my thinking by suggesting two a believe are appropriate subjects for strategic thinking.

Electronic banking may prove to be important in the analysis of the compe implications  of  bank  mergers  and  acquisitions.  A  cornerstone  of  our  current  appro enforcing the antitrust laws is the definition of a local geographic market for the cl products and services - primarily insured accounts and loans and transaction services businesses. On-line banking conducted via a household's or a small business' personal c has  obvious  possible  implications  for  the  reasonableness  of  using  a  local  geographic While current usage of PC banking is too small to affect our methodology significantl judgment this is clearly an area that we need to monitor and study, and, if necessary, to adapt our procedures accordingly. In this regard, I would note that good data on the banking by households and small businesses is a must.

Electronic  banking  raises  similar  issues  for  our  evaluation  of  the  Com Reinvestment  Act  performance  of  banks.  Here  again,  a  fundamental  aspect  of  our  cu approach is definition of the relevant geographic area. These are complex topics and t still clearly out, but, in my view, they are areas that deserve careful watching.

## Federal Reserve Payments System Role

Clearly, an efficient and smoothly functioning payments system is critica health and stability of the financial markets and the economy more broadly. Although surely  room  for  continuing  improvement,  the  U.S.  payments  system  fares  quite  well compared to other countries. As the central bank, the Federal Reserve has a keen in fostering continuing improvements in the efficiency and integrity of the U.S. payments

We work to achieve this objective through several important payments system roles, t regulator, service provider, and facilitator. As regulator, we are always open to your for  revisiting  regulations  that  may  pose  impediments  to  payments  system  innovatio considering changes to existing regulations, we would assess how the change might aff public good. For example, is the original public policy rationale for the regulation no valid? Would the proposed change make society better off?

As service provider, the Federal Reserve is working closely with the indu enhance  the  ACH  marketing  and  education  that  is  needed  to  substantially  increase penetration. The market research that I discussed earlier is important in helping to efforts.  In  addition,  the  Reserve  Banks  are  providing  ACH  EDI  transaction  capabilit customers to facilitate the use of the ACH for vendor payments. In the check service, t Banks are presenting an increasing number of checks electronically (ECP currently rep about 14 percent of Fed check collection volume), are introducing a wider array of che services, and are developing pilot programs to learn more about ECP. To facilitate the of  transactions  that  clear  outside  the  Federal  Reserve,  the  Reserve  Banks  will introducing an enhanced net settlement service, which provides better finality, securi controls than the net settlement service used by most private clearing arrangements toda

Finally, as facilitator, we are eager to hear about your efforts, both th and the failures, and to learn what consumers think. If we are to make informed deci policy  and  regulatory  issues  in  this  rapidly  changing  environment,  we  must  have  a understanding of market developments and the implications of policy choices. I do not the  Federal  Reserve  should  dictate  or  promote  any  specific  'vision'  of  the  future system, particularly with respect to the small-dollar retail payment mechanisms. The ma will be the ultimate judge of the future direction of the payments system. We should un however,  the  payment  mechanism  attributes  customers  are  demanding,  and  the  products services you are developing to meet that demand, so that we can shape policies in the market realities.

## Conclusion

In closing, I hope that my discussion has provided some additional insig the  consumer  side  of  electronic  banking  and  its  implications  for  Federal  Reserve development. I would like to again extend my personal welcome for your suggestions on h improve the climate for payments system innovation, and to share with us your experienc electronic  banking.  The  insights  that  we  obtain  from  an  ongoing  dialogue  with  i representatives need to be augmented with further research in this area. In this regard Reserve  plans  to  undertake  a  major  research  effort  in  1999  that  will  include  su consumers, businesses, and depository institutions about the use of retail payments. T will gather data on the use of various retail payment instruments and the use of tec facilitate  retail  payments,  and  will  also  explore  public  perceptions  about  retai instruments.  We  look  forward  to  sharing  the  results  of  these  surveys  with  you.  They provide both the Federal Reserve and the private sector with a much broader base of inf from which to evaluate policies and initiatives.
