title: Mr. Greenspan testifies on private-sector refinancing of the large hedge fund, Long-Term Capital Management  (Central Bank Articles and Speeches, 1 Oct 98)
description: Testimony by the Chairman of the Board of Governors of the US Federal Reserve System, Mr. Alan Greenspan, before the Committee on Banking and Financial Services of the US House of Representatives on 1/10/98.
text:
Mr. Greenspan testifies on private-sector refinancing of the large hedge fu Long-Term Capital Management Testimony by the Chairman of the Board of Governors of the US Federal Reserve System, Mr. Alan Greenspan, before the Committee on Banking a Financial Services of the US House of Representatives on 1/10/98.

Mr.  Chairman  and  other  members  of  the  Committee,  I  thank  you  for  th opportunity to report on the Federal Reserve's role in facilitating the private-sector the large hedge fund, Long-Term Capital Management (LTCM). In my remarks this morning, will attempt to put into some perspective the events of the past few weeks and disc questions of importance to public policy makers that they raise.

The Federal Reserve Bank of New York's efforts were designed solely to enha the probability of an orderly private-sector adjustment, not to dictate the path tha would take. As President McDonough just related, no Federal Reserve funds were put at r promises  were  made  by  the  Federal  Reserve,  and  no  individual  firms  were  pressure participate. Officials of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York facilitated discussions the private parties arrived at an agreement that both served their mutual self-interest possible  serious  market  dislocations.  Financial  market  participants  were  already  uns recent global events. Had the failure of LTCM triggered the seizing up of markets, su damage  could  have  been  inflicted  on  many  market  participants,  including  some  not  di involved  with  the  firm,  and  could  have  potentially  impaired  the  economies  of  many  n including our own. With credit spreads already elevated and the market prices of ris under considerable downward pressure, Federal Reserve officials moved more quickly to p their good offices to help resolve the affairs of LTCM than would have been the case normal times. In effect, the threshold of action was lowered by the knowledge that mar recently become fragile. Moreover, our sense was that the consequences of a fire sale by cross-default clauses, should LTCM fail on some of its obligations, risked a severe of market liquidity. The plight of LTCM might scarcely have caused a ripple in financia or  among  federal  regulators  18  months  ago--but  in  current  circumstances  it  was  jud warrant attention.

What is remarkable is not this episode, but the relative absence of such e over the past five years. Dynamic markets periodically engender large defaults.

## Events of the Past Few Weeks

LTCM is a hedge fund, or a mutual fund that is structured to avoid regulat limiting its clientele to a small number of highly sophisticated, very wealthy individu seeks high rates of return by investing and trading in a variety of financial instrume founding in 1994, LTCM has had a prominent position in the community of hedge funds, in because of its assemblage of talent in pricing and trading financial instruments, as large initial capital stake. In its first few years of business, it earned an enviabl racking up a string of above-normal returns for its investors.

LTCM appears principally to have garnered those returns by making judgemen on interest rate spreads and the volatility of market prices. In its search for high levered its capital through securities repurchase contracts and derivatives transaction sophisticated  mathematical  models  of  behavior  to  guide  those  transactions.  As  long configuration  of  returns  generally  mimicked  their  historical  patterns,  LTCM's  mathe

models  of  asset  pricing  could  be  used  to  ferret  out  temporary  market  price  anomalie trading both closed such price gaps and earned an extra bit of return on capital for th the nature of the competitive process driving financial innovation that such techniques emulated, making it ever more difficult to find market anomalies that provided sharehol a high return. Indeed, the very efficiencies that LTCM and its competitors brought to financial system gradually reduced the opportunities for above-normal profits. Indeed acknowledged this when returning $2¾ billion of capital to investors at the end of counter these diminishing opportunities, LTCM apparently reached further for return ov by employing more leverage and increasing its exposure to risk, a strategy that was d fail.  Unfortunately  for  its  shareholders,  LTCM  chose  this  exposure  just  as  financi uncertainty and investor risk aversion began to rise rapidly around the world.

In that environment - so at variance with the experience built into its LTCM's embrace of risk on a large scale produced stunning losses. As we now know, by th of  August  the  firm  had  lost  half  its  capital  base.  And  as  September  unfolded,  the continued. The firm, however, apparently did not unwind its positions significantly.

In  our  dynamic  market  economy,  investors  and  traders,  at  times,  m misjudgements.  When  market  prices  and  interest  rates  adjust  promptly  to  evidence  o mistakes,  their  consequences  are  generally  felt  mostly  by  the  perpetrators  and,  th cumulate to pose significant problems for the financial system as a whole. Indeed, the of an effective market economy necessitates that investment funds committed to capital that  do  not  accurately  reflect  consumer  and  business  preferences  should  incur  los ultimately be liquidated. What value is left needs to be redirected to profitable uses more accurately reflect market preferences. By such winnowing of inefficiencies, produc enhanced and standards of livings expand over time.

Financial  markets  operate  efficiently  only  when  participants  can  commi transactions with reasonable confidence that the risk of non-payment can be rational and compensated for. Effective and seasoned markets pass this test almost all of the rare occasions, they  do  not.  Fear,  whether  irrational  or  otherwise,  grips  participan unthinkingly disengage from risky assets in favor of those providing safety and liqu subtle distinctions that investors make, so critical to the effective operation of fin are  abandoned.  Assets,  good  and  bad,  are  dumped  indiscriminately  in  circumstances  o uncertainty  and  fear  that  are  not  conducive  to  planning  and  investment.  Such  circum were  they  generalized  and  persistent,  would  be  wholly  inconsistent  with  the  functi sophisticated economies supported by long-term capital investment.

Quickly unwinding a complicated portfolio that contains exposure to all m of risks, such as that of LTCM, in such market conditions amounts to conducting a fire prices  received  in  a  time  of  stress  do  not  reflect  longer-run  potential,  adding  t incurred. Of course, a fire sale that transfers wealth from one set of sophisticated m to another, without any impact on the financial system overall, should not be a conce central  bank.  Moreover,  creditors  should  reasonably  be  expected  to  put  some  weight possibility  of  a  large  market  swing  when  making  their  risk  assessments.  Indeed,  w examine banks we expect them to have systems in place that take account of outsized moves. However, a fire sale may be sufficiently intense and widespread that it serious markets  and  elevates  uncertainty  enough  to  impair  the  overall  functioning  of  the  e Sophisticated economic systems cannot thrive in such an atmosphere. 1

The scale and scope of LTCM's operations, which encompassed many markets, maturities, and currencies and often relied on instruments that were thinly traded and that  were  not  continuously  quoted,  made  it  exceptionally  difficult  to  predict  th ramifications of attempting to close out its positions precipitately. That its mistak unwound and losses incurred was never open to question. How they should be unwound when those losses incurred so as to foster the continued smooth operation of financia was much more difficult to assess. The price gyrations that would have evolved from a would have reflected fear-driven judgements that could only impair effective market fun and generate losses for innocent bystanders.

While the principle that fire sales undermine the effective functioning of may  be  clear,  deciding  when  a  potential  market  disruption  rises  to  a  level  of  se warranting central bank involvement is among the most difficult judgements that ever c a central banker. In situations like this, there is no reason for central bank invol there is a substantial probability that a fire sale would result in severe, widespread, disruptions to financial market activity.

It was the judgement of officials at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York were monitoring the situation on an ongoing basis, that the act of unwinding LTCM's p in a forced liquidation would not only have a significant distorting impact on market also  in  the  process  could  produce  large  losses,  or  worse,  for  a  number  of  credi counterparties, and for other market participants who were not directly involved with that environment, it was the FRBNY's judgement that it was to the advantage of all including the creditors and other market participants - to engender if at all possibl resolution  rather  than  let  the  firm  go  into  disorderly  fire-sale  liquidation  follow cascading cross defaults.

As President McDonough has detailed, officers of the Federal Reserve Ban New York contacted a number of creditors and asked if there were alternatives to for firm into bankruptcy. At the same time, FRBNY officers informed some of their colleag the  Federal  Reserve  Board,  the  Treasury,  and  other  financial  regulators  of  their activities. The troubles of LTCM were not a complete surprise to its counterparties. LTCM's  earlier  statements  regarding  its  August  losses  were  well  known,  and  sophist counterparties understood the difficulties in closing out large losing positions. In commercial banks among its creditors had already begun taking normal precautionary mea associated with exposure to counterparties whose condition is deteriorating. Still, cr whole  most  likely  underestimated  the  size  and  scope  of  the  market  bets  that  LTCM undertaking, an issue that is currently under review.

On September 23, the private sector parties arrived at an agreement provi capital infusion of about $3½ billion in return for substantially diluting existing stake  in  LTCM.  Control  of  the  firm  passed  from  the  current  management  to  a  commi determined from the outside by the new investors. Those investors intend to shrink portfolio so as to reduce risk of loss and return the remaining capital to the investo practicable. I do not rule out the possibility that the new owners of what is left o decide to keep part of it in business. That is their judgement to make.

This agreement was not a government bailout, in that Federal Reserve funds neither provided nor ever even suggested. Agreements were not forced upon unwilling m participants. Creditors and counterparties calculated that LTCM and, accordingly, thei would be worth more over time if the liquidation of LTCM's portfolio was orderly as opp

being subject to a fire sale. And with markets currently volatile and investors skitti special premium on the timely resolution of LTCM's problems seemed entirely appropriat matter of public policy.

Of  course,  any  time  that  there  is  public  involvement  that  softens  the private-sector losses - even as obliquely as in this episode - the issue of moral hazar action by the government that prevents some of the negative consequences to the privat of  the  mistakes  it  makes  raises  the  threshold  of  risks  market  participants  will subsequently  choose  to  take.  Over  time,  economic  efficiency  will  be  impaired  as uneconomic investments are undertaken under the implicit assumption that possible loss be borne by the government.

But is much moral hazard created by aborting fire sales? To be sure, in wiped out in a fire sale will clearly be less risk prone than if their mistakes were more  orderly  fashion.  But  is  the  broader  market  well  served  if  the  resulting  fear irrational judgements govern the degree of risk participants are subsequently willing Risk taking is a necessary condition for wealth creation. The optimum degree of risk should be governed by rational judgements about the market place, not the fear flowing sales.

The Federal Reserve provided its good offices to LTCM's creditors, not to p LTCM's  investors,  creditors,  or  managers  from  loss,  but  to  avoid  the  distortions  t processes  caused  by  a  fire-sale  liquidation  and  the  consequent  spreading  of  those  d through contagion. To be sure, this may well work to reduce the ultimate losses to th owners of LTCM, but that was a by-product, perhaps unfortunate, of the process.

I should add that, in order to keep incentives working in their favor, the of LTCM apparently also understood the importance of some cushioning of the losses owners and managers of the firm. The private creditors and counterparties in the rescu chose to preserve a sliver of equity for the original owners - one tenth - so that management would have an incentive to stay with the firm to assist in the liquidati portfolio. Regrettably, the creditors felt that, given the complexity of market bets bewildering array of financial contracts, working with the existing management would easier than starting from scratch.

## Some Questions for Policy Makers

Without doubt, extensive study will be required to put the events of the p weeks into proper perspective. As a member of the President's Working Group on Fina Markets, I support Secretary Rubin's call for a special study on the public policy impl hedge funds. While the affairs of LTCM are by no means settled, I would like to pos tentative questions that may have to be addressed.

First, how much dependence should be placed on financial modelling, which, all its sophistication, can get too far ahead of human judgement? This decade is st examples of bright people who thought they had built a better mousetrap that could con extract an abnormal return from financial markets. Some succeed for a time. But while t occasionally be misconfigurations among market prices that allow abnormal returns, they persist. Indeed, efforts to take advantage of such misalignments force prices into bett and are soon emulated by competitors, further narrowing, or eliminating, any gaps. No

how skilful the trading scheme, over the long haul, abnormal returns are sustained onl abnormal exposure to risk.

Second,  what  steps  could  counterparties  have  taken  to  ensure  that  the properly  estimated  their  exposure,  particularly  in  markets  that  are  volatile?  To  an degree, the creditors of LTCM were induced to infuse capital into the firm because they stress test their counterparty exposures adequately and therefore underestimated the uncollateralized exposure that they could face in volatile and illiquid markets. In p reflected an underappreciation of the volume and nature of the risks LTCM had undertak its relative size in the overall market. By failing to make those determinations, its participants failed to put an adequate brake on LTCM's use of leverage. To be sure, s decisions are based on judgements about the soundness of borrowers that are accepted fr parties or, possibly in this case, that are founded on the impressive qualifications principals.  In  some  cases,  such  truncated  risk  appraisals  may  be  accurate,  but  they substitute for a rigorous analysis by the lender of the borrower's overall credit wor risk profile.

Third,  in  this  regard  what  lessons  are  there  for  bank  regulators?  Do commercial bank exposure to LTCM included both direct lending and acting as counterpart the firm in derivatives contracts. A preliminary review of bank dealings with LTCM s that the banks have collateral adequate to cover most of their current mark-to-market with LTCM. The unexpected surge in risk aversion and the dramatic opening up of intere spreads  in  August  obviously  caught  LTCM  wrong  footed.  Counterparties,  including  ba continued to collect collateral for marks to market. What they were not collateralized the losses that might have occurred when prices moved even further and market liquidi up in a fire sale.  Supervisors of banks and security firms must assess whether current regarding  stress  testing  and  counterparty  assessment  could  have  been  improved  to counterparties to take steps to insulate themselves better from LTCM's debacle. More i will be the assessment of whether those procedures are adequate for the future. But thi in which much work has been ongoing. During the fourth quarter of 1997 and the first qu 1998,  supervision  staff  of  the  Federal  Reserve  Bank  of  New  York  and  the  Board  met managers at several major New York banking institutions to discuss their current rela with hedge funds, updating a similar study conducted 3½ years earlier.

Fourth, does the fact that investors have lost most of their capital and may take some losses on their exposure to LTCM call for direct regulation of hedge fun questionable whether hedge funds can be effectively directly regulated in the United Sta While their  financial  clout  may  be  large,  hedge  funds'  physical  presence  is  small. amazing communication capabilities available virtually around the globe, trades can be from almost any location. Indeed, most hedge funds are only a short step from cyberspa direct US regulations restricting their flexibility will doubtless induce the more aggr to emigrate from under our jurisdiction. The best we can do in my judgment is what we d Regulate them indirectly through the regulation of the sources of their funds. We are t monitor far better hedge funds' activity, especially as they influence US financial mar funds move abroad, our oversight will diminish.

In the first line of risk defense, if I may put it that way, are hedge fu and counterparties. Commercial and investment banks especially have the analytic skills the degree of risk to which the funds are exposed. Their self-interest has, with few ex including the one we are discussing today, controlled the risk posed by hedge funds.

supervisors are the second line of risk defense in their examination of lending proc safety and soundness. We neither try, nor should we endeavor, to micro-manage bank l activity. We have nonetheless built up significant capabilities in evaluating the comp practices in OTC derivatives markets and hedge funds. If, somehow, hedge funds were world-wide, the American financial system would lose the benefits conveyed by their including arbitraging price differentials away. The resulting loss in efficiency and co financial value added and the nation's standard of living would be a high price to p mind, too high a price.

Fifth,  how  much  weight  should  concerns  about  moral  hazard  be  given  whe designing mechanisms for governmental regulation of markets? By way of example, we sho note that were banks required by the market, or their regulator, to hold 40 percent cap assets as they did after the Civil War, there would, of course, be far less moral ha fewer  instances  of  fire-sale  market  disruptions.  At  the  same  time,  far  fewer  banks profitable, the degree of financial intermediation less, capital would be more costly, of output and standards of living decidedly lower. Our current economy, with its wide safety net, fiat money, and highly leveraged financial institutions, has been a conscio the American people since the 1930s. We do not have the choice of accepting the benefit current system without its costs.

## Conclusion

For  so  long  as  there  have  been  financial  markets,  participants  have  h occasion to weigh the costs and, especially, the externalities associated with fire-sal of troubled entities against short-term assistance to tide the firms over for a time. balancing  of  near-term  costs  and  longer-term  benefits  that  presumably  led  J.P.  Mo convene the leading bankers of his age - both commercial and investment - in his librar to address the severe panic of that year. Such episodes were recognized as among th occasions  when  otherwise  highly  effective  markets  seize  up  and  temporary  ad  hoc  res were required. The convening of LTCM investors and lenders last week at the Federal R Bank of New York could be viewed in that long tradition. It should similarly be viewed occasion, warranted because of the potential for serious disruptions to markets. We remain mindful where to draw the line at which public-sector involvement ends. The eff week were limited to facilitating a private-sector agreement and had no implications f Reserve resources or policies.

title: Mr. Duisenberg speaks on changes in European financial systems and the contributions of the ECB  (Central Bank Articles and Speeches, 23 Sep 98)
description: Remarks delivered by the President of the European Central Bank, Dr. W. F. Duisenberg, at a conference on 'Monnaie unique et fiscalité de l'épargne: quelle Europe financière?' organised by the European Parliament in Brussels on 23/9/98.
text:
Mr.  Duisenberg  speaks  on  changes  in  European  financial  systems  and  the contributions of the ECB Remarks delivered by the President of the European Central Ba Dr. W. F.  Duisenberg,  at  a  conference  on  'Monnaie  unique  et  fiscalité  de  l'épargne: Europe financière?' organised by the European Parliament in Brussels on 23/9/98.

## 1. Introduction

I  would  like  to  express  my  appreciation  for  the  interesting  exchange  of which has taken place during this round table. As was made clear during the discuss structure of financial systems in Europe will evolve as the single currency is created has already contributed to this evolution in many ways and will continue to do so in th would like to make a few remarks on this topic.

## 2. Changes in European financial systems

European financial systems are evolving within a global environment, which become more liberalised, international and concentrated. Changes of particular importan euro area include technological innovation in payment systems, the supply and trading derivative  products,  and  the  improvement  and  diffusion  of  new  risk  management  techni Moreover, the environment of European financial systems is characterised by the Single with new harmonised pieces of regulation and practices developed on the basis of, not Banking  Co-ordination  Directives,  the  Capital  Adequacy  Directives  and,  importantly context of this Conference, the Investment Services Directive.

The scope and organisation of financial activities in the euro area will al as a result of the creation of the euro. First, money markets are going to be unified. focus of foreign exchange activities will of course shift to currencies outside the eur the behaviour of participants in equity and bond markets is likely to be driven less specific  considerations  and  more  by  precise,  sector-specific  or  issuer-specific  cons This latter development is what some commentators have called the development of a ' risk  culture'.  This  development  is  likely  to  improve  the  effectiveness  of  price  for European bond and equity markets. This, in due time, will contribute to the smooth fun of the financing of the euro area economy, as savings are likely to be channelled more and  swiftly  through  the  economy.  As  such,  the  development  of  a  'credit  risk  cultur therefore be a welcome product of European Monetary Union.

## 3. Contributions of the ECB

Let me now turn to the contributions that the European Central Bank has m and will continue to make, to support the efficient working of financial markets in the

## Price stability

The first and foremost contribution that the ECB aims to make is price st The European System of Central Banks will pursue its primary objective of maintaining stability with determination. This should facilitate the formation of price expectation participants and contribute to financial stability in general.

This  environment  will  be  beneficial  to  the  efficiency  of  savings  allo amongst the various sectors of the economy of the euro area. There are several reasons First,  the  achievement  of  price  stability  should  help  to  reduce  the  uncertainty  rel future path of inflation. This should enhance the information content of real and fin prices  and  improve  the  capacity  of  economic  agents  to  select  investment  options  eff Second, price stability will contribute to protecting the value of savings, thereby undesirable  wealth  re-distribution  effects  that  inflation  may  cause.  Third,  in  the increased financial stability may contribute to reducing the likelihood of occurrence of bubbles.

## Payment systems

A second contribution of the ECB relates to the field of payment systems EMI, and now the ECB, have developed the TARGET system, which will be made available t market participants as from 4 January 1999. The system will ensure the unification o markets in the euro area. It will reduce transaction costs for cross-border payments enhance security with regards to settlement risks and possible payment gridlocks.

The ECB has also prepared, and is about to publish, a set of minimum stan which securities settlement systems should fulfil in order to be used in ESCB credit o This publication and other initiatives taken by the ECB have fostered the increased co between securities settlement systems and depositories of the euro area.

## Market rules and practices

A  third  contribution  of  the  ECB  relates  to  market  rules  and  practices. commentators have recognised that European Monetary Union will contribute to the further the  harmonisation  of  market  rules  and  practices.  In  accordance  with  the  mandates  g treaties and statutes, the European Monetary Institute has taken, and now the European Bank takes, an active role in the promotion of adequate new market conventions and rule euro area, bearing in mind the principles of free competition.

## Monetary policy framework of the ECB

Finally,  financial  markets  will  need  to  take  into  account  the  monetary framework of the ECB. The monetary policy framework of the ECB has been built so as t very  efficient  for  transmitting  monetary  policy,  while  at  the  same  time  being  as  n possible with regard to financial structure. The neutrality and, indeed, market-friendl ECB's framework is apparent in a variety of ways.

First,  neutrality  is  apparent  in  the  way  open  market  operations  are  con Almost all of the ECB's open market operations will be executed through tenders, to broad spectrum of counterparties may submit bids. This will be a transparent and fair Fine tuning open market operations may also be conducted through tenders, the so-called tenders. The ECB and the national central banks will aim at giving the opportunity to in fine tuning operations to all counterparties having an appropriate track record of a money market, if necessary on a rotating basis.

Second, the consideration of neutrality has been a driving factor in the p establishment of the list of eligible assets. Eligible assets are the assets which coun

to post as guarantees for any credit received from the European System of Central Banks. of  eligible  assets  comprises  a  wide  variety  of  assets,  which  have  been  selected  by according to area-wide uniform criteria relating to their credit standing in the whole order  to  promote  a  certain  degree  of  continuity  at  the  start  of  the  Third  Stage  o Monetary Union, a sub-set (the so-called tier two eligible assets) includes assets o importance for certain national banking systems of the euro area. These assets have credit standing as the other assets.

For  monetary  policy  operations,  counterparties  will  be  able  to  use  any  e assets, irrespective of where they are located in the euro area. To this end, national will act as correspondents for each other so as to make cross-border use possible also for which this service is not yet provided by securities settlement systems.

For the record, one may also mention the ECB's system of risk control meas Risk control measures will ensure that the amount of assets provided is always suffici designing its system of risk control measures, the ECB has paid careful attention t market practices in this area.

Finally, and perhaps most importantly, the minimum reserve system of the has been developed so as to be as neutral as possible. The minimum reserve system has t objectives. The first objective is to stabilise money market interest rates. This will requesting  that  average  reserve  holdings  be  above  the  minimum  reserve  requirements monthly periods of time. This will allow the banking system to absorb liquidity shock The  volatility  of  money  market  rates  will,  as  a  consequence,  be  reduced.  Also,  fin operations will not have to be used frequently, which will mean that markets are less a central bank interventions than they would otherwise be. The second objective of the m reserve system is to enlarge the demand for central bank money, so as to enlarge the deficit  of  the  banking  system  vis-à-vis  the  European  System  of  Central  Banks.  Th safeguard the role of the European System of Central Banks as a key provider of liquid banking system.

In the minimum reserve system of the ECB, the reserve ratio will be rather and reserve requirements will be fully remunerated. The reserve ratio will be set at be and 2.5% and will be applied to the deposits, debt securities and money market paper i credit  institutions,  except  for  residual  maturities  above  two  years.  Reserve  holdin remunerated  up  to  the  required  reserve  level,  at  the  rate  of  the  ESCB's  main  ref operation (as averaged over a month).

It may be argued that a less than full remuneration of minimum reserves w increase  the  interest  rate  elasticity  of  central  bank  money  demand.  This  notwithstan European Central Bank has decided in favour of a full remuneration of minimum reserv order  to  avoid  the  potential  distortions  to  fair  and  efficient  markets  that  a  le remuneration could have implied. As a result, the minimum reserve system is unlikely to any delocation of certain parts of the reserve base, hence of savings. Finally, it may a to note that the European Central Bank has also decided not to exempt any credit inst the euro area from the minimum reserve system.

## 4. Conclusion

I am confident that the policy of the ECB has always been, and will conti be, guided by the principle of equal treatment, the desire to foster the development markets in the euro area and the need to avoid undue shifts in economic activity. This contribute to providing an adequate environment for an efficient allocation of savings area.

title: Mr. Duisenberg's statement to the European Parliament's Subcommittee on Monetary Affairs  (Central Bank Articles and Speeches, 22 Sep 98)
description: Address by the President of the European Central Bank, Dr. W. F. Duisenberg, in Brussels on 22/9/98.
text:
Bank,

Mr. Duisenberg's statement to the European Parliament's Subcommittee on Monetary Affairs Address by the President of the European Central Dr. W. F. Duisenberg, in Brussels on 22/9/98.

This is the first time that I, in my capacity as President of the Europea Bank (ECB), have the privilege to appear here at the European Parliament in accordanc Article 109b(3) of the Treaty. Today I should like to inform you, first, of the decisi been taken by the ECB since July and, second, of our schedule for the work still to be during the remainder of 1998. Afterwards I shall be happy to answer your questions.

First and foremost I should like to stress that our preparatory work for Sta of Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) is proceeding on schedule. You may be aware that w held two sets of meetings this month: meetings of the Governing Council of the ECB and General Council of the ECB on 1 September 1998, and an additional meeting of the Gover Council on 11 September 1998. We decided to hold a second meeting in September because felt that with regard to the long lead-time, especially in those areas in which the pre of our counterparties, i.e. the credit institutions, is affected by our decisions, w things forward faster. Today I am in a position to present to you quite a long list decisions taken recently by ECB bodies. I think that the list demonstrates that we have good progress in a number of areas. Let me please elaborate on the most important de relating to the preparatory work for Stage Three of EMU.

## A. State of preparatory work

## 1. Exchange  rate  policy  co-operation  between  the  euro  area  countries  and  other  EU  M States

The General Council endorsed the text of an Agreement between the ECB and t non-euro area national central banks, laying down the operating procedures for an excha mechanism in Stage Three (the so-called ERM II). You will recall that the European Cou Amsterdam in June last year agreed to set up an exchange rate mechanism in Stage Th replace the present European Monetary System (EMS). For this reason, the EMI prepared a Central Bank Agreement on the replacement of the current exchange rate mechanism with a one in Stage Three. It is this Agreement which has now been signed by myself, as Pres the ECB, and by the governors of the four non-euro area national central banks. The s this Agreement by the latter parties implies their acceptance of the operating procedu not, however, imply their participation in ERM II.

For the currency of each Member State participating in the mechanism, a ce rate  against  the  euro  and  a  standard  fluctuation  band  of  ±15%  will  be  defined,  in supported by automatic unlimited  intervention  at  the  margins,  with  very  short-term  f available. However, the ECB and the participating non-euro area national central bank suspend  automatic  intervention  if  this  were  to  conflict  with  their  primary  obj maintaining price stability. In line with the Resolution of the European Council, exc policy co-operation may be further strengthened, for example by allowing closer exchan links between the euro and other currencies in the exchange rate mechanism, where, an extent that, this is appropriate in the light of progress towards convergence.

## 2. General documentation on ESCB monetary policy: instruments and procedures

Last Friday, 18 September 1998, the ECB published a report entitled 'The s monetary policy in Stage Three: General documentation on ESCB monetary policy instrume and procedures'. This report contains a detailed description of the monetary policy in and procedures to be applied by the ESCB in Stage Three of EMU. Hence it provides c institutions  with  the  information  they  need  in  order  to  prepare  for  participation monetary policy operations as from 1 January 1999. The report expands upon and update material contained in an earlier version which was published by the EMI on 23 September

The report first sets out the criteria to be fulfilled by credit institutio be eligible as counterparties to ESCB monetary policy operations. It then presents the the different types of open market operations which might be conducted by the ESCB an ESCB's two standing facilities (the marginal lending facility and the deposit facility) also contains a detailed description of the procedures related to the various types of and  specifies  the  eligibility  criteria  and  the  risk  control  measures  to  be  appli underlying  the  ESCB's  liquidity-providing  operations.  Moreover,  the  report  includ description  of  the  features  of  the  ESCB's  minimum  reserve  system  and  sets  out  sp provisions  to  be  applied  for  the  ESCB's  monetary  policy  instruments  and  procedures transition to Stage Three.

In this context I should also mention that on 11 September 1998 the Gover Council of the ECB endorsed the statistical framework on the basis of a number of rep had  been  prepared  by  the  EMI  -  many  of  which  had  been  published  in  the  past  -  th confirming the ECB's statistical requirements for Stage Three. The reporting framework money and banking statistics of the ECB is included in the 'General documentation'.

Furthermore,  on  11  September  1998  the  Governing  Council  endorsed  a  list eligible securities settlement systems following an assessment of such systems against that had previously been laid down for their use in the credit operations of the ESCB which  indicates  those  securities  settlement  systems  that  will  be  used  by  the  ESCB conditions for their use, is set out in the 'General documentation' as well.

## 3. Technical preparations for the euro banknotes

The  technical  preparations  for  the  euro  banknotes  are  proceeding  accordi schedule. The origination, i.e. the process of converting the designs into banknotes, ha successfully  completed.  A  zero-production  run  will  be  conducted  in  the  autumn  before production starts in early 1999.

The Governing Council of the ECB decided on 11 September 1998 that there wi be  no  national  feature  on  the  euro  banknotes.  It  also  confirmed,  in  line  with recommendations made by the EMI, that the following seven banknote denominations will issued: 5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 200 and 500.

## 4. Schedules for the meetings of the Governing Council and General Council

In addition to its meetings scheduled for 13 October, 3 November and 1 Decem 1998, the Governing Council of the ECB has agreed to hold a further meeting on 22 Dec 1998. The Governing Council's final meeting before the start of Stage Three will be

primarily to fine-tuning its last-minute preparations. The Governing Council has als that during the first year of Stage Three its meetings shall, as a rule, be scheduled to Thursdays every other week, starting on 7 January 1999. Furthermore, the General Counc agreed that the current practice of holding quarterly meetings on the same day as meeti Governing Council should continue in Stage Three.

As far as the information policy of the ECB is concerned, I should like to that the ECB intends to hold a press conference, as a general rule, once a month. Fo three months of 1999, it envisages holding a press conference immediately after the fir of each month. It is my aim to pursue a policy of actively informing the public about decisions and the rationale behind them. In addition to press conferences, the public of the members of the Governing Council and the ECB's regular publications will also co to achieving this goal. In its regular publications, for example, the ECB will report t all aspects relevant to the conduct of the single monetary policy in the euro area. I they will supply a detailed analysis of the developments upon which the respective m policy  decisions  are  based.  Apart  from  the  publications  foreseen  in  the  Treaty,  of Annual Report and the Quarterly Report are the most important ones, the ECB intends to a Monthly Bulletin.

In order to give a well-rounded picture I should like to draw your attentio of the most recent ECB publications, the 'Report on electronic money', before I tur schedule for the remainder of 1998.

## * The 'Report on electronic money'

On  31  August  1998  the  ECB  published  a  'Report  on  electronic  money'.  The report deepens the analysis of the implications of prepaid cards conducted by the EMI and extends it to new forms of electronic money, i.e. software-based electronic money which have since started to evolve. The main findings of the study were published in th of the EMI Council on the issuance of electronic money, which is contained in Chapter III of the EMI's Annual Report 1997.

Although electronic money is not a widespread phenomenon at present, it is to  have  significant  implications  for  monetary  policy  in  the  future.  In  this  regard, ensured that, in particular, price stability and the unit-of-account function of money risk. There are a number of additional regulatory concerns regarding electronic money wh have  to  be  taken  into  account,  such  as  the  efficient  functioning  of  payment  syst confidence in payment instruments, the protection of customers and merchants, the sta financial markets and protection against criminal abuse.

With a view to ensuring monetary policy effectiveness and a level playingand  in  order  to  address  the  regulatory  concerns  I  have  just  outlined,  the  ECB  rega essential that certain minimum requirements be fulfilled (see Chapter 4 of the Report).

I would like to stress in this context that the ECB follows with interest attention the European Commission's work on a directive on electronic money and expects officially consulted in due time.

## B. Schedule for the remainder of 1998

Given the huge volume of work to be completed during the remainder of the it  seemed  to  us  appropriate  to  give  priority  to  those  issues  relevant  to  credit preparatory  work  for  Stage  Three.  The  above-mentioned  'General  documentation'  is example of this, since credit institutions' preparations for participation in ESCB mone operations as from 1 January 1999 were to a large extent dependent on the decisions to by the Governing Council. Given the lead time in this field I consider the approach ado very helpful.

The  need  to  set  priorities  was  also  a  major  factor  in  opting  to  sched decision on euro area's monetary strategy for the autumn of this year. The determina strategy for the single monetary policy is a very important decision to be taken. Nonet outcome  of  our  proceedings  does  not  have  such  a  direct  impact  on  our  counterpa preparations for Stage Three as the operational framework. Moreover, another reason for having taken definite decisions regarding the monetary policy strategy is that the matt very  thorough  consideration.  The  Governing  Council  has  already  started  with  this  dis which will continue for some time. I can assure you that there are no fundamentally opinions within the Governing Council concerning the orientation of our future monetar strategy. In this context, allow me to remind you that the EMI had already achieved consensus  regarding  the  monetary  policy  strategy.  In  particular,  certain  strategie exchange rate targeting or nominal income targeting were explicitly excluded some ti Moreover, it was pointed out that the implementation of the two potential candidate that  had  been  identified,  namely  monetary  targeting  and  direct  inflation  targeting practice, be relatively similar. A combination of elements of both strategies was also as  a  possibility.  Finally,  there  was  no  doubt  within  the  EMI  Council,  that  monetar decisions  should  be  based  on  a  broad  range  of  indicator  variables  and  that  money  wo assigned a prominent role, with either targets or monitoring ranges set for its growt that money demand is sufficiently stable. The Governing Council of the ECB will conti discuss  the  specification  of  the  strategy  along  these  lines  over  the  months  to  c Governing Council will then specify the exact formulation of its strategy and its impl in 1999 before the start of Stage Three.

title: Mr. Ferguson discusses the state of the US economy: near-term challenges and long-term changes  (Central Bank Articles and Speeches, 17 Sep 98)
description: Remarks by Mr. Roger W. Ferguson, Jr., a member of the Board of Governors of the US Federal Reserve System, at the Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City on 17/9/98.
text:
Mr. Ferguson discusses the state of the US economy: near-term challenges and long-term changes Remarks by Mr. Roger W. Ferguson, Jr., a member of the Board of Governors  of  the  US  Federal  Reserve  System,  at the Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City on 17/9/98.

It is a pleasure to be here today to discuss the state of the economy, because -- despite some turbulence of late in financial markets -- there is still g report.  We  are  now  in  the  eighth  year  of  economic  expansion.  Production,  employment incomes have all been rising briskly, and the unemployment rate has declined to its lo since 1970. And at the same time, inflation has remained remarkably subdued.

But  the  prudent  central  banker  cannot  afford  to  focus  exclusively  on  the performance of the past. He must constantly look as well to the future. In that spirit, not only discuss our current economic situation, but I shall also comment on several a believe deserve particular attention in the period ahead. Some of these areas involv risks  to  our  fine  economic  performance,  and  some  involve  potentially  important  st changes to our economy.

Before  I  begin,  let  me  remind  you  that  these  views  are  personal  and  d necessarily reflect the views of other members of the Federal Open Market Committee Board of Governors.

## Recent Economic Performance

As you know, the United States has been experiencing a period of exceptio strong economic growth. Real GDP rose nearly 4 percent over 1996 and again last yea fastest rates of increase, two years in a row, in fifteen years. And activity maintaine of expansion over the first half of this year as well, although growth apparently did some in the spring. This recent performance is especially impressive because it occur face of a substantial reduction in export demand associated with the crisis in Asia.

This  powerful  economic  growth  has  benefited  American  businesses  throug soaring profits. It also has benefited our governments -- federal, state, and local revenues that have come in above earlier expectations. And it has benefited American w through higher incomes and lower unemployment rates than almost anyone predicted. Our labor  markets  have  had  the  tremendous  dividend  of  giving  job  experience  to  people otherwise would be on the margins of the economy -- experience that will serve these well for many years to come. Tight labor markets are welcome, even to central bankers they can be sustained without producing cost and price pressures that will undermine pro

The  driving  force  behind  this  sustained  growth  has  been  domestic  demand, reflected  in  enormous  increases  in  both  consumption  and  investment  spending.  Consump spending has been fueled by rapid growth of employment and incomes. With some 6 mill people added to payrolls over the past two years, and with compensation gains well in inflation, consumers have had the means to boost their spending appreciably. And the mo doubling in the value of the stock market since late 1994 -- only a small fraction of been reversed in recent weeks, I might add -- has made people more comfortable about sp out of current income -- and probably out of accumulated assets, too. It should be no s surveys that measure consumer confidence have recorded historic highs, nor that the

saving rate has declined considerably. The same factors, along with the lowest mortgage some time, have powered home sales to record levels.

Favorable financial conditions, along with exceptionally large price decli computer  equipment,  have  made  it  relatively  cheap  for  firms  to  invest  in  new  pla equipment. And with sales in a solid uptrend, this has produced a remarkable boom in spending. Business fixed investment was up nearly 10 percent last year, and it rose at pace  in  the  first  half  of  this  year.  Even  more  strikingly,  investment  has  averaged annual  growth  over  the  past  five  years,  making  this  the  most  rapid  sustained  expan investment in thirty years. As I shall discuss shortly, this investment may provide some to be optimistic about productivity growth in the period ahead. But, without dou played an important role in helping to boost aggregate demand in recent quarters.

One  important  question  looking  forward  is  whether  the  recent  rapid  growt demand can be sustained. I am not a forecaster, but it is important to know what the among forecasters has been, and most have been expecting growth to slow from its recen One reason forecasters have expected growth to slow is that production for inventories rising  at  an  extremely  rapid  pace  that  was  unlikely  to  be  maintained.  And  indeed, investment  did  drop  down  a  good  bit  in  the  second  quarter,  contributing  importantly quarter's more modest GDP growth. Still, most analysts believe that the rate of stockb at least outside the motor vehicle sector -- probably remained unsustainable and can be to slow further.

A  second  reason  forecasters  have  expected  a  slowdown  is  that  the  impetu consumer spending from annual gains of 25 to 30 percent in share values seemed unlikel sustained. This may seem obvious after last month's drop in stock prices, but lookin earlier in the year even the most optimistic forecasters were expecting stock market well  short  of  the  rates  seen  in  1996  and  1997.  The  impetus  to  spending  from  such increases in household wealth would be considerably smaller than was generated by las outstanding  run-up  in  share  prices.  And  of  course,  last  month's  decline  may  provide reason to expect consumption growth to slow.

## International Risks

A third important reason forecasters have expected slower growth ahead i continuing troubles overseas. The problems faced by our Asian trading partners, inclu persistent  weakness  of  the  Japanese  economy,  and  the  accompanying  strength  of  the already have led to a sharp reduction in the demand for our exports. Indeed, in the f this  year,  the  quantity  of  exports  declined  two  quarters  in  a  row  for  the  first  ti mid-1980s, with shipments to Korea and Japan down sharply. Declines in exports of mach industrial supplies, and agricultural equipment were especially noteworthy. When we inc effect of rising imports as well, net exports subtracted more than 2 percentage points growth  over  this  period,  and  our  trade  deficit  on  goods  and  services  widened  t $175 billion at an annual rate in the second quarter.

I should emphasize that not all of the effects on our economy of the Asian have been adverse. Low prices this year of energy and other internationally traded com including many agricultural commodities such as soybeans and wheat, have benefited mu our nation -- although certainly not our oil industry or our farmers. Those low price part, a decline in the demand from Asia. To put it another way, those nations exporti

other commodities have borne some of the brunt of the sagging Asian economies. Further the favorable financial conditions in this country may have been aided by a 'flight to helped  hold  down  our  long-term  interest  rates  and  stimulate  interest-sensitive  se housing. Thus, the seemingly fortuitous timing of extremely robust domestic demand th offset the reduction in our export demand has not been entirely coincidental.

As with any financial crisis, it is extremely difficult to predict what the bring for the troubled Asian countries. I remain guardedly optimistic that conditions w stabilize in the coming months, and that export demand will start to firm at least year. But that is by no means a certainty.

One particular risk is that the problems that have thus far been most severe may become more severe in other regions of the world. We have already seen this in Russ financial  difficulties  in  other  countries  as  distinct  as  South  Africa  and  Brazil  em worries  and  uncertainties  on  this  score.  For  a  variety  of  reasons,  there  could  b 'contagion' to other countries. First, investors' appetite for international risks ha following the Asian crises. This has led to trouble for countries that are running cur deficits and so are dependent on foreign capital. While most of Russia's problems a grown, for example, more cautious investors probably contributed to precipitating that crisis. Indeed, over the last month it has become apparent that even US financial marke immune to perceptions that risk has increased. Second, as some emerging-market countrie fixed exchange rates respond to market pressures by relaxing their exchange-rate arran those remaining countries attempting to peg their exchange rates may come under incr speculative  pressures.  Third,  countries  that  have  close  economic  ties  to  the  hardest nations certainly are feeling the repercussions of a reduction in demand for their ex greater economic slowdown in Asia could trigger financial problems in those countries, finally, as I noted earlier, countries that are heavy exporters of oil and other primar have been hard-hit by low prices.

In  short,  international  problems  in  Asia  and  elsewhere  are  proving  to  be profound and sustained than many, myself included, were guessing and hoping would be case.  Obviously,  the  effect  of  this  drag  on  our  ongoing  economic  expansion  is  an  a deserves close scrutiny in the months ahead.

## Inflation Developments

But as I noted, the flip side of reduced export demand and a strong dollar the international situation is helping to hold down inflation here at home. This help the  remarkable  fact  that  our  strong  economic  growth  and  low  unemployment  rates coincided with exceptionally favorable news on the inflation front. I cannot overemph importance of this story: rising inflation has sown the seeds of almost every cyclical the last half century.

The consumer price index increased less than 2 percent over the past year. T time consumer inflation was this low was in 1986 when, as in the present instance, co benefited from declining prices of energy products. But even when we exclude volatile f energy items and focus on the so-called 'core' CPI, inflation has been running not much percent, the lowest rate in more than three decades. And a broader measure of prices, price index, has increased only one percent over the past year, held down by rapid decl prices businesses pay for computers and communication equipment.

This inflation performance has been better than most analysts had expected we  should  not  exaggerate  the  extent  of  the  surprise.  True,  most  economists  believe current unemployment rate of 4½ percent is below the level consistent with stable infl indeed  may  already  be  exerting  upward  pressure  on  labor  costs.  But  almost  all  s economists have long realized that unemployment is not the only influence on inflati have emphasized, the strong dollar has led to falling prices for our imports, and low have led to low prices for gasoline and other energy products. Low oil prices also ha hold  down  prices  for  petroleum-derived  products  like  fertilizers  and  plastics,  and reduced  price  pressures  more  generally  by  reducing  firms'  utility  and  transportati Furthermore,  structural  changes  in  the  health  care  system  have  reduced  the  growth  o health care costs. These factors have all contributed to our benign inflation performan need to be vigilant because, just as these factors have worked to the benefit of lo recently, any or all of them may turn around and exert upward pressure on inflation in t

## Changes in the Labor Market

One of the complexities in the inflation outlook involves changes that appe occurring  in  labor  market  practices.  The  extraordinary  rise  in  labor  demand  a accompanying  tight  labor  markets  have  led  to  labor  shortages  in  some  parts  of  the Shortages have been reported for a variety of jobs, with the supply of computer prof especially tight.

To some extent, firms have been responding to these labor shortages by ra wages. And indeed, compensation increases have been growing in size for the past two t years. But firms also have responded to tight labor markets in ways other than simply larger base wage increases. Firms have been making increasing use of various forms of pay, such as hiring and retention bonuses, as a way to attract and retain certain key without granting a general wage increase. These targeted bonuses seem to be most preva information processing workers, but I sense that they are reasonably widespread beyond as well. And these bonuses are often quite sizable. It is not uncommon to hear of hiri of five to ten percent of base salary, or higher.

Firms are changing their compensation practices in other ways, too. Busin increasingly are relying less on base wage and salary increases, and are substituting so variable pay that is tied directly to performance, such as annual bonuses and profit sh or even stock options that extend well beyond senior management.

These changing labor market practices have implications for the functioning economy that are both interesting and, potentially, quite important. For one thing, man bonuses may not be adequately captured by our aggregate wage statistics, so if these bo becoming more prevalent, labor costs may be rising somewhat faster than the publishe would  indicate.  Second,  these  practices  may  lead  to  changes  in  the  cyclicality  o compensation costs. On the one hand, if firms now are able to use targeted bonuses t workers in place of generalized wage increases, this could hold down compensation costs labor markets, thereby making these costs less cyclical. On the other hand, increasi variable pay will tend to make compensation more cyclical than it otherwise would hav Under a profit sharing system, for example, firms make larger compensation payments t employees when times are good than they do when business is slack.

If  the  latter  effect  were  to  dominate,  and  compensation  were  to  become cyclical, it would raise interesting questions about how this change might affect fir behavior. To some extent, of course, firms probably smooth through the cyclical ups an in  their  costs  when  making  price  decisions  in  any  case.  But  such  smoothing  probably perfect,  and  increases  in  fixed  pay  probably  would  exert  some  upward  pressure  on Increased use of profit-sharing bonuses, however, would presumably lead firms to boo employees' compensation precisely when they can most afford to do so. And, conversely, profits are being squeezed, the resulting decline in bonus payments would help ease t cost  pressures.  Thus,  there  may  be  reason  to  believe  that  increases  in  variable  com payments might not lead to the same price pressures as would increases in fixed compe payments.  In  other  words,  increased  cyclicality  of  compensation  gains  might  not  imp change in the cyclicality of price increases.

Finally, the spread of variable pay could lead to changes in employment pa Pay  that  is  more  variable  is  more  tied  to  profitability.  As  profitability  decli compensation, and it is possible that employment may not drop as much as it would in a which compensation is less closely tied to profits. In any event, it will be fascinat these  labor  market  developments  unfold,  and  to  try  to  sort  out  the  implications macroeconomy.

Of course, companies are not moving toward variable compensation schemes alter the macro-dynamics of the economy. Firms are moving to variable compensation sch because  they  hope  these  changes  will  enhance  their  profitability,  in  part  by  raisi productivity. By giving workers a larger and more direct stake in the fortunes of the firms  are  providing  incentives  for  their  employees  to  work  more  efficiently  and  to productivity-enhancing changes to the way products are made and business is conducted hard to know how successful these efforts will ultimately prove to be. Many business pe convinced that variable compensation plans have paid off in terms of higher productivi others are less confident, and say that they hope the changes are boosting productivity is very hard to pinpoint the sources of productivity improvements.

This discussion points to one final aspect of our economic outlook that d mention, namely, productivity growth. In the long run, nothing is as important for our welfare  as  productivity  growth,  for  this  is  what  determines  the  pace  of  increase standards. And the recent productivity data have been impressive: output per hour wor 1¾ percent in 1997 after an advance of more than 2 percent the year before. The big qu whether  this  rapid  productivity  growth  is  temporary  or  is  permanent  --  that  is, productivity has merely displayed its normal short-run response to a step-up in the activity,  or  whether  the  faster  pace  can  be  sustained  for  some  time  even  as  outpu moderates.

The only correct answer, of course, is that we don't know yet. I can cit reasons to be very cautiously optimistic that productivity may be on a more favorable than it was in the 1980s. One reason is the changing incentives within the firm owing t pay that I just discussed, which at least some firms strongly believe has aided their performance.  A  second  reason  for  optimism  is  the  investment  boom  that  I  discussed  e Economic history teaches us fairly convincingly that growth in the amount of capital pe is an important determinant of gains in output per worker.

Furthermore, some analysts have argued that the computerization of our econ is only now beginning to bear fruit, and that we may expect impressive productivity adv people learn to use the new technology effectively. The economist Paul David notes tha several  decades  following  the  initial  development  of  the  electric  motor  for  compa reorganize their production techniques to use the new invention efficiently. By analogy argument hints that the largest benefits of computerization may be yet to come.

This analogy is intriguing, but counterarguments certainly can be made as One reason it took electric power so long to yield benefits is that it took many years technology  to  gain  widespread  use,  in  part  because  of  the  huge  expenditures  requ reconfigure manufacturing plants to use electric power. By contrast, the transition office equipment to mainframe computers, and then to desktop machines, often entails smaller adjustment costs and so has been comparatively rapid. Furthermore, it is easy that, while computers account for a large share of investment, they account for only a of  the  overall  capital  stock,  in  part  reflecting  their  rapid  rate  of  depreciation. computers earn a considerably higher return than other investments that firms might m small  share  imposes  some  limits  on  the  contribution  computers  could  make  to  ov productivity growth.

So, while we can be hopeful that the recent productivity increases may repr faster long-term trend, we should not count our chickens too soon. But you certainly productivity to the list of items I will be following closely in the period ahead.

## Conclusion

With  strong  output  growth,  low  unemployment,  low  inflation,  and  rap productivity growth, these have certainly been good times to be a central banker. But not mean that they are not interesting times, as a glance at the financial pages will Although  our  economy  is  basically  very  strong,  we  also  face  near-term  and  longe challenges, and I hope I have given you a sense of some of the issues that will be on my try to gauge our nation's economic performance in the period ahead.

text:
Mr.  Meyer  reflects  on  recent  developments  in  banking  and  financial markets: implications for bank supervision and regulation Remarks by Mr. Laurence H. Meyer, a member of the Board of Governors of the US Federal Reserve System, at the Fin Institutions Center, University of Tennessee, Knoxville, on 18/9/98.

The banking and financial services industries have been undergoing rapid c in recent years. These changes include the consolidation and increased geographic scop banking  industry,  a  blurring  of the distinctions between various financial in deregulation, and the implementation of financial strategies made possible by improvem computer technology and advances in finance theory. These changes in turn have create opportunities  and  risks  for  financial  institutions  and  new  challenges  for  superv regulators.

My focus today will be on how legislation, supervisory practice and regu standards have to adapt to these changes in order to promote competition for financia and maintain stable financial systems. Markets are moving very rapidly, while legisl regulatory  changes  are  occurring  much  more  slowly.  It  is  important  that  both  legisla regulatory standards quickly catch up to the changes in the market place in order to ma benefits to consumers and minimize the risks to financial stability.

There  are  three  ways  in  which  recent  developments  have  put  pressure legislation, regulatory standards and supervisory practice. First, the job of supervisi become  more  challenging  as  a  result  of  the  increased  size,  geographic  scope,  comp globalization  and  diversity  of  banking  organizations.  Second,  the  effectiveness  of  o foundations  of  the  current  regulatory  framework,  the  risk-based  capital  rules,  has improvements in credit risk measurement facilitated increased use of securitization derivatives to arbitrage those capital rules. These innovations have allowed banks to capital charges for a given set of risks, making reported risk-based capital ratios inc meaningful  and  the  current  standards  progressively  less  effective.  Third,  banks  a financial  institutions,  often  with  the  help  of  their  regulators,  have  found  ways,  a statutory limits, to expand not only the activities in which they engage, but also to c effectively with one another. Market developments and regulatory actions have created with the existing legislative framework underpinning banking and financial services.

I  will  focus  on  three  policy  responses.  First,  I  will  discuss  the  pot increased  market  discipline  to  raise  the  overall  effectiveness  of  the  current  reg supervisory  framework,  responding  to  the  challenge  of  supervising  such  large  and  c institutions, without more burdensome and intrusive regulations. Second, I will empha priority that needs to be attached to updating and refining our capital standards. T discuss the importance of financial modernization legislation.

Before  tackling  the  policy  questions,  let  me  begin  by  reviewing  why  and banks are regulated.

## Why Do We Regulate Banks?

Why do we supervise and regulate banks? The reasons are very straightforw Initially, when banks were the dominant financial institutions, the major purpose was 'systemic  risk'  and  the  impact  on  the  economy  of  bank  failure.  Then  as  the  safety

created to reduce systemic risk, the resultant moral hazard created an even more import to supervise and regulate banks.

Historically, the objective was to protect against a panic-driven flight to or  bank  runs,  that  caused  a  catastrophic  decrease  in  the  money  supply  and  the  col financial intermediation. Today, largely because of deposit insurance and the Federal discount window, flights to currency are not a real concern in the United States. But l solvency problems at large banks and other financial institutions can create systemic and while banks are no longer 'special' the large banks do play a central role in ou system.  Indeed,  the  stability  of  the  electronic,  large  dollar  payments  system,  whi trillions of dollars a day and in which banks play a pivotal role, is critical in li risk. Other potential pressure points, in all of which banks play a key role, include t securities, financial derivatives, and interbank funding markets.

Our very success at virtually eliminating the risk of bank runs in the Unit has led to a second major reason for supervising and regulating banks. Deposit insur discount window, and Federal Reserve payment system guarantees -- the very things tha eliminated bank runs -- create what is called a 'safety net' for banks. The existence o net gives the Government a direct stake in keeping bank risks under control, just as insurance  company  has  a  stake  in  controlling  the  risks  of  policyholders.  Because insurance and other parts of the safety net can never be fully and accurately priced, i for us to monitor and sometimes to act to control bank risks in order to protect the p on taxpayer funds. An equally important, if unintended, consequence of the safety net creates what economists term 'moral hazard' incentives for some banks to take excessiv That is, the safety net creates incentives for banks to take larger risks than otherwis safety net, and potentially taxpayers, may absorb most of the losses if the gamble f incentives are especially strong if the bank is near failure since, at this point, ban have virtually nothing to lose.

## How Do We Regulate Banks?

Bank regulation and supervision can be thought of as a portfolio of regu rules  and  supervisory  practices  that  collectively  aim  to  monitor  and  protect  the soundness of the banking system, so as to control systemic risk, offset moral hazard i and limit the potential call on the taxpayer. This portfolio includes, in no particular set  of  rules  and  practices  relating  to  the  federal  safety  net  itself;  (2)  the  re disclosure and the incentives that promote market discipline of banking organizations rules  that  govern  the  capital  that  banking  organizations  must  hold;  (4)  the  limi activities  that  banking  organizations  may  engage  in;  (5)  the  restrictions  on  wher activities  can  be  conducted  within  banking  organizations;  (6)  prudential  restrictio relationship between banks and their affiliates; and (7) the nature and details of the of banking organizations.

The  more  effective  is  market  discipline  and  the  more  effective  are  c standards, the less there is a need to invoke the more intrusive and burdensome compo the regulatory portfolio. For this reason, I focus particularly on enhanced market dis reform of capital standards. But financial modernization legislation has also focused a the role of activity limitations, restrictions on where activities are conducted withi organization, and the appropriate supervisory framework for more diversified financia organizations that would emerge from such legislation.

## Market Discipline: The Role of Subordinated Debt

To a significant extent, market discipline and regulatory standards are sub The  more  effective  the  former,  the  less  reliance  has  to  be  made  of  the  latter.  B regulatory approach involves significant costs to both the private and public sectors reliance on the market can reduce the cost of achieving a given degree of safety and so the banking system and thereby increase the efficiency of the overall regulatory framewo

But there is a significant trade-off to worry about. A greater reliance on t may  also  increase  systemic  risk.  For  example,  eliminating  deposit  insurance  would  c increase the incentive for depositors to monitor the risk profiles of banks. The pri increased market discipline, however, would, in my view, be unacceptably high -- a sign increased risk of bank runs and hence systemic risk. The key therefore is to find oppor increase market discipline in a way that results in an acceptable trade-off with respec risk and thereby to achieve the optimal balance of market discipline and regulatory stan

Market  discipline  involves  information  and  incentives.  Markets  need  acces information to judge the risk profiles of banking organizations. But, to make market work, there also have to be incentives for banks to respond to the changing judgmen market.

It may be possible to increase market discipline by requiring large, intern active banks to issue a minimum amount of certain types of subordinated debt to the pu appealing aspect of this approach is that subordinated debt holders, so long as they a 'insiders', face only downside risk, and thus their risk preferences are very close to FDIC. Subordinated debt holders would therefore be expected to impose market discipline bank that is quite consistent with what bank supervisors are trying to do, including e banks to disclose more information about their financial condition. Observed risk prem subordinated debt could perhaps be used to help the FDIC set more accurate risk-based insurance premiums, and such debt would provide an extra cushion of protection for tax An  additional  benefit  of  having  subordinated  debt  traded  on  the  open  market  is  th movements  would  provide  a  clear  signal  of  the  market's  evaluation  of  the  bank's  fi condition that, even if it were not used to help price deposit insurance, could serve warning aid to supervisors.

Such an approach would most likely be limited to the largest banks for at le reasons. First, it is the increased size of banking organizations and the financial i the  largest  and  most  sophisticated  banks  that  are  challenging  the  effectiveness  of regulatory  and  supervisory  framework.  It  may  therefore  be  appropriate,  even  essen differentiate  the  regulatory  standards  and  supervisory  practices  at  large,  sophist internationally active banks -- the predominant sources of systemic risk -- from those to small and medium-sized banks. Second, it is unclear just how deep and liquid a m bank subordinated debt would be and what access small and medium sized banks would hav this  market.  Today,  almost  no  smaller  banks,  for  example,  issue  subordinated  debt, majority of the largest banks already participate to some degree in this market. Howeve the largest banks that participate, most of their subordinated debt appears to be he holding company, not by independent third parties. This suggests that the developmen operationally feasible program for mandatory  subordinated  debt  would  require  a  consi amount of careful thought. Still, in my judgment it is thought that might prove very wor

## Reform of the Basle Accord: Updating Risk-Based Capital Rules

Capital supplements the discipline from 'outsiders' -- the market -- by rei the  incentives  of  'insiders'  --  the  owners.  Capital  standards  have  therefore  long foundation of the regulatory approach to safety and soundness in the banking system.

The current capital standards are based on the Basle Accord adopted in 19 most of the world's industrialized nations in an effort to encourage stronger capita banks,  to  include  off-balance  sheet  exposures  in  the  assessment  of  capital  adequacy establish more consistent capital standards across nations. The Accord was a major ad 1988, and has proved to be very useful since then. But in recent years calls for reform to grow.

The Basle Accord capital standard divides bank on- and off-balance-sheet a into four risk buckets, and then applies a different capital weight to each bucket. Th are  intended  to  increase  with  the  riskiness  of  the  assets  in  a  given  bucket.  How relationship  is  rough.  Perhaps  most  troublesome,  the  same  risk  weight  is  applied non-mortgage loans. Thus, for example, a loan to a very risky 'junk bond' company ge same weight as a loan to a 'triple A' rated firm.

While the current capital rules fail to differentiate among the riskiness o the banking book, banks are increasingly doing so, taking advantage of increasingly models for measuring, managing, and pricing risk. These models allow banks to assign i economic  capital  to  the  various  loans  and  allow  banks  to  identify  those  loans  for economic capital is less than that required by the Basle Accord. Banks should then eith remove loans from their banking books for which regulatory capital exceeds economic cap otherwise find ways to make regulatory capital converge to economic capital. Conversely should want to keep loans that their models assign higher capital than required by standard. And, banks have been doing just that, in part through innovations such as sec of loans and credit derivatives.

Banks use securitization, for example, to remove their lower risk loans perhaps they otherwise would not originate -- from their banking books, reducing the a capital charges. In a traditional securitization, a special purpose vehicle sells secur a loan pool and uses the proceeds to purchase the loans from the bank. There might se no problem with this arrangement, as long as banks shed the risks that go along with th this were the case, securitization would simply be a device for shifting to the capita risks associated with the bank loans securitized. Banks would then continue their tradi of originating the loans, but the capital markets would play an increased role in the fu loans.

But, in reality, banks are required to keep part of the risk or provide s enhancement in order to make the securities backed by the loans more acceptable to th market.
