title: Mr. Gramlich reviews the benefits and problems of world capital flows  (Central Bank Articles and Speeches, 15 Sep 98)
description: Remarks by Mr. Edward M. Gramlich, a member of the Board of Governors of the US Federal Reserve System, on 'World Capital Flows' at the Carnegie Bosch Institute, University Center at Carnegie Mellon, Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania on 15/9/98.
text:
Mr.  Gramlich  reviews  the  benefits  and  problems  of  world  capital  flows Remarks  by  Mr.  Edward  M.  Gramlich,  a  member  of  the  Board  of  Governors  of  the  US  Federa Reserve System, on 'World Capital Flows' at the Carnegie Bosch Institute, University Ce Carnegie Mellon, Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania on 15/9/98.

For  many  years  it  has  been  clear  that  free  trade  is  generally  more  ef economically  than  protection.  There  are  still  huge  political  fights  within  countries policies, and there may be occasions when countries are better off deviating from free tra trade normally wins the economic high ground in most policy arguments.

But that is not true, or not as true, for international capital flows. Large world debt levels combined with inadequate management of foreign currency risks have le collapse  of  banking  systems  in  country  after  country,  massive  changes  in  exchange  rates recession  or  depression  in  much  of  the  world  economy.  In  view  of  these  provocations, observers  are  now  re-examining  their  preconceptions  that  free  international  capital optimal.  Particular  countries  such  as  Malaysia  are  clamping  on  exchange  controls,  fr economists such as Paul Krugman are suggesting currency controls as a least bad option, many others are recommending distortionary taxes on some capital flows, and almost everybod least re-examining their preconceptions.

But before this process goes too far, I would like to enter a contrary plea. clear problems with the present system of international lending and borrowing. But there and important benefits as well. We know what the problems are. Let's fix them as soon as and try to preserve the important benefits of international capital flows.

## The Benefits of World Capital Flows

Let  me  start  with  the  benefits  of  world  capital  flows.  Much  of  this  is  s neoclassical  economics,  but  it  bears  repeating  in  these  troubled  times.  Countries'  s investment propensities can differ markedly around the world. If economies were closed to flows,  domestic  interest  rates  would  equilibrate  saving  and  investment  in  each  countr interest rates would vary widely, which means that capital would have a different marginal each country.

Suppose now the world were to be opened up to capital flows. Capital would f out of those countries with low interest rates, where investment prospects are scarce co domestic saving, and towards countries where interest rates are high, where investment pros abundant  relative  to  domestic  saving.  Countries  that  import  capital  would  benefit  from stock of high productivity investments. Countries that export capital would put their savi use. Both countries would gain, and the world economy would also gain because scarce sav better allocated to capital markets around the world.

This all may sound a bit academic, but the process has been very important world's  economic  development.  Countries  undergoing  development  can  sometimes  squeeze  t requisite saving out of their poor economies, as the United Kingdom did in the 19th cen Japan did in the 20th century. Or they can import capital to supplement domestic saving United States, Canada, and Australia did in the 19th century and several countries in East and Asia have done in the 20th century. This imported capital has been very important in th development  process,  and  it  has  often  brought  with  it  other  benefits,  such  as  the  in spreading  of  technological  improvements.  Without  world  capital  flows,  the  general  le development in the world would be far less.

Problems

If that's the story, what's the problem? Why do world capital markets seem causing such anguish, in country after country? Why are countries turning away from open markets? It turns out that there is some fine print that goes with the neoclassical mod world economy has had some trouble with the fine print. Here are some of the ways.

- Exchange rate volatility. Countries trade in different currencies, and e rates are necessary to make the conversions. But in addition to being the for  converting  currencies,  exchange  rates  play  another  important  role  i world economy - they also represent the mechanisms for bringing countries p structures in line in international trade. Suppose one country's prices are for it to compete in world trade, either because it has suffered an adver shock,  has  had  too  much  inflation,  has  too  rigid  labor  contracts,  or  fo other reason. The country can suffer a painful recession to get its prices line.  Or  it  can  let  its  currency  depreciate.  Depreciations  are  not  ab necessary, as is asserted by advocates of fixed exchange rates. But depreci or  currency  fluctuations  in  general,  are  often  far  less  costly  ways  t international  adjustments.  The  next  time  you  hear  someone  complain  abo exchange  rate  changes,  ask  them  what  else  they  had  in  mind  to  rest international equilibrium.

While  exchange  rate  changes  have  this  potentially  stabilizing  effect,  th also be destabilizing. When exchange rates are allowed to fluctuate, they in currency markets according to the demands and supplies of forward-look traders, and they can be very volatile, often overshooting long-term value volatility can destabilize trade and impart significant uncertainty to int lending. Borrowers may borrow in international markets expecting to repay one exchange rate, and when the bill comes due, the exchange rate may di by  a  lot.  Lenders  and  borrowers  can  both  hedge,  but  hedging  is  costly, institutions providing this hedge can go broke.

- Financial institutions. Financial institutions engage in what is known as transformation.  They  take  deposits  from  you  and  me,  which  deposits  can redeemed any time we take out our check book, and make long-term loans mortgage  borrowers  and  businesses.  There  are  fantastic  efficiencies  in process  -  consumers  can  get  higher  returns  on  their  saving,  and  busines borrow and invest in productive equipment. Indeed, banks and other finan institutions play the same role in allocating domestic saving to its best the international capital market plays for international capital.

But  as  with  capital  flows,  there  are  risks.  If  the  banks'  loans  go  b institution  is  in  trouble  and  may  not  be  able  to  redeem  deposits.  Wit country's borders there are often institutions such as deposit insurance t savers, but internationally the risks can be greater.

Given that banks are involved in the domestic saving, investment process, not  surprising  that  they  have  become  heavily  involved  in  the  internat saving,  investment  process.  In  general  this  process  too  has  led  to  worl efficiencies, but here too there are risks. In Japan, for example, the ba been hurt by a massive decline in real estate and other values, which ha many nonperforming loans on their books. In Korea and Indonesia, the ban were hurt by the foreign currency exposure of their borrowers.

- Incentive effects. Incentive effects are always important in economics, ge complicating the analysis of policy measures. Nowhere is this as true as international capital flows.
- One  incentive  problem  involves  what  is  known  as  moral  hazard.  Suppose national governments do intervene to protect the safety and soundness of b That intervention might seem sensible, but it could inspire more risky lend the  banks,  to  let  the  government  pick  up  the  tab  if  things  go  bad.  A problem involves unilateral default on loan payments or currency obligat Defaults would appear to benefit debtors, but in the long run these debto have trouble getting new credit. Or contagion effects. Even if one borro perfectly sound, if other borrowers like it go under, lenders will be rel lend to similarly classified borrowers. Discussions of international capit abound with these incentive effects.
- Transparency. A last issue involves transparency. For the international market to work well, lenders must know the risks and rewards. They must kn the aggregate debt of a country, the exchange rate risks they are taking, on and off-balance sheet liabilities of all relevant banks. When they do n a good picture of these risks, they can get into serious trouble.

While the world financial crisis has hit with uneven force in various countr while local situations have differed, the interaction between these four elements has alm been critical. Sometimes big changes in exchange rates precipitated a crisis, sometimes bi in asset values put the banks in trouble, sometimes moral hazard issues generated unsound l almost everywhere there was a lack of transparency. Once a crisis got going, unilateral de contagion effects spread it to other countries. The result was a broadscale financial col then fed over to the real sector and caused bankruptcies, credit restraints, and recession income losses in turn magnified the financial problems.

## Solutions

Are there any solutions to this mess? Many are calling for an end to open markets,  as  if  the  benefits  are  not  worth  the  costs.  Others  are  calling  for  distortion protect  countries  from  too  much  openness.  Should  we  go  part  or  all  of  the  way  back  to economies?

I remain an optimist and I think not. There may be occasional instances where restrictions are necessary to control extreme capital flows not justified by economic fun Moreover, the world capital system clearly is in need of repair. But I hope we can repair back to a world where saving in whatever country goes to the country that needs it most, an pay the most to the saver. And to a world where international capital flows are an importa for world economic development. Let me discuss some remedies that should help in that proce

- Financial  institutions.  Two  types  of  corrections  are  necessary.  A  fi tantamount to preventive medicine - what should be done when institutions not  in  crisis?  The  basic  need  here  is  for  better  bank  supervision.  Supe must be improved to insure that proper risk management techniques are put place and followed. Previous practices where banks, or those to whom ba made loans, loaded up on short-term hard currency denominated liabilities be  curbed.  Market  discipline  can  also  be  used  to  control  risk,  by  exp

financial institutions to as much market discipline as possible and by l moral hazard problems.

But even with all the preventive medicine in the world, the patient some gets sick, and banks in Japan and a number of other countries surely are. to be done then?

Examination  of  a  number  of  historical  episodes  suggests  that  there  are important elements to dealing with a banking collapse. First, the bank reg must go through the balance sheets, determine the problem loans, take the the banks' balance sheets, sell them, and have the public take whatever were entailed. Second, the troubled institutions must be closed down wit management  replaced  and  shareholders  suffering  losses.  Third,  the  heal institutions must then be recapitalized, preferably by new equity sales in markets. The sooner these steps are taken, the better. The longer they taken, the longer troubled banks will continue incurring losses, engaging i practices, threatening the safe institutions, generating contagion effects performing  the  banks'  all-important  maturity  transformation  function.  In here is a way foreign capital flows can be part of the solution to the because new foreign-owned banks that can perform this maturity transformat function can be invited to participate in credit-starved economies.

- Maturity transformation. While financial institutions perform matu transformation, there is no reason to unduly burden the system. Countries often gotten into trouble when they have done too much maturit transformation -  that  is,  borrowed  from  abroad  at  short  maturities  to  f long-term  investment.  Steps  could  be  taken  to  limit  such  borrowing,  e nationally or through bank supervision. Some economists have used this ide propose taxes on short-term borrowing, though the tax rates necessary to d job could be very high and it might be more effective to use orthodox prin of bank supervision.
- Transparency. A further set of corrective mechanisms involves grea transparency. It must be clearer to lenders and borrowers alike what risk are  taking.  This  requires  better  reporting  by  financial  institutions,  an requires better aggregate statistics on the uncommitted foreign reserve b of  individual  countries.  Transparency  alone  cannot  do  the  job  of  good regulation,  but  it  is  hard  to  imagine  a  solution  to  the  international problems of the day without more transparent accounting.
- The IMF. Last but not least I discuss the IMF. Frankly, my own feeling is an institution like the IMF did not exist, we would want to invent somethi it. Here is an international institution that, at least in principle, can finances of different countries without the accusations of big brother tha come about if the United States alone tried to put itself in this role. Mo can  organize  other  lending  countries  to  bring  support  to  countries  in  n liquidity  assistance,  as  opposed  to  having  the  bill  fall  entirely  on  th States.

Supporting the existence of something like the IMF does not suggest agreem with its exact structure or with all of its policies. The present crisis i international preventive medicine provisions are weak. It may be difficult

IMF to perform this warning system role, but there is clearly a need for warnings  about  the  risks  of  lending  to  certain  countries,  to  prevent  c vulnerabilities from building up as much as they did. The IMF's 'one siz all' recommendations of fiscal austerity should also be re-examined, becau many  Asian  countries  expansionary  fiscal  policies  were  clearly  called indeed, still are called for - while the IMF initially recommended the reve

But the two biggest criticisms of the IMF involve the moral hazard issue exchange  rate  flexibility.  On  moral  hazard,  the  criticism  is  more  or inevitable. Any time there is any governmental attempt to increase safet soundness, moral hazard questions can be raised. In the case of the IMF, there to bail out countries in a liquidity crisis, countries will be mor end up in liquidity crises. The answer, it seems to me, is for the IMF t tight conditions on its lending, so that countries will certainly not loo to getting into debtor status. In terms of underlying structural change, t of the few leverage points the international lending community has on borro countries, and it is important for the IMF to use its tool well.

On  exchange  rate  flexibility,  the  problem  with  the  critics  is  that  they saying the same thing. Some say the IMF is too quick to let the exchange fall, some say it is not quick enough. Both cannot be right at the same tim

As a general rule, the exchange rate flexibility issue is a hard one and to make broad recommendations. Sometimes a country's cost structure is cle out of line, or its inflation rate is clearly too high, and exchange rate seems to be the least costly way to bring prices and wages back into lin exchange rate flexibility will cause capital losses and will raise the cos of future capital transactions. That does not mean that the exchange rate preserved at all costs, but it does mean that capital flows themselves p constraints on the normal international adjustment mechanisms. Given all t is hard for me to take a firm policy on exchange flexibility, and I hav sympathy for the apparent open-mindedness of the IMF on the issue.

Will  these  solutions  be  enough?  Who  knows.  But  I  think  we  all  have  a  stak making the world capital system work better. Before we initiate more artificial restriction flows, we should try to improve the system to take advantage of its very large benefits.

## First statement:

Things are only in their infancy. The issuance of electronic money should gen be restricted to banks. Third statement:

## The  banking  world  will  be  changing  even  faster  -  but  neither  the  size  of financial institution by itself nor applying modern strategies are guarantees of quality.

The  process  of  concentration  in  the  banking  industry  will  continue  and  pro result in fewer banks as well as a general increase in the size of units.

Alternatively or complementary to the massive growth we are seeing in many pla at  present,  specialisation,  the  return  to  core  business  or  measures  denoted  by  the banking', i.e. the attempt to reduce costs by outsourcing activities, shrinking the range banking  services  or  purchasing  outside  services.  From  an  economic  point  of  view  these important  strategies  for  the  banks  in  the  future,  but  outsourcing  must  never  affect  re business or the possibility to control business for the management as well as for the authorities.

## Fourth statement:

## Changes  in  the  banking  scenery  also  affect  supervisors  -  supervision  must  b kept efficient, time has not come for an 'outsourcing' of core functions of supervision.

Supervisors must also react on global integration. One proposal to reform supe is to leave supervision and development of supervisory concepts to a large extent to th respectively to a small group of global players. Supervisors are open to new approaches. however, some fundamental reservations against this proposal.

The  current  proposals  of  self  regulation  do  not  respect  the  context  be stipulating  risk  control  norms  and  the  responsibility  for  preventing  systemic  risks. regulation would simultaneously require that market participants take over major responsi preventing  systemic  risks  and  therefore  setting  up  private  agencies  to  intervene  durin crises. But as long as private institutions are not prepared to install such agencies and responsibility for systemic risks, time for outsourcing of essential elements of supervi come.

## Fifth statement:

## In the information age, central banks can operate as an anchor of prudentia supervision owing to their 'natural' presence in the market.

The central bank establishes contacts with market participants and receives v information almost automatically by virtue of its market presence; similar to a seismogra record tremors in the financial system at an early stage and react accordingly. Moreover

cases  the  central  bank  is  in  a  good  position  to  strive  for  market-enhancing  and  pr justifiable deregulation and technical innovations.

However,  during  liquidity  crises,  central  banks  should  not  assume  an  off prede termined function of 'lender of last resort' because of the associated problem of mora Instead, liquidity crises should be solved by private or semi-private agencies before the central bank. In Germany the Liquidity Consortium Bank serves as an example for such stra case of liquidity problems.

## Annual Review of Monetary and Economic Developments in Fiscal 1997

## Summary

Japan's economic growth slowed during fiscal 1997. 1 The economy, which had been on  a  recovery  path,  began  to  decelerate  with  the  turn  of  the  new  fiscal  year  in  April became increasingly sluggish toward the end of the fiscal year.

Final demand deteriorated toward the end of fiscal 1997. Until recently, net generally followed an upward trend and underpinned Japanese economic activities. In deta exports  expanded,  reflecting  firm  business  conditions  overseas  -  particularly  in  Europ United  States  -  and  also  by  the  depreciation  of  the  yen,  while  real  imports  remained unchanged. However, net exports peaked out toward the end of fiscal 1997, owing to a decr exports to other Asian countries against the background of the ongoing economic adjustment region. Meanwhile, public-sector investment basically trended downward because of tight bud both the central and the local government levels. Business fixed investment maintained a increase during the first half of fiscal 1997, particularly in the manufacturing industry. the  second  half  of  the  fiscal  year,  it  seemed  to  have  peaked  out  reflecting  factor deterioration in corporate profits. Private consumption and housing investment were depres April 1997 mainly in reaction to the surge in demand ahead of the rise in the consumption from 3 to 5 percent. 2

The stagnation became evident from autumn 1997 partly against the background the deterioration in household confidence despite a moderate recovery temporarily observed summer 1997. The stagnation in final demand adversely affected production, corporate prof employment condition. Accumulation of inventories was followed by an adjustment in produc resulting in a decrease in output in the last two quarters of fiscal 1997. Inventories in goods, including construction goods and consumer durables, began to accumulate in spring and this development expanded to producer goods in autumn 1997. Corporate profits plunged second half of fiscal 1997 resulting in a turn to decline for the fiscal year as a whole. In  the  meantime,  the  growth  in  wages  and  sa particularly  overtime  compensation  and  bonuses,  decelerated,  reflecting  reduced  product worsening corporate profits.

Consequently, the positive cycle of production, income, and expenditures tha supported the economic recovery during fiscal 1996 weakened from the beginning of fiscal exerting  downward  pressure  on  the  overall  Japanese  economy. In  light  of  the  above,  there  are  several  issues  which  must  be  dealt  with Japanese  economy  to  regain  a  self-sustaining  growth. In view of this aim, the government set out a comprehensive economic p on  April  24,  1998  including  special  income  tax  reductions.  Expeditious  implementation  o measures and significant results are expected.

The second task is to solve various problems that surfaced after the burstin economic 'bubble' as quickly as possible and to restructure and enhance the mechanism of financial  system.  During  fiscal  1997,  the  government  implemented  measures  to  stabili Japanese  financial  system,  which  included  the  use  of  public  funds. Along  with  the  efforts  to  review  and  to  improve  the  indirect  financing  syst necessary to reinforce direct financing through the expansion of risk capital offered in markets,  thereby  encouraging  the  optimal  allocation  of  funds  in  the  economy.  Thus infrastructure for corporate accounting, disclosure of information, the system of taxation services, and payment and settlement systems must be reviewed and improved expeditiously.

The third task is to make steady progress in the reform of Japan's economic st through  measures  such  as  deregulation  and  revision  of  the  taxation  system. ## Question: Is There a New Economy?

The question posed for this lecture of whether there is a new economy re beyond the obvious: Our economy, of course, is changing everyday, and in that sense it 'new'. The deeper question is whether there has been a profound and fundamental altera the way our economy works that creates discontinuity from the past and promises a signi higher path of growth than we have experienced in recent decades.

The question has arisen because the economic performance of the United Stat the past five years has in certain respects been unprecedented. Contrary to convention and the detailed historic economic modelling on which it is based, it is most unusual f to be falling this far into a business expansion.

Many of the imbalances observed during the few times in the past that a bu expansion has lasted more than seven years are largely absent today. To be sure, labo are unusually tight, and we should remain concerned that pressures in these markets co over to costs and prices. But, to date, they have not.

Moreover,  it  is  just  not  credible  that  the  United  States  can  remain  an prosperity  unaffected  by  a  world  that  is  experiencing  greatly  increased  stress.  Dev overseas have contributed to holding down prices and aggregate demand in the United St the  face  of  strong  domestic  spending.  As  dislocations  abroad  mount,  feeding  back financial markets, restraint is likely to intensify. In the spring and early summer, Open Market Committee was concerned that a rise in inflation was the primary threat continued expansion of the economy. By the time of the Committee's August meeting, the had  become  balanced,  and  the  Committee  will  need  to  consider  carefully  the  pot ramifications of ongoing developments since that meeting.

Some  of  those  who  advocate  a  'new  economy'  attribute  it  generally technological innovations and breakthroughs in globalization that raise productivity a new capacity on demand and that have, accordingly, removed pricing power from the wo producers on a more lasting basis.

There is, clearly, an element of truth in this proposition. In the United example, a technologically driven decline is evident in the average lead times on the p new  capital  equipment  that  has  kept  capacity  utilization  at  moderate  levels  and eliminated most of the goods shortages and bottlenecks that were prevalent in earlier sustained strong economic growth.

But, although there doubtless have been profound changes in the way we orga our  capital  facilities,  engage  in  just-in-time  inventory  regimes,  and  intertwine sophisticated risk-sensitive financial system into this process, there is one important notion that we live in a new economy, and that is human psychology.

The  same  enthusiasms  and  fears  that  gripped  our  forebears,  are,  in  every visible in the generations now actively participating in the American economy. Human are always rooted in a forecast of the consequences of those actions. When the future sufficiently clouded, people eschew actions and disengage from previous commitments. sure, the degree of risk aversion differs from person to person, but judging the way pr in today's markets compared with those of a century or more ago, one is hard pressed significant differences. The way we evaluate assets, and the way changes in those valu our economy, do not appear to be coming out of a set of rules that is different from t governed the actions of our forebears.

Hence, as the first cut at the question 'Is there a new economy?' the answ more profound sense is no. As in the past, our advanced economy is primarily driven human psychology moulds the value system that drives a competitive market economy. And process is inextricably linked to human nature, which appears essentially immutable a anchors the future to the past.

But  having  said  that,  important  technological  changes  have  been  emerging recent years that are altering, in ways with few precedents, the manner in which we production, trade across countries, and deliver value to consumers.

To explore the significance of those changes and their relevance to the pos of a 'new economy', we need to first detail some key features of our system.

The American economy, like all advanced capitalist economies, is continual the process of what Joseph Schumpeter, a number of decades ago, called 'creative destr Capital  equipment,  production  processes,  financial  and  labor  market  infrastructure, whole panoply of private institutions that make up a market economy are always in a stat -- in almost all cases evolving into more efficient regimes.

The  capital  stock  --  the  plant  and  equipment  that  facilitates  our  produ goods and services -- can be viewed, with only a little exaggeration, as continuously down and rebuilt.

Our capital stock and the level of skills of our workforce are effective upgraded  as  competition  presses  business  managements  to  find  increasingly  innovativ efficient ways to meet the ever-rising demands of consumers for quantity, quality, an Supply and demand have been interacting over the generations in a competitive environm propel  standards  of  living  higher. We  have  dramatically  reduced  the  size  of  our  radios,  for  examp substituting transistors for vacuum tubes. Thin fiber-optic cable has replaced huge t copper  wire.  New  architectural,  engineering,  and  materials  technologies  have  enabl construction of buildings enclosing the same space but with far less physical material required, say, 50 or 100 years ago. Most recently, mobile phones have been markedly dow as they have been improved. As a consequence, the physical weight of our GDP is growing very gradually. The exploitation of new concepts accounts for virtually all inflation-adjusted growth in output.

The cause of this dramatic shift toward product downsizing during the pas century  can  only  be  surmised. But every competitive market economy, even one solidly based on a rule of la always  in  a  state  of  flux,  and  its  perceived  productiveness  is  always  subject  to uncertainty that are inevitably associated with endeavors to anticipate future outcomes.

Thus,  while  the  general  state  of  confidence  and  consumers'  and  invest willingness to commit to long-term investment is buttressed by the perceptions of the s the society and economy, history demonstrates that that degree of confidence is subjec variations. description: Speech by the Deputy Governor of the Bank of Sweden, Mr. Lars Heikensten, at World Trade Day '98 held at the Stockholm Chamber of Commerce on 25/8/98.
text:
Mr.  Heikenstein  discusses  the  advent  of  the  euro  and  EMU  in  relation  to Sweden Speech by the Deputy Governor of the Bank of Sweden, Mr. Lars Heikenstein World Trade Day '98 held at the Stockholm Chamber of Commerce on 25/8/98.

I should like to begin by thanking our hosts for the invitation to Worl Day '98.  The  introduction  of  a  new  currency  is  due  in  our  vicinity  in  little  more months' time. This is the first instance in modern times of a large group of sovere establishing  a  monetary  union  with  a  single  currency.  Along  with  the  collapse  of Curtain, the creation of the European Monetary Union is probably the most significant E event since World War Two.

Today  I  shall  be  focusing  on  what  the  birth  of  the  euro  may  mean developments in the currency market. I shall not, however, be attempting to predict t future  strength  or  weakness.  Instead,  I  shall  begin  by  discussing  factors  that  could single  currency  in  the  course  of  the  changeover  and  the  somewhat  longer  term. ## 1. A new currency is created

A new currency will see the light of day in January 1999. Eleven countri Europe are forming a monetary union and will accordingly be having a currency, a moneta exchange rate policy, and a central bank in common. The euro will be the domestic curre major economic area. Today, the euro area's share of world output is around 30 per against around 35 per cent for the United States. As regards world trade, the share external trade amounts to around 17 per cent and the United States around 15 per cent.

EMU is a central component in the process of European integration. This pr was initiated in the 1950s with agreements on the joint control of certain means of p the  European  Coal  and  Steel  Community.  The  idea  was  to  forge  economic  bonds  betwe nations as a way of promoting peace in Europe. The establishment of the Common Market i 1980s was a further step, aiming at freedom of movement within the Community for go services,  capital  and  individuals.  With  the  introduction  of  a  single  currency,  the Europe will come still closer to each other in economic and political terms. At the sam another obstacle to the creation of a large internal market in Europe will be removed.

Thus, EMU is to be seen primarily as one aspect of a larger, political proje analyses,  however,  have  tended  to  concentrate  on  the  union's  pros  and  cons  in  an  ec context.  The  advantages  that  have  been  cited  for  the  participating  countries  incl transaction costs for trading in a common currency, increased transparency and compet the single market, and low, stable inflation. The lack of an exchange rate as an ins stabilisation policy is mentioned as one of the drawbacks.

Sweden's  Parliament  decided  in  December  1997  that  Sweden  would  not  be joining the monetary union from the start, mainly on account of the lack of public sup

decision was made after a committee of experts had reported on participation's advanta drawbacks for Sweden. The commission was basically in favour of Sweden being a member EMU  but  was  of  the  opinion  that,  given  the  disadvantages  considered,  Sweden  should participate from the start. The report gave the Riksbank an occasion to present its appraisal of the mo union. This differed and amounted to a recommendation that Sweden should participate fr start. In  general,  one  can  say  that  a  c nominal  exchange  rate  is  determined  by  the  real  exchange  rate  together  with  differ inflation with the rest of the world. A currency's real exchange rate can be described of goods and services in that country relative to the rest of the world. If a differen grows, a corresponding depreciation of the currency is needed to keep the real excha stable. By reporting equity, deciding div having their shares quoted in euro, companies with transactions in euro might possibly their  access  to  the  euro  capital  market  and  reduce  their  costs  for  handling  curren management of liquidity. Swedish law does not currently permit the use of currencies ot the  krona  but  the  possibility  of  having  other  currencies  as  the  unit  of  account investigated.

Today, many companies invest their surplus liquidity in Swedish kronor, p because  their  dividends  are  paid  out  in  kronor.  If  companies  choose  the  euro  as  th account, this could have consequences for their asset management. One such consequence be  a  preference  for  investing  surplus  liquidity  in  euro.  This  alters  their  investme which  brings  us  back  to  what  I  said  earlier  about  short-run  exchange  rate  move Presumably, however, the portfolio adjustments would be gradual, leaving the krona's ex rate  more  or  less  unaffected  by  the  flows.  And  even  if  the  flows  were  to  be  so  la influence the krona's rate, there is no reason to suppose that they would have a perma on the krona's exchange rate against the euro. These flows would be accompanied by many types of currency transaction.

The krona's long-term level will depend instead on Sweden's economic poli When  economic  policy  is  credible  and  focused  on  low  inflation,  there  are  no  groun believing  that  the  krona  would  go  on  weakening  continuously  or  that  it  would  relinq position in Sweden's economy.

## 4. Concluding remarks

To round off what I have been saying, the development of a currency - be euro  relative  to  the  US  dollar  or  the  Swedish  krona  relative  to  the  euro,  for  ex dependent on the direction and results of economic policy. If the policies in the co

regions we have been discussing are credible, focused on low inflation and successfu longer run the exchange rates ought not to diverge.

The legal framework for economic policy in EMU provides a good foundation f a  credible  low-inflation  policy.  But  it  is  still  important  that  all  the  components policy back up the objective of price stability right from the introduction of the sin The ECB can do this by conducting a credible monetary policy and explaining it clear national governments can contribute by ensuring that combined fiscal policies in the comfortably comply with the Stability and Growth Pact; this is not yet the case. Meas improve labour markets can also help to enhance conditions for the success of the m union.

In the same way, the institutional changes and economic developments in Swe in recent years herald good conditions for a stable krona. The framework for both mone exchange  rate  policy  has  been  strengthened.  The  status  of  the  Riksbank  is  being  mad independent and the budget process is now considerably more disciplined. Certain flow currency market may be generated simply as a consequence of the new currency's introd but what ultimately matters is the economic fundamentals. This suggests that the adve single currency - the euro - will not lead to any marked changes either in the krona's Swedish community or in its value.

title: Mr. Stals discusses 'The many facets of interest rates'  (Central Bank Articles and Speeches, 2 Sep 98)
description: Address by Governor of the South African Reserve Bank, Dr. Chris Stals, at a Breakfast Meeting of the Insurance Brokers Council of South Africa, on 2/9/98.
text:
Mr. Stals discusses 'The many facets of interest rates' Address by Governor of the South African Reserve Bank, Dr. Chris Stals, at a Breakfast Meeting of the I Brokers Council of South Africa, on 2/9/98.

## 1. Introduction

Nobody will deny it that South Africa has extremely high interest rates stage. In the context of South Africa's own historical record and measured against a c of inflation of about 6½ per cent, nominal interest rates are extremely high. In the c world environment, and particularly within the group of emerging market economies, the South African interest rates lies in the upper quartile, but is still beaten by a nu comparable countries. Six of the 24 emerging markets listed in the weekly publicatio Economist, for example, have higher short-term interest rates than South Africa at this

Nobody  will  deny  it  that  the  high  level  of  interest  rates  is  bad  for  t African economy, particularly at the current stage of the business cycle and a rather domestic  economic  situation.  It  is  only  the  few  savers  we  still  have  in  the  countr old-aged people who live off their interest income, who may benefit from these high rates. On the other hand, the high interest rates will most probably reduce consumption with borrowed funds, and also investment in fixed capital, equipment and inventories. T production  capacity  of  the  economy  is  therefore  constrained  by  the  present  adverse conditions. In terms of domestic needs, South Africa now requires a stimulation of the and would prefer lower interest rates to encourage economic development.

There is also a fairly general consensus of opinion that the present high rates were recently forced on South Africa by the international financial situation. T East Asian crisis that started to surface in Thailand more than a year ago spilled o economies  of  many  other  countries.  Even  countries  with  more  stable  economies  suc Australia, New Zealand and Canada were adversely affected by these developments. Emer countries  far  away  from  the  East  Asian  epicentre  such  as  Mexico,  Colombia,  Brazi Venezuela have been infected by the problem. Countries with economies in transformatio as  the  Czech  Republic  and  Poland  also  suffered  and  the  recent  catastrophic  developm Russia cannot be completely divorced from the East Asian crisis. In the end, South Af could not escape from the turmoil.

There are major differences of opinion among economists inside and outsid South Africa on what the reaction of the official macroeconomic policymakers in South should be to soften the blows for the economy. At the one extreme there is the Inte Monetary Fund that believes that much more restrictive monetary and fiscal policies sho been applied in South Africa in recent months to fend off the attacks of international and short-term profiteers.

At the other extreme we find economists in South Africa with major private interests who believe that the Reserve Bank should have kept interest rates artificiall complete disregard of the consequences this would have had for the exchange rate of t and subsequent inflation. There are those who believe that the Reserve Bank should ha more  to  keep  the  exchange  rate  stable,  even  if  it  should  have  required  the  reintro tightening of exchange controls.

There are many naive critics in South Africa who believe that the Reserve B fully responsible for the high interest rates and that the Reserve Bank indeed used i powers to force interest rates to these destructively high levels. In their ignorance that the Reserve Bank can even at this stage pull the rabbit from the hat and insta bring  interest  rates  down  again.  Unfortunately,  in  the  real  world  such  miracles  ar possible.

## 2. What caused interest rates to go up

To  avoid  confusion  in  this  debate,  the  real  causes  for  the  recent  sharp interest rates should be revisited. It will be recalled that in the first quarter of t wide-spread optimism that interest rates in South Africa could decline further during of 1998. The Reserve Bank had already reduced its Bank rate from 17 to 16 per cent in 1997, and to 15 per cent on 9 March 1998. Inflation was declining, foreign portfolio in flowed into the country, the foreign reserves were rising and the exchange rate of th under pressure to appreciate.

However,  the  situation  changed  dramatically  in  May  1998  when  non-residen reviewed their investment strategy and started to withdraw some of the funds they had p invested in South African bonds. During the four months January to April 1998, non-r investors increased their holdings of South African bonds by approximately R16 billio the next four months, that is from May to August 1998, they reduced their holdings o African bonds by about R19 billion.

This dramatic change of strategy had an almost immediate negative effect o overall  demand  and  supply  conditions  in  the  South  African  financial  markets.  The  yi long-term government bonds rose from just below 13 per cent at the beginning of May to of over 21 per cent last week. Other interest rates followed the upward trend and esta extremely high levels we now have for the Reserve Bank's rate for repurchase transacti prime overdraft rate, and the mortgage lending rate of banking institutions.

In  this  process,  triggered  by  a  decline  of  investors  confidence  in  the  e markets of the world, little concern was shown for the depressed conditions in the Sout economy.  No  consideration  was  given  to  the  needs,  desires  or  expectations  of  the  pe South  Africa.  Neither  the  Minister  of  Finance  nor  the  Governor  of  the  Reserve  Ban consulted by the markets before interest rates were forced to higher levels. The whol was driven by external factors that swept across many of the smaller economies of the w a  huge  tidal  wave.  The  switch  from  a  R16  billion  inflow  of  capital  for  investment African bonds in the first four months of 1998 to an outflow of an almost similar amou next  four  months  dramatically  changed  the  demand  versus  supply  conditions  in  the African financial markets. In the situation, it would have required a massive creation by the Reserve Bank to prevent interest rates from rising to the extent they did. Such a money in turn would have added fuel to the inflationary pressures that were already stim the depreciation of the rand.

## 3. What can now be done to bring interest rates down?

It is amazing to read in the financial press in South Africa almost every accusation that the high interest rates in South Africa at this stage are a reflection

Bank's deliberate 'high-interest-rate-policy'. The present level of interest rates is o as being 'artificially' high because of Reserve Bank intervention in the market. The overlook  the  fact  that  the  Reserve  Bank  indeed  raised  the  amount  of  accommodation available  to  banking  institutions  at  the  daily  repurchase  tender  for  central  bank R4.1 billion early in May to R9.8 billion at this stage. This action by the Reserve Ban prevented interest rates from rising even further and, if anything, created an artifici of  interest  rates  in  the  country.  Perhaps  with  some  justification,  this  policy  of  t recently criticised by the International Monetary Fund.

The Reserve Bank also made a huge amount of forward cover available to Sou African  residents  with  outstanding  commitments  in  foreign  currency,  and  to  non-re investors with open rand positions in South Africa with the objective of discouraging t sending more funds out of the country. This policy undoubtedly contributed towards main interest rates at a lower level as the IMF quite correctly pointed out. In South Africa widely criticised for having provided this forward cover, but at the same time also bla 'high' interest rates.

After four months of heavy pummelling by the markets, South Africa now fi itself in a situation where:

- the exchange rate of the rand has depreciated by about 25 per cent;
- interest rates have risen to a level where borrowing from the banking sec the financing of additional economic activity has become almost prohibitiv
- the banking sector has lost a lot of liquidity;

There  is  therefore  an  understandable  pressure  on  the  Reserve  Bank  to something that will bring interest rates down immediately and effectively for all borro South African market. Can the Reserve bank do anything to salvage this situation?

A  simplistic  view  is  that  the  Bank  should  reduce  the  rate  for  its  rep transactions and therefore provide accommodation to banking institutions at a lower c view overlooks the fact that the repo rate of the Reserve Bank is determined on a d through a tender system, and is no longer fixed by the Bank. Should the Reserve Bank t want  to  reduce  the  repo  rate,  it  will  have  to  offer  more  central  bank  funds  ('high money) to the banking institutions.

In deciding on its policy, the Reserve Bank must, however, take into account

- the recent large outflows of funds through the Bond Exchange. An expansion domestic liquidity in this situation could facilitate the outflow of funds;
- existing  relationships  between  interest  rate  margins,  spot  exchange  rat forward  rates.  A  disruption  of  these  relationships  can  easily  lead  t speculative transactions against the rand;
- the continuing high rates of growth in bank credit extension and in the supply; and
- the need to keep inflation in check in the aftermath of a depreciation of t more than 20 per cent since May this year.

In this situation, it will be irresponsible for the Bank to create more mo effort to force interest rates down. Advantages, if any, to be gained from such a pol very short-lived.

A solution in the short-term for the South African dilemma can only come the original source of the problem, that is, from the international financial markets. must  return  to  the  many  international  fund  managers  who  have  decided  in  recent  mont withdraw  substantial  amounts  of  portfolio  investments  from  the  bond  markets  of  the economies around the world. These fund withdrawals not only forced interest rates to levels, but also created turmoil in the foreign exchange markets. A return of stabil markets will pave the way for lower interest rates in South Africa, and in many othe countries of the world. For any individual country such as South Africa to try to br these shackles at this stage will be almost impossible, unless impenetrable brick wa constructed around the South African economy to isolate it from the rest of the world.

## 4. Can South Africa survive with these high interest rates?

As already mentioned, the high level of interest rates at this stage is not with the current needs of the South African economy. There is, however, very little we get ourselves out of the dilemma in the very short-term.

The present unsatisfactory situation emphasises the long identified need fo Africans  to  save  a  greater  percentage  of  our  income  or,  to  put  it  in  more  sensible language,  to  consume  less.  We  must  remember  that,  in  terms  of  the  macro-econo consumption financed with borrowed funds counts as negative saving. By borrowing from b to finance current expenditure, we actually use up tomorrow's income today.

The situation also emphasises once again that the South African total prod machinery  must become more competitive. We must make ourselves not only more self-sufficient in the provision of finance for our own economic development, but al production of the goods and services we need for domestic consumption and real investm other  words,  we  must  reduce  our  dependence  on  the  rest  of  the  world  and  eliminat vulnerability for recurrent balance of payments crises.

As long as these high interest rates are forced on us by the international over which we have no control, a slow-down in total economic activity will be unavo Sensible adjustment to the realities of the situation will, however, avoid a major rece already predicted in some quarters, and feared by many. To delay a spending decision tod not mean a permanent abolition of a justifiable need, but realistic deference to th disciplines and constraints of an adverse global situation, until international condit again.

In  the  meantime,  we  should  not  lose  confidence  in  the  resilience  of  the African  economy,  and  in  its  ability  to  weather  the  current  storm.  Looking  around  th today, we still have, even in the present adverse climate, many reasons for remaining about  the  medium  and  longer-term  prospects  for  the  South  African  economy.  Our  bank system remains sound, our financial markets operate with great efficiency, and a huge demand for goods and services needs but little encouragement to re-stimulate the econom

Mr. Greenspan remarks on income inequality Remarks by Chairman of the Board of Governors of the US Federal Reserve System, Mr. Alan Greenspan, at a symposium sponsored by Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City in Jackson Hole, Wyoming on 28/8/98.

## Income Inequality: Issues and Policy Options

I am pleased once again to open this annual symposium. At the outset, I wish to Tom Hoenig and his staff for assembling a highly capable group of experts to inform us and to discussion on an important issue in the world economy. The study of income inequality - its c consequences, and its potential policy implications - has a long history in economics, althoug always  had  a  high  profile  among  researchers  and  policymakers.  To  borrow  a  phrase  from  Prof Atkinson, income distribution in recent years has been 'brought in from the cold.' In part, tha has resulted from the experience of many industrialized economies with widening earnings inequ the 1980s and 1990s. It has been heightened by interest in the consequences of economic ch developing, newly industrialized, and transition economies.

The experience of industrialized countries, including the United States, with income  inequality  has  spawned  a  great  deal  of  research  on  the  functioning  of  labor  markets sources of shifts in the demand for various types of skills, on the supply responses of workers efficacy of government efforts to intervene in the operation of labor markets. A number of have contributed importantly to this work will be participating in this conference. One sto emerged from that body of research is now familiar: Rising demand for those workers who hav skills to effectively harness new technologies has been outpacing supply, and, thus, the compe those workers has been increasing more rapidly than for the lesser skilled segment of the workf this supply-demand gap has been an important source of widening earnings inequality is now accepted within the economics profession. However, the considerable diversity of experiences countries as well as the finding that earnings inequality has also increased within groups of similar  measured  skills  and  experience  suggest  that  we  may  need  to  look  deeper  than  skil technological change if we are to fully understand widening wage dispersion. In particular, private and public institutions influenced inequality over the past two decades? What roles played by growing international trade and the evolving ways in which production is organized? the participants in this symposium are well-equipped to speak to these issues, and we should l more about the causes of widening inequality during the next two days.

In discussing the extent to which large portions of the population are not re benefits of economic growth, I hope that the participants at this conference will not stop wit of trends in earnings - or, for that matter, even trends in income more broadly defined. Ultima interested in the question of relative standards of living and economic well-being. Thus, we n examine  trends  in  the  distribution  of  wealth,  which,  more  fundamentally  than  earnings  or represents a measure of the ability of households to consume. And we will even want to cons distribution  of  consumption,  which  likely  has  the  advantage  of  smoothing  through  transitor affecting particular individuals or households for just a year or two.

Among these more comprehensive measures, data for the United States from the Fede Reserve's Survey of Consumer Finances suggest that inequality in household wealth - that  is worth - was somewhat higher in 1989 than at the time of our earlier survey in 1963. Subseque 1992 and 1995 surveys - and here our data are statistically more comparable from survey to su they were earlier - showed that wealth inequality remained little changed in terms of the broad 1 Nonetheless, that stability masks considerable churning among the subgroups. One particularly change was an apparent rise in the share of wealth held by the wealthiest families at the expe wealthy families; most of the change occurred within the top 10 percent of the distribution.

Moreover, our research using the survey suggests that conclusions about the distr of wealth are sensitive - although to a lesser degree than income - to the state of the eco

At  the  othe distribution,  owned  principal  residences,  the  values  of  which  are  not  as  sensitive  to  bus conditions,  are  a  typical  household's  most  important  asset.  Another  interesting  finding  is expand  the  definition  of  wealth  to  include  estimates  of  Social  Security  and  pension  wea distribution among U.S. households becomes much more even. 2 This finding suggests that, in addition to factors influencing private wealth accumulation, the evolution of institutional arrangements that has taken place over the last two decades may have played an important role in affecting the distribution of wealth over time.

What about the effect of the recent rise in stock and bond market values? The view is that the growth in mutual funds and other financial investment avenues has allowed in further down in the wealth distribution to take advantage of the strength in equity markets. C figures show that households lower in the income distribution are now more likely to own stoc decade ago. 3 However, between the 1992 and 1995 surveys, the spread of stock ownership and the r prices did not lead to a rise in the share of stock and mutual fund assets owned by the bottom of the wealth distribution. Although their dollar holdings rose rapidly, the increases were no those  for  households  at  the  top  of  the  wealth  distribution.  If  patterns  of  equity  ownersh changed much since 1995, the steep rise in stock prices over the past several years would further increase in the concentration of net worth. This influence could be offset, to some continued broadening in the ownership of equities, particularly through tax-deferred savings Moreover, some additional offset may have occurred through rising house prices, an important middle class families. Our 1998 survey, which is now in the field, will yield a clearer read how wealth concentration has changed and on the relative importance of different assets in that

Despite our best efforts to measure trends in income and wealth, I believe th those measures - by themselves - cannot yield a complete answer to the question of trends in m economic well-being. In the United States, we observe a noticeable difference between trend dispersion of holdings of claims to goods and services - that is, income and wealth - and tr dispersion of actual consumption, the bottom-line determinant of material well-being. Ultimate interested  in  whether  households  have  the  means  to  meet  their  needs  for  goods  and  for  s including those such as education and medical care, that build and maintain human capital.

Using  data  from  the  Consumer  Expenditure  Survey  that  the  U.S.  Bureau  of  Lab Statistics conducts, researchers have found that inequality in consumption, when measured by outlays,  is  less  than  inequality  in  income. 4 These  findings  are  not  surprising.  As  is  well  known, consumers tend to maintain their levels of consumption in the face of temporary fluctuations Variations in asset holdings and debt typically act as buffers to changes in income. Thus, c patterns tend to look more like patterns in income that have been averaged over several years that should remind us of the pitfalls of reading too much into any year-to-year change in our economic well-being.

The  BLS's  consumer  expenditure  data  suggest  a  rise  in  inequality  over  the  1 comparable to that shown by the Census family income figures. However, during the first hal 1990s, inequality partially receded for consumer expenditures while for income it continued to 1). The consumption data used in these calculations include only what individuals purchase di of their incomes and accumulated savings. Recently, researchers have extended the analysis usin complete and more theoretically appealing measure of consumption that includes the indirect services from the stock of durable goods that they already own - houses, vehicles, and major a 5 As one might expect, although this measure of consumption has a profile somewhat similar to t in the current expenditure data over the 1980s and the first half of the 1990s, it shows still inequality overall and a clearer pattern of consumption smoothing during the 1981-83 recession.

The  information  available  from  the  Consumer  Expenditure  Survey  can  be  used calculate  another  interesting  measure  of  the  well-being  of  households:  changes  in  inequali ownership of consumer durables. The BLS staff has updated tabulations of these data that they

for me several years ago (table 2). Of course, ownership rates for household durables clearl income. But for a number of goods - for example, dishwashers, clothes dryers, microwaves, an vehicles - the distribution of ownership rates by income decile has become more equal over time

Even though we may be able to develop an array of measures of current and past t in inequality - such as those that I have described and potentially others that may be pres symposium - we will likely still face considerable uncertainty about how to interpret those me about what the future may hold for the trend and the distribution of economic well-being.

Wealth  has  always  been  created,  virtually  by  definition,  when  individuals  us growing knowledge, in conjunction with an expanding capital stock, to produce goods and serv value. The process of wealth creation in the United States has evolved in a number of import Over the last century, we have learned how to be more efficient in meeting the needs of consu thus  we  have  moved  from  producing  essentials  to  the  production  of  more  discretionary  good services. Moreover, these goods and services have been, over time, increasingly less constrai limits of physical bulk. More recently, we have found ways to unbundle the particular charact each good and service to maximize its value to each individual. That striving to expand the satisfying the particular needs of individuals has resulted in a shift toward value created exploitation  of  ideas  and  concepts  and  away  from  the  more  straightforward  utilization  of resources and manual labor. The new thrust has led to structural changes in the way that we or production  and  the  distribution  of  goods  and  services.  It  has  increased  the  demand  for, compensation  of,  workers  who  have  the  ability  to  create,  analyze,  and  transform  information interact effectively with others. Most important, it has accorded particularly high value to t of advanced computer and telecommunications technologies to the generation of economic wealth.

At  the  same  time,  however,  the  consequences  of  technological  advances  and  t implications for the creation of wealth have become increasingly unpredictable. We have found cannot forecast with any precision which particular technology or synergies of technologies significantly  to  our  knowledge  and  to  our  ability  to  gain  from  that  knowledge.  Even  i technological  change  were  to  occur  at  a  steady  rate,  variations  in  our  capacity  to  absorb advances would likely lead to an uneven rate of increase - over time and across individuals expanded investment in knowledge: Supplies of appropriately skilled workers can vary. In some the initial choices in the exploitation of advances may turn out to be sub-optimal. In other c potential  of  advances  may  be  realized  only  after  extensive  improvements  or  after  complem innovations in other fields of science.

As we consider the causes and consequences of inequality, we should also be mi that, over time, the relationship of economic growth, increases in standards of living, and th of  wealth  has  evolved  differently  in  various  political  and  institutional  settings.  Thus,  ge about the past and the future may be hard to make, particularly in the current dynamic and environment of economic change. We need to ask, for example, whether we should be concerned the degree of income inequality if all groups are experiencing relatively rapid gains in their though those rates of gain may differ. And, we cannot ignore what is happening to the level income while looking at trends in the distribution. In this regard, our goal as central bank clear: We must pursue monetary conditions in which stable prices contribute to maximizing sus long-run growth. Such disciplined policies will offer the best underpinnings for identifying o to channel growing knowledge, innovation, and capital investment into the creation of wealt turn,  will  lift  living  standards  as  broadly  as  possible.  Moreover,  as  evidenced  by  this sustaining a healthy economy and a stable financial system naturally permits us to take the ti efforts on addressing the distributional issues facing our society and on other challenging is remain out in the cold.

title: Mr. Yam discusses 'Intervention true to guiding policy'  (Central Bank Articles and Speeches, 24 Aug 98)
description: Discussion by the Chief Executive of the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, Mr. Joseph Yam, published in South China Morning Post on 24/8/98.
text:
Mr. Yam discusses 'Intervention true to guiding policy' Discussion by the Chief Executive of the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, Mr. Joseph Yam, published in South China Morni Post on 24/8/98.

The current debate revolving around government intervention in the stock and fu markets to deter currency manipulation brought a feeling of nostalgia to me. It made me recall debates on government intervention there were within the administration when Sir Philip Haddo was financial secretary.

I was then, in the late 1970s, a young economist in the Economic Services Branch Government Secretariat, with little responsibility and a lot to learn. Those debates were, some more healthy and more intellectual. There was certainly less mud being thrown around.

But  the  contrast  is  understandable.  Today,  this  is  a  controversial  issue.  T interested parties airing their grievances through punchy and articulate expressions of their philosophical issue of interventionism. This is also an issue in which, in a more politicised and at a time when the community is enduring the pain of economic adjustment, the politically see great political mileage. A government with the whole of the legislature arguably in opposi a vulnerable target.

It  is  so  easy  to  wave  the  banner  of  free  markets  and  condemn  any  governme intervention,  and  be  seen  to  be  righteous  and  knowledgeable;  notwithstanding  that  the  gov concerned has been so successfully running the freest economy in the world. But we must be hum thank those wanting to lecture us on free markets, if only for the purpose of keeping us on our

Hong Kong is changing and one would expect any dynamic city to be different after passage of 20 years. But, surprise, surprise, the policy of positive non-interventionism has Many may have chosen to ignore or forget the true meaning of this policy, but not the adminis the HKSAR. Certainly, I have not forgotten it. And, having worked continuously and closely wi financial secretaries in succession, I can vouch for all of them in their firm adherence to positive non-interventionism. It applies also to the specific case of the current interventio and futures markets. As a firm believer in such a policy, I am responsible for conducting the i

The nostalgia has prompted me to take time off watching the markets to read some o long-forgotten literature on positive non-interventionism. This gives me great pleasure, partic I see the rare sentences and, if I am more fortunate, paragraphs attributable to my drafting the final texts. Yes, Sir Philip was a great financial secretary with a great mind. Even many hold him in high regard. I hope that in quoting him, our stance in the stock and futures marke into a context that our critics may be able better to appreciate.

As early as November 1973, at the Conference on Managers in a Changing Hong Kong Environment, Sir Philip spoke on, amongst other things, the role of public policy. He said Government must accept such responsibilities as are necessary to ensure that management decis not  frustrated  by  imperfections  in  the  operation  of  the  market  mechanism,  leading  to  e inefficiency or social distress which only the Government can remove.'

In  September  1979,  he  talked  about  interventionism  and  the  adjustment  mechani amongst other things, in a speech on the Hong Kong Economy in Transition. He said that: 'A pra view dictates an admission that interventionism can be relevant to the maintenance of economic in Hong Kong even in the general context of a philosophy of positive non-interventionism'. In speech he cautioned against taking for granted the 'efficiency with which [the] essentially adjustment mechanism operates in restoring equilibrium'. He then went on in the same speech to areas that could be collectively referred to as market imperfections which justifies market int

But it was the speech he made to the Federation of Hong Kong Industries in Decem 1980 (and as Principal Assistant Secretary for Economic Services then it was my honour to have in drafting part of the speech) in which he made abundantly clear his stance on the policy non-interventionism. Here I quote two paragraphs of his speech in full.

Sir Philip said: 'I have frequently described the Government's economic policy sta being one of 'positive non-interventionism'. Not surprisingly, perhaps, some have claimed th really just a fancy term for laissez-faire or, less kindly, that it covers up a 'do-nothing' a simply  not  so:  positive  non-interventionism  involves  taking  the  view  that  it  is  normally damaging  to  the  growth  rate  of  an  economy,  particularly  an  open  economy,  for  the  Governme attempt to plan the allocation of resources available to the private sector and to frustrate t market forces, no matter how uncomfortable may be their short term consequences.'

Sir Philip added: 'But in my description of our economic policy stance, I do qual term 'non-interventionism' with the adjective 'positive'. Perhaps in the past I have not spe implications of this adjective clearly enough. What it means is this: that the Government, w with an interventionist proposal, does not simply respond that such a proposal must, by def incorrect. Quite the contrary.

'Generally speaking, or so I would like to argue, the Government weighs up careful arguments for and against an act of interventionism in any sector of our economy and on the d supply side in the light of present and likely future circumstances. The Government then co positive decision as to where the balance of advantage lies. It is true that, more often than to the conclusion that the balance of advantage lies in not intervening; and, I must confess alarmed if we didn't. Yet, in all cases, the decision is made positively, and not by default, a non-outcome  of  a  do-nothing  approach.  But,  there  are  many  examples  of  the  Government  decid usually on the advice of its boards and committees, to intervene, in one way or another, in t of market forces.'

Indeed there are many examples of intervention. We built the airport because, w government intervention, it would simply not have been economically viable. We built roads and We  provided  public  housing,  medical  services,  the  list  is  long.  But  we  tend  to  do  less jurisdictions and so the size of our public sector in relation to gross domestic product i smallest in the world.

Specifically in the monetary and financial systems, there is significant intervent form of the regulation of financial markets and the supervision of financial institutions. Thi because we feel that, in the words of Sir Philip, 'the balance of advantage' lies in so int because 'imperfections in the operation of the market mechanism [may lead] to economic ineffici

In very much the same spirit, we intervened in 1996 and built a real time payment because  the  private  sector  was  not  able  to  come  up  with  this  highly  desirable  piece  of infrastructure. We have been intervening since the beginning of 1990 to develop the Hong Kong debt market, again because the market was considered essential for effective financial inter and, regrettably, the private sector was not able to develop one that is properly structured.

The  linked  exchange  rate  system  is  also  a  product  of  the  policy  of  pos non-interventionism. The Government intervened to fix the exchange rate because we found out i and since, that there is a need for a monetary anchor. In the absence of such an anchor, the currency will be, in mathematical terms, an indeterminate. In other words, it is not somethi free market can determine in the best interest of the community without intervention.

We have had four speculative attacks on our currency since the outbreak of fin turmoil in the region in the middle of last year.

It is very well known to almost everyone in the market that a handful of hedge have on each occasion conducted a double play in the stock futures market and the currency mar have come to realise how this double play works, although it has only become apparent, at leas the third and fourth attacks in June and August this year respectively.

On each occasion, interbank interest rates were pushed higher, to varying degrees, view to engineering a sharp fall in the stock index futures.

While the August episode is still being played out, it is clear that these curren or manipulations, have introduced a large interest rate premium for the Hong Kong dollar ove dollar. This currency manipulation premium amounts to around three to four percentage points. community already in considerable pain, having to go through the inevitable, and already ve economic  adjustment  necessitated  by  financial  turmoil  in  Asia,  we  can  do  without  the  pai disproportionately exacerbated by those manipulating our currency in order to benefit from t stock  futures  positions.  There  is  further  the  serious  risk  of  this  double  play  creating  a over-shooting in the stock and other asset markets, undermining the stability of our otherw financial system.

I must emphasise, however, that I am in no position to judge whether or not the been  overshooting  and,  if  so,  the  extent  of  the  overshooting.  But  we  can  all  see  that  m overshoot badly and uncontrollably if we just look around us in the region. Whatever accusation throw  at  the  Indonesians  -  'crony  capitalism,  nepotism,  corruption,  racism,  poor  macroec management, neglect of financial development' - even if all these were true, they still do no extent of the meltdown of their currency and their financial system, and the distress they ar brutal reality is that they are now in that position.

Markets panic and overshoot, and if we are not careful, we can easily be pushed i situation. And the culprits would be the handful of hedge funds having little or no interest i not to mention in our well being, other than it being a free market which they can manipulate which they can take money, somewhat like an ATM machine, as others have put it.

The HKSAR administration is run by people who have put Hong Kong on the map as the freest economy in the world. It is clear to us that there are, again quoting my great teach 'imperfections in the operation of the market mechanism', possibly leading to 'economic ineff and 'social distress'. So the administration decided to intervene to deter currency manipula rid  of  the  unnecessary  and  unfair  pain  that  has  been  inflicted  on  the  community  as  reflec currency manipulation interest rate premium, and to avoid market adjustments overshooting in p an uncontrollable tailspin.

Consistent  with  Sir  Philip's  view  that  interventionism  should  be  'relevant maintenance  of  economic  stability  in  Hong  Kong',  and  with  Exchange  Fund  Advisory  Committe backing, Financial Secretary Donald Tsang Yam-kuen made the order to intervene in the free market forces.

There has been no departure from the long established policy of posi non-interventionism that has served Hong Kong so well in the past. Those who think that we departed should try and refresh themselves of what this policy really means.

And no one needs to take my word for it. Those are the words of Sir Philip, the a of that policy and someone who commanded and still commands a lot of respect.

Indeed as Monetary Authority chief, I have no responsibility over that policy. It the broad shoulders of Sir Donald Tsang who is carrying it bravely. Let us all make a little e him the support that he needs, spiritual or otherwise, by trying to gain a better appreciatio policy of positive non-interventionism really means.

Whilst on the subject of intervention, may I reiterate that our intervention in and futures market to deter currency manipulation does not imply any weakening of our resolve t to the linked exchange rate system. This resolve has never been stronger. Indeed, as I have elsewhere,  there  simply  is  no  better  alternative  for  Hong  Kong.  The  experience  of  many neighbouring economies in the past year or so underlines why.

As  the  financial  storm  in  this  region  spreads  to  almost  everywhere  now,  and increased intensity, the discipline of currency board arrangements of our linked exchange rat our best safeguard for our long-term prosperity and stability.

## Bank of Japan presents the summary of an article published in the August edition of its Quarterly Bulletin Bank of Japan communication, 31/8/98.

## Release of a Reference Wholesale Price Index Using a Geometric Mean Formula

## Introduction

In recent years, concern about the accuracy of price statistics has risen in ind countries where the statistical bias in price indexes seems to have grown significantly while have generally been stable. 1 The Bank of Japan has worked to improve the accuracy of its Wholesal Price Index (WPI) over the years, but many problems remain to be solved. 2

One such issue is the formula used for calculating the index. Recently, the Bank to publish a reference WPI using a geometric mean formula (WPI-UGM) in addition to the convent index using arithmetic mean method (Laspeyres index). Although the new formula may not succee removing the bias in the current index, the Bank considers that by publishing more data, it users with more information about the possible measurement bias in the present WPI.

1 In the United States, a report titled 'Toward a More Accurate Measure of the Cost of Living' was subm Senate Committee in December 1996 by the Advisory Commission to Study the Consumer Price Index (Boski Commission). This report triggered a series of controversies over the accuracy of the Consumer Price In Chairman Alan Greenspan of the Federal Reserve Board has frequently made references to this issue. In G the Bundesbank published a discussion paper in March 1998 titled 'Problems of Inflation Measurement in Ge Non-Technical Summary' (Hoffmann [1998]). In Japan, too, a paper was published concerning the problem of measurement errors (in Japanese, Shiratsuka [1995]).

2 In general, problems with the accuracy of price indexes can result from (1) factors relating to the fo calculate indexes, as discussed in this paper; (2) failure to adapt statistical samples properly to re consumer  preferences  and  distribution  channels;  and  (3)  failure  to  make  appropriate  adjustments  for  c quality of goods and services. In order to deal with (2) and (3), the Bank revises the weights of goo expenditure on individual items (expenditure shares) every five years, reviews and replaces individual basket when necessary, and makes an adjustment for quality changes between old and new items at the sam Quality adjustment for such goods as personal computers is made by applying an econometric method known 'hedonic regression method.'
