title: Mr. Heikensten discusses recent economic and monetary policy developments in Sweden  (Central Bank Articles and Speeches, 19 Aug 98)
description: Speech by the Deputy Governor of the Bank of Sweden, Mr. Lars Heikensten, at the Local Authorities Economics Seminar in Malmö on 19/8/98.
text:
Mr.  Heikensten  discusses  recent  economic  and  monetary  policy  developments  in Sweden Speech by the Deputy Governor of the Bank of Sweden, Mr. Lars Heikensten, at the Authorities Economics Seminar in Malmö on 19/8/98.

Thank you for the invitation to attend this Seminar and talk about the Swedish ec and monetary policy. I shall begin with a brief account of how the Riksbank operates with it target. In that context I shall also be saying something about economic policy's results in Then  I  shall  consider  the  Riksbank's  appraisal  of  the  Swedish  economy,  as  presented  in  ou inflation report last June, together with subsequent economic tendencies. Finally I shall be the somewhat longer perspective of my opening section. This will tie in with the theme of th and highlight some factors that are of crucial importance for our success in creating a potent economic expansion.

## 1. Inflation target policy-how does it work?

The objective of monetary policy is to keep the value of money stable. This ha defined  more  specifically  as  keeping  the  annual  rate  of  inflation  (measured  as  the  chang Consumer Price Index) at 2 per cent. Around this target there is a tolerance interval of ±1 point which serves to accommodate normal deviations that arise, for instance, from transitory But the possibility of larger deviations than this cannot be ruled out. If they occur, it is i explain their causes and state how inflation is to be brought back into line with the target.

To influence consumer prices, the Riksbank uses its instrumental rate-the repo Simplifying somewhat, one can say that, by altering the marginal interest rate for banks, th influences  other  domestic  interest  rates  and  thereby  the  level  of  economic  activity  in  S consequently the development of prices. It should be noted, however, that in the short and med pricing is also affected by other factors, such as the construction of fiscal policy and the d wages.  That  is  why  the  Riksbank  is  concerned  that,  when  making  decisions,  politicians  and market organisations should also promote low inflation. It is the reason, moreover, for my r these matters at the end of this talk. But in the long run the course of inflation is crucial monetary policy.

Interest rate adjustments have their main effect on prices after an interval of years. Monetary policy decisions therefore have to be based, not on the latest figures for inf the Riksbank's current assessment of future price movements . Our quarterly inflation reports accordingly present ongoing inflation forecasts based on analyses of a large array of economic indicators by  economic  models  and  knowledge  of  relationships  between  different  parts  of  the  economy. inflation assessment is used by the Riksbank in drawing conclusions about the direction of policy. A forecast rate of inflation above the target normally leads to interest rate increa expected rate below the target prompts the Riksbank to lower the repo rate.

Inflation is assessed on a continuous basis. New information-fresh economic stati for instance, or signs of a change in some economic relationships-leads the Riksbank to re current forecast and make the necessary changes. If a new forecast indicates that future in deviate  from  the  target,  then  the  Riksbank  has  to  adjust  the  repo  rate  in  accordance  wit assessment.

However, assessments of future inflation-like any other forecast-are bound to inc an element of uncertainty. Moreover, observers are liable to differ on which future path is mo So it is hardly surprising-rather a healthy sign-that our inflation assessments and monetary p sometimes a subject of lively debate. But while inflation assessments may vary, in Swedish soci there is broad support for focusing monetary policy on price stability.

## 2. Recent years

The  Swedish  economy,  as  we  all  know,  went  through  a  profound  crisis  in  the  e 1990s. This is not an occasion for discussing the causes of the crisis in depth. It will suff the  origins  lay  in  structural  weaknesses  in  Sweden's  economy.  But  the  crisis  also  had  to shortcomings in stabilisation policy in the late 1980s and early 1990s.

Since production stopped falling and growth restarted in the course of 1993, ec developments in Sweden have exceeded expectations in several respects. The average annual grow of above 2.5 per cent is higher than the average in the boom period in the 1980s.

In a way, perhaps this is hardly surprising. The weak exchange rate gave exports a impetus and there was plenty of unutilised capacity. But I do not think many people expected high growth could be combined with low inflation. In these years Sweden has rejected the pol the decades of high inflation and reinstated the time-honoured tradition of annual price incre 2 per cent. Inflation has also been low in an international comparison. Judging from the expe economic agents, a low-inflation regime has now been established.

The composition of growth has also been favourable. After decades of growth that generated to a high degree by rising consumption-with an accumulation of external debt-it is a sign that expansion been associated with strong export demand and industrial investment. One this, the large current-account surpluses since 1994, has made it possible to repay external de

A dramatic turnaround has also been achieved in government finances. Massive bud deficits  have  been  succeeded  by  a  surplus.  This  trend  is  primarily  a  consequence  of  the recovery, just as declining activity was the main cause of the earlier fiscal collapse. But extensive  measures  for  budget  consolidation,  neither  the  economic  upturn  nor  the  improvem government finances would have been feasible.

Tax  increases  and  spending  cuts  on  the  scale  we  have  experienced  in  recent obviously leave their mark. Household income has been sharply restricted, particularly in 199 have public activities.

In  one  respect,  moreover,  the  outlook  is  still  troublesome,  namely  as  r employment. Despite the economic recovery, a rapid expansion of employment has proved diffic achieve. It is worth noting, however, that the number of private sector jobs, in services in p in fact been rising continuously since 1995. But this has not made up sufficiently for the co employment during the 1990s in, for example, the public sector and construction.

After this review of developments in recent years, I shall now discuss the Rik appraisal of the coming twenty-four months, which is the period we need to consider when con monetary policy.

## 3. The message in June

In the latest inflation report last June the Riksbank presented an economic for Sweden and its implications for the path of inflation up to the middle of the year 2000. Our was that the trends in recent years, with high growth and low inflation, would continue in ahead.

The  economic  upswing  was  assumed  to  continue  in  the  forecast  period,  with  ann growth rates around 2.5 per cent this year and 3 per cent in the next two years. The forecast increasing contribution from rising domestic demand, accompanied by a successive fall-off i growth. Private consumption was expected to pick up, partly in view of rising household income.

Notwithstanding the prospect of further good economic growth in the coming years, Riksbank judged that the rate of inflation would remain low and even be less than we had e earlier. The strong demand was certainly assumed to give some increase in inflationary pressu forecast period but not so much as to be a cause for concern. One reason lay in the good pr growth  that  was  also  foreseen,  indicating  that  full  capacity  utilisation  in  the  economy  wo reached in the coming twenty-four months. Although capacity utilisation was high in certain se Riksbank envisaged that in the economy as a whole there would be a capacity surplus.

External inflationary pressure was expected to be low in view of subdued interna inflation, low raw materials prices and a somewhat stronger exchange rate.

Expectations of future inflation among households, financial agents and manufact indicated a belief that future inflation would be low. Thus, confidence in economic policy' price stability seemed to have been firmly established.

The Riksbank noted that the uncertainty in the assessment of future inflation was whether it would be even lower than we foresaw in the main scenario. One of the main factors the crisis in Asia and its conceivable effects on international economic developments and pri were risks of the crisis' effects being greater than assumed in the main scenario in June, demand and low inflation in the rest of the world would lead to an even lower price rise in t economy.

All  in  all,  these  considerations  meant  that  in  the  June  report  the  Riksbank's assessment of inflation in the coming years was adjusted downwards. As the rate of inflation twenty-four months ahead was judged to be below the target, the Riksbank considered that, at l time, there was room for a somewhat more expansionary monetary stance. The repo rate was the lowered 25 basis points.

## 4. What has happened since the June report?

Let us now look at what has actually happened since the beginning of the summer.

## Low pressure from international prices

During the summer the Asian crisis has got worse and the uncertainty about its course seems to have grown. More countries in the region are now expected to show a fall i during the year. One of the main factors behind the deterioration is the weak Japanese econ knock-on effects of the Japanese crisis in other parts of the world are highly uncertain, as in such countries as Russia and China.

An impact from the Asian crisis is now discernible in economic growth in the U States  and  the  United  Kingdom.  These  economies  show  signs  of  a  slowdown  that  can  be  trace decreased exports to Asia but there are also indications that their domestic demand is slackeni

In the euro area, however, growth prospects seem to be more favourable. The reco appears to be firm-to a growing extent as a result of stronger domestic demand-and it looks as inflation will remain low.

The  overall  picture  of  international  activity  is  somewhat  weaker  than  the  Ri forecast in June. International inflationary pressure is low. The extensive economic problem and the unrest in global stock exchanges are contributing to this.

## Swedish economy strong

Economic growth in Sweden seems to be good, however. As expected, the statistics s an accelerating growth of domestic demand, accompanied by a slowdown in foreign trade.

Private consumption is rising strongly and a continuation of this trend is indic number of factors: households' personal economic expectations are still rising, employment is and  disposable  income  is  growing  as  a  result  of  low  inflation  and  a  less  restrictive  fi Uncertainty about share prices could have a contrary effect but the downward movements that ha observed constitute no more than a correction after a relatively strong increase. Since the 1998 the Stockholm Exchange has risen 20 per cent. The statistics also show strong growth fo consumption as well as gross capital formation.

But foreign trade is weakening; export growth is slowing and imports are rising. are several signs that exports will go on slackening; the inflow of export orders has deter confidence has fallen among purchasing managers in manufacturing. However, the weaker exchange may have a contrary effect on exports.

The inflation statistics show that inflationary pressure in the Swedish economy low. In June and July the price level fell 0.2 per cent. This means that for both months the t rate of inflation was 0.6 per cent.

All in all, it looks as though the growth of domestic demand in 1998 may excee assessment  in  the  June  report.  On  the  other  hand,  foreign  trade  may  be  somewhat  weaker  th counted on at that time. Thus, the figures on real economic developments that have been publis the latest inflation report do not seem to call for any substantial revision of the forecast the summer figures for inflation or the regular surveys of inflation expectations altered the the early summer.

## Weaker exchange rate

In the June report we counted on some appreciation of the krona in the forecast During the summer the krona has weakened and I want to take this opportunity of commenting o tendency since June. Most of the weakening has occurred in August. In effective terms (TCW) th has depreciated somewhat more than 3 per cent since the beginning of June, from 119 to 123. Aga US dollar and the German mark the fall in this period amounts to somewhat more than 5 per cen per cent, respectively.

Several explanations are given for the weakening of the krona. A downward tende was already evident in May-June in connection with the repo rate cut. After that the krona see been pulled down by the unrest in Asia, which has hit relatively small industrialised countr dependent on foreign trade. Some observers consider that countries with a high export share materials have experienced a currency depreciation in connection with the price fall for raw That explanation is not really all that applicable to Sweden because it is difficult to show t particularly dependent on raw materials exports.

The stock exchange turbulence is also considered to have had a major effect on the recently in that nonresidents have disposed of Swedish shares, which involves selling kronor currencies. Since the June inflation report there has been no new information that warrants concern  about  economic  development  in  Sweden.  So  the  weaker  krona  does  not  appear  to  refl change in confidence in the economic fundamentals. The traditional indicators of credibility, from price trends in financial markets, convey the same picture. Both the long bond differe Germany  and  the  expected  future  short  interest  rates  point  to  persistently  strong  confide low-inflation policy.

In this context I should like briefly to rehearse the role of the exchange rate i policy. The Riksbank does not target the exchange rate; monetary policy focuses instead on a inflation.  The  exchange  rate  can  be  seen  as  one  of  a  number  of  indicators-albeit  one  of important-that we use to predict inflationary pressure in the Swedish economy. If the krona we strengthens permanently , then thisall else equal -will affect inflation.

The difficulty accordingly lies in assessing the permanence of exchange rate move and incorporating the assessment in the overall picture of inflation. The economic fundamenta an appreciation of the krona in the coming years. For this reason we believe that the current w temporary and will be followed in time by a renewed appreciation. It should be underscored, that  if  the  krona's  weakening  to  date  can  be  regarded  as  permanent,  then  there  are  also  r expecting that the weaker exchange rate will lead to inflation at a higher rate than we foresa report.  That  would  have  consequences  for  monetary  policy,  always  assuming,  of  course,  tha factors have not simultaneously contributed to a better outlook for inflation.

The  recent  weakening  of  the  krona,  together  with  increased  concern  about  conti turbulence in Asia and global stock exchanges, has shown up in money market pricing. The ma earlier assessment was that room existed for further interest rate cuts. Today the picture is This I find entirely natural in that the exchange rate is an important factor in our assessm inflation.

## The overall picture

To  sum  up,  the  new  statistics  since  June  largely  support  the  opinion  about  in prospects  that  we  presented  in  the  latest  report.  The  figures  for  real  economic  activity  a suggest, if anything, that the path of inflation will be lower than in our main scenario in t If so, however, it is presumably a question of marginal revisions. The exchange rate, however, moving as we predicted, has weakened. The assessment of this tendency and how it should be we up with other factors in an overall assessment of inflation prospects is a matter to which t will be returning in the next inflation report on September 28th.

## Concluding remarks

Having presented the Riksbank's picture of current economic developments, I should to return to the somewhat longer time perspective from the beginning of this talk and take u that is the theme for today's speakers. Is there room for expansion in the Swedish economy? In shall concentrate on two fields that are closely connected with monetary policy: the functio labour market and fiscal policy.

The economic policy that has been implemented in recent years, with its emphasi price stability and sound government finances, has had favourable results in a number of resp growth has been combined with persistently low inflation. Moreover, the composition of growth h structurally  desirable,  focusing  on  exports  and  industrial  expansion.  This  helps  to  establ foundation for a sustained increase in future consumption. A reduction of external debt has beg

Prospects  for  the  coming  years  also  look  favourable.  It  seems  that  output  can relatively rapidly by Swedish standards, accompanied by relatively low inflation.

There is reason to emphasise, however, that what we see is hardly the final sol our problems but rather important initial steps towards a more balanced development.

For  one  thing,  the  positive  trend  in  the  Swedish  economy  does  not  yet  apply substantially to the labour market . A downward adjustment in the rate of wage increases towards more reasonable long-term figures has begun but we do not know how permanent it will be. What will in the next round of wage negotiations if capacity utilisation at that time is high? Is the fun

labour  market  in  other  respects  sufficiently  smooth  for  the  adequate  creation  and  filling vacancies? This is a key question. If we do not succeed in finding good solutions in Sweden comes to wage formation and the workings of the labour market, in the longer run it will not b to permit such strong economic expansion as we have experienced in recent years.

Another aspect of economic  policy  that,  like  the  functioning  of  the  labour  mar closely connected with the Riksbank's domain is fiscal policy . In recent years monetary policy has been assisted  in  the  first  place  in  that  the  consolidation  of  government  finances  has  restor foundation  for  economic  policy;  in  addition,  there  has  been  the  more  direct  restraint-in perspective-on demand and price impulses. In recent decades that was by no means invariably th On the contrary, there were periods when fiscal policy accentuated the cyclical movements.

I find it important to issue a warning about repeating mistakes of this type. In of  an  economic  upswing  we  are  now  hearing  calls  for  expansionary  fiscal  policies  in  the increased public spending as well as unfinanced tax cuts. There are strong long-term grounds the upswing in activity to build up government surpluses as a buffer for harder times. That w our future freedom of action in economic policy. It will be easier to cope both with futur downturns and with structural challenges such as an ageing population. A tighter fiscal policy the burden on monetary policy and increases the probability in the years ahead of being able t to  have  low  interest  rates  and  a  stable  economic  development,  with  good  growth  of  producti employment.

title: The changing face of exchange control and its impact on cross-border investment opportunities in South Africa  (Central Bank Articles and Speeches, 23 Jul 98)
description: Address by the Governor of the South African Reserve Bank, Dr. Chris Stals, at the Annual Australia/Southern Africa Business Council Meeting held in Sydney on 23/7/98.
text:
The  changing  face  of  exchange  control  and  its  impact  on  cross-border investment opportunities in South Africa Address by the Governor of the South African Reserve Bank, Dr. Chris Stals, at the Annual Australia/Southern Africa Business Council Meeting Sydney on 23/7/98.

## 1. The history of exchange control in South Africa

The  beginning  of  exchange  control  dates  back  to  1939  when  South  Africa,  a member of the now defunct British Sterling Area, was asked, together with other members Sterling Area, to introduce restrictions on the outflow of funds to non-Sterling Area cou ensured  the  free  movement  of  funds,  emanating  mainly  from  the  United  Kingdom,  within Sterling Area.

After World War II, the Sterling Area exchange controls were gradually phased but in South Africa in 1961 the controls were extended and given a specific South African This  followed  upon  disrupting  internal  political  clashes  (the  Sharpeville  incident), Africa's withdrawal from the British Commonwealth. Exchange control in South Africa was intended to provide some protection to the domestic economy from the adverse effects of la outflows  of  capital.  For  the  first  time,  exchange  control  also  restricted  the  rep non-resident investment funds from the country.

During the period 1961 to 1993, exchange control was extended from time to t mostly  in  reaction  to  a  worsening  of  South  Africa's  internal  political  situation,  and external pressures in general. For example, in 1976, after the uprising of school children proceeds of the sale of non-resident owned securities in South Africa were blocked and e converted into securities rand, tradable only at a substantial discount at a second tier exchange rate. After the United Nations introduced world-wide economic and financial san against South Africa in 1986, a standstill on the repayment of a major part of South Afric indebtedness was introduced, providing for an extended negotiated redemption of the outs amount.

By  the  time  that  the  major  social  and  political  reforms  were  introduced  in Africa in the early nineties, there existed a very comprehensive system of exchange con covered  certain  current  account  transactions  and  the  inflows  and  outflows  of  both  resi non-resident investment funds.

## 2. The phasing out of exchange control

There was general consensus that exchange controls created many distortions i South African economy. Interest rates, the exchange rate, financial asset and property p even  production  costs  in  the  domestic  economy  were  affected  by  the  comprehensive  exch controls.  The  system  prevented  the  important  price  mechanism  of  the  market  economy functioning properly. This led to the maldistribution of scarce resources and the functio economy at levels below its optimum capacity.

After the democratic election for a new Government of National Unity took pla April 1994, and international punitive actions against the South African economy were r there  was  general  consensus  within  the  new  Government  that  exchange  controls  should  al removed. There was, however, major disagreement on how fast the controls should disappear. one extreme were supporters, mostly in the private financial sector, of a 'big bang' appr pleaded  for  the  immediate  removal  of  all  the  controls.  On  the  other  hand,  there  was  s

support for a more gradualist approach and for the dismantling of the exchange controls extended period of time.

The Reserve Bank supported the latter approach, mainly for the following reason

- Years  of  economic  sanctions,  boycotts,  disinvestment  campaigns  and  t withdrawal  of  foreign  loan  funds  from  South  Africa  depleted  the  countr foreign reserves. At the time of the elections of April 1994, the Reserv owned, on a net basis, zero foreign reserves.
- During the long extended period of exchange controls, backlogs developed, a huge pent-up demand for an outflow of capital emerged. Overdue loans had to repaid  to  non-residents,  and  no  South  African  residents  were  allowed accumulate foreign assets of any significance over a period of more than years.
- Distortions were by that time so much embedded in the South African finan structure  that  the  sudden  removal  of  exchange  control  would  not  only  h exerted pressure on the country's low level of official foreign exchange re but could also have forced painful immediate structural changes that would unduly disrupted the domestic economy in the short term.

The  South  African  authorities  therefore  decided  on  a  gradual  phasing-out  o existing exchange controls. Beginning already in 1993, the following relaxations were acc introduced over the past five years:

- As a first priority, all exchange controls applicable to current account tr were removed. South Africa now fully complies with the requirements of Arti VIII of the International Monetary Fund.
- Secondly, controls on non-residents were removed. The debt standst arrangements of 1985 were finally rescheduled towards the end of 1993, and financial  rand  system  (two-tier  exchange  rate)  was  terminated  in  March  1 Non-residents are now completely free to introduce funds for any purpose South Africa, to repatriate such funds and to transfer out of the country and capital gains earned on their investments without restriction.
- Resident corporates (companies) were gradually enabled to make dire investments  in  foreign  subsidiaries,  branches  or  joint  ventures  by  trans limited amounts of funds from South Africa, and by raising funds abroad thr equity and loan issues. In the process, direct investments of about R50 (US $10.7 billion) were acquired by the South African corporate sector ove past four years.
- Resident institutional investors were given permission in June 1995 to div part of their total assets into foreign currency denominated investments. stage,  they  may  hold  up  to  15  per  cent  of  their  total  assets  outside  o Africa.  In  total,  the  financial  sector  has  now  acquired  about  R55  billi $11.8 billion) in the form of portfolio foreign investments.
- Last  year,  in  June  1997,  private  individuals  were  given  permission  to limited investments in their own names outside of South Africa. At this

individual taxpayers in good standing with the tax authorities may invest R400 000 per individual outside of South Africa. A modest amount of fore exchange equal to less than R2 billion has since then been absorbed under concession

- Many other smaller exchange control restrictions were either eased or remo for example on short-term trade financing, inter-bank financing arrangement the transfer of legacies, donations and emigrants' funds. Administr procedures were simplified and banks (authorised dealers in foreign excha were  mandated  to  approve  many  transactions  without  prior  reference  to Reserve Bank.

There  remains  but  one  major  area  for  relaxation,  and  that  is  in  respect restrictions  still  applicable  to  the  so-called  'blocked'  funds  of  former  residents  of  S Apart  from  settling-in  allowances,  the  remainder  of  the  assets  of  emigrants  is  blocked Africa and becomes non-transferable. Income earned on blocked funds, however, is not sub the restrictions.

South Africa has therefore now reached a stage where there are no effective exc controls any more on current account transactions and on the movement of funds of non-res Resident  corporates,  financial  institutions  and  private  individuals  all  have  limited  sc some investments outside of the country and have, on a combined basis, now accumulated more R100 billion of foreign assets. Backlogs that existed in 1994 for the outflow of non-resi have been accommodated in full, and those that existed for the outward investment of resid are gradually being absorbed. On balance, South Africa has now removed more than sevent cent of all the exchange controls of the past.

## 3. The inflow of capital into South Africa

The macroeconomic argument for the removal of exchange control is based on t assumption  that,  on  balance,  in  a  liberalised  economy,  over  time  capital  inflows  wil outflows.  Despite  the  need  to  accommodate  large  accumulated  backlogs,  this  philosophy vindicated by developments in the capital account of the South African balance of payments past four years.

Non-resident investors increased their holdings of South African equities by R63 billion (US $13.5 billion) from 1 January 1995 up to the end of June 1998, and also i net  amount  of  about  R30  billion  (US  $6.5  billion)  in  South  African  bonds.  The  total investment capital inflow of more than R90 billion was mainly used for financing the acqui foreign assets by South African residents, as already mentioned above.

Taking  account  of  the  relatively  large  net  inflows  of  portfolio  foreign outflows to finance foreign investment by residents, and all other capital movements, t account of the South African balance of payments still showed a net inflow of funds from a R53 billion over the period from the beginning of 1995 up to March 1998. The inflows were than sufficient to cover modest current account deficits and to raise the total gross fore reserves of the country to a level of R45 billion (US $9.0 billion) at the end of March 1 level, the total foreign reserves were sufficient to cover about three months' imports o services. In terms of international standards, the level of the foreign reserves is still but at least much more comfortable than at the end of March 1994, when the gross foreign of the country amounted to only R10.3 billion (US $3.0 billion).

One of the disappointing aspects of the capital inflows into South Africa over four years has been the relatively small amount of direct foreign investment made in the co more than 25 per cent of the total inflows represented direct foreign investment, and the as portfolio investment in securities, loan capital and short-term financing facilities.

## 4. Restructuring of the financial sector

The  gradual  removal  of  exchange  controls  was  accompanied  by  some  major restructuring of the financial sector in South Africa. To encourage competition in the ma foreign  banks  were  allowed  to  establish  themselves  in  the  country.  More  than  20  foreig opened up branches or subsidiaries in South Africa, and more than 60 foreign banks now do b in the country through representative offices. Together with about 35 domestic banking ins the South African banking industry is now providing, on a competitive basis, excellent an financial  services  to  the  country.  The  industry  is  healthy,  well-managed  and  subject  to regulation  and  supervision  based  on  the  principles  of  the  Basle  Committee  guidelines  a principles.

While the gradual phasing-out of exchange control continued, the financial ma were  also  restructured,  liberalised  and  made  more  flexible  to  accommodate  almost  exp increases in volumes. In the capital market, three separate specialised institutions wer provide, respectively, for equity trading on the Johannesburg Stock Exchange (JSE), bond tr the  Bond  Exchange  of  South  Africa,  and  trading  in  derivatives  on  the  South  African  F Exchange.

Two years ago, the JSE introduced major reforms to provide for corporate owners foreign ownership (of stock brokers), dual capacity trading, negotiated commissions and e screen trading. The JSE is continuing to improve its facilities by providing for the imm and  dematerialisation  of  stock,  and  for  improved  clearing  and  settlement  arrangements. listing of about 700 different securities, a total market capitalisation of about US $275 turnover  of  about  US  $45  billion  last  year,  the  JSE  is  now  classified  as  one  of  the  m exchanges of the world.

The most spectacular increase in the total volume of transactions over the p years took place in the Bond Exchange of South Africa. Total turnover in this market incre the equivalent of US $553 billion in 1995, to US $927 billion in 1997, that is an increase cent over just two years. The relaxation of the exchange controls made an important contr the development of the Bond Exchange. Total gross transactions by non-residents in this ma year exceeded the equivalent of US $257 billion, or almost 30 per cent of total turnover.

Interest is also growing in the South African Futures Exchange. The total num contracts traded in this market increased from 3½ billion in 1995 to more than 5 billion in

A further important development that flowed from the globalisation process i emergence of a Euro-rand market where the outstanding amount of rand-denominated loans ra by  non-South  African  borrowers  from  non-South  African  investors  now  amounts  to  abo R36 billion. A substantial part of the proceeds obtained from these loan issues was rei South African bonds.

The market in foreign exchange in South Africa is also growing rapidly. The av daily turnover in this market now exceeds US $10 billion. Of particular importance is the in forward cover operations in this market, where South African banks now carry a fully forward sales (or purchases) book of about US $180 billion.

The Reserve Bank recently introduced steps to encourage a more active developm of the domestic inter-bank market for funds. It is the objective to ensure that short-term should  be  flexible,  and  should  fluctuate  to  reflect  changes  in  underlying  market  condit effective  rate  at  which  central  bank  funds  are  made  available  to  banking  institution determined  on  a  daily  basis  through  a  tender  system  for  repurchase  transactions,  ente between the Reserve Bank and banking institutions. This greater flexibility in short-te rates  is  of  particular  importance  in  light  of  the  growing  volume  of,  and  greater  vo short-term international capital movements.

As a further step in the development of the financial system, the Reserve Bank beginning of this year also upgraded the national payment, clearing and settlement system. system provides for an electronic on-line real-time link between participating banks, and fund  transfers  between  these  banks.  It  enables  the  banks  to  monitor  and  manage  their positions continuously, and provides for electronically managed end-of-day settlement of transactions. As from the beginning of October, it will become possible to settle transac intra-day basis as and when instructions are received within the system.

The gradual phasing-out of the exchange controls was therefore accompanied b simultaneous process of liberalising, modernising and upgrading of the domestic financial s the process, the removal of the exchange controls did not create any major disruption in th markets, and the health and soundness of the South African financial institutions were prot

Both  processes,  however,  should  be  seen  as  part  of  the  wider  movement international  financial  globalisation.  Without  introducing  these  changes,  it  would  not possible for South Africa to participate in the process of world-wide integration of financ The removal of exchange controls and the simultaneous upgrading of the domestic financial opened up the way for South Africa's participation in this process.

## 5. The Southern African Development Community

A further consequence of the socio/political/economic reforms in South Africa the past few years was a natural greater involvement for the country in the economic dev process of the African continent. Apart from a more active participation in continental working through the Organisation of African Unity, the United Nations Economic Commission Africa, and the African Development Bank, South Africa is taking an active part in the ac the Southern African Development Community (SADC).

Fourteen  countries  of  the  Southern  African  region  now  belong  to  this  fo agreement  for  economic  co-operation,  with  the  long-term  goal  of  eventual  economic  integ South  Africa  plays  a  leading  role  in  the  development  of  financial  and  investment  co-o amongst the participants in SADC.

Within the structured institutional framework of SADC, a Committee of Governo of  all  the  central  banks  of  the  region  was  established.  This  Committee  introduced  a  n co-operation  projects  intended  to  develop  the  financial  systems  and  markets  of  the  reg approach of the Governors Committee at this stage is first to develop the financial infras each  of  the  countries,  before  venturing  into  the  more  challenging  task  of  macroec co-ordination or integration.

One of the important projects in the work of the SADC Governors Committee is remove remaining exchange controls within the region. Where practicable, countries are enc

to do this even faster than what has been programmed for the overall phasing out of the con envisaged that there will eventually be a relatively free movement of goods, services and this vast area with a total population of more than 180 million people.

## 6. The financial globalisation process

The phasing out of exchange control and the restructuring of the financial sys important  preconditions  for  South  Africa's  greater  participation  in  the  financial  gl process. As can be deducted from some of the statistics quoted in this address, South Afr firmly on the road of greater participation in the expanding international financial market

Recent  events  in  the  wake  of  the  East  Asian  financial  crisis  proved  once however, that the globalisation process is not without risk. The easy movement of large a funds  into  and  out  of  countries  with  relatively  small  economies  can  at  times  be  very  d During  the  four  months  January  to  April  1998,  non-residents  increased  their  holdings  o African bonds, acquired through the Bond Exchange, by more than R16 billion. Over the ne weeks, that is during May, June and the first half of July 1998, they reduced their holdin R12 billion.

Both the inflows and the outflows of capital on this occasion disrupted the African financial markets and complicated the implementation of monetary policy centred medium-term  objective  of  maintaining  financial  stability  in  the  interest  of  optimum  e growth. In the situation and against the background of a rather depressed domestic econ yield on long-term government bonds increased from 12.7 per cent on 30 April 1998, to 1 cent on 6 July, before it declined again to 15.5 per cent last week.

The  Reserve  Bank's  fluctuating  repo  rate  similarly  showed  wide  fluctuations increased from 14.8 per cent in early May to a peak of 24.0 per cent on 22 June, before set at a level of about 21 per cent. All banking institutions in the country were forced t deposit and lending rates by about 6 percentage points since the end of April. The prime rate of the major commercial banks now stands at 24 per cent. With the latest measure of i only 5 per cent per annum, real interest rates are at an extremely high level.

The  exchange  rate  of  the  rand  also  came  under  a  lot  of  pressure.  After relatively stable for a period of about 18 months from October 1996 up to the end of April rand depreciated from R5.05 against the US dollar in the middle of May to R6.62 = $1 on 1998. Since then, the exchange rate appreciated again to fluctuate around the R6.00 = $1 the last few days. At this level, the rand, measured against a basket of currencies, is sti cent down from where it was at the beginning of this year.

Some  critics  do  believe  that  the  removal  of  the  exchange  controls  is  partl blamed  for  this  greater  volatility  in  financial  conditions.  They  advise  South  Africa,  t reintroduce some of the controls, for example, the two-tier exchange rate system. This vi shared by the monetary authorities in South Africa. Despite the gyrations of recent weeks believe that the advantages of participation in the financial globalisation process wil bring more advantages to the South African economy than disadvantages.

## 7. Concluding remarks

The  policies  of  the  phasing  out  of  exchange  control,  the  restructurin liberalisation  of  the  financial  system  and  the  promotion  of  active  participation  in  the financial globalisation, have created many opportunities for cross-border investment in Sou

Foreign  banks,  fund  managers,  institutional  investors  and  manufacturing  concerns  are  ex their financial business with South Africa in the form of:

- conventional short-term trade financing;
- short-term inter-bank financing facilities;
- loans extended for medium and longer-term periods to South African borrowe in both the private and public sectors;
- portfolio investment in equities, bonds and financial derivatives, acquired the various capital market exchanges; and
- direct  investment  in  the  form  of  subsidiaries,  branches,  or  joint  ventur South African undertakings.

Developments in recent years also led to the creation of an active Euro-rand outside of South Africa, and to a greater involvement of South Africa in the economic deve process of the Southern African region.

These  exciting  developments  have  already  created  opportunities,  also  for expansion  of  financial  relations  between  South  Africa  and  Australia.  I  believe  man opportunities  exist  and  are  waiting  for  the  financial  and  other  economic  entrepreneurs Africa and in Australia to be exploited.

Our two countries should not always be regarded as major export competitors i world  markets  for  base  minerals  and  other  commodities.  There  are  also  many  areas  wher economies are complementary and where our policies can be supportive in the global enviro This applies particularly when it comes to our efforts of integrating our financial mark world environment.
author: Chris Stals

title: Mr. Heikenstein discusses the Swedish financial crisis of the early 1990s  (Central Bank Articles and Speeches, 15 Jul 98)
description: Speech by the Deputy Governor of the Bank of Sweden, Mr. Lars Heikenstein, at a seminar arranged by the Swedish embassy held in Seoul, Korea on 15/7/98.
text:
Mr. Heikenstein discusses the Swedish financial crisis of the early 1990s Speech by the Deputy Governor of the Bank of Sweden, Mr. Lars Heikenstein, at a seminar arranged b Swedish embassy held in Seoul, Korea on 15/7/98.

Let me begin with a thank you to the organisers of this seminar. I am honou have the opportunity to share with you some experiences from the Swedish financial crisi early 1990s.

## 1.  Introduction

An IMF study from 1996 showed that in the past fifteen years, 132 of the Fund' member countries had experienced macroeconomic and/or financial crises. Today the figure i higher. Crises are a recurring phenomenon. In spite of every effort to prevent them, I fea will continue to occur. We should therefore use the opportunities to learn from each oth order to avoid making the same mistakes and to find the appropriate correctives sooner.

Needless  to  say,  there  are  no  single  'best  solutions'.  Crisis  situations  a specific in some respects, not least with regard to their structural and political environm not been specific, they would probably never have occurred because they would have been 'sp in advance. Having said this, however, there are a number of globally accepted 'truths' a constitutes a good response to crises.

Discussions  around  crisis  situations  are  usually  divided  into  two  parts: prevention and crisis management. In this presentation I will be focusing on the latter. To the  handling  of  a  crisis,  it  is  useful  to  know  which  factors  generated  the  problems. narrative will include the events that led up to the crisis in Sweden. I will also com developments in Asia, with some emphasis on Korea. Having sketched this background, I wil to  the  actual  handling  of  crises,  explaining  why  we  found  certain  types  of  solutions Sweden - leaving it to you to consider whether the same might apply to some extent to your

## 2.  Background

## The macroeconomy

First, let me say a few words about the macroeconomic background to the cris Sweden. There are both similarities and differences between Sweden and Asia. In the foll will touch on some of them. It should also be remembered that substantial differences a between the Asian countries.

One common factor is the fixed exchange rate . In Sweden this led to high levels of foreign borrowing, particularly in the private sector. In addition it made it difficult gradual overheating of the economy by applying contractive monetary measures - raising i rates tended to increase capital inflows which, to the extent they were monetised, further to the overheating.

Following the deregulation of the domestic financial market, the crisis in Swed also preceded by a rapid expansion of credit ; in the course of five years, private borrowing gr from 85 to 135 % of GDP. The credit expansion coincided with a protracted boom and a signi proportion of the borrowed money was spent on speculation, both in real estate and in assets, such as equity. The real estate speculation in Sweden culminated in a bubble th 1990-91. Shielded by the economic upswing, there had been many misdirected and overly opti investments in various industrial and other projects.

In these aspects I find similarities between Sweden in the late 1980s and th countries  during  the  1990s.  A  feature  common  to  Sweden  and  Korea  was,  moreover,  that domestic financial market was liberalised long before the external capital outflows. This overheating  of  the  domestic  economy  could  not  be  adequately  balanced  by  capital  outflo investment abroad.

But there are also some differences. Other factors that contributed to Sweden' crisis were a relatively deep international downturn and high interest rates in our part of the world in the wake of German reunion. On top of this, our fiscal position was more vulnerable , entering the 1990s with a public debt-to-GDP ratio of around 40 per cent. Sweden's external borrowing ra also high - some 30 per cent of GDP. Besides reflecting the public budget deficit, this ha an  extremely low  private  savings  ratio .  In  some  years  this  ratio  was  actually  negative.  The weaknesses made Sweden highly vulnerable to shifts in confidence in our economy.

## The financial sector

There  were  also  underlying  weaknesses  in  financial  systems.  Let  me  now  turn these.

The financial systems had not adapted to the change from a sheltered environment to a deregulated and much more competitive situation. In the earlier environment, banks had incentive to develop a sophisticated credit culture, involving comprehensive evaluations o projects and collateral. (One important similarity between Sweden and Korea was the overop reliance on collateral and other guarantees, rather than on the viability of the loan p When deregulation was a fact, bank managers saw a chance of gaining market share and incr revenues by taking new risks, but did not clearly see the dangers in a lack of the necessar

One  of  the  major  faults  in  credit  decisions  in  Sweden  was  that  banks  le customers, projects and geographical areas of which they did not have sufficient knowledge. major mistake was that banks accepted high-risk concentrations , not just to individual companies but also to economic sectors, primarily real estate, and to geographical areas. At the crisis, bank loans to real estate, or collateralised by real estate, accounted for more t of all loan losses.

A further weakness was the inability of the banks, as well as of the author register  the  growing  prevalence  of  indirect  concentration  risks.  For  instance,  bank demanded loans denominated in foreign currencies . Interest rates on these loans were lower than o krona loans and as the krona was fixed within a fairly narrow band, there was presumed t exchange risk. The banks borrowed the foreign currencies abroad and on-lent them to cus avoiding  open  exchange  risk  exposures.  However,  when  the  krona  was  attacked  and  the  f exchange rate subsequently had to be abandoned, banks were doubly affected. For counterparties,  perceiving  the  banks'  weakened  position,  reduced  or  withdrew  credit  lin forced the banks to demand either early repayment from customers or loan conversion into d currency. This led, in turn, to sharply increased loan losses because, at short notice, bo unable to raise the larger amounts in krona that were needed to repay the foreign curre which the krona's depreciation had made much more expensive.

Neither had the supervisory authority , the Bank Inspectorate, adjusted . It continued its  traditional  formal  supervision,  ensuring  that  reports,  permits  et  cetera  were  form rather than supervising the actual risks. The authority was also somewhat complacent about be  frank,  the  Central  Bank  and  the  Ministry  of  Finance  should  share  the  blame  for  thi

Sweden had not experienced a financial crisis since the 1930s. Lacking relevant crisis e the authorities did not perceive that the 1980s could pave the way to a new financial decade was, after all, characterised by sustained economic growth, rising bank profits and low loan losses.

The financial weaknesses I have described so far are quite similar in Swede Korea. However, some differences should also be noted:

- In Sweden, banks had built up good capital reserves . Before the onset of the crisis, all th banks fulfilled or surpassed the 8 per cent Basle requirement for capital. So, alt performing and other impaired loans amounted to 15 per cent of GDP in Sweden (a fi that is rather similar to recent estimates for Korea), the original cost to the go rescuing  the  banking  system  amounted  to  only  some  4  per  cent  of  GDP;  since  t moreover, most of this has in fact been recovered.
- Sweden applied restrictive rules to central bank involvement in the banks. Only liquidity support was provided, inter alia in the form of foreign currency deposits to stem th from the banks and to reduce the risk of a credit crunch. This did not involve the R any risks because the State guarantee for banks' repayments also applied to us as a l

## 3.  Triggers

Now,  let  me  turn  to  the  actual  crisis.  It  is  well  known  that  the  event  (o triggering a crisis is often different from the crisis' underlying causes. In the absence factor, countries with substantial underlying problems from time to time have also been abl an acute crisis. The event triggering a crisis is sometimes rather dramatic, such as the of a politician - as in the Mexican case - or a sudden loss of confidence, e.g. due to th of a disappointingly weak fiscal budget. Opinions may differ about what were the most im 'triggers' of the acute crises we are discussing today. Again, I see both differences and between Sweden and the Asian countries.

In our case, a policy shift to the low-inflation regime in the rest of Europe, combined with structural changes and a more hostile international environment (with higher interest rat lower growth, as I mentioned before), made the existing situation unsustainable and trig crisis.

In the early 1990s the government refrained from accommodating the high costs inflationary pressures that had been building up in the 1980s. Under similar circumstances the 1970s and 1980s we had devalued several times. Now there was broad agreement that we s stick to the fixed exchange rate in order to bring inflation down; in this respect, th indeed successful: inflation fell from 8-10 per cent to 2-3 per cent in less than two year of  this,  however,  was  that  real  interest  rates  shot  up.  Structural  reforms  were  also  i particularly in the tax system but also in housing and other areas. One aim of these refo create more market-related incentives for savings and to reduce subsidies. While these cha long overdue, they now came at the worst possible time from a macroeconomic point of view.

In this context, it is relevant to mention the importance of the sequencing of policy changes . In our case, some things, such as financial deregulation, were achieved during t (although  obviously  not  enough)  and  supported  demand  when  this  was  already  strong.  Late when the economy was on its way down, tax changes were implemented that encouraged saving. this should be added the mistake I have already mentioned, of not liberalising outward cap at the same time as the domestic credit market is deregulated.

The crisis culminated in the fall of 1992, when for a few days repo rates wer to  500  per  cent  in  the  vain  hope  of  stemming  currency  outflows.  Interest  rate  hikes contractive  measures  for  defending  the  fixed  exchange  rate  in  the  midst  of  European currency turmoil further exacerbated the economic downturn and added to the banks' loan losses. All i the three years from 1991 to 1993, Sweden's GDP fell by a total of around 6 per cent. Be financial crisis had even been recognised in the summer of 1992, production had probably fallen by 2-3 per cent.

It is my impression that the process in these respects has been quite differen perhaps apart from Thailand. Growth did not drop much before the crisis. More important w direct contagion effects , particularly via financial markets. Other 'triggers' were political , such as uncertainty caused by upcoming elections, and perceived balance of payments problems. In m respects the process - once it had started - was also more rapid in Asia. Perhaps markets all - learnt something from previous crises in Europe and Latin America. They did not see coming but once it started, they reacted more rapidly.

## 4.  Crisis management

I  will  now  turn  to  the  issue  of  how  to  resolve  a  crisis,  once  it  has  erup obviously necessary to tackle macro and micro problems in parallel since the two are interl

As  I  stated  earlier,  I  believe  that  the  origin  of  the  Swedish  crisis  was macroeconomic, due to policy mistakes in the 1980s and early 1990s, and triggered by the shift  to  a  low  inflation  regime.  (Although  there  were  also  structural  weaknesses  in  th sector). The solutions were also primarily macroeconomic in kind. Once the krona peg ha abandoned, demand got a stimulus. The task confronting policy makers was to restore the cr of  economic  policy.  This  required  in  our  case,  given  the  weak  fiscal  position,  very  st measures (some 8 per cent of GDP 1994-98). But it also called for a consistent monetary However, and this is important to underline in the present context, if the financial probl been managed properly, they could easily have been a drag on the macro economy. For exampl taking prompt action it seems that we largely avoided a 'credit crunch', which was a possi worried people a lot at the time. Credit volumes obviously fell, but this could be expla reduction in demand.

Briefly, the important components of the solution for the financial sector were as fo

1. The Government, later confirmed by Parliament, issued an unlimited guarantee stating that no depositors or other counterparties to Swedish credit institutions would suffer a This was a fundamental measure in order to restore confidence in the Swedish banks from  domestic  and  from  foreign  depositors  and  other  counterparties.  The  results  s themselves rather quickly, e.g., in the form of renewed interbank credit lines wit banks.  Also  the  Swedish  public  remained  calm  and  there  were  no  runs  on  the  ba However, the government (Parliament) guarantee and the other measures must also be m known to all interested parties.
2. The mandate to implement the support policies was given to a new agency, the Bank Sup Authority,  which  was  at arm's  length  from  the  political  sphere but  accountable  to  the Government. To avoid conflicts of interest, it was found appropriate not to have the Authority in either the Ministry of Finance, the Central Bank or the Financial Sup Authority.

3. A common framework of measures was constructed for support of the banking system. strategy for deciding which banks to reconstruct and which to liquidate was developed and explained  to  the  general  public.  The  measures  were  designed  to  minimise  costs  f Government and the risk of moral hazard. Consequently, shareholders were not covere the government guarantee and would lose their equity investments to the same degree Government had to provide support for their banks. This provided an incentive to the to  avoid  applying  for  state  support  unless  it  was  absolutely  necessary,  to  mini amount  of  support  and  to  reduce  the  time-period  of  receiving  support.  We  used  a simple, but clear and easy-to-explain, method of identifying banks which should be support  in  order  to  survive  and  those  which  should  be  liquidated  or  merged.  Fir write -down the bank's bad loans. Then you test the bank in a micro- and macroecono model.  If  the  model  indicates  that  the  bank  will  be  adequately  profitable  agai medium-term future it should be given support to survive. But if the model indicates bank will never be profitable again the bank will not be of economic benefit to th and should thus be closed or merged in an orderly manner.
4. Strict valuation rules were used from the onset of the crisis. This was deemed necessary order to restore confidence but the policy was not without risks. All bank assets marked-to-market even if the market, such as that for real estate, was exceptional This  led  to  higher  bank  losses  and  a  weaker  financial  position  than  if  a  somewha flexible  valuation  rule  had  been  adopted.  The  Bank  Support  Authority  hired  exper valuation of various types of assets to ensure that the banks did not over- or und the value of their assets with the aim to motivate requirements for more support. In the rules on when to identify a loan as a non-performing loan and how much to wri were made stricter and with less room for the banks' own judgement.
5. The Swedish government did not take any specific measures to rescue or reconstruct t non-financial companies , neither did it instruct the banks on how to use the support th received.  All  support  was  provided  via  the  banks  and  the  state-owned  asset  manage corporations, leaving them to negotiate the best terms for themselves and their noncustomers. There was a wave of bankruptcies and restructuring of non-financial comp primarily in the domestic sector due to weak domestic demand.
6. The extensive use of Asset Management Corporations (AMCs) in Sweden has become well known abroad. AMCs had, in fact, been established in other countries before the S crisis, so this was nothing new. The special feature in our case is the emphasis on splitting an ailing bank into a good bank and a 'bad part' and transferring the bad assets to the AMC at carefully assessed market values. Once in the AMC, the assets are regrouped and imp in  order  to  become  attractive  to  potential  buyers.  As  soon  as  a  reasonable  pric obtained, the asset was sold. This was sometimes a rather time-consuming process but end the results were probably better than if there had been a quick 'fire-sale' of t is  my  opinion  that  the  use  of  AMCs  is  superior  to  having  the  bad  assets  remain problem banks. The bank staffs are no experts in the field of handling bad assets and obtain the best sales values. Also, the bank management needs to tackle other probl to work hard on future strategic planning for the bank - they do not have time enoug often very large number of complex decisions to be taken on the bad assets.

## 5.  Conclusions

Finally, can we draw any conclusions for Asia in general and Korea in part from the way the financial crisis was handled in Sweden?

First,  I  think  it  is  important,  as  I  said  before,  to  recognise  the  impo macroeconomic  developments.  Once  the  fixed  exchange  rate  had  been  abandoned,  Sweden' economy  experienced  an  export-driven  upturn.  But  it  did  take  a  long  time  for  confidenc Swedish economy in general to return - at least another two years. It is noteworthy that despite the fact that the recovery in growth had started in the summer of 1993. The expla primarily  in  the  fiscal  situation,  to  which  the  financial  sector  and  related  problems substantial contribution - enlarging the budget deficit by perhaps as much as 6% of GDP at On top of this, the krona was depressed for a long time by the repayment of foreign loans.

The financial problems did not have a major impact on economic developments fr 1993 onwards. Once the important decisions concerning the financial sector had been taken not long before the financial aspect of the crisis had disappeared from the headlines. An were already recovering in late 1993 - just a year after the peak of the crisis. This obviously  a  great  achievement  and  it  may  be  worth  briefly  stating  some  of  the  more  im lessons that, in my opinion, can be drawn from this episode of financial crisis management:

1. Confidence needs to be restored rapidly . This was achieved in Sweden as far as the financia sector was concerned. If confidence returns fairly soon, the real effects on the eco not be large. But if, on the other hand, the lack of domestic and/or external confi to persist, this could act as a drag on economic development for a long period. It experience from other countries that the longer the period with a lack of confid more drastic the measures that will be needed to restore credibility. Among other restoring confidence involves being transparent about the problems and about the me for  dealing  with  them.  It  also  means  that  measures  are  implemented  as  stated responsible authorities, without any deviations in timing or application. Just the that  specific  industries  or  other  interest  groups  may  be  receiving  unjustifiably treatment would quickly erode any confidence.
2. Transparency is important . A severe crisis wipes confidence out - rightly so. We realise it was up to Sweden to regain it. To do so, all the cards had to be on the table. T the  losses  and  the  magnitude  of  the  bad  loans  had  to  be  revealed  in  their  enti valuation had to be prudent. If you hide losses initially or are overly optimistic i you risk having to apply again to the international investment community or to taxpa additional support. This, in my view, might jeopardise confidence and legitimacy. I necessary to have highly transparent and fair 'rules of the game' for government su the financial sector, not least to avoid political bickering. The responsibility for falls  primarily  on  two  parties:  the  authorities  and  the  banks.  The  authorities transparent about the broad framework for the solution of the crisis and the banks transparent about their losses and other deficiencies, financial position and need f support.
3. Someone must take the losses . It is important to realise that once the crisis has occurr losses  cannot  be  hidden  and  must  be  dealt  with  in  one  way  or  another.  In  this Swedish  institutions  worked  well.  Party  politics  were  clearly  separated  from  b realities. And the politicians did a good job, realising that bygones were bygones, s fair framework to sort the crisis out. From a political perspective it was importa banks'  owners  were  not  rescued.  People  at  large  had  to  take  substantial  cuts  i standards - at least temporarily. Letting the 'big guys' go unhurt under these circ would have jeopardised the whole operation.
4. The  macroeconomic  policy  mix  for  crisis  management  can  differ .  In  our  case,  there  was obviously not much room for fiscal stimulation of the economy. Considering the much

public  debt,  there  could  be  more  room  in  some  Asian  countries  but  the  potential effects  of  the  financial  losses  also  need  to  be  taken  into  account.  Monetary  pol difficult dual role: it has to strike a balance between stimulating the economy so the burden on the banks and on their borrowers and at the same time ensuring the inflows that are needed to rebuild the depleted foreign currency reserves.

5. On top of this - and perhaps the most important factor - there was political consensus . The government sought and received backing from the main opposition party. That party also allowed to appoint Board members of the Bank Support Authority so that it cou continuously  informed  and  influence  decisions.  That  was  important  both  for  pol legitimacy at home and for credibility abroad - investors could be sure that the s had created would be upheld even if there were a change in government.

Let me end on a positive note. Economically, the crisis in Korea and in many other Asian countries should be manageable although it will probably take time before the r clearly visible. Korea is in far better shape than many other countries, including my own 1990s, given the high rates of potential growth and that the fiscal balances are in reaso However, what actually happens will depend on how the crisis is managed.

That is now precisely the question.
