8 Among others, see Committee on Payment and Settlement Systems (1990a), (1990b), (1993) and (1995).

The Committee's most recent work focusing on banks is a report on real-time gross settlement (RTGS) systems." These systems, which are now in place in most G-10 countries along with many others, protect against gridlock by ensuring final settlement of all transactions, transaction by transaction in real time. The report not only provides an overview of key concepts and principal design features but also describes the risks associated with such systems and some broader policy implications. It addresses the particular differences between systems already in place, the management of liquidity in such systems, and the various procedures used to queue payment instructions. The report is the first of its kind and is likely to prove particularly useful to both emerging and industrial countries still in the process of modernising their settlement systems.

In recent years, the Committee has extended its interest beyond banks to settlement systems for securities and foreign exchange, and clearing arrangements for exchange-traded derivatives. In all cases, the nominal values of the daily transactions are very large. Various reports on arrangements to support securities transactions have been published since 1992, with the latest effort focusing on a disclosure framework for system operators that will allow participants in such arrangements to better evaluate the risks they are running." As for exposure to settlement risk in foreign exchange markets, the Committee has established that settlement exposures are much larger than had previously been thought. In a report published last year,*° they also indicated ways in which participants could reduce such risks and strongly suggested they do so to avoid a punitive response from public sector authorities. Regarding clearing arrangements for exchange-traded derivative instruments, the Committee published a report in March 1997*' which systematically reviewed such arrangements, identified weaknesses and made recommendations for remedying them. As with many other Committee reports, it contains a great deal of factual and comparative information not available elsewhere.

Finally, the Committee recognises that issues having to do with the use of collateral to manage risk, and with the operational reliability of the infrastructure (e.g. business continuity planning, especially with regard to IT services), are also germane to a well-functioning payment system. So too are many legal issues, such as the enforceability of netting agreements and the complications likely to arise from the absence of an international agreement on bankruptcy procedures for internationally active financial institutions. The bottom line is that the task of ensuring timely settlement in all circumstances remains incomplete and the Committee's agenda is still full.

## d. Global participation in the work of the committees

Finally, the increasing efforts made by the various committees to involve non-G-10 countries in their work deserves to be emphasised. The Core Principles were drawn up with the close cooperation of non-G-10 supervisors, and the "Report on cross-border banking" was prepared jointly

44 See Committee on Payment and Settlement Systems 1997a).

See Committee on Payment and Settlement Systems 1997c). 45

See Committee on Payment and Settlement Systems 1996b). 46

See Committee on Payment and Settlement Systems 1997b). 47

with the Offshore Group of Banking Supervisors. Regional supervisory groups meet regularly with representatives of the Basle Committee in attendance, and there has been a significant increase in supervisory training by G-10 supervisors in association with the Secretariat of the Basle Committee. Finally, the Committee has recently initiated joint meetings with regional supervisors on the occasion of its quarterly meetings in Basle. All of these efforts are directed to building a truly global network of supervisors and the wide dissemination of documents, standards and guidelines developed by the Committee in association with others. Similar initiatives have recently been undertaken by the Committee on Payment and Settlement Systems with similar objectives in mind. The Euro-currency Standing Committee had, for many years, "extended" meetings involving representatives of important non-G-10 financial centres. However, it is now actively engaged in discussing how broader participation might be made more effective.

## D. The role of the BIS in crisis management

It has been analytically convenient above to deal separately with the three major components of the international financial system and the BIS committees which support each. This approach also emphasises the comprehensive reach of the Committees' concerns. However, a deficiency of this approach is that it fails to emphasise the relationships between the various components of the system, as well as the further links to macroeconomic variables of interest to central bankers. In fact, it is the complex reality of these interrelationships that makes the pursuit of financial stability such a challenging task and also accounts for the fact that there have been so many financial crises along the way.

Before turning to the role of the BIS in crisis management, it is important to note that, even at the domestic level, a certain "constructive ambiguity" often applies about the potential role of the public sector. This is to avoid bad behaviour and moral hazard on the part of the private sector. Given that no two crises are the same, the amount of pre-planning that can be done is in any event limited. Perhaps the most that can be hoped is that the prospective players in the unfolding drama -the central bank, the Treasury, supervisory bodies and deposit insurance agencies -know each other well and have well-established lines of communications, so that decisions affecting all can be speedily agreed upon. At a moment of crisis, the time allowed for decision-making is not likely to be great. Moreover, as we have seen in South Asia, the failure of domestic policy-makers to take credible policy actions quickly (particularly if these policies have been prescribed in the context of an IMF programme) can result in the market imposing heavy penalties.

The provision of international support to help resolve financial crises with international ramifications should be equally ambiguous if moral hazard is to be avoided."* In any event, liquidity

48 A new but unwelcome form of ambiguity has emerged in the context of the Asian crisis. The short-term liquidity requirements of a number of countries have been so great as to call into question whether the Fund had adequate resources to restore confidence on the part of private creditors. For example, as of July 1996 the

support from the International Monetary Fund to sovereign borrowers must continue to be firmly linked to conditionality and the adjustment of domestic policies. Moreover, support should be provided in such a way as to insure that all the parties whose behaviour contributed to the crisis (both debtors and imprudent creditors) pay some part of the costs. As for liquidity support to internationally active banks, the G-10 Governors have agreed that such support should be provided in the first instance by the homecountry authorities. However, this decision still leaves unclear whether the home authorities will be prepared to do so. The willingness of the Bank of England to allow Baring Brothers to fail is a welcome indicator of this ambiguity. What is also unclear is the extent to which other national authorities might act to support the home authorities in different circumstances. The 1996 agreement between the Federal Reserve and the Bank of Japan, under which the Bank of Japan could obtain dollar funds through repo arrangements, gives some indication of the possibilities in this regard.

Given the scope, increasingly wide participation and regularity of the meetings which take place in Basle, the BIS makes an important contribution to international financial stability by ensuring that policy-makers (at least central banks and other regulators) know each other well and have open lines of communication. This is the institution's most important contribution to crisis management, although not its only one. The international community (in particular the central banks of the G-10 countries) have often found it appropriate to provide bridge loans through the BIS to countries in financial difficulties which are awaiting the receipt of funds from the IMF, the World Bank or other such bodies. Such bridge loans often provide needed liquidity, are an indication of international support for the policy changes normally associated with Fund programmes, and ensure a continuing central bank involvement in the process of crisis management. While this role might be thought less important in the future, given that the Fund can now disburse much more rapidly than before thanks to the new Emergency Financing Mechanism, some possibilities still remain open. For example, in view of its expertise with arranging bridge loans, the BIS might be asked to help draw up multilateral legal agreements to ensure equal and fair treatment of sovereign creditors should loans go bad. Attempts to use bilateral agreements to secure a "second line of defence" in support of the IMF programme for Korea in recent months have become extremely complicated and are not yet complete.

For completeness, it should be noted that the BIS, in addition to providing support for bridge loan facilities, is also prepared to act as a principal and to lend funds on both a collateralised and an uncollateralised basis. Needless to say, the sums available in this fashion must be strictly limited by concerns about prudent behaviour and the continuing good financial health of the BIS itself. Nevertheless, there have been occasions when even the relatively small loans made by the BIS may have been useful in stopping small problems from potentially turning into much bigger ones.

## E. Conclusions

short-term debt (less than one year to maturity) owed by Korean debtors to international banks amounted to almost $70 billion. See Bank for International Settlements (1998c). Private bankers did finally agree to establish a process for rolling over this debt. However, to the extent that this was not purely voluntary, the difference between this procedure and a debt rescheduling is moot.

As the process of liberalisation and globalisation proceeds, markets increasingly replace the dictates of governments and regulators. This is perhaps even more true with respect to financial markets than in other areas of economic activity. As a corollary, the influence of those government bodies which work closely with markets tends to be enhanced. In part, this may explain the perception that both the domestic and the international profile of central bankers has risen in recent decades. Without delving too far into bureaucratic theories of institutional behaviour, the desire to expand their influence may be a further reason explaining why both central bankers and other regulators are increasingly relying on market processes to achieve their objectives. The role and reputation of the BIS has been similarly enhanced in that international cooperation among central banks and other regulators in large part takes place in that forum."

Another change affecting the work of the BIS in recent years has been the growing emphasis being put by governments on issues having to do with financial stability as opposed to price stability and traditional macroeconomic preoccupations. It is of some note that the last four G-7 Summit Communiqués (Halifax, Lyon, Denver and Birmingham) put strong emphasis on such issues while hardly mentioning international macroeconomic policy coordination. It is also notable that, at the semi-annual meetings of the G-10 Governors and Ministers, the General Manager of the BIS has in recent years reported regularly on work being undertaken at the BIS in this area. This is not to say that traditional macroeconomic concerns have somehow become less important. Rather, these recent developments indicate that the BIS, and those who regularly meet there, now seem to have a wider scope for contributing to global economic welfare than perhaps ever before.

The Governing Council first assessed current economic developments in the e area. The general picture is one of continued economic expansion combined with broadl inflation.

As  far  a developments  are  concerned,  inflation  as  measured  by  the  harmonised  consumer  price (HICP) is estimated to have risen slightly in April, to 1.4%, but has not increased fur

Economic  growth  has  been  driven  increasingly  by  dome demand  rather  than  net  exports,  as  might  be  expected  at  this  stage  of  the  cycle consumption and stockbuilding have been the main factors underlying domestic demand to d

In  this  respect,  I  should  like  to  underline  three  aspects.  First,  any dividend' resulting from the current cyclical upturn should be used to bring deficit levels down, rather than relaxing control over expenditure. Second, most Member States go a step further, and indeed improve structural balances as they are not yet in compl the obligations under the Stability and Growth Pact. euro countries. There is currently no sign of exchange rate tensions among euro area c Forward exchange rates are expected to be virtually identical to central rates, suggest pre-announced rates are considered credible. I consider this a remarkable achievement.

Following its review of economic developments, the Governing Council settle number of organisational issues.

- i. It adopted the Rules of Procedure of the European Central Bank. Th will be published in the Official Journal of the European Communities
- ii. It approved, in accordance with the Rules of Procedure, the establis of eleven ESCB committees to assist in the work of the European Syst of  Central  Banks  (ESCB).  The  committees  are  as  follows  (listed alphabetical order): Accounting and Monetary Income Committee, Banking Supervision Committee, Banknote Committee, External Communications Committee, Information Technology Committee, Internal  Auditors  Committee,  Legal  Committee,  Market  Operations Committee, Monetary Policy Committee, Payment and Settlement Systems Committee, and Statistics Committee;
- iii. It formally adopted a budget for the European Central Bank for the se half of 1998 and agreed on the establishment of a Budget Committee assist the Governing Council in ECB budget-related matters;

## (a) Monetary policy issues

The Governing Council decided on the introduction of a minimum reserve syst by the ESCB at the start of Stage Three. Among the three main functions that a minimum system could usefully perform, the Governing Council attaches particularly high import its contributions to the stabilisation of money market interest rates and to the enlar demand for central bank money by creating or enlarging a structural liquidity shorta market.

In the light of the potential burden which a minimum reserve system could i on the private sector and the effects it might have on the financial activity of credit the euro area, the Governing Council has decided on features which fulfil the two money management purposes outlined above, while at the same time allowing an adequate remuner of minimum reserves.

A number of details of the minimum reserve system that will be applied already  specified  in  previous  documents  published  by  the  European  Monetary  Inst Additional features agreed upon yesterday include the liability base, the lump-sum allow the rate of remuneration. Further details are provided in the separate press release that is being iss this morning.

It  is  intended  that  the  precise  features  of  the  minimum  reserve  system published in the form of an EU Council Regulation. For this purpose, the Governing C adopted an ECB Recommendation for an EU Council Regulation on the application of minimu reserves by the European Central Bank. In accordance with the provisions of the Statu ESCB,  the  EU  Council,  acting  by  a  qualified  majority  and  after  consulting  the  Eu Parliament and the Commission, is expected to adopt this Regulation.

The  Governing  Council  also  adopted  ECB  Recommendations  for  EU  Council Regulations concerning the collection of statistical information by the ECB and concer powers of the ECB to impose sanctions. All three ECB Recommendations will be publishe the Official Journal of the European Communities for general notice.

## (b) Foreign exchange issues

The  Governing  Council  decided  on  the  size  and  form  of  the  initial  trans foreign reserve assets to the European Central Bank from the national central banks par in the euro area. Before the end of the current year the Governing Council will also have to an ECB Guideline pursuant to Article 31.3 of the Statute of the ESCB, which will sub operations in foreign reserve assets remaining with the national central banks - inclu to approval by the ECB.

In  connection  with  the  setting-up  of  common  market  standards,  the  Govern Council also reached agreement on a number of issues related to the quotation and publi reference  exchange  rates  for  the  euro.  Specifically,  it  was  agreed  to  recommend  to participants the 'certain' method for quoting the exchange rates for the (i.e. 1 euro = X foreign currency units) and to have daily reference exchange rates f computed and published by the ECB.

## (c) Payment systems issues

The  Governing  Council  decided  on  the  conditions  for  the  participation  o non-euro  area  EU  central  banks  and  credit  institutions  in  the  TARGET  (Trans-Euro Automated Real-time Gross settlement Express Transfer) system. In TARGET the ESCB wil provide  central  bank  liquidity  in  the  course  of  the  day  (i.e.  intraday  liquidity) necessary  to  avoid  delays  in  the  execution  of  payment  orders.  If  intraday  liquidi reimbursed at the end of the day it becomes overnight credit granted by the ESCB, wh evident  monetary  policy  reasons,  cannot  be  offered  to  institutions  outside  the  e Nonetheless,  non-euro  area  EU  central  banks  and  institutions  in  those  countries connected to TARGET.

The Governing Council considered that giving such institutions outside the area unlimited access to intraday credit would have created risks for the conduct of policy that it was not ready to take. ## (d) Legal protection of euro banknotes

Finally, the Governing Council agreed on a number of legal instruments aime enhancing the protection of euro banknotes. title: Mr. Ferguson gives his views on exercising caution and vigilance in monetary policy in the United States  (Central Bank Articles and Speeches, 9 Jul 98)
description: Remarks by Mr. Roger W. Ferguson, Jr., a member of the Board of Governors of the US Federal Reserve System, on the occasion of the Distinguished Speaker Series, held at the Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta on 9/7/98.
text:
Mr. Ferguson gives his views on exercising caution and vigilance in monetar policy in the United States Remarks by Mr. Roger W. Ferguson, Jr., a member of the Board of Governors of the US Federal Reserve System, on the occasion of the Distinguished Speaker Series, held at the Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta on 9/7/98.

## Introduction

These  are  fascinating  times  for  monetary  policy.  As  we  progress  through eighth year of the current economic expansion, economic growth has continued at a robu with unemployment reaching a 28-year low, while inflation has remained remarkably sub To be sure, not all recent developments have been altogether positive, especially consi current situation in Asia. Nonetheless, the performance of the American economy in rece has exceeded expectations in a rather extraordinary fashion.

But recent developments have challenged our understanding of the workings the macroeconomy. Although the recent surprises of both low unemployment and well-beha inflation  have  been  quite  favorable,  they  have  been  surprises  nonetheless  and  no reconcilable  with  each  other  based  on  old  relationships  and  our  earlier  assessmen economy's potential.

These developments have increased the uncertainty about the economic outl and about the appropriate response of monetary policy in general to new developments. I take this opportunity to discuss some implications of this increased uncertainty for th monetary policy.

Before  starting,  let  me  remind  you  that  these  views  are  personal  and  d necessarily reflect the views of other members of the FOMC or the Board of Governors.

## Objectives and Strategy for Monetary Policy

To evaluate the proper strategy for monetary policy, we must first underst Federal  Reserve's  policy  objectives  and  then  recognize  the  parameters  within  which operates in attaining these objectives.

The long-run goal of monetary policy is straightforward. The Federal Reserv mandates  that  we  promote  price  stability  and  maximum  employment.  Sometimes  this  du objective is misunderstood, with the misconception that these inflation and employmen cannot be attained simultaneously -- that there is a tradeoff in the long run between other. It is worthwhile repeating what I am sure all of you already understand well: t goals of price stability and maximum employment are not mutually exclusive. Not so lon mainstream  macroeconomists  thought  that  employment  and  growth  were  by  and  larg independent of inflation in the long run. But the evidence accumulating in the 1990s suggest that low inflation contributes to real economic performance in ways not fully a before. If anything, our approach to price stability, by reducing uncertainty and makin savings and investment decisions easier, seems to have enhanced the growth of productiv GDP, and employment.

This indirect benefit, of course, reinforces the price stability goal. It inflation that monetary policy determines in the long run, and this means that price s straightforward way is elevated to the status of the primary long-run goal of monetary p

Where a tradeoff can appear, and this I think is the source of occasional co is over shorter periods. In the shorter run, inflation may rise and fall depending o economy is operating relative to its potential. When the economy has become overextende output  exceeding  the  economy's  potential,  employment  beyond  sustainable  norms, production  surpassing  normal  capacity  limits,  then  prices  have  tended  to  increase  a faster  rate.  Likewise,  when  aggregate  demand  has  fallen  short  of  the  economy's  po inflation has tended to fall.

And this is where the short-run setting of monetary policy comes into pl moving short-term interest rates, monetary policy can affect other financial condition up  exerting  a  substantial  influence  on  aggregate  demand.  Decisions  by  businesses investment and by households about housing and consumption are altered by changes in i rates  and  other  credit  conditions.  Monetary  policy  also  can  indirectly  impinge  up components of aggregate demand. As a result, in the shorter run, monetary policy can important role in stabilizing the economy from undesired fluctuations in economic act inflation.  The  strategy  for  monetary  policy  geared  towards  these  shorter-run  concern briefly described. It is to restrict monetary conditions when the economy seems on th becoming overheated and inflation is threatening and ease monetary conditions when si weakness in demand appear on the horizon. But it is important that we pursue these s goals keeping in mind our primary long-run goal of price stability.

Of course, other forces besides the state of the economy relative to its can influence inflation in the short run. Even prior to the anomalous experience of re which I will discuss later in detail, supply shocks, such as a sudden hike in oil dramatically affected inflation. Such forces can also cause short-term fluctuations in t that are, at least in part, beyond the control of monetary policy. However, active s policy may still have a role to play as a buffer, helping the economy to absorb such d in the short run, while counteracting any persistent deviations from price stability.

But  monetary  policy  operates  with  a  long  lag,  with  a  policy  change  exhib material effects on  the  economy  (excluding  the  immediate  impact  on  financial  markets several quarters after its implementation. By some estimates it may be almost a year brunt of the effect of an interest rate change is felt on aggregate demand, although t appears sooner in some sectors of the economy than in others. And it may generally tak still for a policy change to alter the course of inflation.

Consequently, active stabilization policy is most successful when pre-emptive, responding to early warning signals or forecasts of unfavorable developm the  inflation  and  employment  fronts.  In  this  regard,  by  identifying  past  regul relationships among economic variables and understanding their conceptual underpinning can use the most recent economic data to update forecasts of where the economy is Based  on  these  forecasts  we  can  then  take  steps  to  adjust  the  stance  of  monetary necessary, in accordance with our objectives.

## Uncertainties: Old and new

To be useful for monetary policy, forecasts of the future health of the e need to be reasonably reliable. Good forecasts rest on theories about empirical regul can be confidently relied upon to provide guidance.

Regrettably, accepted theories are found lacking at times, empirical models down, and forecasts based on them prove unusually inaccurate. If monetary policy were to follow guidelines based on past regularities that are increasingly failing to reflect it  would  unintentionally  introduce  undesirable  gyrations  in  the  economy.  Thus,  hei uncertainties regarding the workings of the economy pose an additional source of stress design.

To ascertain the appropriate framework for policy analysis we must first be of some key sources of uncertainty. In recent years, traditional views of the econom have been most challenged by the phenomenon of declining inflation despite increasing t in  labor  markets  as  evidenced  by  reductions  in  the  unemployment  rate  to  its  lowest almost  three  decades.  Many  believe  that  there  is  an  unemployment  rate,  the  non-acce inflation rate of unemployment (the 'NAIRU'), that would be consistent with a stable i rate,  once  other  short-run  influences  on  inflation  dissipate.  To  these  economists, pressures tend to increase when unemployment remains below the NAIRU and tend to decre when  unemployment  stays  above  the  NAIRU.  For  many  years  proponents  of  this  view considered  6  percent  a  reasonable  estimate  of  the  NAIRU.  Since  1995,  however, unemployment rate has been below this level, and substantially below of late, while inf continued to progress toward our price-stability objective. In response, over the past many observers have revised their estimates of the NAIRU down by half a percentage po more. Yet considerable uncertainty remains about the confidence with which the new est can be relied upon for evaluating inflationary pressures.

The NAIRU never was measured with precision; statistical inference has alw provided a distribution of likely values around a point estimate. And several factors, the demographic composition of the labor force, have long been known to introduce syst variation in its value over time. Nonetheless, the uncertainties about how structural be changing the NAIRU seem unusually large at present and cannot be ignored. And for the present uncertainties have called into further question the basic usefulness of th at least of a point estimate held with any confidence.

A related uncertainty concerns the underlying trend growth of labor produc Until fairly recently, this trend had seemed to have been about constant since the mid there are many that believe that a pickup may have occurred in the last few years, an productivity trend would help to explain the unexpectedly favorable econ growth-unemployment-inflation nexus in recent years. Unfortunately, much as with the NA our understanding of the forces that drive the productivity trend is less than perfect. investment boom of the current expansion has raised the amount of capital for each wor contributed  to  an  increase  in  labor  productivity,  and  it  may  be  that  advancing  tech making the capital stock and workforce more productive. However, some of the recent pic productivity is the normal response to the faster output growth of late, so the degr there is a new higher trend remains an open question.

Another difficulty in assessing the current amount of slack in the economy, third  uncertainty,  concerns  the  divergent  patterns  in  alternative  measures  of  exces Capacity  utilization  in  manufacturing  and  the  rate  of  unemployment  have  historically together over the cycle. Unexpectedly, they have diverged in the current expansion, in surge in investment has kept capacity utilization in the manufacturing sector near i average while labor markets have become tighter and tighter.

Recent  developments  in  South-East  Asia  also  have  contributed  to  uncerta about the current monetary policy environment. One place where the effect of the crisi felt  is  in  the  prices  of  primary  commodities.  Since  such  commodities  are  traded  o markets, lower demand from Asia is reflected in lower prices world-wide, which bene producers  that  use  commodities  as  inputs.  This  development  serves  as  a  short-run  b positive supply shock, to the US economy, one that also helps contain inflationary pre does the more general decline in import prices as the US dollar appreciates.

But the Asian crisis can be expected to continue to have an adverse impa trade-sensitive industries. Some evidence of a deterioration of our trade balance with economies  has  already  appeared.  With  little  historical  guidance  to  draw  from,  h considerable uncertainty prevails regarding the extent to which the present Asian situ contribute to slower US growth as well as the timing of such a slowdown. For instance, expectations that the crisis would have contributed to a slowdown in economic activit this year, the economy's growth in the first quarter of this year exceeded even the performance of 1997. However, more recent data reflecting developments in the second q including  survey  information,  do  give  some  evidence  of  a  slowing  in  the  overall  ec especially  the  manufacturing  sector,  perhaps  due  to  Asian  financial  turmoil.  As  yo suspect, we will continue to watch incoming data quite closely as the year progresses better handle on this situation.

To be sure, uncertainties such as these have loomed large at times in the p we can learn much from those experiences. The uncertainties faced by policymakers duri 1970s  about  the  economy's  potential  provide  an  enlightening  perspective  on  the  p situation.

Following a period of rapid productivity gains during the 1950s and 1960s economy's performance during the 1970s appeared out of line with previous experience. S in  1973,  in  particular,  inflation  rose  more  than  expected,  at  times  considerably' economic growth tended to disappoint expectations for a number of years. At first, it reasonable to assume that the observed productivity'slowdown was temporary. Reflectin assumption,  for  instance,  the  Council  of  Economic  Advisors  gave  a  4  percent  estim potential  output  growth  in  the  1974  Economic  Report  of  the  President,  as  would  hav consistent with the earlier trends.

Increased uncertainty regarding this estimate was evident in the 1975 and Reports, but not until 1977 was the point estimate of potential output growth revised to  3.6  percent.  As  the  economy's  performance  continued  to  disappoint,  further  dow revisions followed, to 3 percent in 1979 and to 2.5 percent to close the decade in 1 several years after the fact was a trend break in productivity recognized as likely to h in 1973. And even today our understanding of the forces contributing to the slowdown entirely satisfactory.

As  inflation  accelerated  as  the  1970s  continued,  critics  blamed  the  F Reserve's operating procedures for placing too little weight on money growth and too m interest rates in the conduct of policy. In response, the Federal Reserve in late 197 emphasis on monetary growth targets. But the FOMC abandoned the strict regime of targ M1  through  reserve  quantities  in  1982  once  evidence  accumulated  that  the  character demand had been altered by the spread of interest-bearing NOW accounts. Later, the brea behavior of M2 velocity during the early 1990s from its earlier historical pattern u indicator properties of that aggregate as well. In 1993, the FOMC de-emphasized the ro broader aggregates in policymaking. Despite recent tentative signs that the relationsh M2 velocity and the cost of holding M2 assets may be returning to its earlier histori uncertainty persists regarding the continued stability of this relationship.

In terms of the performance of inflation and unemployment, the experience o past few years has not been unlike a mirror image of the 1970s. While the consequences more pleasant, unexpectedly low inflation and unemployment do raise some complicated i for monetary policy.

## Strategy in Uncertain Times: Caution and Vigilance

This account of the sources of uncertainty that we face in designing the course of monetary policy should not leave the impression that our task is so dauntin policy waters are unnavigable. But such an account does serve a valuable purpose in re us that in designing policy we should recognize our ignorance as well as trust our knowl

For instance, we need to recognize the difficulties of inferring the true s the economy by interpreting incoming data. How do we know whether unexpected developmen are  just  temporary  moves  away  from  stable  longer-run  relationships  or  are  manifesta changes in the underlying economic structure? In many cases this judgment is difficult with much confidence until considerably after the fact. In the meantime, we must bear that  the  statistical  relationships  we  work  with  are  only  loose  approximations  of  u reality,  which  is  constantly  evolving,  at  least  to  some  extent,  in  response  to technology, consumer preferences, and government policies. Our vision is always obstru some haze. But sometimes the picture is clearer than at other times.

Because  of  these  difficulties  in  assessing  the  situation,  a  balanced  jud required in evaluating whether historical regularities are indeed changing significan not just subject to temporary aberrations. I believe that one should guard against hol truths  that  may  no  longer  be  valid,  but  one  should  also  be  cautious  about  decla permanent changes have occurred, for there are too many examples of proclaimed 'new that did not in fact come to pass. Erroneously dismissing the continued validity of could  result  in  bad  policy  just  as  easily  as  failing  to  correctly  recognize  new  re change occurs.

What  should  be  done  when  uncertainties  seem  particularly  acute?  When  w suspect that our understanding of the macroeconomic environment has deteriorated appre as evidenced by strings of surprises difficult to reconcile with our earlier beliefs, appropriate response is to rely less upon the future predicted by the increasingly un gauges  and  more  upon  inferences  from  the  more  recent  past,  weighing  incoming  data heavily relative to more distant data in trying to discern the new environment.

Even for those of us who take this more pragmatic approach, there are chall Recent data, on which our understanding of the new reality is based, are subject to r more  reliable  or  more  complete  sources  become  available.  Moreover,  there  are  often indices  for  measuring  underlying  economic  circumstances,  requiring  one  to  consider measures simultaneously.

In  the  current  context,  the  considerable  uncertainty  regarding  our  pr estimates  of  the  capacity  of  the  economy  and  its  sustainable  rate  of  growth  in  my suggest  the  need  to  downplay  forecasts  of  inflation  based  on  those  earlier  assessm necessity,  I  believe  heightened  reliance  needs  to  be  placed  on  more  recent  observa inflation and costs for inferring future inflationary pressures. We are not precluded pre-emptively if new information were to tip the balance of risks in the outlook towa inflation, but are naturally a little more cautious in acting on forecasts as long uncertainty persists.

As a consequence, the lead times for pre-emptive action are likely to be And, in my judgment, we may have to rely more on measures other than apparent excess de to get reliable indications of pending changes in inflationary pressures. For instance costs may have to be watched especially closely, and the rate of unemployment perha closely  than  we  are  used  to.  But  a  pattern  of  unsustainable  growth  characterize continuously declining unemployment rate still may increasingly suggest greater infla Even if the limits of the economy's growth potential have moved, there are still limit to be respected.

The  increased  uncertainty  also  implies  that  continued  strong  economic  gr with  low  inflation  is  not  outside  the  realm  of  possibility,  and  by  adopting  a  caut posture we may learn more clearly if that possibility is likely or remote. It should be creation of new jobs, by itself, is a welcomed development. There are benefits to al skill building that occurs on the job. It is important, however, that these jobs be sustainable growth, and not the result of excesses and imbalances.

However,  caution  can  be  excessive,  running  the  risk  that  inflation  may  i reappear and require a more wrenching readjustment than if it had been anticipated. Un should not induce paralysis. We need to be willing to move, even if cautiously, knowing may  have  to  reverse  our  action  if  subsequent  developments  differ  from  our  expect Moreover, we must be willing to act forcefully if information suggesting a threat to o price  stability  becomes  available.  Inflation  is  an  insidious  tax  on  all  of  our  citi impacting  low  and  moderate-income  citizens  more  than  others  because  there  are  fewer available to them to protect their income and their assets against an erosion of purcha If  evidence  of  an  incipient  rise  in  inflation  were  to  appear,  decisive  action  would counterweight  to  minimize  the  building  of  a  temporary  inflationary  aberration  into expectations, which could be disruptive. And this is why caution and vigilance go hand under these circumstances of increased uncertainty.

Moreover, it is at uncertain times such as these that the wisdom underlyi institutional  structure  of  the  FOMC  becomes  most  apparent.  A  committee  with  br representation  can  bring  a  variety  of  perspectives  and  analyses  to  bear  on  difficul problems. In addition, the real-time reports the presidents of the Federal Reserve B from their districts are especially valuable in the decision-making process at times because they afford a contemporaneous sense of what is going on in the economy. Such di

of information sources becomes particularly useful when our earlier assessment of the e potential has been drawn into question by surprises, even pleasant ones.

## Conclusion

A string of favorable surprises yielding strong growth, high employment an inflation is by far the most pleasant environment under which to come to the realizati understanding of the workings of our complex economy is not infallible. A sound economy subdued inflation makes dealing with the greater uncertainty much easier indeed!

The Federal Reserve has an important trust to help safeguard the health United States economy. What we should do in the face of some uncertainty is to act ca while remaining vigilant, to take measured steps when necessary, and to adjust to the unforeseen change. In this way we will raise the odds of achieving our goals of stable maximum employment, not only providing benefits to Americans, but also a stable anchor volatile world economy.

title: Mr. Tietmeyer discusses the role of the IMF in the global economy  (Central Bank Articles and Speeches, 2 Jul 98)
description: Opening address by the President of the Deutsche Bundesbank, Prof. Hans Tietmeyer, at the symposium 'The Role of the IMF in the Global Economy' held in Frankfurt am Main on 2/7/98.
text:
Mr. Tietmeyer discusses the role of the IMF in the global economy Opening address by the President of the Deutsche Bundesbank, Prof. Hans Tietmeyer, at the symposium 'The Role IMF in the Global Economy' held in Frankfurt am Main on 2/7/98.

A mass of analyses, commentaries and proposals have already appeared concerning crisis in some emerging markets and the problems in certain countries in transition. Many have enlighten us, but some have merely created more confusion. I hope that today's symposium will in the enlightening category.

The title of the symposium sums up the main issue: we are living more and more global economy. This has been caused by two driving forces; firstly, political factors: the goods  and  services  markets  worldwide,  which  has  been  gradually  proceeding  for  decades ever-growing liberalisation of capital transactions, and the internal orientation of countrie to market-based structures. Secondly, technical developments are having an ever-increasing im almost perfect information technologies now available, and the highly efficient transportation

These  two  aspects  are  interlinked  and  mutually  reinforcing.  The  political  o strengthens the economic incentives to seek newer and better technical solutions. Conversely, progress creates powerful pressures to liberalise markets as it makes the maintenance of bar and more inefficient and expensive.

The  benefits  and  challenges  of  globalisation  are  inextricably  linked.  Abov globalisation  brings  major  benefits  for  everyone.  The  most  important  benefits  are:  greater through  stronger  competition,  a  better  allocation  of  resources  and,  consequently,  fall Ultimately, the rising standard of living worldwide owes much to the gains produced by globalis

But  it  has  other  noticeable  effects,  too.  Globalisation  demands  considerable flexibility from economies, and, at the same time, credibility from the national political dec And the integration of previously national markets increases interdependency. As a result, na regional crises can no longer be considered in isolation. Contagion is a constant danger in t today and tomorrow.

That  is  why,  in  addition  to  each  country's  primary  duty  to  prepare  for  and  p financial crises in its own territory, joint efforts at the global level are also meaningful And this is without question the task of the IMF.

Some people believe that the recent financial crises would not have happened if th been no globalisation and that, consequently, the gradual opening of markets is the main ca problems. But that view is too short-sighted. The main causes are the misguided or at least ri pursued by the countries in question. Essentially that also applies to the countries affect Their own internal weaknesses make them vulnerable.

It  is  also  true  that  the  global  financial  markets,  with  their  tendency short-termism, are sometimes a factor in making the magnitude of the potential reversal so g country then loses the confidence of investors because of a political error, it is punished har too hard, at least for a time.

The outbreak of the crisis in some Asian countries poses some new questions bec some of the key fundamentals were quite sound: In many cases the public fiscal balance was in s at least was not in excessive deficit. Unemployment was fairly limited. The monetary policy s mostly  quite  restrained,  and  inflation  remained  moderate  for  a  long  time.  For  quite  a  whi account deficits were financed by capital imports apparently unproblematically.

Some indicators even showed an exceptionally positive trend. In particular, the and  investment  ratios  were  comparatively  high,  and  real  growth  in  this  region  was  strong elsewhere.  Until  a  short  time  ago,  the  title  of  such  a  symposium  might  well  have  been  'Th economic miracle'.

On closer inspection, however, it can be seen that the economic successes of recen already carried the seeds of the later crisis: massive short-term capital inflows,  asset  in equity and property markets, in some cases a misallocation of capital, currency appreciation in decreasing  competitiveness  and  growing  current  account  deficits.  These  symptoms  also  poin internal weaknesses and political mistakes: for example, an over-rigid pegging of the exchange dollar and inadequate efficiency of the domestic financial sector.

Certainly,  there  are  good  reasons  for  pegging  an  exchange  rate  to  another  cur Credible pegging to a stable anchor can help to reinforce internal discipline. And it can help risk premium demanded by investors.

But there are other considerations which can become a danger if the exchange r pegged too rigidly: They can make it hard to pursue the objective of internal monetary stabil rate policy becomes a hostage to the exchange rate, for - given strong capital inflows - an rise often has an opposite impact on monetary expansion than the one intended. A persistent st can then arise in comparison with the anchor country which over time can endanger the competit of exports. In addition, the fixed exchange rate encourages residents to borrow in foreign relatively favourable nominal interest rates. However, they expose themselves to substantial r own currency has to devalue.

In this way the policy of rigid exchange rate pegging helped to make some coun vulnerable to a change in mood in the markets and hence to a rapid reversal of financial capita

Moreover, in some cases the domestic financial sector was underdeveloped and not efficient.  Not  infrequently  the  financial  institutions  were  subject  to  political  pressu supervision was not particularly effective.

When the capital began to flow back out of these countries, this soon led, in con with a vulnerable financial sector, to a massive disruption of the economic system. Hence mi monetary policy, omissions in supervising financial institutions and insufficient domestic c structures in some cases made the crises possible in the first place and were largely respons scale of the crises.

A number of Asian countries tolerated the emergence of a bubble economy and eviden did not correctly assess the associated dangers. However, the financial and foreign exchang cannot move out of step with real economic conditions in the long run. A reversal will occur suddenly and mostly in an exaggerated form. That is dangerous for the countries concerned, quite often for others, too.

An overall analysis of the problem must include some further aspects:

Firstly, the crisis has not yet been overcome, despite the IMF's intervention an the reforms initiated in a number of countries. The causes - but also the resistance to soluti deep-seated. It is very hard to change long-established patterns of behaviour and accustomed Yet policy makers in the countries concerned cannot and should not shy away from these challen the self-interest of the countries concerned but also in the interest of others.

It  is  encouraging  that  certain  countries  have  taken  important  steps  to  tack challenges and are reaping the first rewards. That also confirms that the IMF has pointed thes in the right direction.

And  secondly,  some  structural  problems  of  the  Asian  emerging  economies  are  by means unique. Such problems also exist elsewhere, and often have similar causes: in some coun transition the financial sectors are too weak; external debt is often rather short-term and d foreign currency to an excessive extent.

In  some  industrial  countries  there  are  at  the  moment  tendencies  towards  exagge asset prices. One must ask oneself whether the prices reflect the true value of the underlyin whether perhaps the potential for a reversal is becoming too great.

The situation in Japan is a special problem. The efforts to overcome the diffic that country via monetary and fiscal policy means have been unsuccessful so far. But it is not a problem of finding the right macroeconomic course.

It would seem that there is still too little competition on the goods and espe financial markets in Japan. In particular, the problems in the financial sector, which have over years, demand convincing, forward-looking solutions. At the same time a problematic vacuum in some areas and the political response has been too hesitant and vague with respect to the corrections. It is to be hoped that the new announcements  will  soon  be  followed  by  convinc confidence-building actions.

## III

In dealing with financial crises, the Fund has learned many lessons in the past f and  has  accumulated  important  experience  with  the  strategy  of  intervening  very  early  with amounts. The rationale behind this strategy is more or less as follows: the best way to counte confidence in a country, once it has broken out, is to take resolute action to provide co conditioned financial assistance and so to set an unmistakable signal. In my view, however, th this strategy have not been particularly encouraging in a number of cases.

At least three serious drawbacks are apparent: Firstly, the frequent applicatio strategy is simply very expensive for the Fund.

Secondly, levels of financial assistance that are announced very early on act li of benchmark. And in the next crisis  they  are  considered  the  absolute  minimum.  If  the  inte community were to offer less, the countries concerned and the financial markets could well int as indifference, as proof of a kind of benign neglect - or even malign neglect.

And  thirdly,  an  early,  massive  intervention  by  the  IMF  undermines  the  ability financial markets to function in the long run. Functioning markets need not only the chance profits but also the possibility to punish mistakes through incurring losses. Otherwise there a moral hazard. And not only for the policy makers of the countries concerned. The markets, end  up  underestimating  the  risks  because  they  are  confident  of  a  bail-out.  This  leads misallocation of capital and shifts costs on to the public sector.

Basically,  this  reveals  the  central  problem  of  any  form  of  interventionist  e policy: the other players come to expect interventions and anticipate the later measures. On has become clear that an interventionist strategy for managing financial crises can easily le end.

So how can the IMF escape from this dead end on a lasting basis? Naturally, there magic formula. But there are a few general conclusions.

The first requirement is that the Fund should concentrate less on correcting a outcome that has already occurred. Instead it should try to influence the ex ante setting in which the financial markets operate and to improve their functioning.

That begins with improved prevention. Above all, this requires more transparency information  so  that  the  financial  markets  can  form  their  expectations  more  rationally  a realistically and so that the IMF itself can assess the need for action more quickly. Spec means publishing more data (especially on the maturity structure and denomination of externa publishing timelier data and at shorter intervals (if possible, monthly instead of twice-year more  sources,  that  is  not  only  the  data  of  the  borrowers  themselves  but  also  data  from  th financial institutions in the industrial countries.

Improving the data quality of a number of countries will certainly require a su intensification of basic statistical work and more openness. However, the return of benefits i considerable.

The  advantages  of  greater  transparency  are  obvious.  The  countries  concerned  ha greater recognition of the need to take certain action. The 'ownership' of adjustment progr particular, increases. And there are less uncertainties for the market players.

The  limits  of  such  transparency  must  lie  where  confidentiality  and  the  'in openness' of advisory or decision-making processes have to be upheld. But in the integrated today it must also be clear that national sovereignty is increasingly coming up against its lim

The IMF itself can contribute towards more information. But it is not a rating The ultimate responsibility for correctly assessing chances and risks in a given country remai players in the financial markets.

In the broader sense, greater prevention also includes technical support. For exam international community can and should provide support, especially in the field of banking su where a number of emerging economies evidently still have some weaknesses. The BIS recently s the Institute for Financial Stability in order to train expert staff, and the committees of t bank  governors,  which  mostly  meet  in  Basle,  have  now  intensified  their  cooperation  wi representatives of the emerging economies.

In addition, the IMF should take account of the recent experience and specific co of countries when making its policy recommendations. For example, the level of development domestic financial sector needs to be taken into account in assessing the right route to the of capital transactions. And when recommending an exchange rate peg, the country's ability to such a regime needs to be considered carefully.

Finally,  one  aspect  of  prevention  should  surely  be  that  the  IMF,  wherever  eco policy weaknesses are apparent, should exert greater pressure if necessary on the government c before a crisis has broken out, even if the extent to which this can be done publicly is a question.

For the main contribution towards effective crisis prevention must be made, of cou the countries concerned themselves. That applies to emerging economies and countries in trans the poorer developing countries and, not least, to the industrial nations as well.

A  necessary  precondition  for  winning  the  confidence  of  the  markets  is  convin economic and political action (good governance). No one can ignore market mechanisms in the lo without causing economic damage. And political power must not be misused in order to secure pe advantages and to distort the domestic economy with lucrative monopolies.

## V

When a crisis does break out, the IMF should again pay more attention to its catal as a moderator and coordinator. The primary aim must be to maintain or restore the crisis access to private capital.

Therefore  the  IMF  should  contribute  towards  bringing  creditors  and  debtors  tog round the table at an early stage and towards working out market-based solutions. I fully agre Mr.  Michel  Camdessus  said  in  a  recent  interview  in  a  German  newspaper:  'Moral  hazard  ex Overcoming this problem, however, requires the involvement of the private creditors. Their par is the backbone of our activity'.

Clearly, not every case is identical. It is naturally easier to perform the role if - as in some Asian cases - the creditors are in the main commercial banks. In some cases IMF seems to have been rather late in seizing that chance. If the groups of creditors - as i case - are more widely spread and heterogeneous, it may be more difficult to bring all the parties together around one table. On the other hand, if non-banks are involved more heavily, t of a spreading financial crisis in the sense of a systemic risk also tend to be smaller.

The  IMF  should  also  minimise  its  provision  of  financial  assistance  not  least  b these  are  public  resources  which  it  is  distributing.  It  should  therefore  itself  bear  only necessary portion of a financing package. It can define a maturity and an interest rate for which it provides that give the debtor an incentive to repay them as soon as possible. Finall the IMF must make its help subject to certain requirements, that is it must define the conditi is part of the IMF's mandate and is also in the interest of the world community.

In defining the conditionality it is imperative to tackle the underlying causes. time it has become clear that macroeconomic measures alone often do not suffice. In Asia - as - it has become apparent instead that one of the root causes was the insufficient soundness and of the financial sector.

The work of the committees in Basle and the efforts of the Fund have laid the ba appropriate rules and appropriate supervision. The key need now is to translate that into actio of  the  countries  concerned  that  may  not  be  easy.  But  the  gains  will  make  the  effort  wo Moreover, effective financial supervision and robust financial sectors are a prerequisite fo liberalisation of capital transactions as envisaged by the IMF and supported by us.

## VI

Since last autumn the IMF has come under heavy criticism from some quarters - m unfairly  in  some  cases.  The  proposals  for  improving  the  situation  range  from  abolishing altogether to setting up additional institutions.

## Introduction

Britain has a love-hate relationship with Europe. Love, because the UK, too, fa powerful Europe generating peace and free trade relations worldwide. All  told,  however,  the  British  seem  to  be  favouring  Europe.  Newt  Gingrich, Chairman of the US House of Representatives, is wrong. The British are hesitant about European integration, as they have always been. T only joined the EC in 1973, when they were sure of its success. A similar process would se taking place where EMU is concerned. At first, the UK was eager to be in on the process, co liberalizing its capital movements, but it subsequently demanded an opt-out clause so as not t to take further action. ## The desirability of British membership

It would mean a larger zone of exchange rate stability, a larger market, and better chan euro  becoming  an  international  currency. Let me say something about what entry into EMU would mean for the United Kingdom itself. In principle, the British Government is in favour of joining EMU. In October 1997, Gord

said in the House of Commons: 'If, in the end, a single currency is successful, and the econo clear and unambiguous, then the Government believes Britain should be part of it'.

The  UK  could  benefit  materially  from  joining  EMU.  Exchange  rate  stability,  gre comparability  of  prices,  and  larger  money  and  capital  markets  offer  the  British  economy  ad opportunities for growth. It must furthermore be remembered that even if the UK does not join, feeling the impact of EMU. Geographically, the UK may be an island, but it is not economica much  is  evidenced  by  the  degree  to  which  the  British  economy  is  affected  by  the  exchang movements of sterling. That influence being as great as it is, then surely it is better to b table where the policy affecting your economy is determined. That means joining EMU. After all, as the UK remains outside EMU, it will not be permitted to take part in the euro-X group, w economic policies of the euro area are coordinated by the Ministers of Finance.

The City, too, stands to benefit substantially from Britain's participation, beca become part of deeper and more liquid financial markets. Obviously, the City's position as financial centre is not yet in peril. As my colleague, Eddie George, neatly pointed out, th people working in the financial sector and affiliated industries in Greater London equals the of Frankfurt: 600,000. If the UK were to remain outside EMU for a long time to come, some City activities could gradually shifted to financial centres on the continent.

## Policy-making for membership

From whatever angle you look at it, the UK would do well to enter into EMU. Fr where we stand, EMU is incomplete without the United Kingdom. The question is not so much whe the UK should join, as when. Research by the Treasury shows it is too early. Of the five econ developed by the Treasury, the crucial one assesses whether the British business cycle is suf line  with  that  in  other  European  countries  and  is  not  marked  by  major  outliers,  the  quest whether  the  single  monetary  policy  actually  fits  in  with  the  UK's  economic  policy. But apart from the question whether this is an economically favourable time to j are institutional impediments to  the  UK's  immediate  membership  as  well.  For  one  thing,  the population have to voice their approval in a referendum and, for another, the UK still needs exchange rate criterion for joining the monetary union.

Let us take a closer look at these obstacles. First of all, the British Governmen to convince the people of the importance of membership. This will be possible if the advan presented in a convincing way, since the idea of joining monetary union is no longer an unfam But the exchange rate criterion, which applies for countries in search of EMU membership, is more complex and more formal, matter. Countries wishing to join EMU on 1 January 1999 are req to have taken part in the exchange rate mechanism of the European Monetary System for the l years, without the fluctuation margins being exceeded. Countries joining at a later stage a subject  to  the  same  rules.  But  the  exchange  rate  mechanism  which  will  take  effect  a 1 January 1999  differs  from  that  currently  in  force.  In  my  opinion,  ERM2  will  replace  ERM legally, it is not that simple, and my view is not shared by everyone. For the time being, t making any moves to join the new exchange rate mechanism. I understand the UK's reluctance t ERM2, considering its unfortunate experience with ERM1. Although the UK only joined ERM1 in 19 it was already forced to leave in 1992. Naturally they feel that the experience does not bea But the circumstances prevailing at that time, viz. an excessively high entry rate for sterli importantly, a macroeconomic policy which did not fully support the exchange rate objective, way comparable to those in evidence in the UK and Europe today.

Now  let  us  take  a  look  at  Britain's  cyclical  conditions  and  economic  policy exchange rate movements of sterling largely reflect the cyclical divergences between the UK European continents. I already noted, it is crucial to British participation in EMU that, in t its economic development does not diverge substantially from those in Europe. The UK's econom always been subject to greater turbulence, and its business cycle is invariably ahead of t mainland. But the cyclical outliers seem to be decreasing. It is gratifying to note that the p cycle of interest rate policy has made way for a monetary policy aimed at keeping inflation und The Government's economic policy is now also directed at putting a  stop  to  the  well-known pattern of stop-go, boom-bust. Like  the  business  cycles  of  countries  such  as  the  Netherlands  and  Germany,  th Britain will never run exactly parallel to the European average. This is the consequence of c single monetary policy in an area as large as the euro zone. The differences among the coun have to be addressed through their budgets, within the confines of the Stability Pact, and e flexible labour and product markets. In these respects, the UK is streets ahead of the othe countries, and is therefore well placed for EMU.

## Conclusion

Ladies and gentlemen, I have come to the end of my speech. All things considered prospects are good for the UK making a successful entry into EMU somewhere in the first few y the 21st century. The British Government's commitment to membership of EMU, and their refusa adopt a wait-and-see attitude can be regarded advantageous. In the meantime, the British shou say in matters. They are a full-fledged member of the EU, and have been in on the process towa throughout.  Outsiders  should  not  become  outcasts.  From  the  Dutch  perspective  in  particula desirable that the UK should put its mark on the shape of the European economy and EMU, also the  run-up  to  its  participation.  Britain  can  play  an  important  role  in  boosting  the  flexi European labour and product markets. Such a role is needed to stimulate the European economy, offer Europe's 18 million unemployed the prospect of a new job. To quote Helmut Kohl: 'To coo as closely as possible with Britain 'in building Europe', Europe needs the United Kingdom, versa. The European Union needs, above all, that unique British blend of realism and tradi pragmatism and idealism, level-headedness and love of freedom'. With which I could not agree mo

It gives me great pleasure to open this conference, which is a joint arrang Sveriges Riksbank and the Institute for International Economic Studies. For  us  at  the  Riksbank,  as  well  as    for  me  personally,  the  oppo welcoming such a large assembly of leading international experts and central representatives is a notable landmark in the practical task of restoring price stabilit

## Sweden on the way to establishing price stability

There has been something paradoxical about Swedish economic policy.

After the period of generally high inflation that started with OPEC 1, Swed one of the last of the industrialised countries to re-focus economic policy on price s notion that a trade-off exists between inflation and unemployment lived on in Sweden fo than in other countries. At the same time, Sweden has a long tradition in the field of central banki Riksbank, founded in 1668, is the world's oldest, still-functioning central bank. A monetary policy focus on stability,  which  is  one  of  the  themes  for  our  forthcoming  discussions,  has  always important  item  on  the  central  bank  policy  agenda.  A  well-known  Swedish  economist, Wiksell,  was  a  clear  exponent  of  the  idea  in  the  late  nineteenth  century. the Riksbank was the first central bank to declare openly that its monetary policy norm stabilisation.

Notwithstanding this long tradition, after inflation's rising trend in th era, Swedish economic policy's reorientation toward price stability did not begin unt 1980s and early 1990s. That was a decade or so after such realignment had been initiate countries. By then, Sweden had experienced twenty years of inflation that averaged 8 p year. That was the longest inflationary period since the early nineteenth century. In the one hundred and forty years from 1830 to 1970, inflation in Sweden had averaged an rate of 2 per cent. So one can say that in the present decade we have been re-establ roots.

Sweden's policy realignment in the early 1990s was, however, more painful anyone  could  have  foreseen.  One  conceivable  explanation  is  that,  having  waited  long other  countries,  the  road  back  to  price  stability  was  more  difficult  for  us.  There number of exceptional events along the way. What was perhaps the worst bank crisis century erupted in the wake of the 1980s' bubble economy. In  recent  years  the  situation  in  Sweden  has  become  more  stable  and,  wi resolute economic policy, developments have taken a positive turn. The bank crisis h resolved, the economy is in an expansionary phase and inflation expectations are low. step, the credibility of the new regime is being established. Experience in other coun shows that the consolidation of a changeover to a low-inflation regime takes many years.

## Inflation target's historical roots and advantages

The idea of focusing monetary policy on price stability goes back, as I men earlier, at least to Wiksell's arguments a century ago. It seems to me that Wiksell's deflation being as important to avoid as inflation has much to do with the acceptan policy today.

In Sweden and many other countries, the old idea, in the 1950s and 1960s, trade-off exists between inflation and unemployment resulted in an increasingly high trend inflation. When the drawbacks of active economic policies of this type became a people in general and their representatives also feared the other extreme - a monetary consistently aimed at keeping inflation as low as possible. Some countries, of which S one, are basically averse to deflation. So a regime whereby monetary policy has a sy long-term commitment to keeping inflation at a predetermined level of 2 per cent, neit nor less, represents what many people perceive as a balanced approach to avoiding defl well as inflation. This has made it easier to establish the legitimacy of the regime mind.

## Some relevant issues for a practitioner

Let me now turn to some matters which a practitioner finds important and w will also be touched upon during the coming two days.

One  issue  concerns  the  indicator  of  inflation  that  is  appropriate  to  us explicit target. The practical considerations in this respect are complex and are cur debated in Sweden. The consumer price index has the advantage of being familiar to public.  Besides  measuring  trend  inflation,  however,  it  also  gives  information  abo fluctuations that stem from transitory supply-side shocks, for example changes in indi and interest costs. With the CPI as the target variable, the central bank encounters the public discussion because shocks of various kinds are liable to result in temporary from the target. Neither  is  it  entirely  clear  how indicator of underlying inflation should be constructed.

Whichever alternative one chooses, it is essential in my opinion that the bank  be  prepared  to  contribute  to  as  open  a  discussion  as  possible,  so  that  its  a achieving and maintaining price stability is not lost sight of and the public's abili central bank responsible for the conduct of monetary policy is not weakened.

Another issue is the choice of a targeting horizon for the monetary polic relates to the trade-off between output volatility and inflation volatility. As it stan is correct but very difficult to understand.

A long target horizon may w greater variability in the inflation rate but would allow for more gradual interest rat and  smaller  real  economic  fluctuations.  In  our  approach  the  normal  target  horizon between one and two years.

A third issue is the degree of transparency. It is widely agreed that trans not merely compatible with an inflation target regime but actually essential if the r function  properly.  For  one  thing,  the  central  bank  must  be  accountable  for  its  co monetary policy. It  is,  after  all,  important  that  discussion  during  the  meetings  is unprejudiced,  so  that  the  participants  can  listen  to  their  colleagues'  arguments,  c minds in the course of a meeting and accept joint responsibility for the decisions tha At the same time, it is important that each individual is responsible for arguing fo position. ## Monetary policy and asset prices

Finally  some  words  about  a  matter  that  is  not  directly  on  the  agenda  f discussions. I am referring to how monetary policy should respond to asset prices. The bringing  it  up  today  is  threefold.  First,  it  is  a  matter  that  is  widely  discussed international forums as well as in many central banks. Second, as a practitioner I wo encourage our leading international experts present here today to study it further in come  in  order  to  develop  more  knowledge  in  this  area. Now when we are assembled here for an important conference, with interest contributions from a number of the world's leading experts in the field, we would do w temperate in our appraisal of what we believe we know today.
