title: Mr. Meyer discusses issues and trends in bank regulatory policy and financial modernization in the United States  (Central Bank Articles and Speeches, 9 Jun 98)
description: Remarks by Laurence H. Meyer, a member of the Board of Governors of the US Federal Reserve System, at the Bank Administration Institute, Finance and Accounting Management Conference held in Washington, DC on 9/6/98.
text:
Mr. Meyer discusses issues and trends in bank regulatory policy and financia modernization in the United States Remarks by Laurence H. Meyer, a member of the Board of Governors of the US Federal Reserve System, at the Bank Administration Institute, Finan Accounting Management Conference held in Washington, DC on 9/6/98.

It is a pleasure to be here today, and I thank the Bank Administration Inst inviting me to be a part of your discussions.

When  people  think  of  the  Federal  Reserve,  I  am  pretty  sure  that  most  Ameri think  of  monetary  policy,  interest  rates,  international  finance,  and  the  Fed's  macr responsibilities in all of these areas. And, of course, macroeconomics lies at the core central bank does. However, as everyone at this conference appreciates, another major fun the Federal Reserve is the supervision and regulation of banks and bank holding companies. like to use my time this afternoon to discuss some key aspects of this side of the Fed's ac

I will begin by outlining, very briefly, some of the key trends affecting th and financial sector. I will then focus on what I see as the most important challenges trends pose for bank supervisors, and suggest some directions that I believe we should cons thinking  about  how  bank  supervision  should  evolve  over  time.  Lastly,  I  will  discuss legislative efforts to modernize our banking system.

## Key Trends Challenging Bank Supervisors

Surely the most profound force transforming the financial, and for that matte sectors of our economy, is the rapid growth of computer and telecommunications technolo finance, a critical and complementary force is the development of intellectual 'technolo enable financial engineers to separate risk into its various components, and price each co an economically rational way.

Implementation  of  financial engineering strategies typically requires ma amounts of cheap data processing; and the cheap data processing would not be useful with formulas required to compute prices. The combination of the two has led to a virtual explos number and types of financial instruments. Such products have lowered the cost and broade scope of financial services, making it possible for borrowers and lenders to transact d each other, for a wide range of financial products to be tailored for very specific purp financial risk to be managed in ever more sophisticated ways.

Financial  innovation  has  been  the  driving  force  behind  a  second  major  tre banking  --  the  blurring  of  distinctions  among  what  were,  traditionally,  very  distinct financial firms. One of the first such innovations, with which we are all now very fam money market mutual funds. In the 1980s, banks began to challenge whether the Glass-Steaga prohibited combinations of commercial and investment banking. Today, both the regulators a courts  agree  that  Glass-Steagall  does  not  imply  a  total  prohibition.  More  recently, separations of banking and insurance sales have also begun to fall, with support from the and the courts.

A major result of the continued blurring of distinctions among commercial ban investment  banking,  and  insurance  is  a  tremendous  increase  in  competition  for  many  fi services. Greatly intensified competition has also led to increasing pressure for revision the  banking  laws  and  regulations  that,  despite  some  successful  efforts  at  relaxation continue to exert outdated and costly restraints on the banking and financial system.

Indeed,  despite  its  often  frustratingly  slow  pace,  there  seems  little  do deregulation has been a major force for change in the banking and financial services indus decades ago we still had Regulation Q, the Glass-Steagall Act was widely viewed as requ virtual prohibition of combinations of commercial and investment banking, and interstate and branching, let alone combinations of banking and insurance, were barely fantasies eve state level.

The fourth major force transforming the banking landscape is the globalizati only  of  banking  and  financial  markets,  but  also  of  the  real  economy.  The  interact developments in both the financial and real economies have expanded cross-border asset ho trading, and credit flows. In response, financial intermediaries, including banks and secu have increased their cross-border operations. Once again, a critical result of this rapid been a substantial increase in competition both at home and abroad.

The final significant trend I will highlight is the on-going consolidation o banking industry. I think that it is fair to say that the American banking system is cur midst of the most significant consolidation in its history. In 1980 there were about 14,4 the U.S. organized into about 12,300 banking organizations. By the end of 1997, the nu banks had fallen to just under 9,100, and the number of banking organizations to not qui This 42 percent decline in the number of banking organizations was due in part, but only the large number of bank failures in the late 1980s and early 1990s. A more important fa mergers among healthy banks. Since the early 1980s, it has not been unusual to see 400 mergers among healthy banks each year.

While  mergers  have  occurred,  and  continue  to  occur,  among  banks  of  all  siz would emphasize three aspects of the current bank merger movement. First is the high inci 'megamergers', or mergers among very large banking organizations. Several mergers of the la years have been either the largest at the time, or among the largest bank mergers in U. And, of course, that trend continues.

Second, despite all of the merger activity, a large number of medium to small remain in the United States. Moreover, by most measures of performance these small banks ar than a match for their larger brethren for many bank products and services. When a megame announced it is not uncommon to read in the press how small banks in the affected mark looking to take advantage of the business opportunities created thereby. Research seems t their optimism.

Lastly, while the overall number of banking organizations has fallen since 198 does not mean that new, or de novo, entry has not occurred. From 1980 through 1997 some new banks were formed in the United States.

In large part because of the continued viability of smaller banks, while the concentration of banking assets has increased substantially since 1980, measures of loc banking concentration have remained essentially unchanged. Indeed, the stability of loca concentration in the face of such a large consolidation of the banking industry is remar bodes well for the competitive vitality of local banking markets.

While the reasons for bank mergers are varied, the bottom line is that the States is well on its way to developing a truly national banking structure for the firs history. We are not quite there yet, but I do not think it will take too many more years.

## Future Directions in Bank Supervision

## What do all of these changes mean for how we supervise and regulate banks?

## Analysis of Competition

Clearly,  as  the  banking  industry  consolidates  we  need  to  maintain  compet markets.  Competitive  markets  are  our  best  assurance  that  consumers  receive  the  highest products at the lowest possible prices. As I discussed earlier, there are many reasons to in recent years competition has increased greatly in markets for a large number of financi and  services.  This  is  true  for  many  products  purchased  in  local,  regional  and  national However,  in  some  cases  we  still  observe  potential  competitive  problems  with  a  proposed merger. Fortunately, the antitrust laws, as written into the banking statutes, give us maintain  competition  in  such  situations.  These  laws  require  that  the  Board  approve  on mergers that are not expected to substantially harm competition.

Over the past year or so, quite a few applicants have pushed very hard at the frontier for approving merger applications. In response, the Board has occasionally felt c remind applicants, especially those proposing a merger that would affect a large number markets, that substantial changes in market concentrations will receive careful review. when  mergers  would  exceed  the  screening  guidelines,  'mitigating'  factors  must  be  prese mitigating factors I mean conditions that tend to create a more competitive market than is by market concentration alone. The greater the deviation from the screening guidelines, powerful and convincing the mitigating factors must be.

I have personally been particularly concerned with cases where a large numb local markets are affected. In such cases, even if the adverse effect is fairly small in local markets, it seems to me that the cumulative, or total, adverse effect might be signi a large number of markets are affected adversely, I believe that we should be especially assure ourselves that there are substantial mitigating factors. In addition, when a merger a large change in concentration in a market that is, or becomes, highly concentrated, I th to give special attention to the impact on competition.

## Assessing Safety and Soundness

Technological  change,  financial  innovation,  the  acquisition  of  new  powers banking organizations, the increasing geographic scope of banks, and the globalization of markets  all  challenge  our  ability  to  examine  and  assess  the  safety  and  soundness  of  i banking firms. One way that examiners are adapting to this changed world is to focus much attention on the information and risk management systems of banks. The key question they How effectively are these systems measuring and controlling an institution's rapidly chan profile? The emphasis on risk management is most critical at our largest, most sophistic most  internationally  active  banks.  Many  of  these  banks  use  advanced  economic  and  stat models to evaluate their market and credit risks. These models are used for a variety of including allocating capital on a risk adjusted basis and pricing loans and credit guarante

The  development  by  some  banks  of  increasingly  accurate  models  for  measurin managing,  and  pricing  risk  has  called  into  question  the  continuing  usefulness  of  on foundations of bank supervision -- the so-called risk-based capital standards, or the Ba The  Basle  Accord  capital  standards  were  adopted  in  1988  by  most  of  the  world's  industr nations  in  an  effort  to  encourage  stronger  capital  at  riskier  banks,  to  include  off-b exposures in the assessment of capital adequacy, and to establish more consistent capital across nations. The Accord was a major advance in 1988, and has proved to be very usefu

then. But in recent years calls for reform have begun to grow. I will outline briefly on problems we are currently facing with the Basle Accord.

The Basle Accord capital standards divide bank on- and off-balance-sheet asset four risk buckets, and then apply a different capital weight to each bucket. These weigh roughly  with  the  riskiness  of  the  assets  in  a  given  bucket.  However,  the  relationship Perhaps most troublesome, the same risk weight is applied to all loans. Thus, for example, a very risky 'junk bond' company gets the same weight as a loan to a 'triple A' rated firm.

This aspect of the Accord clearly gives banks an incentive to find ways to av regulatory capital standard for loans that their internal models say need less capital th by the Basle Accord. Conversely, banks should want to keep loans which their models say more capital than does the Basle standard. And, guess what, banks have been doing just t so-called 'regulatory arbitrage' may not be all bad, but it surely causes some serious p well. For one thing, it makes reported capital ratios -- a key measure of bank soundnes supervisors and investors -- less meaningful for government supervisors and private analyst ways around this problem is a high priority at the Federal Reserve.

The  arbitraging  of  regulatory  capital  requirements  is  but  one  of  a  host  of conflicts between banks and bank supervisory rules and regulations. Indeed, one can view the long history of bank supervision and regulation as something of a contest between su who want to deter excessive risk taking and banks who seek ways around sometimes ineffici just plain uneconomic, regulations. This long history leads me to seek supervisory strategi in  the  economist's  jargon,  incentive  compatible.  By  incentive  compatible,  I  mean  supe policies and procedures that give banks strong internal incentives to manage their risks pr minimize  the  exploitation  of  moral  hazard.  Put  differently,  we  need  to  design  strate encourage banks, in their own self-interest, to work with us, not against us.

When designing supervisory policy, we should always remember that the first li defense against excessive risk-taking by banks is the market itself. Market discipline c often is, highly effective at deterring excessive risk. Indeed, a primary goal of many regulatory reforms implemented in the wake of the banking and thrift crises of the 1980s 1990s was either to increase market discipline or to make supervisors behave more like th would behave. Market discipline was increased, for example, by raising capital standards mandating greater public disclosure by a bank of its financial condition. Prompt correct rules  that  require  supervisors  to  impose  increasingly  severe  penalties  on  a  bank  as  it condition deteriorates, and the adoption of risk-based deposit insurance premiums are exa encouraging supervisors to act like the market.

The reforms of the early 1990s were a good start. But I believe that there may more that we can do. Such comments may sound out of place today. Times are good, and al everyone seems quite satisfied with the current deposit insurance system. But good times precisely when we should develop ideas for an even more effective system. The crucible of a not always the best time to think up reforms -- witness the error we made in passing t Steagall Act, an error we have yet to correct after 65 years! Indeed, it is in part for t that the Board continues to urge Congress to pass financial modernization legislation. spirit of being forward looking, let me attempt to give you the flavor of one idea that considering.

It may be possible to increase market discipline by requiring large, intern active banks to issue a minimum amount of certain types of subordinated debt to the pub appealing aspect of this approach is that subordinated debt holders, so long as they ar

'insiders,' face only downside risk, and thus their risk preferences are very close to FDIC. Subordinated debt holders would therefore be expected to impose market discipline bank  that  is  quite  consistent  with  what  bank  supervisors  are  trying  to  do,  including  e banks  to  disclose  more  information  about  their  financial  condition.  Observed  risk  prem subordinated  debt  could  perhaps  be  used  to  help  the  FDIC  set  more  accurate  risk-based insurance premiums, and such debt would provide an extra cushion of protection for taxpay additional benefit of having subordinated debt traded on the open market is that price m would provide a clear signal of the market's evaluation of the bank's financial condition t it were not used to help price deposit insurance, could serve as an early warning aid to su

Subordinated  debt  is  not,  however,  without  its  problems.  For  example,  the preferences  of  such  creditors  are  aligned  with  those  of  the  FDIC  only  when  the  bank  is solvent. At or near insolvency, subordinated debt holders may be willing to 'bet the bank to increase the chances that they will not suffer a loss. The fact that the bank closure d in the supervisor's hands is another complicating factor. In addition, it is unclear just liquid  a  market  in  bank  subordinated  debt  would  be,  although  limiting  any  requirements largest banks would ease this concern. For example, at the end of last year only one-half banks with less than $50 million in assets issued subordinated debt, but 83 percent of total  assets  of  $10  billion  or  more  did  so.  However,  it  appears  that  much  of  exist subordinated debt is held by the bank's parent holding company, not independent third parti the question of how deep and liquid a market might evolve remains. For these and other rea operationally  feasible  program  for  mandatory  subordinated  debt  would  require  a  consid amount of careful thought. Still, in my judgment it is thought that might prove very worthw

## The Need For Financial Modernization

Technology and globalization are changing markets all over the world, but pe none have been more affected than the financial markets. Yet in the United States much of framework  has  essentially  not  changed  since  the  1930s.  The  resultant  pressure  on  f institutions to be able to compete has thus been reflected in the search for loopholes and regulatory authorities to find ways within their charter to permit new activities. The p only inefficient, but creates new inequities, institutions that may be producing unintende the misallocation of resources. That is why my colleagues and I are such strong supporter 10, The Financial Modernization Act of 1998, which the House passed last month and the S Banking Committee will be discussing next week.

This bill brings our financial institutions into the 21st century in a frame minimizes  risks  and  inequities.  The  task  it  sets  for  itself  is  not  easy.  Each  set  of institutions  --  and  their  regulators  --  have  special  privileges  and  advantages  that  t maintain  and  limits  and  restraints  that  they  wish  to  shed. The most critical element is that H.R. 10 would permit banks to conduct in the subsidiaries (so-called operating subsidiaries or 'op subs') only the same activities th already conduct in the bank and financial agency activities, which by their nature requi funding and create minimal risk. These limitations, it seems to me, are crucial for seve Banks have a lower cost of funds than other financial entities because of the safety net we  give  the  collection  of  deposit  insurance,  access  to  the  discount  window,  and  acces payments system. text:
Mr. King looks at the UK economy and monetary policy Speech by Mr. Mervyn King, an Executive Director and Chief Economist of the Bank of England, at the Building So Association Annual Conference in Bournemouth on 27/5/98.

Next Monday - 1 June - sees the start of the statutory basis for Britain's new policy regime. An independent Bank of England will, through its Monetary Policy Committee (or set interest rates to achieve an inflation target of 2½%. For over 30 years economic policy in been bedevilled by inflation and the resulting instability of output and employment. Stabili prices and macroeconomic performance more generally - requires a credible commitment to a mon and fiscal framework embracing low inflation and sustainable public finances. That we now have.

But  stability  of  the  economy  is  not  the  same  as  stability  of  interest  rates. interest rates must go up and down according to the state of the economy if the inflation ta met. In contrast, if monetary policy is successful in achieving the inflation target then, pre short-term  interest  rates  will  have  moved  over  the  economic  cycle,  long-term  interest  rate relatively  stable.  And,  from  the  perspective  of  your  borrowers,  whether  on  fixed  or  flo mortgages, what matters is the predictability of the cost of a loan over the life of the mortga fluctuations, within reason, of monthly payments. Timely movements in short-term interest rate means by which both the average cost of a mortgage, and its variability, can be reduced to the necessary to attract loan finance. In so doing we should be able to avoid crisis - and inevi changes of interest rates of the kind that we have seen so often in the past. Indeed, since target was adopted in October 1992 there have been no changes of interest rates of that kind were  decided  at  the  regular  monthly  monetary  meetings.  Moreover,  the  switch  last  May  to  a timetable of meetings for the Monetary Policy Committee - with all interest rate decisions an 12 noon on the Thursday on which the MPC meeting concludes - was a major step forward in redu uncertainty in financial markets.

## Through the Looking Glass .....

So if interest rates must be flexible, in which direction are they likely to mo wish I could tell you. Inflation, as measured by RPIX, rose to 3.0% in April, compared with March. But that jump largely reflected the Budget changes to excise duties which took effect e year than last. That will drop out of the index in the third quarter of this year when RPIX likely to fall back towards its target level of 2½%.

However, this relatively optimistic short-term outlook reflects an extraordinaril inflation environment. The combination of a strong exchange rate (still about 25% above its August 1996), a 20% fall in dollar oil prices over the past year, and an average fall of 9 commodity prices, is holding down retail price inflation. Domestically generated inflation is higher than RPIX inflation. As the one-off effects of the rise in sterling wear off over the next year or so - as indeed they will unless sterling appreciates further - inflation will st the target unless domestically generated inflation declines.

In  the  long  run,  domestically  generated  inflation  is  likely  to  be  close  to  t increase of unit labour costs. At present unit labour costs are rising at about 3½% a year. figures released earlier this month - which showed that average earnings in the economy grew and in the private sector by no less than 5.6% - were undoubtedly disappointing. It is too so how far they reflect the impact of higher bonuses this year than last. In any event, to hit target those rates of earnings growth will have to fall back.

These  high  levels  of  earnings  growth  are  not  the  underlying  cause  of  inflat pressure; they are a symptom of a tight labour market. Equally, the prospects for earnings gro critically on the future path of output and on inflation expectations. The MPC's central proj May Inflation Report is that the pace of output growth will slow. But a slowdown in economic g not, in itself, sufficient to hit the inflation target. The central issue for monetary policy

nominal demand will slow sufficiently quickly to prevent retail price inflation rising when th effects of a high exchange rate and lower commodity prices wear off.

The extent to which domestic demand growth slows down is crucial. At present, we relying on a sharp deterioration in the trade balance to keep output growth down to levels that to rising inflationary pressure. But in the longer-run domestic demand growth must fall from rate of 3½ - 4% to something closer to trend. During 1997 as a whole, consumption grew by 5% growth  rate  is  already  moderating.  And  the  MPC's  central  projection  is  for  a  further  slow domestic demand during this year. That is likely to be brought about by a combination of the monetary tightening that has been put in place over the past year or so. But there are real There  is  a  risk  that  consumption  may  prove  stubbornly  buoyant.  Real  personal  disposable increased by 4.2% last year, and the ratio of net financial wealth of households to their inc an all-time high of over 3. Those factors will support consumption. The latest retail sales fi some  comfort  with  volume  growth  below  that  in  the  middle  of  last  year  when  consumption stimulated by windfall gains, predominantly from the conversion of building societies. (Rarel many, been so grateful, to so few building societies.)

## Highs and lows in house prices

In the past, domestic demand has been sensitive to developments in the housing ma In  the  late  1980s  house  prices  increased  by  40%  in  two  years,  while  consumption  rose  by  ov Borrowing using housing as collateral - so called equity withdrawal - amounted to almost 50% increase in consumption over that period. The impact of rises in house prices on consumption cause and which is effect - remains hotly contested by economists. A rise in house prices lea to an increase in wealth but also to an increase in the cost of housing services. Or, to put if the price of your home goes up, you will not be able to spend more on other things if you w on living in your home. So it is not at all clear that changes in house prices will in fact ha impact on household spending.

Perhaps of greater importance is the role which house prices play in signalling c confidence about the future. In common with other assets, such as equities, house prices ca quickly to news about future economic prospects. And house prices and consumer confidence do s be closely correlated. So house prices may be a leading indicator of sentiment about the eco hence of consumption and domestic demand. But, just like equities, house prices also reflect real interest rates. Since long-term real interest rates have fallen from over 3½% to below past year, it is not surprising that house, and other asset, prices have risen.

Precisely because housing is an  asset,  its  price  is  more  volatile  than  most  go services in the retail price index. As such, it is important to look at house price levels as rates of change. Although house prices have been rising quite rapidly over the past couple of returned to the peak reached in the late 1980s only at the end of last year, and exceeded it time in the first quarter of this year. That, of course, followed the sharp fall in house pri 1990s - house prices fell by over 10% between 1990 and the end of 1992.

For most families, apart from future earnings and pensions, their wealth is domin one  asset  and  one  liability.  The  asset  is  their  home  and  the  liability  is  the  mortgage  on difference between these two is sensitive to the state of the economy. In a low inflation w prices are likely to rise and fall whereas the mortgage liability is fixed in money terms. T has the potential to create large swings in household net worth which may well exacerbate fluct demand and output. The upside consequence was seen in the consumption boom of the 1980s, and opposite was evident in the bust of the early 1990s when falls in house prices meant that a 1½ million  families  had  negative  net  equity  resulting  in  higher  precautionary  saving  an consumption.

The forward-looking information contained in house prices underlines the importanc MPC attaches to measuring them accurately. The recent divergence between the rates of house

inflation implied by the Halifax and the Nationwide indices is both puzzling and unfortunate. of house price inflation recorded by the two indices began to diverge at the beginning of 1997 recently published data suggest that house prices, as measured by the Nationwide index, rose in  the  year  to  April  1998,  whereas,  according  to  the  Halifax  index,  they  rose  by  only  5. household wealth in the year to April 1998 rose by £80 billion more according to the Nationw the Halifax index. Such differences matter in our assessment of the economy.

The Bank of England, together with representatives from the Halifax and Nationwide from the Department of Environment, Transport and the Regions (DETR), have spent a great deal o and effort trying to understand the cause of this divergence and to assess what is really h house prices.

The answer to the first question - what accounts for the divergence? - remains l mystery. The Bank's preferred explanation, reached I have to admit via a process of eliminatio plausible explanations rather than by the existence of incontrovertible evidence, is that th reflects the way in which house prices are 'mix adjusted' to take account of the different ch of  the  houses  bought  and  sold  in  any  one  month.  Changes  in  the  relative  composition  of  t portfolios of the Halifax and the Nationwide over the last year or so are likely to have ma effect.

To answer the second question - what is really happening to house prices? - the Ba developed an alternative measure of house price inflation using data from the Land Registry. T have the advantage that they cover nearly all housing transactions in England and Wales and so comprehensive than the data used by either the Halifax or the Nationwide. However, the Bank est far from ideal. The published Land Registry data are not 'mix adjusted'. And, although the Ban apply a simple mix adjustment to take account of the basic type of property brought and sol county in which the property is located, it is less sophisticated than that used by either Nationwide.

So I would not want to claim in any way that we at the Bank have found the true me of house price inflation. Rather, the Bank estimate was developed in the spirit of trying t guidance to the members of the MPC on the relative weights that they should attach to the co pictures  painted  by  the  Halifax  and  Nationwide  indices.  The  house  price  index  constructed Department of Environment, Transport and the Regions is also helpful in this respect. That ind advantage  that  it  is  constructed  using  a  more  complete  method  for  adjusting  for  the  mix  o transacted  than  the  Bank  estimate,  but  it  is  based  on  only  a  small  sample  -  approximately mortgage-backed transactions.

The Bank estimate suggests that house prices increased by 9.0% in the year to 199 compared  with  6.9%  measured  by  Halifax  and  12.9%  by  Nationwide.  The  Bank  estimate  is  broad consistent with the DETR index, which shows a 7.9% increase over the same period. But further required on this issue which is of importance to us all.

## 'Divided we stand, united we fall'

That brings me to the Monetary Policy Committee and the prospect for interest rate transparency  of  the  new  process  means  that  the  debate  about  monetary  policy  within  the  M explained clearly to the world at large. Hence the reasons why monetary policy is so finely ba I believe, now widely understood.

But it is not just the policy debate which is now more transparent. The voting r each individual member of the MPC is in the public domain. There is a good reason for this. D is  an  incentive  for  individuals  to  cast  their  vote  for  the  policy  most  likely  to  hit  the inflation target. I have little doubt that the prospect of having to defend one's voting re makes  individual  members  of  the  MPC  well  aware  of  their  responsibilities.  There  can  be  no

behind the coat-tails of the chairman, nor disowning a decision subsequently by claiming to ha against a position adopted by consensus. Transparency should improve both the quality of decis the accountability of Committee members.

But there is an additional point which is fundamental to the role of the Monetar Committee. Its purpose is to take technical decisions about the level of short-term interest the issue is one of technical judgment it is better to rely on the collective wisdom of nine p views of only one individual. I have noticed that the highest in the land often rely on team whereas  you  and  I  have  only  one.  Of  course,  it  is  often  tempting  to  take  comfort  from  t confidence with which any one doctor proclaims his or her diagnosis. But the evidence suggest difficult cases reasonable experts can interpret the evidence in different ways. Rather than from one self-confident view, which I would find difficult to challenge, I would like to know balance of professional opinion lies. That  is  why  in  the  case  of  essentially  technical  jud sensible to rely upon collective wisdom, and there are other areas in which we do precisely tha Lords, for example, reach their decisions by aggregating individual judgments, and the same is United States Supreme Court. The MPC is based on the same principle. For such a system to wor crucial that the individual members of the MPC give their best judgment and do not try to artificial consensus.

When policy is clearly off-track, as in the spring of last year, it is not diffi unanimous  decisions,  as  the  Committee  did  through  1997.  But  when  policy  is  finely  bala disagreements about the precise level of interest rate are not only likely but an indication broadly on-track. That is why the motto of the MPC should perhaps be 'divided we stand, uni fall'.

Some commentators have been unable to resist labelling members of the Committee either 'hawks' or 'doves'. There is a fundamental problem with this labelling. It makes no se new system to describe individuals as hawks or doves. Each member of the Committee has the inflation target. Unlike some other central banks, MPC members cannot entertain closet views a attractions  or  dangers  of  slightly  higher  or  lower  inflation.  Their  task  -  to  which  they personally accountable - is to hit the Government's inflation target. So members of the Commi on interest rates according to the economic data, which change from month to month, and the an those data. No one takes a position that higher interest rates are a good or a bad thing out o you drove past an infant school at 40mph, you might well be described as driving dangerously fa you drove at 40mph on a motorway, you might well be described as driving dangerously slowly. A must  be  judged  in  the  light  of  the  circumstances.  In  terms  of  monetary  policy,  that  means positions which members of the MPC take on interest rates will change over time according to the  economy  evolves.  But  if  interest  rates  themselves  cannot  be  predicted,  because  they  d changing economic data, what should be predictable is the way MPC members respond to those da predictable 'policy reaction function', to use the jargon, should, over time, diminish the in market commentators take in the meetings of the MPC and direct that interest to what is happeni economy.

So, as the voting record shows, it is seriously misleading to think of the MPC in fixed camps of 'hawks' and 'doves'. As circumstances change, it is easy to imagine that the shall be 'doves' and the 'doves' shall be 'hawks'. And, over a five year period, since each m the  MPC  is  trying  to  hit  the  same  inflation  target,  I  predict  that  it  will  be  impossible between 'doves' and 'hawks'. What will the commentators call us then? If Britain either has or to join Monetary Union, then the birds may have flown the nest. But if the MPC is still sett rates in Britain, then I hope that we shall be seen as a group that is tediously predictab raising interest rates, sometimes cutting them, but always moving in response to the economi order to hit the inflation target.

title: Mr. Greenspan presents an update on economic conditions in the United States  (Central Bank Articles and Speeches, 10 Jun 98)
description: Testimony of the Chairman of the Board of Governors of the US Federal Reserve System, Mr. Alan Greenspan, before the Joint Economic Committee of the US Congress on 10/6/98.
text:
Mr.  Greenspan  presents  an  update  on  economic  conditions  in  the  United  States Testimony of the Chairman of the Board of Governors of the US Federal Reserve System, Mr. Greenspan, before the Joint Economic Committee of the US Congress on 10/6/98.

Mr. Chairman and members of the Committee, I am pleased to have the opportunity present an update on economic conditions in the United States.

Such an assessment cannot be made in isolation but rather depends critically on happening in the rest of the world and how those developments affect the performance of the A economy. In my previous appearance before this Committee last October, my remarks focused mainl the turbulence that was then evident in world financial markets and, in particular, on the p had  emerged  in  a  number  of  Asian  economies.  The  tentative  assessment  offered  then  was  tha economies of Asia were in for some trying times but that the situation did not seem likely to expansion of this country's economy.

That assessment, I believe, still is essentially correct, although uncertaintie degree of restraint that will be coming from abroad remain substantial. Earlier this year, the most of the Asian countries seemed to be stabilizing in some respects, but, as the events of weeks  have  demonstrated,  the  restoration  of  normally  functioning  economies  will  not  necessa smoothly. In some cases, the adjustments that are needed to improve external balances and t existing  misallocations  of  resources  have  been  accompanied  by  sharp  increases  in  inflatio unemployment,  abrupt  cutbacks  in  living  standards,  and  increases  in  uncertainty  and  insecur heightened social and political pressures that can develop in such circumstances not only intro complications  into  economic  policymaking  but  also  make  it  even  more  difficult  to  foresee  h processes of adjustment will play out across the afflicted economies.

That the American economy would be affected to some degree by spillover from t problems in Asia was never in doubt, even though the timing and magnitude of the impact hav difficult  to  predict  with  much  confidence.  Many  months  ago,  businesses  in  this  country anticipating a worsening of our trade balance with the Asian countries, and incoming economic d since  confirmed  those  expectations.  Meanwhile,  other  influences  on  trade  --  such  as  the  st demand growth in the United States and a dollar that has been strong against a wide array of cu have persisted. In total, US exports of goods and services turned down in real terms in the fi 1998, the first such decline in four years, and real imports of goods and services continued rapidly. The combined effect of these changes exerted a drag of 2½ percentage points on th growth rate of real GDP last quarter. Weaknesses in Asia appear to account for approximately of that deterioration. Not only have export volumes been affected, but producers in both in agriculture also are having to adjust to the lower product prices that have come with slower growth  abroad  and  the  increase  in  the  competitiveness  of  foreign  producers  induced  lar depreciations of their currencies.

But even with substantial drag from the external sector, the US economy has cont to  expand  at  a  robust  pace.  In  the  first  quarter,  real  GDP  grew  even  faster  than  it  ha Employment has continued to increase rapidly this year, and the unemployment rate has fallen reaching  its  lowest  level  since  1970.  Incomes  have  continued  to  climb,  and  gains  in  house business expenditures have been exceptionally strong. Although the data on hours worked sugge growth of the economy has likely slowed this quarter from the first quarter's torrid pace, t slowdown remains in question. Evidence to date of a moderation in underlying domestic spending sparse.

The strength of domestic spending has been fueled, in part, by conditions in f markets. Although real short-term interest rates have been rising, equity prices have moved s credit has been readily available at slender margins over Treasury interest rates, and nomina interest rates have remained near the lowest levels of recent decades. Rapid growth of money t

a further indication that financial conditions are accommodating strong domestic spending, alt still are uncertain how reliable that relationship will prove to be over time.

In  short,  our  economy  is  still  enjoying  a  virtuous  cycle,  in  which,  in  the  c subdued inflation and generally supportive credit conditions, rising equity values are provid for  spending  and,  in  turn,  the  expansion  of  output,  employment,  and  productivity-enhancing investment. The hopes for accelerated productivity growth have been bolstering expectations corporate earnings and thereby fueling still further increases in equity values.

The essential precondition for the emergence, and persistence, of this virtuous arguably the decline in the rate of inflation to near price stability. Continued low product and expectations that it will persist have brought increasing stability to financial markets perceptions  that  the  degree  of  risk  in  the  financial  outlook  has  been  moving  ever  lowe perceptions, in turn, have reduced the extra compensation that investors require for making l taking ownership positions in, private firms.

To a considerable extent, investors seem to be expecting that low inflation and productivity growth will allow the extraordinary growth of profits to be extended into the dis Indeed, expectations of per share earnings growth over the longer term have been undergoing co upward revision by security analysts since 1994. These rising expectations have, in turn, dr prices sharply higher and credit spreads lower, perhaps to levels that will be difficult to economic conditions remain exceptionally favorable -- more so than might be anticipated from h relationships. In any event, primarily because of the rise in stock prices, about $12 tril added to the value of household assets since the end of 1994. Probably only a few percent largely  unrealized  capital  gains  have  been  transformed  into  the  purchase  of  goods  and  se consumer  markets.  But  that  increment  to  spending,  combined  with  the  sharp  increase  in  equ investment, which has stemmed from the low cost of both equity and debt relative to expected p capital, has propelled the economy forward. The current economic performance, with its combina strong growth and low inflation, is as impressive as any I have witnessed in my near half-centu observation of the American economy.

The consequences for the American worker have been dramatic and, for the most p highly favorable. A great many chronically underemployed people have been given the opportun work, and many others have been able to upgrade their skills as a result of work experience, increases in on-the-job training, or increased enrollment in technical programs. Welfare recipi to have been absorbed into the work force in significant numbers.

Government finances have improved as well. The taxes paid on huge realized cap gains and other incomes related to the stock market, coupled with taxes on markedly higher c profits, have joined with restraint on spending to produce a unified federal budget surplus time in nearly three decades. April's budget surplus of $125 billion was the largest monthly record.  Widespread  improvement  also  has  been  evident  in  the  financial  positions  of  state governments.

The fact that economic performance strengthened as inflation subsided should not been surprising,  given  that  risk  premiums  and  economic  disincentives  to  invest  in  productiv diminish as product prices become more stable. But the extent to which strong growth and high utilization have been joined with low inflation over an extended period is nevertheless ext Indeed, the broadest measures of price change indicate that the inflation rate moved down fur first quarter of this year, even as the economy strengthened. Although declining oil prices co this result, pricing leverage in the goods-producing sector more generally was held in check industrial  capacity,  reduced  demand  in  Asia  that,  among  other  things,  has  led  to  a  sof commodity prices, and a strong dollar that has contributed to bargain prices on many import elements in this mix clearly were transitory, and the very recent price data suggest that con inflation  has  moved  up  in  the  second  quarter.  But,  even  so,  the  rate  of  rise  remains  quit

overall. At this point, at least, the adverse wage-price interactions that played so central a inflation higher in many past business expansions -- eventually bringing those expansions to a not appear to have gained a significant toe-hold in the current expansion.

There are many reasons why the wage-price interactions have been so well-containe this expansion. For one thing, increases in hourly compensation have been slower to pick up tha other recent expansions, although, to be sure, wages have started to accelerate in the past co as the labor market has become tighter and tighter.

In the first few years of the expansion, the subdued rate of rise in hourly comp seemed to be, in part, a reflection of greater concerns among workers about job security. We to have moved beyond that period of especially acute concern, though the flux of technology leave many workers with fears of job skill obsolescence and a willingness to trade wage gain security.  This  may  explain  why,  despite  the  recent  acceleration  of  wages,  the  resulting compensation  has  fallen  short  of  what  the  experience  of  previous  expansions  would  have  led anticipate given the  current  degree  of  labor  market  tightness.  In  the  past  couple  of  years workers have not had to press especially hard for nominal pay gains to realize sizable increa real  wages.  In  contrast  to  the  pattern  that  developed  in  several  previous  business  expansi workers required substantial increases in pay just to cover increases in the cost of living, co have been generally well-behaved in the current expansion. Changes  this  past  year  in  prices goods and services have been among the smallest of recent decades.

In addition, the rate of rise in the cost of benefits that employers provide to been remarkably subdued over the past few years, although a gradual upward tilt has become ev late. A variety of factors -- including the strength of the economy and rising equity values, reduced the need for payments into unemployment trust funds and pension plans, and the restruc the health care sector -- have been working to keep benefit costs in check in this expansion. medical area at least, the most recent developments suggest that the favorable trend may ha course. The slowing of price increases for medical services seems to have come to a halt, at time, and, with the cost-saving shift to managed care having been largely completed, the pot businesses to achieve further savings in that regard appears to be rather limited at this poin been  a  few  striking  instances  this  past  year  of  employers  boosting  outlays  for  health  b substantial amounts.

A  couple  of  years  ago  --  almost  at  the  same  time  that  increases  in  total compensation began trending up in nominal terms -- evidence of a long-awaited pickup in the gr labor productivity began to show through more strongly in the data; and this accelerated  i output per hour has enabled firms to meet workers' real wage demands while holding the line increases. Gains in productivity usually vary with the strength of the economy, and the favora that  we  have  observed  during  the  past  two  years  or  so,  when  the  economy  has  been  growing rapidly, surely overstate the degree of pickup that can be sustained. But evidence continues t the  trend  has  picked  up,  even  if  the  extent  of  that  improvement  is  as  yet  unclear.  Signs technological transformation of the economy are all around us, and the benefits are evident n high-tech industries but also in production processes that have long been part of our industria

Notwithstanding  a  reasonably  optimistic  interpretation  of  the  recent  produc numbers,  it  would  not  be  prudent  to  assume  that  rising  productivity,  by  itself,  can non-inflationary future. Certainly wage increases, per se, are not inflationary. To be avoid that  exceed  productivity  growth,  thereby  creating  pressure  for  inflationary  price  increase eventually undermine economic growth and employment. Because the level of productivity is tie important degree to the physical stock of capital, which turns over only gradually, increases growth  of  productivity  probably  also  occur  rather  gradually.  By  contrast,  the  potential acceleration of nominal hourly compensation is surely greater. Still, a strong signal of infla building because of compensation increases markedly in excess of productivity gains has not ye emerged in this expansion. Among nonfinancial corporations, our most reliable source of cons

costs, trends in costs seem to have accelerated from their lows, but the rates of increase in costs and total unit costs are still quite low.

Nonetheless,  as  I  have  noted  in  previous  appearances  before  Congress,  I  re concerned  that  economic  growth  will  run  into  constraints  as  the  reservoir  of  unemployed available to work is drawn down. The annual increase in the working-age population (from 16 years  of  age),  including  immigrants,  has  been  approximately  1  percent  a  year  in  recent  ye employment, measured by the count of persons who are working rather than by the count of jo been rising 2 percent a year since 1995 despite the acceleration in the growth of output per h between employment growth and population growth, amounting to about 1.2 million a year on ave has been made up, in part, by a decline in the number of individuals who are counted as unemp those persons who are actively seeking work -- of approximately 700,000 a year, on average, end of 1995. The remainder of the gap has reflected a rise in labor force participation that to a decline of more than 500,000 a year in the number of individuals (age 16 to 64) wanting not  actively  seeking  one.  Presumably,  many  of  the  persons  who  once  were  in  this  group  have recently become active and successful job-seekers as the economy has strengthened, thereby prev still sharper drop in the official unemployment rate. In May, the number of persons aged 16 wanted to work but who did not have jobs was 9.7 million on a seasonally adjusted basis, slig than 5½ percent of the working-age population. This percentage is a record low for the series, became available in 1970.

The gap between the growth in employment and that of the working-age population w inevitably close. What is crucial to sustaining this unprecedented period of prosperity is closing occurs in a disruptive or gradual, balanced manner. The effects of the crisis in Asia certainly damp net exports further, potentially moderating the growth of domestic production a employment. The strength of domestic spending that has been bolstering output growth and the for labor also could ebb if recent indications of a narrowing in domestic profit margins were be the forerunner of a reassessment of the expected rates of return on plant and equipment. prospects  for  the  return  to  capital  would  not  only  affect  investment  directly  but  could consumption as stock prices adjusted to a less optimistic view of earnings prospects. Finally, unsustainable rise of inventories that has been evident in recent quarters will be slowing at perhaps abruptly. An easing of the demand for labor would be an expected consequence of a slo in either final sales or inventory accumulation. Of course, the demand for labor that is cons particular rate of output growth also could be lowered if productivity were to continue to acce on the supply side of the labor market, faster growth of the labor force could emerge as th delayed retirements or increased immigration.

If developments such as these do not bring labor demand into line with its sust supply, tighter economic policy may be necessary to help guard against a buildup of pressures derail the current prosperity. Fortunately, fiscal policy has been moving toward restraint to although recent budgetary discussions do not appear to be focused on extending that tendency. policy might  need  to  tighten  if  demand  were  to  continue  to  exhibit  few  signs  of  abating  n thereby  threatening  to  place  still  further  strains  on  our  labor  markets.  We  at  the  Feder recognizing  the  powerful  forces  of  productivity  growth  and  global  restraint  on  inflation, perceived to date the need to tighten policy in response to strong demand, beyond what has through falling inflation's upward pressure on the real federal funds rate and the modest inc nominal rate that we initiated in March of 1997. But, we are monitoring the evolving forces ve to determine whether the recent acceleration of costs, albeit moderate, is likely to prove tra start of a more worrisome pattern that may well require a response.

In summary, Mr. Chairman, our economy has remained strong this year despite evide of substantial drag from Asia, and, at the same time, inflation has remained low. As I have in set of circumstances is not what historical relationships would have led us to expect at this business expansion, and while it is possible that we have, in a sense, moved 'beyond history have  to  be  alert  to  the  possibility  that  less  favorable  historical  relationships  will  even

themselves. That is why we are remaining watchful for signs of potential inflationary imbalan as the economy continues to perform more impressively than it has in a very long time.

title: Mr. Heikensten examines EMU and economic policy in Europe  (Central Bank Articles and Speeches, 29 May 98)
description: Speech by the Deputy Governor of the Bank of Sweden, Mr. Lars Heikensten, at JP Bank's Conference at the World Trade Center, on 29/5/98.
text:
Mr. Heikensten examines EMU and economic policy in Europe Speech by the Deputy Governor of the Bank of Sweden, Mr. Lars Heikensten, at JP Bank's Conferenc the World Trade Center, on 29/5/98.

This is not the end. It is not even the beginning of the end. But it is, perhaps, the end of the beginning.

Winston Churchill's declaration in November 1942, after the victory El Alamein, is, I think, applicable - in rather different circumstances - to EMU's co for economic policy in Europe after the weekend at the beginning of May.

Several years of intensive preparations for monetary union now lie behind us work, steeped in economic policy premises as well as technicalities, has been carried o different European settings. Many of the EU Member States have also worked hard both ready on time for EMU by fulfilling the Maastricht criteria and to complete the more and technical arrangements. It is now roughly a month since these processes were crown the historic decisions in Brussels to initiate European monetary union with eleven co couple of days from now, the new European Central Bank will be holding its first meetin

So there are good reasons to shift our attention and look ahead. The conve process has been successful in many respects and monetary union is to start in little mo months time. But once it has started, what challenges will EU's economic policy have What are the rules for this policy? How are the dialogue and decisions likely to deve next few years? These are some of the questions that I shall be considering today.

## 1.  Convergence

A  natural  starting-point  for  a  discussion  of  the  current  economic  situa Europe is the convergence reports that the Commission and the European Monetary Inst (EMI) presented at the end of March.

There are now two other matters that seem to be particularly important an will  no  doubt  receive  more  attention,  both  in  the  European  economic  debate  and  in decision-making processes in economic policy:

- One  has  to  do  with  the  degree  of  uniformity  in  cyclical  activity  an possibility of using judicious fiscal stances in different parts of the monetary union to make up for the absence of national discretion in monetary polic
- The  other  concerns  the  participant  countries'  economic  structures,  not how  their  labour  markets  function and  to  what  extent  they  are  sufficiently flexible both to cope with any shocks to stability and to bring unemplo down to more acceptable levels.

## 2.  Functions

EMU is a historically unique construction, with a common central bank that conduct monetary policy across national boundaries. At the same time, however, eleven governments are to conduct fiscal policies with eleven different budgets, besides mak other  decisions  that  affect  the  functioning  of  their  national  economies,  not  least markets.

## Monetary policy

In  a  monetary  union,  monetary  and  exchange  rate  policy  is,  by  definiti common  concern.  The  monetary  policy  objective  is  price  stability;  without  prejudice objective, monetary policy is to support the general economic policies in the Communi more budget policies focus on stability - and wages stay in line with productivity will be the room to manoeuvre in monetary policy.

The  ECB's  basic  tasks  will  be  to  define  and  implement  the  single  monet policy, conduct foreign exchange transactions, hold and manage the official foreign re the Member States, and promote the smooth operation of payment systems. The national c banks  (NCBs)  will  be  able  to  have  an  active  influence  on  policy,  participate  in  it implementation  and,  perhaps  not  least,  communicate  it  in  their  respective  countries analysis of the euro area will be undertaken centrally to a large extent and the leve rates will  be  decided  by  the  ECB  Governing  Council,  which  consists  of  the  members  o ECB's Executive Board and the NCB Governors of the, initially eleven, participating coun

The  European  System  of  Central  Banks  (ESCB)  has  been  given  a  highly independent  status  so  as  to  be  in  a  position  to  conduct  a  monetary  policy  for  pric without short-run political considerations. But its independence does not relieve the duty to inform and communicate. On the contrary, it accentuates the need for a dial exchange of information. The  common  interest  r normally not be ideal in relation to the economic situation in every country.

The national financial structures also differ considerably, which means t instance,  interest  rate  sensitivity  varies. ## Fiscal policy

Fiscal  policy  is  a  national  concern  but  the  national  room  to  manoeuv conditioned  by  various  EU  regulations.  The  Treaty  has  general  provisions  to  the  eff economic policy is to contribute to the achievement of Community objectives in accordan

the principle of an open market economy with free competition. The Member States are to their economic policies as a matter of common concern and are explicitly required to c them but the decisions are to be made on a national level.

Then  there  are  more  specific  agreements  on  matters  like  the  scale  of  ra value-added  tax,  government  subsidies  and  rules  for  public  procurement.  These  agree which  are  a  limited  constraint  on  the  construction  of  taxes  and  public  spending,  h concluded  mainly  for  purposes  other  than  stabilisation  policy  -  to  promote  competit establish a single market for capital, goods, services and labour.

The fiscal policy rules that have attracted most attention are those for go budgets  and  debt.  The  Maastricht  Treaty  stipulates  that  budget  deficits  are  not 3 per cent and that the government debt-to-GDP ratio ought not to exceed 60 per cent. intended  to  make  monetary  union  candidates  put  their  public  finances  in  order  p participation.

The Stability and Growth Pact has clarified what will apply once monetary has begun. The Pact can be said to consist of two parts: a surveillance mechanism for d an early stage that a country is starting to have budgetary problems and is in danger an excessive deficit, and a mechanism for sanctions on errant countries. The first m covers  all  the  EU  countries  and  requires  them  to  present  a  fiscal  policy  program sanctions mechanism, on the other hand, applies only to countries in the euro area. Th of  the  Pact  is  to  strengthen  political  mechanisms  at  union  level  so  that  budget  di permanently maintained. The  Pact  requires  every  Member  State  to  aim  for  a  medium-term  budgetar position close to balance or in surplus. Fiscal policy accordingly faces new challenges and it is not all that easy t what may happen. At the same time, the scope for will be curtailed in a sense by the Stability and Growth Pact, though this need not be a restriction in practice as long as the objective of medium-term balance or surplus stronger challenge is to be expected from the ongoing integration in the European Unio

EMU may accentuate. This process can be rather rapid, not least in financial markets. I for  goods,  pricing  in  a  single  currency  may  accelerate  the  existing  trend  towards differences in consumption taxes, for example.

## Structural and labour-market policy

Finally some words about structural and labour-market policy. This policy f much less clearly defined than the two I have already considered. It is affected by man rule  systems  at  both  national  and  EU  levels,  besides  belonging  to  the  competence  o different ministers and commissioners. The common agricultural policy and tax harmoni are two examples.

The components of structural policy that concern the internal market - compe laws, the whole of the market for goods and services, the mobility of capital, and lab mobility - are largely regulated at EU level. The competition laws are one example here.

Another component of structural policy is the regulations and other matte apply to the labour market. Many initiatives here have recently been taken at EU level speed things up and comply with political requirements in the Union. In these matters, most decisions have to be made at the national level. But the connection with condi monetary policy is evident: the better the economy can be made to work, the higher the that can be achieved without this generating increased inflation.

Monetary union is likely to accelerate the process towards increased integr Europe. In this way it will also contribute to new demands for structural adjustmen monetary union's primary purposes is, in fact, to stimulate competition and structura primarily to the benefit of consumers in the EU area. At the same time, such a develop probably entail a greater degree of joint action and harmonisation in the Union.

## 3.  Interaction

As I have outlined, monetary union involves a central direction of monetary and  a  broadly  national  direction  of  budget  policy,  though  discretion  in  budget demarcated by the Maastricht Treaty and the Stability Pact, for instance, and is bei curtailed by the gradual extension of international integration. At the same time, stru is to varying degrees a common EU concern. This raises the question of how a balanced can be constructed in such an environment.

## Bodies for decision-making and cooperation

One approach to this question involves describing the EU institutions tha been set up for economic policy decision-making and cooperation.

- Ecofin, as the decision-making body for the ministers of finance and econ is the principal forum in the field of economic policy. It is in this g for example, many of the decisions were taken so that monetary union co start  on  time.  The  budget  policies  of  the  Member  States  have  also monitored  here  and  this  will  continue  under  the  Stability  Pact.  More Ecofin draws up an annual 'budget statement', the Broad Economic Polic Guidelines, containing the principles for economic policy in the EU area.

- Most of the matters on the Ecofin agenda have been prepared by the Monet Committee,  which  besides  representatives  for  each  of  the  fifteen  Mem States (normally an under-secretary of state or a deputy central bank go includes representatives for the Commission and, more recently, for the When monetary union starts, the name of the Monetary Committee will b changed to Economic and Financial Committee but at present it seems that composition  will  be  unchanged  apart  from  the  EMI  being  replaced  by  t ECB.

Work on monetary union has been a heavy burden for these bodies in recent ye Meetings have been protracted and business has ranged from major issues like the Stabi Growth  Pact,  the  new  European  exchange  rate  system  (ERM2)  and  legislation  for  monet union to matters such as the design of the European coinage.

Some of the structure is now changing with the advent of monetary union but its basic features. The preparatory work is over, as is a good deal of the work conn ERM.  A  number  of  processes,  such  as  those  concerning  government  finances,  are  be modified. But this is accompanied by an increased need to discuss issues raised by t monetary union.

Now  that  the  countries  which  will  be  participating  initially  in  monetary have been singled out, moreover, an informal group - the Euro 11 Group - is being se discussions among the ministers of finance and economy in the euro area. The idea is group will concentrate on matters that concern just the participating countries and c greater need for dialogue and cooperation that they perceive in connection with the in monetary  union.  However,  this  is  not  a  decision-making  body  and  all  matters  conside Euro 11 are prepared by the Monetary Committee, in which all fifteen EU Member State represented.

The crucial institutional change is, of course, that as of next year the monetary policy will be fully centralised. The Treaty explicitly states that the ECB swayed by political considerations; its task is to concentrate on monetary policy. But dialogue will be needed with the governments in the EU and euro areas, in the first pla ministers  of  finance  and  economy.  The  Treaty  actually  provides  for  this  in  that  th president may participate in meetings of the ECB Governing Council and even submit mot Moreover,  representatives  of  the  NCBs  and  finance  ministries  will  continue  to  meet Economic and Financial Committee.

Monetary union raises many other institutional questions that I will not b up today. Not the least of these is relations with countries and organisations outside Union. Where, for instance, does the primary responsibility for the exchange rate lie and what about relations between euro area countries and the International Monetary Fund

I now want to hark back to the issues I touched on earlier: fiscal policy i to the business cycle, and how the labour market functions. How will these matters be h the system for economic policy decisions?

## Cyclical disparities and fiscal policy

The past year has seen a general strengthening of economic activity in t area.  This  has  helped  improve  government  finances  and  provided  better  conditions  in respects  for  the  start  of  monetary  union.  But  it  has  been  accompanied  by  increased disparities between the future euro countries. This is clear from a look at how obse revised their growth predictions as compiled, for example, in 'consensus forecasts'. the  euro  countries  divided  into  two  groups  with  higher  and  lower  predicted  GDP  gr respectively, shows that in the past year the gap between these groups has widened. T applies in terms of predicted inflation.

One should not make too much of this; the differences have grown but are small  and  assessments  for  1999  suggest  that  they  will  narrow  again.  But  the  pictu illustrate a problem that will have to be addressed. The single monetary policy is i both stimulating the economy in some countries and curbing it in others. Pressure on fi will accordingly vary across countries. For one thing, differences in automatic stab thus in cyclical sensitivity will automatically lead to country differences in budget another, different degrees of active fiscal policy will be needed to manage tensions th from a single interest rate throughout the monetary union.

This question has been deliberated informally for some time by economic po decision-makers in the European Union. It also underlies the discussions that are now EU's broad economic policy guidelines. In a way, it also contributed to the initiativ German  finance  minister  before  the  weekend  at  the  beginning  of  May,  when  some  fur reinforcement  of  budget  policy  in  the  coming  year  was  achieved  by  agreeing  on  an implementation of the Stability and Growth Pact's objective and an earlier productio annual convergence and stability programmes.

This is ultimately a question for which each country is responsible. Countr fulfil the Stability Pact's criteria will be entitled to a fiscal stance that is more e the ideal for European inflation. Today, moreover, there is cause for concern that cu policy may be too expansionary in some countries. But it is also clear that the cost policy mainly fall on the countries themselves. Higher domestic inflation eventually competitiveness; with exchange rates  irrevocably  fixed,  once  a  cost  crisis  is  there, difficult to rectify. Improved productivity can provide a remedy but achieving it is practice, this presumably leaves either fiscal tightening at a later stage to retard t increases or an adjustment of labour taxes, neither of which is simple.

For the credibility of the EMU project it is important that no country is a such  a  situation  at  the  start.  Countries  with  a  risk  of  high  inflation  are  theref experience strong pressure in various processes, for example in Ecofin. On the whole, i me that the question of adjusting fiscal policies to the ECB's monetary policy will issue. The same applies to how any fiscal adjustments are to be allocated across countr

## Labour market problems

It is an established fact that the functioning of the labour market is a many  Member  States.  A  solution  to  the  employment  question  clearly  presupposes  that European labour market is made to work more smoothly than before. The matter is also d connected  with  monetary  union.  There  will  no  longer  be  any  possibility  of  using  a monetary policy to deal with labour market shocks. It is then all the more importan labour market functions properly.

Employment growth in the EU area has been weak and unemployment in many countries has been high for a long time compared, for instance, with the United State force mobility is also lower than in the United States. But we also know that the Memb differ  considerably.  Some,  such  as  the  Netherlands  and  the  United  Kingdom,  have comparatively  successful  in  generating  new  jobs.  Others  have  done  considerably  worse remedies chosen by the successful countries vary, too. Some have adopted highly decent solutions  and  extensive  deregulation.  Others  have  sought  to  build  up  a  consensus  an minor changes in some public systems.

The  question  of  how  labour  markets  in  Europe  work  and  how  they  can  b improved  is  already  very  much  a  part  of  the  European  agenda.  There  have  been  pol initiatives  in  a  variety  of  contexts  in  recent  years,  including  national  actio employment. These plans include the analysis of labour market laws, effects of tax sys business conditions. Processes are being built up, inspired by the Maastricht Treaty's with budget policy. The annual employment guidelines require each Member State to pres national  action  plan  with  a  view  to  improving  people's  employability,  entrepreneuri flexibility  and  equality.  These  national  action  plans  are  to  be  specific,  with  goa schedules,  so  that  they  can  be  evaluated.  Good  examples  are  to  be  highlighted  so  t countries, if they wish, can adopt them.

Structural questions have been brought to the fore during the British Pre and there have been somewhat more concrete discussions in various committees about ho get  Member  States  in  step  here  as  well.  One  approach  involves  finding  good  exampl different fields, just as in the case of employment, and analysing the structural prob country. This process generates what the British call peer pressure, which can also co the desired national changes coming about.

Once  again,  however,  the  decisions  in  this  field  largely  have  to  be  m national level. But to perhaps an even greater extent than with fiscal policy, the majo a successful national policy will accrue to the country in question. By itself, this s and should facilitate changes. At the same time, the political resistance in most EU c strong.

Some believe that the very fact of monetary union will generate desired refo labour markets. Possibly but not necessarily - when high unemployment rates in recent in many EU countries have failed to produce changes, why, it may be asked, would mon union be more successful? In conclusion, I consider that much work at EU level will be in political education and a search for methods to gain support for changes in this fi not foresee the same pressure in the joint processes as in the case of fiscal policy; need of a common approach.

## Laborious but successful process

I should like to conclude with a summary and some tentative conclusions a the future course of the economic policy debate in the European Union.

1. There  are  important  interfaces  between  monetary  policy,  fiscal  polic structural policy. Problems concerning the composition of fiscal policy workings  of  the  labour  market  affect  the  room  to  manoe uvre  in  moneta

policy. This suggests that a vital dialogue will be needed between di parts of EU's economic policy decision-making system that are involved such  matters.  More  of  a  joint  appraisal  will  presumably  emerge.  N processes and institutions are also likely to develop.

2. The growing need for dialogue and a joint appraisal has already led t tasks  and  developments  for  a  number  of  EU  institutions.  Many  observe consider that this is true of Ecofin, which as a leading actor in the co of EMU has responded to new requirements. One example of a completely new structure is Euro 11, which is designed for the handling of joint is the  euro  area's  finance  ministers.  There  are  many  other  opportunitie dialogue, so those who fear that the ECB will be operating in something vacuum are likely to be mistaken.
3. Issues concerning fiscal  policies  in  EU/EMU  and  labour  markets  have  a arrived on the agenda in other ways, for example at the Monetary Committ This is partly because many consider than monetary union has accentuated need  for  a  joint  European  discussion.  With  monetary  union  soon  to launched, moreover, the agenda has more room for other matters. The Stabi and Growth Pact is one example of earlier initiatives in connection with Various  processes  have  likewise  been  started  to  bring  the  problem unemployment into the limelight.
4. There are strong grounds, in the fields I have discussed, for keeping d making essentially at a national level. The effects of the policies, fo in the labour market, mostly occur in the country in question. There a considerable  country  differences  in  such  matters  as  the  premises  for policy, the structure of government finances, labour market regulations on.  Still,  the  ongoing  integration  of  markets,  which  monetary  union stimulate, is presumably exerting increased pressure for reform.

The process that monetary union is now driving onwards is, in fact, fairly of EU cooperation in general. The European Union is a highly decentralised organisation and political legitimacy are essentially located at the national level. The joint budg Matters move forward in a process where external events, for instance in the global and  political  initiatives  modify  the  agenda.  Problems  are  often  managed  with  ar negotiated  compromises  between  sovereign  states.  Each  new  initiative  and  decision  f platform for the next phase. Monetary union, which is now leading to the appearance items on the agenda, is after all largely a consequence in its turn of earlier decision on the internal market.

This  process  may  sometimes  appear  to  be  rather  random  and  it  often  provi instances  of  uncertainties  and  risks.  But  it  is  a  process  that  has  gradually  brou countries closer together. And monetary union is an another, major step.
