text:
Mr. Erçel speaks on lessons for Turkish policy-makers from the East Asian crisis Address by the Governor of the Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey, Mr. Gazi Erçel, at the Euromoney Conference: Investing In The Future, in Istanbul, on 3/6/98.

It is a pleasure to address you at this new Euromoney Conference being he Turkey. I wish to thank Euromoney and its staff for arranging this conference, which h us reach a better understanding of the Turkish economy and the macroeconomic policies p by the authorities.

I would like to speak today about 'Lessons from the East Asian crisis for T policy-makers'. The financial crisis in the East Asian countries has had strong effe economies of the world, on industrial and emerging market countries alike. Some of thes have made themselves felt very quickly, while others will not run their course for anot three years. I may say that these effects are strong but not dangerous. One area of concern is capital flows to emerging market economies, which may increase spreads and about a capital market retrenchment.

According  to  a  study  conducted  by  the  Institute  of  International  Financ private capital flows to major emerging market economies have slowed only slightly belo 1997 level of $223 billion, but are well below their 1996 level of $304 billion. Bu coming  from  commercial  banks  and  direct  equity  investments  from  private  creditors decrease more than was expected, which means that capital flows will be smaller.

I do not wish to review the origins of the East Asian crisis in detail, bu us  that  it  is  the  structural  weakness  of  domestic  financial  systems  and  the  growin perception of that weakness that triggers a crisis in an economy. Like the Mexican peso East Asian crisis was a classic 'self-fulfilling prophecy' panic initiated by Jeffrey Sa

It is widely recognized that both the Mexican crisis and the crisis in the E countries stemmed from incorrect macroeconomic policies and structural imbalances. Exc rate policies in particular, combined with irresponsible fiscal policies, put enormous balance of payments. Weak domestic financial systems and rapid expansion of domestic c combined with pegged exchange rate regimes, deepen the economies' dependence on short-t external borrowing.

But it is a distinctive feature of the East Asian crisis that it is based private sector than were the public sector crises seen during the 1970s and 1980s. The found for the public-sector-based crises of those years were simpler. Programs support IMF,  and  much  less  government  borrowing  from  international  institutions,  were  the elements  in  the  solution  of  those  crises.  The  private-sector-based  crises  of  today complicated and harder to understand.

Let me follow up this brief summary by focusing my remarks this morning on f main areas where lessons from the recent East Asian crisis may be found.

First, it was the countries' ongoing exchange rate policies that contributed to the build up of crisis conditions. The countries of the East Asian region chose to purs exchange rate policy, or one pegged to the US dollar, for about a decade after the Pla In  the  beginning  these  policies  contributed  to  stronger  growth  and  low  inflation

countries. But starting in 1995, the appreciation of their currencies had begun to th balance-of-payments positions.

Second, to offset the weakness of their economies, the authorities relied on much short-term financing, which concealed the weaknesses of their macroeconomic pol The nature and direction of the flow of short-term international capital had not bee analyzed. The ratios of short-term debt to usable foreign exchange reserves were in th 170-200 percent for Indonesia, Korea and the Philippines, much higher than the average 70 percent for the other major emerging market economies.

Third, transparency of banking systems, including central banks, is essen analyzing ongoing  developments  in  countries'  financial  sectors.  In  particular,  trends off-balance-sheet  items,  cross-border  interbank  funding  and  their  transactions  with centers should first of all be transparent and second should be available for making about the system. The absence of a sufficiently thorough system of banking supervision lack of transparency not only became problematic before the crisis, but also caused c problems later on.

Fourth, the quality of the assets of the banking system is vital for the so macroeconomic policy. In allocating savings to investment use, the banks should be ex careful about the risks that must be taken for a variety of reasons. There are five m risk that the banking system and of course the appropriate authorities have to deal wi risk; foreign exchange risk; maturity risk; loan risk; and market risk. A sound financi the best assurance of efficient monetary and fiscal policies.

In  my  view,  all  four  of  these  factors  contributed  to  the  change  of perceptions and sentiment and produced a cutback in normal financing (in fact, 95 pe external flows to emerging market countries come from the private marketplace). This c in  turn,  weakened  the  external  reserve  positions  of  these  countries.  Then  the  combi weak reserves and a weak financial sector brought on a liquidity crisis.

We are now in a position to draw some lessons from the East Asian crisis. policy  implementation  must  pursue  sound  macroeconomic  policies  in  order  not  to  los confidence of the markets. And second, four main principles must constantly be kept in m

- The currency should not be allowed to appreciate, except as part of a anti-inflation program.
- Any  short-term  international  capital  flows  that  occur  must  be  care examined  to  determine  their  direction  and  nature.  In  addition,  the  r usable  external  reserves  to  short-term  debt  must  be  kept  at  reasonabl internationally accepted levels.
- Weak  banking  systems  have  been  the  most  important  contributors  to  pa crises. A sound and transparent banking system is an absolute requiremen avoiding future crises. Risk-taking strategies should be appropriate to system.  Off-balance-sheet  items  and  cross-border  lending  should  be  un tight discipline. An independent supervisory authority is the best guara efficient, sound, and effective banking supervision.

- Last  but  not  least,  the  pursuit  of  sound  macroeconomic  policies low-inflation environment is an essential precondition for building publ market  confidence.  Confidence  also  requires  that  both  public  and  pri sector institutions be guided by strong, high quality governance and ac ethical rules.

The last point that I want to make is that I disagree with those economi speak of the difficulty of anticipating the East Asian crisis, since these countries h all the ingredients of a perfect crisis recipe:

- An appreciated exchange rate;
- A high and worsening ratio of short-term debt to usable foreign reserves;
- Untransparent off-balance-sheet items in the banking sector;
- A widening current account deficit;
- Steep growth of domestic credits;
- And  a  continuous  decline,  during  recent  years,  in  emerging  marke borrowing spreads without matching improvement in their economic fundamentals.

If someone should combine all these elements, it is conceivable that they succeed in creating a crisis.

But the world's financial centers turned away from the existence of this crisis recipe and turned toward the Turkish economy, for which, ignoring the developm East Asia, they predicted a crisis during the last couple of years.

The Turkish economy does not satisfy the perfect crisis recipe described abo course we have high inflation, a high nominal budget deficit, and high short-term domes but on the other hand Turkey's exchange rate policy, current account situation, the na short-term external debt, and other fundamentals do not indicate an alarming situation.

The East Asian crisis should have greatly improved the ability of economi predict an episode. I would be glad to see some evidence of this improvement.

title: Mr. George gives a central banker's response to the Asian crisis  (Central Bank Articles and Speeches, 28 May 98)

Mr. George gives a central banker's response to the Asian crisis Speech by the Governor of the Bank of England, Mr. E.A.J. George, at the Foreign and Colonial Emerging Ma Conference, in London, on 28/5/98.

Thank  you,  Mr  Chairman.  I'm  delighted  to  participate  in  this  Emerging  Mark Conference, sharing the platform with such distinguished company. I am particularly pleas joined in this session by Guillermo Ortiz - my colleague from the Bank of Mexico.

The  storm  last  year  in  Asia  struck  essentially  the  ASEAN  four  -  Thailand Philippines,  Malaysia  and  Indonesia  -  spreading  subsequently  to  South  Korea  and  intermi battering Hong Kong and elsewhere.

It is still not wholly clear - to me at least - quite why the storm struck sud it did. Most crises of this sort have their origins in some evident macro-economic policy least in hindsight there are usually fairly clear tell-tale signs of expanding fiscal def monetary policies, classically accompanied by evidence of imbalance in the form of acce inflation or a rapidly deteriorating balance of payments. There were such signs, perhaps mo in  Thailand;  but  they  were  not  for  the  most  part  particularly  pronounced  in  Asia.  Some perhaps understand better than I do why the initial infection proved to be so contagious. all your money!

In fact through the first half of the 1990's, and in some cases for much lon countries in question had been remarkably successful. They attracted, by their very succ inflows of capital from the rest of the world, where yields had fallen, in the hope of ach returns.

Again with the benefit of hindsight, it is possible to identify a number of weaknesses in the mechanisms for financial resource allocation in the recipient countries. for example, a general lack of reliable financial information, and a lack of transparency i the  financial  position,  of  both  public  and  private  sectors.  Complex  and  opaque  links government,  financial  institutions  and  non-financial  companies  made  it  difficult  for  ou understand the real nature of their exposures. There was widespread, often informal, government influence over financial flows, which impo also  contributed  to  a  perception  that  much  of  the  borrowing  was  implicitly  under-writte government. The list could go on.

The problem was compounded by the absence of any real perception of exchange ra risk. Borrowers were evidently confident that governments would maintain their exchange ra against the dollar, even when the dollar itself began to strengthen, so that unhedged fore debt, much of it at short-term, appeared to be a cheap alternative to domestic currency The result was a build-up of short-term foreign currency liabilities, by banks and non-ba was not fully appreciated, and which left the Asian economies especially vulnerable to a capital in the event of a change in sentiment. So, once the run started, it was violent and contagious. For a time around th last year there was a significant possibility of a chain of default emanating from Asia tha reverberated right through the global financial system. The immediate task was to contain t

Essentially there are two broad options for dealing with a foreign currency cri is simply to allow financial markets - exchange markets, interest rates, and stock and bond take the strain, and to seek to restore confidence, and to moderate the impact of market m by restrictive macro-economic policy adjustment in the affected country. The second is to t the  financial  market  impact  and  the  extent  of  the  associated  macro-economic  adjustme providing or arranging alternative external financing. In practice these options are not mutually exclusive and the real question is the appropriate balance between them.

Where a country has transparently been pursuing an unsustainable macro-econom policy, most people find it easy to accept that that country should bear the burden and ad though  that  may  be.  Many  people  find  this  harder  to  accept  where,  as  in  the  presen conventional  macro-economic  policies  had,  for  the  most  part,  been  relatively  responsibl were  certainly  adjustments  to  macro-economic  policy  that  needed  to  be  made  -  a  more  fl exchange rate regime in some cases, for example, or a somewhat tighter overall macro-ec stance, with perhaps some adjustment between fiscal and monetary policy. But  there  are  real  dangers  in  extre movements or in excessively severe macro-economic adjustment to contain them. That, essentially, is why it may be in the self-interest of the international to attempt to mitigate the market and macro-economic adjustment pressures by providing fi support. Not surprisingly, too, there is resistance in many countries, including notably the United States, to the idea that public money should be used to bail out private creditors, especially foreign creditors.

In fact, in the critically important case - because of its size - of Korea, th massive official support failed to restore market confidence. And when it became apparent official bilateral financing was in practice available only as the very last resort we central banks as the immediate intermediaries - had to turn to the commercial bank lende major creditor countries and persuade them to extend the maturity of their loans. Like mos it was a dangerous moment. But the banks' constructive response went a long way to stabili immediate situation in relation to Korea - and thereby to the region as a whole. The cred are also now in negotiation with Indonesia's bank and commercial non-bank debtors.

I  can't  pretend  that  we  are  completely  out  of  the  wood  in  terms  of  the  e financial crisis in Asia, but there is now at least a good deal more light between the tree

International attention is now extending to managing the economic fall-out fro year's financial disturbances, against the background of the longer-standing financial and fragility in Japan - which is of course the largest economy in the Asian region. The concer part  to  the  implications  for  global  economic  activity;  but  it  relates  importantly, prospective external payments imbalances within the global economy which will need to be h very carefully if they are not to lead to trade frictions and/or exchange rate volatility.

But attention has also turned to an intensive reappraisal, in all sorts of i fora, of more effective means of preventing, and managing, such situations in the future.

It would have been understandable in the light of the Asian experience if th been some turning back from the path towards greater freedom of international capital mov and there has been some suggestion of this. But on the whole the international debate central banks as well as governments are actively involved - continues to recognise the benefits  of  free  capital  movements  and  the  contribution  that  they  can  make  to  global  e prosperity. The mood is to continue cautiously down that path, but to emphasise the need, for sound macro-economic policies, which everyone accepts as a sine qua non , but also for steps to accompany capital account liberalisation designed to reduce the risks of volatility.

In  a  broad  sense  a  need  for  greater  transpa recognised in relation to public policy, to the relationship between the public and privat corporate governance, accounting standards, and so on. title: Mr. Thiessen reports on globalized financial markets and monetary policy  (Central Bank Articles and Speeches, 27 May 98)
description: Notes for remarks by Governor of the Bank of Canada, Mr. Gordon Thiessen, before La Conférence de Montréal, in Montréal, on 27/5/98.
text:
## Mr.  Thiessen  reports  on  globalized  financial  markets  and  monetary  policy

Notes for remarks by Governor of the Bank of Canada, Mr. Gordon Thiessen, before La Conférence de Montréal, in Montréal, on 27/5/98.

Globalization  -  that  is,  the  growing  integration  and  interdependence  of  n economies - is changing dramatically the economic landscape. Countries are trading more go services,  an  increasing  number  of  firms  now  operate  across  national  borders,  and  sav borrowers have greater access than ever before to global financial markets. Over the pas world trade has grown twice as fast as world output, foreign direct investment three tim and both currency trading and share trading about ten times as fast.

Not everyone agrees that all this is good for individual national economies or world community at large. Among those who take a dimmer view of globalization, one conce that  the  increased  influence  of  international  financial  markets  is  eroding  the  ability governments  to  set  their  own  macroeconomic  policies.  They  also  worry  that  powerful  fin markets may be the main cause of crises such as those in Mexico in 1994-95 and in Southea in 1997.

You will probably not be surprised to hear that I do not share these negativ And today, I would like to discuss one particular aspect of globalization - how national policies work in an environment of globalized financial markets. I will draw heavily on own experience to support the view that monetary policy can continue to function effective increasingly integrated world.  Canada has a long history of being open to global markets services and capital. This interaction with the rest of the world has proven very succes view, and has benefited Canadians and our foreign partners enormously through the years.

With open international markets, Canadians have been able to sell their produc services abroad and to enjoy a wide variety of imported goods, some of which could not re produced at home. And we have been able to set up businesses and pursue investment opportu abroad.  Even  more  importantly,  we  have  been  able  to  use  foreign  savings  to  finance  th investment projects that were necessary to develop our industrial infrastructure and to i production potential, especially in the resource and manufacturing sectors. We have also h to technological innovations and processes developed elsewhere. This has allowed us to c new capital equipment and a skilled labour force more efficiently, thereby improving pro and, thus, our incomes and standards of living.

Nonetheless,  there  are  concerns  in  Canada,  as  well  as  elsewhere,  about  the increase in international financial flows and the implications thereof. How does the free of capital affect the conduct of national monetary policies?

## Capital mobility and the implications for monetary policy

The growing integration of national financial markets, as evidenced by the dr growth in the volume of cross-border capital flows since the early 1970s, has no doubt ch environment in which national economic policies are conducted. Globalization tends to bri policies under closer market scrutiny and to uncover and draw attention to any deep-seated problems that may exist. But I would not conclude from this that we have become captives markets and that we have lost control of our national monetary policies, as some argue.

First, let us be clear as to what 'having control' over one's own monetary actually means. When people talk about an independent or autonomous monetary policy, they take it to mean the ability of a central bank to set domestic interest rates without being

developments outside national borders. This is not realistic - unless of course a country i cut off from the rest of the world! The moment a country wants to make use of foreign sa invest a portion of its domestic savings abroad, a link between domestic and foreign inter inevitable.  As  a  major  user  of  foreign  capital,  Canada  has  long  lived  with  interest  ra closely related to those in the United States and other foreign financial markets.

But even with integrated financial markets, there is still room for monetary independence via exchange rate movements. Thus, monetary policy autonomy requires a flex exchange  rate  regime.  With  a  fixed  exchange  rate,  the  national  authorities  essentially monetary policy of another country - the country whose currency serves as the anchor. If rates go up in the anchor-currency country, interest rates will also have to rise suffi country with fixed exchange rates to ensure that the peg is maintained. Thus, if monetary focused  on  a  fixed  exchange  rate,  the  central  bank  cannot  at  the  same  time  pursue  a objective.

In the case of the European Union, where member countries have decided to ado single currency - the euro - they have essentially opted to give up the potential for an national monetary policy and to transfer the policymaking power to a supranational agen European Central Bank (ECB). Of course, the ability of the ECB to follow an independent Eu monetary policy will require that the euro float against other major outside currencies, US dollar and the Japanese yen.

Thus, in a world of open and integrated financial markets, the exchange rat major channel through which monetary policy actions are transmitted to the economy. Moreo is movements in the exchange rate that permit domestic interest rates to diverge from the counterparts for a period of time. For example, an increase in official interest rates b bank, in response to demand and inflation pressures in the economy, leads to a stronger which also works to restrain those pressures. At the same time, the appreciation of th creates the conditions for other domestic rates to follow the rise in official rates, to now be above those prevailing abroad. This is because the exchange rate is now seen to be expected  value  and  is  thus  likely  to  decline  in  the  future.  Under  these  circumstances markets will bid up domestic interest rates to compensate for the anticipated decline in value of the currency.

Having  clarified  the  issue  of  monetary  policy  independence,  I  would  now  lik discuss the effects of increased capital mobility on the conduct of monetary policy. A hig of capital mobility enhances still further the role of the exchange rate in the monetary process. This is not a bad thing. It just means we have to ensure that we always take th rate into account when considering the monetary policy stance that is appropriate for our economic  circumstances.  That  is  why  in  Canada  we  have  developed  the  concept  of  'monet conditions' to keep track of the combined effect on the economy of movements in both inter and the exchange rate.

With a flexible exchange rate system, the increased role of the exchange rate monetary transmission mechanism also means that it is crucial that investors' expectations currency movements are firmly anchored by clear and credible domestic macroeconomic policie

Thus,  the  central  bank  must  have  a  strong  commitment  to  preserving  the  int value of the currency by keeping inflation low. That is why in Canada we have adopted targets for inflation-control. But this is not enough. The fiscal situation must also be se control. Otherwise, as fiscal deficits and debts keep accumulating, investors will come t inflationary policies will be used in the future to reduce the burden of debt.

Canada's  experience  during  the  Mexican  currency  crisis  of  1994-95,  and  mo recently through the Asian problems, is very instructive in this regard. The Mexican cris the spotlight on our fiscal problems at the time, consequently driving risk premiums in o rates  sharply  higher.  During  the  recent  Asian  crisis,  however,  with  our  public  finances shape,  and  with  clear,  strong  policy  commitments  by  both  the  fiscal  and  monetary  auth financial markets have been more stable and our longer-term interest rates have been fallin

Of course, pressures on the exchange rate can also be triggered by so-calle shocks'. In Canada, such shocks are frequently associated with swings in world prices of commodities. In cases like these, a flexible exchange rate can act as a 'shock absorber' some of the necessary adjustments to the shock to take place through movements in the valu currency.

Canada's long-standing preference for flexible exchange rates has been driven l by the benefits such rates offer in facilitating adjustments to external shocks. This is consideration for us, given our strong reliance on international trade and foreign savings exporter of primary commodities, Canada has often been hit by sharp swings in the world p these products which, in turn, have caused large capital movements. Indeed, the decision our exchange rate in 1950 and again in 1970 (after a short period of fixed exchange rat related to strong inflows of foreign capital associated with a surge in commodity price cases, we chose to allow the Canadian dollar to float up, rather than try to maintain a fi rate and risk a destabilizing inflationary monetary expansion.

Overall, I am persuaded that a flexible exchange rate regime is the best wa country to take advantage of today's integrated capital markets and to deal with the exte that arise from time to time.

## Exchange rate fluctuations: Is taxing currency transactions the solution?

Some critics have argued that integrated international financial markets hav rise  to  large,  short-term  speculative  flows  of  capital  that  can  cause  unwarranted  exc pressures. Such speculative transactions, they say, disrupt domestic macroeconomic polici in  temporary  misallocations  of  resources,  discourage  trade,  and  encourage  further  unpr financial transactions as businesses and individuals seek to protect themselves.

Based on these arguments, some people have resurrected the idea of discoura currency transactions using a tax similar to the one proposed by Professor James Tobin in t

The case for taxing global financial transactions rests on the notion that s will discourage short-term flows, which are viewed as destabilizing, without affecting lo flows that are presumed to be desirable and based on fundamentals.

But short-term flows are by no means all undesirable and destabilizing. And t no  way  of  discriminating  between  useful  flows  and  destabilizing  speculative  ones.  For  e because foreign trade and investment inflows and outflows are not always fully offsetting, capital flows are typically needed to balance out a country's external accounts. These ca occur  in  response  to  actual  and  anticipated  movements  in  the  exchange  rate,  and  thus smooth out exchange rate fluctuations. Because such flows are often driven by small diffe perceived rates of return at home and abroad, they could well be discouraged by a transac On the other hand, speculative flows that actually 'bet' on a sharp movement in a curren rather large expected returns and are unlikely to be discouraged by the tax. In the end, a

tax would likely increase, rather than decrease, exchange rate volatility, as well as re liquidity and raise the cost of capital.

Needless  to  say,  where  financial  market  fluctuations  reflect  changes  in  do macroeconomic policies that put investors at greater risk than before, the tax would be treating the symptoms rather than the cause of the problem.

In all, I find the case for a tax on currency transactions completely unconvinc

## Promoting greater financial market stability

If a tax is not a good idea, how else can we promote greater stability in int financial markets and reduce potential disruptions to domestic policymaking?

I have already talked about the value of a flexible exchange rate system in fa adjustment to 'real' shocks and allowing national authorities to pursue an independent policy.  Flexible  exchange  rates  can  also  be  helpful  in  moderating  the  size  of,  and  aid adjustment to, capital flows.

In addition, governments are increasingly coming to the realization that the international financial stability is best addressed not by retreating into isolation or by distorting, costly restrictions, but rather through sound and transparent domestic economic

International  co-operation  can  also  help.  It  can  help  by  encouraging  count pursue national policies that lead to economic stability, thereby reducing the risk of sud in market sentiment and sharp exchange rate fluctuations. And it can help by setting widely standards  for  transparency  and  disclosure.  Such  standards  should  support  more  informed judgments about the riskiness of investments, especially in emerging market economies, a help avoid the crises that can be triggered by the sudden uncovering of problems.

Following the G-7 Halifax Summit in 1995, a series of international initiat improve the functioning of financial markets have been undertaken, mainly under the auspice International Monetary Fund and the Bank for International Settlements. These initiative enhance the transparency and disclosure of economic and financial data, strengthen the sur of national and global financial systems, develop mechanisms for support in times of cr provide training in financial sector supervision.

Recognizing  the  importance  of  these  efforts,  Canada  has  recently  proposed creation of a new international process to provide 'peer review' of national financial reg supervisory  systems.  Efficient  and  prudently  managed  national  financial  systems  can  red risks, and maximize the benefits, of international capital flows. In this regard, nationa authorities need to ensure that financial institutions have appropriate risk-management place to help minimize risks, particularly with respect to mismatching of maturities and This would make it easier to cope in the event that short-term inflows switched to outflo the main problems in Asia was that domestic financial institutions were borrowing shortforeign currency, to invest in illiquid domestic assets.

## Concluding thoughts

To  summarize,  globalization  has  been  broadly  beneficial  to  the  world  econo International financial markets have facilitated access by borrowers to a larger pool of gl and have enhanced investment opportunities for savers worldwide.

Yes, international capital flows have at times disrupted national financial But such episodes more often than not were caused by unsustainable domestic policies and to the need for adjustment.

In view of the overall benefits of greater access to global capital markets, it serve us well to restrict the free flow of funds. The best way to maximize the benefits globalization and reduce the risks of disruptions to national macroeconomic policies is to these policies are sound and sustainable. In addition, financial systems need to be prudent and supervised - both nationally and internationally.

Here  in  Canada,  we  are  following  this  advice  in  our  domestic  macroeconom policies.  And  we  are  also  strongly  supporting  and  contributing  to  global  initiatives  d promote financial market stability worldwide.
author: Gordon Thiessen

text:
Mr. Carse gives a banking supervisor's perspective on control issues in financ Speech  by  the  Deputy  Chief  Executive  of  the  Hong  Kong  Monetary  Authorit institutions Mr. David Carse, at the BanComp '98 conference in Hong Kong on 25/5/98.

I am pleased to be here this morning to speak to you at the start of this conf internal controls and anti-money laundering. The advertised title of my speech is 'Understa role and needs of the regulator in all authorised financial institutions'. This is a very and I have therefore narrowed it down to focus on the banking supervisor's perspective on issues in financial institutions. I am sure there are many compliance and audit professi audience today, so I trust I should not have too hard a hard job persuading you that go controls are not only important, but crucial to the success of financial institutions. Jus example, what poor internal controls did for BCCI, Daiwa Bank and Barings.

So what advice can I offer you today to help you ensure that your institution meet the same fate? Well, what I will do is to share with you my thoughts on the key elem financial institution's control systems, and highlight some of the areas where other insti gone horribly wrong. I will also talk about one of the key areas of a financial institutio its controls against being used for money laundering.

So let me start by giving you a banking supervisor's view of internal contro first,  what  exactly  do  we  mean  by  'internal  controls'?  The  definition  I  would  suggest, borrowed from the Basle Committee on Banking Supervision, is that internal controls refer ongoing process by which the Board of Directors and management of an institution ensure t institution  meets  three  key  sets  of  objectives.  First,  operational  objectives  -  the  e effectiveness of the institution in using its assets and other resources and in protecting from  loss.  Second,  information  objectives  -  the  reliability  and  completeness  of  fina management information needed for decision-making within the institution and for regulato other external uses. Third, compliance objectives - compliance with applicable laws and re supervisory requirements, and internal policies and procedures, in order to protect the franchise and reputation.

What, then, are the main elements of the sort of control systems needed to a these  objectives?  Basically,  there  are  five  inter-related  elements:  management  oversigh control culture; risk assessment; control activities; information and communication; and m activities. The Basle Committee on Banking Supervision has recently put all this together of fourteen principles for regulators to use in evaluating institution's internal control not propose to run through these one by one, but I would like to pick out one or two poin give you an idea of what I, as a regulator, see as the key ideas.

First, on management oversight and the control culture, the starting point is Board of Directors need to understand the risks run by the institution, to set the accepta these risks, and to ensure that senior management takes the steps necessary to identify, control these risks. Senior management must then take the responsibility to implement the approved  by  the  Board,  to  set  appropriate  internal  control  procedures,  and  to  moni effectiveness of these procedures.

This makes it quite clear where the main responsibility for controls rests - a fairly  and  squarely  on  the  shoulders  of  the  institution's  Board  of  Directors  and management, not just on its compliance and audit departments. However, having said that, e in  an  institution  shares  the  responsibility  to  some  extent.  A  key  task  for  the  Board management is to establish the right culture within the institution, a culture in which th of internal controls is stressed, and high ethical and integrity standards are promoted.

will be determined not simply by what the top levels of management say but what they d example, do the institution's remuneration policies reward risk-taking at the expense of Does senior management display a casual attitude towards breaches of limits? Do they encour right attitude towards regulatory compliance? Is there backing and respect at senior lev internal audit and compliance functions? The response of the senior levels of the organ these kind of issues will determine how personnel lower down actually behave in practice, their attitude to control issues.

Moving on to risk assessment, the important thing is to identify and evaluat factor that could adversely affect the achievement of the institution's objectives. This m the familiar risks of credit risk and liquidity risk, but also risks such as operational r risk, market risk, country and transfer risk, legal risk and reputational risk. And this ongoing process, continually re-evaluating the risks and reviewing the control systems t these risks.

Regarding control activities, the point I would stress is that control activi be  an  integral  part  of  the  daily  operations  of  an  institution.  Examples  of  this  inclu reviews of performance and risk exposure; appropriate activity controls that monitor per and exceptions at the departmental or divisional level; segregation of duties; physical access to assets; periodic checking for compliance with exposure limits; a system of appr authorisations for transactions over certain limits; and a system of verification and rec transaction details and activities. The objective should be to ensure that all areas of the continually in compliance with established policies and procedures.

On information and communication, it should be self-evident that an institutio comprehensive and timely financial, operational and compliance data, and so needs to hav information  systems.  But  having  the  information  is  only  the  first  step.  Equally  import second step, that the information should get to the right people at the right time.

Finally,  on  monitoring,  it  cannot  be  overstressed  that  that  monitoring effectiveness of an institution's internal controls should be a continual and ongoing proc monitoring of key risks should be an integral part of the daily operations of the institut and independent internal audit and compliance functions have an important role to play h requires these functions to have direct access to senior levels of the organisation so t criticisms of systems or transactions cannot be blocked by the line management concerned.

These, then, are what I would regard as the key elements of a financial inst internal controls. As regards how these are applied to individual institutions, my expec banking  supervisor  is  that  any  financial  institution,  regardless  of  size,  should  have system of internal controls that is consistent with the nature, complexity, and risk of its that  responds  to  changes  in  the  institution's  environment  and  conditions.  I  am  not  say expect every institution to be using state-of-the-art risk management and control techn what  I  do  expect  is  that  every  institution  should  have  control  systems  that  adhere  to principles  I  have  just  discussed,  and  which  are  as  state-of-the-art  as  they  need  to  be particular  institution's  activities.  I  also  expect  these  systems  to  be  kept  under  revi change.

Let me now move on to discuss some of the things that can go wrong when contr break down. I will not go into particular case studies, but will try instead to draw toge the common threads of recent problem bank cases. The Basle Committee paper that I menti earlier suggests five such common threads, and I will draw on this in the following remarks

The first, which I have mentioned already, is lack of adequate management over and accountability, and failure to develop a strong control culture within the institut exception, a common feature of recent problem bank cases has been management inattention t laxity in, the control culture of the institution, insufficient guidance and oversight by Directors  and  senior  management,  and  a  lack  of  clear  management  accountability  throug assignment of roles and responsibilities. These cases also reflect insufficient incentives strong line supervision and maintain a high level of control consciousness within business

The second thread is inadequate assessment of the risk of certain banking act whether  on  or  off  balance  sheet.  Many  banking  organisations  that  have  suffered  major neglected  to  continually  assess  the  risks  of  new  products  and  activities,  or  update assessments  when  significant  changes  occurred  in  the  environment  or  business  conditions. recent  cases  highlight  the  fact  that  control  systems  that  function  well  for  tradition products are unable to handle more sophisticated or complex products.

The third thread is the absence or failure of key control activities, such as of duties, approvals, verifications, reconciliations, and reviews of operating performan segregation of duties in particular has played a major role in the significant losses that at banks.

The  fourth  thread  is  inadequate  communication  of  information  between  levels management within the bank, especially in the upward communication of problems. To be effe policies and procedures need to be effectively communicated to all personnel involved in an Some losses in banks occurred because relevant personnel were not aware of or did not und the bank's policies. In several instances, information about inappropriate activities that been reported upward through organisational levels was not communicated to the Board of Di or  senior  management  until  the  problems  became  severe.  In  other  instances,  informat management reports was not complete or accurate, creating a favourable impression of a b situation that was in fact problematic.

The  fifth  and  final  thread  is  inadequate  or  ineffective  audit  programs  an monitoring activities. In many cases, audits were not sufficiently rigorous to identify a control weaknesses associated with problem banks. In other cases, even though auditors problems, they were not corrected by management.

From  these  common  threads,  it  should  now  be  clear  why,  in  the  first  part  o remarks  today,  I  stressed  the  things  I  did  -  management  oversight  and  control  cult assessment, control activities and monitoring, and information and communication. These areas that institutions need to focus on to avoid becoming a 'problem bank case' themselves

Let me move on now to consider the role of the banking supervisor in ensuring an institution's internal controls are adequate and effective. This is an area on which t greatly increased emphasis in recent years. Of course supervisors, like the management of institutions, have always been concerned with the quality of control systems. However, the has been rather piecemeal, and has focused on certain types of risk which are easily qu rather than the more intangible types of risk. What we are trying to do nowadays is to mov a more systematic identification and assessment of the risks facing a bank across the whol its activities and the adequacy of the controls over these risks.

This 'risk-based' approach is intended to focus our attention on what we see institution's key risk areas. Of course, the correct identification of the institution's crucial  in  this.  For  most  of  Hong  Kong's  local  banks,  credit  risk,  liquidity  risk  a

reputational risk remain the highest risk areas, but for individual institutions other for as interest rate risk and market risk also come into the equation. If an institution engag business that we regard as being at the higher end of the risk scale, such as share margin lending for property development, this will also attract our attention. Other things tha our attention include major changes in the operating environment, including new technolog or activities which are experiencing rapid growth; the introduction of new lines of busines or activities; and domestic and foreign acquisitions. In each case we would want to be as any necessary enhancements to the control environment have been made so as to reduce the of adverse and unforeseen effects on the institution.

Different risk areas require different approaches, but essentially our appro start by reviewing the written policies and procedures setting down the controls over a area, and then to look at how the controls work in practice. This may involve a combin reviews of documentation, discussions with staff, and some testing of transactions. The will be a judgement as to whether we believe the controls are effective or need improv improvement is needed we will discuss our recommendations with the management and agree action plan and time-scale for the remedial action.

This may sound to you quite similar in some respects to the work of an instit internal audit department and external auditors. I would agree that there are certainly so features, and indeed we would usually review as part of our own work the work done by th department on identifying areas of potential risk and control problems. Similarly, externa observations  and  recommendations  are  often  very  useful  to  us  in  coming  to  a  judgement effectiveness of an institution's internal controls. However, to supervise an institution supervisor needs, in my opinion, a means of independently verifying that internal controls and  that  all  substantive  risks  have  been  identified  and  considered.  For  this  reason,  o dialogue  with  institutions,  and  our  periodic  on-site  examinations  of  institutions'  ac invaluable.

I believe this oversight can also be beneficial in a practical way to the itself. For example, we may have insights that the institution does not. We may be able institution feedback on how it compares vis-à-vis its peers in similar areas and to indicat which, from our experience, its controls and risk management processes are falling behind I would not want to overplay this 'management consultant' type role, but I think it can be perhaps especially to the smaller, less sophisticated financial institutions. Of course, th that we have the necessary expertise to offer useful advice. This is a constant challeng environment  of  rapid  technological  change  and  product  innovation.  We  have  therefore  tr develop  our  own  treasury  and  securities  specialists  whose  task  it  is  to  review  and  as leading-edge  and  sophisticated  areas  such  as  value  at  risk  and  treasury  and  derivat management.

Let me move on now to the subject of the prevention of money laundering. This key concern for the supervisors of all major international financial centres, and is so should be high on the agenda for the management of every financial institution.

Here in Hong Kong considerable time and effort has been put in over a perio years into ensuring that the banking system follows best international practice on the pr money laundering. Principally, this means following the recommendations of the Basle Comm on  Banking  Supervision  and  the  Financial  Action  Task  Force,  whose  guidance  notes  on prevention of money laundering we have used to develop our own detailed Guidelines to insti The basic thrust of these Guidelines is to provide that institutions should have in place effective  policies,  procedures  and  controls  to  combat  money  laundering,  covering  essent

such as procedures for account opening, customer identification and record keeping as well systems for reporting suspicious transactions and training of staff.

Please be in no doubt as to how seriously we regard adherence to these Guide The reason for this is simple. To paraphrase the health warning on a packet of cigarette laundering  can  seriously  damage  your  health'.  Being  associated  with  money  laundering seriously undermine confidence in an individual financial institution and potentially in system as a whole. We are presently seeing this demonstrated in the case of the Mexican system, which is embroiled in a money-laundering scandal.

So  what  steps  can  a  banking  supervisor  take  to  ensure  that  institutions  ar everything they can to protect themselves from being used for money laundering? The first to make sure that the Guidelines issued to institutions are kept up-to-date as techniques of  money  laundering  evolve,  and  to  ensure  that  institutions  revise  their  own  internal accordingly. We have recently revised our Guidelines and issued them as a convenient bookl pleased  to  say  that  demand  for  this  has  been  high  and  we  have  issued  over  5000  copies booklet. However, Guidelines need to be put into practice. To ensure that senior managem focused on the need for this, money-laundering controls are a regular agenda item for our meetings with management. They are also a regular topic for our on-site examinations. Duri examinations we review an institution's policies and procedures, look at their records of transactions, and interview staff at random to check that they have been trained to identif transactions  and  to  follow  the  appropriate  procedures  for  account  opening  and  cu identification. We may also commission external auditors' reports if we think it necessary.

So how do institutions in Hong Kong rate on combating money laundering? Perha the best indicator of their vigilance against money laundering is the number of reports of transactions  made  to  the  Joint  Financial  Intelligence  Unit  (JFIU).  These  numbers  sugg institutions are certainly improving, as both the number of reports, and the number of making reports, has been increasing over time. The number of reports made to the JFIU ro only  264  in  1992  to  4210  in  1997.  Our  own  on-site  examinations  also  suggest  that  the awareness, and the training of staff, is improving. So, overall, institutions are doing we there is always room for improvement, and I would urge those with responsibility for this relax their guard.

This brings me to my concluding remarks. I started out today by talking abou important elements of a control system, and how banking supervisors assess the effectiv institutions' controls. I discussed some of the common threads of recent 'problem bank' c the control issues they highlighted. Finally, I stressed the importance of controls in the laundering prevention. While I hope this was of interest to you, and at least gave you different perspective on some familiar issues, I think I should end by saying that I cer claim to having all the answers. Please do not sit back and expect the banking supervisor guidelines telling you exactly what you need to do. While I hope my advice may be of some h responsibility for ensuring that your institution has the right controls and the right cu So  I  hope  this  conference  provides  you  with  some  useful,  practical  ideas  for  improvi institutions' controls when you return to work.

title: Mr. Greenspan gives a testimony on the global financial system and the role of the IMF in the Asian crisis  (Central Bank Articles and Speeches, 21 May 98)
description: Testimony of the Chairman of the Board of Governors of the US Federal Reserve, Mr. Alan Greenspan, before the Committee on Agriculture of the US House of Representatives on 21/5/98.
text:
Mr. Greenspan gives a testimony on the global financial system and the role o the IMF in the Asian crisis Testimony of the Chairman of the Board of Governors of the U Federal Reserve, Mr. Alan Greenspan, before the Committee on Agriculture of the US Hous Representatives on 21/5/98.

The  global  financial  system  has  been  evolving  rapidly  in  recent  years. technology  has  radically  reduced  the  costs  of  borrowing  and  lending  across  traditional borders, facilitating the development of new instruments and drawing in new players. Infor transmitted instantaneously around the world, and huge shifts in the supply and demand f naturally follow, resulting in a massive increase in capital flows.

This  burgeoning  global  system  has  been  demonstrated  to  be  a  highly  effic structure that has significantly facilitated cross-border trade in goods and services and, has  made  a  substantial  contribution  to  standards  of  living  worldwide.  Its  efficiency  ex punishes  underlying  economic  imprudence  swiftly  and  decisively.  Regrettably,  it  also  app have facilitated the transmission of financial disturbances far more effectively than ever

Three years ago, the Mexican crisis was the first episode associated with o high-tech international financial system. The current Asian crisis is the second.

We do not as yet fully understand the new system's dynamics. We are learning and need to update and modify our institutions and practices to reduce the risks inherent regime. Meanwhile, we have had to confront the current crisis with the institutions and we have.

Many argued that the Asian crisis should be allowed to run its course without from  the  International  Monetary  Fund  or  the  bilateral  financial  backing  of  other  nati asserted that allowing this crisis to play out, while doubtless having additional negati growth in Asia, and engendering greater spill-overs onto the rest of the world, would not a large or lasting impact on the United States and the world economy.

They  may  well  have  been  correct  in  their  judgment,  and  some  would  argue  t events  over  the  past  six  months  have  proved  them  right;  we  have  so  far  avoided  the continuing downward spiral that some feared. There was and is, however, a small but not ne probability that the upset in East Asia could have unexpectedly large negative effects on J America, and eastern and central Europe that, in turn, could have repercussions elsewhere, the United States. Thus, while the probability of such an outcome may be small, its conseq my judgment, should not have been left solely to chance. We have observed that global f markets, as currently organized, do not always achieve an appropriate equilibrium, or at l time to stabilize. Moreover, the effects of the Asian crisis on the real economies of the affected countries, as well as on our own economy, are only now just being felt.

Opponents  of  IMF  support  for  member  countries  facing  international  financ difficulties also argued that such substantial financial backing, by cushioning the losses investors, encourages excessive risk-taking. There doubtless is some truth in that, though has been the expectation of governments' support of their financial systems that has been obvious culprit, at least in the Asian case. In any event, any expectations of broad ba turned out to have been disappointed. Many if not most investors in Asian economies have suffered substantial losses.

Moreover, the policy conditionality, associated principally with IMF lending, dictates  economic  and  financial  discipline  and  structural  change,  helps  to  mitigate  so

inappropriate risk-taking on the part of governmental authorities. At the root of the p been poor public policy that has resulted in misguided investments and very weak financial Convincing  a  sovereign  nation  to  alter  destructive  policies  that  impair  its  own  perfor threaten contagion to its neighbors is best handled by an international financial institu the IMF. What we have in place today to respond to crises should be supported even as we improve  those  mechanisms  and  institutions.  Some  observers  have  also  expressed  concern whether we can be confident that IMF programs for countries, in particular the countrie Asia,  are  likely  to  alter  their  economies  significantly  and  permanently.  My  sense  is consequence of this Asian crisis is an increasing awareness in the region that market cap practiced  in  the  West,  especially  in  the  United  States,  is  the  superior  model;  that  is greater promise of producing rising standards of living and continuous growth.

Although  East  Asian  economies  have  exhibited  considerable  adherence  to  man aspects  of  free-market  capitalism,  there  has,  nonetheless,  been  a  pronounced  tendency government-directed  investment,  using  the  banking  system  to  finance  that  investment.  G record of real growth rates of close to 10 percent per annum over an extended period of tim surprising that it has been difficult to convince anyone that the economic system practi Asia  could  not  continue  to  produce  positive  results  indefinitely.  Following  the  break increasing awareness, bordering in some cases on shock, that their economic model was inco or worse, has arguably emerged in the region.

As a consequence, many of the leaders of these countries and their economic adv are endeavoring to move their economies much more rapidly toward the type of economic sy that we have in the United States. The IMF, whatever one might say about its policy advi past,  has  played  an  important  role  in  this  process,  providing  advice  and  incentives  th sound money and long-term stability. The IMF's current approach in Asia is fully supporti views of those in the West who understand the importance of greater reliance on market reduced  government  controls,  scaling  back  of  government-directed  investment,  and  embr greater transparency -- the publication of all the data that are relevant to the activiti bank, the government, financial institutions, and private companies.

It  is  a  reasonable  question  to  ask  how  long  this  conversion  to  embracing  m capitalism in all its details will last in countries once temporary IMF financial support an end. We are, after all, dealing with sovereign nations with long traditions, not alway with market capitalism. But my sense is that there is a growing understanding and apprec the  benefits  of  market  capitalism  as  we  practice  it,  and  that  what  is  being  pres IMF-supported programs fosters their own interests.

Similarly, it is a reasonable question to ask whether the US authorities sh seek greater assurance that the ongoing process of reform in the IMF's policies and opera produce additional concrete results before we agree to augment the IMF's resources. I have believe that the management and staff of the IMF are committed to a process of change. We somewhat  more  difficult  task  in  convincing  the  IMF's  membership  as  a  whole  of  the  nee change. However, I am confident that our leverage in this regard would be reduced if th States failed to agree promptly to the proposed increases in the IMF's resources.

Accordingly, I continue fully to back the Administration's request to augmen financial  resources  of  the  IMF  by  approving  as  quickly  as  possible  US  participation  in Arrangements to Borrow and an increase in the US quota in the IMF. Hopefully, neither will to  be  needed,  and  no  funds  will  be  drawn.  Although  the  tendency  in  recent  months  t stabilization in the East Asian economies is encouraging, clearly those economies are not woods  as  recent  events  attest.  Moreover,  we  have  not  yet  put  in  place  the  strengtheni

international financial architecture that would enable us in the future to place less re IMF to deal with potential systemic crises. Thus it is better to have the IMF fully equippe response to a pending crisis is essential.

title: Mr. Heikensten examines economic policy and the fight against inflation in Sweden  (Central Bank Articles and Speeches, 27 May 98)
description: Speech by the Deputy Governor of the Bank of Sweden, Mr. Lars Heikensten, at the Meeting of Almega-Affiliated Employers' Associations on 27/5/98.
text:
Mr. Heikensten examines economic policy and the fight against inflation in Sweden Speech  by  the  Deputy  Governor  of  the  Bank  of  Sweden,  Mr.  Lars  Heikensten,  at  the  Meeting

Almega -Affiliated Employers' Associations on 27/5/98.

Thank you for the invitation to attend your meeting and talk about economic poli inflation.  Today  I  shall  begin  with  a  brief  review  of  the  historical  background  to  the  f inflation in the Swedish economy. It is worth recalling that more than eight years have pass was decided in Sweden that combating inflation would have top priority. This policy has been consistently ever since. After a couple of initial years that were troublesome in many ways, have been encouraging and Swedish stabilisation policy now looks good even in a European compar This  will  be  followed  by  a  discussion  of  three  policy  fields-fiscal  policy,  labour  market formation-that  are  closely  linked  to  monetary  policy,  as  well  as  some  remarks  about  compe conditions in Sweden's economy. Successful results in these policy fields enlarge the room to m in monetary policy. In conclusion I shall consider some topical monetary policy issues, inc current appraisal of inflation and monetary policy's construction.

## 1.  The fight against inflation and its results

High inflation characterised Sweden's economy for a number of years in the 1970s 1980s, a period that clearly illustrates an inflation economy's negative consequences. Repeate were  made  to  rectify  the  economic  imbalances  by  means  of  devaluations  and  fiscal  stimu development remained unstable. The problems with inflation were then accentuated when the fin markets were deregulated. Prices and wages rose steeply and Sweden was caught in wage-price s The  occurrence  of  price  bubbles  made  investment  decisions  more  hazardous  and  led  to productivity. A high level of inflation became a permanent feature of our economy. As monetar at that time was focused on maintaining a fixed exchange rate, fiscal policy ought to have been

Bit by bit, there was a growing awareness across party political lines that in t run this economic policy strategy was not viable, a perception that had already dawned on most in our part of the world in the early 1980s. It was now that low inflation in Sweden came to b necessary condition for achieving stable and sustained growth and thereby high employment. Th clearly  expressed  officially  for  the  first  time  in  the  Budget  Statement  in  January  1991. inflation was given pride of place on the economic policy agenda. The final policy objectives same as before but the perception of the conditions that were needed to attain them had changed

This realignment of stabilisation policy occurred, however, at a time when the policy's  negative  consequences  had  begun  to  leave  their  mark.  Due  to  the  high  level  of manufacturing, for example, economic growth in Sweden was weak. In addition, a rising real inte coincided with a period when the tax reform made savers and investors more sensitive to inter All this had a marked downward effect on domestic demand.

The drop in output-almost 6 per cent in the course of three years-meant in turn government finances worsened dramatically. From a surplus at 4.2 per cent of GDP in 1990, the balance swung to a deficit of 12.3 per cent in 1993. In this period, moreover, registered un shot up from 1.7 to 8.2 per cent.

In a way, the economic crisis in the early 1990s can be said to have been gener political decisions. The combination of a stabilisation policy realignment with some structur did play a part in the course of the crisis. But it should also be underscored that such m broadly  essential.  The  problem  was  not  so  much  the  measures  that  were  implemented  when inflationary bubble had already developed as the fact that policy had not been realigned earlie

In recent years, economic developments in Sweden have been favourable. Growth h been stronger than in the high phase in the late 1980s and it has proved possible to combine g with  low  inflation.  A  couple  of  years  after  the  realignment  of  economic  policy,  inflation

sharply to around 3 per cent. Moreover, the reduction of current inflation has been accompa downward  revision  of  inflation  expectations.  Today,  neither  households,  firms  nor  financia agents perceive any serious threat from inflation in the coming five years.

Government finances have also improved markedly since the effects of the acute cri the early 1990s were overcome. After rapid budget consolidation, a surplus of 1.6 per cent is 1998. Government debt has been reduced since 1995. Still, the restoration of confidence did t time.  There  were  strong  and  persistent  doubts  about  both  the  determination  and  the  abili Government and the Riksdag (Sweden's parliament) to carry out the proposed measures.

Finally it is worth noting that the steps for reorienting economic policy on stab taken  with  a  consensus  that  was  considerably  broader  than  is  sometimes  suggested  by  the  p debate. A good foundation for the years ahead has now been laid, although high unemployment is serious problem for Sweden's economy. The positive picture is underpinned by institutional re the budget process and the status of the Riksbank.

## 2.  Three fields of importance for monetary policy

Now  I  should  like  to  turn  to  some  issues  or  policy  fields  that  are  of  major importance  for  monetary  policy.  They  are:  fiscal  policy,  the  labour  market,  wage  format competitive conditions in the Swedish economy. It is generally the case that the more price supported  by  other  policy  fields,  the  greater  the  contribution  monetary  policy  can  make economic policy goals.

## Good fiscal foundation but storing up for lean years is advisable

Fiscal policy is relevant for monetary policy in a number of ways. Fiscal decisio the room to manoeuvre in monetary policy not only via their direct impact on demand-and henc inflation-but also by how they influence economic policy's credibility. A fiscal policy that i as  being  untenable  in  the  longer  run  can  raise  doubts  about  the  overall  policy  commitment inflation and stability. To this should be added fiscal policy's influence on the macro economy in which taxes are levied and public revenue is spent influence the behaviour of households which  may  thereby-generally  in  the  longer  run-alter  the  economy's  inflation  propensity.  T however, I shall not be developing this aspect.

In the first respect-fiscal policy's impact on economic activity-the picture is cl in recent years the fiscal stance has been very tight. Of course, this has contributed to t inflation and in this sense it has assisted monetary policy. With the current fiscal proposals ahead, however, the stance will not be as tight as before. But to some extent the growth of income is still being restrained by the overall change in taxation and public spending.

As regards credibility, there has been a marked improvement. Last year the Govern laid down a long-term objective for government finances which goes further than the average corresponding  commitments  in  Europe.  Over  the  business  cycle  the  budget  balance  is  to  ave surplus of 2 per cent of GDP. The Riksdag has approved this objective.

The Riksbank finds this objective reasonable. A budget surplus over the business can  contribute  to  a  speedier  reduction  of  government  debt,  which  is  currently  high.  This  w greater freedom of action for future economic policy, which is particularly important in tha public finances are no doubt still relatively sensitive to the cyclical economic situation. But further challenges in store for fiscal policy. An ageing population implies new and growing req for example. Another matter that may alter the conditions for fiscal policy is the increased mo bases, which in some respects may make it difficult to maintain present levels of taxation.

Better wage settlements but what about the next round?

As things now stand, fiscal policy will continue to provide good room to manoeuv monetary policy in the coming years. So what about the contributions from the labour market a formation?

Of the aggregate value-added in the Swedish economy, wages make up almost 70 pe cent. Wage trends are therefore crucial for the path of inflation. For many years, the wage ri has been above the rate in most other countries in Europe. But as we all know, instead of Swedish employees a better real wage, the outcome has been the reverse. In the 1990s the rate increases in Sweden has been curbed but the negotiated increases in the 1995 round were ab European average.

As I mentioned earlier, economic policy in Sweden has been focused on low infla since 1991. A consistent implementation of this policy, with an inflation target, clarifies th game for wage formation. High wage increases are liable to boost inflation, which necessitat interest rates.

The  inflationary  consequences  of  the  wage  increases  can  be  modified  if  product growth is good, as has been the case in recent years. But at least a part of this productiv achieved at the expense of jobs; this is one aspect of the process whereby higher labour cos stronger rationalisation and maybe also an increased capital input. In this way, too, and not the higher interest rates directly affect demand and employment, a rapid wage rise is liable jobs.

Against this background, the outcome of the latest wage negotiations is better earlier years. Agreements for the next three years have been concluded at levels around 3 per It has been said that this takes wage drift into account but that is probably not entirely th one should no doubt count on wage drift averaging around 1 per cent. ## 4.  Conclusion

Stabilisation  policy  in  Sweden  was  realigned  in  the  early  1990s  and  focused  o inflation.
