title: Mr. Tietmeyer discusses the benefits, opportunities and pitfalls of financial and monetary integration  (Central Bank Articles and Speeches, 18 May 98)
description: Address by the President of the Deutsche Bundesbank, Prof. Hans Tietmeyer, at the 1998 Mais Lecture at the City University Business School, in London, on 18/5/98.
text:
Mr. Tietmeyer discusses the benefits, opportunities and pitfalls of finan and  monetary  integration Address  by  the  President  of  the  Deutsche  Bundesbank, Prof. Hans Tietmeyer,  at  the  1998  Mais  Lecture  at  the  City  University  Business  Sch London, on 18/5/98.

First of all, I wish to thank you very much for your kind invitation.  I a to  have  the  opportunity  to  give  this  year's  Mais  Lecture  and  to  share  with  you  som thoughts.  It  is  a  great  honour  for  me  to  be  invited  to  continue  the  sequence  of  o personalities  who  have  established  and  maintained  the  tradition  and  reputation  of Lecture with their talks.

At the same time, I am happy to be here in London once again. For every vi London  is  a  wonderful  city  full  of  culture  and  history.    For  a  central  banker,  Lon addition, a large and efficient financial centre. Its strong points include, not least infrastructure  in  economics  and  business.  The  City  University  Business  School  is  mak important contribution to that.

I should of course like to add: I come from a financial centre on the c which likewise has some strong points. And experience shows: competition is always stim for both sides. Thus, the two financial and monetary centres, London and Frankfurt, go s towards symbolising tonight's topic: Financial and Monetary Integration: Benefits, Oppo and Pitfalls.

I

I should like to begin with the hypothetical question: What will historian future  regard  as  the  most  important,  forward-looking  features  of  the  close  of  the century? Perhaps they will point to the following three features:  Firstly: following of  the  competition  between  the  political  systems,  the  competition  of  the  economic between a market economy and a centrally planned economy likewise seems to have come to end.  At  any  rate,  the  state  socialist  model  as  a  competitor  of  the  free  market  ec foundered - not only because it was dissolved in and together with the Soviet Union former  sphere  of  influence;  what  is  more,  it  is  no  longer  a  serious  reference  mode development of emerging economies; not even for China.

Secondly: economic historians may, later on, perhaps see the present time period of dramatic technical and economic upheaval - of 'creative destruction' in Schu phrase. In particular, basic innovation in microelectronics is being reflected in lots innovations  which  are  now  more  and  more  reaching  application  status  and  in  many  pr innovations becoming increasingly marketable.

And  thirdly:  we  contemporaries  are  speaking  more  and  more  of  an  era progressive  economic  integration,  at  both  a  regional  and  a  global  level.  Globalisat keyword in today's discussion.

These three features are of course interlinked. The victory of the market e system and the decline in transportation and communication costs are fuelling global in Global  competition,  in  turn,  is  fostering  the  search  for  new  applications  of  the possibilities. And especially in a dynamic period with large adjustment requirements

all  sectors  of  the  economy,  a  centrally  planned  economy  is  especially  inferior  to economy.

All  three  features  have  a  common  thrust.  They  work  in  the  direction overcoming  national  frontiers  and  administrative  barriers.  The  old  dream  of  interna therefore holds out the promise of coming true.

But the more this open, increasingly barrierless world becomes reality, th evident it grows that this is not a perfect or simple world. On the contrary: in the former east-west conflict, conflicts within countries or in individual regions have less common. Indeed, some conflicts which had previously been obscured have only now c to  light.  And  the  technological  changes  and  economic  globalisation  are  not  only  a  s greater  prosperity.  They  at  the  same  time  pose  huge  challenges.  The  developed  ind countries are particularly feeling the need for reform in their labour markets and soc systems. This is especially true of countries in continental Europe.

II

Progressive economic integration is, of course, not a new phenomenon. But are many indications that this process has accelerated and intensified in the last te quantitatively and qualitatively.

Economic integration is a comprehensive process. It is increasingly affect real  economy.  The  international  interdependence  of  national  economies  is  increasing. quality is emerging. For the growing interdependence is no longer based solely or pri trade in finished products or commodities. Especially, the process of developing and p goods is being increasingly split up internationally. This is possible because nation have become increasingly permeable and communications have become more intensive, becau transportation  and  communication  costs  have  fallen  sharply,  and  because,  in  partic emerging economies have likewise become more integrated in the world economy; this, a all, markedly facilitates direct investment there.

The front runners of such integration are of course the global financial They are able to take the best advantage of the disappearance of transaction barriers a technological options. In a world of increasing real economic interdependence, and wit financial markets, the question of monetary integration is also becoming more urgent.

The calculability and appropriateness of monetary relationships is becoming important. Globalisation  therefore  increases  the  overall  pressure  to  pursue  a  stabil monetary policy everywhere. If a country, especially a bigger one, drops out, this may integrated world economy, to serious damage due to volatile financial market prices. A why  many  countries  are  switching  over  to  monetary  cooperation,  or  even  to  pegging exchange rates.

One part of Europe is now going a radical step further. Eleven EU countrie enter into monetary union on a durable basis at the end of this year. That union will t single  supranational  monetary  policy  decided  by  a  supranational  and  politically  ind central bank.

A number of countries will closely watch the outcome of this experiment, w may change Europe considerably. This is true in particular of those countries of the Union which do not wish to join the monetary union as yet. Accession candidates in cen eastern Europe, too, will of course watch developments with keen interest. But countrie parts  of  the  world  as  well  will  focus  their  attention  on  the  euro  area.  This  is  b countries  in  South  America  or  Asia  are  beginning  at  least  to  contemplate  the  opti monetary union. Even if they still have a long way to go.

## III

What  is  it  that  prompts  sovereign  states  to  follow  this  basic  trend economic integration, even if of course it does not always lead as far as is planned for

Essentially, three more or less major benefits may be derived from any fo economic integration: Firstly, more integration leads to more competition. Competitive enhances  efficiency.  Secondly,  integration  changes  market  structures.  Markets  become Enterprises are able to exploit economies of scale. National economies can specialise t extent. Resources are fed into a larger pool, from which they can be allocated more e And market breadth increases. The consumer can choose from a wider range of products of Thirdly,  integration  reduces  information  and  transaction  costs.  This  applies  in  pa monetary integration, too.

But - what is invariably true is also true of economic integration: there thing as a free lunch.

First  of  all,  it  is  helpful  to  distinguish  between  market  integration  a integration. Market integration mainly implies dismantling barriers and obstacles. The markets  can  grow  together.  Policy  integration  goes  further.  It  also  implies  that coordinate or even harmonise the general direction of movement in individual sectors of policy, or individual parameters.

The  countries  which  join  an  integration  process  must  clearly  appreciate potential problem areas:

First  problem  area:  market  integration  going  beyond  national  borders  p increased domestic challenges. For instance, integration in the international divisio accelerates  structural  change  and  calls  for  more  internal  flexibility,  especially  o market. And liberalising capital movements places demands on the domestic financial which must be able to handle international capital flows that may rapidly change directi

Second  problem  area:  to  be  really  efficient,  market  integration  wit elimination of barriers may require a minimum of policy integration. This applies, for to some protection provisions for products and in the production process. Different ta may of course likewise distort cross-border goods and financial flows. And if capital m globalised, different approaches to monetary policy may contribute to volatility. Such may have a strong impact on financial and real investment.

But, and this is the third problem area: policy integration is itself a sword.  It  may  make  markets  more  efficient.  But  it  can  also  contribute  to  curbing competition.  That  may  involve  risks:  an  excessive  tendency  towards  centralisation  ma

which does not take sufficient account of diverging conditions. The delineat responsibilities may become blurred if mixed responsibilities arise with undue bureau the  worst-case  scenario,  efficient  policy  solutions  may  no  longer  be  implemented. innovation is blocked.

Countries must be able to come to terms with these three risks and problem in  their  efforts  to  coordinate  or  integrate  their  policies,  if  they  are  to  secure integration. Striking the right balance here is not always easy.

## IV

The  financial  markets  are  something  like  the  flywheels  of  globalisation capital  movements  and  efficient  financial  markets  greatly  facilitate  direct  investm provide the basis for transactions and for the safety of payment flows, which are th equivalent of real integration.

The global financial markets promote and strengthen market structures. They make  it  possible  for  investment  in  emerging  economies  to  be  funded  privately,  rath officially, today on a much greater scale than previously. Capital is allocated today, used to be, in accordance with economic, rather than political, criteria.

Conversely, the integration of the emerging economies into the global fin markets  provides  new  investment  outlets  for  savings.  This  must  also  be  seen  agai backdrop  of  the  ageing  populations  in  most  industrialised  countries.  They  in  partic accumulate and invest capital today so as to be able to maintain their relative standa in the future, too.

And the global capital markets have assumed a role which is bearing fruit disciplining of national policies. They offer opportunities, but also pose a risk, to c fail to follow the economic constraints. Nowadays they are an effective part of the c balances.

These  important  benefits  of  the  international  capital  markets  are  some wrongly disregarded in the ongoing debate.

But the financial crises being encountered by some east Asian countries ha course,  highlighted  the  risks,  too.  A  number  of  emerging  economies  have  become  sw integrated in the global financial markets. Not all of those countries have adjusted t structures at the same pace and as thoroughly. That makes them vulnerable. Two weakness particular, may become their Achilles heel: a domestic financial sector which is unable large capital flows in a sufficiently sound manner, and an overly rigid exchange rate one or more other currencies.

Exchange rate pegging can in some cases and for some length of time prod positive effects. An overly rigid exchange rate peg, however, can have probl consequences: It may jeopardise the competitiveness of an economy, and especially exp may fetter domestic interest rate policy. It thereby makes it more difficult to figh periods of heavy capital inflows. And it may tempt residents to borrow in foreign cur relatively favourable nominal interest rates. These consequences may make a country vul as we have seen already in the Mexican case in 1994-5.

In  addition,  some  risk  factors  are  inherent  in  the  market.  The  intern financial markets mostly have a tendency towards short-termism. A major part of inter lendings  and  borrowings  is  at  fairly  short  term.  And  they  quite  often  tend  to self-reinforcing herd instinct in periods both of euphoria and of scepticism.

Both  factors,  any  domestic  weaknesses  and  the  properties  of  the  interna financial markets, may cause a potential for a reversal in sentiment for a currency t Mostly triggered by some special economic or political change or other, the exchange currency may go down very fast, in many cases to an overly low point. An 'undershooti the appropriate relationship occurs. Such a slump in the value of a currency can hit t of the country concerned with a massive force, especially if that country is heavily i foreign currency.

What is to be done? Two points in particular are important:

Firstly, the functioning of  the financial  markets  must be maintaine strengthened. On the one hand, to this end the markets need more, better and more up information  on  the  level,  maturity  and  denomination  pattern  of  the  debts  of  poten countries. Sufficient transparency is of particular significance for the functioning of markets. On the other hand, the IMF must not encourage moral-hazard attitudes on the investors and recipient countries by bailing out private investors. Losses ca misjudgements and enforced adjustment in the event of wrong behaviour are as much an in part of a functioning market as are profit opportunities. And crises should not invaria rollback on the part of private investors. Private funding of investment is in principl public funding. Ways must be found to safeguard the long-term interests of private i Though there is probably no panacea, various approaches are being considered, and rig The IMF above all has to act as a catalyst maintaining or restoring countries' access capital. A policy of bailing out private investors is heading in the wrong direction.

Secondly, it is important for countries to eliminate their domestic weakne prevent  them  from  arising  in  the  first  place.  This  includes:  being  careful  about  o exchange rate pegs, strengthening domestic supervision of the financial system, and a strengthening domestic competitive structures in the goods markets and in the financial

V

Cynics might now say that Europe should make sparing use of the advice: careful with exchange rate pegs'. After all, eleven European countries are actually o towards monetary union. And hitherto they have also largely linked their mutual exchang though not always without any problems in the past.

Monetary union  does  in  fact  represent  a  maximum  of  policy  integration  in monetary  field.  Monetary  policy  is  not  merely  coordinated,  but  unified.  And  that  wil good, because in practice this step cannot be reversed.

There  were  of  course  also  some  other  options.  With  the  European  Moneta System, Europe's approach has for a long time been that of an exchange rate arrangeme fixed but adjustable parities; at times there have been some considerable difficulties end the system has proved largely successful. That goes in particular also for the peri

widening of the  fluctuation margins. Nevertheless, this approach falls short of ful integration and the strategy of a single currency.

At the time, your country above all proposed another, less ambitious soluti full  monetary  union;  I  am  referring  to  the  adoption  of  a  parallel  currency,  to  be common currency. That would probably have triggered a currency competition. Depending o design, that solution could, however, also have adversely affected the scope for monet of  the  central  banks  of  the  existing  hard  currency  countries  and  thus  jeopardi anti-inflation policy. A parallel currency would presumably have got stuck. It might per been able to crowd out weaker currencies, but whether also a currency of the D-mark's would at least be doubtful. This is true, at any rate, of the specific form of mon activities discussed at the time.

Be  that  as  it  may,  in  the  Maastricht  Treaty  a  more  far-reaching  soluti adopted. A large majority in the EU opted not merely for a common currency. It also w single currency. There are sound economic reasons in favour of a single currency; inc also  sound  political  reasons,  at  least,  if  a  more  thorough-going  political  integrat sought.

Above  all,  the  single  currency  makes  it  possible  fully  to  exploit  the  e benefits of integration. Competition will be given maximum encouragement in the single by the complete transparency of prices. Factor allocation will no longer be impaired by exchange  rate  uncertainty.  Exchange-rate-related  information  and  transaction  costs minimised by a single currency. The euro financial markets will have an optimum dept breadth.

But  what  applies  to  economic  integration  in  general  also  applies  to  mon integration  in  particular:  These  benefits  will  not  come  automatically  and  not corresponding challenges.

How can monetary union secure the benefits? What risks are looming?

Monetary union is faced with three major challenges: Firstly, the aforemen benefits for the goods and financial markets will materialise only if the euro remain stable.  Only  then  will  the  euro  lead  to  full  price  transparency,  reduce  costs  and attractive  investment  currency.  Secondly,  monetary  union  must  not  trigger  or  exa economic tensions. Broadly speaking, an essential requirement that must be met is: one all. And, thirdly, monetary union must not give rise to political tensions between the states.

These challenges arise against the backdrop of the specific conditions pr by monetary union. The euro will be legal tender in an area which consists of largely national  states  whose  policies  -  other  than  monetary  policy  -  will  largely  rem responsibility. That may lead to a dilemma between the requirements of a supranational c and the political pattern in Europe, which will continue to be determined by the nati and their policies.

The euro needs a high degree of flexibility in the economies of the parti countries.  But  there  is  no  European  economic  and  structural  policy  which  can  ordai necessary flexibility from above. And even if there were a responsibility at the Europea

doing so, the possibility could not be ruled out that, ultimately, the result would be rather than more flexibility. At the same time, there is no regional revenue equalisat comparable to the systems operated in a national state. A social and transfer union c must not make up for any lack of flexibility and competitiveness, for the upshot would be not only less flexibility, but possibly also more political disagreement.

At the same time, however, the euro needs discipline on the part of nationa policy,  at  least  as  far  as  fiscal  deficits  are  concerned.  Otherwise  there  is  a  ris because large debts in some countries will attract the savings of the euro area as a contribute to  higher  interest  rates  for  everyone.  Fiscal  policy,  however,  will  large national responsibility. That is why it is so important that the Growth and Stability prove to be effective in the future.

How can the euro function against this background? The 'classical' answer o Werner Group in the early seventies (of which I was a member at the time) was: Europe m up a political union parallel to the monetary union. Thus, supranational political str supposed to ensure that Europe met the requirements of a supranational currency.

Maastricht  adopted  a  different  approach.  It  left  the  rift  between  supra money and national policy structures. To that extent, it has sometimes been dubbed 'a with a limp'. If, however, there is no supranational political authority to meet the req a supranational currency, then the participating countries must do so on their own in their own accord or in their own interest.

The Maastricht Treaty therefore also set important rules for the fiscal dis member  countries.  And  compliance  with  those  rules  is  likewise  jointly  monitored.  Ho what ultimately will be crucial for the functioning of the Stability Pact will, abov countries' ability and willingness to abide by those rules on a sustained basis.

A monetary union, under the Maastricht Treaty, therefore needs a large measu common  'stability  culture'  in  all  participating  countries.  And  another  point:  the function as a depoliticised currency only in this specific form. The ultimate moneta i.e. monetary stability, must  not  be  subordinated  on  a  discretionary  basis  to  other monetary policy must be conducted by a politically independent central bank.

That may be considered in some quarters to be an overly German postulate. But still, one could live however, eleven countries try subordinating their common currency to their respective primary political objectives, things will really get pretty chaotic in the union.

That way, the euro would gain the confidence neither of the citizens nor financial markets. The upshot would, rather, be all too likely to be permanent politi The euro must not come under the influence of the domestic interests of individual c Monetary policy must be geared to the situation in the euro area as a whole, taking res for maintaining stability of the common currency. Some of the incidents in Brussels d first weekend in May may in this context have been a timely warning, and a lesson to b by all.

There can be no doubt that monetary union implies the irreversible loss sovereignty of the participating countries in the monetary sphere. In Germany, this also means the loss of a symbol of economic reconstruction war.

Monetary  union  thus  reinforces  an  overall  trend  towards  global  econo integration, especially also as  a  consequence  of  the  global  financial  markets:  the  n forfeits some of its freedom to shape events. In some countries and some quarters ther fears about the immediate forfeiture of sovereign rights, as in the case of the curren about  an  uncontrolled  dynamic  integration  process  which  will  -  automatically,  as  i relegate the nation state into the background.

Here in the U.K. (but not only here) there seems to be some concern abou uncontrolled political integration drive in Europe: the fear of a 'superstate of Europe'. this fear is manifest to some extent in continental Europe, too, there is, at the same more concern about an uncontrolled economic integration drive caused by increased competition In Germany, there is, in addition, concern that the stability of the euro might not mat D-mark.

text:
Ms. Hämäläinen discusses achieving a credible currency for Europe Address by the Governor of the Bank of Finland, Ms. Sirkka Hämäläinen, at the Frankfurt Inter Banking Evening on 5/5/98.

…First of all I would like to thank the hosts of this evening for giving opportunity to address this distinguished audience in these historical surroundings. honour and privilege for me.

With the historical decision reached at last weekend's European summit, we know  that  a  common  monetary  policy  will  become  reality  for  eleven  EU  countries  at beginning of next year. A long, intense process - a process that has had its doubters along the way - has now passed an important milestone.

Setting forth on this historical project was in itself a tremendous achieve the real challenges still lie ahead. The participating countries must now make this pro and achieve its intended objectives. The project must deliver unquestioned monetary sta efficiency  to  the  euro-area,  and  thereby  provide  a  solid  basis  for  growth  and  emplo Europe.

As part of the overall stabilization and convergence achieved by the parti countries  and  as  a  result  of  the  strengthening  of  market  confidence,  we  have  se convergence in interest and exchange rates. This will ease the transition to a singl policy, but the crucial question remains: How do we make the euro credible from the that the ESCB doesn't have to resort to an unnecessarily tight monetary policy?

At the end of the day, strong credibility is what ensures low inflation exp low inflation and low interest rates.

Credibility  is  built  up  from  many  elements,  building  blocks  if  you  will though  the  ECB  starts  its  operations  without  a  track  record  and  without  its  own  h credibility, a number of these critical elements already exist. All in all, I would l seven building blocks that are important for the ESCB's credibility.

1. The first building block is the credibility the ECB may inherit from the national ce of the participating countries. All NCBs in the euro area have conducted monetary aimed  at  price  stability  and  convergence  in  accord  with  the  principles  of  the  M Treaty.
2. The  second  building  block  is  the  ESCB's  uncontested  independence.  This  will institutional credibility from the outset.
3. The third building block is the transparency and clarity of the ECB's strategy and ECB's  primary  final  objective  is  price  stability.  This  final  objective  will  befo operationalized and quantified in a way that is meaningful and understandable to the and the public at large.

The  ECB's  monetary  policy  will  be  geared  towards  a  'domestic'  objective,  internal stability within the euro area while the euro is allowed to float against other worl The fact is that the share of foreign trade in GDP for the euro area is approximatel

as for the US, about 10 per cent, so the exchange rate will probably not have muc impact on the euro area price stability or the monetary policy stance, even indirectl

Certainly, it would be expedient to quantify and to announce the target ' price sta example,  in  the  form  of  a  target  range  or  an  approximate  value.  This,  and  what  k intermediate  monetary  aggregate  targets  could  or  should  be  used  to  communicate monetary  policy  stance  to  the  markets,  the  public  and  policy-makers,  are  stil consideration. I will therefore not go further into this topic, except to note tha monetary policy strategy and the definition and specification of its policy will be first and most important issues on which the ECB must decide.

The problem of intermediate targets is that we lack Europe-wide empirical evidence stability of demand-for-money functions and on the monetary policy transmission mecha in general. What we can say with certainty at this point - and this is not too produc the analysis of the monetary policy transmission mechanism will be a truly challengi The financial market and structural changes produced by the single currency, as wel general  continuous  structural  changes  in  the  financial  markets  due  to  globaliza transforming the transmission processes.

- All  the  central  banks  carefully  distill  vast  amounts  of  data  and  examine  many  d indicators before they decide on policy. Thus, quantitative targets are not perhaps s for the internal decision-making process of the central bank. But they are very imp communication with the markets and the public. How useful they are for this purpose d very much on their predictability.
4. The  fourth  building  block  -  which  partly  covers  the  previous  one  -  is  the  wide openness of the central bank towards the markets, the public and policy-makers, not o strategy and targeting but also in its analyses and reasoning behind its decisions.

A high degree of market transparency is natural for any central bank operating in environment,  because  transparency  essentially  increases  the  efficiency  of  monetary Without  doubt,  the  ESCB  has  to,  and  will,  consider  all  possible  means  and  chann achieve it.

Another  central  aspect  of  openness  is  what  is  loosely  called  'democratic  account Confidence of the public and the political decision-making bodies that represent the of utmost importance for the credibility of an independent central bank. This confi only be achieved if information provided by the central bank to the public is clear, is a healthy dialogue between the central bank and political decision-making bodies.

The Maastricht Treaty provides a framework for accountability at the European level; legislation of the member states provides a similar framework for national accountabi euro  will  require  the  acceptance  and  support  of  citizens  and  policy-makers  i participating member state. Thus, accountability at the national level will be very i

In practice, democratic accountability should be the outcome of constructive communi between  the  central  bank  and  political  decision-making  bodies  -  connected  with  co central bank independence. There should not be any genuine conflict between the centr on the one hand and the other policy-makers and the public on the other hand because share a common ultimate goal under EMU, monetary stability and economic growth.

5. The fifth building block, and one of the most important elements in the credibility is the stance and discipline of fiscal policies, both in individual member states an area as a whole.

Fiscal policy affects credibility in two ways. The first has to do with how well nat policies cope with differences in the business cycle and in the monetary policy tra mechanisms of the member states. Under a single monetary policy, national fiscal p need  to  be  far  more  active  and  flexible  than  at  present  to  deal  successfu country specific  growth  and  inflation  differences.  Both  room  to  manoeuvre  at  the level  and  the  Stability  and  Growth  Pact  explicitly  demand  that  the  public  finance member state are balanced and healthy.

The second aspect of fiscal policy, closely connected to the first, is the overall de policy discipline in the euro area. Curbing inflation expectations and achieving th target  are  the  more  easily  attained  with  low  interest  rates,  the  more  disciplined policy at the European level.

It is of vital importance that a close and constructive dialogue is organized and between the ministers of finance of the participating countries (EURO-11) and the E Central  Bank.  Such  a  dialogue  does  not  in  any  way  endanger  the  ECB's  independence pursue its legislated objective price stability.

Simultaneously, the role of national central banks and their dialogue with the nati policy  authorities  will  continue  to  be  essential;  in  achieving  an  appropriate  mon fiscal policy mix at the European level, and in ensuring balanced economic perform each country under the single monetary policy.

6. The sixth building block of credibility for the European Central Bank and the stabi euro, is a high standard of economic and monetary analysis within the ESCB. High-q work encourages confidence in the expertise of the system in a new environment wher analysis  and  know-how  must  cover  the  entire  euro  area.  Here,  the  skills,  knowled expertise accumulated in national central banks will be put to good use in the prep the single monetary policy.

As you have noticed, I have repeatedly stressed the importance of national central ba European  System  of  Central  Banks.  Let  me  say  very  firmly  that  I  am  not  doing  it parochial concerns or motives. What we need is an ECB that is strong and efficient. I eleven-country constellation the ECB needs to mobilize the support of the national banks.

The governors of the national central banks will have a central role in the Governin of  the  ECB  where  decisions  on  monetary  policy  as  well  as  decisions  on  systems institutional arrangements will be made. Operations and transactions will be decentra carried  out  in  the  national  central  banks.  The  skills  and  accumulated  knowledge national central banks will form an integral part of the preparation of joint dec NCBs will also play a major communications role by providing information at the na level and helping to define the fiscal and monetary policy mix for both the nationa entire  euro  area.  And  finally,  the  national  central  banks  will  bear  a  great  respo

ensuring the legitimacy of the independent ESCB through their contributions to trans and democratic accountability.

7. While I stress here the role of the national central banks, I also want to stress that the seventh, and one of the most important building blocks of the credibility a of the euro and the efficiency of the single monetary policy will be the ability of t of the national central banks to base their analyses, actions and decisions on the the euro area as a whole.

Although  one  of  the  tasks  of  any  governor  of  a  national  central  bank  is  to  bring information and viewpoints into the decision-making process, there is no conflict interests of the euro area.

Adopting a euro area-wide viewpoint will be a demanding and immediate challenge for European System of Central Banks. This challenge makes me believe that it is not a go to  publish  the  minutes  and  the  voting  positions  of  the  Governing  Council  meetings though transparency and accountability of the European System of Central Banks are important.  The  publication  of  the  discussions  and  voting  positions  could  easily dramatization of national differences of opinion at the expense of euro-level views.

*       *       *

During  the  1990s,  Finland  has  gone  through  severe  adjustments.  We  ha consolidated our public finances and achieved credibility for our monetary policy. For the single monetary policy is a natural continuation of this process. In global, expect financial markets, a small country has poor possibilities to ensure its exchange rate rate  stability,  even  with  a  highly  disciplined  fiscal  and  monetary  policy  and  sound fundamentals. For us, the stability and credibility that we expect from EMU, and its are of vital importance.

text:
## Mr. Liebscher discusses the role of a national central bank within the ESC

as  illustrated  by  the  OeNB Address  by  the  President  of  the  Austrian  National  Ban Dr. Klaus Liebscher, held at the 26 th Economics Conference of the Oesterreichische Nationalbank on the topic 'Economic Policy 2000', in Vienna on 7-8/5/98.

## Introduction

Just a few days ago, the key political decisions which will pave the way t were  taken  at  the  summit  in  Brussels.  Based  upon  the  preparatory  work  of  the  Eur Monetary  Institute,  the  Commission  and  ECOFIN,  the  Council  of  the  Heads  of  State  o Government agreed last weekend to start Stage Three of EMU on January 1, 1999, with e countries. At the same time, the bilateral exchange rates for the participating curre are to form the basis for their euro conversion rates, were preannounced. The European Bank  will  be  formally  inaugurated  in  Frankfurt  on  June  30,  and  EMU  will  commence schedule  on  January  1,  1999.  These  developments  have  provided  the  financial  markets reliable  points  of  reference  that  will  contribute  substantially  to  a  calculable  dev exchange rates and interest rates until the onset of EMU.

The general public and the financial markets are now convinced that EMU w become reality in just a few months' time. By comparison, people know much less abou institutions that will be responsible for the single monetary policy and, in particul relationships among them. Will there still be a place left within EMU for today's natio banks? And if so, which tasks are they going to keep once monetary policy is made in Fr These are questions that are frequently asked. And the answers are indeed quite complex.

The basic institutional framework of the European System of Central Banks as defined ESCB/ECB Statute

A superficial glance at the ESCB/ECB Statute lets things appear quite simple

- The establishment of the ECB in mid-1998 will coincide with the foundatio the European System of Central Banks (ESCB). The ESCB will consist of th ECB and the national central banks (NCBs) of the EU member states. Fro January  1,  1999,  the  ESCB  will  have  the  sole  responsibility  for  the monetary policy within the euro area. In performing its tasks, the ESCB w independent of any political instructions and will be committed to the p objective of price stability.
- The ESCB will be governed by the ECB's decision-making bodies, led by th ECB  Governing  Council,  which  will  consist  of  six  members  of  the  ECB Executive Board, including the ECB President and Vice-President, as wel the governors of the NCBs of the euro area. Monetary policy decisions wi

taken centrally, by a simple majority of the ECB Governing Council and ba on the principle of 'one member, one vote'.

- The ECB Executive Board will conduct monetary policy in accordance with t guidelines and decisions adopted by the ECB Governing Council. In doing it will issue the necessary instructions to national central banks.
- The national central banks will form an integral part of the ESCB and accordance  with  the  guidelines  and  instructions  issued  by  the  ECB. conducting operations within the ESCB's field of competence, the ECB w rely on the national central banks whenever possible and appropriate.
- Finally, a so-called 'General Council' will be constituted as a decision-making body. It will assume responsibility for the coordinatio exchange of information between the euro area and EU central banks whi have not yet adopted the single currency, but will not exercise any influ the monetary policy of the euro area.

Much  will  also  depend  on  the  direction  in  which  the  European  Union  will moving  as  a  whole.  To  the  extent  to  which  integration  advances,  to  which  national become more and more insignificant and to which political union increasingly takes s parallel  development  might  take  place  within  the  ESCB.  Political  and  general  eco integration of the Community and experience with a single monetary policy will - as I expect - influence each other in a mutually beneficial process.

title: Mr. Stals elucidates monetary policy objectives in South Africa in the environment of financial globalisation  (Central Bank Articles and Speeches, 11 May 98)
description: Address by the Governor of the Reserve Bank of South Africa, Mr. C. Stals, at the Monthly Meeting of the Bank for International Settlements in Basle on 11/5/98.
text:
Mr.  Stals  elucidates  monetary  policy  objectives  in  South  Africa  in  t environment of financial globalisation Address by the Governor of the Reserve Bank of South Africa, Mr. C. Stals, at the Monthly Meeting of the Bank for International Settlements in 11/5/98.

## 1.  Background

Major political and social reforms in South Africa in recent years creat expectations, and many demands are being made on the Government for the social upliftm the people. In defining its macroeconomic strategy, the South African Government first a Reconstruction  and  Development  Programme (RDP)  in  1994  in  which  legitimate  needs were  identified.  The  total  cost  of  implementation  of  the  RDP,  however,  as  could  ha expected,  by  far  exceeded  what  was  affordable.  This  was  confirmed  by  the  publicat mid-1996  of  a Macroeconomic  Strategy  for  Growth,  Employment  and  Redistribution (GEAR),  which  concentrated  more  on  the  supply-side  of  the  economy.  GEAR  provided programme for macro-economic restructuring that is intended to raise the growth potenti country over a five-year period from 3 to 4 per cent to 6 per cent per annum.

In the Government's macroeconomic strategy, monetary policy was tasked wi the  responsibility  of  maintaining  overall  financial  stability,  or  of  protecting  the currency. It was assumed that the objectives of neither the RDP nor GEAR would be atta unless overall financial stability is maintained.

The instruction to the Reserve Bank to secure financial stability also ap the South African Reserve Bank Act, and was recently written into the new Constitution Republic of South Africa. In terms of Section 224(1) of the Constitution:

'The primary object of the South African Reserve Bank is to protect the value of the currency in the interest of balanced and sustainabl economic growth in the Republic'.

The  Constitution  also  provides  for  the  protection  of  the  independence  o Reserve Bank:

'224(2)  The South African Reserve Bank, in pursuit of its primary object, must perform its functions independently and without fear, favour or prejudice, but there must be regular consultation between the Bank and the Cabinet member responsible for national financial matters'.

The macroeconomic strategy of the Government, and particularly the GEAR pa of  it,  is  often  criticised  and  there  are  strong  pressures,  emanating  mainly  fr organisations,  for  the  total  rejection  of  this  programme.  The  disciplined  monetary applied in terms of the above mandates from the Government are also often denounced by pressure groups. The Reserve Bank is from time to time castigated for not following a p will provide more money at lower interest rates for the purpose of financing the social programmes of the country.

## 2.  The main objective of monetary policy

The  mandate  from  Parliament  to  the  Reserve  Bank  is  not  explicit  on  w 'protection of the value of the currency' really means. This obviously opens up the malignant attacks on the Bank, whatever objectives might be pursued.

The main objective of the Bank, however, is to bring inflation down. Ove twenty years from 1972 until 1992, inflation in South Africa fluctuated between 10 an cent per annum, with an average of about 15 per cent. This was obviously too high, a was general public support for determined efforts by the Bank since 1990 to reduce infl single digit level. Since 1992, the rate of inflation has been contained within the level, fluctuating between 5 and 10 per cent. Over the twelve months up to March 19 consumer price inflation equalled 5.4 per cent, and at the production level, prices ros by 2.3 per cent.

In the absence of a formal quantified guideline from the Government, the Re Bank defined its goal for inflation as a rate that will be more or less in line with t of inflation in the economies of South Africa's major trading partners and competitor present world environment, this will require a rate of inflation of even lower than 5 p

The Reserve Bank is often criticised for being obsessed with inflation, unnecessarily depressing the domestic economy, in its efforts to reduce inflation. S those recently produced by Michael Sarel, an economist at the International Monetary F thrown against the Bank.

## 3.  The monetary policy model of the Reserve Bank

In 1986, South Africa introduced the M3 money supply as an anchor for monetary policy. Annual targets, or guidelines, for an acceptable rate of growth in M3 were announced by the Bank, and decisions to influence overall liquidity in the banking sector, or to chan rate,  were  triggered  by  substantial  deviations  in  actual  money  supply  growth  fr predetermined guidelines.

To  control  the  money  supply,  the  Reserve  Bank  obviously  had  to  manage  t amount of liquidity available within the banking sector, and had to accept realistic i With  fairly  stable  relationships  between  the  money  supply  and  aggregate  demand,  the served South Africa well for a relatively long period of time. In 1987/88, for example, growth in M3 was close to 30 per cent, and the rate of inflation 20 per cent. In 1992, M3 was reduced to 8 per cent, and inflation declined to a single digit figure for the 1993.

In recent years, however, with the major changes particularly in South Af international financial relationships, the money supply model lost some of its useful the past four years, the rate of increase in the money supply has persistently stayed level of about 15 per cent, being about 5 full percentage points above the annual guide Reserve Bank. Over the same period, total bank credit extension increased by about 16 per annum, a rate of growth that is also regarded as excessive by the Reserve Bank.

And yet, gross domestic expenditure declined from 5 per cent growth in 199 1½ per cent last year, and inflation remained well under control. After a depreciation

of 22 per cent in 1996, inflation rose correspondingly from 5 per cent to almost 10 per later. Over the past twelve months, however, inflation has come down again to the level 5 per cent per annum.

These developments forced the Reserve Bank to reconsider its monetary pol model and to follow a more eclectic approach in which a strict financial (monetary) p used as a basis for monetary policy decisions. This financial package includes:

- n movements in the money supply and its components M1, M2 and M3 ;
- n changes in total bank credit extension, both to the Government and private sector;
- n the level of interest rates and the structure of the yield curve;
- n changes in the gold and foreign exchange reserves;  and
- n movements in the exchange rate of the rand.

In terms of Reserve Bank analyses, the main reasons for the breakdown in money supply model in recent years have been:

- n the  almost  explosive  increases  in  volumes  on  the  various  finan markets;
- n the reintermediation in the banking sector of certain financial trans such as direct lending by foreign banks to South African non-bank pri sector institutions;
- n the absorption of many new workers from the subsistence sector in market economy;  and
- n the  effects  of  large  and  volatile  international  capital  flows  o liquidity, interest rates and the money supply.

The  debate  in  South  Africa  at  this  stage  about  the  monetary  policy  mod whether South Africa should not, at this juncture, follow the example of many other and introduce a formal inflation target as an anchor for its monetary policy.

## 4.  Other objectives of monetary policy

Effective monetary policy is, for obvious reasons, not only dependent on principles applied by the central bank, but also on the infrastructure or the archit which we operate. In summary, over the past few years, we had to restructure our bankin our financial markets, and the national payment, clearing and settlement system to su process of gradually introducing the South African financial system in the global marke

Bank regulation and supervision are, at this stage, a responsibility of th Bank, but there are serious proposals for following the recent examples of the United and Australia to remove these functions from the central bank. The present regulatory very much based on the risk management approach as prescribed by the Basle Committee, on the Core Principles. The major change in the South African banking sector in recent the introduction of more than 20 new foreign banks and additional foreign competition opening of more than 60 representative offices of foreign banks in South Africa.

The  financial  markets  were  also  encouraged  to  modernise.  The  Johannesbu Stock  Exchange  (JSE)  introduced  major  reforms  to  provide  for  corporate  ownership,  f

ownership  (of  stockbrokers),  dual  capacity  trading,  negotiated  commissions,  and  el screen trading. It is continuing to improve its facilities by providing for the immob dematerialisation  of  stock,  and  for  improved  clearing  and  settlement  arrangements.  T turnover on the JSE last year amounted to about US $45 billion.

Major changes were also introduced in bond trading, and the total turnover Bond  Exchange  of  South  Africa  last  year  amounted  to  the  equivalent  of  US  $927  bil Non-residents accounted for $257 billion.

The  daily  turnover  in  the  market  for  foreign  exchange  in  South  Africa exceeds $10 billion.

A Euro-rand market developed in Europe where the total amount of outstand Euro-rand bonds now exceeds R37 billion.

To stay in step with the financial globalisation process, the Reserve Bank also  upgraded  the  national  payment,  clearing  and  settlement  system.  The  new  system provides for:

- n an electronic on-line real-time link between participating banks;
- n secure  fund  transfers  between  banks  through  Reserve  Bank  settlemen accounts;
- n a better management on a continuous basis of the liquidity positio banks;
- n electronically  managed  end-of-day  settlement  of  interbank  transacti and
- n from the beginning of October, settlement of large transactions on a basis as and when instructions are received by the system.

## 5.  The financial globalisation process

The implementation of sound monetary policies and the establishment of a s and well-managed banking sector, effective financial markets, and an efficient national clearing and settlement system, were regarded as important preconditions for the exte South Africa's participation in the process of financial globalisation.

As  a  further  important  element  of  the  process,  South  Africa  is  also  rem exchange controls on a gradual and structured basis. There are, at this stage, no more controls on any current account transactions; all controls were removed on non-resident now free to bring funds into South Africa and to repatriate funds for any purpose; rest residents to make investments outside of the country have been eased for corporates, in investors  and  private  individuals,  who  may  make  foreign  investments  within  fairly  g prescribed limits. These limits are being raised gradually until they will become ineffe

The South African approach on financial globalisation is that it is in the the country to have access to foreign funds, and that we must therefore apply domestic and other macroeconomic policies that will make the country attractive to the foreign in

Furthermore, policies in South Africa must be flexible enough to adjust q and decisively to changes in foreign investor sentiment. When capital inflows subside, into outflows, as a minimum:

- n the exchange rate must be allowed to absorb part of the shock;
- n an outflow of capital must reduce liquidity in the banking sector;
- n interest rates must be allowed to rise;  and
- n some  inflationary  pressures will develop that will require, immediately, more restrictive monetary and fiscal policies.

a

These  adjustments  will  obviously  not  be  painless,  but  will  provide  a  ba re-establishing confidence in the shortest possible time.

title: Mr. Camdessus shares his views on a new financial architecture for a globalized world  (Central Bank Articles and Speeches, 8 May 98)
description: Address by the Managing Director of the International Monetary Fund, Mr. M. Camdessus, at the Royal Institute for International Affairs in London on 8/5/98.
text:
Mr.  Camdessus  shares  his  views  on  a  new  financial  architecture  for  a globalized  world Address  by  the  Managing  Director  of  the  International  Monetary  Fu Mr. M. Camdessus, at the Royal Institute for International Affairs in London on 8/5/98.

The G-7/G-8 Summit will be held in Birmingham next week. High on the Summit agenda will be the issue of how to renovate the architecture of the international fina in the face of the tremendous changes under way in the global economy. The Asian cri been so unexpected in many of its aspects, so broad, so cruel in its human consequenc even before the crisis has run its full course - the leaders of the world want to em design of a new architecture. This is certainly the right thing to do, and the venue of could  hardly  be  more  fitting.  Like  many  other  cities  in  advanced  countries,  Birming experienced the forces of change in the global economy first hand - from the loss of industries to the challenge of finding new employment opportunities. Moreover, two ce ago, this city was at the heart of the Industrial Revolution, an era that, like our own, extremely  rapid  change.  At  that  time,  intellectuals  of  all  schools  of  thought  use frequently in Birmingham - every full moon, I understand - and bring their reflections the challenges of their new world. This was the so-called Lunar Society, which inclu personalities as Matthew Boulton, James Watt, Erasmus Darwin (grandfather of Charles) William Small - a friend of Benjamin Franklin and Thomas Jefferson, all with wide-r interests, all sharing a sense of optimism and responsibility for building a better wo what a blessing it would be if the G-7/G-8 - our new Birmingham group - were to be insp such an example when dealing with their pressing agenda!

As a modest preface to their work, I would like to share with you my per views on the need for change the Asian crisis reveals, the building blocks available architecture, and the work already under way at the IMF and, in the best traditions o House, to fly a few kites and suggest some further steps for the longer term.

*  *  *

## Change is needed

As in the days of the Industrial Revolution, we are now at a defining mome human history. The question before us is straightforward: how to utilize the full p globalization to improve the living standards of all - particularly the poorest - whi the risks it entails, such as those we have seen materialize so brutally in Asia, and equally  pernicious,  even  if  less  spectacular,  of  the  continuous  marginalization  of countries. What kind of new architecture of the global system could achieve this? The must be deduced from a proper analysis of the most recent crises.

Contrary to what we saw during the debt crisis of the 1980s, the problems i were not almost exclusively macroeconomic in nature; even if these countries suffere them,  from  some  deficiencies  in  this  respect,  by  and  large  they  had  long  track  re successful  economic  management.  Rather,  in  a  context  dramatically  changed  by  a  m realignment between the dollar and the yen, and important differences in short-term yie other factors helped trigger the crisis:

- the weakness of their public and private banking and financial structures
- an  unsustainable  accumulation  of  short-term  financing  -  particularl interbank lending, which Alan Greenspan refers to as the Achilles' heel

- international financial system - which made countries particularly vuln to a sudden shift in market sentiment.
- and, last but not least, deep-seated problems of governance, corruptio what US commentators call 'crony capitalism'.

Together with the macroeconomic problems, these three major factors had to addressed  for  our  response  to  the  crisis  to  be  pertinent.  If  you  examine  our  prog Thailand, Korea, and Indonesia, you will see that we have tried to deal with these fa they will have to be taken into consideration in the future in whatever efforts are u avoid the recurrence of crises. But even that will not suffice. In view of the enormous economic cost of the Asian crisis, no wonder we hear many radical suggestions as to avoid  such  losses  in  the  future.  There  are  calls  for  us  to  do  a  better  job  of  pr preventing  crises,  addressing  their  social  impact  more  effectively,  stopping  specul properly regulating this 'casino economy', seeing to it that investors bear the full c mistakes, stabilizing the international monetary system, providing for more p accountability of our institution, etc., etc.

We cannot deny the basic justification of these - at times vociferous change. No doubt there are at least some elements of validity in each of them. Taken they tell us that, at this stage, world public opinion expects its leaders to design an common  house  with  an  audaciously  modern  architecture,  and  not  limit  themselves  to plumbing and interior decorating of the old mansion.

But, as responsible architects, let us start by recognizing the building hand. Indeed, they are substantial.

## Seven building blocks

The  first  of  these  building  blocks  is  the  tremendous  potential  for  grow prosperity globalization provides countries fully integrating into the global economy. sources  of  dynamism  are  there,  engendered  by  new  information  technologies  and  unif financial  markets.  The  question,  then,  is  how  to  discipline  and  channel  these  forc growth will be sustainable and more broadly shared and the fundamental desire for great will be more fully satisfied.

The  second  building  block  is  integration.  By  integrating  themselves  int mainstream of the globalizing world economy, the poorest countries will avail themsel most powerful instrument of acceleration of development, while, if they preferred to do they would expose themselves to the risks of marginalization, abandoning several genera economic stagnation and poverty.

The  third  building  block  is  the  universal  consensus  on  the  importance increasingly open and liberal system of capital flows in order for globalization to de promises.

The fourth building block is what we could call the 'golden rule' of transp now truly seen as the key for modern management, economic success, and rational behav global markets.

The sixth building block could be a set of standards and codes of best pr this  could  require  a  few  words  of  elaboration.  More  and  more  we  observe  an  emer recognition  that  the  global  markets  still  suffer  from  the  kind  of  anarchy  that  af domestic  financial  markets  here  in  Europe  during  the  nineteenth  and  the  beginning twentieth  centuries  -  that  is,  until  various  scandals  and  crises  led  to  the  crea institutions and rules as securities and exchange commissions, banking supervision, ac standards, disclosure and prudential rules, and so forth. Last, but not least, the seventh building block is the option for the mu approach  to  handle  problems,  which  are  now  more  and  more  global  in  nature.  And  the instruments of such an approach will have to be the Bretton Woods institutions themsel me be immodest for a moment. The experience they have accumulated, the quality of thei their demonstrated ability to address new economic challenges promptly and efficientl them a major asset of the world community and a central pillar of a new architecture, they continue adapting themselves, reforming themselves, to this new world. These  seven  building  blocks  have  been  neglected  or  unevenly  utilized  for long. Assembled in the right way, they could offer a rock-solid foundation for a new system. Assembling them, nevertheless, will be hard work, each of them implying that interests or perverse practices be challenged. And, as with all transitions from one era to another, we can expect uncertainties to persist for some years to come. This makes it all the more urgent to on this new architecture right away.

## Initial steps for a new architecture

In fact, a number of significant steps are already under way. title: Mr. Tietmeyer discusses EMU - after the Brussels Summit  (Central Bank Articles and Speeches, 7 May 98)
description: Address by the President of the Deutsche Bundesbank, Prof. Hans Tietmeyer, at the spring meeting of the Institute of International Finance in Rome on 7/5/98.
text:
Mr. Tietmeyer discusses EMU - after the Brussels Summit Address by the President  of  the  Deutsche  Bundesbank,  Prof.  Hans  Tietmeyer,  at  the  spring  meeting  o Institute of International Finance in Rome on 7/5/98.

I

In Brussels last weekend some momentous decisions were taken.

Now we can be sure about

- -the participation of eleven countries,
- -the bilateral rates at which the participating countries will irrevo the exchange rates of their currencies upon the start of monetary union -the candidates for the offices of the President, Vice-President and th
- four members of the Executive Board. This means that the composition the ECB Governing Council, in future comprising 17 members, is likewis clarified.

It is, I think, advisable to distinguish between the substance of the deci some  of  the  events  in  Brussels.  Not  everything  that  happened  last  weekend  in  Br contributed  to  the  necessary  expectation  that  the  euro  will  be  a  really  supranat depoliticised currency. I hope, however, the learning process will go on and some of t accompanying the weekend decision will be forgotten shortly. For the future what count is the substance of the decisions.

The suggestions with regard to the nominations of the Executive Board of ECB are to be viewed favourably overall. The persons involved are acknowledged expert monetary and banking issues, and for the most part have many years of experience in the monetary policy. And the reactions by the markets were clearly positive. Some analysts talking of a 'dream-team'. But, of course, even the most promising dream-team has to ma big points in reality.

The EMI has already endorsed the nomination. And we are sure: the Europea Parliament  will  do  the  same  in  the  next  few  days,  so  that  the  ECB  can  be  establi scheduled on the first of June.

II

In  several  respects,  the  Brussels  decisions  already  alter  European  mon policy-making  today  (and  not  merely  in  January 1999).  The  policies  of  the  national banks -  although  national  responsibility  still  reigns,  formally  speaking,  until  the year - are from now on influenced even more by European considerations.

The phrase of 'de facto monetary union' was used sometimes in the past. Af all, many observers spoke of a 'de facto monetary union' in connection with the EMS ba 1991-92 - a notion that soon turned out to be an illusion. But during the seven-month period until the start of formal monetary union, there is certainly far more justific phrase than there was then.

Firstly,  subject  to  the  well-known  time-lags,  the  monetary  policies  of participating national central banks exert an impact on the entire euro area. Hence it not to introduce any national inflationary pressures into the monetary union.

Secondly, upon the entry into monetary union at the end of the year, if not uniform money market rates will pertain. On account of the increase in mutual interdep in  Europe,  monetary  policy  cooperation  between  the  national  central  banks  will  have reinforced, even though final responsibility will rest with the individual national cen

There  will  presumably  also  be  a  further  convergence  of  central  bank  r However, such convergence need not take place at the very beginning of the interim Limited interest rate differences and exchange rate movements may well continue to ex some time.

It  cannot  yet  be  predicted  where  the  common  level  of  central  bank  rates actually be by the end of the year. That depends primarily on monetary and anti-infl policy  developments  throughout  'euroland',  with  the  larger  countries  naturally  b particular responsibility on account of their greater economic weight.

In this connection, the future course of the 'mix' of fiscal and monetary p the individual countries will certainly play a part. After all, in future undesirable will not only exercise an impact on the domestic economy. From now on all 'euroland'-c banks have to take that into account.

## III

As  soon  as  the  European  Central  Bank  has  been  set  up,  the  ECB  Governin Council will have a number of important decisions to take before the start of monetar For, needless to say, European monetary policy must be fully operational from the very of monetary union. In particular, that calls for

- -a forward-looking, empirically-backed strategy, and
- -an effective arsenal of instruments.

The European Monetary Institute has already done a good deal of prelimin work on both those subjects. Although a consensus has been reached on most issues, a n of options and details are still unresolved. It is on these that decisions are still re be, majority decisions. In any case, the new ECB Governing Council will in part be com differently from the existing EMI Council.

As  regards  the  monetary  policy  strategy,  two  models  have  emerged  from  t EMI's preliminary work: the strategy of direct inflation targeting and that of targeting stock. We at the Bundesbank believe that our proven monetary targeting strategy is app in principle for the euro area, too. At all events, studies suggest that the demand f the euro area is actually likely to be even more stable than that in national markets.

Above all, a monetary targeting strategy has the advantage that it invol inherent commitment on the part of the central bank, and sets a standard by which the bank must let itself be judged. Hence a monetary targeting strategy may be a major ele building up the European Central Bank's reputation. Moreover, a monetary targeting st

provides  a  dependable  framework  to  which  the  markets'  expectations  can  be  geared. forward-looking and indicates unwelcome developments at an early stage. However, initi may not be possible to rule out major volatilities in the movement of the money sto owes something to the existing differences in countries' financial market patterns.

Hence it no doubt makes sense to supplement the monetary targeting strategy some  features  of  direct  inflation  targeting.  Then  the  European  Central  Bank  would  h elucidate its policies against the background of its money stock target and its price e Such a twofold transparency, in which it seems to me the money stock target should certain primacy, could help the single monetary policy to build up a reputation swif initial phase.

The European Monetary Institute has also elaborated some proposals relatin the range of policy instruments and its structure. The central banks are broadly ag number of instruments. That applies in particular to

- -the marginal refinancing facility,
- -the deposit facility, and
- -the open market instruments in the form of repo transactions (with maturities).

Repo transactions have meanwhile been accepted by all the national central b as an effective policy instrument consistent with market conditions.

The marginal refinancing facility is  intended  as  a  safety  valve  in  the  e short-term  liquidity  bottlenecks  in  the  money  market.  It  restricts  upward  swings  i market rates and thus steadies the money market. The deposit facility likewise has a effect, by offsetting short-term liquidity surpluses. It constitutes a floor for money Hence the two facilities virtually lay down the limits of the interest rate corridor.

I know that the topic of minimum reserves is no favourite of the banks. Even advise  the  ECB  to  make  limited  use  of  minimum  reserves,  not  so  much  as  a  manageme instrument but rather as a basis instrument. Minimum reserves, as a durable basis ins enhance the responsiveness of money demand to changes in interest rates, and thus can monetary policy more effective.

So  as  to  guarantee  the  uniformity  of  the  money  market  in  the  euro  area monetary policy operations of the central banks in 'euroland' should be settled on a basis. For that purpose, a cross-border large-value payment system - known as TARGET being set up. Since TARGET is attractive to the private sector as well, a disagreement about the conditions of access. In the main, it revolves around the conditions on whi and central banks outside the euro area are to be granted intra-day credit.

There  are  good  reasons  for  arguing  that  participants  in  another  monetary cannot be granted the same terms of access in every respect as participants within the union. It seems to be only logical that those who wish to benefit fully from the adv TARGET will also submit to the monetary policy constraints imposed by the euro area. events,  the  monetary  policy  of  the  euro  area  must  not  be  undermined  by  recourse TARGET system.

Viewed as a whole, there are signs that the instrumental prerequisites for monetary policy consistent with stability will soon all be met. Although that is not condition, it is certainly a necessary condition, for a stable euro. And the euro must b is to unfold in full its undoubtedly great potential for economic benefits. It is onl currency that in future it will be able to play a major role as a global reserve and currency, alongside the dollar. And it is only as a stable currency that the euro will contribution to the stability of the international financial system.

IV

But the stability of the international financial system also depen developments outside Europe. At the moment, after all, international organisa governments,  central  banks  and  private  financial  institutions  (such  as  the  IIF)  as engaged in drawing conclusions from the dramatic course of events in South-East Asia. observers are debating these conclusions in the rather imprecise terms of a radical ref structure of the international financial system, with ideas ranging from the abolition and World Bank - without replacement - to illusionary notions of a new Bretton Woods s or even a World Central Bank.

I am sure that all these extreme positions do not stand a chance in the rea In point of fact - as the discussions three weeks ago at the spring meeting of the IMF Bank in Washington showed - the key issue is how and in which direction the existing can be strengthened.

Unfortunately,  the  crucial  importance  of  well-functioning  markets  for  s international finance is often underrated. In South-East Asia, at any rate, the functi markets was obstructed in two respects:

- -externally,  by  clinging  too  long  to  exchange  rate  parities  which become unrealistic, and
- -internally, by investment decisions which were not geared adequately sustained profitability.

Any contribution to the prevention and solution of such crises cannot but en the markets' ability to function. And in this context it is not very helpful if the emphasises its financing role and steps in at an early stage with overly large financia That  only  creates  moral  hazard  problems.  This  is  because  such  financing  may  easi misconstrued  as  an  invitation  to  the  countries  concerned,  as  well  as  to  other  en countries, to refrain from undertaking essential structural reforms.

Private investors, too, are tempted to pay less heed to the risks. Charles was  quite  right  to  draw  attention  to  these  moral  hazard  problems  in  his  recent  let chairman of the Interim Committee.

In  my  opinion,  improving  surveillance  is  a  much  more  promising  approach Besides macroeconomic data, financial market data should be monitored more closely tha been the case hitherto. What we chiefly need, in my view, is more, and more up-to-date, countries' foreign currency debt. This is a challenge addressed to borrowers and lenders

The IMF should endeavour to obtain more, and above all better, data especi from the debtor countries. For the markets' ability to function, it is essential that data collected should be more transparent, more complete and more up-to-date. It is onl basis that the IMF can perform its primarily catalytic task. That strengthens the stru international financial system. And it should also be considered whether governments th comply with such transparency requirements should be publicly admonished.

The  challenge  extends  to  creditors,  too.  At  the  BIS  we  are  discussing  a moment how the time-lags in the provision of data can be substantially reduced. In pa the  crises  in  South-East  Asia  have  demonstrated  how  important  timely  information  o maturity and the currency of loans may be.

I  greatly  appreciate  the  fact  that  the  Institute  of  International  Financ buttresses efforts to bring about greater transparency among creditors. After all, this a certain extra workload on creditor banks. But the responsibility for crisis preventi rests on both sides - on the multilateral organisations and the private financial inst And if a crisis does erupt despite all the efforts at prevention, it can mostly only be private investors, too, pull their weight - pull their weight, that is, in a spirit self-interest.

Charles Dallara was therefore undoubtedly right when he wrote:

'In  this  era  of  globalization,  both  market  participants  and  multilatera institutions have crucial roles to play; the more they understand each othe the  greater  the  prospects  for  better-functioning  markets  and  financial stability.'

Of course, both sides have their own rules and responsibilities. But the their common interests and responsibilities too.

In  the  market-based  financial  world  of  today  and  tomorrow  multilate institutions can only play a limited role. Bailing out the private investors would n beyond  the  limits  of  the  available  reserves;  it  would  -  and  this  is  even  more  im undermine  the  proper  functioning  of  the  private  markets.  I  am  happy  to  mention  th IIF-members seem to share this view.
