title: Mr. Macfarlane reports on monetary policy and financial stability in the Australian Economy
description: Opening statement by the Governor of the Reserve Bank of Australia, Mr. Ian Macfarlane, to the House of Representatives Standing Committee on Financial Institutions and Public Administration in Melbourne on 7/5/98 (slightly abridged).
text:
## Mr.  Macfarlane  reports  on  monetary  policy  and  financial  stability  in  the

Australian  Economy Opening  statement  by  the  Governor  of  the  Reserve  Bank  of  Australia Mr. Ian Macfarlane, to the House of Representatives Standing Committee on Financial Insti and Public Administration in Melbourne on 7/5/98 (slightly abridged).

## 1. Introduction

## Mr Chairman,

It is a pleasure to be here in front of your Committee for the third time unde arrangements set out in the Statement on the Conduct of Monetary Policy . I hope this meeting will be as successful as its predecessors in helping to lift the level of understanding of mon financial stability, the Australian economy and, of course, the region more generally. I al have found our Semi-Annual Statement on Monetary Policy a useful source of information and a reasonably clear statement of our views.

It is especially pleasing that we are meeting here in Melbourne for the firs you  remember,  Mr.  Chairman,  the  attempt  to  do  so  last  November  was  foiled  by  a  clash Melbourne  Cup  week  and  the  attendant  shortage  of  hotel  rooms.  Fortunately,  the  Vict Government has not been able to put on a sporting extravaganza to foil our plans this time.

## 2. Review of last time

As  on  the  previous  occasion,  I  would  like  to  start  today  by  recognisin accountability includes being accountable for what was said last time. I will do this by how the past six months have turned out against the background of what I told the Commit were expecting last November. At that time, I summarised our expectations by saying that I 1997 would prove to be a good year for economic growth, with GDP growing by about 4 per that inflation would remain below 2 per cent for a while, but with a tendency to pick up through 1998, and that there was a good chance that unemployment would decline. I said ve about the current account and balance of payments, as the outlook for Asia was still very u

We  had  only  two  quarters'  data  on  economic  growth  in  1997  at  the  time  of previous meeting - now we have all four. The ABS records that GDP grew by 3.6 per cent ov four  quarters,  and  non-farm  GDP  by  3.8 per cent,  slightly  less  than  the  4  per  cent  t expecting. I do not think there is any point in making much of this small difference.

The  other  reason  that  I  would  not  make  much  of  this  small  difference  is  th outcome  for  the  labour  market  turned  out  to  be  a  bit  better  than  we  expected.  The unemployment rate in the first half of 1997 was 8¾ per cent. When we met in November, the recent figure we had was 8.6 per cent. The run of numbers we have received over the pa months have been either 8.2 per cent or 8.1 per cent. So if you look across the past 12 think you could see a reduction in the unemployment rate of ½ per cent or so. So over the 1997 a combination of good growth and moderate outcomes on wages made some inroads into o unemployment rate.

On inflation, I have little to add to what I said last time. Underlying inflati 1½ per cent over the past 12 months. We are still expecting that it will rise over the nex largely  because  falling  import  prices,  which  were  pushing  inflation  down,  have  given increasing import prices. In fact, the fall in the exchange rate has meant that wholesale have  risen  by  7.7  per  cent  over  the  past  12  months,  and  import  prices  made  their  firs contribution  at  the  retail  level  to  the  CPI  in  the  March  quarter  after  seven  quarters

detracted from it. These changes are not alarming, but they do tend to suggest that we ha the low point in the inflation cycle.

So I feel reasonably comfortable with our earlier assessment, except in one r last  time  we  met,  the  full  extent  of  the  Asian  slowdown  was  still  uncertain.  In  fact, interesting that as recently as six months ago, most discussions treated the ASEAN Four as known extent of the Asian slowdown. We did not know at that stage, although the possibil flagged, that Korea would join them, that Indonesia would deteriorate significantly furthe Japan would suffer a relapse into recession. When we take these developments into accoun clear  that  a  bigger  external  contractionary  effect  now  has  to  be  factored  in.  I  will  r subject in more detail later.

## 3. Prospects for 1998

## (a) General

So much for 1997 - what about 1998? In the absence of the external shock from 1998 was shaping up to be, if anything, a stronger year than 1997. There was nothing in th dynamic of the economy which was pointing to a slowdown, and we had every reason to exp growth of 4 per cent plus. That will no longer be the case, and we are now looking at growt 1998 of something more of the order of 3 per cent. This would probably mean that after a which the unemployment rate came down, we might be looking at a year in which it flattens o

I  have  already  mentioned  the  outlook  for  inflation  when  I  reviewed  the  pre year's results. Broadly speaking, we think that the trough in the inflation rate has passed back again into the 2-3 per cent range, but it is not doing so in an alarming way. We expec that range by the end of this year, and it probably will rise a bit during next year.

## (b) Balance of payments

Another part of the economy which in Australia has always been closely watche the current account of the balance of payments. With domestic demand in Australia growin above trend, but with a number of our major export markets declining, it is an arithmetica that the current account has to widen, as it has. This is not a sign of an economic policy trust markets will treat it accordingly. A number of people, including myself, have made that on this occasion the widening of the current account deficit is not the result of exc in domestic demand, nor is it the result of declining competitiveness because of high inflation, nor is it a counterpart to a large budget deficit. For these reasons, we exp arouse the same excitement as it has in the past, though you can never be sure. At pr expectation is that the current account deficit in 1998 will be about 5½ per cent of GDP, look at the cyclical behaviour of the current account over the last two decades, you could it touching 6 per cent for a time.

Imports are probably slowing from their very high growth rate in the second h last year, but not by much according to the March quarter figures. Over the course of 199 expect them to show their usual behaviour, that is to grow by a few percentage points f domestic demand. Exports, on the other hand, cannot hope to keep up last year's pace of cent, and a small positive figure is probably what we can expect.

Most  of  our  exports  -  our  rural  products  and  metals  and  minerals  -  are  so worldwide, rather than country-specific, markets. If we cannot sell zinc or copper to Korea to another country: the same goes for our rural exports. It means that for two-thirds of

what we earn is a function of world demand, not of the demand from our specific (largely trading partners. At the end of the day, the prices for these commodities adjust to clear and that has been happening. The prices of Australian commodity exports have fallen by 9 over the past year when measured in terms of a neutral basket of currencies. At the same Australian dollar has fallen against this neutral basket of currencies, so our commodit Australian dollars - what our exporters actually receive - have gone up slightly. Even for exports - coal and iron ore - where prices are renegotiated annually, the Australian doll contracts which commenced in April this year were higher than in the contracts a year earli an example of the market adjusting - in this case, the foreign exchange market - to shield sector (but not the whole economy) from the worst of the Asian downturn.

## 4. Asia

Having  made  these  points,  I  do  not  want  to  give  you  the  impression  that downplaying the effects of Asia. To the contrary, the biggest difference between the way our immediate future today and the way we viewed it a year ago is clearly the external have received from Asia. While it is true that the Australian business cycle is always aff world business cycle, the current Asian crisis is the first significant identifiable ext have had for a long time. The last time I can remember something as specific as this was O 1979, but that was on a much bigger scale and affected the whole OECD area more evenly. current Asian crisis is unusual in that Australia has a bigger exposure to it than any country (other than the two who are actually part of the crisis - Japan and Korea).

We  have  always  been  very  conscious  of  Australia's  vulnerability  to  a  s contraction in Asia. But it has always been our hope, and certainly the guiding princip Australia's policy, that the economic problems in Asia could be minimised by prompt action this awareness of possible danger ahead that lay behind Australia's very quick response t crisis, and the Reserve Bank's willingness to put funds from its balance sheet at the Go disposal to ensure that Australian participation was not delayed. It also explains why Aus only country other than Japan to be a part of all three Asian support packages - those fo Indonesia and Korea.

Australia has done what it can to help minimise the Asian fallout, but clearl have turned out worse than we had hoped for. The crisis has spread further than was at fi likely, it is resulting in larger falls in output and employment in the countries concerne it has been compounded by the relapse of the biggest Asian economy - Japan - into recessio started  as  a  currency  crisis  in  Thailand  is  leading  to  widespread  suffering  in  a  rang countries.

Of  course,  those  countries  have  some  deep-seated  economic  policy  deficienci weak  banking  sectors,  too  much  of  what  is  called  'crony  capitalism',  too  much  gover direction of investment (including implicit underwriting of loans) and insufficient discl accounting  standards,  etc.  These  deficiencies  are  common  to  most  countries  at  earlier development than ours, and they have been around for decades. They did not deter massive inflow for most of this decade, and I suppose it must be galling for some of these countri to sermons on their deficiencies delivered by international bankers who, until recently, to ply them with loans. We all have to agree that these countries made policy errors; tha the course. Yet I agree with Paul Krugman who, when commenting on the current situation, 'Yet governments are no more stupid or irresponsible now than they used to be; how com punishment has become so much more severe?'

These countries have had to make a very rapid adjustment to their external po to stop their exchange rates from falling below the extremely low levels they reached lat

They could not rely on a resumption of capital inflow to stop the problem, so the only fe was to return their current accounts to surplus. This has involved very tight policies, a in domestic demand, and very large falls in imports. For the three countries in IMF progra estimate that imports have already fallen by between 30 and 40 per cent. Even though ther been  enough  time  to  expand  exports  in  line  with  their  improved  competitiveness,  their accounts  have  already  moved  into  surplus.  Australia's  exports  to  these  countries  appear already fallen roughly in line with their falling imports. Thus, we have received the ef trade flows quite early in the piece. In time, when their exports pick up, we should get from this even if their domestic demand remains weak.

## 5.     How have we coped?

To date, we have coped quite well, largely because we were in good shape going it with strong domestic demand and low inflation. This was in part due to the fact that we expansionary monetary policy action between July 1996 and July 1997.

The  other  way  in  which  we  have  coped  well  is  that  our  financial  markets behaved very sensibly. It is true that our exchange rate has depreciated against the US against major currencies in general, but this is an understandable market reaction to the in our international trading environment. Apart from a minor panic in January, the whole pr been very orderly.

The bond market too has performed very well. International and domestic inves have clearly drawn a distinction between Australia and our Asian neighbours, and we have n any rise in risk premia on Australian bonds. Indeed, we have improved our position over th and Australian borrowers can now borrow in A$ at or below the same rate as equally credi US borrowers can borrow in US dollars. The Australian share market has also risen over the months and, even though it has not performed quite as well as some overseas markets, is hi its former peak in mid-1997.

What  is  the  implication  of  Asia  for  the  conduct  of  monetary  policy?  The  si answer is that it makes it more difficult. The Australian economy has suffered an external significant reduction in demand for our exports, which will lead to lower export volumes cases and lower export prices in others. This will show up in some combination of lower gr a widening of the current account of the balance of payments. Because of the fall that has our exchange rate, it will also show up as higher inflation than otherwise. Even if we foresight, we cannot adjust policy in a way which would avoid these outcomes altogether.

The best we can hope for is a combination which minimises the longer-run disru to  our  economy.  Choosing  the  monetary  policy  to  achieve  this  is  not  an  easy  task.  It constantly reviewing our position in the light of changes to the economy, and our forecast events. Importantly, it will be heavily influenced by how the Asian situation develops. I the only reason we are foreseeing any slowdown in growth in 1998 is because of the Asian there was nothing in the domestic economy that pointed in that direction - in fact, it poin growth. I suspect that in the future evolution of our policy, Asia will be the major influe

As you know, the Board of the Reserve Bank met on Tuesday and did not make an change to the setting of monetary policy. There had been some speculation over the precedin that we might ease, but the majority of observers expected no change. Our on-balance vie same as the majority of outside observers: that is, we judged that the present setting is As we see it:

- The  present  stance  of  monetary  policy  provides  a  low  interest  r environment  which  is  working  to  support,  rather  than  restra growth. Credit is readily available, borrowers seem to regard cur interest  rates  as  attractive,  financial  wealth  is  rising,  as  i sector leverage.
- Developments  in  the  exchange  rate  and  interest  rates  charged financial  intermediaries  since  the  last  reduction  in  the  cash  r July last year have worked to magnify the effects of lower offi rates.  The  exchange  rate  has  come  down  against  major  currencies and competition among banks has reduced interest rates to busine and personal borrowers.
- The  most  likely  outcome  over  the  next  12  months  at  the  presen policy  setting  is  for  inflation  to  return  to  its  target  range domestic  demand  to  remain  at  or  above  trend  growth.  With  a significant reduction in net exports, GDP will probably grow bel its  trend  rate,  but  some  growth  slowdown  in  the  short  run  is unavoidable result of the external shock.
- Our  measured  approach  to  date  has  served  us  well  in  that  it maintained  confidence  in  Australian  financial  markets.  That, course, does not rule out further changes in policy, but it does i a  constraint  in  that  it  means  monetary  policy  has  to  be  adju credibly.  We  do  not  wish  to  jeopardise  Australia's  current  go international  standing  or  revive  memories  of  when  Australia  wa regarded  as  a  'boom  and  bust'  economy.  We  gain  a  lot  from  our current reputation for stability - not only does it reduce our bor costs, but we can raise equity more cheaply, and we have become more attractive place for direct foreign investment.

Of course, we recognise that it would also be a mistake to stick too long to of policy in the name of stability if there were good reasons to move. We have to be consci risks to our current assessment, and constantly review them. The major downside risk which see is the possibility that the effect of the Asian and Japanese situations might prod slowing  in  the  Australian  economy  than  our  current  expectations,  perhaps  indirectly  by growth substantially in other trading partners or by seriously dampening domestic demand income or confidence effects. Such an outcome is not in our view the most likely one some probability.

title: Mr. Gunnarsson reports on some aspects of economic conditions and current prospects in Iceland  (Central Bank Articles and Speeches, 31 Mar 98)
description: Address by the Governor of the Central Bank of Iceland, Mr. Birgir Isl. Gunnarsson, at the Bank's Annual Meeting on 31/3/98.
text:
Mr.  Gunnarsson  reports  on  some  aspects  of  economic  conditions  and current  prospects  in  Iceland Address  by  the  Governor  of  the  Central  Bank  of  Iceland Mr. Birgir Isl. Gunnarsson, at the Bank's Annual Meeting on 31/3/98.

On behalf of the Board of Governors of the Central Bank I welcome you to t 37th  Annual  Meeting  of  the  Bank.  The  Bank's  Annual  Accounts  for  1997  have  today  bee ratified by the Minister of Commerce, and the Bank's Annual Report has been published Report gives an overview of the Bank's operations and a detailed description of econom monetary developments in the past year, as well as of the Bank's monetary policy objecti measures. I will discuss some aspects of economic conditions and current prospects, those that are most closely linked to the Central Bank's areas of responsibility.

## Economic Growth

GDP  grew  sharply  in  1997  for  the  second  year  in  a  row.  It  is  estimated growth was 5 percent, compared with 5.5 percent in 1996. Economic growth in Iceland du these two years has been far higher than in other industrial countries. In the Europ growth was 2.6 percent and in the United States 3.8 percent; in Japan, which has faced in recent times, growth was only 1 percent. The British economy has strengthened in years and growth is estimated to have been 3 percent in 1997. The rapid growth of the d economy inevitably raises the question of whether this is consistent in the long run economic stability that has been achieved in recent years. The growing current accoun clearly  preaches  caution  and  underscores  the  need  for  sufficiently  tight  monetary  a conditions.

Growth in 1997 was primarily driven by growing private consumption and fix investment. Private consumption rose by 6 percent and fixed investment by 9.9 percent the last two years fixed investment has increased sharply following many years of cont Investment  in  power-intensive  industry  has  played  an  important  role,  as  has  invest commercial buildings. Housing investment has also begun to recover during the last two but not sufficiently to offset the decline in the previous year.

## Current Account Deficit

The current account deficit turned out smaller in 1997 than had been expect just in excess of 8 billion kronur. Merchandise imports grew by 5.9 percent in volum with consumer goods accounting for three-fifths of the increase and investment goods than a third. Here it needs to be borne in mind that it may have been mere coincidence imports for power-intensive industrial projects were recorded in 1997 or 1998. More ap have been recorded in 1998 than expected. Merchandise exports grew by less than 2 perc volume terms, which is not a particularly good performance. The growth of exports is in slow in relation to, for example, the expansion of world trade. Thus, it can be said export growth is as much the cause of the current account deficit as the expansion of demand.

## Business Profitability and the Labour Market

The external conditions of the economy in 1997 were largely unchanged fr 1996, and were on the whole favourable. Business profitability seems to have been fair although not as favourable as in 1996, because of the wage increases at the beginning o

and large depreciation and interest charges related to the high levels of investment years, especially in the fisheries. The labour market situation improved furt unemployment declined to 3.9 percent on average, having come down from a peak of 5 per in 1995. Real wages grew by 5.7 percent in the course of 1997, and were at year-end highest level since 1989.

## Prices

Inflation remained subdued in 1997, or 2.2 percent in the course of the ye 1.8 percent on average between 1996 and 1997. The Central Bank had, in the wake of the settlements, forecast somewhat higher inflation but wage increases did not translate increases to the extent shown by past experience. Productivity growth was higher than e and the rise in import prices lower. In addition, the Central Bank's measures restra increases, as I will discuss in greater detail shortly. In January, the Bank forecast would average 2.6 percent between 1997 and 1998, and 2.3 percent in the course of the seems clear that inflation during the first quarter of this year has been lower than January.

## Government Finances

In 1997, the Treasury recorded a welcome surplus of 1.3 billion kronur on a basis  despite  tax  cuts,  a  rise  in  the  wage  bill  and  special  interest  payments  asso government bond redemptions. In order to compare the outcome with the budget it is nec to exclude the special interest payments of 3.5 billion kronur. Thus adjusted, the surplus was 4.7 billion kronur. A Treasury surplus had not been recorded since 1984. accrual basis, which includes accrued interest and pension liabilities, the Treasury' appear  to  have  been  close  to  balance  in  1997.  The  Treasury  repaid  debt  during  th Amortization of foreign debt exceeded new borrowing by 6.5 billion kronur, or the equiv 5 percent of the Treasury's foreign debt; this marked the first time since 1986 that a of foreign debt exceeded new borrowing. Domestically, new borrowing exceeded amortizat by 3.4 billion kronur.

While this turnaround in the Treasury's finances is certainly to be welcom is,  nonetheless,  a  somewhat  mixed  blessing.  It  is  a  matter  of  concern  that  the improvement  in  the  Treasury's  finances  in  1998  is  less  than  warranted  by  the  aut stabilizers  alone  and  that,  all  other  things  equal,  the  degree  of  fiscal  restraint demand in 1998 will be less than last year. In preparations for the 1999 budget it is paramount  importance,  in  light  of  economic  conditions,  to  aim  for  a  substantial  T surplus. The same considerations, of course, apply to the implementation of the 1998 and any excess revenue should be used to improve the financial balance rather then en extra spending. I say this because there are limits on what monetary policy can accom restrain domestic demand in the current circumstances.

Local  government  finances  deteriorated  somewhat  in  1997.  The  combined revenue deficit of the 14 largest municipalities was 2.9 billion kronur. It is estimat government  debt  increased  from  36  billion  kronur  to  42  billion  kronur  in  1997.  G government debt in relation to GDP declined from 56 percent in 1996 to 52.7 percent i which, in light of the Maastricht limit on government debt of 60 percent of GDP, is a f debt position.

Monetary Developments

The Central Bank's principal target remains price stability. The Bank's mon instruments primarily influence inflation in the long run, and it is generally accepte stability  is  an  important  precondition  for  economic  growth  and  improved  living  sta Domestically there is a good consensus about this goal, as is the case in most countr central banks pursue the same or a similar objective.

In an open economy such as the Icelandic one a stable exchange rate is nece for favourable price developments. A stable exchange rate has, therefore, been an inte target for monetary policy. The Central Bank implements monetary policy mainly by sett own interest rates and by intervening on the money market. In the short run the Bank influence the exchange rate through the purchase and sale of foreign currency.

Given  the  conditions  that  prevailed  in  1997,  there  was  clearly  a  dang overheating which led the Central Bank to pursue a tight monetary policy. After the B raised money market rates in the fall of 1996 the differential between domestic money rates and those in main trading partner countries widened to 3 percentage points. Th necessary  response  to  the  growing  uncertainty  about  the  outcome  of  the  pending negotiations, and it led to an acceptable equilibrium for some time. However, some c outflow was experienced during the first weeks of 1997 until the outline of the wage se began to emerge. The wage settlements eased fears of rising inflation and increased co in a stable exchange rate. The Central Bank, nevertheless, maintained unchanged intere and considerable currency inflow took place through July. International reserves grew t of 36.2 billion kronur at the end of July, up 5.2 billion kronur from the beginning despite the repayment of some of the Treasury's foreign debt.

The Central Bank thought it desirable that the exchange rate of the krona strengthen  somewhat  to  lessen  pressures  on  the  domestic  market  and  dampen  infla pressures. The Bank's measures undoubtedly contributed to lower inflation than expected.

Monetary  developments  changed  course  at  the  beginning  of  August.  Currency outflow commenced anew and bond market yields began to rise. This change was the resul increased purchases of foreign securities by residents, a stop in the relending of fo and an increase in general bank lending. The differential between domestic and foreign market rates had also narrowed because of interest rate rises in some neighbouring c When it had become clear that this was not a temporary situation, the Central Bank re by raising interest rates by 0.3 percent in mid-November. The interest rate had an i impact, the exchange rate of the krona strengthened and the currency outflow stopped. end of the year, the exchange rate index was 0.9 percent below the central rate of the range  after  having  strengthened  on  the  whole  by  1.4  percent  in  the  course  of  th International reserves stood at 27.8 billion kronur at year-end, down 3 billion kronur earlier.  Reserves  are  now  about  27  billion  kronur.  The  Central  Bank's  short-term liabilities were close to zero at year-end, where they in fact remain.

## The Bond Market

Bond market reforms were continued in 1997. In 1996, the Central Bank decid to withdraw from the long-term market and reached custodian agreements with three secu firms following a bidding process. The Bank handed over to the firms a part of its s portfolio and at the same time ceased to be a market maker in government bonds, gover notes  and  housing  bonds.  The  experience  from  these  agreements  is  positive  and  they

renewed in March 1997. The new agreements were more extensive than the earlier ones, a their wake two banks announced that they would engage in market making for certain clas government securities in the same manner as the custodial firms. It is not unlikely custodial agreements will become unnecessary and that the Central Bank will no longer n be involved in ensuring adequate market making in the long-term market. Both the Treasu the State Housing Authority began to reorganize the classes of bonds they issue, with of improving the price determination of government guaranteed bonds and raising turno the secondary market.

## The Central Bank's Monetary Policy Instruments

In  1997,  the  Central  Bank  began  preparing  changes  to  its  monetary  pol instruments.  The  purpose  was  twofold:  first,  to  level  the  playing  field  for  domest institutions with respect to their access to facilities at the Central Bank, and, sec the operating environment of domestic credit institutions to the environment prevaili European Economic Area.

These  changes  have  been  modelled  on  the  instruments  designed  for  th prospective  European  Central  Bank,  which  will  be  established  on  July  1  and  for commence  operations  on  January  1,  1999.  Under  the  auspices  of  the  European  Moneta Institute,  the  precursor  to  the  European  Central  Bank,  work  has  proceeded  on  design monetary  instruments  of  the  bank.  The  Central  Bank  has  followed  this  work  to  the possible. Some issues, such as concerning reserve requirements, will not be resolved u the European Central Bank has been established. The Central Bank may therefore adjust it when the situation in Europe becomes clearer.

The first step in changing the Central Bank's instruments was taken on Mar and covered the following. The liquidity requirement of deposit banks was abolished. auctions  of  14-day  repurchase  agreements  replaced  the  tap-sale  of  these  agreement government  guaranteed  securities  and  the  Central  Bank's  certificates  of  deposit  qu collateral for repurchase agreements rather than only Treasury bills and certificates The Central Bank will auction 14-day certificates of deposit when it feels the need to liquidity. The direct sale of 45-day certificates of deposit will cease, but 90-day cer continue  to  be  sold.  A  new  overnight  facility  for  credit  institutions  subject requirements  was  established  at  the  Central  Bank.  Collateral  for  overnight  loans provided by government guaranteed securities held by the credit institutions.

The  next  step  in  these  changes  will  take  place  on  April  1  when  new  r governing reserve requirements will take effect. The reserve base will be widened to in foreign borrowing of credit institutions while the reserve requirement ratio will be the change is intended to be broadly neutral with respect to required deposits, thus change  neutral  from  a  monetary  policy  perspective.  The  reserve  requirement  ratio  wil percent on obligations under 1 year to maturity but 1.5 percent on obligations tied than 1 year. Also, the reserve requirement will cover more institutions than before, institutions subject to reserve requirements will have access to facilities at the Cen will  be  possible  to  meet  the  reserve  requirement  more  flexibly  than  has  been  th Indexation of required deposits will be abolished but the interest rate on them will set on the basis of prevailing yields.

The last step in these changes will be taken on May 21 when the first calcu based on the new rules concerning reserve requirements will be done. At the same tim so-called discount quota, which is a facility that the Central Bank has offered to dep will be abolished. The Bank will also close the foreign currency accounts of deposit ba held.

Since 1987 the Central Bank has targeted interest rates to achieve its mo policy objective rather than targeting the money supply or base money. The access that banks have to liquidity at the Central Bank is therefore flexible and at their own disc the Bank's interest rates among the factors influencing the extent to which the draw on from the Central Bank. At the outset, the long-term market was most important to the Bank but as the money market and the foreign exchange market developed during 1992 1993, the Bank began to focus its activities on them. The Central Bank's instrument rat the  yield  it  requires  on  repurchase  agreements  with  credit  institutions.  This  arran similar to the most common practice among industrial countries, and is based on the that central bank instrumental rates largely determine money market rates. Money marke then influence price developments, with price stability being the ultimate objective, t channels. First, they have a strong direct impact on currency flows and the exchange r capital movements have been liberalized. Second, they affect the interest rates of dep and the entire interest rate spectrum, which in turn influences consumption and invest thereby  affect  the  level  of  demand  on  goods  and  labour  markets.  Thus,  the  Central achieves its objective whether it targets prices directly or indirectly by having the e as an intermediate target.

The  changes  that  the  Central  Bank  implemented  at  the  beginning  of  Marc concerning repurchase agreements had two components. On the one hand, the definition o collateral  that  qualified  for  repurchase  agreements  was  widened  to  include  again, intermission, all market listed government guaranteed securities and central bank cert deposit.  The  purpose  of  this  change  is  to  level  the  positions  of  the  various  go securities,  as  varying  positions  in  regard  to  liquidity  transactions  with  the  Centra influence  their  relative  market  yields.  It  is  clear  that  such  limitations  do  not Iceland's  neighbours.  In  addition,  the  stock  of  outstanding  Treasury  bills  has  shru recent  period,  which  has  caused  a  shortage  of  these  bills  for  deposit  banks  to  use repurchase agreements with the Central Bank. The other change is, as mentioned before, practice of offering repurchase agreements on tap has been abolished and replaced by a auction of the agreements, as is done in many industrial countries. The Central Bank c discretion  choose  to  auction  reverse  repurchase  agreements instead of straightf repurchase agreements.

Neither of these changes alters the course of monetary policy. However, the have the effect of reversing the rise in money market rates that had occurred in Ja February, when the interbank rate rose to 8.3 percent because of the shortage of Trea on the market. This moved money market rates back to the level the Central Bank had aim when it set its interest rates in November, a range of 7.2-7.4 percent. It is always de is precisely the right level of money market rates in light of the situation on and p the foreign exchange market in the short run and for the goods and labour markets 1hence.  The  Central  Bank's  current  assessment  is  that  the  level  of  the  interest  r November provides sufficient restraint to ensure price stability in the period ahead. this assessment is under constant review in light of the development of a host of indic

## Foreign Exchange Market

The  foreign  exchange  market  was  reorganized  in  1997.  The  exchange  rat quotation meetings were abolished and replaced by a continuous market. Furthermore, m participants  other  than  the  Central  Bank,  now  six  institutions,  replaced  the  Bank  a makers  on  this  market.  The  arrangement  is  now  similar  to  that  among  many  neighbour countries. The Central Bank's transactions on the foreign exchange market are now alway own initiative, and should be view as intervention aimed at influencing the exchange r new market arrangement has greatly improved the flow of information about market condi and made the market more active. Also, all information about pressure on the exchange r appears instantaneously and the volume of transactions has grown sharply. Total turnove foreign  exchange  market  was  162  billion  kronur  in  1997,  and  had  doubled  since  1996 addition, the participation of the Central Bank in foreign exchange market transactions 82 percent of turnover in 1996 to 37 percent in 1997. So far this year turnover has co increase and the share of the Central Bank has declined to 13.2 percent. Average daily has been about 2 billion kronur this year. Daily fluctuations in the exchange rate inc result of last year's change, but not much when compared to what is common among ot countries.  Since  mid-1993,  or  for  almost  5  years,  the  exchange  rate  of  the  krona  h deviated more than 2.1 percent from the central rate.

## Yields on Domestic Markets

Money market yields declined in the course of the year until the Central raised its rates in November after which they rose. Yields on 3-month Treasury bills ro percent where they stood at year-end. A low Treasury borrowing requirement at times ca shortage of Treasury bills. Demand for Treasury bills was also boosted because of in interest in them for liquidity management.

Yields on indexed bonds changed little during the first half of 1997 but the second half the yield on government bonds and housing bonds fell sharply, albeit u This  decline  was  partly  the  result  of  the  low  Treasury  borrowing  requirement.  The  y non-indexed government bonds also declined sharply in 1997, although also unevenly, t percent at year-end. Yields on both indexed and non-indexed bonds have continued to fa year, with the yield on government guaranteed indexed bonds now well below 5 percent w some had regarded as the floor.

Although money and bond market yields declined in 1997 the lending rates commercial and saving banks changed little. These rates have now begun to come down. Profitability of deposit institutions

The profitability of banks improved during 1997. Current information on pr of the commercial banks shows a substantial increase compared with the preceding year. combined return on equity was 9.2% in 1997, compared with 8.2% in 1996 and 5% in the y before that. Nonetheless, profitability varied widely among them, and the different c that they faced complicate comparisons. Landsbanki (the National Bank) and Búnaðarbanki Agricultural Bank), for example, incurred large irregular expenses related to the final of their pension obligations, which cannot be expected to recur in future. Provisions for loan losses have fallen sharply among all the banks. At the same time, the six larg banks recorded some decline in profitability compared with the previous year, and thei

on  equity  was  8.5%.  I  should  underline,  however,  that  profitability  varied  widely individual savings banks.

## Reforms to the Banking System

There  now  appears  to  be  widespread  agreement  that  efficiency  needs  to improved  in  the  banking  system  in  order  to  lower  costs  and  make  domestic  banks  m competitive in relation to foreign competitors, which will seek a market share in Ice necessary to take advantage of the opportunity provided by the incorporation of the st into limited liability companies and the prospective sale of shares in them. Certain go be kept in mind. Effective competition on financial markets needs to be secured, alth merger of institutions should not be excluded if it can improve efficiency and profita important question arises whether the state as owner of three strong institutions shou lead in the necessary restructuring or whether powerful institutional investors are ne the job. Foreign investors with experience in banking are one option. The latter appro however,  prevent  the  Treasury  from  realizing  the  full  value  of  its  assets  in  the institutions. The wide distribution of share holdings will also undoubtedly be an is debate. This is by no means a simple matter and desirable goals may not be fully consis main goal must be to ensure effective competition and efficiency improvements in the op of credit institutions.

## Pension Funds

It is estimated that the assets of the pension funds which are available pensions, stood at 345 billion kronur at the end of 1997, an increase of more than kronur, or 12.7 percent, in the course of the year. The composition of pension fund a change somewhat. Holdings of market listed securities expanded by 25.6 billion kronur holdings of other securities declined by 3.7 billion kronur. At the end of 1997, the pe held  21.7  billion  kronur  worth  of  domestic  shares.  The  pension  funds'  holdings  of securities  grew  sharply  in  1997,  or  by  12.6  billion  kronur,  about  one-half  of  whic shares.  At  the  end  of  1997,  the  pension  funds  held  foreign  securities  valued  at  22 kronur.

## Payment Intermediation

Over the last two years, the Central Bank has increasingly turned its atte payment  systems,  both  to  specific  payment  forms  and  to  settlement  systems.  The  Bank released  two  reports  on  this  subject,  one  on  electronic  payment  forms  and  another comparison  of  payment  intermediation  in  Iceland  with  international  practice.  In  rece there has been growing international concern that settlement systems do not adequately account settlement risks. Two responses have been adopted. First, strong conditions ha imposed  on  net  settlement  systems  which  lower  risk,  and  plans  have  been  laid  fo contingency  that  a  settlement  party  is  unable  to  meet  its  obligations.  Second,  net systems have been abandoned in favour of real-time settlement, in which each transac recorded immediately and permanently, rather than transactions being netted, for exampl end  of  the  day.  It  now  appears  to  be  generally  accepted  that  settlement  systems,  w central bank provides settlement services, should be real-time systems. In light of th the  Central  Bank  began  in  co-operation  with  financial  institutions  a  review  of  d settlement systems with the view of bringing them into line with best international pra aim is to establish a real-time settlement system in 1999. The operation of a real-time

system  will  be  a  precondition  for  participation  in  the  European  Central  Bank's  TA settlement system should it become available.

## Financial System Stability

Securing the sound operation of financial institutions is a task of steadil importance for the Central Bank. By law, the Central Bank is required to protect the system and support sound money and securities transactions. Central banks pursue this t variety  of  ways.  They  carefully  follow  those  macroeconomic  developments,  which  imp money flows and thus the profitability of financial institutions. Securing payment and systems is a central bank task across the world. Central banks are also lenders of la financial  institutions  and  need  to  be  prepared  to  lend  resources  in  excess  of  wh normally be required. The Central Bank of Iceland has partly performed this task thr Bank Inspectorate which has been built from the ground up in the Bank and is closely l some of the Bank's other activities, for example in regard to a joint database. Par currently debating draft legislation, which calls for the creation of a new supervisory which would combine all supervision of financial institutions. I cannot deny that th Bank is opposed to these ideas for reasons I discussed at this venue last year, and I into the issue in any more detail now. However, since the government's wishes in this became clear the Central Bank has co-operated wholeheartedly with the Ministry of Comm in preparing the best possible legislation in this area and in securing the necessary the Central Bank and the new supervisory institution and also to ensure that The Cent will have all necessary opportunities to guard a sound and effective financial system central banks, which do not have supervision among their responsibilities, such as in and the United Kingdom, much work has been put into defining the relevant tasks of the bank. The Central Bank is bound to seek models in these countries when it becomes cle the Bank Inspectorate will depart.

## European Monetary Union

There  are  now  9  months  until  the  member  countries  of  the  European  Union which meet the requirements of the Maastricht Treaty and become members of the Europ Monetary Union, adopt a new currency, the euro. There is now little to suggest that thi happen on January 1, 1999 and the European Central Bank will be established this comin 1. The Central Bank has thought it necessary to follow these developments closely, not order to be able to analyze the impact on Iceland and the options available to Iceland environment.  In  June  1997,  the  Central  Bank  released  a  report European  Monetary  Union, Creation  and  Impact. The  Bank  will  release  interim  reports  on  this  issue  as  the  occa warrants. At this stage, it is premature to say what impact the Monetary Union will Icelandic exchange rate policy or on the options Iceland will face. I will, nevertheles words about the subject as it appears from the perspective of the Central Bank. The o now that 11 countries will form the Monetary Union at the outset. These countries acco only 33 percent of Iceland's external goods trade. The initial impact will therefore no as significant as has been suggested in the domestic debate. Only when the United Ki joins the Monetary Union will more than one half of Iceland's goods trade be with coun the union.

But  which  options  will  we  have  as  regards  exchange  rate  policy  when  t Monetary Union has come into existence? Theoretically the options are: 1) the current 2) a floating exchange rate; 3) a unilateral link with the euro; 4) a bilateral link

and 5) introducing the euro as legal tender in Iceland. This list does not include mem the Monetary Union, as that is only available to members of the European Union.

Three  factors  need  to  be  considered  when  weighing  these  options:  first, success they will produce in terms of low inflation and economic stability; second, h are they to narrow interest rate differentials vis-à-vis abroad; and, third, the flexibility they o in case of external shocks, whether positive or negative.

The current arrangement calls for the maintenance of a trade-weighted exch rate index within 6 percent on either side of a central rate. The arrival of the e prevent  the  continuation  of  this  arrangement.  The  euro  would  be  assigned  a  weight currency basket consistent with the Monetary Union members' share of Iceland's external This approach will, however, not yield any progress towards narrowing interest rate dif vis-à-vis those abroad beyond the growing credibility that economic stability will achi own in due course. title: Ms. Rivlin remarks on lessons drawn from the Asian financial crisis  (Central Bank Articles and Speeches, 23 Apr 98)
description: Remarks by the Vice-Chair of the US Federal Reserve System, Ms. Alice M. Rivlin, before the Hyman P. Minsky Conference on Financial Structure at The Levy Institute in Annandale-on-Hudson, New York on 23/4/98.
text:
Ms. Rivlin remarks on lessons drawn from the Asian financial crisis Remarks by the Vice-Chair of the US Federal Reserve System, Ms. Alice M. Rivlin, before the Hym Minsky  Conference  on  Financial  Structure  at  The  Levy  Institute  in  Annandale-on-Hudson, York on 23/4/98.

## Toward A Better Class of Financial Crises: Some Lessons from Asia

Drawing  lessons  from  the  Asian  financial  crisis  has  become  a  minor  indus partially offsetting the impact of the crisis on developed economies -- at least for ec contributes to conference budgets, airline revenues, bar tabs, and the length of academi The opining classes can turn almost any bad news into an excuse for more meetings in be settings like Bard College.

Some of the talk has been devoted to the blame game. Was the crisis (or rath rolling  set  of  interrelated  crises)  home-grown,  that  is,  brought  on  by  ill-conceived over-leveraged companies, lax banking supervision and crony capitalism in the borrowing cou Was it the greed, inattention, or herd instinct of the lenders? Or was it the inherent international capital flows? Did the IMF step in just in time to avert total meltdown or provide  early  enough  warning?  Did  the  conditions  imposed  on  borrowers  help  restore  in confidence or further undermine it?

The quick answer is that all of the alleged culprits bear part of the resp International flows of capital can be unstable -- what flows in can quickly flow out -- a enormous escalation in the volume of private capital flows, coupled with the advent of sim communication in all the world's markets, has greatly increased the exposure of economies turnarounds in cross-border flows. Decades of rapid growth and apparently unending capital had made the Asian emerging markets, until recently known as 'tigers', believe they were from  the  reversals  of  investor  confidence  that  beset  other  parts  of  the  world  and  pr incaution that led to over investment in some sectors, inflated equity and real estate pric ill-thought-out  projects,  public  and  private.  Close  relations  between  companies,  ba governments created false senses of security, as well as uneconomic 'policy' loans and inv Weak supervision of financial institutions and markets, on top of traditions of secrecy and governmental transactions, aggravated the crises when things turned down. At the sam foreign investors and creditors asked too few questions, were hesitant to reign in the gal that had laid so many golden eggs, and reinforced each other's reluctance to be the first As  tensions  were  developing,  the  IMF  pointed  to  some  of  the  dangers  without  getting response, and missed some others, as did the much-vaunted market gurus and rating agencies the crises hit, the IMF quickly crafted rescue packages that imposed serious structural conditions  of  aid,  inevitably  making  some  mistakes  in  the  process,  but  arresting  the downward spiral and restoring enough confidence to allow the countries to get their policie to support the climb back to economic health. No one thinks the climb will be easy, but t is that the worst is over.

Now  the  talk  has  shifted  to  the  more  difficult  subject  of  what  the  inter community can do to prevent, mitigate and manage financial crises in the future. The stakes for industrial and emerging market countries alike. When international capital markets func they help achieve rising standards of living for both creditor and debtor countries. When crash, they bring incredible hardship to ordinary workers and their families -- often peopl been pulled out of their traditional occupations and communities by economic change and ma nothing to fall back on.

Two  sets  of  prescriptions  are  relatively  uncontroversial,  albeit  deceptively achieve.  First,  the  world's  capital  markets  and  the  machinery  designed  to  stabilize  th function better with more complete, accessible and timely information flows. Investors c better decisions and lenders can exercise more discipline over borrower behavior if they accurate  and  more  complete  information  and  have  it  sooner.  Both  international  and  do officials  can  monitor,  supervise  and  warn  of  impending  danger  only  if  they  know  the Improving transparency should apply not only to businesses and banks, but to official bod national and international. It's important to know what a country's budget deficit really i and off budget) and what its exchange reserves really are, including any operations in t markets. The Asian crisis was certainly exacerbated by lack of information of many sorts, accurate data on reserves.

There  is  currently  a  great  flurry  of  activity  in  various  international  for standards of accounting and reporting on business, banking and governmental activity and sheets.  Progress  will  be  made.  But  one  should  not  expect  too  much.  Although  post  morte financial  crises,  especially  reviews  of  investor  decisions  that  went  sour,  feature  a  g if-only-we-had-known rhetoric, in actual fact a great deal of information usually turns been available which no one ever looked at or effectively analyzed. For transparency to people need to actually want to look -- and too often those who are making high profits wo not hear bad news.

Second, a major sustained international effort is needed to strengthen the s functioning and supervision of financial systems in emerging market countries. A clear recent economic history (and not just in emerging market countries) is the crucial impo strong  banks  and  other  financial  institutions,  adequately  capitalized  and  able  to  ma overseen by serious prudential supervision and an independent well managed central bank. In countries can ill-afford to be sanctimonious on this score -- many of us have experienced t effects of poor prudential supervision or lack of political will to close failing financia but good management and strong supervision of financial institutions is clearly a key to wi economic shocks.

Here, too, consensus is strong and serious activity is underway under the ae variety of international bodies, perhaps too many, to evolve clear rules for financial sup help countries implement them. The task will require time, patience and resources. It is n examiners,  but  bankers  who  need  training  in  how  to  do  their  jobs  in  modern,  fast internationally exposed economies. Strengthening financial systems, including improving co governance, goes hand in hand with efforts to improve transparency and information flow investors,  shareholders,  supervisors  and  international  agencies  --  and  both  will  requir effort and run into significant resistance.

The  first  two  prescriptions  are  preventive,  designed  to  reduce  the  frequen amplitude of financial crises. But no one with a sense of history -- or reality -- belie can be eliminated. Hence, a third prescription also appears on everybody's list, albeit w agreement on what it means, namely, private creditors should take on a greater portion of of resolving future international financial crises. Sharing the burden is a far more diff come  to  grips  with  conceptually  than  either  the  need  for  greater  transparency  or  the stronger, better supervised financial systems. Not much intellectual structure yet exists about burden-sharing in international financial crises. Moreover, cross-border financing so rapidly and market instruments are morphing so fast that designing ways of sharing the like changing the tires on a moving car -- pretty exciting and not obviously doable.

The  task  cannot  be  set  aside,  however,  for  at  least  two  reasons.  First,  th resolving international financial crises is outrunning the likely resources available for The volume of cross-border flows has grown precipitously and the cost of breakdown has es with it. High speed traffic on a six lane freeway moves a lot of people to their destinat the pile-up in a wreck is a lot more expensive than on a winding two lane road. If rec continue, managing the next crisis will call for more resources than taxpayers in the Un and  other  developed  countries  are  likely  to  feel  comfortable  turning  over  to  the  IMF international organizations, even if they are reasonably confident that the borrowing cou pay the loans back, as experience indicates they will.

Second, and far more important, the perception that official resources can be on  to  bail  out  creditors  (directly  or  indirectly)  arguably  generates  moral  hazard.  It  c excessive risk-taking by lenders and funding of less economically defensible projects. I channel financing into less stable forms whose overuse makes crises more likely to occur. episodes, direct investors and holders of equity and long-term debt have taken serious l short-term  lenders,  especially  interbank  lenders,  have  been  largely  protected.  While  a trouble has understandable reasons for not wanting to cut itself off from short-term bank for  using  its  scarce  international  resources  to  keep  this  lifeline  attached,  the  resu reinforce  excessive  dependence  on  debt  rather  than  equity  and  on  short,  rather  than  lo financing.

Both reasons combine to create an urgent need for serious and creative thought part  of  the  international  community  about  how  to  'bail  in'  private  sector  financiers, reduce the impact on the financial resources of official institutions like the IMF, the Wor the regional development banks, to reduce moral hazard leading to excessive risk-taking, short-term inter-bank borrowing, and to improve risk assessment.

Designing  mechanisms  for  appropriate  burden  sharing  among private secto investor/creditors  is  inherently  hard  because  it  runs  into  some  very  sticky  and  fu dilemmas. The basic principle from which all borrowing and lending must proceed is that who  use  other  people's  money  have  a  firm  obligation  to  pay  it  back.  Hence,  a  suspens payments  or  a  work-out  arrangement  must  be  clearly  rare  and  exceptional,  resorted  to extreme situations. Raising fears that suspensions are likely or work-outs normal could unn increase  the  cost  of  capital,  cause  drastic  reductions  in  cross-border  flows  and  dimi incomes of debtors and creditors alike. Yet having no known or understood process for deal default  can,  as  has  been  seen  in  Asia,  lead  to  inequitable  burden  sharing,  high  offici potential future moral hazard.

A related basic dilemma involves the timing of a suspension of payments. Autho have to hold off long enough to be sure there is no other choice, but not wait so long th are running for the doors and irreversible damage is already done.

The problem is, of course, not entirely new. International borrowers have gott trouble  before,  and  precedents  for  workouts  have  been  developed  --  Paris  Club  procedu resolving sovereign debts to public creditors; London Club for resolving sovereign debts banks. But each crisis is different from the last. A critical element in the Mexican cris was  the  threat  of  default  on  dollar-indexed  Mexican  short-term  bonds  (tesebonos 1 )  for  which  no work-out process existed. Dealing with bond holders (who are likely to be numerous and sc is more complex than dealing with lending governments or a relatively small (and known) g

1 Tesebonos were technically denominated in pesos.

international banks. The recent Asian crises posed still another problem. The borrowers governments, but private banks and corporations, a situation that may be typical of future one that adds greatly to the legal and organizational complexities of sharing the burden distress.

When the debt in question is sovereign debt, whether to banks or other lend may not be hard to re-establish stability and confidence in the sovereign. The IMF can le to solve the borrowing government's immediate liquidity problem while the government works debt restructuring with its creditors. IMF rules permit 'lending into arrears' in these cir

If  the  creditors  are  bondholders,  as  they  were  in  Mexico,  the  situation difficult. IMF rules do not at present permit a government borrowing from the IMF when it to pay its bondholders. Even a small minority of the bondholders can use their bargaining obstruct a resolution of the crisis in hopes of getting a better deal. After the Mexican c resolved with the help of significant new official lending to Mexico, the international focused on how to improve the bargaining position of the debtor government with its bondho such a crisis should arise in the future.

The 'Rey Report' on Sovereign Liquidity Crises (named for its author, Jean-Jac Rey of the Central Bank of Belgium) was a major effort by the G-10 countries to learn the l Mexico. It recommended two new steps:

- First, the IMF should expand its willingness to lend into arrears to co situation in which a sovereign was making a good faith effort to work out restructuring with its bondholders.
- Second,  it  recommended  that  bonds  issued  in  international  markets  cont clauses that would facilitate debt restructuring if it became necessary. could be added to provide for debt-holder representation in negotiations w sovereign or qualified majority voting on changes in terms. Such clauses w make it harder for minority creditors to block restructuring or exact a price than necessary to satisfy the majority.

Neither of these recommendations received much official attention until the crisis hit. Although the recommendations were not actually germane to the situation in Asia reviewed the recommendations at its Interim Committee meeting in April 1998 and action near future seems more likely than a year ago. Perhaps the official community will alway crisis late.

Unlike  the  sovereign  debt  crises  in  Latin  America,  the  situation  in  Asia  i private debts (of banks in Korea, corporations in Indonesia, and some of each in Thailand) creditors, mostly banks. Hence, it was inherently harder, as currency values plummeted and all but disappeared, to design ways either to restore stability or to organize work-outs.

An additional complication was the fact that, although the debts were private of them involved varying types of implied government guarantees. In Korea, the Finance M ill-advisedly volunteered that the Korean government would honor foreign debts of Korean When the Korean banks experienced difficulty rolling over their international bank loans, of Korea provided the reserves they needed to repay the loans, in effect delivering on the but rapidly depleting the central bank's reserves in the process. Guarantees of this sort moral hazard. Pre-crisis, they result in more bank lending than would otherwise have tak and when trouble begins they may accelerate a bank run. But much less explicit guarantees

trouble as well. Where governments are heavily intertwined with banks and companies, as ha normal  throughout  much  of  Asia,  foreign  lenders  and  investors  may  well  assume  that government  will  not  allow  favored  operations  to  fail.  One  of  the  challenges  of  mitiga managing future crises, therefore, is finding ways to discourage emerging market governmen guaranteeing private debts or being so closely involved with private enterprises that these are seen as immune from market forces.

The expectation that future borrowers in international markets will be mostly enterprises, greatly increases the importance of the first two prescriptions -- increasing and  strengthening  financial  system  surveillance  --  not  just  to  prevent  and  mitigate  cri manage them when they happen.

In an economy that tolerates secrecy in business and financial dealings and information disclosures are limited, firms with fairly shaky fundamentals may be able t easily  in  a  boom.  They  will  be  carried  along  by  the  general  optimism,  since  everyone  w believe the best and there is no tradition of asking hard questions anyway. But in a cr participants tend to believe the worst. To contain the crisis and restore confidence, it both for managers and public authorities to be able to deliver the bad news and be belie markets. If there is no tradition of accurate, high quality information that can be reli participants and bank depositors are likely to believe that things are substantially wor really are and proceed to prove it by their actions. A culture of transparency and time information  can  serve  as  an  economic  stabilizer  in  both  directions.  It  can  restrain  th enabling investors to assess risk more accurately, and it can cushion over-reaction once a slide  begins.  But  such  a  culture  cannot  be  built  quickly,  and  even  where  it  exists, assiduously maintained.

Similarly,  prudential  supervision  of  financial  institutions  may  be  thought primarily  valuable  for  crisis  prevention  --  useful  for  ensuring  that  financial  inst adequately capitalized, don't take unacceptable risks with other people's money, and that ones are required to shape up or go under. Once a crisis hits, however, it is important t distinguish strong from weak institutions, those that ought to be rescued from those that closed. Unless supervision has been effective on an ongoing basis, however, the supervisor be able to tell strong from weak and will not be able to find out fast enough to prevent institutions then go down with the bad. It is actually in the long-run interest of financ that aspire to be the survivors of a shake-out to insist that supervisors are well informed a high standard.

Another lesson of recent events in Asia has been the importance of clear, enfo bankruptcy laws in dealing with a crisis, as well as helping to prevent one. Bankruptcy p opportunity, not only for closing down truly insolvent enterprises in an orderly way, but troubled ones by allowing them to cut a deal with their creditors, restructure their obliga on operating on a sounder basis. But bankruptcy procedures cannot be rapidly invented or fi in a crisis. For bankruptcy procedures to mitigate crises effectively and help to get surv feet, there has to be a 'culture of bankruptcy' which operates in good times as well as ba creditors, lawyers and courts have to be used in the process, know what to do, be able, be have done it before, to cut the deals that will minimize the damage and keep potentially enterprises afloat. Asian countries, most obviously Indonesia, found that since their mod experience had been primarily one of boom and growth, they had inadequate bankruptcy law little 'culture of bankruptcy' to help manage a sudden negative turn of events.

Improving transparency, supervision and bankruptcy procedures will help emerg market  economies  grow  more  sustainably  (albeit  perhaps  slower)  and  manage  downturns  be

when they happen. But the conceptually hard questions involve international collective a how it can manage major crises more effectively.

Once a crisis hits one country, especially a country of significant size an with  others,  the  whole  international  community  has  a  strong  interest  in  rapid  action markets  and  prevent  the  contagion  from  spreading  and  engulfing  others.  At  this  momen community looks to the IMF to act quickly, provide liquidity and restore confidence, espe confidence that the crises has bottomed out and will not be part of a continuing downwar Asia in 1997 was a demonstration of how fast the dominoes could fall.

When  the  root  cause  of  the  problem  is  inappropriate  macro-economic  poli especially big budget deficits and easy money combined with a pegged exchange rate, it may difficult for the IMF to restore confidence by injecting enough liquidity to pay short-te foreign currency in return for rapid changes in policy. When macro policy is not obviously culprit, restoring confidence may be harder and more expensive.

Injecting new money in exchange for reforms may still be the primary answer, bu patience  of  taxpayers  wears  thin  as  amounts  escalate  and  it  is  perceived  that  some  c creditors  are  being  bailed  out  with  official  international  resources  --  creditors  who calculated the risks more accurately and should bear the cost of not having done so, so the it again.

Some  have  asked  whether  official  resources  could  be  saved  and  moral  haza reduced  by  designing  an  automatic  international  bankruptcy-like  process,  known  in  advan which a standstill could be triggered, followed by a set procedure for sharing the burden the relevant creditors. Serious thought is being devoted to this issue. It is not hard to i approach, but all crises are different and applying a cooky cutter solution could well do than good.

The next few years will be a testing time for what I think of as the 'cros community', meaning the organizations, public and private, dedicated to making the cross relationships (especially business and financial ones) work better. The 'cross-border co includes mega firms that produce goods and deliver financial services on a worldwide sc associations of accountants, lawyers, bankers, securities dealers, insurance underwriters kinds of financial regulators as well as general international financial institutions (th World  Bank)  and  more  specialized  ones  such  as  the  Bank  for  International  Settlements, regional development banks -- to mention only a few of the more obvious members of a burge species.

The benefits of cross-border trade and capital flows for raising the world sta living are clear, but so are some of the costs -- especially the costs to ordinary people o in the backwash when there is a crisis. If these costs are not taken seriously and methods mitigate  and  manage  financial  crises  better,  a  wave  of  political  backlash  against  c foreigners  and  what  we  all  think  is  'progress'  could  result.  One  lesson  of  recent  cri factories, banks, shiny buildings, and eager investors do not by themselves create the und of  modern  economic  society  able  to  withstand  shocks  with  minimal  damage.  That  takes addition to good fiscal, monetary and other public policies -- an infrastructure of laws a and expectations that cannot be built overnight or imposed from the outside. The challeng cross-border community will be to work closely with emerging market economies to help them this infrastructure in ways that work for them. Wading in and saying, 'do it our way' wo The  process  will  involve  continuous  interaction  and  adaptation  and  may  well  result  i functioning economies in the so-called developed world, as well.

title: Mr. Desario reports on growth prospects and implications for supervision of asset management  (Central Bank Articles and Speeches, 9 Apr 98)
