text:
Mr.  Desario  reports  on  growth  prospects  and  implications  for  supervision  of asset management Address by the Director General of the Bank of Italy, Dott. Vincenzo De at the conference 'Asset management: insurance companies versus banks' held in Rome on 9/4/

## 1. Introduction

The growth of asset management has been a common feature of the financial syst of all the leading industrial countries. In Italy, the growth has been especially rapid i years, under the influence of both cyclical and structural factors.

The professional management of savings has always been a characteristic aspec financial intermediation. Its scope was originally limited to the management of individual estates and the provision of financial advice.

The mandate  to engage in financial investment conferred by savers (as management) does not place intermediaries under an obligation to repay the nominal value principal invested, nor does it guarantee the achievement of a given yield. The scope of has become much broader; it now involves a wide range of different financial intermediar instruments and a much larger pool of investors.

The sharp increase in financial flows has led intermediaries to operate in a v markets and expand the number of innovative products they offer. The ranks of those involv grown: banks and insurance companies have been joined by investment houses and investment management companies, the savings of high-income customers by those of lower-income work and pensioners, and individual investors by institutional investors.

The  operational  overlap  between  different  categories  of  intermediary  and substitutability of different types of instrument have increased. Competition has become both the domestic and the international level. The need to achieve a critical mass in orde in a market where the geographical boundaries and the supply of products are changing rap prompted reorganizations, concentrations and the formation of conglomerates.

The  expansion  of  asset  management  has  been  a  major  driving  force  in  finan innovation and has contributed everywhere to the erosion of institutional segmentation a pressure to change the organization of controls.

I shall look first at the evolution of asset management at the international le analyzing its development in Italy and the role of banks and other intermediaries. In v opportunities and risks that this development entails, I shall also address supervisory is legal framework established recently with the consolidated law on financial markets and the closer and more effective cooperation between authorities, both in Italy and in internation

## 2. Asset management in the industrial countries

The rapidity of the growth of the international asset management industry is r in the share of the financial instruments it offers in households' portfolios and the i institutional investors.

Between 1982 and 1994 - a period for which comparable figures are available was  a  significant  shift  in  the  composition  of  households'  portfolios  in  all  the  lead countries: while the share of financial assets held as bank deposits declined, that of pro by insurance companies, investment funds and pension funds grew steadily.

Significant  differences  between  countries  nonetheless  persist  within  this  c trend.  At  the  end  of  the  period  considered,  the  proportion  of  households'  financial consisting of managed assets was one-sixth in Italy and France, one-fourth in Germany and two-fifths in the United Kingdom and three-fifths in the United States.

During the same period, the assets of institutional investors (insurance com investment  funds  and  pension  funds)  increased  in  relation  to  the  total  volume  of intermediation and gross domestic product. Differences in the role of institutional inve various countries are captured by the latter indicator: the assets under their management to 30 per cent of GDP in Italy and Germany but amounted to more than 200 per cent of GDP United Kingdom and Japan (Table 1).

The disparity in the size of the sector in the different countries does not from identifying a number of shared structural determinants of the growth in asset manageme

The  first  and  most  important  is  the  gradual  aging  of  the  population,  which demand for pension-related financial instruments. The difficulties faced by public pensio reinforce this trend: asset management has grown the most in countries whose pension syst primarily based on private pension schemes; where public systems play a major role, the s developed later and grown more slowly.

The tight limits on budget deficits imposed by the stability pact among the c participating  in  the  Economic  and  Monetary  Union  will  accelerate  recourse  to  private arrangements, giving additional impetus to the growth of institutional investors in Italy, Germany.

The  liberalization  of  capital  movements  at  the  end  of  the  1980s  was  an  eq important propulsive factor. New opportunities to diversify financial investments were ope savers in countries that had previously imposed foreign exchange restrictions. It became p construct portfolios with the desired combination of risk and return; at the same time, it difficult  to  manage  portfolios,  increasing  the  importance  of  the  services  offered  by intermediaries.

The decline in the rate of inflation in recent years, together with the res macroeconomic stability, has been another factor contributing to the growth and has encou shift in financial resources towards longer-term assets and, above all, the stock market.

The spread of asset management has not had the same features everywhere. In United States, the process has been accompanied by a considerable reduction in the role of the countries of continental Europe the latter have retained a significant position and i have been the main actors in promoting the growth of the sector.

In  reality,  the  growth  of  asset  management  does  not  necessarily  lead  to  b disintermediation: the competition triggered by the changed preferences of savers, new te and more refined financial instruments, and the evolution of the legal framework does not f one  type  of  intermediary  but  rather  modifies  the  characteristics  of  financial  intermed financial products as we know them today.

Asset management, defined as the all-inclusive professional management of savi is destined to produce lasting changes in the structure of the financial system we have i three  main  directions:  greater  concentration  in  the  production  of  asset  management  ser expansion of financial assets in relation to real wealth, and an increase in the impor securities market.

˝

The search for optimal size in asset management activities, internat diversification strategies and the need to create efficient integrated structures for the distribution of financial products have given rise to mergers between some of the world' intermediaries.

The growth in asset management has contributed to financial deepening in the l industrial countries. Between 1982 and 1994 the ratio of gross financial assets to real from 0.8 to 1.6 in the United States and from 1.5 to 2.5 in the United Kingdom.

Institutional investors are channelling an increasingly large volume of funds the  financial  markets.  The  arbitrage  activities  they  engage  in  and  their  ability  to  tr volatile financial assets give breadth and depth to the securities market, reinforcing i allocation of savings and the redistribution of risk. It is worth noting the introduction credit instruments and the growing recourse to techniques for securitizing of bank loans.

The connection between the development of asset management and the growth of t stock market is shown by the fact that at the end of 1995 the shareholdings of UK pensi were greater than the total capitalization of the Italian and German stock markets.

In  certain  circumstances  the  behaviour  of  institutional  investors  could  acc tensions in securities markets. In markets of insufficient depth, price fluctuations are amplified by the use of dynamic hedging techniques or the imitative behaviour of managers to reduce the risk of performing less well than their competitors.

## 3. The growth of asset management in Italy

In Italy, the spread of asset management products has increased appreciably in years, approaching the levels achieved in the other leading countries.

Between  1990  and  1997  the  aggregate  comprising  investment  funds,  portfol management services, pension funds and life insurance companies' technical reserves increas 150 trillion lire to just under 1,000 trillion, rising from 8.5 to 33 per cent of total d assets (Table 2).

The  increase  was  especially  large  in  1997.  Net  fund-raising  by  investment tripled by comparison with 1996 and amounted to 143 trillion lire. In the first nine mont the net inflow of resources to portfolio management services nearly doubled to 64 trillion premiums paid in respect of life insurance policies grew more moderately, increasing by 44

The  differences between  the products offered by  the various categories intermediary have narrowed. About one-quarter of the funds raised by portfolio management s were  reinvested  in  investment  funds.  In  the  insurance  industry  there  has  been  strong  g products with a more pronounced financial component, such as single premium policies, s which increased by 125 per cent in the first nine months of 1997.

The impressive increase in asset management in 1997 was boosted by the declin interest rates that accompanied the fall in inflation. Small investors entrusted professio with savings that had previously been invested in government securities as they sought to their returns, inter alia through capital gains.

The  shift  from  personal  investment  to  asset  management  has  led  to  a  gre diversification of households' and firms' investment portfolios. Nonetheless, considering

˝

assets  held  directly  or  indirectly  by  savers  shows  that  the  redistribution  of  final instruments is taking place gradually. In the past two years the substantial reduction in demand  for  government  securities  has  been  largely  offset  by  the  increase  in  the  subscri investment funds. Only in part has it translated into purchases of listed shares and espec securities.

The preference for asset management is likely to be reinforced by the recent c in the tax treatment of financial assets. The new procedures for the taxation of financ based on an all-inclusive approach, relieves investors in managed asset instruments from send  in  returns  and  requires  the  intermediaries  providing  the  service  to  settle  the liabilities. The new rules also standardize the procedures for individual and collective i simplification that should enhance operational efficiency.

The flow of funds to institutional investors and to the securities market re adequate response in terms of the supply of financial instruments. Greater recourse by fi market, through debt and equity issues, will enable the productive economy to benefit fro substantial  saving  capacity  and  give  intermediaries  an  opportunity  to  expand  their  in banking services.

The  supply  policies  of  banks,  especially  the  leading  Italian  banking  groups played a key role. Capitalizing on professional asset management is now a central strategic it is in line with customer preferences, helps offset the downward trend in interest incom productivity through a better utilization of labour, and consolidates the fiduciary rela savers.

In  1996  managed  asset  services  contributed  substantially  to  banking  gro profitability,  producing  gross  revenue  of  more  than  4  trillion  lire  or  around  one-third profit.

In the same year banks and their subsidiaries handled 70.4 per cent of all m assets in Italy, up from 63 per cent in 1992. Considering investment funds and portfolio ma services  only,  at  the  end  of  1997  the  volume  of  assets  managed  directly  or  indirectly amounted to four-fifths of the total. Banking groups have strengthened their central ro management; overall, there has been no significant impact on the volume of funds intermedi the credit system.

Over  the  past  five  years  the  fund-raising  policies  of  the  bank-controlle management companies have transformed the rankings in this sector; the number of bank-cont companies in the top five has risen from two to four.

Marketing  capabilities  and  the  fiduciary  relationship  with  customers  have banks  a  competitive  edge  over  other  financial  intermediaries.  The  expansion  of  the  dis network  in  years  past  through  the  progressive  diversification  of  channels  (branches, salesmen, marketing agreements) has produced very extensive coverage of the territory.

A survey of the banking system conducted by the Bank of Italy found that at t of  1995  portfolio  management  services  were  offered  by  more  than  60  per  cent  of  all  ban insurance products by over 70 per cent, and investment fund units by 80 per cent.

Insurance  products  are  increasingly  simple  and  standardized,  which  has  facil their marketing via bank networks and financial salesmen. In the first nine months of 1997 of life insurance products sold through bank networks was 33 per cent, compared with 25 pe the same period of 1996; the share marketed through agents dropped from 42 to 36 per cent.

˝

## 4. Banks and other intermediaries: competition and integration

The Italian financial system was historically bank-oriented rather market-oriented.  It  did  not  offer  valid  opportunities  for  portfolio  diversification:  t investment was restricted to one instrument - bank deposits - offering modest yields and value that was stable over time.

In the last fifteen years Italians' high propensity to save, the increasing government securities, the launch of investment funds and the liberalization of capital m vements have enormously enlarged the role of the financial markets and the opportunities for divers

There nonetheless remain risks for the economy as a whole that the markets d help to control and which financial theory defines as 'non-diversifiable'. Such risks are with the economic cycle or the alternation of periods of financial euphoria and panic, whi generate broad swings in asset prices and thus affect households' wealth. In such circums important  role  is  played  by  intermediaries  that  perform  the  function  of  converting  ris balance  sheets  through  the  supply  of  such  non-negotiable  instruments  as  bank  deposi defined-benefit life insurance products.

Financial  innovation  continuously  redefines  the  interaction  between  markets intermediaries. It is this process that determines the ability of the financial system growth of the economy and offer instruments with adequate safeguards for households' and savings.

The growing competition between instruments, types of intermediary, a intermediaries  and  markets  thus  does  not  eliminate  some  of  the  features  that  disting operations of banks, insurance companies and securities intermediaries.

Banks  necessarily  have  a  large  portion  of  their  assets  tied  up  in  non-neg assets - loans. They retain a central role in the provision of payment services. They a channel for the transmission of monetary policy impulses, owing to the convertibility of de legal tender.

Insurance companies are characterized by the production of instruments that offer customers a guaranteed return even for the long term.

Securities intermediaries are geared to efficient trading in securities. The they issue do not carry the obligation of redemption at face value and are not means of pay

The  intensification  of  competition  is  a  force  for  the  increasing  integra specialized intermediaries within group structures.

The  reasons  for  integration  are  often  to  be  found  precisely  in  the  field management,  where  the  overlapping  between  banking,  insurance  and  securities  business  is pronounced.

Competition spurs the drive for ever greater size, permitting adequate diversi and  the  exploitation  of  economies  of  scale  in  the  supply  of  individual  and  collect management services. The recent wave of mergers among the leading global intermediaries con the link between the enlargement of the market, the increase in competition and the effort to achi critical  mass.  For  instance,  the  merger  between  Union  Bank  of  Switzerland  and  Swiss Corporation, already the third and fifth-largest European banking groups at the end of 199

˝

Competition and concentration are bound to intensify with economic and monet union, which will eliminate the residual segmentations based on the currency of denomina financial products.

In  the  drive  for  efficiency,  Italian  intermediaries  have  also  begun  to  c functions  that  were  once  performed  by  different  operational  units  and  not  always  integ operational or administrative terms. They are rationalizing the production and distributi different asset management services within group structures, but they have not yet attain needed in order to compete at the European level.

Italian intermediaries can defend their position in the domestic market effe capitalizing on their customer relations and distribution capabilities. With respect to cer investors, however, such as firms, foundations and wealthy individuals, the distribution ne minor  importance,  and  foreign  intermediaries  are  likely  to  be  increasingly  effective  co Over the longer run, the spread of electronic sales networks and other marketing innovat intensify competition in standardized products for the retail market as well.

The acceleration of mergers and takeovers within the Italian banking industry growing  recourse  to  forms  of  integration  between  credit  and  insurance  institutions  re commitment  to  enhance  the  competitiveness  of  the  financial  system  and  to  reposition  the within the European market.

Alongside the major intermediaries there is still room for local operators, success  requires  highly  specialized  production  strategies,  aimed  at  particular  instru markets. Alternatively, these banks could concentrate on strengthening their distribution c perhaps  through  agreements  with  large-scale  asset  management  institutions  that  do  busine number of different financial market centres, in order to obtain more sophisticated product their customers a broader range of services.

## 5. The new regulation of asset management

The erosion of the geographical and product barriers between markets, the creat complex and internationally ramified groups, the increasing competition between different intermediaries  and  the  growth  of  securities  markets  have  enhanced  the  investment  oppor available to vast numbers of small investors; they have also called for a major effort regulatory framework and the organization of supervision in order to protect the savings in the stability of intermediaries.

The  revision  of  the  regulations  governing  the  various  financial  sectors,  p response  to  the  process  of  harmonization  within  the  European  Community,  has  eliminate competitive  inequalities  between  different  intermediaries  operating  in  the  same  markets instruments  for  exercising  control  in  order  to  counter  the  risks  arising  from  the  new organization of financial activity.

In Italy, the Consolidated Law on Financial Markets has responded to the pro posed by the new and diversified structure of supply by thoroughly overhauling the rules financial intermediaries and markets.

˝

The statutory innovations will allow Italian intermediaries to diversify and the range of services they provide, adopt more flexible organizational structures and comp equal footing with foreign firms.

The earlier legal framework restricted the scope for innovation, especially in of collective investment, where new types of investment funds could only be introduced by legislation.

The extensive recourse made to secondary instead of primary legislation has re the constraints on the diversification of products and services. In particular, the Minist is charged with the task of defining the principal characteristics of the various types funds, with special reference to eligible assets (listed securities, unlisted securities, whether  the  fund  is  open  or  closed-end,  and  the  nature  of  potential  customers  (small institutional investors).

The Bank of Italy is charged with regulating the management of investment fu portfolios. In addition to the earlier tasks associated with the prudential supervision of for collective investment in transferable securities (UCITS), it is now responsible for est procedures and prohibitions for investment activity and for the limitation and diversificat

The  most  important  innovation  is  the  elimination  of  the  separation  bet management  on  an  individual  basis  and  that  on  a  collective  basis  with  the  creation  of manager, the 'asset management company'.

Investment  firms,  banks  and  trust  companies  continue  to  be  allowed  to  pro individual management services directly, while asset management companies are allowed to p both  individual  and  collective  management  services  on  an  exclusive  basis.  The  possib operating across the board will enable them to achieve higher levels of productive efficien

The right to provide the two services jointly, which is consistent with the Community directive currently under discussion on the collective management of assets, me needs  of  intermediaries  and  puts  them  in  a  better  position  to  satisfy  the  preference customers. At the same time, the prohibition on the supply of other services is an importa against conflicts of interest.

Major changes in the direction of greater flexibility have also been introduc organizational level. In particular: the management and promotion of funds may be separa entrusted to different companies; managers may delegate investment activity within a set for  the  allocation  of  resources;  and  in  the  field  of  individual  management  services investment firms may entrust the execution of management contracts to third parties, for p portfolio or even the entire portfolio, subject to written authorization by the customer. of  considerable  autonomy  in  the  organization  of  production  reflects  the  belief  that  the management services is a complex business with high fixed costs and large economies of scal

The importance of group structures in the financial industry and the related strengthen prudential controls suggested extending the scope of the rules on consolidated s to  financial groups having at  least one investment firm or  asset management  com Responsibility for issuing the regulations lies primarily with the Bank of Italy, which i define such groups for supervisory purposes and draw up the prudential rules to be appl consolidated basis.

The division of supervisory responsibilities according to purpose has been con and  further  clarified  for  all  intermediaries.  Consob  is  entrusted  with  ensuring  the  t

˝

correctness and regularity of trading, while the Bank of Italy is responsible for the cont protecting investors and ensuring the capital adequacy and stability of intermediaries.

Faced with the continuous and at times tumultuous development of financial mar the debate on the optimal organization of supervisory controls sometimes appears to be con an excessively abstract level. The experience of recent years shows that supervisory arr must be constantly adapted to the situations created by financial and technological innovat

The  transfer  of  vast  sums  to  the  care  of  professional  managers  by  small belonging to a wide range of social groups raises special issues with regard to financi Naturally, there is no derogation from the principle that the result of delegated investm on the performance of the management scheme, which may involve both lower-than-expected r of  return  and  capital  losses.  Managers  nonetheless  have  a  special  responsibility  to  saf value of such savings. It is indispensable that management choices should correspond to profiles accepted by investors and, more generally, that the rules on risk diversificati observed. The prudential limits on operations established and monitored by the authorities great importance.

The structural changes under way in the Italian financial system require the d supervisory regulators to intensify their coordination efforts. Effective cooperation among enhances the effectiveness of controls, and the ability to forestall instability is the k the efficiency gains that the growth of financial markets makes possible.

The  consolidated  law  imposes  an  obligation  on  the  authorities  to  collab inter alia by exchanging information; they cannot invoke official secrecy in their dealings w other. The importance of coordination is thus confirmed, in recognition of the dangers that cooperation is likely to entail for the integrity and efficiency of the financial system time collaboration must be informed by the principle of minimizing the costs borne by thos to supervision.

The  globalization  and  increasing  competition  between  financial  centres  that accompanied the growth in asset management have also spurred a far-reaching reorganization securities markets. The consolidated law completes the innovations introduced by Legislativ 415/1996, which provided for the privatization of the stock exchange and the securities mar management of the markets is entrusted to limited companies that have private sector shar and  self-regulatory  powers  in  matters  such  as  the  admission  of  financial  instrume intermediaries to the market, as well as their exclusion and suspension.

Consob is charged with the supervision of the regulated markets; the Bank of has been given a primary role for the markets that are important for monetary policy purp screen-based government securities market (MTS) and the interbank deposit market (MID).

## 6. International coordination

The response to the growing integration of markets has been to complete the r of financial regulations, with the creation of a system of controls that is basically neutr to the nature of intermediaries and based on cooperation among supervisory authorities.

The  internationalization  of  finance  results  in  cooperation  among  the  authori different  countries  becoming  of  fundamental  importance.  The  increasing  openness  of  fi markets  makes  the  exchange  of  information  indispensable,  requires  a  flexible  interpret cooperation  agreements  and  calls  for  the  coordination  of  corrective  measures.  The  links

˝

supervisory bodies must be permanent, not restricted to crisis situations, and must invol authorities responsible for controlling intermediaries and those with powers over markets.

The growth of asset management, where the activities typical of institutions e in banking, insurance and securities investment services intersect, has fostered the rise conglomerates.

The presence of these complex organizations creates new channels for the spre possible crises; their international ramification and the existence of different types of increase the difficulty of coordinating the supervisory bodies involved.

Generally speaking, the emergence of a small group of very large global oper with  substantial  capital  and  highly  diversified  portfolios  strengthens  the  financial emergence  of  such  a  group  nonetheless  faces  the  international  community  with  the  probl forestalling  the  possibility  of  an  insolvency  and  defining  instruments  on  an  adequate handling such an event.

The  supervision  of  financial  conglomerates  is  hindered  by  the  existenc unregulated  entities,  but  problems  also  arise  where  all  the  components  are  subject  to controls. In the case of capital adequacy, it is necessary to avoid double and multiple ge can result in the group as a whole failing to have adequate capital even though the individ satisfy their respective capital requirements.

The ramification and strategies of groups can reduce the effectiveness of ind supervisory authorities' prudential controls and make it less easy to overcome company cris

Risk control in the more complex financial conglomerates is often centralize single operating unit; the correspondence between company structures and lines of business exist; group activities are no longer covered by supervisory controls, which are divided type of institution and product. Regulators are likely to encounter greater obstacles to performance of their tasks because functions that are crucial to the sound and prudent mana the undertaking subject to supervision are carried on in a different jurisdiction.

Awareness of these difficulties has led to an intensification of cooperative international  fora.  At  the  beginning  of  1996  the  Basle  Committee  on  Banking  Supervisio International Organization of Securities Commissions (IOSCO) and the International Associa Insurance Supervisors (IAIS) set up the Joint Forum on financial conglomerates and charged the task of addressing the supervisory issues raised by these complex financial organizatio

In  particular,  the  Joint  Forum  has  studied  the  practical  means  of  facilit exchange of information among supervisory authorities, at both the national and the inte levels, and has examined arrangements for facilitating the coordination of control activi ordinary circumstances and in crises. It has also drawn up a list of principles aimed a more effective supervision of regulated institutions within financial conglomerates.

The  proposals  put  forward  by  the  Joint  Forum  primarily  concern  the  methods evaluating  the  capital  adequacy  of  conglomerates  and  verifying  the  integrity  and  ex requirements for corporate officers and significant shareholders. Common reporting forma been  prepared  for  use  by  authorities  in  order  to  improve  their  understanding  and  analys structure and operations of conglomerates.

The possibility has been examined of identifying one authority to act as coor with the aim of facilitating the exchange of information, permitting an overall assessment

˝

of the riskiness and capital adequacy of groups, and improving the consistency of prudentia and the timeliness of corrective measures. This hypothesis nonetheless requires that consid given not only to the benefits just mentioned but also to the danger that supervisory ac made  more  complex  and  the  safety  net  seen  as  having  been  extended  to  all  the  componen conglomerates, including those that are unregulated.

As things stand today, coordination among supervisors has to rely on their pra exchanging information, the knowledge each has of the others' operating procedures and obj and trust in the opinions they express.

Last  February  the  documents  prepared  by  the  Joint  Forum  were  distributed supervisory  authorities  and  market  participants  for  them  to  put  forward  their  observa suggestions. It is important that financial industries, including Italy's, analyze the p carefully, in order to contribute to enhancing their effectiveness and utility, to the ben of all market participants.

## 7. Conclusions

The growth in asset management represents a major structural change and is com to all the leading industrial countries. In Italy, the growth of the industry has acceler conjunction  with  the  fall  in  interest  rates  over  the  last  two  years.  The  shifts  in  i strategies,  the  recomposition  of  their  assets  and  the  links  created  between  the  differ intermediary suggest that the growth will not peter out once Italian interest rates come into lin those prevailing in the other countries that will be part of the European Monetary Union.

The management of savings by institutional investors benefits from the develop of the securities markets and, at the same time, contributes to their efficiency. It does imply the disintermediation of banks. In Italy, the supply policies of the major banking g sustained the expansion of management services. The increasing competition, at the interna well as the domestic level, is stimulating the search for larger size through mergers and that often give rise to financial conglomerates.

The changes under way modify the exposure to systemic risk, the channels for propagation  of  crises  and  the  latter's  potential  impact.  The  greater  ramification  of  t market is likely to reduce the probability of a single intermediary's difficulties spreadi of the system. Nonetheless, the number and size of today's financial markets and institut that it may prove more difficult to limit the effects of a crisis where one does occur.

Despite the progress made in adjusting the regulatory framework to the new rea financial  markets,  supervisory  authorities  are  faced  with  new  challenges;  the  most  i concerns the coordination of their action, both domestically and internationally.

The crises that have occurred in the last few years show how fast tensions transmitted  across  countries,  markets  and  intermediaries.  Macroeconomic  instability  is interact with elements of financial instability, spreading to the jurisdictions of sever authorities, central banks and governments and involving international organizatio globalization proceeds, the asymmetry between the integration of markets and the multiplicity of regulatory  authorities  increases  the  difficulty  of  carrying  out  supervision,  calls  fo integration of supervisory action.

Coordination  and  the  timely  exchange  of  information  can  increase  the  abili forestall crises and help overcome them when they do occur.

˝

The  reform  of  the  securities  market  and  the  opening  of  finance  to  interna competition have broadened and strengthened the structure of Italy's financial system and its allocative efficiency. Firms and households can turn to new intermediaries and new inst

Firms can tap a wider range of sources of external finance, raise long-term d above all, make greater use of equity capital. In this way they can achieve a more soli structure that is better able to sustain investment. Households have greater scope to di financial portfolios with products that in the long run permit higher real rates of return.

In today's new conditions of monetary stability, the possibility of earning hig at low risk that was a feature of the last twenty-odd years will no longer exist. In orde advantage of the opportunities offered by the development of the securities markets, inte will have to make their investment choices keeping a close eye on economic fundamentals and capital solidity and earnings prospects.

It is not only intermediaries who must be fully aware of the growing complex financial intermediation and of the related risks, but also the investors who entrust the savings.

title: Mr. Stals addresses the topic 'Implications for the South African financial sector of the process of financial globalisation'  (Central Bank Articles and Speeches, 8 May 98)
description: Speech by the Governor of the South African Reserve Bank, Dr. C. Stals, at the Tenth Annual 'Beeld' Economist of the Year Banquet, held in Johannesburg on 8/5/98.
text:
Mr.  Stals  addresses  the  topic  'Implications  for  the  South  African  financi sector of the process of financial globalisation' Speech by the Governor of the South African Reserve Bank, Dr. C. Stals, at the Tenth Annual 'Beeld' Economist of the Year Banquet, h Johannesburg on 8/5/98.

## 1. Lessons from the East Asian crisis

Recent developments in certain East Asian countries focused attention on the pitfalls for the smaller economies of the world on the road to financial globalisation. Th the collapse of financial markets in East Asia may differ from country to country, but a fe shortcomings in the economies of the afflicted countries were identified:

Firstly,  in  many  countries,  inappropriate  macroeconomic  policies  were  appli defend  artificial  exchange  rates,  and/or  to  maintain  interest  rates  at  untenable  low  l countries  were  highly  successful  for  many  years  and  they  achieved  remarkably  high  av economic growth rates over an extended period of time. Based mainly on an industrious and labour force, they were able to remain competitive, despite the emergence of underlying we in the economic fundamentals.

Secondly, the financial systems did not keep pace with the changing macroecono environment. Banking institutions were not properly regulated and monitored, and financial were distorted by undue governmental intervention. In some cases, there were insufficient d of  basic  information  that  could  have  enabled  investors  to  make  a  better  assessment deteriorating situation at an earlier stage.

Thirdly, the countries became overly exposed to foreign capital flows, and vul balance of payments positions developed that could not be managed once confidence faded. current  account  deficits  were  no  longer  covered  by  total  capital  inflows,  and  the  with short-term funds from some countries exacerbated the situation.

Fourthly, bad governance in public and private sector institutions did not re seriousness of the underlying adverse developments, and did not take timely corrective acti the bubble finally burst, the situation had already advanced to a stage where only costly macroeconomic restructuring could salvage these economies.

The experience of the afflicted East Asian countries provides ample evidence vulnerability  of  the  smaller,  emerging  market  economies  in  the  environment  of  fi globalisation. Other countries, including South Africa, can also be subjected by the glob markets to similar painful corrections, although it might be for completely different re lesson for South Africa from the East Asian crisis is therefore to be alert, to be cautio aware of the harsh but not unreasonable disciplines of the global markets.

## 2. South Africa and financial globalisation

Over the past few years, the South African financial sector has moved quite the road of globalisation. In the Annual Report for 1997 of the Bank Supervision Departmen Reserve  Bank, interesting  information  has  been  made available about  developments  in  the African banking sector in 1997.

There  are  now  more  than  20  foreign  banks  operating  in  South  Africa  thro locally-established  branches  or  subsidiaries,  and  more  than  60  foreign  banks  with  repre offices in South Africa. South African banks are also extending their activities to the

world  and  during  1997  obtained  permission  from  the  Registrar's  Office  to  establish  mor 45 branches, subsidiaries, and representative offices in other countries around the world.

At  the  end  of  1997,  the  total  South  African  banking  sector  utilised  more R35 billion in foreign funding, and carried loans extended by them in foreign currencies R17½  billion.  The  foreign  liabilities  and  foreign  assets  of  the  South  African  bankin respectively, represented but small percentages of the total assets (or total liabilities) sector,  estimated  at  about  R440  billion  as  at  31 st December  1997.  Foreign  funds  as  a  source  of financing of the activities of South African banking institutions are, however, still incre

It is well-known that non-resident investors have become very important partic in the South African financial markets. ## 3. Consequences for the South African economy

## 4. Economic forecasting: a difficult task

Against  the  background  of  the  international  integration  of  financial  mark becomes much more difficult to predict developments in financial aggregates, such as inter exchange rates and the inflation rate. 4. Be willing to acknowledge a wrong forecast and produce a new one. Most peop who take note of your forecasts have in any case already forgotten the la that you made.
5. Remember  the  assumptions  which  form  the  basis  of  every  forecast.  They  a often so unrealistic that the forecast is also nearly worthless.
6. Make forecasts on the basis of objective analyses, and not on what suits book or the book of your clients. It doesn't help to be popular but wrong.

## 5. Concluding remarks

The integration of South Africa in the world financial markets is an on-going that is linking developments in the major  financial aggregates  in  this  country  more  and developments in the rest of the world.

Because of this process, economic forecasting has become much more complex. No only  changes  in  the  South  African  situation  influence  developments  in  important  fi aggregates, such as interest and exchange rates, but also events in remote places such as I

Economic  forecasters  have  great  responsibility,  not  only  to  provide  consiste sensible forecasts, but also to understand and explain the shortcomings of even their best to remember that even bad forecasts can sometimes become self-fulfilling.

description: Co-speaker's address by the President of the Deutsche Bundesbank, Prof. Hans Tietmeyer, following the lecture 'Achieving a Credible Currency for Europe' held by Dr. Sirkka Hämäläinen, Governor of the Bank of Finland at the International Frankfurt Banking Evening on 5/5/98.

speech.

## Mr.  Tietmeyer's  address  at  the  International  Frankfurt  Banking  Evening

Co -speaker's address by the President of the Deutsche Bundesbank, Prof. Hans Tietmeyer, fo the lecture 'Achieving a Credible Currency for Europe' held by Dr. Sirkka Hämäläinen, Gover the Bank of Finland at the International Frankfurt Banking Evening on 5/5/98.

I

Sirkka,

First of all, thank you very much for having come and for your extremely inter

You have spoken to us this evening with dual authority:

- -on the one hand, as the Governor of a highly successful national centra and,
- -on the other, as a prospective member of the ECB Executive Board.

In the face of such concentrated authority in your address, there is hardly pertinent that I can add.

I can only emphasise one of the core sentences of the speech you addressed NCB governors, and which is certainly true of the Board members as well:

'The interests of the entire euro area must always come first.'

Without  any  doubt,  this  rule  is  the  crucial  cornerstone  of  the  ECB  in  ach credibility.

The  topic  of  our  gathering  this  evening  is  'Achieving  a  credible  currenc Europe'.

Nominating  Sirkka  Hämäläinen  to  the  Executive  Board  of  the  ECB  is,  however without any doubt an invaluable step on the way to a credible currency for Europe.

I am sure that you, Sirkka, will be a jewel in the crown of the - hopefully euro.

By the way, in Brussels a number of men were likewise earmarked for the Execut Board. But they are, of course, not so important - not, at least, this evening.

Sirkka, sincerest congratulations! We are all delighted that you are going to Frankfurt central banker.

I wish you, for our own sakes, every success.

- -To begin with, of course, on the way to your definitive appointment.
- -And particularly in your office here in Frankfurt, from the summer onwards

However, not everything that happened last weekend in Brussels contributed t necessary expectation that the euro will be a really supranational and depoliticised curren

I would like to make three remarks on the decisions which were taken in Brusse weekend.

1. The compromise reached in Brussels over the weekend on filling the offic President of the European Central Bank is a decision taken by the political authorities take note of and on which I do not want to make any further comments.
2. The suggestions made with regard to the nominations for the Executive Bo of the ECB are to be viewed favourably overall. The persons involved are acknowledged e on monetary and banking issues, and for the most part have many years of experience field  of  monetary  policy.  That  certainly  goes  for  Professor  Dr.  Otmar  Issing,  who appointed for eight years. It is to be hoped that the appointment process will be comp soon, and the European Central Bank thus established.
3. The  European  Central  Bank  must  endeavour  from  the  start  to  build  up necessary confidence in the sustained stability orientation of its policies, and must its independence of political influences. As a member of the future ECB Governing Cou shall strongly support any such policy.

III

Sirkka,

Frankfurt will become your new place of action.

I wish that you will feel happy here in Frankfurt. And I am sure that will provided that you are able to get to know Frankfurt a bit.

For if every one of the eleven national parliaments - like parts of the French Assembly - in future wanted to hold regular consultations with the members of the ECB Exe Board, you would not get to see very much of Frankfurt, other than the airport.

I hope that will not be the case.

I also hope that you will like Frankfurt. Of course, I don't suppose Frankf compete with Helsinki in every respect. But in many ways it can.

In  terms  of  culture,  too,  Frankfurt  has  a  great  deal  to  offer.  After  all, banking go well together. It is no accident that the great Finnish composer Jean Sibelius o

'It is only among bankers that I have ever come across an appreciation of music; it is very rare among artists, who prefer to talk about money.'

˝

Another reason why you may feel at home in Frankfurt is that - in my opinion are a number of common features in the Finnish and German mentalities.

Both national mentalities are inclined to speak their mind clearly and frank possible that both the Finns and the Germans do not always express themselves with that and  fluency  that  so  distinguishes  the  representatives  of  those  civilisations  which  w influenced by Rome.

But  Finns  and  Germans  alike  are  conspicuous  for  a  strong  sense  of  realism clear-cut, if sometimes somewhat harsh, powers of judgement, and for a healthy attachment native land.

Finns like a clear, straightforward approach, rather than convoluted affectedne

That goes equally for their approach to Europe. Finnish professions of faith in may not always sound so effusive and euphoric. Understandably, they also set great store independence.

On the other hand, the Finns stand by Europe

- -not only when the sun is shining,
- -and not only when they are receiving money from Brussels.

Finland is on the periphery, if at all, only in geographical terms; in politi is in the heart of Europe.

V

It no doubt owed something to the sense of realism in the thinking of our two that a 'stability culture' evolved, and was consolidated, in both our countries.

And in both countries the respective central bank plays a major role in cement stability culture. The high international reputation of Finnish anti-inflation policy owes to your efforts and your personality, Sirkka.

So, you will likewise appreciate the 'stability culture' which Frankfurt has in

You once said that it is the lot of a strictly stability-oriented central bank unpopular.

I can assure you of one thing: here in Frankfurt it is possible for a central b both stability-oriented and popular at the same time. Being a guardian of stability in Frankf something special, I must say.

And I am convinced that Finns have a particular gift for that.

That is because stability orientation has something to do with long-termism, a with  staying-power.  And  Finns  are  proverbially  unbeatable  in  the  kinds  of  sport  that staying-power.

˝

And another thing: once the euro has got going, it will have to pass its ' Elch-Test ' (an expression that was last year's 'word of the year' in Germany). And we Germans are relieved that somebody from Finland is helping at the steering wheel. For the Finns are the experts in all matters relating to Elks and how to deal with them.

## VI

Incidentally, there are also some interesting similarities between our two curr

What strikes one first, of course, is the common name.

At the time when a proper name for the single European currency was being sou instead of the three letters E-C-U, many Germans suggested calling the single currency Mark after the  Finnish  currency.  'For  unfathomable  reasons',  however,  that  suggestion  failed  to  me general approval.

Another  extremely  interesting  parallel  is  that  both  currencies  are  older  th respective, nowadays independent, states.

As  you  will  no  doubt  know,  the  introduction  of  the  D-Mark  preceded  t establishment of the Federal Republic of Germany, even if only by a short period.

The 50th anniversary of the introduction of the D-Mark will remind us again o A ceremony to mark that occasion will take place in Frankfurt's Paulskirche on June 20.

But  the  less  than  one  year  that  the  D-Mark  is  older  than  the  Federal  Repub Germany  is  nothing  in  comparison  with  the  pacesetter  role  played  by  the  Finnish  markka markka was actually introduced over 50 years before independent Finland was born.

Hence we are all the happier that the Finns are prepared to let the markka be a into the euro. And that change is actually meeting with more approval in Finland than in Ge

But  there  has  been  one  problem  in  connection  with  Finland's  qualification monetary union. A few months of membership in the exchange rate mechanism of the EMS a lacking.

When we in the Bundesbank were drafting our Convergence Report, we racked our brains wondering what we could do. Strictly speaking, Finland ought to have joined the winter 1995-96.

But we in the Central Bank Council then recalled that, as everybody knows, the are always somewhat downcast and despondent in winter. That is because of the lack of sunsh

We thought it would be unfair to expect the Finns to take such an important de as joining the ERM in the depths of winter.

But after a fine summer it was very much easier for the Finns to take that step

And so we agreed in the Central Bank Council of the Bundesbank not to express criticism of Finland in this matter.

˝

We found that all the easier since Finland's successes in the field of stabil have been of such a lasting nature. And that, of course, is what matters most.

In the other case in which a few months of ERM participation were lacking, b way, things were not quite so easy.

## VII

Sirkka, once again, thank you very much for your address, and the very best wis you in your new and important assignment.

I am sure our cooperation will be as confident as it has already been in the years.

title: Mr. Greenspan examines the crises in Asia, considers the existence and provision of safety nets and ponders possible policy responses to problems in the international financial system  (Central Bank Articles and Speeches, 7 May 98)
description: Remarks by Chairman of the US Federal Reserve System, Mr. Alan Greenspan, before the 34th Annual Conference on Bank Structure and Competition of the Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago on 7/5/98.
text:
Mr. Greenspan examines the crises in Asia, considers the existence and provisio of safety nets and ponders possible policy responses to problems in the international fin system Remarks by Chairman of the US Federal Reserve System, Mr. Alan Greenspan, before 34th Annual Conference on Bank Structure and Competition of the Federal Reserve Bank of Chi on 7/5/98.

Events  in  Asia  over  the  past  year  reinforce  once  more  the  fact  that,  whi burgeoning  global  system  is  efficient  and  makes  a  substantial  contribution  to  standards worldwide, that same efficiency exposes and punishes underlying economic imprudence swiftl decisively.  These  global  financial  markets,  engendered  by  the  rapid  proliferation  of  cr financial flows and products, have developed a capability of transmitting mistakes at a far throughout the financial system in ways that were unknown a generation ago. Today's intern financial  system  is  sufficiently  different,  in  so  many  respects,  from  its  predecessors reasonably be characterized as new, as distinct from being merely a continuing evolution past.

As a consequence, it is urgent that we accelerate our efforts to develop a soph understanding  of  how  this  high-tech  financial  system  works.  Specifically,  we  need  s understanding  if  we  are  to  minimize  the  chances  that  we  will  experience  a  systemic  di beyond our degree of comprehension or our ability to respond effectively. We need it if continue to make progress in reducing settlement risk in foreign exchange markets and to sound infrastructure for payments and settlement systems generally. And we need it if we ar confidence in our processes of supervision and regulation.

In this regard, I intend to focus my remarks this morning on three related topi start by examining the crises in Asia, which, along with the one in Mexico just a few provide the first evidence of how crises arise in the new system, especially the central ro play. I will note that, while the support provided to banks by public safety nets appea element of stability in the new system, it has also been part of the process that engen crises. Next, I will consider why, if the existence of safety nets can encourage crises, w provide  them.  Finally,  I  will  consider  possible  policy  responses  to  some  of  the  system' problems and tensions. Put differently, can we learn to stabilize our burgeoning, sometime new international financial system so that we can realize its full potential?

*

*

*

Let  me  start  with  Asia.  In  hindsight,  it  is  evident  that  those  leveraged  e could not provide adequate profitable opportunities at reasonable risk in the 1990s to surge in capital inflows. That surge reflected in part the diversification of the western e huge capital gains to a sector of the world which was perceived as offering above averag Together  with  distortions  caused  by  a  long-entrenched  government  planning  ethos,  the  f investment  resulted  --  some  would  say  inevitably  --  in  massive  deadweight  losses.  As slowed, burdened by fixed-cost obligations that were undertaken on the presumption of con growth,  business  losses  and  nonperforming  bank  loans  surged.  The  capital  of  banks  in economies -- especially when properly accounted for -- eroded rapidly. As a consequence, sources dried up as fears of defaults rose dramatically.

In  an  environment  of  weak  financial  systems,  lax  supervisory  regimes,  and  v assurances  about  depositor  or  creditor  protections,  the  state  of  confidence  so  necess functioning of any banking system was torn asunder. Bank runs occurred in several countr reached crisis proportions in Indonesia. Uncertainty and retrenchment escalated.

In short, the slowing in activity in Asia exposed the high fixed costs of a economy, especially one with fixed obligations in foreign currencies. Failures to make induced vicious cycles of contagious, ever rising, and reinforcing fears.

It is quite difficult to anticipate such crises. Every borrower, whether a nonbank company, presumably structures its balance sheet to provide a sufficient buffer ag emergence of illiquidity or insolvency. The scramble by borrowers to protect their balan when this buffer is unexpectedly breached can lead to a surge in the demand for liquidity produces a run on the financial system. In this context a preventive effort to lessen the probabilities of such crise for  example,  by  bolstering  the  financial  system's  buffer  through  more  capital  or  improv supervision -- may not in itself further insulate a country from crisis if financial ins faced with a lower cost of capital or lower spread on their debt, leverage away the incre Indeed, one form of moral hazard is that an initially sound financial system that attra premia could merely induce a ratcheting up of the risks that a nation's borrowers choose t This is not to disparage endeavors to bolster financial systems. Mr.  Gaddum  discusses  the  euro,  US  dollar  and  the  world  economy Dinner speech by the Deputy Governor of the Deutsche Bundesbank, Mr. Johann Wilhelm Gaddum, on th occasion  of  the  Joint  Conference  of  Konrad-Adenauer-Stiftung  and  Aspen-Institut,  Ber Washington DC on 6-8/5/1998.

There is no doubt about it. The European Central Bank will come into operatio

July 1.

That also means that the euro is on its way, and that will bring about cha Europe. But is it only Europe that will be affected?

I very much appreciate having this opportunity to explain the views of the De Bundesbank on this matter to such a well-informed audience here in Washington.

Recently, in a well-known US newspaper, I saw a cartoon which captured what my mind - is the widespread ambivalence concerning the future prospects of the euro.

The cartoon showed a group of experts (presumably economists) sitting at a r table and apparently discussing the future outlook for the euro. The chairman of this gro gets carried away and exclaims: 'I bet you 10 to 1 that the euro will be a success!' E others at the table nods vigorously in agreement with this forecast, replying: 'I think so one of the group adds somewhat timidly: 'But in dollars.'

Begun as a foreign policy concept, the idea of European monetary union (EMU) h taken on economic significance during the past few  years as a result of  the  globalisat markets. So far, there has been little discussion of this international dimension of EMU.

EMU will create a currency area which, when all 15 states of the European Un have become members, will have a population of approximately 370 million whose gross dome product will represent about 38.3% of the GDP of all OECD states. This will change the re importance of the world's currencies.

It  therefore  seems  reasonable  to  suppose  that,  when  stating  what  we  expec monetary union, we have to explain, firstly, what the European Central Bank will mean for and particularly for Germany and, secondly, what it may mean for our friends and partners parts of the world.

II

Konrad Adenauer always incorporated the idea of European cooperation into Germa policy, and since then - yes, right up to the present day - this has been a central featu policy.

All  German  governments  have  had  this  objective  in  mind.  And  the  idea  of monetary union has always  played an important role in this.

In the light of this it is not surprising that in Germany both the government opposition  support  the  project  of  monetary  union  -  despite  the  considerable  reluctanc population.

Both prior to and after the signing of the (Maastricht) Treaty the Bundesba outlined  in  its  statements  what  monetary  union  will  mean  for  Germany  (and  for  the participating states).

At the request of the Federal Government the Bank issued a further comment March 26, that is to say, shortly before the decision taken last weekend.

It  was  only  to  be  expected  that  the  Bundesbank's  analysis  of  the  degre convergence  reached  within  the  European  Union  incorporates  light  and  shade,  opportunitie problems. This comment by the Central Bank Council was anything but an excuse for euphoria.

The Bundesbank has not  resolved to reject monetary union because of the inhe problems. In addition to making its analysis, it has nevertheless made it clear what resp policy makers will incur as a result of monetary union.

First of all, I shall outline the positive points:

- Exchange rate tensions within Europe have declined appreciably.
- Inflation rates are very similar and are no more than somewhere between 1 and 2.0%.
- Capital market rates are now very close to the German rate.

The challenges, however, are as follows:

When  their  bilateral  exchange  rates  are  fixed  irrevocably,  the  participa monetary union are giving up not only an economically compensatory mechanism - the excha rate - for ever. They have also to accept an adjustment over the long term of the differen and political traditions in the member states to the new supranational framework and to national interests in favour of this new dimension.

In  a  monetary  union,  which  by  definition  transcends  the  sovereignty  of participating  nation  states,  discrepancies  may  arise  time  and  again  that  must  be  solve national economic, fiscal and social policy measures and not through the monetary policy a uniformly throughout the union.

EMU will increase the competition for inward investment in the participating s The more flexible a country's goods, financial and labour markets are the better it will compete.

For this reason, the policy of reform which has been in force over the past fe must not be abandoned or applied less vigorously. On the contrary, it must be intensified.

Fiscal policy has a particular role of responsibility in monetary union.

Fiscal  policy,  in  contrast  to  internal  and  external  monetary  policy,  whic union-wide responsibility, will remain the responsibility of the member states. Consequen particularly  important  that  the  public  authorities  can  prove  that  their  financial  posi permanently sound footing.

If  they  are  to  fulfil  this  requirement,  some  member  states  will  have  to

BIS Review   39/1998 particular effort.

˝

A permanently sustainable financial position on the part of member states is e if conflicts between them are to be avoided and, moreover, if conflicts between the respec and the single stability-oriented monetary policy are to be avoided.

So much for the Bundesbank's basic concern.

We have always thought it was important to make it clear that, if European mon union was a worthwhile objective, it could not be achieved without a measure of sacrifice.

Monetary union provides all the advantages of a fairly large homogeneous mar freed from exchange rate fluctuations. But from its participants it demands economic and discipline.

The  combination  of  monetary  policy  uniformity  and  political  diversity  p problems.

It was in this connection that President Chirac spoke of an adventure.

The two largest member states of the union, Germany and France, have differ traditions.

On the one hand, there is Germany's fortunate experience with a Bundesbank tha independent in its monetary policy decisions.

Conflicts with the government of the day, whether it be Adenauer's, Schmidt' Kohl's,  have  done  nothing  to  change  that.  In  the  event,  they  have  actually  strength Bundesbank's standing.

France, on the other hand, sees monetary policy as an instrument of the gover in power. The recent amendments to the statutes of the Banque de France represent a cha approach which was necessitated by the provisions of the Maastricht Treaty and which was unpopular.

The political compromise reached in the dispute concerning the appointment of first president of the ECB has to be seen against this background.

The aim of the eight-year term of office which is laid down in the Treaty and cannot be extended is to ensure the independence of the incumbent. The fact that it is pre ruling that has been called into question confirms fears that not all of the ramifications independent monetary policy have yet been finally accepted by the governments concerned. Li independence of the Bundesbank, it is something that we shall probably still have to fight

## III

Although the integration of the world economy began a long time ago, a signif acceleration occurred in the 1980s and 1990s.

This is seen in the trends in international capital flows and in the financial an even greater degree than it is in foreign trade.

˝

However,  a  gigantic  step  is  now  being  taken  with  the  introduction  of  a  s currency in a large part of the global financial market.

The  fragmentation  into  many  national  capital  markets,  a  phenomenon  which particularly apparent in the case of the bond markets and which has arisen as a result of t of different currencies (and therefore of different interest rates), will be a thing of the

The national markets in Europe will compete with each other more intensively they do now. They will gradually lose the specific national features that they now have.

The  large  cross-border  euro  capital  market  will  accelerate  the  trend  to globalisation.  This  will  encourage  processes  of  concentration  and  yet  provide  opportun specialise in market segments which need a particularly intensive degree of management know

The volume of transactions on the future euro bond market will approach the si the undisputedly dominant US market today.

If today's US market is about six times larger than the German market, it will about 1.6 times larger than the euro market.

The euro will take over the role of the D-Mark.  The tripolar world capital consisting of the dollar, the euro and the yen is gradually emerging.

The depth and breadth of the euro market, which will be greater than the dept breadth  of  the  present  national  markets,  will  become  more  attractive  to  internationally customers for and suppliers of capital.

In  contrast  to  the  situation  in  the  United  States,  we  will  have  several  s issuers in one single currency area. This competition with respect to creditworthiness nee disadvantage.

The greater attractiveness of the European market will increase its efficiency professionalism of the market players. What does all of this mean for the German capital ma

With the loss of the D-Mark, Germany, and particularly the German bond marke will lose a major competitive advantage.

The  currency  which  has  been  the  anchor  for  the  European  Monetary  System  and which  over  a  period  of  some  decades  has  become  the  most  important  investment  and  res currency after the dollar will disappear.

We have been trying for some years now to make up for the approaching loss of competitive advantage we have as a result of the D-Mark.

The German capital market had to be prepared for the euro. Structural weakne had to be removed.

The German capital market is now in a strong starting position and is equipp meet the competition from other financial centres.

˝

German bonds set the benchmark for the yield curve in Europe. Repo business switched back from London to Frankfurt.

The  German  futures  exchange  now  handles  more  than  70%  of  the  Federal Government's contracts. The Bunds, too, have returned from London to Frankfurt.

However, one thing is clear to us:  in the long run only a stable euro will ha chance of taking over the role of a reserve, investment and transaction currency.

Only  a  stable  single  currency  will  provide  the  European  Community  with  t opportunity to play a major role in the world economy and to do so with correspondingly influence than it has today.

## IV

What does this mean for our friends and partners in other parts of the world? hardly showed any interest in the European debate on monetary union at first; then, in the things had taken on a more concrete shape, they reacted in astonishment. For a long time project was regarded in non-European countries as having no chance of success.

A sarcastic but not at all untypical comment which I would like to quote may as an example of this attitude:

'It's a lunatic idea but, to be honest, one that I thought would collapse of stupidity. Unfortunately, it hasn't, and so here goes.' (Samuelson, January 1997)

Even  US  economists  for  the  most  part  reacted  sceptically  to  the  idea  of  a currency in Europe when they considered its economic justification.

On  the  other  hand,  the  European  advocates  of  the  EMU  project  were  seldo prepared to answer this criticism.

Presumably  the  reason  for  this  was  that  from  the  outset  they  had  suspected Americans were being particularly critical about European efforts at integration because th this development through the eyes of competitors.

However,  internationally  successful  currencies  are  not  simply  establishe politicians  by  decree.  They  have  to  stand  their  own  in  competition  with  other  currencie financial markets.

I am certain that it will take some time before the euro will be able to asse the international markets and represent a genuine competitor for the US dollar.

At least in the past structural changes in the international currency pattern only very slowly. One only needs to think of the time it took for the dollar to replace sterling.

It  was  no  different  when  the  D-Mark  was  being  established  as  an  internati currency: that took years, if not decades.

In its competition with the dollar the euro will have to acquire for itself degree of trust. This is something it will not inherit.

˝

However,  Americans  and  Europeans  alike  can  only  benefit  from  the  competitio between these two major currencies for the confidence of investors.

The  disappearance  of  exchange  rate  risks  on  the  European  market  will  prov interesting investment opportunities in Europe for US enterprises, too.

The increase in world trade that can be expected from EMU will also benefit th economy.

The European economies which enter into this monetary union will be compelled dismantle  market  rigidities  (especially  in  the  labour  markets)  if  they  want  to  survi intensified international competition and be able to meet the consequences of external sho currency area.

The IMF is right in describing the labour markets as the Achilles' heal of th project.

Politically, the development of a system of transfers between the participatin has no chance at the moment. The unsatisfactory situation in the labour markets therefore change in policy inevitable.

This will ultimately have positive repercussions for Europe's trading partner including the United States.

Another  reassuring  point  is  that  the  Maastricht  Treaty  rules  out  the  possib policy makers using the exchange rate of the euro as a foreign trade policy instrument.

A more productive European economy with sound monetary and fiscal policies i likewise not only in Europe's interests but also in the United States'.

I am quite sure that the entire international monetary system will profit fr predictable monetary and fiscal policies in European monetary union.

## V

In  Washington  it  is  naturally  impossible  to  speak  of  the  international  mo system without addressing yet another aspect of European monetary union, namely the impact imminent European monetary union on the debate that is currently being held - especially light of the east Asian crisis - in the United States (and elsewhere) on the future role of

Now  and  again  one  hears  fears  voiced,  especially  in  the  United  States,  abou potential threat the EMU poses for the global leadership role of the Bretton Woods insti agree with those who urge reforms at the IMF and the World Bank.

The  need  for  reform  may  be  due  just  as  much  to  the  structural  changes  in financial markets as to the changes in the importance of world trading partners.

text:
Mr. Kelley discusses the Year 2000 issue Testimony of Mr. Edward W. Kelley, Jr.,  a  member  of  the  Board  of  Governors  of  the  US  Federal  Res System,  before  the  Committee  on  Commerce,  Science,  and  Transportation  at  the  US  Sen on 28/4/98.

I  am  pleased  to  appear  before  the  Committee  today  to  discuss  the  Year  2 computer systems issue and the Federal Reserve's efforts to address it.  The stakes are nothing  less  than  the  preservation  of  a  safe  and  sound  financial  system  that  can  c operate in an orderly manner when the clock rolls over at midnight on New Year's Eve a millennium arrives.  So much has been written about the difficulties ascribed to the challenge  that  by  now  almost  everyone  is  familiar  with  the  basic  issue  -  specific information  generated  by  computers  may  be  inaccurate  or  that  programs  may  be  termin because they cannot process Year 2000 dates.  The Federal Reserve System has developed executing a comprehensive plan to ensure its own Year 2000 readiness, and the bank supe function is well along in a cooperative, interagency effort, to promote timely remed testing by the banking industry.  This morning I shall first focus on the potential mac consequences of the Year 2000 issue.  Then I shall discuss actions being taken by th Reserve System to address its internal systems, including Reserve Bank testing with de institutions, and its bank supervision efforts.

## The Macroeconomic Effects of the Millennium Bug

The Year 2000 ('Y2K') problem will touch much more than just our financi system  and  could  temporarily  have  adverse  effects  on  the  performance  of  the  overa economy as well as the economies of many, or all, other nations if it is not corre spectrum of possible outcomes is broad, for the truth of the matter is that this episo We have no previous experiences to give us adequate guideposts.  A few economists alrea suggesting that Y2K-related disruptions will induce a deep recession in the year 2000 probably  a  stretch,  but  I  do  not  think  that  we  shall  escape  unaffected.    Some  of frightening scenarios are not without a certain plausibility, if this challenge were b But it is not being ignored.  While it is probable that preparations may in some instan be inadequate or ineffective, an enormous amount of work is being done in anticipatio rollover of the millennium.  It is impossible today to forecast the impact of this ev range of possibilities runs from minimal to extremely serious.  In that spirit, let me you some of the ways in which the millennium bug already is influencing the US economy discuss some of the possible outcomes for economic activity early in the next century.

Corporate  business  is  spending  vast  amounts  of  money  to  tackle  the  Y problem.  To try to get a handle on the magnitude of these Y2K expenditures, we have r the most recent 10-K reports filed with the SEC by approximately 95 percent of the fir Fortune  500.    These  are  the  largest  businesses  in  our  economy,  with  revenues  of $5½ trillion  annually,  and  are  likely  to  be  on  the  cutting  edge  of  efforts  to  de millennium bug.  Before the end of the decade, these firms report that they expect to s $11 billion in dealing with the Y2K problem.  (Of this total, financial corporations a expenditures of $3½ billion, while companies in the nonfinancial sector have budgeted around $7½ billion.)

These estimates undoubtably understate the magnitude of the Y2K reprogramming efforts.   In  culling through the 10-K reports, we  found that  many  com

reported incurring no additional costs associated with Y2K remediation efforts.  I d firms are unaware of the problem.  Rather, I suspect that some firms did not view t spending as having a 'material' effect on their bottom line, and some companies probab funded Y2K programs with monies already budgeted to their information technology funct Making an allowance for all costs - whether explicitly stated or not - and recognizing Fortune  500  firms  are  only  part  of  the  picture,  an  educated  guess  of  the  sunk  cost remedial efforts in the US private sector might be roughly $50 billion.  To put this n perspective, the Gartner Group has estimated that Y2K remediation efforts will total $600  billion  on  a  worldwide  basis.    The  US  economy  accounts  for  about  one-fifth  of output, and thus our estimate seems broadly consistent with the lower end of their ran the experience of our own Y2K efforts to date, I would expect to see costs rise furth these Y2K programs are fully under way - ultimately pushing costs up within the Gartner range.

Corporate efforts to deal with the Y2K problem are affecting economic activ a variety of ways.  On the positive side, an important element in some Y2K programs replacement of  aging  computer  systems  with  modern,  state-of-the-art  hardware  and  sof Such capital expenditures - which I should note are not included in the $50 billion cos will raise the level of productivity in those enterprises, and, in general, the need Y2K problem has increased the  awareness on the part of senior executives of the com and  importance  of  managing  corporate  information  technology  resources.    The  incr replacement demand also has contributed to the spectacular growth recently in this c computer hardware and software industries  - a process that  I would  expect to contin while  longer.    But,  ultimately,  we  are  largely  shifting  the  timing  of  these  i expenditures:  Today's added growth is likely 'borrowed' from spending at some time future.  And, if analyzing the dynamics of this situation were not already complicate some  firms  may  'freeze'  their  systems  in  the  middle  of  1999  -  effectively  forgo installation of new hardware and software systems just before the millennium.  This, t influence spending on computer equipment - shifting some of it from 1999 into 2000.

While Year 2000 remediation efforts may give a temporary boost to econom activity  in  some  sectors,  the  net  effect  probably  is  negative.    I  suspect  the  majo expenditures should be viewed as increased outlays for maintenance of existing systems are additional costs on businesses.  Other than the very valuable ability to maintain i into the year 2000, few quantifiable benefits accrue to the firm - and overall produc are reduced by the extra hours devoted to reprogramming and testing.  Conservative es suggest that the net effect of Y2K remediation efforts might shave a tenth or two a y growth of our nation's overall labor productivity, and a more substantial effect is some of the larger estimates of Y2K costs are used in these calculations.  The effec gross domestic product are likely to be somewhat smaller than this but could still tota a percentage point or so a year over the next two years.

The  United  States  is  not  alone  in  working  to  deal  with  the  millennium Efforts by our major trading partners also are under way, although in many cases they are not yet at so advanced a stage as in this country.  In Europe, the need to reprogra systems to handle the conversion to the euro seems to have taken precedence over Y2K e although  there  may  be  efficiencies  in  dealing  with  the  two  problems  at  once.    The difficulties of Japan and other Asian economies certainly have diverted attention and in those countries from the Y2K problem, increasing the risk of a Y2K shock from one o of these countries.  But, on the positive side, large multinational corporations are a of the Y2K problem, and their remediation efforts are independent of national boundarie

But what if something slips through the cracks, and we experien failure of some 'mission critical' systems?  How will a computer failure in one indus the ability of other industries to continue to operate smoothly?  The number of possibl of this type is endless, and today no one can say with any confidence how severe a disruptions could be or how a failure in one sector would influence activity in others.

We have many examples of how economic activity was affected by disruptions the physical infrastructure of this country. ## Background on Federal Reserve Year 2000 Preparations
