title: Mr. Crockett discusses financial stability and international capital flows  (Central Bank Articles and Speeches, 13 Feb 98)
description: Keynote address by the General Manager of the Bank for International Settlements, Mr. Andrew Crockett, to the 33 rd Seacen Governors' Conference in Bali on 13/2/98.
text:
Mr.  Crockett  discusses  financial  stability  and  international  capital  fl Keynote address by the General Manager of the Bank for International Settlements, Mr. A Crockett, to the 33 rd Seacen Governors' Conference in Bali on 13/2/98.

Financial stability has always been a major responsibility of central banks. years, it has become even more important because of the increased capacity of financial di to spill over into the real economy. One need look no further than the difficulties current economies  in  East  Asia  to  appreciate  the  consequences  of  weak  financial  systems.  The maintaining  stability  has  also  become  more  complex:  liberalisation  and  innovation  have benefits but they have also made national financial systems more vulnerable, bo domestically-generated stresses and internationally-transmitted disturbances.

In my remarks this morning, I will begin by reviewing some of the forces makin change in the financial environment. Then I will consider the implications of the change taking place for central banks' task of preserving monetary and financial stability. Final and draw one or two concrete lessons from our most recent experience.

## Basic trends in the international financial system

It is no exaggeration to say that the international financial system is und process  of  unprecedented  change.  Among  the  most  significant  driving  forces  are  advanc communications  and  information  technology.  By  dramatically  lowering  the  cost  of  fina transactions  and  broadening  the  dissemination  of  financial  information,  these  advanc expanded trading and investment opportunities and are exercising powerful effects on the structure of financial intermediation. One notable effect has been to enhance the role whose task it is to transmit information about the value of assets among borrowers and len in turn is forcing traditional intermediaries to redefine their roles.

A  second  important  force  for  change  is  innovation,  which  has  permitted development of products that facilitate the pricing and management of risk. This too has the  effective  bundle  of  financial  services  on  offer.  By  allowing  risks  to  be  hedged, non-financial  enterprises  to  focus  on  their  comparative  advantages.  But  they  also speculation, and the more rapid adjustment of positions taken. They also strengthen linkage markets in ways that are not yet fully understood.

Another key impetus to change, though also a consequence of it, has been ma liberalisation. This applies both to the removal of constraints on the activities of dif financial  institutions  within  a  given  market,  and  to  the  liberalisation  of  cross-bo movements and rights of market access. As a result of liberalisation, a broader range of can now provide financial services; and an increasing number of both markets and institu active across national boundaries. This has greatly extended the reach of competition and modernisation of market practices in far flung centres.

A  consequence  of  the  forces  for  change  I  have  just  described  has  been  a expansion in the scale of financial activity relative to overall economic activity, and of as against purely domestic activity. This in turn has generated unquestioned benefits in te efficient global resource allocation. At the same time, the greater masse de manoeuvre in financial markets has increased the power of market expectations to reinforce or undermine official And the growth of the financial superstructure relative to the economy as a whole means sustained disruption to the financial system now has potentially broader economic effects have been the case previously.

## Consequences of Changes in the financial environment

For  emerging  markets,  the  consequence  of  these  trends  has  been  that  they rapidly become integrated in international capital markets. This has had a number of ad Private debt or portfolio inflows in response to economic liberalisation have expanded size less than $40 billion per year over the period 1983-1990, to an average of about $200 bil in  the  last  five  years.  These  capital  inflows  have  provided  additional  resources  to domestic savings and support high levels of investment. Foreign direct investment has al sharply.  This  has  in  many  cases  been  a  vehicle  for  the  transfer  of  technology,  and  in competitive spur to domestic industry. And the market disciplines that accompany greater e openness have provided timely and forceful penalties on inappropriate policies. By the sa they have reinforced the premium on strong and sustainable macro-economic policies.

But  greater  capital  market  integration  and  larger  capital  flows  have  also beneficial consequences. These have been much in evidence in the experience of Asian count the past year. In a different form, however, they were behind the Mexican economic crisis and indeed some of the problems encountered in the European Monetary System in the early 1 When countries have become excessively dependent on foreign inflows, their sudden revers generate significant adjustment difficulties. Let us consider what has now become a typical of events, with a view to drawing some lessons that can help avert costly crises in the fut

Countries  undertaking  strong  stabilisation  and  structural  reforms  have  often themselves  a  magnet  for  foreign  capital.  Capital  inflows  have  been  even  greater  when  d economic  growth  in  the  receiving  countries  has  accelerated,  and  when  low  interest  rate sending countries has encouraged lenders to reach for higher yields. The inflows, in turn, contributed  to  inflationary  pressures  (when  there  is  a  fixed  exchange  rate)  or  led  t appreciation (when the exchange rate regime is more flexible). Either way, external compet has tended to deteriorate and a balance of payments deficit has emerged.

A  balance  of  payments  deficit  is  a  natural  counterpart  of  a  situation  in domestic  investment exceeds  domestic  saving.  In  itself,  therefore,  it  is  no  bad  thing. financed by capital inflows that are liable to dry up or be reversed, it can put the coun in a vulnerable position. A feature of capital flows in the new, more integrated internat markets, is that a high proportion has been in the form of short term lending, denominated currency. This has been encouraged by significant interest differentials in favour of th country, and an exchange rate regime that has masked the risk of exchange rate changes.

Thus, when growing payments imbalances, or some external event, causes invest to re-evaluate the sustainability of exchange rates, there is liable to be a sudden withdr This can quickly lead to a currency crisis, with all the consequences we have seen in rece Then, if there are financial weaknesses within the domestic economy, the negative effects and growth can multiply.

## Lessons of the Recent Crisis

With what I have just said as background, allow me to consider certain preli lessons that can be drawn from the current crisis. Naturally, a more thorough analysis prevent such crises in the future will have to await a longer perspective on events.

A first lesson is that even economies with relatively strong fundamentals, an sound macro-economic policies, can fall victim to sudden loss of confidence. Why should t One reason is that even good macro-economic policies require adjustment in the light of circumstances. This flexibility was not always there in the case of the countries most aff

˝

crisis.  Let  me  expand  a  little  on  what  I  mean.  When  strong  capital  inflows  are  pushin exchange rate and undermining external competitiveness, monetary policy often finds itse acute dilemma. On the one hand, higher interest rates may be required to dampen an inve boom.  On  the  other,  lower  interest  rates  may  be  needed  to  moderate  the  inflow  of  sho speculative funds. In these circumstances, monetary policy needs assistance from fiscal budget surplus may be needed to curb domestic demand, and to provide the financial resou sterilise the foreign exchange inflow.

Flexibility is also needed in the area of exchange rate management. I do not me countries  should  always  adopt  freely  floating  exchange  rates.  That  would  not  necessari optimum policy in emerging markets, whose financial systems are not fully developed. For ex Hong Kong and Argentina have successfully operated a currency board type system for the several years. But the exchange rate regime must be adapted to the capacity of domestic p institutions to take the burden of adjustment. Where political or other factors make it domestic adjustment mechanisms to take the strain of reversals in capital flows, then the rate has to be the safety valve. If the exchange rate regime makes it difficult to make ti in the external value of a currency, then disequilibria can build up that add immeasura abruptness and costs of the eventual adjustment.

This is not just the recent experience of East Asian countries. It was the exp Mexico in 1994-5; and it was a substantial part of the explanation of the turmoil in th Monetary System in 1992-3. I know from the experience of my own country, where I was clo involved in decision-making at the time, that it is extraordinarily difficult to make c exchange rate peg that has come to symbolise an overall macro-economic strategy. I also kn the penalties for not making an adjustment in time are severe. Which leads me to the concl governments should seek an exchange rate regime that avoids this dilemma unless, as is per case in countries with currency-board arrangements, they are prepared to accept the full logic of fixed rates.

So  much  for the  macro-economic origins of currency crises.  What of t macro-economic  responses.  Some  have  argued  that  the  stringent  monetary  and  fiscal  po advocated by the IMF are inappropriate, because they intensify the financial problems of firms and deepen the internal recession. While I have some sympathy for this view, I am cannot  see any  easy  policy  alternatives  when  a  country  finds  itself  in  a  full-scale  cr conditions, the first priority is to restore external confidence, and this can rarely be a a clear commitment to monetary restraint. Perhaps the most important lesson is the need external assistance and to adopt corrective policies before problems reach the crisis sta policy response can be more accurately targeted to the underlying causes, and the macro-e consequences can be less severe.

One of the clearest lessons of the experiences both in Mexico and in East Asi role  of  weaknesses  in  the  financial  system  in  propagating  economic  disturbances.  Thi consequence of the growing integration of international capital markets, and will certai reversed. If anything, markets are likely to be even more closely tied together over time several more specific lessons to be drawn from this recognition. In the first place, libera domestic financial system, and in the openness to the world capital market must be accompa measures  to  strengthen  prudential  regulation  and  supervision.  For  those  countries  that capital  account  restrictions,  this  means  that  the  dismantling  of  capital  controls  will carefully  phased  and  sequenced.  It  may  also  mean  that  existing  prudential  safeguards, liquidity  ratios,  reserve  requirements,  exposure  limits  and  controls  over  currency  and mismatches in banks' portfolios, may have to be strengthened.

˝

More  generally,  however,  the  recent  crisis  has  revealed  that  many  banking financial systems continue to embody practices that make them vulnerable. These practices inadequate  internal  controls,  non-transparent  accounting  standards,  weaknesses  in  loan procedures,  lax  licensing  provisions,  insufficient  capital  adequacy  requirements,  and closure procedures, among others. Because these weaknesses are widespread, and because the no  internationally  accepted  standard  of  banking  prudence,  the  Basle  Committee  on  Ba Supervision  promulgated  last  year  a  set  of  25  'Core  Principles'  for  banking  super Implementing these principles should make an important contribution to strengthening banki financial systems around the world.

The  Core  Principles  represent  an  important  new  step  in  the  work  of  the  B Committee.  For  that  reason,  I  would  like  to  draw  your  attention  both  to  certain  aspec philosophy underlying their preparation, and to some of the specific recommendations. In place, the Core Principles are intended to be comprehensive in their coverage. That is t apply  to  all  phases  in  the  life  of  a  bank,  from  initial  licensing,  through  continuing through closure procedures for institutions that are unable to meet minimum standards. They comprehensive  in  their  institutional  scope:  they  are  intended  to  apply  to  both  dome internationally  active  banks,  coming  from  industrial,  emerging  and  less-developed  eco Lastly, and very importantly, they have been drawn up with the active involvement of sup from a wide range of countries, including most of the key emerging market economies, inc some central banks represented here.

Let me now turn to some of the specific recommendations, and to ways in wh bank supervision can work to strengthen bank soundness. One of the key foundations of th Committee's approach over the years has been the focus on risk-weighted capital adequacy remains as important as ever, but it is clear that the way in which the current standards has not prevented major episodes of instability. Part of the problem lies in the fact tha attention is given to the fact that the minimum capital requirements are just that: minim be acceptable for a strong, well-managed, well-diversified institution in a major financi likely to be inadequate for a bank operating in a more volatile environment, where credit risks are much greater. Some supervisors in emerging markets have recognised this and h higher minimum standards. Singapore and Argentina are good examples in this regard. I hop initiative will be followed more generally.

But it is not simply the formal capital ratio that needs to be considered. In countries banks fail despite the fact that they were in apparent compliance with minimum ratios shortly before their collapse. This points to deficiencies in accounting standards, simply, allow bad loans to be classified as good. Bank supervisors will have to insist on rigorous standards of loan classification and bad debt provisioning. They will also have greater transparency in financial accounts, so that problems can be identified before th life-threatening proportions.

Of course, at the root of balance sheet weaknesses are poor lending decisions. of  these  can  be  prevented  by  better  banking  supervision.  Improved  information  on  bo conditions  is  clearly  a  first  step.  A  comparison  by  lenders  of  the  return  prospects  of projects with return requirements prevailing internationally is another. Other sources of e certainly be tackled. Some of these arise from what has come to be called 'insider' or 'c lending. A variant of this practice is the policy loans that are encouraged by political au for whatever reason, are unwilling to make direct budgetary provision for expenditures. principles make it clear that credit decisions by banks should be made purely on economic This means that credit officers in banks should have the training and the mandate to make decisions; and that supervisors should have the independence to enforce best practice in they supervise.

˝

Before leaving the subject of how to strengthen financial systems, I would make a more general point about leverage. We all know that banks can get into trouble when too-highly leveraged; in other words when their capital becomes too small relative to thei such a case a relatively small decline in the quality of a portfolio can set alarm bells r lead to a run, with the consequent need to liquidate assets in fire-sale conditions. It is that minimum capital requirements are such an important part of prudential regulation. But leverage is not a problem only  for banks. It can apply to other financial institutions important, outside the financial sector.

When,  as  in  many  Asian  countries,  debt-to-equity  ratios  become  very  high, companies concerned become excessively vulnerable to a re-evaluation of their profit pros relatively small decline in asset values can wipe out equity, and thus lead to premature fo lenders.  One  of  the  most  important  lessons  of  the  recent  crisis  is  the  need  for  no corporations  to  hold  higher  levels  of  equity  capital.  It  is  tempting,  of  course,  when growing rapidly, to exploit the possibilities of leverage to increase the return on equ institutions, and their supervisors, have a responsibility to counteract this temptation b that potential adverse scenarios are recognised and properly factored in to the pricing of

One  of  the  reasons  why  bank  borrowing  has  played  such  an  important  role financing  investment  in  emerging  markets  is  that  bond  markets  are  relatively  underdevel many  of  these  countries.  A  key  task  is  therefore  to  provide  the  necessary  infrastru encouragement for the growth of long-term debt markets. It is good to note that several authorities in the Asian region are now treating this as a matter of priority. Once such b are  established,  they  should  prove  attractive  for  corporate  borrowers  seeking  to  red vulnerability to a liquidity crunch.

I have so far been speaking about lessons that borrowing countries can learn f recent crisis. But there are also important lessons for those countries whose institutions the  expansion  and  subsequent  collapse  of  cross-border  lending,  as  well  as  for  the  int community in its handling of the strains that can accompany greater international mobility Let  me  therefore  turn  to  what  the  major  creditor  countries  could  do  differently,  befo something about international arrangements more generally.

Banks in the major creditor countries have participated fully in the enthusi investment  in  rapidly  growing  emerging  markets.  This  already  happened  in  the  1970s  in America, and led to the debt crisis that began in Mexico in 1982. As a result of that banks  were  for  a  while  much  more  circumspect.  But  by  the  1990s  they  were  already  len substantial  amounts  in  Asia,  buoyed  by  the  perception  that  the  Asian  economies  had macro-economic fundamentals, including low inflation rates, modest public debt and very hi of domestic saving and investment. This led lenders to overlook points of vulnerability. A know,  a  significant  part  of  foreign  lending  went  to  over-leveraged  companies  and  to  f institutions with weak balance sheets.

With  hindsight,  we  can  say  that  the  lending  banks  made  the  crisis  worse  by lending  too  much,  and  then  withdrawing  loans  too  precipitately.  Both  these  problems  m tackled. In the first place, banks must be given the means and the incentive to make bet decisions. Relevant information about the condition of borrowing institutions and countrie made more transparently available; and banks must be encouraged to act on it by knowing th will not be bailed out from bad lending decisions. Secondly, if a crisis does develop, wa found to reduce the tendency of private lenders to withdraw funds at the first hint of trou

˝

Before  concluding,  I  want  to  say  something  about  international  responses  t problem of strengthening financial stability. When a crisis develops, it is entirely approp use the mechanisms of international co-operation to help moderate and resolve the crisis. this involves a central role for the IMF, as well as for groupings of countries with a clo the speedy restoration of stability. But are there ways in which the international commu make  its  influence  more  effective?  In  other  words,  are  there  initiatives  that  can  be  t international level that would help prevent crises, and resolve those that nevertheless occ effective manner?

As I noted earlier, confident answers to these questions can only be given w have  a  greater  perspective  on  the  reasons  why  the  recent  crisis  occurred  and  spread.  B tentative conclusions are already possible. In the first place, the international communi better job of establishing standards by which the various actors in international capital to be bound. These need to include standards of transparency with regard to relevant macroe data and indicators of financial system soundness. Such data will facilitate assessment of by domestic authorities, by market participants, and international institutions. arrangements for surveillance, for example through peer reviews as agreed at Manila, can h domestic authorities to danger signals that may not be visible to them. I have already ref Core Principles of banking supervision. These will need to be elaborated in the coming mo years, and their implementation carefully monitored. Where necessary, countries that need come up to international best practice should receive technical assistance.

In  addition to  core  principles  of  banking  supervision,  standards  will  be  ne other areas, such as accounting and disclosure practices for borrowers and lenders. Ways wi be found to codify prudent behaviour in managing international borrowing and lending. In al the  more  advanced  financial  centres  will  have  to  give  a  lead.  In  my  judgement,  it  w unacceptable for the industrialised countries to call for the adoption of standards in markets that they are not prepared to adopt themselves.

Concerning  crisis  resolution,  one  thing  that  is  clear  is  that  ever-large financing  packages  are  not  the  answer.  The  key  to  successful  crisis  resolution  is  to confidence of the private sector, without provoking moral hazard. This means finding ways the private sector is involved in crisis resolution from the start. The ideal is for priv form  committees  that  work  out  mutually  agreed  rescheduling  packages  with  borrowers  fa liquidity difficulties, as indeed happens in national jurisdictions. For the cases (hope number) where this does not work, ways will have to be sought that replicate at the int level the impact of insolvency procedures at the national level. In any event, the private be allowed to simply await rescue by the international community.

## Concluding remarks

I have tried to offer some preliminary thoughts on the lessons that we can dra the events in Asia during the recent eight months. You and others are engaged in reviews fr we shall undoubtedly learn more. But a number of issues have emerged that need to be addr we are to avoid similar incidents in future. I have argued that expanded capital flows h themselves, been the root source of the current crisis. However, to harvest the benefits action is required by domestic authorities and the international community in a number of a and foremost, a premium needs to be placed on sustainable and responsive macroeconomic pol In  this  regard,  more  critical  examination  of  exchange  rate  policies,  particularly  in accumulated  foreign  currency  indebtedness,  is  needed.  Second  is  the  imperative  of  ef strengthen financial systems. There is now a core body of principles on which to draw which the  accumulated  experience  of  supervisors  and  regulators  in  a  variety  of  countrie implementation, both in industrial and emerging market economies, should be a matter of

both for domestic authorities and the international financial community. Thirdly, there i promote transparency to avoid excesses building up unnoticed. This will require improvem accounting and disclosure practices and in international banking statistics, and an exten dissemination standards to cover domestic financial conditions. And, finally, as I noted a my remarks, arrangements for crisis resolution need to involve burden sharing with the priv to lessen moral hazard risk.

It would clearly be presumptuous to assert that by addressing these and other i be identified in due course, we shall avoid crises in the future, or handle more smoothly t occur. It would be equally hazardous to expect that there are ready and easy answers in these areas. I am confident, however, that the Asian economies struck by crisis will eme and vigorous from the measures they are undertaking, and that the international community responsive to the lessons it has learnt from your experience.

title: Mr. Thiessen reports on the future performance of the Canadian economy  (Central Bank Articles and Speeches, 25 Mar 98)
description: Notes for remarks by the Governor of the Bank of Canada, Mr. Gordon Thiessen, to the Canadian Club of Winnipeg, in Winnipeg on 25/3/98.
text:
Mr.  Thiessen  reports  on  the  future  performance  of  the  Canadian  economy Notes for remarks by the Governor of the Bank of Canada, Mr. Gordon Thiessen, to the Can Club of Winnipeg, in Winnipeg on 25/3/98.

It can take anywhere from one to two years for monetary actions to have thei effect on the economy. Because of this, the conduct of monetary policy must be based on a what the economy will be like -- not tomorrow, not in a month -- but rather in one to two y

That is why in speeches in Vancouver and Toronto last year I spoke about wher Canadian  economy  might  be  heading  in  the  future;  what  this  might  imply  for  our  econ performance  over  the  medium  term;  and  what  should  the  contribution  of  monetary  policy Understandably,  these  important  issues  can  get  pushed  aside  because  of  the  public  focus current economic situation and on recent movements in short-term interest rates and in th value of the Canadian dollar.

Today, I would like to use this opportunity to revisit these medium-term iss doing so, I will be underlining the crucial role played by productivity improvements in our performance. The best place to start is with a brief review of the recent record.

## Recent economic performance

As we approach the end of the decade, we can take satisfaction in the good eco performance of the past two years and in the notable improvements in our economic fundame The Canadian economy has expanded at an average annual rate of 4 per cent since mid-1996 even with the dampening effects of the Asian crisis, it is expected to continue to grow a pace  this  year.  This  should  contribute  to  further  gains  in  employment  and  reduce  the  a unused capacity.

Inflation is low, and we are committed to keeping it low. Last month, togethe the federal government, we announced that we would extend our target of holding inflation range  of  1  to  3  per  cent  to  the  end  of  2001.  Moreover,  government  deficits  have  v disappeared, and the ratio of public debt relative to the size of our economy is finally on path -- for the first time in about 25 years. Low inflation and improved fiscal health rep contributions towards the sounder economic fundamentals I mentioned a moment ago. They ar doubt the main reason why our interest rates have been below US rates.

The other key area where there have been important improvements in recent year in  the  private  business  sector.  Since  the  early  1990s,  Canadian  businesses  have  take challenge of structural adjustment, which their US counterparts had started several years response  to  the  gathering  momentum  of  technological  change,  globalization,  and  heigh competition.

With the benefit of low inflation and low interest rates, Canadian business been investing in new technology and streamlining their operations to enhance productivit success in doing so will be crucial to our future economic performance.

## The importance of productivity growth

Why this emphasis on improving productivity? Whether viewed from the perspecti of an individual firm or of the economy as a whole, it is almost impossible to overemph importance of rising productivity for overall performance and prosperity.

Productivity  growth  is  what  allows  firms  to  hand  out  real  wage  increases, holding their production costs down and remaining profitable.

From  a  broader  perspective,  productivity  growth  is  a  key  element  that  deter economic welfare and the general well-being of a society. At any point in time, our perc how well we are doing economically is probably influenced by where we happen to be in the c fluctuations that affect any economy. But over the longer term, the trend in productivity the economy as a whole is the basis for growing incomes and rising standards of living.

Now, I know that for some people any discussion of the need to increase produc can  be  rather  unsettling.  They  tend  to  associate  improvements  in  productivity  in  an  i company with downsizing and layoffs. And from there it is only a short step to the belief economy-wide  productivity  gains  can  only  mean  a  more  difficult  job  market  and  hi unemployment.

But the history of industrial economies shows that growth in productivity has gone  hand  in  hand  with  improved  overall  employment  conditions.  This  is  borne  out  by experience of countries like Japan in the 1980s and, more recently, the United States and Kingdom. That was also our experience in Canada during the 1950s and 1960s.

## Canada's productivity record

So how has Canada fared in the productivity department since the 1950s and 19 Not all that well, I'm afraid. After a relatively strong showing from the end of the Second to the early 1970s, our productivity performance became rather lacklustre. Productivity estimated to have slowed from an average rate of about 2 per cent in the 1950s and 1960s to 1 per cent in the 1980s and 1990s, although it has picked up recently with the recovery in activity.

I should note that economists do not fully understand why productivity  grow Canada (and, indeed, in other industrial countries) has slowed so sharply since the mid-1 not propose to try to untangle this puzzle today. Nonetheless, there are a few points I w make with respect to the Canadian situation.

The sharp rise in the world price of oil in the 1970s no doubt dealt a major Canadian industry. Because of our climate and because of the importance of primary comm production in our economy, we are major users of energy. Adapting to higher energy costs c took considerable time.

˝

In my view, two other important factors inhibited productivity improvements th much of the 1970s, 1980s, and early 1990s: large fiscal deficits and high inflation.

Government deficits through the 1980s and early 1990s tended to crowd out pri sector investment by appropriating an ever-increasing share of Canadian savings. It was, possible for businesses and governments to get foreign financing. But the accumulation o public sector debt and the rapid buildup of foreign indebtedness eventually resulted in premiums being built into our interest rates. High inflation through the 1970s and 1980s ha effect on interest rates. For these reasons, interest rates were high, even after adjustin This discouraged some of the investment that would have contributed to gains in productivit

Moreover, because high inflation increases uncertainty about the future, bus and individuals seek protection from its ravages or try to profit from it. Either way, sca resources were diverted from productive investments towards hedging and speculative investm

I do not mean to suggest that the factors I have mentioned here explain all productivity problems. But they no doubt worked against the investment that was needed to adjust to both the oil price shocks of the 1970s and the global forces of the past two dec make headway in terms of productivity growth.

Let me now turn to the question of what we can expect in terms of productivity future.

## Future productivity trends and Canada's economic potential

Increases in productivity do not just happen. We need to work hard to achieve In  a  world  of  rapid  technological  change  and  intense  international  competition,  t opportunities  and  incentives  for  productivity  gains  --  provided  we  do  what  is  necessar advantage of the possibilities.

Productivity  comes  from  the  interaction  of  business  investment  in  new  ca equipment, a skilled labour force, and the adoption of new technology. It takes entreprene innovation to pull it all together. Typically, this interaction works best when businesses stable, low-inflation economic environment and when markets are competitive. Producers ar under pressure to perform in terms of price, quality, and service.

With low inflation, a balanced fiscal position, and low interest rates, the policy  environment  is  better  now  than  it  has  been  for  over  25  years.  This  should  pro underpinnings for solid economic growth and increased savings and investment in the future.

With this support from improving economic policy conditions, business investm has indeed been buoyant, particularly since mid-1996, and notably in high-technology equ such as computers. As well, more and more businesses, led by high-tech enterprises, are re have introduced new production technologies. Progress has also been made in learning new

˝

removing labour market rigidities, and improving the adaptability, flexibility, and effic labour force. But more undoubtedly needs to be done in this area.

It is likely that these trends will continue in the future, and will spread to have been lagging behind. With ongoing technological change, deregulation, trade liberaliza intensified  global  competition,  the  pressures  and  incentives  are  certainly  there  f productivity gains.

Thus, the trends are positive, and the direction of our economy is clear. Wha clear is just how much our economic performance will improve. We cannot attach precise est to future growth in productivity. Neither can we judge the end results of the major structu that have taken place in the private sector of the Canadian economy. Because of this, we ne a somewhat agnostic view about the production potential of the Canadian economy and abou lowest unemployment rate that can be sustained over time.

## Monetary policy response -- making the most of the economy's production potential

What are the implications of all this for the conduct of monetary policy?

When  we  at  the  Bank  look  one  to  two  years  into  the  future  to  set  a  cours monetary policy, we must take into account changes in the trends that affect the potent economy to produce over time. At the same time, we must recognize that our ability to pre potential is restricted by the many uncertainties involved.

In these circumstances, the best way for monetary policy to help the economy r its potential is to focus on encouraging a sustained economic expansion over time. How d this? By keeping inflation low. As we move towards full capacity over the next year or so, important to set monetary conditions at levels that forestall a resurgence of inflation an boom and bust cycles that go with it.

A  responsible, credible  monetary  policy  will  allow  us  to  explore  the  limits economy's capacity to produce, to create jobs, and to support rising standards of living. US experience amply demonstrates the advantages and benefits of such a policy.

I believe that the recent extension of the inflation-control targets and the credibility  of  those  targets  give  monetary  policy  more  scope  to  test  the  limits  of  ou potential than at any time since the 1960s.

Now that I have discussed the rationale behind the Bank of Canada's medium-t strategy, let me explain our recent actions to raise the Bank Rate.

As  I  said  earlier,  the  underlying  momentum  of  the  Canadian  economy  remain positive. Despite the problems in Asia, Canada's external environment is still favourable strength  in  our  major  non-Asian  trading  partners,  particularly  the  United  States.  In  ad

˝

dampening effects on domestic demand from the fiscal consolidation efforts of the past four diminishing.  And  monetary  conditions  continue  to  support  the  economic  expansion.  Given circumstances, the persistent decline in the external value of the Canadian dollar through and  January  implied  a  further  easing  in  monetary  conditions  that  looked  to  us  to  be  e Moreover,  the  speed  of  the  decline  in  the  currency  risked  undermining  investor  confid Canadian dollar assets. That is why we took action.

## Concluding thoughts

Let me conclude by summarizing my main points today.

For much of the period since the 1960s, we have not had conditions in place would allow the Canadian economy to fully realize its potential. With low inflation and fiscal position, we now have the foundation that should permit us to move towards full cap to explore what our economy can deliver in terms of sustained growth in output and employme better standards of living.

Canada's  private  sector  has  been  responding  to  the  universal  challenges  of technological change, globalization, and heightened competition by undertaking major restr initiatives to become more efficient, productive, and competitive. Although we do not know just how much more productive we are going to be as a result of these initiatives, the reason for optimism.

The best contribution the Bank of Canada can make to this process is by continu provide a stable, low-inflation environment. With an eye to the medium term, this will requ a  course  for  monetary  policy  that  will  ensure  that  the  Canadian  economy  reaches  full smoothly and then continues to grow over time at a non-inflationary and therefore sustaina The  longer  economic  growth  is  sustained,  the  more  benefits  we  will  see  in  terms  of  i incomes and employment.

title: Mr. Carse speaks on banking supervision in Hong Kong and the lessons learned from the financial crisis in Asia  (Central Bank Articles and Speeches, 27 Mar 98)
description: Speech by the Deputy Chief Executive of the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, Mr. David Carse, at the Asian Investment Conference 'Asia: Meeting the Challenge' held in Hong Kong on 27/3/98.
text:
Mr. Carse speaks on banking supervision in Hong Kong and the lessons learned from  the  financial  crisis  in  Asia Speech  by  the  Deputy  Chief  Executive  of  the  Hong  Kong Monetary  Authority,  Mr.  David  Carse,  at  the  Asian  Investment  Conference  'Asia:  Meeting Challenge' held in Hong Kong on 27/3/98.

1. I am pleased to be here this morning to speak to you on the topic of the sup lessons which Hong Kong can learn from the region and specifically from the crisis which has Asia since July of last year. This is a drama that is still being played out and we have not y final act. But I do not think that it is too early to make some kind of judgment about what wen the lessons that can be drawn for the future.

## The Asian Crisis

2. I think that it is fair to say that the Asian crisis has surprised almost e speed and intensity and the ease with which it spread from country to country. Even those sceptical  about  the  Asian  miracle  did  not  really  expect  anything  like  this.  Of  course, warning signs such as the current account deficits in a number of countries such as Thai these could be regarded as the natural consequence of the heavy demand for investment in economies. The Asian economies were certainly not fault-free, but in general they not ex classic signs of gross macroeconomic weakness that normally lead to a balance of payments Governments ran fairly prudent fiscal policies, savings were high and inflation rates reas Even if policy mistakes were made, the punishment does not really seem to fit the crime.

3.  Why  then  have  exchange  rates  fallen  by  as  much  as  they  have  and  why  ha economies in the region been so severely crippled? It is generally agreed that a large answer lies in the weakness of financial and banking systems in the region, which have ampl initial effects of external shocks and economic downturn. In  essence,  banking  systems  t already in weak health before the crisis broke were not up to the task of intermediating l of capital. They have been part of a vicious circle whereby loss of confidence in the curre loss of confidence in the banking system that further undermines the currency. This is the country' syndrome. It therefore follows that strengthening of the banking system must be p cure of the Asian disease and the means of preventing a recurrence. Banking supervision important part to play in this strengthening - hence the topic of my speech today.

## The weaknesses in Asian banking systems

4. Before I go on to discuss the supervisory lessons that can be learned, It is to consider in more detail the precise nature of the weaknesses that were apparent in som not all, of the regional banking systems.

## Over-expansion of bank lending

5. A number of economies experienced rapid growth in bank credit during the 19 often  fuelled  by  inflows  from  abroad.  Much  of  this  lending  was  made  without  proper assessment and went into unproductive sectors such as property and the equity markets. Thi up  asset  prices  and  encouraged  further  lending.  When  capital  outflows  reversed  (because realization that exchange rates were over-valued) this led to a decline in asset prices whi

the  position  of  both  banks  and  borrowers.  The  resultant  rise  in  bad  debts  undermined confidence in the solvency of the banking system, making it difficult for banks to roll external borrowing and provoking further outflows. The weakness of the banks made them reluctant to lend, which further weakened the financial position of borrowers. This is t which Paul Krugman has described as 'financial excess and then financial collapse' 1 .

## Excessive reliance on short-term foreign currency borrowing

6. What was particularly dangerous was that a combination of pegged exchange ra relatively high domestic interest rates and moves towards financial liberalization encour in a number of economies to borrow heavily in foreign currencies to fund the lending boom. this borrowing was short-term, giving rise to a maturity as well as a foreign currency either on the part of the banks or the companies to which they on lent. When the initial currencies emerged, domestic borrowers that had previously never had to think about hedgi foreign currency liabilities rushed to do so, turning a slide in the currency into an ava who were too late were left with liabilities to the banks that were vastly inflated in domestic currency - and the banks were left with the resultant bad debts and a crippled finance the routine needs of their customers.

## Captive banks

7. Why were banks not more discriminating in their credit choices and decisions of  the  explanation  is  that  in  a  number  of  economies  banks  were  ordered  or  persuaded government  to  lend  heavily  to  particular  industries  and  companies.  In  other  words,  th 'captive  banks'.  This  allowed  the  companies  concerned  to  become  over-leveraged  (and vulnerable to economic downturn) and directed resources into unprofitable investments. Th concerned had little incentive to develop proper lending skills.

## Concentration risks and connected lending

8. Moreover, banks in some economies were over-exposed to single borrowers, of those connected with the lending institution. Such lending is usually of poor quality, not made at arm's length, and means that the shareholders have  no  real capital  at  stake  in (because it has effectively been lent back to them).

## Failure to recognize bad debts

9. Having landed themselves with bad debts, banks failed to face up to the pr In  particular,  systems  for  loan  classification  and  provisioning  have  been  inadequate.  A capital  ratios  have  been  overstated,  and  insolvent  or  near-insolvent  banks  have  been  a continue in business and to build up further losses. Banks have been allowed to accrue i non-performing loans, thus overstating revenue and capital.

## Lack of transparency

1

Paul Krugman, 'What happened to Asia?', January 1998

˝

10.  All  this  has  been  made  worse  by  a  lack  of  transparency  in  regional  ba systems. Failure to disclose the true scale of bad debt problems has weakened market disc bank management and reduced the need for them to face up to the problems. Public confide banking  systems  has  been  undermined  because,  with  no  credible  information,  depositors investors assume the worse in even relatively sound banks and rush to take their money out.

## Moral hazard

11. The final ingredient has been the perception that many banks in the regi effectively  government-guaranteed.  This  has  created  a  problem  of  moral  hazard  whereby management  can  afford  to  indulge  in  reckless  lending  behaviour  because  they  believe government will bail them out if they fail. Similarly, depositors have less incentive t creditworthiness of the banks with which they place funds.

## Weakness in supervision

12. How did Asian banks get into this state of fragility? Inadequate regulat supervision, coupled with an explicit or implicit government guarantee, have attracted mu blame, leading Paul Krugman to describe Asian banks as 'over-guaranteed and under-regula Inadequate  supervision  cannot  be  the  whole  story  since  a  number  of  the  weaknesses  aris circumstances which are not the direct responsibility of banking supervisors. There were s in macroeconomic policy, in particular the maintenance of unsustainable exchange rates. Th undoubtedly also political interference in banks, in terms of both policy lending and p supervisors not to take action against well-connected owners of banks. Another fundamental was weakness in the infrastructure of business laws that made it difficult for banks to tak collateral and to put insolvent companies into liquidation. We must also bear in mind the f ultimate  responsibility  for  poor  lending  and  risk  management  practices  must  rest  w management of the banks themselves. However, having said all this, there have undoubtedl failures in supervisory policies and practices, as demonstrated by the reform measures th being put in place in a number of countries.

## The Basle Core Principles

13. Reform is not an easy task. But at least supervisors in individual coun now in a position to tap into an international network of technical cooperation and assist them  to  bring  their  systems  up  to  scratch.  At  the  centre  of  this  international  effort Committee  on  Banking  Supervision  which  is  taking  on  a  leadership  role  in  devising  super standards that can apply to all countries and not just the G-10 countries which sit on the In particular, the Committee has produced a set of Core Principles that are intended to pr of  minimum  requirements  for  effective  banking  supervision.  Supervisory  authorities  arou world are being encouraged to endorse the Core Principles and to implement them as quic possible. The IMF will have a role to play in checking that countries are indeed taking se in this direction.

14. The Core Principles are not earth shattering. They have not unveiled som secret of how to supervise banks. All they do is to summarize what are generally agreed fundamentals of a sound system of supervision. This includes the following main elements:

˝

˝

- Clear responsibilities and objectives for the supervisor set out in a suit framework
- Operational independence for the supervisor and the necessary resources t the job
- A proper licensing regime for banks
- Sound prudential regulations and requirements that address the main type risk faced by banks
- The means to enforce supervisory requirements and gather information thro on-site examination and off-site review
- The power to take action against problem banks, including closure
- The ability to conduct consolidated supervision and to cooperate and exch information with other supervisors at home and abroad

15. These may seem like statements of the obvious. But the necessary measures evidently  not  fully  in  place  in  a  number  of  countries  in  the  region.  Reforms  are  n implemented, in some cases with the help of the IMF and the World Bank. These include t limits on loan growth and on lending to sectors such as property; tightening of the loan c framework and provisioning requirements; more disclosure of non-performing loans; strengt of on-site examination to introduce a more risk-based approach; and enhanced legal powers supervisors to take prompt action to deal with problem banks. In a number of countries, banks and finance companies have been closed down or are being merged and efforts are being to realize as much value as possible from their bad assets. From my discussions with my su colleagues in the region I know that they are serious in their efforts and I wish them ever

## The lessons for Hong Kong

16. This sentiment recognizes that it is also in Hong Kong's interest that stability returns to the region. As I have already indicated, one of the special features disease  is  that  it  has  been  extremely  contagious.  And  although  the  Hong  Kong  economy financial  system  have  remained  in  pretty  good  health,  they  have  not  been  totally  immun suggests that we too have lessons to learn from the crisis.

17. Hong Kong's supervisory system does indeed compare well with internatio standards.  A  review  which  we  conducted  last  year  showed  that  we  had  addressed  all  the covered by the Basle Committee's Core Principles and that we fully complied with all but them. In the latter cases, we are in partial compliance. This does not however mean that complacent for the following reasons:

- First, the Basle Core Principles are, as I have indicated, minimum sta and we should where possible be aiming for best practice
- Second, the environment being faced by banks is changing at an accelera rate and we need to be sure that our supervisory system keeps pace with th
- Third, even our robust monetary system can be subject to external shocks the banks need to take this into account in the way in which they manage business.

18.  The  latter  point  needs  some  further  elaboration.  As  you  will  be  aware, Kong's monetary policy is built around exchange rate stability in the form of the link b Hong Kong dollar and the US dollar. This is backed up by the currency board system which r the monetary base of the banking sector - the notes and coins in circulation and the clear held with the HKMA - to be fully backed by foreign currency. When the Hong Kong dollar is pressure as it was at the end of October 1997 and again in January of this year, the HK Hong Kong dollars from the banks in exchange for US dollars and the monetary base shrinks tightening of liquidity will in turn cause interest rates to rise, perhaps sharply so. Thi the inflows and restore stability to the exchange rate.

19. It is important to realize that this is an automatic process and that the no room to maneuver to prevent the rise in interest rates from taking place. To do so counter to the basic principle of the currency board and would risk prolonging any atta Hong Kong dollar.

20. I think that there is now a better understanding of how the currency board works. In addition, our determination to adhere to the system and to defend the linked exc has been clearly demonstrated. This should help to deter future speculative attacks on the dollar. However, we have to acknowledge that the possibility of short term interest rates exist under the currency board mechanism and the banks therefore need to take this into a the way in which they run their business and manage their balance sheets.

21. Bearing this in mind, I draw three main supervisory lessons from the re crisis and its impact on Hong Kong:

- First,  it  is  important  for  banks  to  maintain  a  strong  balance  sheet  t withstand the interest rate fluctuations to which I have referred and main confidence of the public. Banks in Hong Kong score well in this respect bu not something that can be taken for granted. I think that it is true to say banks did expand their loan books too rapidly during the mortgage boom in 1 As a result, loan to deposit ratios came under some strain. The banks wer exposed  to  growing  interest  rate  risk  because  a  substantial  proportion  o assets are linked to best lending rate while their liabilities are linked This has been a reminder of the need to maintain sound fundamentals: high ca adequacy  and  liquidity  ratios;  prudent  loan  classification  and  provisioni sound risk management.
- A  second  and  related  lesson  from  the  region  is  that  banks  need  to  bewar excessive lending to finance overheated asset markets. This increases the le of their customers, exposing the banks to increased credit risk if prices fa course is what has happened in the property market in Hong Kong, although banks have so far been protected by their prudent lending policies and by t that  much  of  their  property  exposure  is  related  to  the  residential Notwithstanding  the  good  outcome  so  far,  we  believe  that  the  Asian  crisi reinforced the need for restraint in the growth in property lending and i forms of asset-based finance, such as share margin financing and taxi loans.

˝

- The  third  lesson  is  that  increased  disclosure  and  transparency  are  neces reduce market uncertainty and limit the risk of contagion. The disclosure news  can  be  uncomfortable,  but  it  does  serve  the  useful  function  of  pu pressure on management to run their business prudently and to deal quickly any  problems  which  may  arise.  Hong  Kong  has  made  considerable  progress  in recent years in terms of disclosure of information by banks. We intend to b this  during  the  course  of  1998  by  recommending  new  measures  such  as  mor disclosure about non-performing loans and more specific guidelines for in recognition by banks.

## Review of the Hong Kong banking sector

22. We will be building these lessons into our supervisory approach during the of 1998. More generally, as I have already mentioned, we also have to ensure that our keeps up with market developments and takes account of new types of risk that may emerge. F reason, we have recently commissioned a firm of consultants to carry out a study of the sector in Hong Kong over the next five years.

23 The study has two objectives. The first is to examine the strategic outlook banking sector in Hong Kong during the five-year period. This will include an assessmen strengths and weaknesses of the banking sector and the opportunities and threats with wh faced, taking into account the impact of global and local trends and issues. Among the is examined will be the costs and benefits of certain features of the current regulatory sys the remaining interest rate rules and the one branch policy) and the potential impact of these features. I should add however there is no presumption that changes to the current system should, or will, be made. We are going into this with an open mind.

24. The second objective of the study is to consider the adequacy and effective the  HKMA's  current  approach  to  banking  supervision  and  to  make  recommendations  for  a changes that seem required in the light of the strategic outlook for the banking sector. include  any  changes  that  needed  to  be  made  to  the  organizational  structure  of  our  sup function within the HKMA and the supervisory policies, guidelines and techniques which w The study will also examine whether we have the necessary resources to do the job.

## Conclusion

25. In conclusion, the Asian crisis has been a major 'wake-up' call to superv the region and has given fresh impetus to international efforts to raise supervisory sta point  which  bears  repeating  however  that  tightening  of  supervision  is  not  the  whole particularly if the effect is simply to impose more rules on the banks. More external reg indeed have to be the short-term response in a number of countries, particularly those whe government guarantees have been given to depositors. However, the long-term solution must devising a supervisory approach which gives the right incentives for management of banks responsibility for their own actions.

title: Ms. Phillips reviews major milestones, key factors and future directions of the OTC derivatives market  (Central Bank Articles and Speeches, 26 Mar 98)
description: Remarks by Ms. Susan M. Phillips, a member of the Board of Governors of the US Federal Reserve System, before the International Swaps and Derivatives Association, 13th Annual General Meeting in Rome on 26/3/98.
text:
## Ms. Phillips reviews major milestones, key factors and future directions

the OTC derivatives market Remarks by Ms. Susan M. Phillips, a member of the Board o Governors of the US Federal Reserve System, before the International Swaps and Deriv

Association, 13th Annual General Meeting in Rome on 26/3/98.

## Lessons and Perspectives

Thank you for inviting me to speak at this annual meeting of ISDA. When vis Rome, we are all conscious of the rich history and grandeur of the Roman Empire. This puts  into  perspective  the  short  history  of  the  swaps  and  derivatives  market  --  desp come  a  long  way,  the  market  for  over-the-counter  derivatives  is  still  relativel Nonetheless, it is not so young that it cannot benefit from a reassessment of its past with an eye toward using those lessons to inform and guide the future.

## Major Milestones

At meetings such as this one, it often is the practice to review major eve development of the over-the-counter (OTC) derivatives market and to chronicle its grow milestones of the market are often recorded as the introduction of new products, be the swaps, interest rate swaps, caps, collars, floors, or credit derivatives. While this products in their historical context, it does not provide a framework against which t subsequent  evolution  of  products  and  the  market.  An  alternative  approach  that  may  b informative is to focus on OTC derivative dealers and how their role in the market has that is, to chronicle changes in the ways dealers conduct their business and manage From this latter perspective, the first stage in the evolution of OTC derivatives was c by matched transactions. ## 1. The history of money reflects the history of the world

The history of money by far outdates the history of central banking. The Ri of Sweden and the Bank of England are recognised as the oldest central banks in the wor yet, they were only established during the seventeenth century. The use of various inst money dates back at least 5,000 years.

In antiquity, money took the form of ornaments and household utensils and In  Egypt,  circa  2000  BC,  rings,  anklets,  necklaces  and  bracelets  were  used  extens common  means  of  exchange. Mr.  Meyer  addresses  the  competitiveness of financial centres  from  a  Swiss perspective Address by the Chairman of the Governing Board of the Swiss National Bank, Mr. Hans Meyer, at the International Bankers Club Luxembourg, held in Luxembourg on 23/3/98.

Both Luxembourg  and Switzerland are major financial centres in Europe.  The performance and competitiveness of the financial services industry are thus of key economic and social importance to both countries. I should like to use this opportunity to say a few words on the subject from what may be a somewhat unusual perspective.

The factors which determine the competitiveness of an industry are basically the same as those determining the success of the entire economy. In both cases, we are looking at a multitude of quite diverse factors with varying degrees of importance. Today, I would like to single out just three of them which  I  believe  are  of  particular  significance:  economic  stability,  social  equilibrium  (i.e.  political stability),  and  the  human  factor.  Although each  of  these  elements  could  be  dealt  with  separately,  they should ultimately be viewed in a broader context.

Let's start with economic stability. I define this as a state of balanced development across the economy as a whole, characterised by steady growth, a modest inflation rate and low unemployment.

One of the main prerequisites for achieving such a state is the ability not only to create but to sustain an appropriate economic framework. This is primarily an objective for monetary policy, fiscal policy and competition policy. The main goal of monetary policy is to maintain price stability. This is of course not an end in itself, but a means to an end. A non-inflationary climate facilitates the free play of market forces and keeps socially damaging developments at bay. Fiscal policy must, basically, aim in the  longer  term  to  balance  the  public  budgets.  As  with  monetary  policy,  it  is  a  question  of  steady, ongoing  efforts.  This  should  be  no  surprise,  considering  that  the  whole  spectrum  of  public  sector activities  is  reflected  in  the  public  budgets.  This  in  turn  raises  the  question  of  what  services  the  state should  perform,  who  should  pay  for  them  and  how  public-services  can  most  efficiently  be  provided. Where  competition  policy  is  concerned,  the  aim  is  to  create  conditions  conducive  to  the  free  play  of market forces. In recent decades, it has unfortunately not always been possible to gain consensus support for the idea of free competition, which is still regarded with scepticism and suspicion by many people. Provided that free competition is able to develop in a stable environment, there can be little doubt that it is the best means to assure optimal use of available resources. When things go wrong, it is generally due not to the principle of free competition itself but to the lack of a stable environment.

I would like to stress once again that the task of creating a stable economic framework is a  never-ending one: it  is  a  question  of  constantly  working  towards  -  but  never  actually  reaching  -  the intended goal. Success in this endeavour is not just a question of thinking things through in a consistent way but, above all, of adopting a persevering and workmanlike approach.

Economic stability in the sense of a balanced development of the economy as a whole is the sine qua non for a financial centre. It is essential if investors are to gain sufficient confidence in the prospect of sustainable business success. Stable prices, low interest rates, modest rates of taxation and a solid currency are the crucial factors.

To what extent - if at all - is a financial centre reliant on its economic hinterland? This question is less easy to answer. Although a well-balanced interdependency might seem to be desirable here as well, this is not necessarily confirmed by experience. In fact, there never seems to have been any close correlation, and with modern technology enhancing the mobility of people, goods and services, the links have become even looser. Our two countries at least are proof of the fact that there need not be any close correlation between the importance of a country's economy and that of its financial sector.

Talking  about  economic  stability,  I  referred  to  the  need  for  perseverance.  This  is precisely where I see the link with social and political stability. The central task of any community is to provide its members with the greatest possible degree of security, freedom and general welfare. The last

of  these  factors  -  the  general  welfare  of  the  population  -  is  dependent  precisely  on  the  creation  of  the appropriate  economic  framework  I  mentioned  earlier.  I  should  add  that  this task can  only  be accomplished if a sufficient number of citizens actively help in shaping developments. This is especially the case in the sphere of fiscal policy.

In the wake of extremely dynamic growth, public budgets have grown considerably in all developed countries over the past few decades. While the original purpose of this spending was to meet a pressing and legitimate need such as in the area of social security - there has been a growing disparity between the claims made on the public purse and the willingness to generate  the  necessary  resources. Today,  we  have  reached  a  point  where  this  trend  needs  to  be  reversed.  However,  neither  rules  and regulations  nor  government  ordinances  can  achieve  this  alone.  Instead,  we  have  to  take  small  but persistent steps to rectify the situation both from the spending and the revenues side, and - not least of all - to improve productivity. Because such ongoing measures need the backing of the community, the chances of success tend to be greater in smaller communities than in larger ones.

Our experience suggests that a federally structured society based on direct democracy is well  suited  to  achieving  the  interaction  between  economic  and  political  stability  I  have  just  outlined. Here again, though, I should add that we are always on the way towards our goals and will never actually meet them.

Even in the conditions we enjoy, it is not easy to reach the necessary consensus.

This brings me to  the  'human  factor'.  The  background  conditions  I  have  been  talking about are aimed in no small measure at enabling  individuals  to  develop  their  own  interests  as  well  as those of society. This symbiosis is essential to the prosperity of the economy as a whole.

Where human resources are concerned, what is needed most of all is adequate training, motivation and the right mentality. Over the course of time,  the  development  of  the  economy  and  the associated structural change have constantly thrown up new challenges for everyone involved. This can be  seen,  for  example,  in  the  phenomenon  of  structural  unemployment,  arising  from  an  imbalance  in supply and demand for specific skills. Although the need for continuous training and retraining is nothing new, it has now become an urgent concern. But qualifications alone are not sufficient. They only come into their own when the people in question are also motivated.

If we were to restrict ourselves purely to economic activities, we could leave it at that. But after what I said about the correlations between the economy and society, there is clearly more to it. In  a  democratic  community,  we  don't  just  need  'economic  subjects'  who  contribute  their  skills  in specific areas and with the right mentality. We also need citizens who are willing and able to concern themselves at all times with developments in the community and to help shape these developments.

If progress is to be made towards achieving balanced - and therefore stable growth, it is especially important that individuals should be able to  identify  with  the  community  as  a  whole.  Clear interdependencies  with  the  economy  emerge  here  as  a  key  aspect  of  social  coexistence.  Only  if  the individual members of society are assimilated into a balanced and flourishing economic environment will they  identify  with  society  to  the  extent  that  they  work  actively  towards  its  goals  -  which  in  turn  is essential  to  the  successful  shaping  of  the  appropriate  economic  framework.  The  resulting  social equilibrium, i.e. political stability, creates the necessary  confidence  in  a  stable  and sustainable development that is so essential to a financial centre.

Today, there is a tendency for people to retreat into the role of the pure economic subject. I  see  this  as  a  worrying  development,  and  indeed  as  posing  a  threat  to  both  the  economy  and  society. Based on what I said earlier, the economy and society can only flourish in a balanced environment. But this balance can only be achieved if the citizens are aware of their dual responsibility and act accordingly.

We have talked about economic stability, political stability and the human factor. These are the elements which define the substance of a financial centre, and the necessary symbiosis between them hinges on the actions of the  individual.  But  we  should  not  forget  the  importance  of  other  major aspects  such  as  a  clearly  defined  legal  system  and  a  properly  functioning  technical  and  organisational infrastructure.

I  would also like to address another aspect that is of particular importance  to  a  central bank: the stability of the system. Maintaining stability in the financial sphere should not be viewed in isolation, as it is closely interlinked with the human and economic factors discussed earlier.

Political and economic stability, the quality of the human contribution, a clearly defined legal order and an efficient infrastructure are the keys to the success of a financial centre.  To  this,  we should add a reputation which is founded upon a sound attitude and a good track record, going beyond the criteria we have enumerated.

Stability  of  the  financial  system  is  a  concern  primarily  for  the  market  participants themselves. Furthermore, it comes within the remit both of the bank supervisors and of the central bank, which is responsible for monetary policy. As you know, responsibilities and powers are kept separate in my  country,  the  task  of  supervising  the  banks  being  assigned  to  an  independent  body,  the  Federal Banking  Commission.  Discussion  about  whether  it  would  be  preferable  to  unite  the  two  institutions under  one  roof  has  been  going  on  for  a  long  time.  Both  solutions  clearly  have  their  advantages  and disadvantages,  each  of  which  may  be  weighted  differently  depending  on  the  requirements  of  society. Consequently, the debate must be pragmatic and not dogmatic. We believe that our approach has proved its  worth  and  do  not  see  any  need  for  radical  change.  It  is  clear,  though,  that  the  separation  of responsibilities and powers can only function on a basis of close cooperation and trust.

I should like to touch upon two areas in which fundamental changes are needed. First, the financial systems have obviously been becoming more complex with regard to the roles played by their major participants. The traditional approach of focusing supervisory activities on the banks thus seems less and less appropriate. A more comprehensive supervisory system, covering the financial markets as a whole, would be preferable, with particular attention being paid to the transparency of market activities.

Moreover, bank supervision should take account of the increasingly international nature of  the  financial  markets.  There  would  appear  to  be  good  reason  to  call  for  a  globalisation  of  the supervisory system. But globalisation is one of those 'in' words that has to be treated with caution. As a matter  of  fact,  individual  financial  markets  are  still  embedded  in  a  national  economic  and  social environment. What we need is for cooperation between the national supervisory bodies to be gradually intensified  -  which  is  in  fact  happening.  True  supranational  supervision  is  still  a  long  way  off,  as  the necessary economic and social framework is lacking.

For this reason, I should now like to focus on the role that an individual central bank has to play in helping to safeguard the stability of the financial system.

I  have  already  spoken  about  the  general  prerequisites  needed  for  a  financial  market  to flourish. Within the scope defined by the operating conditions mentioned, market players are basically responsible themselves for what they do or don't do. Their prime concern is to stay solvent at all times by adopting sound business practices and putting an effective organisation in place. To prevent problems from  occurring,  the  responsible  bodies  at  the  individual  banks  must  be  able  at  all  times,  and  with  a minimum of delay, to accurately assess their risk situation and to take rapid and appropriate action.

Of course, it is never possible to rule out the possibility of an individual bank running into difficulties. In such cases, a solution must first be sought through the market. Solidarity among the other market players should provide a 'first line of defence'. Seeking funds from the central bank can only be contemplated in the last instance - hence the expression 'lender of last resort'. Obtaining credit from the central bank presupposes that the liquidity requirements are only temporary. If the solvency of a

bank is in peril because of a threat to its capital, the problem is a matter for the supervisory authorities and possibly for the state itself. In practice, the boundary between liquidity and solvency problems can be a fluid one.

In my view, it is important for everyone involved not to lose sight of these principles which are in fact quite simple. It should not be assumed that the central bank might take action beyond the limits outlined. But this does not mean that it cannot assist in the search for solutions, as far as they do not involve extending further credit.

If the problems of individual banks multiply, there is a danger that liquidity may dry out throughout  the  entire  system.  In  such  a  case,  the  central  bank  would  basically  be  able  to  supply  the market with the necessary liquidity. However, it may then come into conflict with the requirements of a policy  geared  to  economic  stability.  Consequently,  the  short-term  benefits  of  an  easing  of  monetary policy should be weighed against the longer-term risks.

I would like to sum up my thoughts as follows:

1. Three  factors  are  of  prime  importance  to  the  competitiveness  of  a  financial centre: economic  stability, political stability and  the 'human  factor'  (i.e. professionalism, motivation and mentality). Although these factors can each be viewed separately, it is the interaction between them that really counts.
2. Economic stability, in the sense of a balanced development of the economy as a whole, is made possible by the existence of an appropriate economic framework. This  is  created  first  and  foremost  by  monetary  policy,  fiscal  policy  and competition  policy.  Economic  stability  provides  the  financial  services  industry with a favourable climate in terms of low inflation and interest rates, moderate tax levels and appropriate exchange rates.
3. Favourable  economic  conditions  are  planned  and  implemented  as  part  of  the process  of  social  coexistence.  This  can  best  be  achieved  when  the  largest possible number of the community's members are involved.
4. 4 Individuals are at the same time citizens and economic subjects, thereby creating a crucial interdependency. Proper integration into a balanced economic environment  is  an  important  prerequisite  for  developing  a  sense  of  common purpose  -  in  other  words,  identifying  with  society  and  thus  also  displaying  a willingness  to  actively  help  shape  its  progress.  This  ultimately  means  that economic  and  social  development  can  only  progress  in  a  sustainable  and balanced way if an appropriate equilibrium can be maintained between them.
5. Even  at  a  time  when  global  economic  and  social  developments  are  becoming more  and  more  closely  intertwined,  being  an  integral  part of a national community still  plays  an  important  role.  It  is  still  essential  that  these  national communities should strive first and foremost to keep their own house in order - a house, though, which should not just be stable but open as well.
6. Ensuring  the  stability  of  the  financial  system  is  one  of  the  core  tasks  of  the supervisory authorities and  of  the  central  bank  in  its  capacity  as  lender  of  last resort. However, the market players' sense of individual responsibility is also of key  importance.  If  a  third  party  is  to  offer  assistance  in  a  system  run  on  free market principles, this can and should be seen as nothing more nor less -  than helping the others to help themselves.
